Expect roughly 1.5 to 2.5 hours for a careful read, with most of the time spent on the theory.201:T4cc,The system has three main components. First, Kaggle-MLE Factory converts historical Kaggle competitions into executable MLE tasks with task descriptions, public data, and metrics. The Interaction Harness preserves experimental state and candidate submissions while leaving action selection to the model, instead of forcing a fixed workflow. Second, hierarchical agentic SFT transfers tool use, coding, and MLE optimization skills through selected trajectories and segments. The selection is guided by execution outcomes, which is important because long trajectories are noisy: successful runs can contain unhelpful branches, and failed runs can still contain useful local behaviors. Third, Windowed Interaction Reinforcement Learning uses completed experiments as window boundaries. The decisions made since the previous experiment result form an execution window, and those decisions receive a shared outcome-based reward. This gives a denser and more causally aligned signal than final-task reward, while avoiding the overly local view of single-turn rewards. WIRL also uses local progress rewards, asynchronous rollout collection, and policy correction to handle expensive experiments and policy drift during online learning.202:T618,The authors do not propose a new detector. Instead, they reuse an existing three-tier candidate-generation pipeline and evaluate eight fully specified cleaning policies on top of it. Tier 1 performs exact and near-exact matching after normalization of whitespace, casing, and LaTeX macros. Tier 2 performs lexical matching using 13-gram and 8-gram coverage plus a 128-permutation MinHash/LSH Jaccard estimate. Tier 3 performs semantic retrieval with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B and cosine similarity. A subset of lexical and semantic candidate pairs is then adjudicated by an existing LLM judge into same, subsumes, variant, or different. The eight policies differ in how much they trust exact matches, lexical heuristics, semantic thresholds, and LLM-judge outputs.

The strongest part of the paper is the evaluation design. The authors build a new independently and blindly dual-reviewed reference set of 594 training-benchmark pairs, split in advance into calibration and held-out partitions. The held-out split is disjoint not only in benchmark items but also in training-example clusters, so policy tuning is tested on genuinely unseen corpora and questions. They also sample 80 candidate-bearing training items and review every candidate edge attached to each item. That enables item-level false-removal measurement: a training item counts as wrongly removed only if none of its candidate edges is truly contaminating. This is more faithful than pair-level precision, which can overstate conservativeness when one item has both true and false candidate matches.203:T49f,The audit covers 16 open RLVR math corpora and 6 benchmarks: MATH-500, GSM8K test, AIME24, AIME25, AIME26, and AMC23. After normalization and corpus-specific deduplication, the study analyzes 1,673,514 corpus-specific training items corresponding to 1,197,691 unique underlying problem texts. Evaluation uses 594 manually reviewed pairs plus 80 fully resolved item-level samples.

The central empirical result is clear: the common heuristic “remove if semantic similarity exceeds a fixed threshold” becomes unreliable as the threshold is relaxed. Candidate-frame recall improves, but manual review shows that at permissive thresholds, most sampled removals are false removals. In other words, semantic retrieval is useful for candidate generation, but weak as a direct removal rule. The paper also reports the cost of each policy in retained corpus size and source-composition shift, showing that cleaning decisions affect not only how much data remains but also which sources remain. The abstract does not expose the full policy-by-policy table, but the paper’s contribution is less about naming a single best policy and more about making the trade-offs visible and auditable.204:T887,方法名叫 Mosaic，核心是两层优化信号。

第一层是 session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation。普通 broadcasting 做法是先按任务内 rollout group 的 outcome reward 做 GRPO 式标准化，再把同一个 trajectory advantage 广播给所有 token。Mosaic 认为这样忽略了 session 使用效率，于是在“相同 outcome”内部再看 session count 的相对排序。直观上，若两条轨迹都成功，使用更少 session 的那条应得到更高 advantage；若两条都失败，反而不应简单惩罚 session 多的轨迹，因为失败样本仍需要探索空间。论文因此设计了一个有界调制项，用 session 数在同 reward 组内的 rank 去修正 trajectory-level advantage。这里有两个关键约束：一是调制不能打乱由 outcome reward 决定的主排序，二是调制幅度要受控，避免 session 偏好压过任务成败本身。作者强调它的作用不是替代 outcome signal，而是拉开 homogeneous-reward group 内部的 advantage 间距，提高学习信号分辨率。

第二层是 session-level advantage shaping。作者把每个 session 对最终 outcome 的边际贡献视作一种 immediate reward。做法上，是比较包含该 session 与不包含该 session 时的 outcome 增益，得到 session-level marginal gain；然后按 session type 分开做 group-relative normalization，再把这个 shaping signal 与上面的 trajectory-level advantage 结合。之所以要按 session type 分开归一化，是因为不同类型 session 的边际收益分布不同，例如压缩 session、主 agent session、fork 出来的子 agent session，其长度、功能和对最终成功率的贡献尺度都不一样，混在一起标准化会让某些类型的信号被系统性放大或压小。

整体上，Mosaic 形成了一个层级目标：trajectory-level signal 负责长期、全局、结果导向的优化；session-level shaping 负责局部、短程、边际贡献导向的优化。并且整个方法保持 critic-free，仍沿用 group-relative 的思路，而不是额外训练 value model。这是它和 PPO-style token/value advantage 路线的主要区别。205:T45f,This is not a pretraining paper in the narrow sense, but it matters for the pretrain-to-post-train interface, especially for long-context agents, tool-using systems, and reasoning models with explicit context management. Its contribution is meaningful in three ways. First, it treats session structure as part of the optimization problem rather than an implementation detail. That is important because modern agent execution increasingly departs from the single-context assumption used during RL training. Second, it proposes a hierarchical, critic-free advantage design, which fits the current preference for GRPO-like large-scale RL pipelines that avoid training an additional value model. Third, it explicitly encodes an efficiency preference: successful trajectories should ideally use fewer sessions, while unsuccessful ones should retain room for exploration. That idea is relevant beyond this benchmark, including memory agents and systems with context rewriting. Still, the scale of contribution is best viewed as a solid improvement in agent RL objective design, not a shift in core language model pretraining.206:T8d3,Mosaic introduces a two-level optimization signal.

The first component is session-aware trajectory-level advantage estimation. In the standard broadcasting setup, one computes a GRPO-style normalized trajectory advantage from outcome rewards within a rollout group, then assigns that same advantage to all tokens across all sessions. Mosaic argues that this ignores session efficiency. It therefore refines the trajectory-level signal using the relative ranking of session counts within trajectories that share the same outcome. Intuitively, if two trajectories both succeed, the one using fewer sessions should receive a larger advantage. If both fail, however, extra sessions should not be penalized in the same way because failed samples still serve exploration. The paper implements this through a bounded modulation term based on session-count ranking inside homogeneous-reward groups. Two design constraints are central: the modulation must not overturn the primary ordering induced by outcome reward, and its magnitude must remain controlled so that session preference does not dominate task success. The point is not to replace outcome supervision, but to increase advantage resolution within reward-tied groups.

The second component is session-level advantage shaping. Each session is assigned an immediate shaping signal based on its marginal contribution to the final outcome. Concretely, the method estimates a session-level marginal outcome gain, normalizes it with group-relative statistics separately for each session type, and combines this shaping term with the trajectory-level advantage. The type-conditioned normalization is important because different session types have different gain distributions. A compaction session, a main-agent session, and a forked subagent session differ in length, function, and contribution scale. Pooling them into one normalization scheme would distort the signal.

Together, these two components form a hierarchical objective: the trajectory-level term provides a global, long-horizon, outcome-oriented signal, while the session-level shaping term captures local marginal effects. The method remains critic-free throughout, staying closer to GRPO than to PPO-style value-based token advantage estimation.207:T6a1,Experiments are conducted on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B as the base model, under two representative multi-session settings: context compaction and subagent forking. Mosaic outperforms both single-session and multi-session agentic RL baselines. The headline number is up to 10.1% relative accuracy improvement over the broadcasting baseline, while also reducing the average number of sessions per trajectory from 3.17 to 2.35. That matters because the gain is not coming from spending more sessions; it comes from better session utility and allocation.

Ablations show that both parts of the method matter. Removing the session-aware trajectory modulation reduces within-group advantage discrimination and hurts sample efficiency. Removing session-level shaping makes it harder for the policy to learn which sessions have real marginal value. The analysis section adds several useful observations:
1. Session-count-aware modulation increases advantage variance within same-reward groups, which helps when outcome rewards are too coarse and many samples tie.
2. Different session types indeed exhibit different marginal-gain distributions, validating the need for type-conditioned normalization.
3. Training changes the agent’s session usage pattern toward fewer but more useful sessions, suggesting that the objective shapes reasoning structure rather than merely adjusting token probabilities.

The abstract-level material does not expose the full table of absolute scores or all training-budget details. For reproduction or cost–benefit judgment, the main experiment section and appendix should be checked for rollout counts, group size, KL settings, and the exact session segmentation rules.208:T41c,The main study uses four released 7B SimpleRL base–RL pairs, three out-of-domain multiple-choice benchmarks including MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and ARC-Challenge, and six public harness extractors. Across positive reported gains, 82% of the gain is attributed to answer format. When all nonzero reported gains are pooled, the share drops to 75%. Independent LLM readers still estimate a 77% format share. On identical outputs, the gap between the largest and smallest gain reported by different harness extractors has a median of 15 percentage points. A concrete ARC-Challenge example shows a boxed-answer extractor reporting a 30.6-point gain, while the fixed extractor reads only a 9.8-point gain. The paper also reports a useful control: on in-domain MATH-500, where both base and RL models already tend to box answers, format gain is close to zero. For one larger 32B pair trained with a different recipe, almost none of the split gain is format gain, suggesting the phenomenon depends on scale, recipe, and the base model’s original formatting behavior.209:T80d,The core idea is to replace an undivided single-agent loop with a structured multi-agent system, AutoSFT, built around two requirements: isolate execution from analysis, and maintain complementary analytical views during proposal generation. The paper first formalizes automated SFT data research. A base checkpoint M0 and an initial candidate pool D0 are fixed. At round t, a recipe Rt assigns sampling weights to examples in Dt, while newly written rows can extend the pool to Dt+1. Training always restarts from M0, producing Ct = train(M0, Rt). Evaluation under a fixed protocol returns benchmark scores, per-example failures, training dynamics, and comparisons to earlier rounds; this bundle is Ft. A research policy π then maps Ft and history H<t to the next data action at.

The authors define six data-engineering action types and use them as an analysis lens for what the agent actually explores. The single-agent baseline exposes two failure modes. First, execution and analysis compete for the same context window, so raw command outputs and logs consume context that should have been used for data diagnosis. Second, a single proposal stream reinforces recent local successes and leads to action collapse, mostly toward category reweighting.

AutoSFT addresses this with three agent roles. A meta-agent manages each round. An executor handles training, conversion, and evaluation separately, returning only file paths and short status summaries, which keeps low-value execution traces out of the main reasoning context. Analysis subagents inspect the same round from four complementary angles: training data, failure cases, training signals, and prior rounds. Each proposes one data action. A synthesis subagent writes new data for capabilities that are weakly covered in the current pool, which extends the search space beyond selection and repair. The paper adds these components incrementally under controlled settings so that performance changes can be attributed to system structure rather than to extra compute or altered training conditions.20a:T609,The experiments are designed to test whether system structure changes the behavior of automated data research, not to maximize absolute benchmark scores. The corrected single-agent loop still reaches only one stable action family, mainly category proportion adjustment, and fails to sustain broader data operations such as repair, replacement, or capability completion. Adding the executor roughly halves context loss, supporting the claim that execution traces were crowding out analysis. Adding the multi-view analysis subagents broadens the action range and improves best IFEval by +6.5. Adding the synthesis subagent yields a further +3.4 on IFEval and +2.9 on IFBench by covering undersupplied capabilities.

The training setup is intentionally controlled. The trainer is a fixed three-epoch SFT script, and every recipe within a comparison is capped at the same token budget. Each round retrains from the same base checkpoint rather than continuing from the previous round’s model. This means research history is carried only through the data pool and recipe, not through model state, which makes attribution cleaner. The paper also tests transfer to code, where no ready-made capability taxonomy is available. In that setting, AutoSFT improves MBPP+ by +3.7 over a single-agent baseline that does not improve. The most useful experimental takeaway is the decomposition of gains: executor fixes context contamination, analysis subagents fix proposal diversity and action collapse, and synthesis fixes coverage gaps in the candidate pool.20b:T6fd,ReasonUni is built on a unified multimodal model with a shared discrete token space, instantiated in the paper with an X-Omni-style pure AR architecture. Images are quantized into visual tokens by a visual tokenizer, text remains language tokens, and visual inputs and outputs share the same semantic codebook. This gives one backbone two conditional policies: understanding p(theta)(T|V) and generation p(theta)(V|T). The paper’s critique of prior reconstruction methods is that they mostly supervise the model to describe what is already present. That encourages copying and preservation, but does not force explicit reasoning about intended edits, structural changes, or invariances. ReasonUni changes the training problem into reasoning-driven editing. Given a source image, an edit instruction, and a target image, the model first generates a textual description of the desired target state, then generates the target image conditioned on that description. The intermediate text is therefore not just a caption; it is a reasoning-bearing representation of the post-edit world state. To jointly optimize both stages, the paper introduces TreeGRPO. For the same input, the model samples multiple reasoning paths, each treated as a branch. Under each branch, it samples multiple generated images as leaves. Rewards are then used at two levels: leaf rewards are aggregated to produce a more reliable branch-level signal for the understanding module, and within-branch normalization guides the generation module under a fixed target-state description. The key idea is structured credit assignment. A reasoning path is judged by the distribution of images it induces, which reduces the noise of single-sample feedback and lets image-level rewards shape the intermediate reasoning process.20c:T4dd,From the provided full-text sections, the paper reports consistent gains on both understanding and generation benchmarks relative to UAE, X-Omni, and related baselines. On the generation side, compared with UAE, ReasonUni improves by up to 5.98 points on DPGBench, 13.00 on WISE, and 16.78 on GenEval++. On the understanding side, it improves both perception and reasoning on MMBench; the logical-reasoning subset gains 6.77 points over X-Omni, whereas UAE gains 3.38 on the same subset. That is an important result because it suggests the benefit is not merely better visual-detail reconstruction. The paper also claims that understanding gains extend across all 12 evaluated benchmarks, which argues against the method being narrowly tuned to one editing setup. The experiments that matter most conceptually are likely the ablations between perception-only reconstruction and reasoning-augmented reconstruction, TreeGRPO versus flatter or staged optimization, and the extent to which the method reduces the usual understanding-generation interference in unified models. However, the provided text does not include the full tables, model sizes, training-set scale, or optimization hyperparameters, so those details cannot be filled in reliably.20d:T490,This is best skimmed as a training-objective paper for unified multimodal models, not as a settled recipe for multimodal pretraining. Start with the introduction and place it relative to Janus, TokenFlow, UAE, and RecA. Janus and TokenFlow mainly address architecture or codebook alignment; UAE and RecA use reconstructive post-training; ReasonUni adds an explicit reasoning-bearing target-state stage. Then focus on the method section, especially the dual-policy formulation and the two-level reward structure in TreeGRPO. That is where the paper’s real contribution sits. In the experiments, check three things first: how the target-state descriptions are evaluated or validated, whether branch-level reward aggregation actually stabilizes optimization, and whether the understanding gains are concentrated on reasoning-heavy benchmarks rather than pure perception tasks. A 40-minute read is enough to extract the main idea. The deeper questions are whether the intermediate reasoning text becomes a useful latent scaffold or just a training-time crutch, and whether pure AR image-token generation will eventually cap the quality ceiling of this unification route.20e:T6f7,The method, Replay-Selected Hindsight Distillation (RSHD), has three main stages. First, after standard GRPO samples a group of completions for a problem and the verifier scores them, the same policy writes a short note for each failed attempt, describing what likely went wrong and what to try next. The note writer never sees the reference answer. These notes are not treated as supervision; they are prompts for targeted re-exploration. Second, the model re-solves the same problem with the note in context, generating fresh replay trajectories that are scored by the same final-answer verifier. A note is accepted only if its replayed attempts outperform the original group. This replay test is the key safeguard. It filters out plausible but misleading self-diagnoses. The paper reports that about one in nine notes explicitly states the answer, and roughly three in five fail the replay test, which makes the filtering step essential rather than optional. Third, successful replay trajectories from accepted notes are distilled into the plain-prompt policy, so the deployed model does not need notes at inference time. Importantly, this distillation branch is kept separate from GRPO’s own reward normalization. That separation avoids mixing two different signals: relative reward-based policy improvement and imitation of verified better behavior. Compared with higher-temperature retries, RSHD conditions exploration on a diagnosis of a specific failure. Compared with hindsight methods that reveal the answer, it avoids train-test leakage. Compared with direct self-reflection supervision, it requires external verification. Compared with re-scoring failed rollouts, it transfers only newly verified behavior rather than increasing the probability of the original mistake.20f:T56f,The experiments cover competition math and free-form science QA, across multiple model families and sizes, comparing GRPO against GRPO plus RSHD. The most important result is not a single headline score but where the gains appear: improvements are strongest on the hardest problems and carry to out-of-domain benchmarks. The motivation is quantitatively grounded. If per-sample success probability is 0.1, an 8-sample group is all-fail more than 40% of the time. In the authors’ math training run, roughly half of the groups at the hardest MATH level carry no gradient. That explains why a method targeting all-fail groups can matter disproportionately. On cost, the extra overhead is training-time generation only, roughly doubling sampled tokens per step, with no inference-time change. The analysis also shows that a meaningful fraction of accepted notes come from all-fail groups, meaning the method recovers supervision exactly where vanilla GRPO has none. Another useful observation is that trained models solve problems in fewer tokens and hit the budget limit less often, suggesting that the distilled signal improves search efficiency, not just final accuracy. The full tables are not included in the provided excerpt, but the reported note statistics already make the central point: note generation is noisy, and replay selection is what turns that noise into useful supervision.210:T6a8,EliteReplay has two stages. Before RL training, the frozen base model is used to build an elite archive with MAP-Elites. This is a key design choice: simply replaying random correct samples from the base model would mostly recover frequent strategies and still underrepresent rare ones. MAP-Elites discretizes a behavior-descriptor space into cells and keeps at most one high-quality solution per cell, so the replay set is explicitly balanced over distinct strategy types rather than over raw sample frequency.

During post-training, the model is optimized with GRPO plus a small replay loss on the archived elite solutions. The replay term acts as an anchor, encouraging the policy to keep assigning probability to diverse correct strategies while still allowing RL to improve task reward. This differs from generic KL regularization or entropy bonuses. KL-to-reference constrains overall drift from the base model but does not specifically protect low-probability correct strategies. Entropy regularization encourages spread, but spread alone does not guarantee preservation of distinct correct solutions. EliteReplay is more targeted: it stores verified, behaviorally distinct solutions and explicitly rehearses them.

Another important technical point is the definition of diversity. The paper evaluates diversity at the level of solution strategies, using a deterministic structural description extracted from the solution itself. This matters because surface-form variation is a poor proxy in SQL: many strings differ syntactically while implementing the same strategy. The deterministic strategy extractor makes the evaluation more stable and better aligned with the intended notion of diversity.211:T62e,The experiments are centered on text-to-SQL, which is a good testbed because many questions admit multiple equivalent correct queries and some are genuinely ambiguous. On BIRD, EliteReplay reaches 74.8% pass@128, essentially matching a strong baseline, MaxRL, at 73.7%, but increases the number of distinct correct strategies per question from 6.2 to 9.1. So the method preserves more meaningful variation without giving up high-budget correctness. On the out-of-distribution Spider benchmark, EliteReplay achieves 93.2% pass@128, outperforming the strongest baseline by 6.3 points while producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies.

The retention results are especially important. EliteReplay retains 62% and 60% of the base model’s correct strategies on BIRD and Spider, respectively, at least 23 points better than any baseline. That indicates the method is not merely generating a different set of diverse outputs; it is specifically preserving the base model’s existing correct behavioral support. On AmbiQT, which tests ambiguous questions, EliteReplay covers both interpretations on 27.0% of examples versus 14.2% for the strongest baseline. This is a strong sign that preserving diverse correct strategies has direct functional value.

The main ablation logic compares plain RL, ordinary replay, and replay built from a QD archive. The takeaway is that naive replay is insufficient because the base model’s own sampling distribution is already skewed toward frequent strategies. The QD archive is what makes rare but useful strategies visible during training.212:T6db,The method, Subspace Tuning (SST), computes an SVD for each weight matrix W, takes the top-k left and right singular vectors, and projects the optimizer’s final update ΔW onto the orthogonal complement of those principal subspaces before applying it. The key detail is that SST projects the applied parameter update, not the raw gradient. That distinction matters because stateful optimizers such as Adam transform gradients through momentum and coordinate-wise rescaling; a projected gradient does not guarantee a projected final step. By acting on the actual update written into the weights, SST becomes optimizer-agnostic.

The projection is bilateral: it removes components aligned with principal singular directions on both the output side and the input side. This is stronger than a one-sided constraint and is meant to preserve the dominant mapping structure of the pretrained matrix. Conceptually, SST freezes the high-energy spectral structure and pushes adaptation into the tail subspace.

The paper also addresses a practical limitation of a fixed protected basis. If the SVD basis is computed once and never updated, the allowed complement can become too restrictive as training progresses. SST therefore includes a refresh mechanism that periodically recomputes the SVD on the current weights. This trades off stricter preservation against continued adaptability: no refresh gives stronger protection, while refresh allows the protected subspace to track the evolving model and frees capacity for further learning.

Methodologically, SST is positioned as a composable constraint rather than a standalone fine-tuning paradigm. It can be combined with full-parameter tuning, SDFT-style recipes, and different optimizers such as Adam or Muon.213:T97c,The empirical section is broad and is designed to test the central claim from several angles: can the model learn new tasks, retain prior capabilities, stay behaviorally close to the base model, and accumulate skills across stages? The domains include Science, Medicine, Pathology, Finance, and Tool Use. The paper evaluates both standard SFT and SDFT, and tests compatibility with Adam and Muon.

The headline result is that SST can preserve an extremely large fraction of principal singular directions while still matching or nearly matching unconstrained fine-tuning on target-task performance. The paper explicitly states that even when protecting the top 99% singular directions, SST still learns the new task, whereas standard SFT causes substantial forgetting. This is strong evidence that the non-principal spectral subspace contains enough adaptation capacity in overparameterized LLMs.

Scaling trends are also important. As model size increases, forgetting under SST shrinks further; from 8B onward, retained performance stays within roughly 1% of the base model, while unconstrained SFT degrades much more. The data-scaling result is equally telling: with more fine-tuning data, standard SFT forgets progressively more, but SST remains comparatively flat while still improving target-task accuracy. That suggests SST is not merely “learning less.”

The paper also goes beyond task accuracy. SST reduces KL divergence from the pretrained model by 2–4× relative to unconstrained recipes. On thinking models, standard SFT collapses natural reasoning length, while SST preserves the original reasoning-length behavior much better. When added to SDFT, SST also reduces fabricated reference-solution attributions, indicating better behavioral fidelity.

The sequential fine-tuning experiments are especially relevant for continual learning. In two-stage and three-stage chains, skills learned earlier remain largely intact under SST as later stages are added, whereas standard SFT degrades dormant skills whenever a new stage is trained. This is closer to the real deployment setting than one-shot forgetting tests.

The most explicit numbers visible from the provided content are: 2–4× lower KL, forgetting within about 1% from 8B onward, and successful learning even while protecting the top 99% singular directions. The detailed per-domain values appear in Table 1, Table 4, and Figures 1, 2, 3, 8, 9, and 10.214:T61b,Read this one by mechanism first, then by evidence. Start with the introduction and Sections 2.1–2.2. That is the conceptual center of the paper. Then read Section 2.3 to understand why a fixed complement subspace can become a bottleneck and why basis refresh is needed.

In the experiments, begin with Figures 1, 2, and 3 to establish the core pattern: target-task learning is preserved while forgetting is reduced, and the effect improves with scale. Finish with Figures 9 and 10, which are the most relevant for real continual learning because they test multi-stage accumulation rather than one-step adaptation.

Three questions are worth digging into. First, why do principal singular directions appear to carry more general capability, and how does that connect to prior observations on spectral drift, low-rank adaptation, and RL-style updates? Second, how large is the usable capacity of the tail subspace, and how does it vary with model size, layer type, and task difficulty? Third, is there a stable scaling relationship between protection ratio, refresh frequency, and adaptation quality? That could matter for continual pretraining recipes.

A quick pass takes around 25–35 minutes. A careful read with formulas and multi-stage results deserves at least an hour.215:T426,The paper formulates response generation as an undiscounted episodic MDP: the prompt is the initial state, tokens are actions, transitions append tokens deterministically, and the scalar response reward is assigned at EOS. It then derives policy-gradient estimators under samples drawn from a behavior or inference policy. A key distinction is made between sequence-level importance sampling, which uses the product ratio over the whole response, and token-level importance sampling, which applies local ratios per decoding step; these estimate different quantities. The main technical point is that, without ratio regularization, the weighted score has zero expectation, so constant reward shifts vanish. After clipping, truncation, or masking the ratio, this zero-mean property generally fails. The proposed fix is to use the covariance between the reward and the regularized importance-weighted score as the estimand, equivalently centering the score term as well as the reward. When the ratio is not regularized, this reduces to the standard policy gradient.216:T7a2,方法名 MRTPO（Multi-Reward-to-Token Policy Optimization）。它保留 GDPO 的关键优点：对每个 reward 在 rollout group 内单独标准化，避免 reward collapse（不同 reward 组合被同一个 advantage 混掉）。核心变化在于：对每个 reward k，不再把该 reward 的 group-normalized advantage 均匀分给所有 token，而是先估计“哪些 token 与 reward k 相关”，再按相关性做归一化分配。

相关性估计来自 self-replay + privileged information：每个 verifier 在评估时依赖某些信息（例如：正确 SQL 的参考、执行错误信息、工具调用的规范/约束、指令中的某条约束文本等）。MRTPO 对同一条已采样的 response y 做两次 teacher-forcing 式的重放（replay）：一次在“包含 reward k 的 verifier 信息”的上下文下，一次在“移除该信息”的上下文下，得到每个位置 t 的 next-token 分布 p_t^{(+k)} 与 p_t^{(-k)}。用 token-wise Jensen–Shannon divergence 作为差异度 d_{k,t}=JSD(p_t^{(+k)}||p_t^{(-k)})，把它解释为该 token 对 reward k 的敏感度/相关性。然后把 reward k 的优势 A_k^{(j)}（来自 group 标准化）按 d_{k,t} 在 token 维度上归一化，得到 token advantage A_{k,t}^{(j)}，再把所有 reward 的 token advantage 聚合成最终 A_t^{(j)} 进入 PPO/GRPO 的 clipped surrogate objective。

与已有方法的区别：GDPO/SAW 等主要解决“每个 reward 在 response-level 贡献多少”（reward weighting / normalization），但仍是 token-uniform；OPSD 类自蒸馏方法是直接拟合带 privileged info 的 teacher 分布，目标函数形态不同，且不显式做多 reward 的 credit 分解。MRTPO 的关键取舍是：不需要额外生成（仍用同一条 response 重放），不需要 token 标注，不引入额外模型；代价是每个 reward 需要额外两次前向重放来算 JSD（计算开销随 reward 数 K 增长）。217:T4bb,MRTPO (Multi-Reward-to-Token Policy Optimization) keeps the standard PPO/GRPO clipped objective intact and changes only the per-token advantage A_t. For each reward k, it constructs two replay contexts for the same sampled response: one with the verifier’s information for reward k available (+k), and one with that information removed (-k). It then teacher-forces the response under both contexts to obtain next-token distributions p_t^(+k) and p_t^(-k) at every position t. Token relevance is measured as d_{k,t} = JSD(p_t^(+k) || p_t^(-k)). The group-normalized advantage for reward k is redistributed across tokens proportionally to d_{k,t} (with normalization over t), yielding reward-specific token advantages that are then aggregated across rewards.

Key distinctions: GDPO/SAW decide reward contributions at the response level but remain token-uniform; OPSD-like on-policy self-distillation fits a privileged teacher distribution directly rather than explicitly decomposing multi-reward credit. MRTPO’s main trade-off is compute: relevance estimation requires extra forward replays per reward, scaling with the number of rewards K, but it avoids extra sampling, extra models, and token-level labels.218:T61f,The framework has two stages. In stage one, the system starts from roughly 17.8K theorem statements collected from public formal corpora, mainly NuminaMath-LEAN and Lean-Workbook. For each theorem, a model is prompted to produce a proof attempt in a single pass, as numbered natural-language steps paired with corresponding Lean tactics. A key design choice is that the model never receives Lean execution feedback during generation. This preserves genuine model errors instead of repaired trajectories, which is exactly what a verifier needs to learn from.

In stage two, the formal proof is compiled in Lean. All steps before the first failing tactic are labeled correct; the first failing step and all subsequent steps are labeled incorrect. The authors recognize that Lean failure is not always a mathematical failure: some failures are purely syntactic or due to formalization mismatch. To reduce such false negatives, they add a second model call that reads the Lean error message, attempts one syntax repair, and classifies the failure as mathematical versus merely formal. Only proofs whose first failure is judged to be mathematical are kept. For fully compiling proofs, there is an additional consistency check to ensure the natural-language steps actually express the same mathematics as the formal proof.

This yields 10,634 labeled proofs and 152,005 step labels, plus a held-out 200-proof benchmark called LeanPRM-Bench. Verifiers are then trained purely on natural-language inputs, so Lean is only used once during data creation, not at inference time.219:T535,The main empirical result is a controlled comparison against PRM800K-style human supervision. With the same model, the same training recipe, and the same number of updates, LeanPRM-Verifier-4B outperforms the PRM800K-trained verifier on four out of five benchmarks. The gains are large: +14.4 exact step-label accuracy on LeanPRM-Bench, +9.7 on Hard2Verify, and +9.4 on IMO-GradingBench.

The paper also evaluates proof selection in a best-of-N setting on IMO-level problems. The LeanPRM-trained verifier selects correct proofs noticeably more often than random, while the PRM800K verifier stays close to chance. This is an important sanity check: the model is not merely learning stylistic preferences, but something closer to proof validity.

Another useful result is scale consistency. The improvement from LeanPRM supervision appears across all tested model sizes, from 0.6B to 8B, on LeanPRM-Bench, Hard2Verify, and IMO-GradingBench. Given that the dataset is only 10.6K proofs, this suggests that supervision quality and domain alignment matter more than raw label count in this setting.

The most informative ablations are the ones around filtering and label construction: whether syntax-repair filtering is used, how much noise comes from formal-only failures, and how robust the gains are across model scales and benchmarks.21a:T4e8,A controlled head-to-head comparison between two supervision channels with careful confound control.
- Filtered SFT: sample teacher solutions once, filter by final-answer correctness (and separately analyze completeness filtering), then train via token-level cross-entropy (behavior cloning).
- OPD: run student rollouts; at each step the teacher provides token-level supervision (distribution/score) on the student’s prefixes; train the student to match the teacher on those visited states (DAgger-style).
Key design choices:
1) Nested data budgets with fixed update counts per method to avoid “more steps” artifacts.
2) Training-time logging of token-role divergence and explicit completion diagnostics.
3) Error decomposition: separate performance gaps into (a) completion rate differences and (b) correctness conditional on completion.
4) Mechanism probing: analyze teacher behavior on student-generated prefixes and test five OPD variants to see whether the completion collapse is robust to objective tweaks.
A notable empirical claim is that the completion collapse is an attractor induced by the on-policy feedback distribution: starting from an SFT-initialized student, continued OPD quickly erases the previously learned completion behavior.21b:T4c1,Setup: Qwen3-VL 2B student distilled from an 8B teacher; tasks are ChartQA and Geometry3K.
Main findings:
- Geometry3K (teacher fails to finish ~22% within the token budget): with 900 training problems, OPD reaches ~63% test completion vs ~76% for SFT, and trails SFT by 7.9 accuracy points (about -10.5 to -5.3). About 6.6 points of the gap come from instances where only one method produces a concluded answer.
- SFT → OPD regression: continuing OPD from an SFT-trained student drives the rollout termination/completion back to the plain-OPD level within ~40 training steps; final test completion ends around ~62%, close to zero-shot.
- ChartQA (more reliable teacher completion): OPD shows a small, non-robust data-efficiency edge. OPD with 300 questions gets 0.826 accuracy, within 1.4 points of SFT trained on 3,000 (0.840). Under a fixed SFT training-length protocol, OPD leads same-budget SFT by 2.7 points (per-seed interval roughly +0.6 to +5.8). With tuned SFT training length, the OPD advantage shrinks to ~1.1–1.5 points with intervals including zero.
Takeaway: OPD is competitive at small budgets mainly when the teacher reliably completes; otherwise OPD inherits non-completion and loses materially.21c:T40c,The method is Adaptive Stage-Aligned Policy Optimization, or ASPO. It combines SAPO and AFSD. The trained model is a step-level safety monitor that receives the task and visible history, then outputs a concise rationale and a structured verdict before the next action is executed. The data pipeline builds step-level annotations from existing corpora, adds a violation taxonomy and intervention windows, and extends coverage through multi-agent red-teaming. SAPO performs prefix-local policy optimization: responses are compared only against other responses sampled at the same prefix, then scored with a time-aware intervention schedule. It also allocates a fixed update budget to each decision class, so abundant safe steps do not overwhelm the learning signal. AFSD adds reasoning supervision through self-distillation. On intervention steps, the teacher sees step annotations; on benign steps, it uses rules mined from the monitor’s own false alarms, supplying explanations for why the monitor should continue instead of stopping.21d:T601,The training setup is GRPO. A step samples B prompts and n responses per prompt. Rewards are binary and converted to within-prompt advantages. The gold reward checks the final answer against a reference answer. The majority-vote reward marks responses correct if their final answer matches the most frequent answer among the n samples for that prompt.

Near the sampling policy, the GRPO update is a sum of prompt gradients. If the majority answer for a prompt is correct, the MV and gold prompt gradients are identical. The entire difference between the two batch updates comes from prompts where the majority answer is wrong. The paper decomposes the MV update relative to the gold update into shrinkage and misdirection. Shrinkage is the component along the gold direction and mainly changes the effective step size. Misdirection is the orthogonal component and is the part that changes the optimization direction.

The key claim is that misdirection is controlled by cross-prompt coherence of label errors. Independent wrong labels can be frequent and still average out at realistic batch sizes. Coherent wrong labels, such as a reward that systematically prefers confident outputs, frequent outputs, or outputs favored by a learned reward model, leave a directional bias that batch averaging cannot remove. To test this directly, the authors use per-response gradient sketches, allowing multiple reward functions to be evaluated on the same model samples and compared as update directions rather than as final training curves alone.21e:T5fa,The empirical study uses five models from two model families. The main measurement is directional agreement between batch updates. MV updates align with gold updates about as well as two independent gold updates align with each other. After correcting for prompt-sampling noise, the cosine between MV and gold is statistically consistent with 1. The paper also reports that, at practical batch sizes, a prompt’s own gradient accounts for less than 1% of the change in that prompt’s output, supporting the batch-level interpretation.

Controls match the proposed decomposition. Randomly flipping up to 30% of gold labels leaves the update direction essentially unchanged, because the induced errors are incoherent. In contrast, rewards that consistently favor frequent answers, confident answers, or responses preferred by a learned reward model fall short of the gold direction, because their errors share structure. Training runs show the limits of the equivalence. The local gradient match holds at examined checkpoints, but MV and gold training do not become identical. Gold training remains ahead on held-out majority accuracy, while MV mainly sharpens single-sample answers. On held-out problems whose initial majority answer is wrong, MV training turns them into correct-majority problems at roughly three times the rate expected from resampling alone. The introduction also cites TTRL on Qwen2.5-Math-7B, where MATH-500 maj@64 improves from 66.4 to 85.2, as a motivating case that a prompt-level account cannot explain.21f:T970,方法上，论文的核心不是提出新的 latent reasoning 模型，而是提出一套统一诊断工具，并在 21 个 model-task 配置上系统跑通。实验网格覆盖两类 backbone：GPT-2 和 Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct；三类任务：ProsQA、PrOntoQA、GSM8k；三种训练 recipe：COCONUT、CODI、SIM-COT-COCONUT。这里最有信息量的是后两者与 COCONUT 的对比。COCONUT 是把 hidden state 直接回灌成下一步输入，不直接监督每个 latent slot 的语义；CODI 在答案位置对齐 latent 与 written reasoning；SIM-COT-COCONUT 则在保持 latent inference 机制和 slot budget 不变的前提下，加上 per-step supervision。作者还做了 continued-training control，用来区分“多训练了一点”与“确实加了逐步监督”这两件事。

围绕 RQ1，作者设计了 deletion + replacement 的组合干预。删除 latent slots 只能回答“有没有依赖链”；替换则进一步区分依赖的是位置还是内容。替换有三种：噪声、数据集均值向量、另一道题的 latent vectors。这个设计很讲究，因为如果删除有害但各种替换都几乎不影响答案，就更像是 placeholder/position dependence；如果换成别题的 slots 比直接删除还更伤，才更像模型真的在读链内容。

围绕 RQ2，作者不是只 probe 最终答案，而是对每个 slot、每一层同时 probe 最终答案、候选答案、以及每一步 reasoning step，并用 permuted-label null 做对照。这样能区分“答案早就可读”“路径信息分散存在”“步骤是否按顺序布局”“是否存在 candidate superposition”等不同现象。论文的一个关键发现正来自把 probe 结果和 RQ1 的因果结果并排看：可读不等于可用。

围绕 RQ3，作者分析 latent trajectory 的 step size、最后显著变化位置 L、是否早早 settle，并做 mid-chain editing：在链条中途把前缀替换成另一个样本的 twin prefix，观察最终答案是跟着被编辑内容走，还是保持原答案。这个测试比单纯看轨迹几何更强，因为它直接问“已经收敛的状态还能不能被后续 latent step 改写”。整套方法最后汇总成一个 taxonomy：placeholder chain、collapsed/superposed chain、step-dependent causal chain 等都不是互斥说法，而是对应不同任务、训练方式和测量维度下的不同链类型。220:Ta5b,论文最重要的结果集中在逻辑任务与算术任务的分化，以及不同 recipe 的差异。

1. 逻辑任务上，COCONUT 经常在链开始前就已经把答案编码出来。作者发现，在 ProsQA 和 PrOntoQA 这类逻辑任务里，最终答案在 question 的最后 hidden state 上就已经可被读出；latent slots 的状态变化也很快收敛，后续 slot 只做很小更新。更关键的是，删除整条链通常几乎不改变预测，论文摘要里给出的量级是：在逻辑任务上，删除无监督 recipe 的链，最多只改变 3 个答案。这说明这些 latent steps 在很多配置里并没有承担形成答案的因果角色。

2. 逻辑任务上，per-step supervision 会改变“链的形状”，但不必然改变“链的内容因果性”。SIM-COT-COCONUT 能把 reasoning steps 更整齐地一一映射到不同 slot，形成 ordered layout；删除链会明显伤性能，说明模型开始依赖链。但作者进一步发现，在某些配置里，替换链内容并不会改变答案。也就是说，模型依赖的可能是 slot 的存在、顺序、长度或结构，而不是其中承载的具体语义内容。这是全文最值得记住的结论之一。

3. 算术任务上，三种 recipe 都表现出更明显的 content dependence。也就是删除链会伤性能，替换内容也会改变答案，说明 latent chain 在 GSM8k 这类任务里更像真实计算轨迹，而不是占位结构。论文没有在给定片段里展开所有具体表格数字，但从摘要和方法描述可以确认：作者把 arithmetic cell 作为与 logical cell 对照的核心证据，说明 latent reasoning 的有效性不是统一成立，而是任务相关的。

4. probe 结果方面，逻辑任务中的无监督链往往“答案早可读、路径分散存储、候选不共存于单 slot”。这与一些先前工作提出的 candidate superposition 或 collapse 现象并不矛盾，而是说明不同论文测到的是不同维度。per-step supervision 则能让 step k 更集中地出现在 slot k，但这种可解释布局本身仍不能证明模型在用它。

5. state dynamics 方面，作者报告逻辑任务中的 latent states 往往早早 settle；而算术任务中状态沿链持续移动，mid-chain edit 更容易改变最终输出。这进一步支持“逻辑任务里链常是冗余或占位，算术任务里链更像真实中间计算”的判断。

从实验设计角度看，最有价值的不是某个单点提升，而是作者把 21 个配置放进同一套干预—probe—轨迹分析框架里，得到了一组可比较、可复现的判据。221:T44a,For pretraining and alternative language modeling research, the value is methodological and diagnostic. First, it provides a causal analysis protocol for latent reasoning, rather than relying on surface indicators such as accuracy, probe readability, or trajectory geometry. Second, it shows that latent-chain behavior depends strongly on task type and training recipe. On logical tasks, COCONUT often already contains the answer before the latent chain starts, so the chain can be redundant or placeholder-like. On arithmetic tasks, chain content is much more likely to be genuinely used. Third, it clarifies what per-step supervision does and does not buy: it can impose an ordered step-by-slot layout and induce dependence on the chain, but that dependence may still be on structure or position rather than semantic content. This matters beyond latent CoT. The same caution applies to iterative LMs, any-order generation, diffusion-style language modeling, and test-time compute methods: extra computation steps are not evidence of useful intermediate reasoning unless causal use is established.222:T96e,The paper does not introduce a new latent reasoning model. Its main contribution is a unified diagnostic framework evaluated over 21 model-task configurations. The grid spans two backbones, GPT-2 and Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct; three tasks, ProsQA, PrOntoQA, and GSM8k; and three training recipes, COCONUT, CODI, and SIM-COT-COCONUT. The comparison between COCONUT and SIM-COT-COCONUT is especially informative because the latent inference mechanism and slot budget are held fixed, while per-step supervision is added. Continued-training controls are used to separate the effect of extra training from the effect of explicit step supervision.

For RQ1, the authors combine deletion with multiple replacement interventions. Deletion only tests whether the model depends on the chain at all. Replacement distinguishes dependence on position from dependence on content. They use three replacements: noise, dataset-mean vectors, and latent vectors from another problem. This is a careful design. If deletion hurts but all replacements leave the answer unchanged, the chain behaves more like a placeholder. If replacing with another problem’s slots hurts more than deletion, that is stronger evidence that the model actually reads chain content.

For RQ2, the probing setup is broader than prior work. Instead of probing only the final answer, the paper probes every slot and every layer for the final answer, candidate answers, and each reasoning step, with permuted-label null baselines. This allows the authors to distinguish early answer readability, distributed path information, ordered step layouts, and candidate superposition. The key point is not probing alone, but probing interpreted jointly with the causal verdict from RQ1.

For RQ3, the paper studies trajectory evolution through step size, the last substantial change position L, and mid-chain editing. In the editing test, the chain prefix is replaced partway through with a twin prefix from another example, and the final answer is checked for whether it follows the edited content or remains anchored to the original computation. This goes beyond geometric description and directly tests whether a seemingly settled latent state can still be revised. The final taxonomy organizes behaviors such as placeholder chains, collapsed or superposed chains, and step-dependent causal chains into a single framework rather than treating them as competing claims.223:Ta82,The central empirical result is the split between logical and arithmetic tasks, together with the effect of training recipe.

1. On logical tasks, COCONUT often has the answer available before the latent chain begins. In ProsQA and PrOntoQA, the final answer is frequently readable from the last hidden state of the question prefix itself. Latent states also settle early, with only small subsequent updates. More importantly, deleting the entire chain usually leaves predictions almost unchanged. The abstract gives the key scale: for the unsupervised recipe on logical tasks, deletion changes at most three answers. This is strong evidence that many latent steps in these settings are not causally responsible for answer formation.

2. On logical tasks, per-step supervision changes the organization of the chain, but not necessarily its content-level causal role. SIM-COT-COCONUT lays out reasoning steps in a cleaner one-step-per-slot manner, and deletion now hurts performance, indicating chain dependence. But in some configurations, replacing the chain content still leaves answers unchanged. That means the model may depend on the existence, order, or structural pattern of slots rather than the semantic information stored in them. This is one of the paper’s most important findings.

3. On arithmetic tasks, all tested recipes show stronger content dependence. Deleting the chain hurts, and replacing content also changes answers, which makes the latent chain look more like a genuine intermediate computation trace on GSM8k-style problems. The provided text does not include every table entry, but the paper clearly uses arithmetic cells as the main contrast against the logical-task results.

4. The probing results show that, on logical tasks with unsupervised chains, the answer is often readable early, path information is distributed across slots rather than neatly ordered, and no single slot consistently holds both candidates. This helps reconcile prior reports of candidate superposition, collapse, and unused chains: different papers were measuring different properties.

5. In the dynamics analysis, logical-task chains tend to settle early, whereas arithmetic-task chains continue to move across slots and are more sensitive to mid-chain edits. This supports the broader interpretation that logical-task chains are often redundant or placeholder-like, while arithmetic-task chains more often participate in actual computation.

The most valuable part of the experiments is not a single performance gain. It is the fact that 21 configurations are analyzed under one intervention-probe-dynamics framework, producing comparable criteria rather than isolated anecdotes.224:T6af,Read it in the order of problem setup, causal tests, probing, dynamics, then taxonomy.

Start with Figure 1 and the first part of the introduction. That figure is the backbone of the paper. It defines the three research questions and the five tests, and the rest of the paper is easiest to follow once that structure is clear.

Next, focus on the RQ1 section with deletion and the three replacement interventions. This is the strongest evidence in the paper because it separates content use from placeholder use. Pay attention to why deletion alone is insufficient, and why replacing with another example’s latent slots is a stronger test of semantic dependence.

Then read the RQ2 probing results. Do not interpret probe accuracy in isolation. The paper’s main lesson is that readable latent states are not evidence of reasoning unless the same states are also shown to matter causally.

After that, read the RQ3 trajectory and mid-chain editing analysis. This part clarifies whether the chain is still computing across slots or whether it settles early and merely carries a stable representation forward. Watch for step size, the last-change statistic L, and whether edited prefixes redirect the final answer.

Finish with the taxonomy section. It is not just terminology. It is a practical framework for classifying latent-chain behavior and for designing future experiments. If time is limited, Figure 1, the main RQ1 results, the logical-versus-arithmetic comparisons in RQ2, and the taxonomy summary are enough to capture the paper’s core argument in about 30 to 40 minutes. For replication or follow-up work, read the intervention construction details and the continued-training controls carefully.225:T475,The experiments use SmolLM3-3B with 36 layers and OLMo3-7B with 32 layers, including 16 training checkpoints for each model family. Baselines include the logit lens, Jacobian lens, supervised probes, and point-cloud distance measures. In OLMo3-7B, after layer 16 of 32, the logit-lens direction is about 75 degrees away from the model's own lexical readout, and the Jacobian lens is about 77 degrees away; even four layers before the output, both are still at least 40 degrees off. LexFrame[1] recovers the native-frame readouts from the middle layers onward and matches the model's final prediction in both content and confidence much earlier than fixed lenses. One round of prefix attention closes most of the gap left by LexFrame[0]. The frame supports early exit that skips more than two fifths of the layers, remains faithful across training checkpoints while the logit lens degrades, and gives attribution signals that are more faithful than attribution patching. Point-cloud distances are weak predictors of the effect of replacing a state, because lexical readout directions mostly lie outside the main directions of state variation.226:T697,The paper is methodologically careful rather than algorithmically flashy. The dataset contains 225 temporal facts across six domains: FDA, finance, sports, people, SEC, and chemical. A common cutoff of 2026-02-16 is used, and changes announced or effective before that threshold are excluded, making the benchmark genuinely post-cutoff. Each item has both an outdated value and a current value, enabling both open QA and claim-check evaluation.

The evaluation has two layers. One is a deployed setting with the proprietary model Luna under its native web search. The other is controlled retrieval: Luna plus six open-weight configurations all receive the same frozen top-10 Brave search menu, with a common search/open/find tool interface. The ground-truth page is guaranteed reachable by preserving its organic rank when present or inserting it at a seeded position otherwise. This design isolates model behavior from retrieval variance.

A key contribution is the behavioral decomposition of reading depth from tool traces: snippet-only episodes, opened-but-not-cited episodes, and integrated episodes where the model cites a page it actually opened. This makes it possible to localize failures to shallow evidence use rather than retrieval miss. The paper also evaluates citation faithfulness, counting cases where the cited page contradicts the answer. Finally, it runs two controlled analyses: directly supplying the source page to test whether failures come from navigation, and layer-wise readouts to test whether retrieved values enter the model’s internal state. The mechanistic result is subtle: the retrieved value is promoted, but the stale value is not suppressed enough.227:T617,The main empirical picture is clear. Search helps all models: under frozen retrieval, enabling search improves claim-check accuracy by 27 to 42 points, and open-question accuracy reaches 85.8% to 95.4%. So the retrieval menu is useful; the issue is not simple retrieval failure. What varies sharply is reading behavior. With the same search results, models answer 2.6% to 76.0% of episodes without opening any page. In its native deployed search, Luna stays snippet-only in 53.6% of episodes.

Those shallow episodes are much less reliable. Pooled across seven configurations, snippet-only episodes produce stale answers 6.4% of the time, versus 1.3% when the model cites a page it opened. Unfaithful citations are also concentrated in snippet-only behavior, again at 6.4%. This is one of the most useful findings in the paper: many failures come from acting on snippets as if they were sufficient evidence.

The controlled interventions sharpen the diagnosis. Providing the source page directly removes some errors, showing that part of the problem is tool use and page selection. But some failures remain. In those residual cases, layer-wise analysis shows that the retrieved value does influence internal predictions, so the model is not simply ignoring evidence. Instead, stale parametric knowledge remains too strong. The closed-book baseline supports the benchmark design: Luna gets only 23.3% open-question accuracy without search (24/103), indicating that the task genuinely measures use of updated external evidence rather than ordinary memorization.228:T458,The labeling scheme is built from Monte Carlo rollouts. For selected prefixes of a generated reasoning trace, the model samples continuations, and the fraction that reach a correct answer estimates the continuation value. If the initial problem state is already unrecoverable, the trace is labeled a capability gap. If an incorrect trace remains recoverable at all evaluated prefixes, it is a near miss. If it first becomes unrecoverable partway through, it is a pit, and that transition point defines the pit step. The experiments use Qwen3 4B and 8B in thinking mode on hard math problems from DeepMath-103k and the MATH training split. Reasoning traces are split by blank lines and merged so each step has at least 400 tokens. The probe family includes a confidence probe trained on final labels, combined/value probes trained on rollout rates, a failure-type classifier reading transcoder activations, and pointer-style probes trained to predict pit steps. Baselines that use no hidden states include classifiers based on trace/problem variables and a length rule that predicts a late step from trace length.229:T468,The results show limited failure-type signal and weak localization. On incorrect 8B traces, the confidence probe remains calibrated for final correctness at the final step, but at a 0.5 cutoff it misses 81% of pits and 47% of near misses. After controlling for four trace/problem variables, the pit-versus-near-miss difference exceeds the prespecified 0.08 effect margin at 8B; at 4B it is nonzero but below the margin. A combined probe trained on rollout rates changes the failure-type ordering: for 8B, the confidence probe assigns a higher final-step score to a random pit than to a random near miss with probability 0.76, while the combined probe gives 0.40. A classifier on transcoder activations separates capability gaps from pits better than the strongest non-hidden-state baseline by 0.055 AUROC at 8B, meeting the 0.05 margin; the 4B gain is 0.049 and does not meet the margin. Pit-step localization is the weakest part: at 4B, the pointer probe beats the length rule in 0 of 10 runs; an ensemble beats it only under one of two loss weightings; at 8B, the tested value probe is below the length rule across five seeds.22a:T434,OPRD has three main components. First, Multi-Scope Reminder supervision separates global and local corrective signals. A Global Reminder converts final test diagnostics into trajectory-level guidance, while a Turn-local Reminder is anchored to an environment observation and applies only to the next decision. This avoids diluting local feedback over a long context or applying it to unrelated turns. Second, a two-stage cold start performs Coding SFT followed by Instruction-Following SFT, so the model becomes more responsive to constraints, feedback, and reminders before distillation. Teacher and student are initialized from the instruction-following checkpoint. Third, outcome-based routing is applied to reminder-free on-policy student rollouts. Verified successful rollouts become autoregressive self-imitation targets. Failed rollouts are handled by a teacher that re-evaluates the same student-generated prefixes under reminders, and the student matches the teacher distribution with Top-100 reverse KL. At inference time, the trained student runs without reminders.22b:T732,The system has two main components. The first is 3DCodeVerse-2M. Instead of merely aggregating public code, the authors perform substantial representation unification and executabilization. They collect diverse 3D sources, including CAD construction sequences, Blender scripts, Shadertoy programs, Three.js / React Three Fiber projects, Thingiverse assets, and more. They then convert heterogeneous formats into runnable source code: for example, DeepCAD construction sequences are translated into CadQuery programs, and Articraft geometry routines are inlined while preserving URDF articulation specifications. Each sample is packaged as a standalone executable program with source files, assets, textual descriptions, provenance, and available verification records. The hard part here is not scale alone, but removing specialized or unavailable dependencies so that samples can actually run in the declared environment. The second component is the 3DCodeVerse Harness. It decomposes a complex 3D project into a DAG of coding and assembly tasks, lets multiple agents generate and integrate source files, executes and renders the result, and then uses an independent judge agent plus spatial consistency checks to evaluate it. The spatial checks are important because they prevent visually plausible but geometrically invalid outputs from scoring well. Feedback is converted into localized repair objectives, enabling repeated execution-evaluation-revision cycles. This differs from generic ReAct-style loops because the process is centered on executable artifacts, structured verification, and targeted repair rather than open-ended natural-language reflection. The harness is also designed as a data engine: it records successful programs, failed attempts, targeted repairs, and preference comparisons for later SFT and preference learning.22c:T453,The headline results are straightforward. Fine-tuning on 3DCodeVerse-2M substantially improves executable 3D code generation: on 3DCodeBench, execution rates reach 84.9% for a 9B model and 92.9% for a 27B model. This suggests the dataset is effective at teaching models to produce runnable 3D programs. In addition, the Harness improves generation quality by 15.5 to 29.1 points over one-shot generation across coding agents, indicating that iterative execution-judging-repair is necessary for complex 3D projects rather than a marginal add-on. The paper also emphasizes support for projects with thousands of lines of code, which makes the setup closer to real software engineering than static object generation. A useful detail is that evaluation is split into execution success, visual assessment, and spatial/structural checks, making it stricter than render-only evaluation. If reading the full paper, the most informative details are likely the dataset composition, environment coverage, conversion failure modes, the separate gains from judge versus spatial checks, and the taxonomy of common errors.22d:T974,核心做法是构建一个 agent-native 的研究环境 Athanor，而不是只给 agent 一个 shell 和若干脚本。系统把 post-training 研究拆成少数高频原子操作：提交训练作业（athanor job）、请求评测（athanor eval）、引入公开数据（athanor data）、保存/拉取/提交工件（athanor artifact）。agent 在自己的 sandbox 中写代码、读日志、分析结果，但真正的训练执行、评测、数据去污染、工件持久化由环境统一管理。这样做有两个直接好处：一是 agent 不必反复搭建训练基础设施，研究迭代速度更高；二是所有动作都被记录，便于追踪 lineage 和防止评测泄漏。

系统设计里有几个关键点。其一，研究状态外化。作者明确认为长周期研究不能依赖 agent 的上下文窗口，因此把 job history、evaluation results、notes、checkpoint lineage、workspace git commit、journal entry 等都持久化，agent 和队友可以读取这些记录继续工作。这相当于给 agent 提供了一个“外部研究记忆”。其二，评测隔离。开发集由冻结 evaluator 执行，最终 held-out suite 对 agent 完全不可见，只在 campaign 结束后由 operator 打分，避免 agent 通过反复 probing 过拟合最终测试。其三，数据入口控制。新数据只能通过 athanor data 引入，并经过 decontamination 后进入共享 data pool，减少训练数据污染评测的风险。其四，并行与异步执行。每个 researcher agent 占用一个 8-GPU node，在共享 GPU 池上并行发起训练和评测任务，允许多个假设同时推进，而不是串行试错。其五，团队协作。agent 可以读队友的 notes 和 results，也可以抓取队友 checkpoint 继续做增量实验，形成研究分工和 checkpoint lineage。

从研究范式上看，这篇工作强调的不是某个 RL 算法或某个数据合成技巧，而是“把研究流程编程化”。作者的设计判断是：如果没有受管控的执行层，agent 会把大量时间耗在调环境、查故障、重复造轮子上；而一旦把训练、评测、数据接入、artifact 管理做成稳定 API，agent 才能把能力真正用在假设生成、证据分析和实验决策上。这和很多只评估 agent 是否会写训练脚本的工作不同，后者往往忽略了真实研发里最耗时的部分正是执行与验证。22e:T420,The paper is not mainly about finding a better post-training recipe. It asks a harder question: how to turn post-training research itself into a process that an agent can execute autonomously, over long horizons, on real GPUs, under clean evaluation constraints. The task is framed as AutoPostTrain: starting from a raw base model, public data, and a sealed held-out evaluation, with no external teacher models, can an agent run the full research loop by itself? That loop includes diagnosing weaknesses, importing and cleaning data, writing and modifying training code, changing objectives or algorithms, tuning hyperparameters, analyzing results, and deciding what to try next. The target is a single generalist checkpoint that improves multiple capabilities at once, not a collection of benchmark-specific specialists. The real difficulty is therefore not one training run, but long-running asynchronous experimentation, state persistence, evaluation isolation, decontamination, failure recovery, and evidence-based iteration under engineering friction.22f:T9cd,The central contribution is Athanor, an agent-native research environment rather than a loose collection of scripts. The system exposes a small set of high-frequency atomic operations for post-training research: launch a training job (athanor job), request evaluation (athanor eval), import public data (athanor data), and save/fetch/submit artifacts (athanor artifact). Agents work inside their own sandboxes, where they can write code, inspect logs, analyze checkpoints, and keep notes. But the actual execution layer is managed by the environment: training runs, evaluation, decontamination, artifact persistence, and record keeping are all handled centrally. This reduces repeated infrastructure work and makes the full research process auditable.

Several design choices are doing most of the work. First, research state is externalized. The paper explicitly treats long-horizon research as something that cannot live inside the agent context window. Job histories, evaluation results, notes, checkpoint lineage, git commits, and journal entries are persisted so that agents, or teammates, can resume from prior evidence. This is effectively an external research memory. Second, evaluation is isolated. Development evaluations are run by a frozen evaluator, while the final held-out suite is never exposed to the agents and is only scored after the campaign. This prevents direct overfitting to the final test. Third, data ingress is controlled. New datasets enter through a dedicated interface and are decontaminated before joining the shared pool, reducing leakage into evaluation. Fourth, the system supports asynchronous parallel execution. Each researcher agent has access to an 8-GPU node, and multiple training and evaluation jobs can overlap across shared nodes. Fifth, collaboration is built in. Agents can read teammates’ notes and results, fetch their checkpoints, and continue from existing lineages.

The deeper methodological point is that the paper treats research as a programmable process. The claim is not that agents lack ideas, but that without a managed execution substrate they waste time on setup, debugging, and rebuilding the same machinery. By turning training, evaluation, data ingestion, and artifact management into stable APIs, the system lets agents spend more of their capability on hypothesis generation, evidence interpretation, and experimental decision-making. That is a meaningful departure from work that only measures whether an agent can write a training script.230:T76b,From the available full-text content, the experimental setup is intentionally strict. The starting point is Qwen3-4B-Base, treated as a raw base model. The agent team must produce a single post-trained generalist checkpoint that improves six capabilities at once. Training is restricted to public data. External teacher models are disallowed. Final performance is measured on a held-out suite that the agents never see. The system runs on real GPUs, with each researcher agent assigned an 8-GPU node, and training/evaluation jobs execute asynchronously over long-running campaigns where failures are expected.

The main experimental contribution is therefore protocol realism rather than a single headline metric. The paper makes the setting harder than prior work along several axes: one unified checkpoint instead of per-benchmark specialists; sealed held-out evaluation instead of an open loop; no teacher model assistance; and full-stack autonomy from data handling to algorithm changes to result analysis. Those choices make the outcome a more faithful measure of research ability rather than prompt engineering or benchmark gaming.

What is clear is the intended evaluation focus: whether agents can sustain progress under real training friction; whether the system supports parallel multi-agent research; whether the research record is rich enough for recovery, audit, and reproducibility; and whether the final submitted generalist checkpoint improves over the starting base model on the sealed suite. When reading the full paper, the most important result sections are likely the comparisons across agent configurations, the effect of the Athanor execution layer, collaboration vs. isolated work, and analyses of failure modes under sealed evaluation.231:T88d,A good reading order is: problem definition, system design, protocol, then results and case studies.

Next, read the sections on interfaces and state management. Focus on how the paper defines atomic research operations, what is delegated to the agent, and what is enforced by the environment. Finally, spend time on failure analyses and trajectory examples, not just final scores. If the paper includes journal snippets or checkpoint lineage examples, those are worth close reading because they reveal the actual bottlenecks in automated research today.

If time is limited, 40–60 minutes on the introduction, system overview, protocol, and main results is enough to get the core idea. For a deeper read, include appendices on safeguards, decontamination, and lineage tracking.232:T41f,SpecAgent separates tool actions into read-only actions and state-changing actions. The weak model is allowed to execute read-only calls while drafting, because these calls do not modify the environment and can be removed from the history if they are wrong. When the weak model reaches the first state-changing action, such as submitting an answer or modifying a record, execution is paused. The strong model then reviews the drafted segment in one prefill pass, commits the longest semantically valid prefix, and repairs the first rejected step. This differs from routing, where one model still generates each step; from collaborative agents, which decide the actor step by step; and from conventional speculative agent methods, which often require exact agreement with the strong model’s own generated action. The key design choice is to accept alternative valid progress rather than only actions that match the strong model. The cost model relies on replacing sequential strong-model decoding with parallel strong-model prefill over drafted segments.233:T4de,OS-Helix frames hybrid GUI/code computer use as end-to-end policy learning.
- Unified action space: the model emits either GUI atomic actions (mouse/keyboard) or code/shell execution actions under one policy.
- Environment/data foundation: application–artifact composition pairs versioned desktop applications with authentic file artifacts to instantiate diverse, reproducible Ubuntu states.
- Trajectory synthesis pipeline: an Exploration Agent briefly explores the initialized state to propose grounded instructions; a separate Evaluator Agent builds mostly rule-based evaluators to score/filter trajectories, enabling scalable collection of hybrid demonstrations.
- Training recipe: (i) SFT on filtered hybrid trajectories to internalize action semantics and modality routing; (ii) online RL in executable desktop environments to improve success.
- Optimization fix: early RL increases the fraction of code actions while degrading success; the paper attributes this to token-length asymmetry (short GUI actions vs long code blocks) causing token-based optimization signals to be dominated by code. Each refinement phase performs local value calibration so that the inherited critic is adapted to the new actor distribution, reward definition, and execution horizon. For the early phase, the paper uses Lyapunov stability analysis to connect stable step size with local sharpness. Since early pre-training lies in a highly sharp region, a large learning rate before sufficient warmup violates the stability condition. This explains why warmup is not just a smoothing heuristic but a way to wait until the landscape becomes less sharp. For the late phase, the loss is locally approximated by a quadratic around a minimum, and the stochastic dynamics are analyzed under gradient noise. The resulting depth-flatness trade-off says that lower noise emphasizes loss minimization and produces deeper minima, while higher noise regularizes sharpness and pushes toward wider basins. Because the theory identifies η/B as the relevant noise-scale term, increasing batch size and decaying learning rate become two related ways of reducing stochasticity.239:T437,The main experiments use LLaMA-2 style models with 93M and 170M parameters, trained on FineWeb-Edu with context length 1024. Evaluation uses a held-out validation split of about 50M tokens. The empirical results support three claims. First, local sharpness is very high at the start of pre-training and then drops, matching the sharp-to-flat picture. Large peak learning rates without enough warmup lead to loss spikes or plateaus. Second, larger peak learning rates require proportionally longer warmup within the tested regime.
