On real correctness labels over 22 routing families and 68 training runs, the conditional test finds replicated evidence in 12/176 family-probe-view cells, all from five DeiT attention-residual families; none passes the additional same-width noise criterion.2ad:T89c,方法核心是对冻结 LLM 某一层、某一 token 位置的 residual state h 做双编码分解。作者学习两个轻量模块：语义编码器 Es 和价值编码器 Ev，再配一个解码器 D，把 h 压成低维的 zs 与 zv，并要求二者承担不同职责。关键设计不是简单平行分解，而是 one-way semantic→value mixing：价值编码允许读取经过 stop-gradient 的语义信息，用来做“语义条件下的价值识别”；但价值损失的梯度不能反向塑造语义编码器。这样做的理由很明确：价值判断依赖上下文，完全独立分解会丢掉条件信息；但如果让价值监督自由回流到语义通道，又会把语义表示污染成价值友好的表示。

训练数据单位是 semantic-value quadruple：(x+, xp+, x-, xp-)。其中同一场景下，x+ 与 xp+ 是同价值的释义改写，x- 与 xp- 是对立价值的释义改写。监督信号围绕这个结构展开。第一类是 reconstruction，防止塌缩，保证 (zs, zv) 还能重构原始 hidden state。第二类是 swap consistency：在同场景、异价值的样本之间交换 value code，保持 semantic code 不变，要求重构后的表示对应“同语义、换价值”的状态；同时还要求 paraphrase 下 value code 稳定。第三类是 regularization，包括 topic de-confounding 和 decorrelation，前者通过 adversarial suppression 压制 zv 中的话题捷径，后者减少 zs 与 zv 的冗余耦合。推理时不直接生成文本，而是先在表示空间做编辑：固定 zs，把 zv 替换成目标 value prototype 或目标 value code，得到重构差分 Δh，再把这个 residual delta 注入原模型继续解码。

和常见 dense steering、sparse steering、或者直接在 residual 上做线性方向加减相比，这里的区别有三点。第一，它不是假设“价值方向”天然存在，而是显式训练一个可编辑接口。第二，它承认 value 识别需要语义 grounding，因此不是强行独立，而是做单向依赖。第三，它把编辑目标定义成 residual delta from reconstruction，而不是直接覆盖 hidden state，这样更像局部修正，理论上损伤更小。2ae:T8ed,从给出的全文内容看，实验设计是这篇最值得看的部分，虽然当前截取内容没有完整表格数字。作者在两种 instruction-tuned backbones 上验证方法，并且不是只看“价值对齐是否成功”，而是同时看 semantic preservation、benign refusal、以及表示层面的 leakage。实验大致分四组。

第一组是 matched split probes。作者把 learned codes 与任意等维切分、以及若干 ablation 做对比，检查 zs 是否更能预测场景/语义而更少泄露 value，zv 是否更能预测 value 而更少携带 topic。这个实验用来证明分解不是参数量或维度分配带来的假象，而是训练目标真的塑造了选择性表示。

第二组是 2×2 ablation，用来拆开 one-way mixing 与 inference-time gating/编辑机制的作用。也就是区分：性能提升到底来自训练时的语义到价值单向混合，还是仅仅来自推理时更温和的门控注入。作者强调有一个 matched mixing-by-gating ablation，说明他们专门控制了“模型容量和编辑形式相近，但没有 stop-gradient 单向结构”的对照。这一点很关键，因为很多 disentanglement 论文最后其实只是多了个更灵活的编辑器。

第三组是 steering 效果比较。对比对象包括 dense steering、sparse steering、direct prompting 等。结论是：在相近 value alignment 水平下，这个 semantic–value interface 能更好保留原场景语义，并减少 benign refusal。也就是说，它改善的是 trade-off，而不是单纯把 alignment 指标拉高。

第四组是输出层评估。除了自动指标，作者还用了 non-generative fidelity metrics 和 human ratings，去判断编辑后回答是否仍保留人物、事实、数量、约束和任务。这个选择是合理的，因为只看生成文本与参考答案的 lexical overlap，无法判断“价值变了但事实没变”这种细粒度目标。

由于截取内容未包含完整 appendix 表格，参数量、层位选择、code 维度、具体提升幅度和显著性数字无法可靠复述。能确认的是：作者在两个 backbone 上都报告了更好的 preservation/alignment trade-off，并且 architecture-matched ablation 支持 one-way mixing 的必要性。2af:T8bc,The method operates on a frozen residual-stream state h from a chosen layer and token position. A lightweight dual-encoder interface maps h into a semantic code zs and a value code zv, with a decoder reconstructing h from the pair. The central design is not a symmetric disentanglement, but a one-way semantic-to-value pathway: the value encoder is allowed to consume semantic information through a stop-gradient bridge. This reflects the authors’ view that value recognition is context-dependent and therefore should be semantically grounded. At the same time, value-related losses are prevented from flowing back into the semantic encoder through that path, so the semantic channel is not reshaped to serve value discrimination.

Training uses semantic-value quadruples: two paraphrases with one target value under the same scenario, and two paraphrases with a contrasting value under the same scenario. The losses are organized into three groups. Reconstruction prevents collapse and keeps the latent pair tied to the original hidden state. Swap consistency is the main structural supervision: within a scenario-matched opposite-value pair, value codes are swapped while semantic codes are held fixed, encouraging the decoder to represent “same scenario, different value framing.” Additional paraphrase consistency encourages value stability across rephrasings. Regularization includes topic de-confounding, implemented adversarially to suppress topic shortcuts in zv, and decorrelation-style penalties to reduce redundancy between zs and zv.

At inference time, the model does not overwrite the hidden state directly. Instead, it fixes zs, edits or replaces zv with a target value code or prototype, reconstructs the edited hidden state, computes a residual delta, and injects that delta back into the frozen backbone. Compared with dense or sparse steering baselines, the differences are clear: it explicitly learns an editable interface rather than assuming a pre-existing linear direction; it allows value recognition to depend on semantics rather than enforcing strict independence; and it applies edits as reconstruction deltas, which are intended to be more local and less destructive than direct activation replacement.2b0:T8b7,The experimental design is the strongest part visible from the provided full text, even though the excerpt does not include all tables and exact numbers. The method is evaluated on two instruction-tuned backbones, and the evaluation is not limited to whether value alignment succeeds. It also measures semantic preservation, benign refusal, and representational leakage.

The first block of experiments uses matched split probes. The learned codes are compared against arbitrary equal-size partitions and ablated variants to test whether zs better captures scenario semantics with less value leakage, and whether zv better captures values with less topic information. This matters because it checks whether the factorization is genuinely selective rather than a byproduct of dimensionality or extra parameters.

The second block is a 2x2 ablation that separates the effect of one-way mixing during training from the effect of gating or editing at inference time. The paper explicitly mentions a matched mixing-by-gating ablation, which is important: it controls for the possibility that gains come merely from a more flexible editor rather than from the asymmetric semantic grounding itself.

The third block compares downstream steering quality against dense steering, sparse steering, and direct prompting. The reported conclusion is that, at comparable value alignment, the proposed interface preserves semantics better and reduces benign refusals. So the gain is in the trade-off frontier, not simply in maximizing alignment.

The fourth block uses output-level assessments beyond standard generation metrics, including non-generative fidelity measures and human ratings. That choice is sensible because lexical overlap is a poor proxy for the target behavior here: the desired edit changes normative framing while preserving facts and constraints.

The excerpt does not expose the appendix tables, so I cannot reliably restate exact parameter counts, latent dimensions, layer choices, or effect sizes. What is clear is that the paper reports consistent improvements in the alignment-preservation trade-off on two backbones, and that architecture-matched ablations support the necessity of the one-way semantic-to-value design.2b1:T6b4,Start with the introduction, especially the distinction between values and surface style. The paper is careful about defining values as context-dependent normative priorities rather than generic stylistic attributes, and that framing explains why a naive style-transfer factorization is not enough.

Then focus on the method section: the quadruple construction, the one-way semantic-to-value mixing path, the exact placement of stop-gradient, and the swap-consistency objective. This is the conceptual center of the paper. The key question to keep in mind is why the value encoder should read semantics, but the semantic encoder should not be shaped by value losses. If that asymmetry makes sense to you, most of the method follows naturally.

In the experiments, prioritize three things: the leakage or split-probe results, the 2x2 ablation isolating one-way mixing, and the preservation-versus-alignment trade-off plots. Those are more informative than any single scalar score. If time is limited, read the main experimental conclusions first, then inspect the appendix for loss weights, layer selection, prototype construction, and failure cases.

Three follow-up questions are worth thinking about. First, whether this interface is specific to values or can generalize to other steering dimensions such as toxicity, helpfulness, persona, or political stance. Second, whether editing a single layer and token position is expressive enough for long-range normative behavior, or whether a multi-layer interface would be needed. Third, whether the quadruple supervision pipeline scales to broader and noisier value spaces. A quick but useful read is around 25 to 40 minutes; a careful appendix pass will take longer.2b2:T4af,The authors formalize search as a candidate graph G(C,E), where nodes are partial candidates and directed edges encode dependencies. A candidate is represented as a set of literals, and each round expands and verifies leaf candidates. A binary verifier indicates whether a candidate remains consistent with the target. There are N agents, each verifying up to m candidates per round and sharing verification results with d neighbors. The key dynamical variable is A_t, the total number of active incorrect candidates across agents. When A_t decays to zero, the system reaches the absorbing solved state; when it grows or persists, the search process remains active and unsuccessful. The paper introduces four search types: needle, chain, hierarchical, and factorizable search. These classes differ in how much a verification result from one branch can prune other branches. The theoretical analysis derives task-dependent critical degrees d_c. Factorizable search benefits most from communication because local evidence can be reused across otherwise separate parts of the search space. Needle-like search benefits less because a discovered fact usually provides little reusable pruning information.2b3:T41a,The paper introduces Approval Laundering as a taxonomy of approval–execution binding failures. It organizes the space into six failure modes: Scope, Argument, Temporal, Tool, Delegation, and Semantic laundering. The unifying idea is that a human approves action A under an explicit policy, but the harness executes A' without requesting renewed approval. The contribution is primarily formal and empirical rather than algorithmic. The authors define a falsifiable approval policy, distinguish it from subjective operator intent, and then design reproducible tests around different credential-binding surfaces. A key point is that many failures do not involve the model changing the literal command string at all. Instead, the mismatch arises from repository-local hooks, session-scoped grants, tool indirection, delegated execution, or UI/rendering mismatches that alter the downstream effect of an otherwise approved action. This makes the work different from prior benchmarks centered on command risk classification or over-broad scope inference.2b4:T8da,方法分成三层。第一层是数据。作者构建了 SWE-Intervene，从 Open-SWE-Traces、SWE-Hero、SWE-chat 的自然软件工程轨迹中抽取 action-level decision node。每个样本保留任务、完整 pre-action context、agent 提议动作，以及三类标签。Hard-Pause 的自然样本部分来自 SWE-chat 的 AskUserQuestion 交互。标签由 GPT-5.5 按人工制定准则标注，再经过两阶段人工审核，25.3% 的候选被剔除，最后得到 5,680 个训练样本和 1,243 个测试样本，并对下游 benchmark 做了去重。

第二层是监督构造。HiSentinel 的关键不是直接拿 pre-action context 做分类，而是先训练一个 privileged teacher。teacher 在训练时能看到 proposed action 以及该动作的 recorded execution result，因此它的判断带有 hindsight evidence。然后把 teacher 的干预判断蒸馏给一个 causal student sentinel，student 在部署时只能看到轨迹前缀和待执行动作。这样做的原因很明确：如果直接用人工或启发式在 pre-action 空间打标签，很多“看起来合理但会把轨迹带偏”的动作很难标；而 teacher 可以借助执行后果把 supervision 变得更接近最终任务完成。

第三层是反馈生成。作者把“是否干预”和“如何反馈”拆开优化。sentinel 先做三分类决策；若需要介入，再由单独的 feedback adapter 生成简洁、证据约束的指导语。Redirect 对应最小必要修正，Hard-Pause 对应明确指出需要的人类信息、权限或授权。这个拆分是合理的，因为决策头追求校准和低误报，生成头追求可执行性和最小干预，两者目标不同。

从问题设定上看，这篇工作和常见 process critic 的区别在于时机。process critic 往往在动作执行后根据最近几步给反馈，trajectory diagnosis 更偏事后定位 decisive error；HiSentinel 把边界前移到 action proposal 与 environment execution 之间，试图在环境状态被污染前阻断错误。和简单的 prefix anomaly detection 也不同，它不是检测“看起来奇怪的动作”，而是预测该动作是否会降低 eventual task completion，并区分 agent 自主可修复与必须人工介入两类情况。2b5:T94e,The method has three main pieces. First, the dataset. SWE-Intervene is built from natural software-engineering trajectories drawn from Open-SWE-Traces, SWE-Hero, and SWE-chat. Each instance preserves the task, full pre-action context, and exact proposed action, and is labeled as Allow, Redirect, or Hard-Pause. Natural AskUserQuestion interactions from SWE-chat provide Hard-Pause examples. Labels are produced by GPT-5.5 under human-written guidelines, then filtered through a two-stage human audit that rejects 25.3% of candidates. The final dataset contains 5,680 training instances and 1,243 held-out test instances, with explicit de-duplication against downstream benchmarks.

Second, hindsight-distilled supervision. A privileged teacher is trained or prompted with access to the proposed action and its recorded execution result. This gives the teacher post-action evidence when judging whether intervention would have improved the trajectory. Those judgments are then distilled into a lightweight causal sentinel that only sees the trajectory prefix and proposed action. This is the key design choice: instead of asking annotators or heuristics to guess from incomplete pre-action context, the training signal is informed by what actually happened after execution.

Third, feedback generation is optimized separately from intervention classification. The sentinel first decides whether to intervene. If intervention is needed, a dedicated feedback adapter generates concise, actionable guidance: minimal correction for Redirect, or a specific request for missing human information, authorization, or access for Hard-Pause. This separation makes sense because the classifier needs calibration and low false positives, while the generator needs usefulness and brevity.

Relative to prior work, HiSentinel differs from process critics and trajectory diagnosis in timing. Process critics usually react after execution; diagnosis methods localize decisive errors retrospectively. HiSentinel moves the decision boundary to the gap between action proposal and environment execution, aiming to prevent state corruption before recovery becomes expensive or impossible. It also differs from generic anomaly detection: the target is not whether an action looks odd, but whether executing it is likely to hurt eventual task completion, and whether the agent can self-correct afterward.2b6:T683,The motivating statistics are strong. On 1,184 failed CLI-agent trajectories from Terminal-Bench, half of the decisive errors occurred by around step 7, trajectories became unrecoverable around step 12, and the first observable failure signal appeared only around step 16. Prefix monitoring detected only 3.7%–8.7% of failures before lock-in. That directly motivates pre-execution intervention.

The dataset is modest but curated: 5,680 train and 1,243 test instances, including 1,122 natural test cases and 121 AUQ-derived cases. The explicit benchmark de-duplication is important, since trajectory overlap can easily inflate apparent intervention quality.

The deployed sentinels are lightweight, at 0.6B and 1.7B parameters. Evaluation is done at two levels: offline intervention and feedback quality on in-domain and external diagnosis benchmarks, and end-to-end coding-agent performance on SWE-bench Verified mini and Ask-or-Assume. The reported metrics include task completion, unnecessary interventions, and inference overhead. In the provided full-text excerpt, the main result tables are not visible, so it would be unsafe to invent exact gains. What is clear from the setup is that the paper evaluates the right objective: not just classification accuracy, but whether the sentinel improves completion while avoiding excessive interruption and keeping latency acceptable.

The most important ablations to verify in the full paper are likely: with vs. without hindsight teacher, with vs. without AUQ-derived Hard-Pause supervision, and joint vs. decoupled decision/feedback training. Those are the places where the paper’s central claims should cash out.2b7:T5a8,Core represents a reasoning trajectory as a stack of decisions. Each decision has a stable identifier, dependencies, and a canonical key that preserves type, value, dependency context, and occurrence identity when needed. A proposer, which may be an LLM or a deterministic policy, returns a finite ordered list of candidates for the next decision. The verifier returns pass, fail(C), or unknown. A fail(C) output is only eligible for hard caching when C is a sound conflict core: no valid complete solution can contain all decision keys in C. The controller keeps a stack and a set of learned nogoods. Before verifying a candidate, it checks whether the resulting state contains a cached core; if so, the candidate is skipped without another verifier call. When a certified failure is found, Core optionally minimizes the core, inserts it into the cache, removes stored supersets, and backjumps to the latest decision contained in the core. Later decisions are discarded because they cannot repair a conflict that does not mention them. If all candidates at a level are exhausted, their explanations can be resolved into an exhaustion core. Unknown verifier outputs can extend the stack provisionally, but they cannot create hard constraints. The formal guarantees require sound verification, sound cores, finite branching and depth, and exhaustive proposals; under these assumptions, uncapped search is complete and does not prune valid solutions.2b8:T5b8,The paper audits a Dr. Zero-style proposer-solver loop after training. For each scheduled step, it saves the source document, the adopted pseudo-label, and the five solver responses used to compute proposer reward. An independent evidence-based auditor builds a reference from the source and judges the saved labels and responses; unsupported cases are left unresolved rather than forced into a binary label. The metrics separate several effects: T_P is pseudo-label correctness, T_S is solver-response correctness, A is the in-loop match rate, F is false-agreement mass where the label and solver response match but are both wrong, and L counts correct solver answers denied credit by a wrong label. Two mitigations are tested. Multi-sample verification samples the same model three times with the source and three times without the source, admitting a proposal only when the majorities are compatible. This improves label quality but adds six generations per candidate and does not fully remove the failure. CrossFit is the main intervention. Source documents are split into two groups. One auxiliary solver trains only on group A and scores questions generated from group B; the other trains only on group B and scores questions from group A. These cross-fitted scores shape proposer reward, while the main solver still trains on all admitted questions. This blocks the direct path where a solver is rewarded for repeating an error learned from the same source.2b9:T551,The method is simple, but the experimental control is strong. Mid-Harness keeps the generator, execution harness, and serving setup unchanged. It only inserts an intermediate wrapper: given the same interaction history, sample several candidate actions, apply a verifier, and forward only the selected action to the original harness. This makes it possible to separate two questions: whether the generator already contains useful alternatives, and whether a verifier can identify them before execution. The paper varies candidate width, verification mechanism, and verifier capability. A key setting is self-verification, where the same model both generates and verifies. In that regime, wider sampling helps little, which indicates that the bottleneck is discrimination rather than candidate diversity. The paper compares pointwise and pairwise verification and finds pairwise comparison works best, likely because candidate actions differ in intent, semantics, and environmental fit in ways that are easier to judge relatively than absolutely. The authors then distill a verifier initialized from the generator using pairwise judgments from GPT-5.6 Sol, while leaving the action generator unchanged. This is a useful design because it separates the upper bound enabled by a strong verifier from the portion that can be recovered by a practical local verifier.2ba:T555,The main experiments use a fixed TMAX-9B generator on TerminalBench-Lite. There are three key findings. First, with a strong verifier, GPT-5.6 Sol raises Pass@1 from 50.00% for the base agent to 68.03%, showing that the generator already produces many useful alternatives that the default pipeline fails to select reliably. Second, under self-verification, increasing candidate width yields only marginal gains, and pairwise verification is the best among the tested mechanisms. Third, distilling a verifier from GPT-5.6 Sol pairwise responses improves Pass@1 from 54.76% to 57.14% without changing the generator. The gain is smaller than using the frontier verifier directly, but it confirms that part of the opportunity can be recovered through verifier training alone. The disagreement analysis is also informative: the main remaining gaps are command semantics and execution feasibility, meaning the verifier still struggles to predict what a command will actually do and whether it will work in the current environment. The paper also shows compatibility with trajectory-level scaling. Mid-Harness improves both parallel scaling with Best-of-T trajectories and sequential scaling with Sequential Refine. In particular, TMAX-9B plus one round of Sequential Refine and Mid-Harness outperforms Best-of-T at T=7 while using less than half the estimated token cost.2bb:T720,The method is called Retrospective World Modeling (RWM). Instead of relying only on a forward model of the form P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t), the agent is also trained to reason backward and infer the action responsible for an observed transition, conceptually P(â_t | s_t, s_{t+1}). Importantly, this is not presented as a standalone inverse-dynamics model bolted onto the side. The retrospective capability is integrated into the unified policy network and used directly for policy optimization.

On top of this, the paper introduces Self-Consistency Reward (SCR). The intuition is simple: if the action chosen by the policy is also the action that the retrospective model would infer from the resulting transition, then the action is more causally grounded and should receive higher intrinsic reward. If the two disagree, the policy is acting in a way that is poorly explained by the actual environment dynamics. This turns the usual observe-predict-act loop into a closed loop with retrospective verification. The authors explicitly distinguish SCR from curiosity-style bonuses. Curiosity rewards novelty or prediction error and tends to encourage exploration; SCR is designed as an exploitation-oriented regularizer that favors actions whose consequences can be consistently explained after the fact.

A technically important part of the paper is its treatment of reward hacking. Retrospective consistency can be gamed if the model exploits superficial transition cues or if the retrospective module is given too much contextual information. The paper therefore studies different reward formulations and context regulation strategies to prevent leakage and shortcut solutions. That section is central to judging whether the method is learning causal grounding or merely benefiting from an overly informative auxiliary signal.2bc:T652,The paper evaluates the method on multiple agentic tasks and reports a headline improvement in average success rate from 8% to 81%, together with stronger generalization. Because the gain is large, the experimental setup matters a lot: readers should check task difficulty, action space, observability, and whether training budgets are matched. From the full text, the intended comparison is not only against plain RL agents but also against agents equipped with prospective world modeling, so the claimed benefit is specifically from retrospective verification rather than from adding another auxiliary head.

Two experimental messages stand out. First, RWM with SCR improves convergence speed and action effectiveness in long-horizon settings, suggesting that retrospective consistency provides denser credit assignment than sparse task rewards alone. Second, the ablations indicate that this signal needs to be internalized into policy optimization; using retrospective reasoning only as an analysis tool or side objective is weaker. The paper also compares alternative reward formulations and context regulation strategies, explicitly measuring the impact of reward hacking mitigation.

Given the aggressive headline number, the most useful reading strategy is to verify where that 8%→81% jump comes from: whether it is averaged over all tasks, concentrated on a subset of hard environments, or dependent on specific partial-observability settings. If the setup is sound, the main takeaway is that retrospective consistency can materially improve long-horizon RL training, not just next-state prediction quality.2bd:T408,Start with the introduction and Figure 1 to understand the conceptual distinction between prospective and retrospective world modeling. Then go straight to the definition of SCR in the method section. The exact form matters: whether it is based on action matching probability, log-probability, margin, or another consistency score determines whether the method behaves more like reward shaping, an auxiliary objective, or an implicit verifier.

In the experiments, prioritize three parts: the main results table to see where the gains occur, the ablations removing the retrospective module or SCR, and the analysis of reward formulations and context regulation. Those sections tell you whether the method is robust or just exploiting a favorable setup. For a skim-level read, 25–35 minutes is enough. If reading more deeply, a useful follow-up question is whether the same idea could transfer to LLM tool-use trajectories, where one could score actions by whether the resulting state change makes them retrospectively explainable.2be:T85b,The paper formulates recursive social improvement as an RL problem over a population of N agents. Agent i faces its own task distribution D_i and is rewarded only on its own tasks. Each round has two decisions. First, the agent chooses a learning action: search privately, observe a peer, or abstain. Second, it chooses a task action by executing a skill from its current library. A skill can be a simple option in a controlled environment or a full skill file in the LLM setting.

A central design choice is token accounting. Search, observation, and acting all draw from the same budget, and the cost of discovering a copied skill is counted as part of the total social-learning cost. This avoids the common mistake of treating copied knowledge as free.

The experiments proceed in two stages. In the controlled stage, options have known value structure, allowing the authors to test whether established social-learning algorithms can in principle yield an advantage. In the LLM stage, agents write, revise, and exchange skill files for instruction-following tasks. These skill files are inference-time textual procedures rather than weight updates. Policies are implemented by fixed-weight LLMs learning in context: the model decides whether to revise its own skill, copy a peer’s skill, or act.

The paper also makes an important distinction between two notions of success. Efficient social learning means better performance per token. Effective social learning means higher final performance than independent learners at the same total cost. This distinction is one of the strongest parts of the paper because many multi-agent results show speed or cost gains without showing superiority under matched compute.

The authors further test simple interventions such as reserving tokens for acting and requiring some private search. These do not resolve the core issue. Another notable analysis tracks skill lineage over time. Copied skills are often revised again, so the process is not mere imitation. But most final skills end up tracing back to only one or two early revisions, indicating rapid lineage collapse and path dependence.2bf:T6d7,The empirical picture is consistent and informative. In the controlled environment, a hand-designed social-learning policy does achieve a social advantage. That shows the setting itself does not rule out social learning. The failure appears when LLMs are used as the policy controllers.

Across tested LLMs, populations with peer observation are 30% to 52% less efficient than solo populations of the same model. In other words, useful social information exists, but the models do not manage it well enough; they reduce exploration too aggressively.

In the skill-file experiments, peer access changes learning speed and cost but not the matched-cost conclusion. With peer access, GLM-5.3-Flash achieves on average 1.3 percentage points higher held-out accuracy over the course of learning. GPT-OSS-120B uses about one-third fewer learning tokens. These are real benefits, but they are benefits in trajectory shape or efficiency, not in final performance at equal token cost. When learning tokens are matched, neither model shows a clear advantage over independent learners.

The lineage analysis is especially useful. Skills are copied and then revised again, so there is genuine recursive improvement. But by the end, most agents’ skills descend from only one or two of the population’s earliest revisions. This explains the main negative result: copied options often beat what an agent found alone at that moment, yet population-level exploration collapses, so the group does not surpass independent search overall.

The paper is careful not to oversell a benchmark win. Its strongest evidence comes from matched-token comparisons that separate “social learning looks smarter” from “social learning is actually better under equal cost.”2c0:T4bf,A good reading order is: formal problem setup, controlled environment results, LLM skill-file experiments, then lineage analysis. About 30–45 minutes is enough for a solid skim.

Pay attention to four parts. First, the RL formulation, especially the two-stage action space and the token accounting. That is what makes the comparisons meaningful. Second, the distinction between efficient and effective social learning. It is the paper’s cleanest conceptual contribution. Third, the contrast between the controlled environment and the LLM setting, because it localizes the failure to the policy controller rather than to the availability of social information. Fourth, any lineage or ancestry figures, since they explain why populations collapse onto a few early discoveries.

If you work on self-improvement, agent training, or inference-time optimization, the natural follow-up question is whether explicit RL, population-based training, or better incentives could learn a stronger copy-versus-search policy than a generic in-context LLM policy. Another useful angle is the connection between transferable skill files and post-training practices such as trajectory reuse, distillation, and synthetic curricula.2c1:T445,SkillSeek is a deterministic two-stage retriever exposed as an MCP server, so it can be used by harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenHands without changing the agent implementation. Stage 1 uses a BGE-base bi-encoder with 110M parameters and 768-dimensional embeddings to score all indexed skills by cosine similarity and retrieve the top 20. Stage 2 uses a bge-reranker-v2-m3 cross-encoder with 568M parameters to jointly score each query-skill pair and return the top 5. The indexed text is not the full SKILL.md body. It is the skill name and description plus a Tool-REX v3 structured profile containing four tags: file type, primary operation, and two secondary operations. This is a practical design choice: name and description alone often miss the surface forms needed by the reranker, while appending the full body adds noise. The Tool-REX tags are generated offline by an LLM, and online retrieval uses no LLM tokens. The analysis also swaps the stage-2 reranker for Qwen3-Reranker variants and commercial rerankers while keeping the bi-encoder and indexing format fixed.2c2:T40a,The evaluation uses the 89-task SkillsBench benchmark over a 4-by-11 grid of pool, backbone, and retrieval method settings. Several numbers are useful. Loading all skills into context is not effective: even with a small 192-skill pool, pass rate stays around the no-skill baseline while token cost rises by 59%. Adding more retrieved skills is also non-monotonic: one relevant skill gives a +17.8% pass-rate lift, two to three skills give +18.6%, and four or more drop to +5.9%. In the headline 34K-skill pool with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, the SkillSeek variant using Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B reaches a 0.442 pass rate, matching Liu et al. (2026b)’s liu_refined loop. The default bge-reranker-v2-m3 version improves pass rate by +5.7% over no skills, compared with +9.0% for liu_refined. The cost gap is large: liu_hybrid increases the agent loop cost from $27.41 to $39.43, while liu_refined reaches $51.30 with a separate refinement agent. SkillSeek runs on CPU, uses zero online LLM tokens, and keeps cost near the no-skill floor at $27.54.2c3:T47b,The paper models memory use as U(q, M), the observable behavior of a system given query q and memory state M. The observation may include retrieved memories, ranking, or the final memory-dependent response. It then separates failures into two groups. Query-related failures keep M fixed and change q, such as paraphrases that should retrieve the same memory or unsupported queries that should not retrieve unrelated records. Memory-state failures keep q fixed and change M, such as stale records outranking updated records, conflicts being handled incorrectly, or deleted memories still being retrieved. U-Fuzz starts from memory checkpoints produced by normal interactions, builds test seeds from associated queries, and mutates one input dimension at a time. Query mutations preserve meaning, redirect to another supported target, or turn the request into an unsupported one. State mutations update, delete, or modify unrelated memories. Each mutant is validated before execution, and mutation obligations ensure systematic coverage of applicable operator-target pairs. Search is guided by observed memory behavior, not by hidden failure labels.2c4:T42b,SAGE has three components. First, it builds self-explored priors by traversing interactive elements on real devices, constructing a deduplicated UI transition graph, and using a multimodal annotator to synthesize task-trajectory pairs from reachable paths. Second, it creates drift-aware perturbations. The drift taxonomy comes from comparing old and new app versions and includes step insertion or deletion, entry-point and path shifts, control renaming, goal-mismatched detours, and distracting alternatives. Perturbation operators transform clean priors into a distribution that approximates deployment-time retrieval noise, with deterministic reliability labels. Third, it trains a reliability-gated policy. The policy first predicts a reliability variable r in {Follow, Partial, Ignore}, then generates the action conditioned on that decision: p(a|·)=Σr p(r|·)p(a|·,r). This factorization makes the agent explicitly check whether the retrieved path matches the current goal and state before acting, rather than blindly conditioning on retrieved trajectories.2c5:T7c5,The formulation starts from minimum-token segmentation with a vocabulary budget. Each document is represented as a byte-level DAG whose edges are candidate substring occurrences. Byte edges are always available; multibyte edges are available only if the corresponding string is selected into the vocabulary. Given a vocabulary, minimum-count encoding is just a shortest path in the usable subgraph. The coupling difficulty is that selecting one token type enables all of its occurrences across the corpus.

The main idea is an occurrence-level Lagrangian relaxation. Each candidate occurrence gets a non-negative price lambda_e. On the document side, segmentation becomes a shortest-path problem with edge costs increased by these prices. On the vocabulary side, each token type accumulates the total bid of all its priced occurrences, and the lower bound subtracts the sum of the top-K bids allowed by the vocabulary budget. This yields a computable lower bound without a generic LP solver: shortest paths per document plus a global top-K selection over token bids. The paper argues that maximizing over prices recovers the LP relaxation, while validity of the reported bound is checked separately with an exact integer checker.

A useful extension is the boundary-licence formulation. Instead of only comparing the two endpoints—fully regex-constrained versus fully unrestricted—the method allows a budget on how many vocabulary entries may cross regex cuts. That produces a compression frontier and makes the design question continuous: how much compression can be recovered by permitting a small number of cross-boundary tokens.

The paper also keeps compression and prediction separate. Compression is analyzed through certified token-count intervals. Prediction is evaluated on held-out data with an explicit vocabulary and decoding protocol, because unrestricted vocabularies change token frequencies, context granularity, and effective predictability, not just sequence length.2c6:T52e,The headline result on English Wikipedia is a certified boundary tax: regex boundaries increase the optimal token count by 28.3% to 36.8%. That is a large effect, showing that pre-tokenization boundaries materially constrain the compression optimum. BPE is only 2.1% above the constrained lower bound, which supports the claim that under a fixed regex regime BPE is already close to the best achievable compression. But BPE is 10.9% above the unrestricted lower bound, which explains why boundary-relaxing methods can still obtain substantially shorter sequences. These are not contradictory findings; they refer to different optimization problems.

The multilingual study covers 12 languages. Unrestricted fitted dictionaries compress better, but they have higher mean test bits-per-byte in every language. With independent tuning and evaluation seeds, the direction remains in 11 of 12 languages. This is the most practically relevant result for LM researchers: fewer tokens do not necessarily mean easier prediction or lower held-out loss.

The boundary-licence experiments are also important, even if the abstract only hints at them. They show how compression improves as a limited number of cross-boundary vocabulary entries are allowed, which is more informative than a binary constrained-versus-unrestricted comparison.2c7:T7f3,技术上分三层。第一层是机制定位。作者从 softmax backward 的标准形式 dS = P ⊙ (dP - δ) 出发，其中每一行的 δ_i = Σ_j P_ij dP_ij，本来保证 dS 每行求和为 0，这对应 softmax 对行平移不变。FP8 attention 的常见实现为了省算，会用保存下来的输出 O 来近似这个 row correction，即 δ_i^stale = <dO_i, Ô_i>。在高精度或前后向操作数一致时，这个捷径成立；但在 FP8 下，forward 用的是量化后的 P、V 得到 Ô，backward 又用重新量化后的 dO、V 得到 dP̂，两边的量化误差来源不同，导致 δ_i^stale 不再等于真正与 dP̂ 匹配的 correction。

第二层是误差如何影响训练。作者推导出 stale delta 会让 dS 的每一行出现非零残差 ε_i = Σ_j dS_ij^stale。这个残差不是无害的，因为它等价于在 matched gradient 上额外加了 ε_i P_ij 这一项。若 ε_i<0，会推动该行 logits 变尖；若 ε_i>0，会推动其变平。表面上看，不同行的残差可能互相抵消，但映射到 channel 维度后并不会自然抵消。作者观察到某些被“偏爱”的通道会持续受到同向压力，尤其体现在 key 侧 RMSNorm gain 被系统性推高，随后形成选择性放大，训练越久越明显。

第三层是修复方法 Delta-Matching。核心思想不是简单提高某个张量精度，而是让 backward row correction 使用与 backward 真实乘法路径一致的量。作者从未量化的 softmax 概率 P 和由 FP8 backward operands 在 FP32 中相乘得到的 dP̂ 出发，重新构造匹配的 δ，使 softmax gradient 的零行和不变量在给定数值假设下恢复。文中还特别说明，只把 dO 保留成 BF16 并不够，因为概率量化带来的不一致仍在。Delta-Matching 的价值在于它不依赖额外保存一个高精度 forward output，也不要求改 attention 结构；它针对的是 backward correction 这个具体失配点，因此可以直接嵌入 native block-scaled FP8 attention kernel。2c8:T822,实验设计比较扎实，重点不只是“最终分数更高”，而是把失效边界画出来了。首先在机制验证上，作者拿 1.67B GDN/GQA 训练末期 checkpoint 的 BF16 重算激活，去探测 FP8 kernel 在 6 个 attention layer、32 个训练窗口上的行为。结果显示，在 dS 量化之前，stale delta 造成的归一化 row-sum residual 中位数大约在 1.1e-2 到 4.7e-2，这已经不是可忽略的舍入噪声量级。

规模实验覆盖 569M、1.67B、5.29B。569M 上，stale-delta hybrid 只表现为较温和的 validation loss gap，下游任务大体还能保住；这解释了为什么一些早期工作在 sub-billion 规模上看起来“FP8 attention 也能训”。但到 1.67B 和 5.29B，训练前期还能跟住 BF16/FP32 mixed-precision reference，之后 loss 开始持续抬升，并带来下游性能下降，而且 5.29B 更早出现拐点，符合“误差积累且随规模加速”的判断。

作者还测试了多种可能的缓解手段。QK normalization 能减轻甚至避免某些配置下的灾难性崩溃，但仍留有明显性能差距；NoPE 在保留位置敏感 recurrent 层时只能延后退化；head dimension 从 128 提到 256 没有根治作用。这些结果说明问题不是某个架构细节偶然触发，而是 attention backward 数值约束被破坏后的普遍现象。

在架构泛化上，作者不只测标准 attention，还测了 Gated DeltaNet + MLA 的 hybrid，以及 KDA + GQA 的组合，stale-delta failure 都存在。在线性层精度、模型结构、训练阶段变化下，Delta-Matching 都能把训练 loss 和整体下游表现拉回到 BF16/FP32 mixed-precision attention reference 附近。

长上下文实验也很关键。按 Kimi K2 / DeepSeek-V3 风格 recipe，从 8K 扩到 64K，并把学习率降下来后，stale-delta baseline 相对 BF16/FP32 的 training-loss gap 要到大约 19k optimizer steps、约 20B tokens 后才超过 0.01。这个结果很有信息量：如果只做短程 context extension 验证，很容易误判为“方法没问题”。2c9:T7df,The technical story has three parts. First, the paper localizes the failure. Softmax backward has the form dS = P ⊙ (dP - δ), where δ_i = Σ_j P_ij dP_ij for each row. In exact arithmetic this guarantees that each row of dS sums to zero, reflecting softmax shift invariance. Many efficient implementations reuse the saved forward output O to compute the row correction, using δ_i^stale = <dO_i, O_hat_i>. This shortcut is valid when the forward and backward quantities are numerically consistent. Under FP8, however, O_hat comes from quantized forward operands, while dP_hat is formed from separately quantized backward operands. The two paths no longer match, so the shortcut becomes stale.

Second, the paper analyzes how this mismatch affects optimization. The stale correction induces a nonzero row residual ε_i = Σ_j dS_ij^stale. That residual adds an extra term ε_i P_ij to the matched gradient. Negative ε_i sharpens a row of logits; positive ε_i flattens it. Even if row-wise residuals nearly cancel globally, they do not cancel channel-wise after projection through Q/K/V. The authors show persistent pressure on selected channels, especially visible as systematic upward drift in key-side RMSNorm gains. This creates selective amplification over training rather than zero-mean noise.

Third, the proposed fix is Delta-Matching. The key idea is to compute the backward row correction from quantities that are actually consistent with the backward path: unquantized softmax probabilities P and FP32 products formed from the FP8 backward operands. Under the stated numerical assumptions, this restores the zero-row-sum invariant. The paper also shows that simply keeping dO in BF16 is insufficient, because the mismatch caused by probability quantization remains. Delta-Matching is attractive because it does not require storing an auxiliary high-precision forward output and does not depend on architectural changes. It directly patches the numerical inconsistency at the backward correction step.2ca:T81e,The experiments are strong because they map out the failure regime instead of only reporting end metrics. For mechanism validation, the authors probe the FP8 kernel using BF16-recomputed activations from final 1.67B GDN/GQA checkpoints, across six attention layers and 32 training windows. Before dS quantization, stale delta produces normalized row-sum residuals around 1.1e-2 to 4.7e-2 on average row medians over nonzero-gradient rows. That is far above negligible rounding noise.

The scale study covers 569M, 1.67B, and 5.29B models. At 569M, stale-delta hybrid training shows only a modest validation-loss gap and largely preserves downstream quality. This helps explain why earlier small-scale studies could appear encouraging. At 1.67B and 5.29B, however, stale-delta runs initially track BF16/FP32 references, then diverge later with rising loss and degraded downstream performance. The onset is earlier at 5.29B, consistent with cumulative error that accelerates with scale.

The paper also tests several mitigations. QK normalization can prevent catastrophic collapse in some settings, but it still leaves a substantial performance gap. NoPE delays degradation but does not remove it. Increasing head dimension from 128 to 256 does not solve the problem either. This is useful because it shows the issue is not an artifact of one architecture choice.

Generality is tested beyond a single attention design. The stale-delta failure appears in hybrids combining Gated DeltaNet with MLA, and KDA with GQA. Across architectures, training stages, and linear-layer precision settings, Delta-Matching recovers training loss and overall downstream performance close to BF16/FP32 mixed-precision attention references.

The long-context extension result is especially informative. Using a Kimi K2 / DeepSeek-V3 style recipe to extend from 8K to 64K with a lower learning rate, the stale-delta baseline does not exceed a 0.01 training-loss gap over BF16/FP32 until roughly 19k optimizer steps, about 20B tokens. This shows why short extension runs can miss the problem entirely.2cb:T559,Start with Sections 3.2 to 3.4. The main thing to understand is why the zero-row-sum property is not a cosmetic identity but the backward expression of softmax shift invariance, and why the saved-output shortcut breaks under FP8. Then read Figure 3 carefully. It is the bridge from local numerical inconsistency to long-horizon optimization damage, especially the channel-selective amplification story. After that, go to the scale and context-extension experiments in Section 4, focusing on the contrast between 569M, 1.67B, and 5.29B, and on the delayed failure during 8K to 64K extension.

Two details are worth extra attention. First, the paper shows that matching output-gradient precision alone is not enough. That is a broader lesson for low-precision training: local precision patches often fail if forward and backward are still inconsistent at the algorithmic level. Second, the mitigation results for QK norm and NoPE are useful because they separate error sensitivity from error source. They make training less fragile, but they do not repair the broken invariant.

For a fast read, spend most time on the derivation of stale delta, Figure 3, and the 1.67B main pretraining results. For implementation or reproduction, the appendices matter because the numerical assumptions and residual definitions are important to interpret the proof and the measurements.2cc:T8e9,实验部分信息量比较足，且不只停留在 ImageNet 分类。

1. 视觉监督训练：作者用约 1M 参数的 core 去初始化 85M 参数的 ViT-Base，再在 ImageNet-1K 上训练，top-1 相比随机初始化提升 +2.2 个百分点。这是最核心的 headline result，因为它说明一个很小的 recurrent core 可以迁移到大得多的目标模型，并带来稳定收益。

如果回到预训练视角，最值得核对的细节是：语言模型实验的规模、token 数、训练步数、与 procedural warm-up 本身相比的差距有多大，以及收益是否主要体现在早期收敛还是最终 loss 也持续更优。当前片段没有完整表格，这些数字需要看原文。2cd:T7c0,The method is called Procedural Core. It has two stages.

Stage one trains a very small recurrent auxiliary transformer on procedural data instead of warming up each target model directly. The auxiliary model is a minimal recurrent ViT with only three unique blocks: an input block, a recurrent middle block, and an output block. The objective and procedural data setup follow prior procedural warm-up work. The key idea is not to maximize the auxiliary model’s standalone performance, but to force useful computation into a compact reusable parameter set through depth-wise sharing. Recurrence acts as a compression mechanism: if deep transformers partly implement block-recurrent programs, then a recurrent model is a natural place to store that structure compactly.

Stage two expands this compact core into a target transformer of arbitrary width and depth. Depth is handled by unrolling the recurrent block across layers. Width is handled by tiling or expansion rules that map the smaller learned weights into a wider model. The result is a deterministic initialization procedure, not a new warm-up run for each target architecture.

The novelty has three layers. First, it turns procedural pretraining from a repeated training stage into a reusable initialization asset. Second, it uses recurrence as the transfer format, rather than directly interpolating or transplanting warm-up weights. Third, the paper goes beyond reporting gains and studies why the method transfers: depth-wise sharing appears to spread computation across a broader set of directions, including lower-energy components that matter for transfer; in ViTs, the strongest effects concentrate in the attention value/output pathway and suppress high-norm token outliers.

From an LLM perspective, the most interesting part is that the same idea is tested not only in vision but also in natural language and code modeling, which argues for a more general transformer prior rather than a vision-specific trick.2ce:T894,The experimental section is substantial and goes well beyond ImageNet classification.

1. Supervised vision training: a roughly 1M-parameter core is expanded to initialize an 85M-parameter ViT-Base, then trained on ImageNet-1K. This gives a +2.2 point top-1 improvement over random initialization. This is the central result because it shows that a very small recurrent core can transfer to a much larger target model.

2. Representation-sensitive downstream tasks: the gains are not limited to classification. Reported numbers include ADE20K semantic segmentation improving from 26.6 to 28.8 mIoU, ImageNet-S zero-shot segmentation from 32.3 to 42.9 mAP, VOC07 localization from 9.9 to 18.4 CorLoc, and NYUv2 depth estimation improving from 1.104 to 0.998 RMSE. This pattern matters: segmentation, localization, and depth all improve, which suggests the initialization changes internal representations rather than only helping classifier fitting.

3. Self-supervised and cross-domain transfer: the paper also reports gains for DINO, so the effect is not tied to supervised labels. More importantly, the method also helps language models trained on FineWeb-Edu and code models trained on CodeParrot. The excerpt does not expose exact language-model loss or perplexity numbers, but this is what separates the work from a standard CV initialization paper.

4. Baselines: Procedural Core beats both random initialization and structured initialization baselines such as Trockman and Kolter (2023). So the result is not just “any non-random start helps.”

5. Mechanistic analysis: the paper argues that recurrence spreads useful computation across a wider set of directions, especially lower-energy ones, and that in ViTs the effect concentrates in the attention value/output pathway while suppressing high-norm token outliers. This is important because initialization papers often stop at empirical gains; here there is at least a plausible mechanism to inspect.

Start with the introduction and make the distinction from prior procedural warm-up work precise: the goal is not another warm-up stage, but a reusable core that captures its benefit.

Then read the method section carefully, especially the figure and the part describing the three unique blocks, recurrent training, and the expansion rules in depth and width. The key conceptual question is why recurrence should be a better carrier of transferable structure than simply training a small feed-forward transformer.

A focused read will take around 45 minutes. The most useful follow-up questions are: how the gains scale with model size, how much is lost relative to running a full procedural warm-up on the target model, and whether this initialization interacts with tokenizer choice, data curriculum, or training cooldown recipes.2d0:T981,技术核心是把当前层的 full weight gradient 分解成 LoRA 可访问部分和不可访问部分。对注入 LoRA 的线性层，设有效权重为 W_base + sBA。给定当前 batch 的输入激活 X 和反向信号 δ，完整权重梯度可恢复为 G_raw = δ^T X（按文中记号，batch 和 token 维展平后计算）。作者证明，由当前 A、B 的欧氏梯度所诱导出来的等价权重空间梯度，恰好张成当前 LoRA 参数化的 tangent space，也就是所谓 LoRA-accessible gradient space。于是可以把 G_raw 正交分解为切空间内的分量和法向分量；后者被称为 normal gradient。

这个 normal gradient 有两个关键性质。第一，只要它非零，取其负方向，在固定当前 adapter 与其他权重的局部条件下，是当前 batch loss 的下降方向。第二，它与当前 LoRA 一阶可达的所有方向都正交，因此不是通过改 adapter 学习率、初始化或梯度重标定就能补回来的。这也是作者为什么不继续做 LoRA factor 的优化修补，而是直接把 normal 分量用于更新 base weights。

GDLoRA 的实现分成两条支路：adapter branch 仍然是标准 LoRA + AdamW；normal branch 则从同一次前向/反向中恢复 full gradient，投影到当前切空间的正交补上，得到 normal gradient，然后直接更新 base weights。这里有两个实现细节值得注意。其一，作者只对 normal branch 做 token-count normalization，即按输入位置数归一化梯度幅值，保持方向不变，目的是让不同序列长度或 token 数下的 normal update 更稳定。其二，base weights 不维护额外的 momentum / variance buffer，也就是不用 Adam 状态去追踪这条支路，从而避免像 FFT 那样为全量参数付出 optimizer-state 内存。这样做的取舍很明确：用更“轻”的 base update 换取部分 full-gradient 信息，而不是完全复制 FFT 的优化器行为。

和已有方法相比，差异也很清楚。Fira 试图用低秩投影近似 full-rank adaptive update，但需要周期性 SVD 或复用投影基，存在梯度子空间漂移问题。LoRA-GA、LoRA-Pro 则仍停留在 adapter 参数化内部，改善的是 LoRA 所诱导的权重梯度与 full gradient 的对齐程度。GDLoRA 直接承认当前 LoRA 切空间之外还有信息，并显式抽取这部分正交分量来更新 base weights，因此方法逻辑更直接。2d1:T95c,The method starts from a LoRA-injected linear layer with effective weight W_base + sBA. Given forward activations X and backward signals delta for the current batch, the unconstrained full weight gradient can be reconstructed as G_raw = delta^T X after flattening batch and token dimensions. The key theoretical result is that the set of equivalent weight-space gradients induced by Euclidean gradients on A and B coincides exactly with the tangent space of the current LoRA parameterization. This defines the LoRA-accessible gradient space.

Once this space is characterized, the full gradient can be orthogonally decomposed into a tangent component and a normal component. The latter is called the normal gradient. This component has two important properties. First, when nonzero, its negative is a local descent direction for the current batch loss when the current adapters and other parameters are held fixed. Second, it is orthogonal to every first-order direction available through the current LoRA factors, so it cannot be recovered merely by better initialization, rescaling, or re-optimizing the adapter gradients within the same parameterization.

GDLoRA uses two update branches. The adapter branch is standard LoRA optimized with AdamW. The normal branch reconstructs the full gradient from the same forward/backward pass, projects out the tangent-space component, and directly applies the remaining normal gradient to the base weights. A notable design choice is that token-count normalization is applied only to the normal branch, to stabilize update magnitude across different numbers of input positions while preserving direction. Another important choice is that the base weights do not maintain additional momentum or variance buffers. This is how the method avoids the optimizer-state overhead of FFT. In effect, GDLoRA supplements LoRA with a lightweight base-weight update that carries information unavailable to the current low-rank factors.

Compared with prior work, the distinction is clear. Fira approximates full-rank adaptive updates through projected gradients and periodically refreshed low-rank bases, which introduces basis-refresh trade-offs. LoRA-GA and LoRA-Pro improve how adapter gradients approximate the full gradient, but still remain inside the LoRA-induced update space. GDLoRA instead explicitly extracts the orthogonal complement and uses it directly.2d2:T5a4,The experiments span natural language understanding, mathematical and commonsense reasoning, and image classification. The main empirical claim is that under matched adapter and optimizer configurations, GDLoRA improves average performance by about 2% to 4% over standard LoRA and often approaches, or in some settings matches, full fine-tuning.

The emphasis on matched configurations matters. The paper is not claiming gains from extra trainable parameters or full optimizer states. It is testing whether the normal-gradient branch consistently adds useful information beyond what LoRA can express at first order. The most informative comparisons are therefore against standard LoRA, FFT, and methods such as Fira, LoRA-GA, and LoRA-Pro.

The ablations to pay attention to are the ones that isolate the mechanism: whether token-count normalization is necessary for the normal branch; how much is gained by combining LoRA updates with normal base-weight updates versus using either alone; how the method behaves at different ranks; and whether the benefit shrinks as rank increases. If the paper’s interpretation is correct, the gain should be more pronounced at lower ranks, where the LoRA tangent space is narrower and the normal component is more likely to contain important descent directions.

This is not a large-scale scaling-law paper. The value lies in making the missing-gradient story concrete, measurable, and empirically useful.2d3:T4e1,Read this paper with one question in mind: is LoRA limited mainly by low-rank capacity, or by the restricted first-order update space of its current parameterization? Start with the introduction and the theorem-level characterization that the accessible gradient space equals the tangent space. That is the conceptual center of the paper. Then read the definition and properties of the normal gradient carefully, especially why it is a local descent direction and why it cannot be represented by first-order perturbations of the current LoRA factors.

After that, inspect the algorithm section to see that GDLoRA reuses signals already available from a standard backward pass rather than introducing an expensive second-order or repeatedly decomposed procedure. In the experiments, focus on the main comparison tables against LoRA and FFT, then the comparisons with Fira, LoRA-GA, and LoRA-Pro, and finally the ablations on token normalization, rank, and base-weight update design.

A 30-minute read is enough to capture the main idea. If you want to judge whether it is practical for large-model training, spend extra time on the appendix details about compute overhead, memory accounting, and how full-gradient recovery is implemented in practice.2d4:T4e8,The paper uses Partial Information Decomposition to separate multimodal information into four channels. Redundant information R is accessible from either modality. Unique information U_1 and U_2 is accessible only from modality 1 or modality 2. Synergistic information S is accessible only when both modalities are present together. The proposed scaling law writes data loss as a sum of four independent power-law curves. Each curve receives only the relevant data stream: R can be reduced by either modality, U_1 by modality 1 data, U_2 by modality 2 data, and S only by the paired count n_p. This differs from prior L(N, D_1, D_2) forms because it gives paired data its own causal role rather than folding it into modality counts. The experimental protocol is built to isolate this variable. Unpaired examples are represented by a learnable null vector plus a modality-presence bit. At test time, both modalities are always present. Cross-entropy is the main loss, with accuracy checked separately. The main sweeps fix architecture and parameter count, folding finite-model effects into E_N, while appendices repeat Digits and VQA under different architectures and parameter sizes to check that the qualitative conclusions are not tied to a single model.2d5:T5ca,The paper evaluates three settings. Digits combines MNIST images and AudioMNIST spectrograms in a four-digit classification task where the four positions correspond to U_1, U_2, R, and S, giving explicit control over the information channels. VQA trains classification heads on top of frozen pretrained embeddings; this setting is dominated by the text modality and is useful for observing how unpaired data helps non-synergistic information. NLVR2 finetunes a pretrained multimodal transformer on a task where mutual information is largely synergistic and unimodal models remain near chance. Across settings, the authors sweep total data D, compute budget C, paired count n_p, and multiple random seeds. They count D as D_1 + D_2, the sum of unique examples per modality. As p approaches 1, the number of unique rows decreases; training steps are fixed, so fully paired data sees more epochs but the same number of gradient updates. This counting convention favors unpaired data, making improvements from higher p more attributable to pairing itself. The main findings are consistent: pairing ratio has a large effect on loss; laws without p cannot capture the observed curves; only paired data reduces synergistic loss; unpaired data reduces redundant or unimodal loss only up to the relevant floors; and synergy shows a threshold-like acquisition pattern. The provided text does not include exact fit-error numbers for the proposed law, so no additional numeric claims are added.2d6:T42e,The authors study an online teacher-student model with a single softmax layer trained by cross-entropy. Inputs are sampled from an isotropic Gaussian and RMS-normalized, mirroring hidden states before an LM head. A fixed teacher matrix produces hard one-hot labels from the argmax of its softmax output. The student learns with different optimizers. The setup preserves the key nonlinearity behind peaked distribution learning: reducing loss requires both growing the student weight norm, which sharpens the output distribution, and aligning the student direction with the teacher. The analysis decomposes the loss into a radial channel, controlled by norm growth and softmax saturation, and a tangential channel, controlled by directional misalignment. These channels decay with exponents α_r and α_t. SGD places both near one third. Adam produces a different dynamic regime, with α_r near one half and α_t near zero. Across seven optimizers, the exponents obey the relation 2α_r + α_t = 1, which yields the same tuned data scaling L*(D) proportional to D^{-1/3}.2d7:T4d9,LUDI changes the UDLM recipe in two places. First, it introduces a less uniform loss. The usual KL objective for UDLM matches the reverse transition to the exact posterior, but part of the objective encourages the prediction distribution to remain too uniform. With a large vocabulary, this weakens the clean-token signal and hurts few-step reverse generation. The authors simplify and approximate the original objective, decompose it into three terms, and remove the term that pushes predictions toward uniformity. The resulting loss drives each reverse transition more directly toward the clean token. Second, LUDI adds per-token time embeddings. A global diffusion time does not tell the model which individual positions are likely corrupted. Token-level time embeddings provide corruption hints for each position, letting the model identify reliable condition tokens and uncertain target tokens. This enables confidence-based sampling similar in spirit to masked diffusion models: generate easy or high-confidence tokens first, then use them as context for harder positions. Unlike MDLMs, LUDI keeps the uniform vocabulary prior rather than a mask-token prior. Unlike AR models, it does not force a strict left-to-right generation order.2d8:T534,The method, REST (REpresentation-Supervised Thoughts), augments the standard final-answer cross-entropy with four differentiable losses on the latent thought itself. The theoretical setup argues that CE on the final answer does not penalize bad intermediate representations as long as the correct answer remains sufficiently likely, so recursive systems can accumulate representational errors over rounds and across agents.

REST targets four properties. Causality requires the thought to preserve information needed to reproduce the correct output. Minimality pushes it to discard information irrelevant to that output. Separability prevents semantically distinct inputs, especially those with different output distributions, from collapsing to similar latent thoughts. Stability encourages the thought to reflect the distribution over plausible outputs rather than a single sampled answer trace. These losses are added to CE with tunable weights.

Implementation-wise, the paper studies both a multi-agent latent recursive system and a single-agent variant where a model feeds its own hidden states back as the next reasoning step. Importantly, REST does not change the architecture or inference procedure; it only changes the training objective. That makes the paper more about missing supervision than about a new system design.2d9:T432,The evaluation spans MATH500, GPQA-Diamond, MedQA, AIME2025/2026, LiveCodeBench-v6, and MBPP+. Under matched training budget, identical training data, and the same latent budget, REST improves over CE-only by +3.5 points on average in the multi-agent setting and +3.3 in the single-agent setting. The best configurations reach +7.5 and +6.5 points, respectively. For a skim-level read, these are the main numbers to retain.

The paper also reports that REST decodes 15.4% more tokens on average at inference. The authors attribute this to a higher rate of convergence to a final answer. That is an interesting trade-off: better latent supervision improves accuracy, but not necessarily by reducing visible decoding cost in the current setup.

The analysis sections matter more than usual here. The paper claims that CE-only systems exhibit thought collapse and retention of irrelevant information, while REST-trained systems better satisfy the targeted properties. Those diagnostics are central to judging whether the method is doing more than adding another auxiliary loss.2da:T4e1,The model follows the standard LoopLM decomposition: a Prelude P, a shared recurrent core F, and a Coda C, written as C ∘ F^K ∘ P during training. At inference, the number of recurrent applications can be changed to r. The study first uses minimalist LoopLMs under controlled pretraining settings, fixing effective training depth while varying the number of physical layers and recurrent loops. This isolates the effect of recurrence from total training depth. The paper then studies two design axes. The first is where non-recurrent computation should be placed. Output-side non-shared blocks help preserve knowledge behavior, especially when the model is under-unrolled, while input-side non-shared computation tends to help reasoning extrapolation. The second is how the recurrent core should be conditioned. Initial-state injection can hurt knowledge robustness when over-parameterized. The proposed history-state injection instead conditions on relative changes from intermediate states, giving the recurrent core access to trajectory information. Timestep conditioning lets the shared core behave differently at different loop indices. A lightweight channel-wise parameterization combines history-state injection and timestep conditioning.2db:T42a,The experiments compare inference budgets below, at, and beyond the training horizon on both knowledge and reasoning tasks. A simple LoopLM can continue improving beyond its training horizon, and some configurations outperform non-recurrent counterparts under comparable training compute. The behavior is task-dependent: reasoning tasks can benefit from extra loops, while knowledge tasks may degrade. Harder reasoning examples do not consistently gain more from additional recurrence, which weakens the view that recurrence automatically allocates computation to difficult cases. Models with the same effective training depth but different physical-depth and loop-count configurations show different scaling curves. Ablations show that output-side non-recurrent blocks improve knowledge robustness under shallow unrolling, input-side blocks are more useful for reasoning extrapolation, and the joint conditioning design outperforms BaseLoop and the individual conditioning variants under extended inference budgets, with Fig. 7(c) serving as the central comparison.2dc:T8ee,方法分成 TES 和 ACS 两条线。

TES，token-error supervision，在原生 router 之外增加一个轻量的 error head。这个 head 以共享的 token 表示为输入，为每个 expert 预测一个误差分数。然后用 native affinity 对这些 expert-wise error 做加权聚合，使聚合后的预测误差去拟合该 token 实际观察到的 next-token cross-entropy。训练好后，TES 不只是做一个辅助预测；它还在路由阶段把预测误差反馈到 expert 排序里：论文采用从 native affinity 中减去一个按比例缩放的 log-error 项，再做 top-K 选择。直观上，若某 expert 对当前 token 预测误差更高，就降低它被选中的相对优先级。这个设计保留了原有 top-K 稀疏预算，也不改 expert aggregation policy。

ACS，affinity-concentration supervision，则更克制。它不引入额外 head，也不在推理时改路由公式，而是直接用 realized token loss 去监督已选 expert 的归一化 affinity 概率的平方项。作者的解释是，这相当于根据 token loss 去调节路由分布该更尖锐还是更平坦：某些 token 上应更集中地押注少数 expert，另一些 token 上则不应过度集中。它是一个 headless 的对齐方式，参数和推理开销都更小。

监督目标上，论文主要用 Itakura–Saito divergence，也试了 ENLL。理论分析部分给出的关键结论是：对 TES 而言，两者都把聚合误差预测推向相同的期望目标，但对 LM 优化的梯度影响不同。若预测误差与真实误差一致，IS 不改变原始 CE 更新；ENLL 会相对放大低损失 token 的梯度权重。这个分析很重要，因为它说明“把 token error 接进 router”不是只有一个实现细节问题，而会改变训练动力学。

和已有方法相比，这篇工作不是重新设计一个全新 router，也不是增加更复杂的 expert selection 网络，而是在保留原生 MoE 结构和 top-K 预算的前提下，把 token-level error 作为显式监督接入路由。它的优点是兼容现有 backbone，改动小；局限是监督信号来自 realized CE，本身受当前模型状态影响，可能更适合 fine-tuning 或后期 router 校正，而未必直接适合早期大规模预训练。2dd:T942,The method has two variants: TES and ACS.

TES, or token-error supervision, augments the native router with a lightweight error head. From the shared token representation, the head predicts an error score for each expert. These expert-wise predicted errors are then aggregated using the native affinity weights, and the aggregate is trained to match the realized next-token cross-entropy for that token. At inference and training time, TES does more than auxiliary prediction: it modifies expert ranking by subtracting a scaled log-error term from the native affinity before top-K selection. Intuitively, experts predicted to incur higher error are down-weighted in the routing decision. This preserves the original sparse execution budget and the architecture’s native expert aggregation policy.

ACS, or affinity-concentration supervision, is the lighter alternative. It adds no extra head and does not alter inference-time routing with an extra transformation. Instead, it directly supervises the squared probabilities of the normalized selected-expert affinities using the realized token loss. The effect is to encourage the routing distribution to become sharper or flatter depending on token difficulty. In other words, it shapes how concentrated the native router should be, without introducing a separate error predictor.

For supervision, the paper mainly uses Itakura-Saito (IS) divergence and also studies ENLL. The theoretical section is important. For TES, both objectives target the same expected token-error quantity, but they induce different optimization dynamics. When predicted and observed token error match, IS leaves the original CE update unchanged, whereas ENLL relatively upweights lower-loss tokens. That is a meaningful distinction: adding token-error supervision is not merely an auxiliary loss choice, but a change to how gradients are distributed.

Relative to prior MoE routing work, the contribution is not a new router architecture. It is a way to keep the native MoE design and top-K budget intact while explicitly supervising routing with token-level error. That makes the proposal easy to graft onto existing backbones. The likely limitation is that realized CE is itself model-state dependent, so the method may be better suited to fine-tuning or late-stage router correction than to the earliest phases of large-scale pretraining.2de:T525,Experiments are run on two backbones, Granite 3.1 and OLMoE-1B, across four multiple-choice QA benchmarks. The main comparisons are against standard CE fine-tuning and a parameter-matched Dual Affinity baseline.

On Granite, ACS-IS improves average accuracy by 2.1 points over CE fine-tuning with frozen native affinity. TES-IS improves over the parameter-matched Dual Affinity baseline by 2.3 points on Granite and 0.5 points on OLMoE, averaged across the four benchmarks. Under stronger supervision, TES reaches a 2.94-point gain on Granite ARC-Challenge.

These results support two conclusions. First, direct token-error supervision can improve routing in practice, not just in theory. Second, the better mechanism depends on the backbone and task: some settings benefit more from explicit error prediction, others from headless affinity shaping. The paper also keeps the native top-K execution budget unchanged in all variants, which matters for deployment realism.

From a pretraining perspective, the empirical scope is still limited. The paper does not show large-scale pretraining loss curves, routing stability during long runs, or how expert specialization evolves under these objectives. The evidence is therefore best read as a routing-supervision prototype rather than a validated MoE pretraining recipe.2df:T7d2,The method has three layers. First, the paper builds an error model for MLA dual-path quantization. MLA stores a shared low-rank content latent and a decoupled RoPE key cache. Quantization errors in the content path propagate through attention matching, value aggregation, and their interaction. Errors in the RoPE path enter mainly through the RoPE-induced QK logit term. Across six models from four families, the authors show that under matched cache reconstruction error, RoPE-path quantization causes substantially larger attention-output distortion. They then explain this with an operator–error model based on attention sensitivity to logits, how quantization error energy is allocated across subspaces, and how error directions couple with sensitive operator directions.

Second, they propose QuantMLA, a function-aligned dual-path quantization framework. The key design choice is not to use one shared quantization objective. Instead, each path gets its own offline-fusible transformation space and its own functional target. For the content path, the objective is attention-output reconstruction: optimize the quantized representation so that the downstream attention output is preserved, rather than merely reconstructing the latent tensor. For the RoPE path, the objective is positional QK reconstruction: directly preserve the position-sensitive QK term, since that is the main route through which RoPE errors affect outputs. The paper also derives a theoretical bound linking this objective to output distortion.

Third, the paper includes a native low-bit MLA attention backend. Unpacking and dequantization are fused into the attention computation instead of restoring high-precision tensors first. This matters because cache compression only translates into real serving gains if bandwidth and intermediate memory traffic are reduced at execution time. The evaluation therefore includes not only kernel-level behavior but also end-to-end vLLM serving under the same scheduling policy.2e0:T5cf,The analysis spans six models from four MLA families, with total model sizes ranging from 16B to 1T parameters. The main empirical results are threefold.

First, the paper reports what it describes as the first joint INT4 caching result for both the content cache and the RoPE cache in MLA, with only minor accuracy degradation. That is the central quality result, because prior MLA quantization work largely avoided low-bit RoPE caching. Second, in a more aggressive setting, it further compresses the content cache to INT2 while keeping the RoPE cache at INT4, and still maintains competitive performance on difficult reasoning and coding benchmarks. This supports the paper’s main analysis: the content path is materially more compressible than the RoPE path. Third, on the systems side, it reports up to 3.59× KV-cache compression at 128K context length and up to 5.168× whole-job output throughput relative to BF16 in the evaluated cache-pressure workload under the same native vLLM scheduling policy.

The most useful ablations are not just score tables. They establish a chain of evidence: matched reconstruction error does not imply matched functional distortion; path-specific objectives outperform generic reconstruction objectives; and a native low-bit backend is necessary to realize the memory savings as actual throughput gains. The full benchmark-by-benchmark numbers are not fully visible in the provided text snippet, but the main trends and claimed gains are clear.2e1:T4aa,Read it in three passes: mechanism, method, then system. They then run controlled needle-in-a-haystack retrieval while sweeping the source phase. The standard pipeline scores all K trajectories with an EF verifier, keeps a subset, then applies regression tests, LLM-generated tests, and a final EF selection step. LatentSift instead collects hidden states while the policy is generating candidates, adding no extra LLM tokens. It represents each trajectory through three channels: reasoning states, environment-observation states, and function-call states. During training, states from successful and unsuccessful trajectories are stored in positive and negative banks. At inference time, candidate states are compared with these banks, step-level distance margins are aggregated, and channel-level ranks are fused conservatively so that a candidate must look good across the behavioral channels.
