If reading more deeply, spend time on the ablations and human-evaluation protocol, since unified models usually fail at task interference before they fail on headline metrics.600:T875,AgentBrew has three stages. First, it collects a one-shot raw trajectory corpus in the target environment. The agent explores the live state of the application, proposes grounded tasks, and executes them. Importantly, the collected trajectories are not filtered by quality. This design choice is central: in real applications, interaction is expensive and success rates are low, so discarding most trajectories is not viable.

Second, the framework performs retrospective task inference. Instead of treating the original instruction as the only valid label, it infers what the trajectory actually accomplished by looking at the action sequence, tool calls, state transitions, and final outcome. This produces an aligned instruction-trajectory pair. The motivation is clear: many trajectories fail at their original goal but still complete some related or partial task. If trained against the original instruction, they become mislabeled supervision; if discarded, they become wasted data. Retrospective inference repairs this mismatch by relabeling behavior according to realized effects.

Third, AgentBrew applies PMI-based credit assignment. The total information a trajectory provides about its inferred instruction is written as pointwise mutual information, and then decomposed into additive per-action contributions using the chain rule. Intuitively, an action receives high credit if it substantially increases the evidence that the inferred task has been accomplished, and low credit if it is redundant, ineffective, or off-target. These per-action credits are then used as sample weights during policy training, amplifying gradients from informative actions and suppressing noisy ones. This is a more data-efficient alternative to rejection sampling or trajectory-level filtering, because useful local behavior can be retained even inside globally unsuccessful trajectories.

Conceptually, the method sits between behavior cloning and offline RL. It does not optimize with online interaction, and it does not assume a reward model or verifier. Instead, it reconstructs latent task structure from raw logs and then performs weighted offline policy learning.601:T57d,The evaluation is conducted on three real MCP applications: GitHub, Notion, and PostgreSQL. These are live, stateful tool environments rather than simulators, which makes the setup more convincing than synthetic agent benchmarks. AgentBrew improves over the Qwen3-32B base model by +8.7 accuracy and +9.7 score on average, and it even surpasses the larger Qwen3-235B. Against rejection sampling, it gains +5.9 accuracy and +10.3 score. That comparison is important: it suggests that better supervision extraction from the same raw data can matter more than scaling the base model.

The paper also provides mechanism-level evidence. One line of analysis tests whether retrospective task inference really converts failed trajectories into usable supervision. Another examines whether PMI-based action weighting is better than uniform weighting or trajectory-level selection. The ablations indicate that removing either task inference or action-level credit assignment leads to clear degradation, which supports the claim that the gains come from finer-grained supervision rather than simply from using more data.

A notable aspect of the setup is that all learning after data collection is fully offline. There are no iterative on-policy rollouts to rescue the method. This makes the result more meaningful for real deployment settings, where additional environment interaction is often the main bottleneck.602:T53b,This one is worth a close read. Start with the introduction and problem setup to internalize the exact constraints: real API environments, no verifier, no simulator, and single-batch offline learning. Then focus on the two core method sections. First, read retrospective task inference carefully: how the inferred instruction is generated, what evidence from the trajectory is used, and how the method avoids producing vague or behavior-inconsistent relabels. Second, go through the PMI-based credit assignment in detail. It is worth checking the derivation of how trajectory-level PMI is decomposed into per-action terms and how those credits enter the training objective.

In the experiments, prioritize the main comparison tables, the rejection-sampling baseline, and the ablations on task inference and credit assignment. If there are qualitative examples or human evaluation snippets, they are especially useful because the main risk of this framework is whether relabeling is genuinely faithful. Three good questions to keep in mind are: whether task inference merely reframes failure as success, whether PMI credits are stable or biased toward superficially informative actions, and how well the framework might extend to longer-horizon or more state-dependent agent settings. A full careful read should take around 45–60 minutes.603:T514,The central idea is soft router anchoring: gently pull the router toward the base router’s routing tendencies during training, without freezing it.
- Router Prior Bias (RPB): a training-time logit bias that attracts router logits toward a prior read from the frozen base router, while leaving router parameters trainable.
- Retention is measured at three levels, with the bias hook removed at evaluation (bias-free measurement): (1) per-expert utilization, (2) token-level top-k expert selection overlap, and (3) expert co-activation community structure (measured via NMI on co-activation graphs).
- Empirical pattern: soft anchoring methods (RPB and several alternative objectives that constrain router parameters/probabilities) achieve better downstream performance and retain top-k/community structure, while re-applied LBL mainly preserves utilization.
- Causal separation via interventions: enforcing the same prior as a hard assignment preserves community structure as well or better but reduces performance; shuffling prior content at fixed soft enforcement (within-community shuffle) barely changes performance. This supports the claim that the gain comes from soft enforcement/training dynamics rather than community preservation per se (community retention is a footprint, not the cause).604:T62d,The method, CLWM, augments a standard latent world model with a contrastive counterfactual objective over action-conditioned futures. The base architecture remains familiar: a recurrent belief encoder summarizes history, stochastic latent dynamics model future evolution, and planning is done by imagined rollouts in latent space. The key change is in the training signal. Instead of only optimizing observation, reward, and continuation prediction, the model is explicitly trained to separate imagined futures when different interventions lead to different control-relevant outcomes.

The central object is an action-conditioned latent summary, Φ(h_t, α), obtained by rolling out a candidate action sequence α from belief state h_t. Positive and negative pairs are defined by intervention outcome rather than pixel similarity. If two interventions are behaviorally different, their latent futures should be pushed apart even when their near-term observations are visually similar. If two trajectories are outcome-equivalent, their latent summaries should align despite nuisance visual variation. The paper highlights hard counterfactual negatives as the critical ingredient: these are exactly the cases where standard predictive objectives tend to collapse distinct futures.

The authors also introduce diagnostics beyond task success: counterfactual separability, intervention-outcome prediction, and model-exploitation rate. These metrics are useful because they can audit inherited representations, including pretrained encoders, without requiring the CLWM objective itself.605:T463,KPI (Key Path Identification) refines a standard SAE-steering pipeline. Starting from a set of ‘positive’ SAE features correlated with the target behavior (faithfulness), it builds an interaction graph among these features using a small development set. Nodes are candidate positive features; edges represent activation/causal dependencies across layers (and potentially within-layer interactions), motivated by the observation that a strongly steering feature often requires upstream features to activate it. KPI then defines key features via graph structure—high indegree features are treated as bottlenecks/aggregators—and constructs key paths by anchoring on a key layer with strong steering effect and tracing back through preceding layers’ key features. Steering is applied only on features along these key paths, aiming to remove redundant features that dilute the intervention. The paper further connects the intervention to attention dynamics: key-path steering increases attention to context-provided ‘golden answer’ tokens and shows a gradual formation of knowledge-selection behavior across depth.606:T579,Two key components.
1) TaskPilot: an online, policy-adaptive task synthesis loop. Starting from real repository snapshots, it generates candidate tasks, runs rollouts with the current checkpoint to estimate learnability, keeps tasks within a target difficulty window (neither unsolved-always nor saturated), and uses policy feedback to adjust tasks toward that window. Training proceeds in iterations: when a checkpoint saturates on validation, it triggers a new synthesis/calibration round, so the task distribution co-evolves with the policy. This differs from offline difficulty filtering over a large static pool.
2) Leaf harness: a simplified Claude-Code-like tool interface designed for compact models. The authors found Qwen3.5-4B frequently fails to terminate under R2E-Gym/SWE-Agent (about 96% trajectories hit the turn limit). Leaf exposes five typed tools (read/write/edit/glob/bash) and uses a natural termination rule (no tool call => terminate), removing brittle “finish action” requirements. During RL, model-generated reasoning/text/tool calls are trained on; prompts and tool outputs stay in context but are masked from loss.
RL setup: DPPO with async rollouts plus a log-length penalty for concise generations; five rounds of (synthesize tasks -> RL). They also discuss a consolidation procedure to recover useful tool-use behaviors that may be forgotten across later iterations.607:T416,The approach, as implied by the introduction, is:
1) Diagnose three AR issues for reasoning: step-wise sampling noise compounding with depth; probabilistic outputs mismatching logical necessity (hallucination probability cannot be driven to zero architecturally); and linear decoding being a poor fit for graph-structured reasoning.
2) Replace token-level sampled trajectories with deterministic transitions in a learned latent state space, where “reasoning” becomes iterative application of operators over latent states.
3) Positioning against existing mitigations: RLHF/RAG/constrained decoding are framed as probability-reduction within AR; tree/search prompting changes structure but still relies on sampling.

What remains unclear (and is critical for pretraining relevance) is the concrete instantiation: how the latent representation is learned, how operators are parameterized, what the training loss is, whether the system is end-to-end differentiable, and how it scales to large corpora without collapsing into an implicit AR model.608:T802,The model consists of a compressor C_phi and a compression-aware decoder G_theta. For each retrieved document d_i, the method appends m_i = floor(L_i / tau) special compression tokens, runs an encoder over the full sequence, and uses the final hidden states at those compression-token positions as the compressed continuous representation. These compressed document embeddings can be precomputed offline for the corpus, so online serving only needs retrieval plus decoding over the compressed sequences.

The main novelty is the training recipe rather than the architecture. Stage I, Pure Distillation (PD), differs from standard KD in a simple but important way: it trains only on examples where the uncompressed RAG teacher is correct. Standard distillation would also transfer the teacher’s mistakes. PD uses the teacher only where it provides reliable supervision, giving the compressed model a strong initialization without forcing it to internalize the teacher’s failure modes.

Stage II, Hard Exploration (HE), is the key step. Reinforcement learning is applied only to queries on which the uncompressed RAG fails. This is a targeted exploration strategy. Instead of spending RL budget on the full data distribution, including easy cases already handled well by imitation, the method concentrates optimization on the subset where imitation is provably insufficient. The intended effect is not just error correction. It is to encourage the compressed model to discover computation patterns better suited to dense compressed inputs, and therefore capable of surpassing the token-based teacher.

Methodologically, this is a selective optimization recipe: use high-confidence supervision to enter a good basin, then use exploration only on high-value hard cases. Relative to prior soft-compression work, the differences are threefold: distill only correct teacher responses, apply RL only on teacher-failure cases, and explicitly allow the compressed model to deviate from the teacher rather than treating the teacher as the final upper bound.609:T61b,The evaluation covers five open-domain QA benchmarks and, importantly, extends retrieval depth beyond the common top-5 setting to a much wider range from top-5 to top-30. That matters because both the cost of uncompressed RAG and the challenge of compression grow with retrieval depth. The headline result is that DEX-Comp achieves performance comparable to, and in some settings better than, the uncompressed RAG baseline while using 16× compressed context and delivering about 4× to 24× inference acceleration. It also outperforms prior soft-compression baselines.

The ablation logic is one of the stronger parts of the paper. Distillation alone yields a competent compressed model, but it does not reliably break the teacher ceiling. RL over the full dataset is less efficient and less stable because it wastes exploration budget on examples that do not need it. The PD+HE combination performs best, supporting the claim that “correct-only imitation” and “teacher-failure-only exploration” are complementary. The paper also reports generalization across datasets and backbone models, which suggests the recipe is not tied to one specific compressor-decoder pair.

The provided full-text excerpt does not include the complete result tables, so exact per-benchmark EM/F1 numbers, parameter counts, and RL hyperparameters cannot be reproduced here with confidence. Still, the confirmed quantitative details are already meaningful: 16× compression, 4×–24× speedup, evaluation from top-5 to top-30 retrieval depth, and five open-domain QA datasets.60a:T656,For a quick read, start with the introduction’s diagnosis of why soft compression underperforms, then read the definitions of Pure Distillation and Hard Exploration, and finally inspect the main result tables and retrieval-depth plots. The most important sections to read carefully are the ones that define the supervision signal.

First, check how the paper determines whether the teacher is correct or incorrect, because the whole recipe depends on that partition. Then inspect the RL objective: reward design, normalization, and any mechanisms used to prevent overfitting to benchmark answer patterns. Those details determine whether the method can transfer to other latent or compressed modeling settings.

Second, focus on the analysis experiments: correct-only distillation versus full-output distillation, fail-case-only RL versus full-data RL, performance as retrieval depth increases, and robustness across backbones or datasets. If there are case studies, they are worth reading closely to understand what “surpassing uncompressed RAG” actually means—better multi-document aggregation, better robustness to distractors, or simply correction of teacher mistakes.

Two deeper questions are worth keeping in mind while reading. Does compressed input genuinely induce a different internal computation strategy, or is the gain mostly due to better sample weighting? And can this selective RL recipe be reused for tokenizer migration, latent-token decoders, or pretrain-to-posttrain targeted exploration? A skim read should take about 25 minutes; a careful read of method and ablations, around 60–90 minutes.60b:Ta3b,GEPARD 是一个 decoder-only 自回归 transformer，输入文本，输出神经 codec 的离散音频 token，不做文本生成，只预测音频序列和结束标记。骨干基于 Qwen3.5 风格结构，但做了关键裁剪：保留 14 层、hidden size 1024、8 个 attention heads，约 500M 参数；加上音频接口和 voice cloning 后总参数约 555.7M。作者强调 backbone 必须保持“stock”——也就是标准 full-attention transformer，不在自回归循环中插入自定义算子，以保证兼容标准 vLLM 和 FlashAttention-2。

一个重要细节是，他们移除了原始 Qwen3.5 中的 LinearBlock，只保留 full attention。文本 embedding 和 tokenizer 继承自预训练 Qwen，其余 backbone 基本从头训练，因为结构变化后旧权重不再兼容。作者给出的理由主要是经验性的：在相同条件下，纯 full-attention 版本听感更好，同时更适合 vLLM。这个判断还不算严格验证，但符合系统目标。

音频侧使用 NVIDIA NanoCodec，22kHz、21.5 fps、1.89 kbps，把语音离散成 codec token 序列。模型的核心设计原则是：所有非标准模态变换都放到 prefill 或离线阶段。具体包括三点。

第一，zero-shot voice cloning 不在解码环中做动态 cross-attention，而是先用冻结的音频压缩器提取说话人表示，形成 K=8 个 speaker prefix tokens，作为输入前缀一次性送入 backbone。这样 speaker conditioning 成为普通 prefix conditioning，而不是逐步参与解码的额外模块。

第二，针对超短文本生成时常见的 runaway 或 skip 问题，作者提出“short register”分析，把它视为序列过短导致的分布异常和停止行为失衡。他们用文本重复等 augmentation 在 prefill 阶段补偿，而不是在推理时加入动态规则。文中还提到用 entropy 和 stop-probability probe 做诊断，这部分更像训练动态与失败模式分析。

第三，CFG 不在 serving 时做双路前向，而是先离线生成带/不带 CFG 的配对样本，再用 DPO 把 CFG 带来的偏好蒸馏到单路模型，且使用长度与质量归一化的 reward scaling。这个点对基座研究者最有意思，因为它体现的是“把昂贵推理策略蒸馏进参数”的思路，和 speculative decoding 之外的另一类 serving-aware training 很接近。

整体上，GEPARD 不是在 codec 结构或语音 tokenization 上做新算法，而是在标准 LM 骨干、codec 接口、prefix conditioning、offline preference distillation 之间做了一个尽量不破坏 serving 栈的组合设计。60c:Ta95,GEPARD is a decoder-only autoregressive transformer that takes text as input and emits discrete neural-codec audio tokens. It does not generate text; it only predicts audio tokens and an end-of-speech signal. The backbone is Qwen3.5-inspired but simplified: 14 blocks, hidden size 1024, 8 attention heads, about 500M parameters; the full model including audio interface and voice cloning is about 555.7M parameters. A central design constraint is that the backbone must remain a stock full-attention transformer, with no custom operations inside the autoregressive loop, so that standard vLLM and FlashAttention-2 can be used directly.

A notable architectural choice is the removal of Qwen3.5’s LinearBlock layers, leaving only full attention. The text embeddings and tokenizer are inherited from pretrained Qwen, while the rest of the backbone is effectively retrained because the structural change makes the original weights incompatible. The justification is empirical and system-driven: the pure full-attention version sounded better in informal comparisons and is easier to serve with vLLM.

On the audio side, the model uses NVIDIA NanoCodec at 22 kHz, 21.5 frames per second, and 1.89 kbps, turning speech into discrete codec tokens. The overarching principle is to move all non-standard modal computation out of the decode loop.

First, zero-shot voice cloning is implemented as prefix conditioning. A frozen audio compressor extracts a speaker representation once during prefill, producing K=8 speaker tokens that are prepended to the input. This avoids dynamic cross-attention to speaker features during decoding.

Second, the paper studies a failure mode for very short utterances, called the “short register” problem, where AR TTS models may loop indefinitely or skip words. Instead of adding runtime control logic, the authors address it through prefill-side text augmentation, such as text repetition, and analyze it using entropy and stop-probability probes.

Third, classifier-free guidance is removed from serving. Rather than running conditional and unconditional passes at every generation step, the model uses offline paired generations and DPO to distill CFG behavior into a single-pass model, with reward scaling normalized by length and quality. This is arguably the most transferable idea for foundation-model researchers: expensive inference-time behavior is converted into a training-time preference signal and baked into the weights.

Overall, the paper is not proposing a new codec or a new speech tokenization method. It is a serving-aware integration of a standard LM backbone, discrete audio tokens, prefix-based speaker conditioning, and offline preference distillation.60d:T840,The evaluation is presented in two stages. In an early concept-validation setup on a rented RTX 5090, a single-stream vLLM run achieved an RTF of about 0.040 and a TTFA of about 0.032 seconds, roughly 25× faster than real time. This serves as a sanity check that the vLLM-native design is viable. In the more realistic production-style setup, using server-class GPUs and a full SSE streaming harness, the end-to-end system including backbone and neural codec reaches about 0.067 RTF and about 0.046 seconds TTFA/TTFB in single-thread mode. Aggregate throughput scales nearly linearly up to 256 concurrent streams, reaching around 204× real-time throughput. The reported practical operating range is 64–128 streams per GPU, where each stream still maintains interactive performance with RTF below 0.75.

The model size is about 500M for the backbone and 555.7M overall. The audio tokenizer is NanoCodec at 21.5 fps and 1.89 kbps. The authors explicitly state that the model is not aiming for top-tier speech-quality metrics; on Seed-TTS-eval it sits in the middle range. That is important for interpreting the paper correctly: the main result is not absolute MOS or intelligibility, but real-time and concurrent serving within a standard LLM stack.

The paper also analyzes two interesting phenomena. One is the short-utterance failure mode, where 1–2 word inputs can trigger runaway generation or skipped words; entropy and stop-probability probes are used for diagnosis. The other is representation leakage in voice cloning: speaker similarity on unseen voices is limited, and the authors attribute part of this to leakage in quantized representations rather than treating it as a generic quality issue. WavLM speaker embeddings are used for evaluation.

The provided excerpt does not include the full result tables, so exact before/after numbers for DPO-based CFG distillation, short-register compensation, or multilingual performance cannot be reproduced safely here. Still, the reported latency, throughput, model scale, and codec configuration are sufficient to locate the paper’s main contribution.60e:T5a1,From a foundation-model perspective, three parts deserve attention. First, read the introduction carefully for the constraint definition: why many TTS architectures are incompatible with stock vLLM, and how the paper turns “do not modify the decode loop” into a hard design rule. Second, read the architecture section with focus on the speaker prefix, the audio interface, and the decision to keep a pure full-attention backbone. Third, read the sections on CFG distillation via DPO and the short-register analysis, since those contain the most transferable ideas.

Do not read it as a conventional TTS paper centered on quality metrics. The more useful question is how online complexity is shifted into offline training or prefill: speaker conditioning moved to the prefix, CFG distilled into weights, and short-utterance failures addressed through data and training rather than runtime heuristics. Those choices are relevant to speech LM serving and to unified multimodal LMs more broadly.

The most useful artifacts to inspect are: the architecture overview and input formatting, the short-register diagnostic plots, especially entropy and stop-probability probes, the DPO pipeline used to distill CFG, and the concurrency/latency curves for TTFA and RTF. A 30-minute skim is enough to decide whether the paper is relevant. A 60-minute read is better if the goal is to extract design principles for speech LM or multimodal LM systems.60f:Ta52,方法核心叫 Speculative Uncertainty, SU。输入是一个大 agent 在最近 k=3 个 step 内生成的 reasoning-action 轨迹窗口，目标是预测当前 step 的 action 在执行前是否会满足一个外部可验证目标 Ω，在文中就是“代码执行不抛异常”。

关键做法有三层。

第一层，是把 speculative decoding 反过来。作者引入一个小型开源 draft model q，对黑盒 agent p 已经生成出的 token 序列做 teacher-forced scoring。也就是给定前缀 (x, y<t)，让 q 输出下一个 token 分布，再去读 agent 实际生成 token yt 在 q 下的概率。这样一次前向就能得到整条轨迹的 token-level 信号，不需要访问 p 的 logits，也不需要重复采样。文中提到至少提取了三类逐 token 信号，摘要截断处能确认其中包括 cross-likelihood 以及 draft 自己的 argmax 与 agent token 的偏差类信息；从方法描述看，核心是利用 q 与 p 在局部条件分布上的一致性/不一致性来近似失败风险。

第二层，是 phase-aware feature extraction。作者观察到 agent 轨迹不是同质 token 流，而是明显分成 reasoning phase 和 action phase。reasoning 段自由度高、熵高、语言噪声大；action 段受工具调用语法、参数格式、代码片段结构约束更强，熵低，但也更直接决定执行是否成功。如果像 HTC 那样把整段 token 概率简单平均，reasoning 段会淹没 action 段中真正与失败相关的信号。SU 因此按 harness 的消息结构把 token 标成 reason/action 两类，分别统计特征，再送入校准器。这个设计不是简单 feature engineering，而是在利用 agent 轨迹的生成机制差异。

第三层，是轻量校准。作者没有训练复杂判别器，而是用线性 calibrator 把 phase-aware 特征映射成“下一步 action 会通过验证”的概率。这样做有两个好处：一是样本效率高，便于跨 agent 迁移；二是输出可直接作为 gate/routing/human intervention 的决策分数。部署时，SU 插在 code generation 和 execution 之间。如果预测失败概率高，就先 veto 当前 action，触发更便宜的 replan，而不是进入 execute-fail-retry 循环。

和已有方法相比，区别主要有三点：一，不需要白盒访问；二，不需要多次采样；三，不把轨迹当作均质序列，而是显式建模 reasoning/action 两阶段。作者还强调 draft model 的训练目标并不敏感，说明这里更重要的是 draft 作为一个通用语言先验和局部一致性探针，而不是某种专门蒸馏出来的精确替身。610:T991,The method, Speculative Uncertainty (SU), operates on a fixed lookback window of the most recent k=3 agent steps. Each step contains a reasoning span followed by an action span. The target is a calibrated probability that the current action will satisfy a verifiable objective Ω before execution; in the coding setting, Ω is whether execution succeeds without exceptions.

The first ingredient is reverse speculative scoring. A small open-weight draft model q is run in teacher-forcing mode over the black-box agent trajectory produced by model p. For each token, q conditions on the prefix and assigns probability to the token actually emitted by p. This yields token-level cross-likelihood style signals in a single forward pass, without access to p’s internals and without repeated sampling. The method relies on disagreement between q’s local distribution and p’s realized tokens as a proxy for downstream failure risk.

The second ingredient is phase-aware feature extraction. The paper argues that agent trajectories are structurally heterogeneous. Reasoning spans are high-entropy and linguistically noisy; action spans are lower-entropy, more syntax-constrained, and more directly tied to execution success. If one averages token scores over the whole trajectory, as in prior holistic calibration approaches, the action-relevant signal gets diluted by the reasoning phase. SU therefore separates reasoning and action tokens using the harness structure and computes features for each phase independently before calibration.

The third ingredient is a lightweight calibrator. Rather than training a heavy classifier, the paper uses a linear calibration layer to map phase-aware features to a failure likelihood. This keeps the method sample-efficient and easier to transfer across agents. In deployment, SU is inserted as a gate between code generation and execution: if the predicted failure risk is high, the system triggers a cheaper replan instead of entering an execute-fail-retry loop.

Relative to prior work such as trajectory calibration with white-box log-probabilities, the differences are clear: no white-box access, no repeated sampling, and explicit modeling of reasoning versus action phases. The paper also notes that the exact draft-model training objective matters little, which suggests the draft is acting more as a generic language prior and consistency probe than as a tightly matched student of the target agent.611:T6d2,The evaluation is conducted on two agentic coding benchmarks, explicitly including SWE-Bench Verified and DA-Code, with additional zero-shot transfer to an out-of-distribution benchmark. The deployment policy is a pre-execution veto gate: if SU predicts high failure likelihood, the action is blocked and the agent replans.

The headline deployment result is a reduction of per-call execution error rate by 6 to 8 percentage points, alongside a 14% to 19% reduction in average token cost. This is important because the method is not merely improving a calibration metric; it is reducing the expensive retry loop that dominates practical agent cost.

A central ablation concerns phase awareness. The paper’s main claim is that treating the trajectory as a homogeneous token stream weakens the signal, because the high-entropy reasoning portion overwhelms the action-specific failure cues. The reasoning/action split appears to be one of the main contributors to performance over prior holistic scoring baselines.

Another useful result is that the draft model need not be large or highly specialized. A distilled 4B draft is reported to be sufficient, the training objective of the draft matters little, and a draft-calibrator setup trained on one agent transfers to other agents substantially better than an untrained baseline. That makes the method more plausible as a reusable deployment component rather than a benchmark-specific fit.

The most informative parts of the experimental section are likely not the absolute calibration numbers alone, but the transfer results: across agents, across benchmarks, and across draft-model choices. Those are the tests that determine whether SU is genuinely robust under realistic black-box conditions.612:T5b5,This is a skim paper. The main value is the problem framing and the signal design, not architectural complexity. Start with the introduction to understand the deployment constraints that rule out white-box probing and repeated sampling.

Then read the method with three questions in mind: how the draft model scores the completed trajectory; how reasoning and action spans are segmented and featurized; and how the calibrator is trained against the verifiable objective. The choice of a short lookback window, k=3, is also worth noting because it reflects a trade-off between local relevance and long-horizon noise.

In the experiments, focus on four items: comparison against uncertainty baselines such as holistic trajectory calibration; ablations for phase-aware versus phase-agnostic features; sensitivity to draft-model size and training objective; and transfer across agents or benchmarks. Those sections will tell you whether the method is robust or merely tuned to one setup.

If time is limited, 15 to 25 minutes is enough for the introduction, method overview figure, main results table, and the key ablation table. If reading more deeply, the most interesting question is which token-level signal actually carries the predictive power: low cross-likelihood, top-1 mismatch, local entropy, or some combination. A second question is whether the reasoning/action decomposition is specific to coding agents or can generalize to broader tool-using agents.613:T461,RSM-full is an online clustered-memory pipeline with two main design choices:
1) Cosine-gated max-member merge write rule: maintain an L2-normalized centroid μ_m per atom/cluster. A new chunk embedding h merges into an atom if cosine(h, μ_m) ≥ τ OR cosine(h, any member in atom) ≥ τ; otherwise create a new atom. The max-member condition makes merging more permissive than pure centroid thresholding, aiming to reduce fragmentation and mis-clustering under streaming drift.
- τ calibration: per embedding space, set τ ≈ Q0.70 of pairwise cosine similarities using ≤50 unlabeled validation examples.
- Write complexity: O(Md) per chunk.
2) Atom-aware grouped context packer: retrieve top-K atoms, rank members within each atom, and pack retrieved chunks grouped by atom (with headers and temporal ordering) rather than a flat relevance-sorted concatenation. The intent is to preserve local coherence and reduce attention interference from interleaving unrelated snippets.

Higher-rank storage/quantization options are mentioned as deployment paths but are not the core explanatory mechanism in the main text.614:T499,EuroAlpaca starts from 51,760 Alpaca Cleaned examples and produces a near-parallel resource for English plus 50 European languages and regional varieties. Near-parallel means that examples remain aligned by source identifier and task intent, while target-language content may be rewritten when literal translation would invalidate the task. The pipeline treats each record as a structured instruction-following instance. A sample-level policy first routes the example to either field-wise machine translation or task-level localization. For translatable examples, a field-level policy decides whether each field should be translated or preserved, which is important for labels, URLs, code, paths, required output strings, and other fixed artifacts. For examples that depend on linguistic form, such as grammatical errors, rhyme, alliteration, word length, acronym formation, or phonological constraints, the system reconstructs a task-equivalent target-language instance. A final validation stage checks cross-field coherence and target-language consistency. The decision, rewriting, and validation modules use an 8-bit quantized google/gemma-4-31B-it with specialized prompts.615:Ta58,方法上有三层。第一层是实验设计。作者在 51M 到 253M 参数的模型上，系统比较 AdamW、ADANA、Muon、SOAP，OT 因子从 1× 到 256×。每个 optimizer、每个模型规模、每个 OT 点都单独 sweep base learning rate，并以最终 validation loss 选优，而不是拿一套固定超参横扫全轴。评价指标用 token multiplier：在同一模型规模、同一 loss 下，baseline optimizer 需要多少 token 才能达到目标，相对于被比较 optimizer 的 token 数之比。大于 1 说明被比较方法更省 token。

第二层是把优化器行为统一解释为“记忆时间尺度”问题。论文把 momentum 的 EMA 和记忆窗口联系起来：固定 β 对应固定 memory horizon；β 越接近 1，历史梯度保留越久。weight decay 则从参数遗忘的角度进入分析：在 decoupled weight decay 下，参数本身也像是对历史更新做指数衰减平均，因此 weight decay 也对应一个参数级 memory window。这样一来，momentum、二阶矩 EMA、weight decay、learning-rate decay 都可以放到“训练过程中系统记忆如何变化”的框架下讨论。

第三层是 recipe 改造。全文有几个关键点。其一，学习率 schedule 的偏好会随 OT 改变，短 horizon 和长 horizon 可能偏好不同 schedule，甚至出现反转。其二，最佳 weight decay 不是常数，经验上近似按 sqrt(OT) 放大；作者还讨论了 log-time weight decay，让参数遗忘时间尺度随训练进程更合理地变化。其三，对固定-memory optimizers，长 horizon 通常需要更长的 momentum memory，但 memory 变长后最优学习率也要相应下降，因此 memory 和 LR 需要联合调。其四，作者提出 momentum cooldown：在训练末期 learning rate 衰减时，对 ADANA 的 momentum schedule 加一个上界或回落规则，限制末段 memory timescale 继续无限拉长。直觉上，如果 LR 已经很小而 memory 还在变长，优化器会过度依赖很久以前的梯度统计，末期适应性变差。这个 cooldown 与 log-time weight decay 叠加后，ADANA 在高 OT 区间的表现明显改善。

从和现有方法的区别看，Muon / SOAP 代表更强的矩阵级预条件，但 memory 仍是固定的；ADANA 的核心不是更复杂的 preconditioner，而是让记忆长度随训练时间增长，更贴合长训 regime。论文的主要新意不在提出全新 optimizer，而在把“optimizer scaling across horizon”做成了一个完整问题：超参如何随 OT 缩放、不同 optimizer 的优势来自哪里、哪些收益是常数倍，哪些会随 horizon 扩大。616:T892,实验覆盖 51M、111M、253M 三档模型，OT 从 1× 一直到 256×。核心结果有几类。

1. 超参最优点随 horizon 明显漂移。作者显示，最优学习率 schedule 会在 overtraining 轴上发生偏好反转；最佳 weight decay 系数近似按 sqrt(OT) 缩放，而不是固定不变。对固定-memory optimizers，OT 越高，通常越偏好更长 memory；但 memory 拉长后，最优 base LR 要下降。联合调 memory 和 LR，在最低和最高 OT 处收益尤其明显。

2. ADANA 的末期 recipe 很关键。加入 momentum cooldown 后，ADANA 在 terminal LR decay 阶段的损失进一步下降；再叠加 log-time weight decay，收益会累积。论文把这解释为：scheduled-memory 方法在长训中有优势，但如果不控制末期 memory timescale，会在收尾阶段留下额外偏差。

3. optimizer outscaling。相对 AdamW，ADANA 的 token multiplier 会随 OT 增长而上升，说明它不是固定常数倍改进，而是在更长 horizon 下越来越占优。作者指出，这个增长趋势接近 DANA 理论在 power-law random features 下给出的 equivalent-OT exponent 预测，即接近 2-κ 的标度。相比之下，Muon 和 SOAP 在大部分 OT 区间对 AdamW 的优势更像近似常数倍；SOAP 在最高 OT 处可能还有进一步增益，但整体不像 ADANA 那样呈现清晰的随 horizon 扩大的 outscaling。

4. optimizer 排名会变。低 OT 时，矩阵预条件方法 Muon / SOAP 明显领先，ADANA 起步落后；随着 OT 增大，ADANA 逐渐追上并超过 Muon，并与 SOAP 接近竞争。这说明如果只在 Chinchilla 附近做 benchmark，会低估 scheduled-memory optimizer 的长期价值。

5. 作者还做了 joint model-token loss fit，以及 floor-decay likelihood profile 分析，试图区分 ADANA 的 outscaling 来自两种机制中的哪一种：一是 token-decay exponent 更好，也就是 loss 随 token 增长下降得更快；二是 finite-model high-token loss floor 更低，也就是在固定模型规模、极长训练下能逼近更低的极限损失。全文的结论是两者都可能参与，但高 OT 优势不能简单归结为单一常数项改善。617:T9cc,The study is built in three layers. The first is experimental design. The authors compare AdamW, ADANA, Muon, and SOAP on models from 51M to 253M parameters, across overtraining factors from 1x to 256x. For every optimizer, model size, and OT factor, they sweep the base learning rate independently and select by final validation loss. Performance is summarized with a token multiplier: at fixed model size and target loss, how many tokens the baseline optimizer needs divided by how many the compared optimizer needs. Values above one favor the compared optimizer.

The second layer is a memory-timescale interpretation of optimization. Constant momentum implies a fixed effective memory window over past gradients. Weight decay is treated analogously, but at the parameter level: under decoupled weight decay, parameters forget past updates exponentially, so weight decay also defines a memory timescale. This framing lets the paper discuss momentum, second-moment averaging, weight decay, and learning-rate decay in a common language of memory and forgetting over training time.

The third layer is recipe adaptation. Several findings stand out. Preferred learning-rate schedules are not invariant across OT; short and long horizons may favor different schedules, and the preference can reverse. Optimal weight decay is not constant either; empirically it scales roughly like sqrt(OT). For fixed-memory optimizers, longer horizons generally prefer longer momentum memory, but the optimal learning rate then decreases, so memory and LR must be tuned jointly. The paper also introduces a momentum cooldown rule for ADANA during terminal learning-rate decay. The intuition is simple: if the learning rate is shrinking while the optimizer memory keeps growing, the optimizer can become overly anchored to stale gradient information late in training. Bounding the memory timescale in the cooldown phase improves final performance, especially when combined with log-time weight decay.

Relative to prior work, Muon and SOAP represent stronger matrix-level preconditioning but still use fixed memory. ADANA’s distinguishing feature is not a more elaborate preconditioner, but a memory schedule that grows with training time. The paper’s main contribution is therefore not just another optimizer comparison. It turns horizon-aware optimizer scaling into a concrete empirical problem: which hyperparameters should scale with OT, which gains are roughly constant-factor, and which gains truly grow with horizon.618:T834,The experiments cover three model sizes, 51M, 111M, and 253M parameters, and OT factors from 1x to 256x. Several results are central.

1. Optimal hyperparameters drift strongly with horizon. The preferred learning-rate schedule can reverse across the overtraining axis. The best weight decay coefficient scales approximately as sqrt(OT), rather than remaining fixed. For fixed-memory optimizers, higher OT usually favors longer memory, but the optimal base learning rate decreases as memory grows. Joint tuning of memory and LR matters most at the lowest and highest OT settings.

2. ADANA is sensitive to end-of-training treatment. Adding momentum cooldown improves ADANA during terminal LR decay, and the gains compound with log-time weight decay. The paper interprets this as a mismatch between ever-growing memory and late-stage small learning rates if no cooldown is applied.

3. ADANA outscales AdamW. Its token multiplier relative to AdamW increases with OT, indicating a gain that grows with training horizon rather than staying constant. The trend is reported to be close to the equivalent-OT exponent predicted by DANA theory on power-law random features, near 2-kappa. In contrast, Muon and SOAP deliver roughly constant token-multiplier advantages over most of the OT range, though SOAP may improve further at the highest OT values.

4. Optimizer ranking changes with horizon. At low OT, Muon and SOAP are clearly ahead, while ADANA starts behind. As OT increases, ADANA catches up, surpasses Muon, and becomes competitive with SOAP. This is one of the paper’s most important empirical messages: benchmarking only near Chinchilla can systematically undervalue scheduled-memory methods.

5. The paper also fits joint model-token loss curves and uses floor-decay likelihood profiles to ask where ADANA’s outscaling comes from. The analysis separates two possibilities: a better token-decay exponent, meaning loss falls faster with more tokens, and a lower high-token finite-model loss floor. The evidence suggests the long-horizon advantage is not reducible to a single constant offset.619:T717,Read it in four passes: setup, hyperparameter scaling, ADANA-specific mechanics, and loss-fit interpretation.

Start with the introduction and the definitions of overtraining factor, token multiplier, and memory timescale. Those definitions are the conceptual backbone of the paper. In particular, the treatment of both momentum and weight decay as memory mechanisms makes the later plots much easier to interpret.

Then focus on the experiments for learning-rate schedules, weight decay, and memory tuning. The key point is not merely which optimizer wins, but how the optimum moves with OT. If your interest is recipe design, prioritize the figures showing schedule reversal, weight-decay scaling near sqrt(OT), and the tendency of longer horizons to prefer longer memory.

Next, read the momentum cooldown section carefully. That is the most methodologically interesting addition in the paper. It explains why scheduled memory helps in long training, and why the final decay phase needs an explicit cap on memory growth. Read this together with the log-time weight-decay discussion; the coupling between optimizer memory and parameter forgetting is one of the paper’s strongest ideas.

Finally, study the joint model-token loss fits and floor-decay likelihood profiles. The goal is not to memorize the fitting procedure, but to understand how the authors decompose long-horizon gains into exponent improvement versus lower asymptotic loss floor. Readers interested in scaling laws or optimizer theory should spend extra time here.

If time is limited, read the introduction, the memory-timescale framing, the main hyperparameter-scaling results, the momentum cooldown section, and the final loss-fit analysis. A full careful read is about 1.5 to 2 hours; a result-oriented pass can be done in about 40 minutes.61a:T43f,PlaidQ is a 0.7B continuous diffusion language model for code completion. The large vocabulary creates a memory bottleneck because dense reconstruction would materialize a large probability tensor; SWVR addresses this with an exact streamed kernel that matches the dense loss and gradients without storing the full tensor. The first is regime characterization. Using gpt-oss-20b as the main case, the paper focuses on models trained with an unusually large auxiliary load-balancing coefficient, λ_aux = 0.9, far above the typical 0.001–0.01 range used in systems such as Mixtral or Switch Transformer. This pushes mean routing probabilities toward the uniform prior 1/E. The authors then argue for two consequences. One, pruning can improve local LM metrics because removing low-contribution experts concentrates routing mass onto the remaining experts, which may sharpen token assignment enough to lower perplexity while still harming task performance. Two, any global importance score washes out domain-specific micro-signals: an expert that is mildly useful for math but not code will look average once scores are aggregated over all tokens.

The second part is MESA, Minimax Expert Score Allocation. Instead of assuming a single globally valid expert ranking, MESA computes domain-aware scores and iteratively boosts experts associated with the currently worst-affected domain under the tentative pruning plan. The objective is explicitly minimax: reduce the largest domain-specific degradation rather than optimize average retention. This is the main conceptual difference from frequency-based or activation-aware pruning methods such as REAP. Those methods still rely on a stable global notion of importance; MESA assumes that such a notion may not exist under over-dispersed routing and therefore reallocates score mass to preserve fairness across domains.61d:T63a,The main experiments are on gpt-oss-20b, with Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct used as a standard-routing control. The most important result is the perplexity–accuracy disconnect. Across five pruning configurations on gpt-oss-20b, the expected negative correlation between perplexity and downstream accuracy disappears. The paper reports Spearman ρ = 0.70 on GSM8K (with p > 0.1) and ρ = -0.10 on GPQA. A striking example is that random pruning achieves the lowest perplexity, 40.95, yet gives the worst math performance, while REAP has the highest perplexity, 145.04, but preserves much stronger downstream behavior.

A second result is the capability trade-off across pruning signals. Activation-aware pruning, represented by REAP, preserves competition-style math better, reaching 73% on AIME 2025, but loses badly on science QA, with GPQA at 47.72% versus 65.48% for a stronger alternative, an 18-point gap. Frequency-based methods show the opposite tendency on some domains. This supports the paper’s claim that weak domain specialization survives inside an apparently uniform router and different pruning signals damage different capabilities.

A third result is the benefit of MESA on worst-case retention. At pruning ratio r = 0.25, MESA achieves the smallest worst-domain degradation. On a per-benchmark comparison, it beats REAP on 7 of 11 benchmarks, with 5 statistically significant wins. On Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct, the same perplexity–accuracy pathology does not appear, which strengthens the argument that the issue is regime-specific rather than a generic property of expert pruning.61e:T47d,For a quick read, focus on three things. Another useful follow-up is whether domain-aware regularization should be introduced during training, instead of trying to recover fairness only at pruning time.61f:T703,The method starts by separating queries into two behavioral types. Local queries mostly attend to nearby tokens. Global queries, associated with TRTs, attend back to distant earlier context. The paper then shows that these global queries are not scattered arbitrarily in query-embedding space; they form a small number of similarity clusters. This motivates beacon queries: a compact set of representative queries intended to approximate future global revisiting patterns.

At eviction time, BeaconKV does not score historical KV entries using only recent queries. It also keeps a small set of beacon queries. A token is retained not only if it matters to the current local decoding state, but also if it is important to one of these representative global queries. This gives the system a way to protect tokens that may not look useful now, but are likely to be revisited later.

Because decoding is online, beacon queries cannot be obtained by offline clustering over the full query history. The paper therefore proposes Continual Farthest Point Sampling, an online procedure that incrementally selects geometrically diverse queries while keeping memory bounded. Intuitively, it maintains a compact cover of the query space seen so far. Compared with storing the full query history, this is memory efficient; compared with using only recent queries, it preserves information about potential future global attention patterns.

Methodologically, BeaconKV is training-free. It does not modify model weights and does not require distillation or calibration. Its main distinction from RPC and R-KV is not a better redundancy score, but an explicit treatment of future-query mismatch: future important queries may differ from recent ones, and a small representative set can partially bridge that gap.620:T537,The evaluation covers four open reasoning models: R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, R1-Distill-Llama-8B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-14B. Benchmarks include AIME24, MATH-500, LiveCodeBench, and GPQA-Diamond, spanning math, coding, and science reasoning.

Several headline results matter. First, across a range of cache budgets, BeaconKV generally outperforms RPC and R-KV, with accuracy gains of up to 31.7 percentage points. That large gap suggests that under aggressive compression, the dominant issue is wrong eviction rather than raw capacity alone. Second, under strong compression, peak GPU memory can be reduced by up to 5.8x while keeping accuracy close to full-KV inference. Third, throughput improves by more than 4.3x over the uncompressed baseline, so the benefit is not only fitting longer traces but also improving practical serving efficiency.

The most informative ablations are the mechanism checks: TRTs indeed exhibit long-range attention; global queries show cluster structure in embedding space; recent-query-only scoring fails to cover these future revisiting needs; and adding beacon queries better preserves the tokens that full-KV inference would later rely on. When reading the paper, the attention visualizations, query-geometry analysis, and the trade-off between beacon count and cache budget are the parts with the most signal.621:T425,This is a skim paper, but it is worth reading beyond the result tables. Softmax attention already computes normalized reductions over exp(τ q·k), so the remaining issues are removing the softmax normalization and incorporating the key-dependent Gaussian factor into the values. Two reductions are given. The prescale variant reads the log-sum-exp values produced by attention backends, multiplies the normalized output by exp(lse), and applies the query/key norm corrections. It is algebraically compact, but the exposed logits do not support the needed differentiable path through the public PyTorch API. The reweight variant avoids reading logits by augmenting queries and keys with two extra coordinates and values with an auxiliary channel. A single scaled_dot_product_attention call returns both the desired numerator and a correction term, whose ratio recovers the unnormalized Gaussian sum. This version is fully compatible with PyTorch SDPA and autograd, including flash-backed backward kernels. The paper also treats practical fp16 issues: underflow of the correction term, mean-shifting q and k to reduce overflow risk, padding dimensions to multiples of 8, and the FlashAttention constraints on D and C.623:T6ae,The method has two coupled pieces: ConsensusBench and ConsensusPR. The central hypothesis is that correct final answers are usually reached through a small set of stable intermediate outcomes, such as solved subproblems, validated constraints, case splits, or applied lemmas. Different correct trajectories may vary in wording, but they often converge on these checkpoints. The paper calls them consensus nodes. Construction proceeds by sampling N rollouts per prompt, keeping the correct ones, extracting intermediate conclusions from those trajectories, and clustering semantically equivalent conclusions into shared nodes. This is an important design choice: the target is not to imitate one canonical solution path, but to recover objective checkpoints that multiple successful paths pass through. Based on these nodes, the authors define ConsensusPR, a rule-based process reward that densifies the original terminal reward along the reasoning path. They also introduce three evaluation metrics: Final Answer Accuracy for endpoint correctness, Node Coverage Rate for how many consensus nodes a trajectory reaches, and Tokens per Node for reasoning efficiency. The metric design is tightly aligned with the failure modes they identify: NCR captures partial progress, while TPN distinguishes concise reasoning from verbose but uninformative chains. A practical advantage is that ConsensusPR plugs into existing GRPO and DAPO/RLVR pipelines without training a separate process reward model. Unlike PRMs, which try to score the quality of each step, ConsensusPR only checks whether the trajectory reaches verifiable intermediate states. That makes the signal more discrete, more objective, and easier to scale.624:T452,The experimental story has four main parts. First, the paper presents a case study of four reward-mismatch types under outcome-only supervision; this is not just motivation, but the basis for the benchmark and metric design. Second, ConsensusBench is used as an evaluation asset to show that models with similar final-answer accuracy can differ substantially in node coverage and reasoning efficiency. Third, ConsensusPR is integrated into GRPO and DAPO-style RL training, where it improves not only final performance but also process quality, measured by higher node coverage and lower tokens per node, while maintaining training stability. Fourth, the paper emphasizes the efficiency advantage over PRM pipelines: no human process annotation and no separate reward-model training. EvoHarnessBench defines the harness as the set of tools an agent can call, the procedural skills it can reuse, and the specialist agents it can coordinate with. Each harness stream is a sequence of cumulative stages H1 ⊆ H2 ⊆ ... ⊆ HT, so later stages only add capabilities and never remove old ones. Streams are built along three axes: tools, skills, and agents.

Two design choices matter. First, each task is assigned to the earliest stage at which it becomes solvable, and it must require at least one newly introduced capability. This helps separate adaptation to new capabilities from retention of old ones. Second, capabilities are released from common core capabilities toward the long tail, which is meant to mimic real harness growth in deployed systems.

The benchmark supports two evaluation modes. In deployment evaluation, no experience is carried across stages; each harness version is evaluated independently. This isolates the direct effect of harness expansion: does a larger capability pool help, or does it mostly distract? In self-evolving adaptation evaluation, persistent artifacts such as memory, prompts, or learned skills can be updated within each stage and then carried forward, while the underlying model weights remain fixed. This tests whether accumulated experience helps or hinders adaptation under a growing harness.

The benchmark is reasonably large: 17 controlled harness streams, each with 3 to 6 cumulative stages, 802 unique tasks, 1,510 axis-specific evaluation examples, 520 executable tools, 42 latent reference skills, and 62 specialist agents. The paper evaluates representative single-agent and multi-agent systems under both modes.627:T540,The empirical message is mostly diagnostic. First, harness expansion is not free. Agents can lose competence on tasks they previously solved even though the underlying model is unchanged and the required capabilities are still present. That is the benchmark’s evidence for harness-induced forgetting. Second, self-evolving adaptation is inconsistent. Gains vary substantially across stages, axes, and environments, which suggests that simply accumulating memory or prompts is not a reliable answer to harness evolution. Third, retention and adaptation often pull in opposite directions: methods that preserve earlier competence better can be worse at exploiting newly introduced capabilities, while methods that adapt aggressively can sacrifice old-task performance.

The main concrete numbers visible from the full text excerpt are benchmark-scale statistics: 17 streams, 802 tasks, 1,510 evaluation examples, 520 tools, 42 skills, and 62 specialist agents. The paper evaluates representative SAS and MAS systems, but the excerpt provided here does not include the full per-system score tables. That makes this paper more useful as a benchmark-design read than as a leaderboard read. The most informative results are the performance trajectories over harness stages and the contrast between deployment mode and self-evolving adaptation mode.628:T4b7,For a quick pass, read the benchmark definition and the two evaluation modes first. Under the cue, civilian casualties are primary for 12 models and success for 8; nine models switch from success to civilian casualties, and none switch in the opposite direction.62d:T629,The paper proposes a framework, not a new metric. It starts by defining a taxonomy of behavioral correctness assumptions, then operationalizes each assumption through controlled response transformations. The assumptions are split into two groups.

1. Correctness-preserving assumptions: transformations that should not change correctness with respect to the reference, such as paraphrasing, stylistic variation, or equivalent reformulation. A reliable evaluator should assign similar scores before and after the transformation.
2. Correctness-altering assumptions: transformations that should reduce response quality, such as removing relevant information, adding factual errors, introducing logical inconsistency, or injecting irrelevant content. A reliable evaluator should lower the score accordingly.

Two design choices matter. First, the transformations are intended to isolate one property at a time, so score changes are attributable rather than confounded. Second, the framework is evaluator-agnostic: it can probe lexical, character-level, semantic, LLM-based, and hybrid evaluators under the same behavioral test suite. In that sense, the work is closer to a stress-testing methodology than to a leaderboard.

The paper also studies repeat-run variability, evaluator configuration sensitivity, and test-suite reproducibility. These are especially important for LLM judges, whose outputs can vary with prompts, decoding settings, or model versions. An evaluator that looks good on aggregate but is unstable across runs or configurations is risky as a training signal.62e:T445,The empirical study covers a broad range of reference-based evaluators, including lexical overlap methods, character-level methods, semantic similarity methods, LLM-based evaluators, and hybrid systems. The main result is not that one family dominates everywhere, but that assumption-level analysis reveals distinct behavioral profiles that aggregate benchmark scores often hide. Lexical methods tend to be brittle under surface-form changes and therefore violate some correctness-preserving assumptions. Semantic and LLM-based methods are usually more robust to paraphrase, but may be less sensitive to certain correctness-altering transformations or more variable under configuration changes.

The paper also reports stability analyses across repeated runs, evaluator settings, and independently generated test suites. The key takeaway is that the proposed diagnostic framework itself appears reproducible enough to support meaningful evaluator characterization. For practical use, the most informative results are likely the per-assumption breakdowns rather than any averaged summary score.62f:T652,DART stands for Depth-as-Target. The central design is to augment DINOv2 with a pixel-space depth reconstruction head, so the model keeps DINOv2’s self-distillation-based representation learning while also predicting pseudo depth maps. The key choice is what the paper does not do: it does not build an RGB-D encoder that requires depth at inference, and it does not follow the standard MAE-style route of feeding depth as an input modality. Instead, depth is used as auxiliary supervision during pretraining only. This matches the deployment constraint in surgery, where reliable depth input is often unavailable.

The motivation in the paper is comparative. Off-the-shelf DINOv2 and DINOv3 pretrained on natural images do not transfer well enough to surgical imagery. MAE-family methods, including RGB-D variants such as MultiMAE, also fail to close the gap in the authors’ setting; the paper explicitly notes that MultiMAE underperforms a single-modality MAE baseline in their surgical pretraining setup. That negative result is important because it justifies moving depth supervision into a DINOv2-style framework rather than continuing along the MAE path.

Technically, the training objective is a combination of the original DINOv2 objective and a depth reconstruction loss. The depth supervision comes from off-the-shelf pseudo-labeled dense depth rather than real depth sensors, which lowers the data barrier and makes the recipe scalable. The contribution is therefore not a new architecture but a domain-aware pretraining recipe that injects geometric supervision without changing inference requirements.630:T47e,From the provided full-content excerpt, several experimental comparisons are clear. Across these regimes, supervising a single randomly selected token per trajectory consistently improves reasoning. Selecting only one or two tokens with extreme teacher-student probability gaps often matches or outperforms dense OPD. The paper reports a non-monotonic sparsity curve: performance first degrades as supervision is reduced, but can recover under extreme sparsity and exceed dense supervision. Ablations show that the sign of the token signal matters. Additional experiments on coding reasoning, Llama models, and other algorithmic settings are used to check that the phenomenon is not limited to Qwen3 math training.632:T5d4,RISE constructs a synthetic teacher by extrapolating the displacement between a current RLVR-updated checkpoint and a trailing anchor checkpoint. Let π_{θ_n} be the policy at iteration n, updated by RLVR to π_{θ'_{n+1}}. Choose a representation map φ that embeds a policy into a vector space where linear operations are meaningful (parameters or logits/distributions). Define the recent improvement direction as Δ = φ(π_{θ'_{n+1}}) − φ(π_{θ_n}). The self-extrapolated teacher is obtained by projecting further along this direction with scale β:

φ(teacher) = φ(π_{θ'_{n+1}}) + (β−1)·Δ, with β>1.

Two instantiations are emphasized:
- Weight-space extrapolation (φ=θ): θ_future = θ'_{n+1} + (β−1)(θ'_{n+1}−θ_n), essentially task arithmetic with an extrapolation coefficient; the teacher is an explicit model.
- Logit-space extrapolation (φ=logits / next-token distributions): extrapolate at the output distribution level (implemented via a geometric mixture / distributional extrapolation), producing token-level targets without necessarily materializing a full parameter-space teacher.

Training alternates RLVR and OPD in a recursive loop: RLVR grounds the direction (so extrapolation is not amplifying arbitrary drift), and OPD distills the extrapolated teacher into the student via token-level KL/CE. Key design knobs are β, anchor lag, and the choice of φ, each trading off compute, stability, and how “local” the teacher remains to the student.633:T526,An end-to-end pipeline:
- Web-graph construction: represent a web corpus as a directed hyperlink graph; improve out-link recall by merging a semantic mirror (RDF triples) with rendered markup.
- Task synthesis: sample an answer-anchored seed page, expand to a local subgraph, distill noisy pages into a connected entity graph, then generate a multi-hop question over that graph.
- Anchor removal / entity rewriting: abstract away directly searchable anchors so the task requires evidence composition across hops rather than single-query lookup.
- Dual-criteria verification: keep only tasks that are both sufficiently difficult and objectively checkable.
- Trajectory collection + filtering: roll out a strong teacher, then apply multi-stage filtering at both trajectory and turn levels to remove low-signal steps (irrelevant browsing, broken evidence chains, hallucinated citations).
- Training: start with filtered SFT; then do RL against live web search with an in-cluster judge and an observation summarizer; use iterative “SFT–RL climbing” where successful RL rollouts are fed back into the next SFT round to stabilize learning and improve sample efficiency.
- Evaluation: hold tool interface, context budget, and judging fixed; compare two inference regimes (with vs without CM) to quantify harness impact.634:T665,The authors fix a standard OPD setup and then vary the data. OPD supervises the student on trajectories sampled from the current student policy, matching the student distribution to the teacher distribution along student-generated prefixes. The paper starts from the sequence-level reverse KL and uses its exact token-level decomposition. In practice, the main implementation is student top-k OPD: at each step, compute the KL only over the k tokens with highest student probability, after renormalizing both student and teacher on that subset. This choice is practical: much cheaper than full-vocabulary KL, but denser than sampled-token supervision.

On top of this setup, the paper runs three layers of analysis. First is 1-shot OPD: sample a single training example and ask whether training on only that example can still improve the student, and whether it overfits. Second is difficulty analysis: bucket examples by difficulty and compare the downstream gains from easy, medium, and hard subsets, including examples beyond the capability frontier of both teacher and student. Third is mechanism analysis: test whether the gains are explained by high token entropy or by long CoT trajectories. The evidence supports the latter. The paper also analyzes token categories and finds that alignment improves especially on structural reasoning tokens such as “Alternative” and “Wait,” suggesting that the student is learning reasoning organization patterns. Based on these observations, the authors propose a simple difficulty-driven data selection rule: train on hard examples rather than trying to cover a large generic dataset.635:T4d4,The experimental story is straightforward. The default setup uses DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B as the student and JustRL-DeepSeek-1.5B as the teacher, with top-k OPD as the main training objective. First, 1-shot OPD consistently helps across sampled single examples, and training remains stable up to 2,000 steps without obvious overfitting or policy collapse. Second, hard examples outperform easy and medium ones. More strikingly, even when those hard examples are so difficult that training accuracy stays at 0% for both teacher and student, validation accuracy still keeps improving. That strongly suggests the useful signal lies in the process, not the final correctness. Third, the paper argues against a simple high-entropy-token explanation and instead shows that longer CoTs lead to better teacher-student alignment over long horizons and expose rare reasoning patterns such as self-reflection. The pipeline has only two stages. The executor produces an initial answer A0. The reviewer sees the problem and A0, then emits accept/reject plus a written critique. If rejected, the executor revises once to produce A1. There is no planner stage, specifically to avoid extra confounds.

The key methodological choice is a paired design. The executor solves each problem once, and the exact same A0 is reviewed under every reviewer condition. This removes executor sampling variance from condition-to-condition comparisons. The four conditions are: no review, self-review, a cross-family mid-tier reviewer, and a weak reviewer. The executor is Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite with 52% standalone accuracy on the task set. The mid-tier reviewer is gpt-oss-20b. The weak reviewer is Llama-3.1-8B, which can solve essentially none of these problems on its own. The benchmark uses 100 numeric-answer Olympiad math problems from Omni-MATH, filtered to allow exact automatic grading with no LLM judge.

The main contribution is not a new pipeline architecture but the rejection-outcome decomposition. Instead of counting rejections or final accuracy alone, the paper tracks what each rejection actually did: fix a wrong answer, damage a correct one, fail because the executor ignored the critique, or induce a wrong correction. This decomposition exposes two common evaluation mistakes. High rejection rate does not imply useful review, and low observed damage does not imply reviewer quality if the executor simply refuses to follow bad critiques. In other words, reviewer quality and critique uptake are separate variables and must be analyzed separately.638:T69e,The headline result is straightforward. The fixed executor solves 52 out of 100 Olympiad math problems correctly. Replacing no-review with a cross-family mid-tier reviewer raises final accuracy to 64%, a gain of 12 percentage points with p=0.0005, and with zero damaged correct answers. This shows that a reviewer does not need full task-solving ability to create net value if it can reject the right cases.

Self-review is the more revealing condition. It achieves the highest detection rate, yet yields no significant accuracy gain. The paper reports that self-review rejects about 2.1 times as often as the effective mid-tier reviewer, but repairs only about one-third as many answers. It also falsely rejects 35% of the executor’s correct answers. The crucial detail is what happens after those false rejections: whenever the executor actually follows the critique, the revised answer becomes wrong. Cases that appear harmless are harmless only because the executor ignored the critique. This is the empirical basis for the paper’s claim that apparent self-review safety is often revision inertia in disguise.

At the low end, the weak reviewer is effectively inert. It changes none of the 100 final answers while roughly doubling token cost. That gives a practical capability floor: below some threshold, review neither repairs errors nor triggers useful revisions, and only adds overhead.

There is also an implementation detail worth noting. An initial run revealed truncation in the mid-tier reviewer’s outputs, so token limits were adjusted and documented. That matters because reviewer usefulness depends on complete critiques; truncation can directly distort rejection quality.639:T4a0,For a quick read, focus on the Introduction and Method to understand the paired design and the rejection-outcome decomposition. First, the authors define a behavioral acoustic-evidence sensitivity score by evaluating each model under three conditions: original audio, silent audio, and mismatched audio. Averaging silence and mismatch is a sensible design choice: silence removes information but also creates an unnatural input condition, while mismatch preserves natural acoustics but breaks semantic alignment. First, after fine-tuning, replacing the audio with silence or unrelated audio causes substantially larger accuracy drops than in the original instruction-tuned models. The effect is strongest on benchmarks designed to suppress text-only shortcuts, especially ADQA-Bench. Second, layerwise interventions show a temporal separation: Audio→Options matters most in early-to-middle layers, while Options→Answer becomes most important in middle-to-late layers. In other words, acoustic evidence is injected into option representations earlier, but those modified representations influence the actual answer selection later. That aligns with the attention results: training seems to strengthen the conversion of grounded representations into final decisions more than the mere presence of audio information.
