The emphasis is on relative degradation patterns and layer localization rather than headline absolute scores.63e:T4b6,SharedSAE is a TopK sparse autoencoder with shared latent indices and model-specific encoders and decoders. Each model tokenizes the same text with its own tokenizer, and a window aligner constructs spans whose decoded text matches across models, producing aligned residual-stream activations. Each model’s encoder maps its activation into the common latent dictionary. For latent selection, the method normalizes selection scores across models, sums the normalized votes, and applies a joint TopK to choose one shared index set. The selected magnitudes are not normalized, so each model retains its activation scale information. Each model reconstructs its own activation with its own decoder, and a cross-stream rescaling term makes codes from one model reconstruct other models’ activations, tying the same latent index to similar features across models. During training, vote-source dropout selects the TopK indices from a randomly chosen single model with probability 0.5, which makes solo-model inference in-distribution. For adding a new model, frozen-dictionary adaptation trains only the new model’s encoder, decoder, and biases while keeping the shared latents and their descriptions fixed.63f:T7e2,技术上，这是一篇偏理论说明的 note。第一部分从标准 SFT 出发，把条件最大似然写成对真实 teacher conditional q_true(y|x) 的 forward KL 投影：最小化负对数似然等价于最小化 E_x[KL(q_true(.|x)||p_theta(.|x))] 加上与参数无关的熵项。这个重写的作用，是把 SFT 明确成“用参数化模型逼近一个目标条件分布”。随后作者引入层次贝叶斯任务模型：先从任务空间采样函数 f，再在任务内采样 few-shot context D_k 和 query。对任意 in-context predictor M(D_k, x)，在 log-loss 下的最优解是 Bayes posterior predictive。Transformer 预训练若在跨任务分布上最小化期望 log-loss，那么在容量和数据足够时，它学到的理想对象就是这个 posterior predictive。这里的关键不是再证明一遍 ICL is Bayes，而是把它和 SFT 放到同一个“近似目标分布”的语言里。

后半部分把这个模板推广到 KL-regularized RL、OPD 和 test-time search。虽然给出的全文片段主要覆盖 Part I，但从摘要与行文结构可以看出，作者采用的是统一的 Gibbs posterior 形式：q*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x) exp(U(x,y)/β)，其中 U 可以是 log-likelihood、reward、advantage 或 search-induced utility。SFT 对应 U=log q_data 或等价的 teacher log-density；KL-regularized RL 对应 reward-weighted posterior；OPD 则是在 student on-policy 轨迹上，用 teacher 分布去近似某个参考后验；search / CoT 则可被看成 test-time 对 latent reasoning path 的 posterior reweighting。这个统一视角的关键区别在于，它不把这些方法按“训练范式”分开，而是按“先验 + 效用 + 近似器”来分解。这样能更清楚地解释：为什么 reverse-KL 风格的 policy matching 往往 mode-seeking，为什么 SFT 的 forward-KL 更像覆盖 teacher 支持集，以及为什么 few-shot demonstrations 有时像给 posterior 提供额外观测，有时却会和 RL 后的 policy 发生冲突。640:T46f,This note is not proposing a new training recipe. It is trying to give a single probabilistic lens for several procedures that are usually discussed separately: few-shot ICL, SFT, KL-regularized RL, on-policy distillation, and test-time search / chain-of-thought. The central claim is that they can all be written in the same two-step pattern: first construct a generalized Bayes or Gibbs posterior from a prior/reference policy plus a utility signal; then fit a parametric model or policy to approximate that posterior or its posterior predictive. The paper focuses on two key identifications. First, under a hierarchical task distribution, few-shot ICL targets the Bayes posterior predictive. Second, SFT is a forward-KL projection onto a teacher conditional distribution, while KL-regularized RL and OPD approximate reward- or advantage-reweighted posteriors under a reference policy. The framework is meant to explain why ICL and SFT can partially substitute for each other, why few-shot prompting can behave oddly on RL-tuned reasoning models, and why OPD, RLHF/RLVR, and search-based inference are less disjoint than they appear.641:T436,Its value for pretraining research is conceptual rather than algorithmic. It gives a cleaner interface between pretraining, post-training, and test-time adaptation by forcing three questions: what is the target distribution, what role does the prior/reference model play, and whether training and inference-time search are approximating the same posterior or optimizing different objects. For pretraining researchers, two points matter. First, ICL is framed not as a prompting trick but as amortized Bayesian inference learned during pretraining; that changes how one thinks about task mixtures, context structure, and data organization. Second, the differences among SFT, OPD, and KL-regularized RL become easier to localize: KL direction, posterior temperature, utility definition, and approximation family. That helps explain why some post-training signals preserve the pretraining distribution while others overwrite it more aggressively. The contribution is moderate in scale and mostly about unification, but it is useful for thinking about the pretrain↔post-train loop.642:T806,The paper is a theory-oriented note. Part I starts from standard SFT and rewrites conditional maximum likelihood as a forward-KL projection onto the true teacher conditional q_true(y|x): minimizing expected negative log-likelihood is equivalent to minimizing E_x[KL(q_true(.|x) || p_theta(.|x))] up to an entropy term independent of the model parameters. This matters because it makes SFT explicitly a problem of approximating a target conditional distribution. The paper then introduces a hierarchical Bayesian task model: sample a task function f, then sample within-task demonstrations D_k and a query. For any in-context predictor M(D_k, x), the Bayes posterior predictive is the unique minimizer of expected log-loss. If a Transformer is pretrained over the same task distribution, then in the infinite-data/infinite-capacity limit its optimal predictor is exactly that posterior predictive. The point is not merely to restate “ICL is Bayes,” but to place ICL and SFT inside the same language of target-distribution approximation.

The later sections extend the same template to KL-regularized RL, OPD, and test-time search. The visible excerpt mainly covers Part I, but the abstract and setup make the intended form clear: q*(y|x) ∝ π_ref(y|x) exp(U(x,y)/β), where U can be log-likelihood, reward, advantage, or a search-induced utility. SFT corresponds to a likelihood-defined target; KL-regularized RL corresponds to a reward-weighted posterior; OPD can be viewed as fitting the student to a teacher-defined posterior on student-generated trajectories; and search / CoT acts like posterior reweighting over latent reasoning paths at inference time. The useful decomposition is not by training stage but by prior, utility, temperature, and approximation family. That decomposition clarifies why reverse-KL style policy matching is often mode-seeking, why forward-KL SFT is more support-covering, and why few-shot demonstrations sometimes behave like extra observations for posterior updating but can also conflict with an RL-shaped policy.643:T6da,The method has two modules. GUT-Q is the uncertainty quantification component. For a given problem, the model is sampled multiple times to produce multiple reasoning chains. The chains are then merged into a directed acyclic graph by identifying semantically equivalent reasoning steps with an NLI model. Nodes represent step-level semantic states; edges represent possible transitions between steps. This is the key move: instead of scoring each sampled chain independently, the method approximates the latent reasoning space induced by token-level stochasticity.

On top of that graph, the paper defines graph complexity as a combination of two signals. One comes from token-level distribution statistics, intended to capture local uncertainty during generation. The other comes from graph topology, intended to capture how that local uncertainty unfolds into global branching structure. The claim is that this joint quantity is a better estimator of reasoning uncertainty than sequence-only or self-prompting approaches.

GUT-O is the optimization component. Since full graph construction is expensive and not directly usable online during RL, the paper introduces a proxy uncertainty measure and uses its negative value as reward. The design choice is important: optimizing only answer correctness does not explicitly discourage unstable or nonsensical intermediate branches, while optimizing shallow signals such as length or entropy may not align with reasoning quality. GUT-O tries to bias the model toward trajectories that are both lower-uncertainty and still task-effective. This differs from self-consistency or reranking methods, which improve outputs at inference time by sampling more; GUT-O attempts to shift the model distribution itself.644:T4bc,From the full-text excerpts provided, GUT-Q is evaluated on 4 LLMs and 5 datasets against 45 uncertainty baselines, using selective generation as the downstream testbed and AUROC, AUPRC, and PRR as metrics. The reported result is that GUT-Q performs best overall in this comparison, suggesting that graph-based reasoning-space estimates separate reliable from unreliable generations better than single-sequence statistics or simpler diversity measures. GUT-O is tested across 4 model scales and 5 datasets, with the main finding that RL with the uncertainty proxy reduces reasoning uncertainty and also improves accuracy.

The experimental framing is stronger than a simple correlation study. The paper checks whether the uncertainty score is useful for abstention or selective answering, and then checks whether it can function as an optimization signal. That said, the main caveat is methodological cost and attribution: graph construction depends on repeated sampling plus an external NLI model. The critical question is how much of the gain comes from the graph formulation itself, versus extra sampling budget and the quality of semantic merging. The ablations around these components are therefore central.645:T4d2,For a skim-level read, start with the overview figure and the formal definition of GUT-Q, then read the reward construction in GUT-O, and finally inspect the main selective-generation table. Around 25–35 minutes should be enough to capture the main idea.

What to focus on:
1. The exact definition of reasoning uncertainty. The paper is not measuring generic predictive uncertainty; it is measuring instability in branching reasoning trajectories.
2. The graph construction pipeline. Check how step boundaries are defined, how semantic equivalence is decided with NLI, and whether logically distinct steps could be over-merged.
3. The decomposition of graph complexity. Understand what the token-statistics term contributes versus the topology term, and whether they partly measure the same phenomenon.
4. The proxy used in GUT-O. Ask whether it tracks the full graph complexity well enough to be a meaningful RL reward.
5. The ablations. The most informative ones are likely: removing NLI merging, using only topology, using only token statistics, and varying the number of samples.

If the goal is only to decide whether to follow up later, the method overview, complexity definition, and the main comparison table are sufficient.646:T45e,The method has two main parts. First, the paper localizes refusal. Instead of treating the residual stream as the universal readout site, it distinguishes the fresh write from the accumulated residual. In transformers this is the attention output; in SSMs it is the selective-scan block output; in hybrids the relevant write sites are examined separately. Linear harm probes are trained to separate harmful from benign prompts, and the strongest decodability appears at the architecture-specific write site rather than in the accumulated residual.

Second, the paper tests cross-architecture alignment and causal transfer. It uses a Procrustes rigid rotation to align one model’s representation space to another’s, allowing only rotation, not reshaping. A refusal direction learned in a transformer is mapped into the target architecture’s space, then removed or gated at the target write site. If this transported direction still controls refusal, the result is stronger than simple linear separability: it suggests the models share a genuinely similar representation rather than merely a shared label boundary.647:T52d,The main target model is Falcon-Mamba-7B, with Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B as transformer references, plus validation on RWKV-6 and Zamba2-7B. Several results stand out. 1) On a surface-controlled subset, a harm probe at the write site reaches AUROC 0.99, while a surface-only probe scores 0.54, indicating the probe is not just detecting jailbreak wrapper text. 2) A single rigid rotation transfers the transformer refusal direction into SSM and hybrid spaces; removing that direction weakens refusal, most clearly for the transformer-SSM pair and at the Mamba write site in Zamba2. 3) A matched-magnitude control shows that directions estimated at the write site causally control refusal, whereas directions estimated in the accumulated residual degrade substantially. 4) The detector-triggered gate is used as a causal test rather than as a defense claim. On Falcon-Mamba, prefix-injection attack success drops from 98.0% to 5.0%. Under a suffix attack optimized through the gate, the detector still fires on all 100 attacked prompts and attack success remains at 1.0%, down from 15.0%. The paper is careful to note that this gate is not stronger than a simpler baseline that always emits a fixed refusal once the detector fires. What transfers across architectures is the refusal direction, not a superior defense recipe.648:T517,The main technical idea is an agentic attacker equipped with a search harness. Instead of explicitly enumerating all possible payloads and injection sites, the paper treats the attack surface as a latent space induced jointly by the environment, the benign user task, and the malicious injection task. To search this space, the attacker is given reconnaissance tools of two kinds: tools for understanding the environment and task context, and tools for understanding candidate injection vectors and their constraints.

The attacker then performs structured reasoning over possible strategies, explores promising subspaces, and uses victim-agent feedback plus environment-state changes to adapt future attempts. A key design choice is explicit strategy management. The paper argues that without tracking explored directions, pruning unproductive branches, and maintaining search state, larger compute budgets lead to redundant exploration and weaker scaling. In that sense, the search harness is what turns prompt injection from one-shot payload generation into an iterative attack process. The study is conducted in a white-box environment setting, which makes the attack surface visible to the attacker and isolates the role of test-time search more cleanly; black-box transfer is left for future work.649:T451,From the available full text, the experiments are organized to show two main findings rather than to optimize a single benchmark number. First, increasing attacker test-time compute improves both vulnerability discovery and exploitation across heterogeneous tasks. This is the central empirical claim and supports the paper’s argument that fixed-budget evaluations can underestimate real-world risk. Second, ablations indicate that explicit strategy management matters: when search tracking and redundancy control are removed, gains from larger budgets degrade because the attacker wastes compute revisiting similar attack directions.

The visible content does not include enough complete tables or setup details to safely restate exact percentages, sample counts, or significance values. What is clear is that both user-task completion and attack success are evaluated through binary outcomes tied to final environment-state changes, which is a stronger setup than relying only on a language-model judge. That makes the benchmark closer to executable agent behavior than to text-only jailbreak scoring.64a:T52f,The authors build a controlled continued-pretraining setup. The base objective remains autoregressive next-token prediction. They select 36 recent documents as self-contained knowledge units: 12 computer science arXiv papers, 12 U.S. federal appellate legal opinions, and 12 PubMed Central medical case reports. The documents are chosen after the OLMo-2 pretraining cutoff, with absence checked using the Infini-gram API. For each document, they construct several forms of evidence. Paraphrases generated with GPT-4.1 serve as a control for linguistic variation. Auxiliary views generated with GPT-5-mini include textbook-style explanations, Stack Exchange-style Q&A, and blog-style expositions. Prerequisite knowledge is generated as textbook material. Contextual knowledge is collected from cited arXiv papers and cited legal opinions; the medical setting is excluded from this part due to the lack of a comparable citation structure. Learning is measured with LAMA-style probes, including factual probes and probes intended to test broader understanding. The experiments compare repetition, paraphrasing, auxiliary views, contextual knowledge, prerequisite knowledge, and teacher strength under controlled token budgets. The paper also examines how these data choices change layer-wise encoding and compression of knowledge.64b:T49b,The main findings are clear. First, repetition is necessary for new knowledge acquisition; paraphrasing helps, but its benefit is concentrated at smaller batch sizes and weakens as batch size grows. This suggests that paraphrasing partly improves gradient coverage rather than always adding new conceptual information. Second, when the token budget is fixed, allocating tokens away from repeated original documents and toward auxiliary views improves both understanding-oriented probes and factual recall. This is the strongest result because factual recall is often assumed to benefit mainly from repeated exposure. Third, auxiliary views remain useful even when they are not generated by the strongest teacher model. Fourth, contextual and prerequisite knowledge help when the model lacks relevant prior knowledge. The scale trend is also important: larger models integrate diverse views more effectively, encode knowledge with better parameter efficiency, and shift learning toward middle and later layers. The concrete setup includes 36 source documents across 3 domains with 12 documents per domain; exact accuracy gains should be read from the paper’s figures and tables.64c:Ta53,方法核心可以概括成三部分：模型结构、训练流程、无损采样。

一，模型结构：diffusion-augmented LLM。Uno 不是训练两个独立模型，也不是给 AR 模型外挂一个外部 drafter，而是在同一个 Transformer 架构的每一层里保留标准 AR 权重，同时增加一组轻量 diffusion 权重。AR 路径继续定义标准 next-token distribution，决定最终质量；diffusion 路径则学习在固定上下文下对一个 token block 做并行去噪或并行 proposal。作者强调这组 diffusion 权重是 lightweight 的，因此额外参数和训练成本都受控。这里和 MTP 的差别也很清楚：MTP 是在 AR 头上直接预测未来多个位置，仍然围绕因果链式建模；Uno 则引入离散 diffusion 过程来生成整块 token proposal，建模形式不同，也更适合做并行 refinement。

二，训练流程：先 AR，后 diffusion distillation。训练分两阶段。第一阶段完全按常规 NTP 训练 AR 权重，得到高质量基模型。第二阶段冻结 AR 权重，只训练 diffusion 权重，让它通过 Diffusion Distillation 学会从 AR 分布中提出高质量 block proposal。这个设计有两个关键好处。其一，最终语言分布仍由 AR 模型定义，因此不会因为 diffusion 训练不稳定而伤害 base quality。其二，已有开源 AR 模型可以后加 Uno 模块，不需要从头重训整模型。文中还说明既可以 from scratch 联合构建，也可以对现有 open-weight AR LLM 做 augmentation。

三，Ψ-Spec sampler：无损并行采样。采样器的目标不是直接信任 diffusion 输出，而是把 diffusion proposal 与 AR verification 结合起来，形成类似 speculative decoding 但不需要外部 draft model 的机制。直观上，diffusion 模块并行提出一个 token block 的候选，AR 模块在一次或少量并行评估中验证这些候选，并通过接受-拒绝或等价校正步骤保证最终样本严格来自原始 AR 分布。作者把这一点称为 lossless acceleration。相比普通 speculative decoding，Uno 的 proposal 与 verifier 共用同一主干架构，避免了双模型部署；相比把 AR 模型硬转成 d-LLM 的做法，它没有把目标分布替换成 diffusion 近似分布，因此不存在“速度上去了但分布变了”的问题。

文中还提到 Ψ-Spec 支持 inference-time scaling：在固定上下文长度下增加额外 denoising 步数，可以换取更好的 proposal 质量。这一点有点像在推理时调节 compute budget，但它作用在并行 proposal 质量上，而不是传统 AR 的逐 token 深思。64d:T862,实验结论很集中：Uno 在质量-速度前沿上优于多类基线，而且这种收益在大 batch 下仍然存在。

第一，比较对象覆盖了三类主流路线：speculative decoding 方法，如 EAGLE-3、DFlash；开源离散 diffusion LLM，如 Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion、DiffusionGemma；以及专有 d-LLM Mercury 2。作者声称 Uno 在这些对比中都取得更好的 speed-quality tradeoff。这里最关键的不是单点速度，而是“在保持 AR 分布无损的前提下”仍能拿到可观加速。

第二，速度结果强调 batch size 维度。文章明确报告，Uno 相对 base AR model 的加速在所有评测 batch size 上都能保持，包括“AR 权重本身在该设备上能容纳的最大 batch”。这是全文最重要的实验信息之一，因为很多 d-LLM 的优势只在 batch-size-1 或很小 batch 下明显，一旦并发上来，额外 denoising 计算会吞掉收益。Uno 由于把 AR 作为 verifier、diffusion 作为轻量 proposal，并且共享同一架构，作者认为它在高吞吐 serving 下仍能维持 up to 2× speedup。

第三，训练成本方面，作者强调 diffusion 权重训练开销很小，因为 AR 主干先训练好后被冻结，后续只做 diffusion distillation。虽然给出的片段没有完整参数表，但从方法设计看，额外成本主要来自轻量层内增广，而不是再训一个完整 drafter。

第四，文章还报告了 end-to-end RL training 的加速。原因很直接：RL 后训练里 rollout generation 往往是主要瓶颈，如果单次生成能无损提速，那么整体 RL wall-clock 也会下降。这个结果对 post-train 与 pretrain 接口很有意义，因为它说明一种 pretrain-compatible 的建模增广，能直接改善后续 RL 训练效率。

由于提供的全文片段没有完整实验章节细节，无法可靠列出具体模型参数量、训练 token 数、每个 benchmark 的精确分数和延迟表。精读时应重点核对三类数字：不同 batch 下的 tokens/s 或 latency；接受率或平均每步接受 block 长度；以及 RL 训练端到端 wall-clock 改善幅度。64e:T5a1,This matters for foundation-model research in at least three ways.

First, it offers a pragmatic interface between AR and diffusion. Instead of replacing AR pretraining with diffusion, it uses diffusion as a parallel proposal mechanism on top of a high-quality AR distribution, with exact AR verification to preserve the distribution. That avoids the long-standing issue that diffusion LMs still struggle to fully match strong AR models in quality.

Second, it cleanly decouples quality parameters from speed parameters. The AR weights determine the response distribution; the diffusion weights are optimized only for generation speed and can be trained after freezing the AR backbone. This is an important design pattern for the pretrain–posttrain interface: not every inference-time capability needs to be baked into the full model during base pretraining.

Third, the paper evaluates acceleration at realistic batch sizes rather than only at batch size one. That is highly relevant for modern serving and agentic workloads, where concurrency is the norm. If the reported results hold, this makes diffusion-based parallel decoding relevant not only for low-latency single-request settings but also for high-throughput serving and RL rollouts.

The contribution is larger than a small decoding tweak. It proposes a unified modeling interface in which AR and diffusion coexist inside one architecture and are connected by an exact sampler.64f:T81c,The method has three main components: the model architecture, the training pipeline, and the exact sampler.

First, the architecture is a diffusion-augmented LLM. Uno does not train two separate models, nor does it attach an external drafter to an AR model. Instead, each transformer layer keeps the standard AR weights and adds a lightweight set of diffusion weights. The AR path continues to define the standard next-token distribution and therefore determines final quality. The diffusion path learns to produce parallel proposals for a block of tokens under a fixed context. This is different from multi-token prediction: MTP adds future-token heads to an AR model, while Uno introduces a discrete diffusion process for blockwise proposal and refinement.

Second, the training pipeline is staged: AR first, diffusion distillation second. The AR weights are trained in the usual way with next-token prediction. Then they are frozen, and only the diffusion weights are trained through diffusion distillation so that they learn to propose token blocks aligned with the AR distribution. This design has two major advantages. It protects the base model’s quality because the final language distribution remains defined by the frozen AR model. And it makes the method modular: an existing open-weight AR LLM can be augmented into Uno without retraining the full model from scratch.

Third, the Ψ-Spec sampler provides lossless parallel generation. The diffusion module proposes a block of tokens in parallel, and the AR module verifies those proposals through a correction procedure analogous in spirit to speculative decoding. The key point is that the final samples are still drawn exactly from the original AR distribution. This is what distinguishes Uno from lossy block decoding and from approaches that convert an AR model into a diffusion model and accept a distribution shift. The paper also claims that Ψ-Spec supports inference-time scaling: additional denoising at fixed context length can improve proposal quality, giving a compute-quality tradeoff at inference.650:T7b0,The experimental message is focused and strong: Uno improves the speed–quality frontier against several classes of baselines, and the speedup persists at larger batch sizes.

First, the comparisons cover speculative decoding methods such as EAGLE-3 and DFlash, open diffusion LLMs such as Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion and DiffusionGemma, and the proprietary diffusion model Mercury 2. The central claim is that Uno achieves better speed–quality tradeoffs than all of them while remaining lossless with respect to the AR distribution.

Second, batch size is a central axis of evaluation. The paper explicitly states that Uno’s speedup over the base AR model persists across all tested batch sizes, including the largest batch that fits on the device with the AR weights. This is one of the most important empirical results, because many diffusion-based decoders look attractive only at batch size one and lose their advantage under realistic concurrency. Uno reportedly reaches up to 2× speedup even at the largest supported batch size.

Third, the training overhead is claimed to be small. Since the AR backbone is trained once and then frozen, the extra cost comes mainly from learning the lightweight diffusion weights rather than from training a second full model.

Fourth, the paper reports end-to-end RL training acceleration. This is plausible because rollout generation is often the dominant cost in RL post-training. If generation is sped up without changing the target distribution, overall RL wall-clock time should improve as well. That makes the method relevant beyond inference serving.

When reading the full paper, the most important numbers to verify are throughput or latency across batch sizes, acceptance statistics or effective block lengths, and end-to-end RL speedups.651:T691,This one deserves a careful read. A good order is: problem framing, sampling correctness, training cost, then system-level gains.

Start with the introduction and method overview. The key is to understand what the paper is and is not trying to replace. It is not replacing AR pretraining, and it is not trying to build a better standalone diffusion LM. It is building an exact parallel sampler for an AR distribution.

Then read Section 3 closely. You want to understand what diffusion weights are added at each layer, how they interact with the AR backbone, why they are lightweight, and why freezing the AR weights preserves quality. This section determines whether the method is genuinely practical.

Next, read Section 4 very carefully. The Ψ-Spec sampler is the heart of the paper. The crucial question is how the proposal, verification, and correction steps guarantee that the final samples are still drawn from the AR distribution. If that argument is sound, Uno belongs in a very different category from ordinary lossy block decoding.

In the experiments, prioritize four kinds of figures: speed–quality frontiers, speed versus batch size, comparisons against speculative decoding at high batch sizes, and end-to-end RL training time. In the ablations, focus on diffusion-weight size, denoising steps, block size, and the effect of freezing versus jointly training the AR backbone.

If time is limited, read the introduction, Sections 3 and 4, and the main experimental figures; that should take around 60–90 minutes. For a deeper pass, go into the appendix for the exactness proof of the sampler, complexity analysis, and the details of augmenting existing AR models.652:T442,AdaptiveSpec has two adaptive components. The first is margin-based lossy verification. At the first mismatch between the draft token and the target model’s top-1 token, the method checks the ratio between the target probability assigned to the drafted token and the target probability of its own top-1 token. If the ratio exceeds a threshold, the drafted token is promoted and accepted. The rule uses logits already computed by the target model, requires no semantic-equivalence verifier, and avoids FLy’s dependence on a downstream window of W tokens without further mismatches. The second component is dynamic tree shaping. At each decoding step, the system adjusts the draft-tree parameters, including n_steps, top-k, and ndt, using a draft confidence score based on the draft model’s top-1 probability and a rolling acceptance history. Confident steps receive more aggressive draft expansion; uncertain steps contract draft computation to avoid spending nodes where acceptance is unlikely. The combined system adapts both the draft phase and the verification phase at every step.653:T70d,The method has three stages. The first is a chunk-summarization diagnostic task. The authors concatenate multiple documents from short-text summarization datasets into long contexts, keep the original document boundaries, and ask the model to identify semantic chunks and produce keywords for each chunk. This is intended to require hierarchical parsing and semantic compression rather than simple span retrieval.

The second stage is head scoring. For valid generations, the method traces attention from generated keyword tokens back to corresponding source tokens in the input. A head receives a high summarization score if output keywords consistently attend to salient source content within the correct chunk. This differs from retrieval-style head scoring because it rewards the ability to compress and reconnect to source meaning, not just local matching or high raw attention mass.

The third stage is budget allocation. A fixed budget is always reserved for sink tokens and a recent sliding window, reflecting the practical importance of system prompts and recent turns. The remaining compressible middle region is allocated across heads in proportion to normalized summarization scores. A water-filling-style reallocation step prevents a few very high-scoring heads from monopolizing the budget and redistributes excess capacity to other useful heads. Within each head, token retention still uses a standard cumulative-attention criterion similar to SnapKV. So SGD-KV is not replacing token selection; it adds a more informed head-level allocation layer on top. Compared with DuoAttention, it uses continuous rather than binary head prioritization. Compared with HeadKV or AdaKV, its head importance signal comes from a dedicated summarization probe rather than directly from downstream behavior.654:T6af,The experiments use Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M and Qwen3-32B. One important detail is that the HuggingFace Qwen2.5-7B-1M checkpoint reportedly performs poorly on multi-turn dialogue tasks, so the authors further fine-tune it before evaluation. That means some care is needed when interpreting the results. The main benchmarks are MRCR, which stresses long multi-turn retrieval and reference tracking, and ETHIC, which emphasizes broad information coverage over long contexts.

Empirically, SGD-KV matches or outperforms prior head-aware compression methods on both models. On Qwen3-32B with chain-of-thought reasoning, both SGD-KV and HeadKV are clearly better than DuoAttention, suggesting that fine-grained budget allocation is more effective than binary head grouping for complex reasoning. On the fine-tuned Qwen2.5-7B-1M model, SGD-KV becomes increasingly favorable as context length grows, overtaking DuoAttention beyond 128K and showing the strongest robustness at the 1M-token scale. The headline number from the abstract is up to 75% KV-cache memory reduction while maintaining strong accuracy at contexts up to 1M tokens.

A particularly useful result is on ETHIC: with only 25% of the KV cache retained, SGD-KV on Qwen3-32B reaches an average score of 28.38, close to the full-KV baseline at 28.53. That suggests the method preserves the right historical information for high-coverage tasks. The appendix also includes generalization checks across different summarization datasets, comparisons of score distributions across head types, and visualizations of final budget allocation. Those analyses support the main claim that a distinct subset of heads is especially important for long-range aggregation.655:T452,For a skim, start with Figure 1 and the first half of the method section. The key question is whether the proposed diagnostic really identifies summarization heads rather than just heads that happen to fire on the probe. Then read the main MRCR and ETHIC tables, focusing on the comparison between binary head grouping, prior head-aware allocation methods, and SGD-KV. About 20 to 30 minutes should be enough for the main thread. Three caveats are worth keeping in mind. First, the extra fine-tuning on Qwen2.5-7B-1M complicates clean attribution. Second, the summarization probe may favor generative aggregation heads and underweight retrieval or positional heads that still matter in some tasks. Third, the validation is concentrated on long-context understanding benchmarks; it is less clear whether the same allocation strategy transfers to code, tool use, or tasks dominated by local dependencies.656:T543,Two main pieces:
1) Direct-P for noncausal forward inference: the authors keep HAO AI Lab’s two-query Blackwell schedule (16-warp CTA, TMA-fed K/V ring buffer, dedicated MMA warp for QK/PV, two softmax warpgroups in ping-pong, separate correction/store warps) and replace only the stage that converts score fragments into the scaled probability operand consumed by PV. Direct-P maps normalized scores directly into MXFP4 probability codes and normalizes the same rounded values that PV will consume, aiming to remove format-conversion overhead and scale movement that otherwise dominate once GEMMs shrink.
2) Causal training path with forward-to-backward quantization handoff: instead of reconstructing a separate BF16 score/probability pipeline in backward, forward passes quantized Q/K payloads, their scales, and the softmax normalizer to backward. Projection/gradient epilogues also publish FP8 row/column views needed by gradient GEMMs. Backward reconstructs probabilities from this saved low-precision state. The paper is explicit about precision boundaries: learned projections remain a separate boundary, so it is not end-to-end pure FP4 training.
The hardware analysis attributes remaining limits to tensor-memory ownership and constrained overlap, motivating an additional allocatable score destination with compatible issue semantics.657:T413,Skim path that preserves the technical story:
- Start with the Introduction to internalize the bottleneck claim (softmax/probability stage dominates once GEMMs are FP4-fast) and the precision scope (“full FP4” only for Q/K/P/V operands).

Time: ~30–45 minutes to get the main ideas; longer if you plan to port the kernel or reproduce results (then include Appendix E).658:T5fa,The key methodological move is preregistration plus a full audit trail. The authors froze the protocol in advance, including acceptance thresholds: same-window repeat rankings had to reach Spearman 0.90, and byte-identical next-day replays had to reach 0.99 agreement. They then refused to repair the protocol after seeing the data. This is what gives the negative result force.

Several design choices matter. First, they built an append-only audit chain: request bodies, hashes, exclusions, valid task groups, replay pairs, and recorded metadata are all pinned and traceable. That rules out the usual explanation that the requests were not actually identical. Second, they decompose instability into distinct observable modes: within-window fluctuation, cross-day drift, and amplification caused by structured outputs such as rankings, where a tiny token-level change can invalidate or reorder an entire record. Third, they add prospective attribution experiments rather than stopping at a failed gate: same-day versus cross-day comparisons, four-provider comparisons, self-hosted controls, and constructed-error calibration. These help separate endpoint instability from task difficulty or judge incapacity. Fourth, the paper connects systems-level nondeterminism to measurement failure. Batch-dependent kernels, serving-time batching, and silent deployment changes were already known in systems work; the paper shows how these low-level effects become fatal once the output is used as a structured ranking or thresholded gate.659:T56e,The headline numbers are strong and easy to interpret. Across two campaigns, the audit covered 52,988 request attempts. The authors are careful not to treat this as the effective sample size; the actual analyses rest on 31 valid task groups, 100 replay pairs, and 10 constructed-error conditions. The first preregistered gate failed badly: same-window repeat rankings achieved only Spearman 0.400 against a required 0.90. The second gate also failed: byte-identical next-day replays agreed at 0.78 against a required 0.99.

Equally important is what did not fail. Requests were delivered successfully, schemas were valid, request-body hashes matched the frozen plan, and all recorded metadata fields remained constant. In other words, the engineering record looked clean while the measurement record was unstable. That is a major empirical point: standard API logs are not enough to establish reproducibility. The supplementary comparisons appear designed to answer whether the issue is specific to one provider or endemic to black-box shared serving, and whether self-hosting reduces the instability floor. The constructed-error calibration is also important because it asks a sharper question than average accuracy: even if the observer can detect obvious errors on average, is its variance low enough for threshold-based scientific use? Under the tested configurations, the answer is no.65a:T4c4,Start with the introduction and the preregistered thresholds. The paper is strongest when read as an instrument audit, not as another judge-bias study. Then go to the protocol and audit sections: frozen requests, hash-based identity, exclusion rules, valid-unit definitions, and the exact procedures for same-window repeats and next-day replays. Those sections determine whether the negative result is methodologically clean.

After that, focus on the mechanism decomposition and the attribution supplements. Three questions are worth tracking while reading: why ranking outputs amplify tiny generation differences; how shared-endpoint batching, kernels, and deployment changes surface as black-box drift; and why provider metadata is too weak to support reproducibility claims. If time is limited, prioritize the main failure tables, the same-day versus cross-day breakdown, the self-hosted control, the constructed-error calibration, and the appendix material on the audit chain and disclosed exclusions. The deeper payoff is in thinking through downstream consequences: how judge noise propagates into data filtering or RL reward signals, and what minimum reporting standard should replace bare model-name disclosure.65b:T545,There are two central ideas. The first is a within-item contrast between original benchmark items and semantically equivalent paraphrases. Since the intended skill is held fixed, a systematic advantage on the original item can be interpreted as memorization of surface form rather than genuine capability. This is framed as differential item functioning in psychometric terms. The second is calibration: instead of treating the paraphrase gap as an ungrounded heuristic, the authors fine-tune 74 models with known doses of contamination and use them to map observed original-versus-paraphrase gaps to estimated contamination levels.

The paper then shifts from per-model detection to leaderboard-level analysis. It distinguishes uniform contamination, where many models benefit similarly and rankings stay stable, from differential contamination, where some models benefit more and rankings can change. Within an IRT-style anchor-linking view, contaminated items are non-invariant anchors. The analysis therefore asks whether removing or accounting for those items materially changes model ordering. This is the main departure from string overlap methods, membership inference statistics such as Min-K%, or canary-based memorization tests. Those methods can indicate exposure, but they do not directly answer whether the leaderboard itself is wrong.65c:T55b,The empirical setup has two stages. First comes calibration. The authors build 74 fine-tuned models with known contamination doses and test whether the paraphrase-gap signal is sensitive, monotonic, and interpretable. This is an important part of the paper because many contamination studies lack calibration, making null results hard to interpret. Second comes measurement on real models. They collect per-instance responses from 47 publicly released models and evaluate them on ARC, GSM8K, HellaSwag, and MMLU using both original items and semantically equivalent paraphrases.

The main result, consistent with the title and the body of the paper, is that contamination does inflate absolute scores but rarely reorders large-model leaderboards. In other words, the dominant pattern is shared inflation rather than rank-changing differential advantage. The key evidence is not just the presence of contamination signals, but the relative stability of leaderboard order after accounting for suspect items or invariance violations. The excerpt provided does not include the full result tables, so I will not invent exact point gains, correlation values, or Kendall tau numbers. When reading the paper, the main tables to verify are the calibration curves, benchmark-specific estimated contamination levels, and the ranking-stability statistics before and after correction.65d:T4aa,For a skim, focus on three parts. First, read the problem framing in the introduction, especially the distinction between score inflation and rank distortion. That is the paper’s main contribution. Second, read the method section that defines anchor-item invariance, differential item functioning, and the original-versus-paraphrase contrast. The key question is why this contrast can isolate memorization rather than ability. Third, inspect the calibration figures and the main leaderboard-stability results. You want to check two things: whether the contamination proxy is actually calibrated against known doses, and how much model ordering changes after accounting for contaminated items.

A good reading order is: framing and motivation, calibration experiment, main results on the 47 public models, then the ranking analysis. Around 25 to 35 minutes should be enough to extract the main message. Two points are worth deeper scrutiny. One is whether paraphrases truly preserve item difficulty, especially for math and commonsense tasks. The other is whether RL post-training can mask contamination signatures, which would limit interpretability for closed or heavily post-trained models.65e:T479,The method has two layers. First, the paper defines and estimates step advantage. A CoT is segmented into steps. For each step, the authors take the prefix up to that point and run Monte Carlo rollouts to sample continuations and final answers, estimating expected reward from that prefix. Comparing expected reward with and without the step gives the step’s advantage. This avoids prompt rewriting and avoids relying on manually designed perturbations; it measures marginal contribution directly on the original trajectory. Second, they turn noisy step-level estimates into analyzable structure. A changepoint-based procedure identifies whether a trace contains steps whose advantage confidently exceeds an effect-size threshold, separating informative from uninformative traces. They then ask whether judges can predict these labels or scores from text alone, using both prompted judges and critics fine-tuned on advantage-derived supervision. Performance is compared not only to simple baselines but also to a noise ceiling induced by rollout uncertainty, which is important for interpreting how much decodable signal is actually available.65f:T504,The experiments span multiple generator models, datasets, and both thinking and non-thinking settings. Three findings stand out. First, important steps are sparse: many sentences that look like reasoning have near-zero advantage. The opening geometry example captures this well: two self-checking steps look similar in text, yet one changes success probability negligibly while another raises it from about 52% to about 94%. Second, judge performance is strongly asymmetric. Larger zero-shot judges beat a prevalence baseline, but remain far below the noise ceiling. Fine-tuned critics improve substantially and get close to the ceiling on incorrect traces, yet recover only a small share of the decodable signal on correct traces. This suggests that in successful reasoning, the state changes that matter are often not fully externalized in the text. Third, the paper uses advantage trajectories to study reasoning dynamics and finds that gains from scale and from thinking mode are driven mostly by stronger answer priors before the first reasoning step, rather than by the answer being discovered progressively during the CoT. The paper also reports that uncertainty-management steps are disproportionately important in correct responses, for both thinking and non-thinking models.660:T49a,The empirical evidence is concrete. In the motivating GRPO run on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B, 150 steps produced a 2.6–2.8 point pass@1 gain on a held-out EvalPlus split across three runs, with p-values of 0.064, 0.078, and 0.077. However, 91–94% of newly passing items passed on the first turn, while turn-2-or-later rescues stayed flat at 6–9 out of 540. The apparent lack of multi-turn repair was traced to tool calls never becoming actions. On BFCL v4, changing only the serving adapter moved the same model from 0.00 to 0.96 / 0.19 on simple_python / multi_turn_base. The 2×2 template-parser decomposition showed zero main effects and all gain in the interaction. On τ-bench’s 115 retail tasks, the same swap changed server-parsed calls from 0 to 636. Replaying vLLM’s hermes extractor over 4,254 deduplicated first turns found no case where the server failed to parse an output that its own rules accepted. Qwen2.5-Coder emitted bare calls rather than the <tool_call> envelope, while Qwen2.5-Instruct emitted the envelope but often broke the JSON inside it. In a verl AgentLoop setting at 7B, 45 of 115 generations contained a complete call, yet none became an action.661:T82c,The contribution is an evaluation framework rather than a new optimizer. On the continuous side, the authors use standard synthetic functions including Branin, Hartmann-3, Hartmann-6, Ackley, and Rastrigin. Domains are normalized to [0,1]^d and objectives are converted to maximization. A key design choice is that they do not only test the canonical form of each function. They also create disguised variants by applying bijective transformations to the input domain and output range, specifically to reduce the chance that the model exploits memorized patterns tied to familiar function names, coordinate systems, or known optima. This is one of the most important parts of the paper because it separates optimization behavior from benchmark recognition.

The LLM is treated as a batch policy. At each step, the prompt contains previously queried points, their objective values, and the remaining budget, and the model proposes q candidates with q in {1,2,4}. They compare single-turn prompting, where each round is reconstructed from scratch, against multi-turn interaction, where the model keeps the conversation and can reflect on prior reasoning. The total oracle budget is fixed at N=120, with 2d initial points, so comparisons across batch sizes are budget-matched. Performance is measured with regret, especially simple regret.

For the discrete setting, they use the PMO molecular optimization benchmark. Here the model proposes molecules in SMILES form and deterministic oracles score them. This setting is naturally aligned with language models: SMILES is a discrete sequence representation with local compositional semantics, so the model can leverage priors from pretraining about symbolic patterns, local edits, and constraint-aware generation. The paper’s deeper point is that LLM optimization behavior is strongly representation-dependent. In numerical spaces, the model has to infer geometry from tabulated histories, which is not a native strength of language pretraining. In molecular string spaces, the task is much closer to structured generation and guided rewriting.662:T5bf,From the full text provided, the continuous experiments use a fixed total budget of N=120, batch sizes 1, 2, and 4, and 2d initial points, across standard functions ranging from low to moderate dimensionality. The authors evaluate both canonical and disguised versions of the objectives. The main empirical takeaway is not a single headline number but a pattern: frontier LLMs can sometimes rival strong classical baselines such as Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization with expected improvement, yet their performance is brittle. It changes materially with task transformations, dimensionality, and batch size. In other words, the models are not consistently reliable numerical optimizers.

The molecular results are stronger. On PMO oracles, the frontier reasoning models are reported to be highly sample-efficient and to frequently outperform specialist methods while using only a fraction of the oracle evaluation budget. That budget efficiency is the important result in a black-box optimization setting.

The model family under study is Anthropic’s Sonnet 4.6, Opus 4.8, and Opus 5, which allows the paper to compare generations within a single frontier reasoning family. The excerpt does not include the full result tables, so it would be inappropriate to invent exact averages or win rates here. Still, the experimental matrix is broad enough to support a structural conclusion: the gap between continuous and discrete performance is systematic, not anecdotal.663:T636,The method has two stages. Stage one builds structured compositional supervision. Instead of crude object swapping, the pipeline starts from real images sampled from LAION-400M. Qwen3-VL-32B extracts a structured scene graph-like description with objects, attributes, and relations. A sampled schema decides how many objects and attributes to keep. Conditioned on this schema and a five-level matching taxonomy, the MLLM generates one retrieval query and five captions. The five levels are: full match, partial presence, attribute error, object error, and full mismatch. Z-Image-Turbo then synthesizes one candidate image per caption, yielding a graded candidate list rather than a flat positive/negative set.

Stage two performs distillation. The synthesized data first fine-tunes a reranker, producing Core-Reranker. Then the reranker’s listwise compositional preferences are distilled into the embedding model, producing Core-Embed. The paper compares standard contrastive learning, pairwise CoSENT, and listwise Rank-KL. The main conclusion is that listwise supervision is the right fit for this setting because the target is not just “correct vs incorrect” but an ordered similarity spectrum. Rank-KL works by matching the embedding-induced ranking distribution to the teacher reranker’s distribution over the whole candidate list. Another useful detail is the diagnostic on Matryoshka dimensions: increasing representation dimension helps binding-sensitive subsets much more than simple lexical substitutions, which motivates distillation beyond merely widening the embedding.664:T59f,There are three main experimental messages. First, the paper validates the capability gap between reranking and embedding. A representative example shows that both the backbone and the reranker rank fine-grained compositional candidates correctly, while embedding similarity fails. The Matryoshka sweep supports the same story: on two SugarCrepe++ subsets, increasing the representation dimension from 512 to 1536 barely changes Replace Attribute, from 0.773 to 0.777, but improves the more binding-sensitive Swap Attribute from 0.589 to 0.623.

Second, the objective comparison is important. CoSENT and Rank-KL both outperform standard contrastive learning under the five-level supervision, and Rank-KL is the strongest overall. This suggests the gain is not only from better hard negatives, but also from using an objective aligned with ordered supervision.

Third, the end results are solid. Core-Reranker-8B reaches 82.7% total average on compositional reasoning benchmarks, surpassing the previous best reranker. Core-Embed-8B achieves the best total average among evaluated embedding models. On MCMR, Core-Embed-8B improves R@1 from 0.375 to 0.412 over its backbone, while preserving performance on standard retrieval sets such as COCO and Flickr30K. The graded held-out evaluation protocol is also a meaningful contribution because it measures whether the model learns relative compositional similarity, not just binary correctness.665:T6b4,The method, FactoSR, follows a two-stage recipe: supervised spatial fine-tuning first, then factorized reinforcement learning. In the SFT stage, the model is taught to produce structured outputs that separate observation, localization, reasoning, and final answer. In the RL stage, the authors build on RLVR with GRPO-style optimization, but replace the usual single correctness reward with a multi-objective reward design.

There are five reward components. A format reward keeps outputs structurally valid during RL. An accuracy reward preserves standard final-answer supervision. The key novelty lies in three geometry-aware rewards. The XY reward enforces cross-view planar consistency and correspondence, encouraging the model to identify the correct region before answering. The Z reward targets 3D localization and relative depth ordering, which is critical for front/back, near/far, and occlusion reasoning. The T reward enforces temporal cycle consistency and reversible camera-motion reasoning, pushing the model to remain coherent over sequences rather than treating frames independently.

This is not an architectural change to the backbone. It is a change in task decomposition and training signal design. Relative to prior spatial RLVR work, the differences are clear: it moves from final-answer-only rewards to factorized rewards, from mostly single-view reasoning to multi-view and temporal settings, and from implicit language-space reasoning to explicitly geometry-constrained optimization. The trade-off is also clear: the approach depends on datasets and annotations that support verifiable XY/Z/T rewards, so scalability and transfer will depend on how broadly those rewards can be instantiated.666:T59b,The headline results reported in the paper are gains of 5.9% on VSI-Bench and 4.5% on All-Angles-Bench, while maintaining decent general multimodal capability. The experimental story is less about one benchmark and more about whether the factorized rewards produce separable gains on separable spatial skills.

The key ablations compare SFT only, SFT plus standard RLVR, and SFT plus FactoSR-RL. The paper’s main claim is that answer-only RL helps somewhat, but remains unstable on depth, cross-view correspondence, and temporal consistency. Adding XY/Z/T rewards yields larger improvements on tasks that require explicit geometric reasoning chains. Reward ablations further support the decomposition: removing XY hurts cross-view localization and correspondence; removing Z weakens relative depth and occlusion judgments; removing T degrades camera-motion and temporal reverse-reasoning tasks. The authors also emphasize stronger generalization than pure SFT, arguing that RL encourages strategy learning rather than memorization of static patterns.

From the provided full-text excerpt, there is no reliable complete table of model size, training steps, or dataset scale, so those details should not be overstated. What is clear is that this is an SFT-plus-RL enhancement on top of an existing VLM, with the main contribution in reward design and spatial-temporal data construction rather than large-scale pretraining from scratch.667:Te4a,整体架构由三部分组成：一个基于 LLaDA 2.0 的冻结 dLLM-VLM 负责多模态理解，一个 connector 把理解侧 hidden states 投到生成条件空间，一个 6B 单流 Diffusion Transformer 负责图像合成。关键点不在“模块很多”，而在职责边界划得很清楚。

1. 先学视觉先验，再学语言对齐
作者反对从训练一开始就重度依赖图文对。原因有两个：一是 caption 贵且噪声大；二是在低分辨率训练阶段，caption 中描述的细节常因下采样而不可见，导致条件和目标不匹配。为此，他们先做 image-only pre-training 和 mid-training，让 DiT 先把自然图像分布学扎实。这里不是无条件生成，而是借助冻结 VLM 从“同一图像区域”提取条件表示，让条件和生成目标天然对齐，避免外部 caption 带来的语义漂移。这个设计很像在做一种自蒸馏式的视觉条件建模：监督信号主要来自真实图像本身，语言只在后期逐步接入。

2. 统一理解、生成、编辑，但不强行共用所有路径
文本生成和编辑共用同一条语义条件路径：文本、视觉上下文和结构化 reasoning trace 先进入 dLLM-VLM，再经 Residual Query Adapter 和轻量 Transformer connector 送入 DiT。编辑任务则额外引入 reference-image pathway，而且这个路径直接进 DiT，绕过 VLM。作者这样做的原因很实际：编辑时既需要高层语义指令，也需要像素级或局部外观证据；如果全部压进 VLM hidden states，参考图像细节容易损失。因此他们同时使用 SigLIP-VQ 特征和 clean VAE latent，分别提供语义级和像素级参考信号。这个设计说明作者没有把“统一”理解成单一路径，而是按信息类型分层接入。

3. progressive training pipeline
训练分阶段推进：先在 256 分辨率做 image-only pre-training；再做 aspect-ratio-bucketed mid-training，继续扩展视觉先验；之后在 512 和 1024 分辨率引入 paired language alignment；再对 text-rich 和 portrait 数据做 targeted refinement；最后做 generation-editing joint training。这里有两个关键取舍。其一，数据配比上始终保持 real-data-dominant，整条生成训练链约 2.2 亿样本，其中 98% 是真实图像，SFT 阶段真实图像占比也保持在 70% 以上。作者承认这种路线在早期 benchmark 收敛可能慢于 synthetic-heavy 配方，但长期 realism ceiling 更高。其二，训练目标不是一次性混训所有能力，而是按“先分布、后条件、再任务整合”的顺序推进，这和大模型训练里常见的 annealing / curriculum 思路一致。

4. 稳定性与优化
DiT 全面使用 parameter-free RMSNorm，而不是带可学习缩放参数的归一化。作者的意图是减少大模型 diffusion 训练中的尺度漂移和额外不稳定因素。优化器选 Muon，也是在强调大规模从头训练的稳定与效率。虽然从给出的片段里看不到完整优化细节和对比表，但论文把这两点列为 recipe 的核心组成，说明它们不是边角工程，而是支撑 6B DiT 训练成功的重要条件。

5. TwinFlow 蒸馏到 Turbo
部署侧使用 TwinFlow，把原始多步 diffusion 模型蒸馏成 2–4 步的 LLaDA-Image Turbo。方法上结合了 distribution-matching distillation 和 self-adversarial flow training。值得注意的是，作者把 Turbo 视为同一家族的部署变体，而不是另起一个轻量模型。这意味着训练时就考虑了 teacher 分布是否适合后续 few-step student 拟合，属于“为蒸馏而设计主模型”的思路。668:T65f,This is highly relevant to foundation-model pretraining. Its significance is not just that it trains a 6B DiT, but that it makes several training decisions explicit and backs them with a full recipe. Four contributions stand out.

First, it argues clearly for decoupling visual-prior learning from language alignment. The generator is trained to model image distribution first, and paired supervision is introduced later. That is closely analogous to the separation between broad pretraining and later alignment in LLMs, and it is a useful design pattern for multimodal foundation training.

Second, it shows a concrete role for a diffusion language model beyond understanding alone. The frozen LLaDA2.0-Mini-based VLM acts as a semantic conditioning hub that unifies text, visual context, and reasoning traces. This gives a practical answer to how an understanding model and a generation model can be separated without becoming disconnected.

Third, the paper contributes a serious large-scale training recipe: parameter-free RMSNorm throughout the DiT, the Muon optimizer, and a progressive curriculum over data type and resolution. For training large DiTs from scratch, these choices matter more than many cosmetic architectural tweaks.

Fourth, few-step distillation is treated as part of the main model family rather than an afterthought. In that sense, LLaDA-Image is not just a model but a full pipeline from prior learning to alignment, editing, and deployment. This should matter for open image-generation pretraining, and it also has direct relevance to unified multimodal pretraining and AR-plus-diffusion style systems.669:T1037,The system has three main components: a frozen dLLM-based VLM built on LLaDA 2.0 for multimodal understanding, a connector that projects understanding-side hidden states into the generator conditioning space, and a 6B single-stream Diffusion Transformer for image synthesis. The key is not the number of modules, but the clarity of their roles.

1. Learn the visual prior first, then align to language.
The authors explicitly avoid heavy dependence on paired image-text data at the beginning of training. Their argument is practical: captions are expensive and noisy, and at low training resolutions many captioned details are no longer visible after downsampling, which creates condition-target mismatch. Instead, they begin with image-only pretraining and mid-training so that the DiT first learns the natural image distribution well. This is not purely unconditional generation. A frozen VLM extracts conditioning signals from the same image region that the DiT is asked to generate, which keeps condition and target tightly matched without relying on external captions. Conceptually, this resembles a form of self-distilled visual conditioning: the image itself provides most of the supervision signal, while language is introduced later.

2. Unify understanding, generation, and editing without forcing a single pathway for everything.
Text-to-image generation and editing share the same semantic conditioning route: text, visual context, and structured reasoning traces are encoded by the dLLM-VLM, then passed through a Residual Query Adapter and a lightweight Transformer connector into the DiT. Editing adds a separate reference-image pathway that goes directly into the DiT and bypasses the VLM. This is an important design choice. Editing needs both high-level semantic instructions and low-level appearance evidence; if everything is compressed into VLM hidden states, reference fidelity can be lost. To address this, the model uses both SigLIP-VQ features and clean VAE latents, providing semantic-level and pixel-level reference signals respectively. The paper’s notion of unification is therefore layered rather than monolithic.

3. Progressive training pipeline.
Training proceeds in stages: image-only pretraining at 256 resolution, aspect-ratio-bucketed mid-training to strengthen the visual prior, paired language alignment at 512 and 1024 resolution, targeted refinement on text-rich and portrait data, and finally joint generation-editing training. Two design choices matter here. First, the data mixture remains real-data-dominant throughout. The full generation pipeline processes about 220M samples, 98% of them real images, and the real-image share stays above 70% even during supervised fine-tuning. The authors explicitly acknowledge that this may converge more slowly on early benchmarks than synthetic-heavy mixtures, but they argue that it yields stronger realism at convergence. Second, capabilities are not mixed all at once. The curriculum follows a distribution-first, conditioning-next, task-integration-later order, which is very much in line with annealing and curriculum ideas in large-model training.

4. Stability and optimization.
The DiT uses parameter-free RMSNorm throughout rather than a learnable affine normalization. The motivation is to reduce scale drift and unnecessary instability in large-scale diffusion training. The optimizer is Muon, again chosen with training stability and scalability in mind. The provided excerpt does not include the full optimization ablations, but the paper presents these choices as central parts of the recipe rather than minor implementation details.

5. TwinFlow distillation to Turbo.
For deployment, the original multi-step model is distilled into 2–4-step LLaDA-Image Turbo variants using TwinFlow, which combines distribution-matching distillation with self-adversarial flow training. An important point is that Turbo is treated as a deployment variant within the same family, not as a separate lightweight model. This suggests that the teacher is trained with downstream few-step distillation in mind, which is a more integrated view of training and serving.66a:T8fd,The experimental results support several distinct claims.

First, on overall capability, LLaDA-Image performs strongly on Qwen-Image-Bench, LongText-Bench, CVTG-2K, and GEdit-Bench, covering photorealism, prompt alignment, bilingual Chinese-English text rendering, and instruction-guided editing. The emphasis is on balanced capability rather than optimizing a single aesthetic metric. That matters because many open models still lag badly on text rendering or reference-preserving editing.

Second, the data strategy is a central empirical result. The paper argues that image-only pretraining followed by progressive language alignment is not only viable, but preferable in the long run to synthetic-heavy paired training from the start. Synthetic mixtures may improve early benchmark numbers faster, but they also inject artifacts and caption bias that hurt realism later. The full generation pipeline uses about 220M samples, with more than 90% of training in image-only stages and 98% of samples coming from real images. Those numbers make the intended shift in supervision very concrete.

Third, the system scale and deployment profile are explicit. The main generator is a 6B DiT trained from scratch, while the understanding module is built on a frozen LLaDA2.0-Mini backbone. The release includes four checkpoints: Base and Turbo, plus FP8 variants of each. The Turbo models run with only 2–4 sampling steps, which substantially lowers inference cost.

Fourth, editing performance comes from the unified architecture rather than a separate editing backbone. Text-to-image and editing share the semantic path, while reference images are injected through an additional DiT-side pathway. This allows the model to balance instruction following and reference preservation on editing benchmarks such as GEdit-Bench. That is an important result for unified multimodal generation systems, where many models still trade off editability against fidelity.

The provided excerpt does not include full score tables, FID values, or detailed human-evaluation numbers, so those should not be fabricated. The reliable hard facts are: a 6B DiT, roughly 220M training samples, 98% real images, more than 90% image-only training stages, more than 70% real-image share during SFT, and 2–4-step Turbo inference.66b:T74e,This one deserves a careful read. Do not start from the benchmark tables. Start with the introduction and model design, because the paper is really about training philosophy and system decomposition. The three questions to keep in mind are: why learn the visual prior before language alignment, why route editing through an extra reference path instead of only through the VLM, and why insist on a real-data-dominant recipe.

A good reading order is:
1. Introduction: identify the three main threads—data decoupling, unified architecture, and few-step deployment.
2. Model Design: focus on the interfaces among the frozen dLLM-VLM, the Residual Query Adapter, the connector, and the single-stream DiT. This is where the division of labor between understanding and generation becomes clear.
3. Training pipeline: this is the most valuable section for pretraining researchers. Pay close attention to stage boundaries, data composition, resolution transitions, when paired data is introduced, and how refinement data is selected.
4. Stability and optimization details: look for the rationale and any ablations behind parameter-free RMSNorm and Muon, especially whether they matter more at larger batch sizes, higher resolutions, or longer training runs.
5. Editing and Turbo distillation: if you care about unified multimodal generation or deployment, read these sections closely, especially the reference pathway and the TwinFlow objective.
6. Experiments: prioritize ablations on data mixture, the necessity of the image-only stages, the effect of real-data ratio on realism and alignment, and the quality-speed trade-off between the original model and Turbo.

If time is limited, spend at least 60–90 minutes on the method and training recipe. If you work on diffusion LMs, unified multimodal pretraining, or AR-plus-diffusion systems, this is worth taking notes on.66c:T452,The authors formulate OPD as training on on-policy autoregressive states s=(x, y_<i). The student samples rollouts under its current policy, and the teacher supplies a next-token distribution at each visited prefix. The student is then updated toward the teacher on those visited states, typically through a token-level KL or cross-entropy loss. The key move is to treat a query as a generator of states, not as a single training item. To quantify this, the paper defines state coverage: states visited by full-data OPD are grouped into semantic clusters, and a query set is scored by the fraction of those clusters reached by its rollouts. This avoids exact-prefix matching, which would be too sparse, and gives a better proxy for the supervision OPD actually sees. The second diagnostic is absorption rate, the fraction of the remaining teacher-student gap closed by one update. This separates insufficient data coverage from slow algorithmic uptake. The paper then tests the same account in multi-teacher OPD, off-domain prompting, content-free prompting, and a controlled comparison with one-shot RLVR.66d:T4ad,The phenomenon is tested across four task domains and three model families. One-shot OPD continues to improve for hundreds of optimization steps and recovers most of the full-data OPD gain, even in cases where the student never solves the training query. The full-data reference contains about 17k queries. The most important measurement is state coverage: one query already reaches 71.5% of the states visited by full-data OPD, with most of that coverage appearing within the first 100 steps. Sixteen semantically diverse queries reach 98.9% coverage and match full-data training. The absorption-rate analysis shows similar decay patterns for one-shot and full-data OPD, indicating that the run length is governed more by how slowly OPD absorbs dense teacher supervision than by a lack of new prompts. In multi-teacher OPD, 16 diverse queries per domain are enough to match full-data training. Off-domain WildChat prompts and content-free templates remain nearly as effective as the full training set. In a controlled one-shot comparison, OPD achieves more than twice the validation gain of RLVR over 1000 steps because its token-level signal persists after the outcome reward has been exhausted.66e:T46f,Read it closely. Start with the Introduction for the paper’s decomposition into state supply and absorption rate. Then inspect the OPD objective and the definition of state, since the paper’s state is an autoregressive prefix rather than a high-level environment state. The main empirical phenomenon is in Section 3; focus on whether the one-shot gain could be explained by memorization, solved trajectories, or model-family artifacts. Section 4 is the core section: read the state-coverage construction, the semantic clustering procedure, the 71.5% single-query result, the 98.9% sixteen-query result, and the diverse-query selection ablations. Section 5 is the second key section because absorption rate is what supports the claim that OPD is limited by uptake speed. Sections 6 and 7 are useful for generalization: multi-teacher routing, content-free prompts, off-domain prompts, and the RLVR comparison all test whether the state-level explanation survives outside the one-shot setup. If available, the appendix details on clustering, rollout sampling, teacher-logit access, temperature, and query selection are worth checking.66f:T543,LeanGRPO removes update-stage recomputation through a systems redesign with two pieces. First, it changes the data-parallel layout. Instead of assigning different prompts to different GPUs and generating multiple local samples per prompt, all GPUs process the same prompt while each rank generates a different sample. This reduces the need for each rank to retain multiple computation graphs for the same prompt group.

Second, it introduces two recompute-free schedules. LeanGRPO-Retain simply enables gradient tracking during rollout and keeps the selected-timestep graphs alive until terminal rewards and group advantages are available, then reuses those graphs for backpropagation. It is simple but activation memory grows with the number of selected timesteps.

LeanGRPO-Reweight is more subtle. During rollout, each selected-timestep graph is immediately consumed through a provisional backward pass, producing a provisional gradient and allowing saved activations to be released right away. Once the terminal reward and advantage are known, the provisional gradient is corrected using that advantage, recovering the same policy gradient in exact arithmetic. This shifts the memory burden from retained activations to stored provisional gradients. The paper positions both schedules as objective-preserving rather than approximate shortcuts.670:T8bb,文章的核心设计是把 supervision 当成“随训练演化的状态”，而不是固定标签。围绕这个抽象，框架分成三个模块，但作者强调它们是互补的 intervention points，不是必须串行执行的流水线。

第一块是 Active Data Selection。目标是在训练预算和标注预算有限时，决定哪些样本进入训练、哪些样本需要外部标注、哪些样本转入弱监督路径。实现上覆盖 verified difficulty filtering、基于模型不确定性的选择、以及 probe-calibrated selection 等。这里的关键不是某一种打分器，而是把“是否值得花 rollout/annotation 成本”前置成显式决策。

On top of that abstraction, the framework organizes the lifecycle into three modules, which are presented as complementary intervention points rather than a mandatory sequential pipeline.

The first module is Active Data Selection. It decides which examples should be retained for training, which should receive external labels, and which should be routed to weak supervision. Implementations include verified-difficulty filtering, model-based uncertainty selection, and probe-calibrated selection. The important design choice is that budget allocation is made explicit before expensive rollout and annotation are spent.

The second module is Weak Supervision Construction. It allows unlabeled examples to participate in RLVR by constructing pseudo-targets, enforcing agreement across views, or assigning target-free rewards. The framework covers methods such as TTRL, Co-Rewarding, EMRL, and Intuitor under a shared interface. This matters because weak supervision no longer requires rewriting the rollout-to-update loop; it becomes a localized change in supervision semantics.

The third module is Training-Time Supervision Refinement. Since supervision can become unreliable due to noise, policy drift, or reward hacking, the framework supports online reassessment and revision using reward dynamics, representation geometry, and rollout evidence. This includes methods such as TraPO, GeoMin, and online label refinement. The deeper point is that supervision quality should be revisited as the policy changes, not fixed once offline.

At the systems level, DE-Venus follows a minimal-invasion design. It keeps verl as the execution substrate for rollout generation, optimization, validation, and checkpointing, and inserts method-specific logic only at the boundaries where supervision semantics change. Persistent sample identity and supervision state are stored through a shared Parquet convention, while verl-compatible batches carry targets, rewards, selections, and advantages during online optimization. Reusable services handle voting, verification, uncertainty estimation, reward construction, evidence analysis, and validation logging. For a first pass, Introduction, the framework overview figure, one example per module, and the main results table should take about 25–35 minutes.674:T59e,The method has three parts. First, the authors recover the prior direction. Given the unembedding matrix W and an empirical unigram distribution p_unigram, they solve a linear least-squares problem over the frequent-token subset to find a vector d_prior such that softmax(W d_prior) reconstructs the unigram distribution as closely as possible. This requires only the output weights and token counts from a corpus, with no model forward passes. They argue that the recovered direction is unique under the fitting procedure and show that it is absent at random initialization but emerges through training. Second, they derive a tempered Bayesian interpretation. For any final prediction state y_pred, they decompose it into λ d_prior plus an orthogonal component. Plugging this into the softmax yields a factorization of the predictive distribution into a unigram prior raised to the power λ times a context-dependent likelihood term. This gives λ a clean probabilistic meaning: λ=0 removes the prior, 0<λ<1 tempers it, λ>1 sharpens it, and λ<0 inverts it. Third, they validate the mechanism dynamically and causally. They vary contextual informativeness through coherent context, shuffled tokens, short contexts, and ambiguous prompts, and track λ. They also intervene directly on the prediction state along d_prior and compare against norm-matched random-direction perturbations to test whether this axis is functionally special.675:T59b,The experiments cover Llama, Qwen, Gemma, and Pythia, from 0.4B to 405B parameters. Four results matter most. First, existence and universality: a single direction reconstructs the unigram prior with low KL error across all tested families, suggesting this is not an artifact of one architecture or recipe. The paper also shows that the direction is not present at initialization and appears only after training. Second, context dynamics: λ decreases as coherent information accumulates, but not merely when token count grows. Shuffled or semantically weak contexts do not reduce λ in the same way, which supports the claim that λ tracks information rather than length or position. Third, causal intervention: increasing the projection along d_prior pushes predictions toward the unigram prior, while decreasing it makes predictions rely more on contextual evidence. Random directions with matched magnitude do not produce the same effect, so d_prior is not just a post hoc statistical fit. Fourth, scaling behavior: the paper reports that in the high-context regime, λ often decreases with hidden dimension across families, hinting that larger models suppress default priors more effectively when context is informative. This part is more observational than fully explained. The analysis is mostly done on the frequent-token subset because long-tail BPE tokens make unigram estimation noisy; the default support fraction is c=0.7.676:T406,The main setup uses GPT-2 small, d=16, and six latent positions on ProsQA.
