This differs from ordinary PCA compression: high variance is not assumed to imply transfer; the question is which PCs encode stable behavioral signal.678:T7ec,The paper introduces a unified framework of attention-indexed models, where multi-layer and multi-head attention-only architectures are expressed through finitely many quadratic token interactions of the form 1/sqrt(d) x_i^T S_ij x_k, with S_ij being d-by-d extensive-rank matrices. The technical contribution has two main parts.

First, it separates the static and dynamic descriptions. In the high-dimensional limit d→∞, the population loss is shown to depend on only finitely many trace-type order parameters, even though the original parameter space is Θ(d^2). So the loss landscape admits a finite-dimensional macroscopic description. However, online SGD is richer: for both tied and untied factorizations, the updates generate an infinite hierarchy of joint matrix moments, and no fixed finite set closes the dynamics in general. The authors then prove that the empirical trajectory converges to a deterministic infinite-dimensional ODE, and that finite-order truncations approximate this limiting dynamics with exponentially decaying error. This is the key methodological result.

Second, the paper analyzes parameterization-induced implicit bias by comparing three representations of the same effective attention: direct optimization of S, tied factorization S=WW^T, and untied factorization S=UV^T. Direct optimization suffers from an information-exponent bottleneck: when first-order correlation vanishes, SGD can remain trapped in an uninformative phase on the d^2 log d sample scale. In the tied case, the PSD structure provides an automatic symmetry-breaking mechanism. Under a mild non-degeneracy condition, this enables weak recovery at Θ(d^2 log d) samples. In the untied case, the mechanism is different: there is a fast-slow decomposition. Quantities such as 1/sqrt(d) Tr(UV^T) evolve on a fast timescale and create a boundary layer; the slower matrix-moment dynamics then proceed from the state selected by that fast transient. Weak recovery occurs only if this early shift breaks the relevant symmetry.679:T5e8,The empirical component is mainly numerical validation of the theory rather than large-scale model benchmarking. The important results are threefold.

First, the paper shows that finite-order truncations of the infinite moment hierarchy provide accurate approximations, with error decreasing rapidly as the truncation order increases. This supports the practical tractability of the otherwise infinite-dimensional ODE description.

Second, it compares the three parameterizations under uninformative initialization. Direct optimization of S remains bottlenecked when first-order correlation is absent. The tied PSD factorization achieves weak recovery on the Θ(d^2 log d) sample scale. The untied factorization can either recover or remain uninformative, depending on which symmetry branch is selected during the fast boundary-layer dynamics. The important takeaway is the difference in phase behavior and sample complexity, not a single benchmark number.

Third, numerical trajectories match the theoretical ODE predictions, indicating that the high-dimensional limit is not merely formal. The paper also highlights a sharp distinction from finite-rank sequence-indexed models, where a finite set of order parameters often closes the dynamics; here it does not.

The first is environment reconstruction. Starting from public terminal-agent trajectories, the system replays file operations and restores each file to its pre-edit state, so the resulting workspace starts unsolved. Because trajectories usually reveal only a partial view of the original workspace, replay alone produces incomplete environments. A completion agent then fills in missing files and dependencies while trying not to leak the solution. This design choice is important: it avoids generating environments from scratch, which often hurts realism, and it also avoids requiring access to the original repository, which may be unavailable.

The second part is task expansion. The framework does not only recover the original user intent; it also synthesizes new tasks over the reconstructed environment. Breadth expansion links related environments and creates cross-workspace tasks, such as porting a feature from one project to another or connecting two components. Depth expansion turns a single-round task into a multi-round interaction. After one round is completed, a user agent issues grounded follow-up requests based on the changed workspace, or asks for fixes when a round fails. This yields stateful, evolving tasks rather than static instructions.

The third part is verification and data generation. For each new task, an agent writes a verifier inside the container, and only trajectories whose tests pass are kept. Qwen3.7-Max is then used as a teacher to solve tasks again in these reconstructed environments, and the resulting trajectories are used to train Qwen3.5-27B. The key point is the data-generation paradigm: reconstruct the environment first, then let a stronger model produce fresh, verifiable solutions, instead of treating historical trajectories as final supervision.67c:T476,The reported scale is substantial. Another important detail is that every synthesized task is paired with a verifier and filtered by test success, so the quality of executable supervision is doing a lot of the work.67d:T782,方法由两部分组成。第一部分是 dynamic per-trajectory rubric。不是为整个任务分布预先写一套固定 rubric，而是先根据任务指令生成初始 criteria，再结合每个 rollout 暴露出来的子目标、失败模式和执行路径，对 rubric 做扩展，最后把同一 group 内多个 rollout 提出的 criteria 合并成共享 rubric 集合。这样做的原因很直接：固定 rubric 往往覆盖不到长轨迹里真实发生的分叉和失败细节，而按轨迹动态生成可以让 judge 评价的是“这条轨迹实际试图完成了什么、卡在了哪里”，不是抽象模板。

第二部分是 distribution of rubric-conditioned advantage。标准 GRPO 对同一 trajectory 的所有 token 使用同一个 advantage；DRACO 改成先让 judge 对 rubric 中每个 criterion 给 verdict，再把 criterion 与轨迹中负责该 criterion 的步骤对齐，然后用一个闭式规则把 criterion-level judgment 分摊成 per-step advantage。论文强调这个分配规则满足若干形式性质，包括总量守恒、符号保持、长度无关等，目的是避免 credit 在长轨迹里被无控制地稀释，或者因为轨迹更长而系统性偏置。这里的关键不是“做 step reward”本身，而是 step reward 不依赖终局 verifier，也不依赖 learned reward model，而是直接从 rubric verdict 推出。

训练上仍然套在 GRPO 框架里：对每个任务采样一组轨迹，judge 对每条轨迹按动态 rubric 打分，再把 rubric verdict 重新分配到步骤，形成替代统一 trajectory advantage 的 step-level advantage。论文还比较了 frontier judge 与 self-judge，说明 judge 质量会直接影响 credit 质量。与已有 process reward 或 step-level RL 方法的差别在于，很多先前方法仍然锚定 gold answer、unit test 或 terminal reward；DRACO 刻意去掉了这些训练时真值依赖。67e:T6ef,DRACO has two main components. The first is dynamic per-trajectory rubric generation. Instead of writing one fixed rubric for the whole task distribution, the judge first proposes criteria from the task instruction, then extends those criteria using what each sampled rollout actually attempted, where it failed, and which subgoals emerged during execution. The criteria proposed from all trajectories in the same GRPO group are merged into a shared rubric set. The motivation is straightforward: fixed rubrics under-specify long trajectories, while rollout-conditioned rubrics can evaluate what the policy concretely did rather than what a generic template expected.

The second component is rubric-conditioned advantage redistribution. Standard GRPO assigns one scalar advantage to every token in a trajectory. DRACO asks the judge to score each rubric criterion, aligns criteria to the steps responsible for them, and then applies a closed-form redistribution rule to produce per-step advantages. The paper emphasizes several formal properties of this rule, including conservation of total push, sign preservation, and length independence. These properties are meant to prevent the usual failure mode where long trajectories dilute credit or where trajectory length itself introduces systematic bias.

Training remains within the GRPO framework: sample a group of trajectories, score them with a frozen judge under the dynamic rubric, and replace uniform trajectory-level advantage with redistributed step-level advantage. A notable design choice is that the method does not rely on a learned reward model and does not anchor step rewards to terminal verifiers or gold answers. That is the main distinction from much of the prior process-reward and step-credit literature.67f:T662,The main experiments are on AppWorld. The paper states that this is the first RL training result on AppWorld that never accesses the environment’s ground-truth unit-test signal during training. On AppWorld TN, DRACO reaches 85.3 TGC@1, which is a +15.9 point gain over the untrained policy. It also transfers zero-shot to τ-bench and performs at or above a verifier-trained run under the same budget. The key point is not only the absolute score, but that outcome-blind training remains competitive with verifier-based RL.

The ablations separate the two components: dynamic rubric alone, redistribution alone with a fixed rubric, and the full method. The two parts appear complementary. Dynamic rubrics improve coverage and task adaptation, while redistribution improves signal density and credit precision. The paper also compares against a coarse outcome-reward baseline, showing that a single trajectory-level scalar is much weaker for long-horizon learning.

Not all ablation numbers are visible in the provided excerpt, but the experimental structure is centered on signal source, credit granularity, and judge quality.680:T8b7,The central idea is environment evolution. The paper starts from a multi-turn learning objective, models agent-environment interaction as a Markov process, and then introduces a higher-level decomposition of execution into alternating scenarios and skills. From this view, environment difficulty is decomposed into three factors: scenario novelty, skill rarity, and execution length. Intuitively, an environment becomes harder when it requires the agent to enter less common scenarios, apply rarer skills or skill combinations, and sustain a longer meaningful execution chain.

A key step is to move from model-dependent negative log-likelihood to a policy-independent notion of difficulty under a reference distribution T. This is meant to separate environment difficulty from model weakness. In other words, the authors do not want to define an environment as difficult merely because the current policy fails on it. With this formulation, environment generation no longer needs to depend on on-policy rollouts.

The implementation uses a loop-engineered multi-agent harness that incrementally modifies a seed environment along one of three directions: increasing scenario novelty, increasing skill rarity, or increasing execution length. Each modification must preserve executability, task validity, and the verifier. This produces verified lineages of environments with gradually increasing difficulty. The lineage design matters: instead of generating entirely new environments from scratch, the method performs local, controlled, traceable edits on already verified environments, which makes curriculum construction more manageable. Training then schedules these evolved environments generation by generation so that the policy continues to receive non-saturated learning signals over time.

Compared with co-evolution, the main differences are that the process is off-policy and that difficulty increase is explicit and structured rather than driven by current rollout failures. The trade-off is that the quality of the difficulty definition and the evolution harness becomes central: if those are weak, the system may generate environments that are harder in superficial ways but not actually more learnable or more useful.681:T612,The paper reports 200-step long-horizon RL experiments on Qwen3.6-27B and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. Another important result is that evolved environments continue to provide useful RL signal even after the seed environments have already been used for SFT. That suggests the method is not merely replaying the original distribution, but is actually pushing the environment family into new difficulty regimes. Compared with agent-environment co-evolution and ensemble baselines, the paper claims that off-policy evolution yields longer-lasting learning signals and slower saturation during training.

From an evaluation standpoint, the paper is trying to validate three things: whether the evolved environments are genuinely harder, whether that hardness generalizes across models, and whether the harder environments translate into downstream benchmark gains. A sublayer reads them through a pre-map, applies attention or an FFN, writes the result back through a post-map, and transports the existing residual state through a learned matrix H_res. Standard HC leaves H_res unconstrained, so its singular values can cause exploding or vanishing transport. mHC projects H_res onto the Birkhoff polytope of doubly stochastic matrices, usually with Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations. This caps the largest gain at one, but does not lower-bound the smallest gain. The paper decomposes stream states into a mean component and inter-stream difference components, showing that doubly stochastic transport preserves the mean while shrinking differences. Identity HC avoids this shrinkage but removes cross-stream mixing. oHC instead constrains H_res to SO(n), the group of rotations. This keeps all singular values equal to one, so the transport is norm-preserving in every direction while still mixing streams. For four streams, the paper gives an exact SO(4) parameterization using a pair of unit quaternions, avoiding iterative projection.684:T4ab,The method is called Declarative Attention (DA). The model is prompted to emit parseable control tags inside its chain-of-thought, declaring the attention scope it needs at each phase of generation. An inference-side state machine reads these tags online and constructs the attention mask dynamically. DA defines three modes. <global> allows access to the full context and is used when the model needs to survey or search broadly. <focus> commits the model to a specific region of the context, restricting attention to that region. <local> limits attention to recent generated tokens, avoiding long-context reads altogether. This is the key departure from prior sparse-attention methods: the selection signal comes from the model’s own generated reasoning trace, not from hidden-state proxy scorers, recency heuristics, historical attention statistics, or an auxiliary scan over the cache. The paper also includes a practical implementation in vLLM using block-aligned, in-place KV-cache masking compatible with FlashAttention. Another notable point is that the protocol works zero-shot on off-the-shelf models, without task-specific fine-tuning or hand-designed partitions for each benchmark.685:T4cc,The evaluation covers 15 long-context tasks, with main results reported on Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-27B. A lightweight self-attention scoring head then maps those hidden states to an N×K item-position score matrix M, where Mij measures the affinity of item i for rank position j. Instead of generating ordinals one token at a time, the model solves for the maximum-weight bipartite matching between items and positions using the Hungarian algorithm or LAPJV, which directly yields a valid permutation.

This design makes several deliberate choices. It reads scores from prefill hidden states rather than output logits, based on the claim that the comparative information needed for ranking is already encoded by the backbone’s self-attention during prefill. It delegates permutation validity to the solver rather than asking the model to learn it, so duplicate or missing ordinals cannot occur. And it keeps the additional head lightweight, so the method removes sequential decode cost without introducing another heavy model.

The paper also compares multiple scoring-head variants and analyzes the role of self-attention in the readout stage. That is an important detail. If a simple independent head were enough, the ranking signal would be mostly item-wise. If a self-attention head helps substantially, then extracting the permutation still requires modeling competition among candidates even after prefill. The paper’s framing suggests the latter, which is why the contribution is more than just parallel classification: it is a structured decoding formulation tied to assignment.688:T5a9,The headline result is roughly a 64× speedup over an autoregressive LLM on both proprietary data and Amazon Beauty, while maintaining similar ranking quality. One latency breakdown is especially informative: with an explicit reasoning trace, the teacher takes about 1807 ms per request, of which only about 28 ms is prefill. That means the overwhelming majority of time is spent in sequential decoding. Without reasoning, the teacher emits about 39 tokens; with reasoning, about 657 tokens. This makes clear how badly decode cost can scale when a generative ranker produces intermediate text in addition to the final ordering.

The most useful experimental comparisons are: teacher AR decoding versus hLLM on the quality-latency trade-off, ablations over different scoring heads, and analyses isolating the contributions of the backbone and the self-attention layers. The central empirical question is whether a single set of prefill hidden states is sufficient to recover the teacher’s ranking. The paper’s answer is largely yes, though the fidelity depends on the readout head and training setup.

One caveat is that the reported speedup applies mainly to the reranking decode stage, not necessarily to the full retrieval-plus-ranking system. Also, the assignment solver is polynomial-time, but for typical slate sizes it is far cheaper than hundreds of autoregressive decode steps. That distinction matters when interpreting the 64× figure.689:T427,For a skim, start with the introduction and problem formulation. The two numbers to remember are that prefill is cheap and decode is expensive, and that the output is a permutation rather than free-form text. Then go straight to the score-matrix construction and assignment decoding in the method section; that is the conceptual core. In the experiments, prioritize the latency breakdown, the quality comparison against the AR teacher, and the ablations over scoring heads. The main thread can be read in about 20–30 minutes.

If the goal is to judge whether the idea generalizes beyond reranking, focus on how the paper argues that prefill hidden states already contain the ranking information. That claim is more important than the exact ranking metric. Also pay attention to whether the self-attention head is truly necessary. If it clearly outperforms simpler heads, that suggests structured output readout still needs explicit modeling of candidate interactions. That is the part most relevant to broader work on non-AR decoding and constrained generation.68a:T563,XMerge has two components. The first is cross-axis selection. Each block is scored along two axes: relative magnitude, which measures the size of the residual displacement, and Block-Influence, which measures directional change between input and output hidden states. The two scores are standardized across eligible layers and combined with a maximum. A block is considered quiet only when neither axis is large. This max rule is intentional: an average could hide a large angular change with a small magnitude score, or the reverse. The second component is reconstructive layer merging. Instead of dropping a layer, analytically folding weights, or adding a learned replacement module, XMerge distills the original adjacent two-block mapping into one existing standard Transformer block. For calibration inputs, it caches the pair input h_l and the original pair output h_{l+2}, then optimizes all parameters of the surviving block so that the single block maps h_l directly to h_{l+2}. After k merges, the result is an ordinary L-k-layer Transformer with no extra inference-time parameters, no task labels, and no end-to-end fine-tuning. The closest contrast is with methods such as ReplaceMe, LLM-Streamline, and analytic merge/fold approaches; XMerge is distinctive because it reconstructs with a full existing nonlinear standard block while preserving the serving interface.68b:T6a2,The method has three main ingredients. First, the authors approximate the Hessian with the empirical Fisher, using the standard assumption that a converged pretrained model is near a local optimum. They reshape the full gradient vector into a matrix G and show that the Fisher admits an exact decomposition as a sum of Kronecker products. After expressing the relevant expectation in terms of E[G⊗G], they take its SVD and recover a representation of the form J(w)=Σ_i σ_i U_i⊗V_i. The approximation comes from truncating this sum to the top-r components.

Second, they avoid explicitly constructing the enormous n^2 by m^2 matrix. Instead, they use an implicitly restarted Arnoldi solver that only needs matrix-vector products. The key identity is (G⊗G)vec(V)=vec(GVG^T), which turns the expensive operation into smaller dense multiplications on reshaped gradients. This is what makes the method scalable.

Third, they do not rely on the low-rank Kronecker term alone. They compute the Fisher diagonal exactly and combine it with the truncated decomposition. This hybrid design is sensible: the low-rank term captures correlations, while the exact diagonal preserves per-parameter scale. In practice, that should be more stable than either a pure diagonal approximation or a pure low-rank one.

Compared with K-FAC-style approximations, block-diagonal Hessians, or layerwise curvature proxies used in quantization, the distinguishing feature is the explicit attempt to preserve cross-layer interactions. The paper is not mainly about within-layer second-order structure. It is about whether off-diagonal coupling is strong enough to predict super-additive damage under joint perturbations.68c:T868,The experiments span four LLM families from 350M to 7B parameters. Even without the full tables in the provided text, the main empirical findings are clear.

First, the paper reports direct evidence of substantial non-diagonal Fisher/Hessian structure in large language models. This matters because it validates, at realistic scale, the claim that diagonal approximations miss important information. Across multiple model families, value projection layers emerge as the most sensitive components and also show the strongest cross-layer correlations. Other module types behave less uniformly and appear more architecture-dependent.

Second, the proposed curvature scores correlate strongly with compression damage. The authors evaluate quantization and sparsification and show that layerwise Fisher/Hessian values track performance degradation well, better than cruder independent-layer approximations. In other words, layers with larger curvature are more likely to cause larger perplexity or task-performance drops when perturbed.

Third, they run inter-layer corruption experiments rather than only single-layer ablations. When two strongly coupled layers are compressed or corrupted together, the resulting degradation exceeds the sum of their individual effects. The off-diagonal curvature terms predict this excess damage. This is one of the most important results in the paper, because it shows that cross-layer structure is not just mathematically elegant; it explains real failure modes.

Fourth, they study post-corruption recovery. After damaging selected layers, they fine-tune different candidate layers and find that updating the layers most strongly coupled to the corrupted ones yields the best recovery. That is a practical result: the best repair target is not always the damaged layer itself, but sometimes the layer most tightly coupled to it.

The numbers worth remembering are the scale range, 350M to 7B, and the reduction from quadratic to linear memory complexity. The evaluation is also broader than a single compression setting: quantization, sparsification, joint corruption, and post-corruption fine-tuning are all included.68d:T566,This is a skim paper, not one that requires line-by-line derivation. Focus on three parts.

First, read the method section for the main chain of ideas: why the Fisher can be written as a sum of Kronecker products, what exactly is approximated by truncation, and how Arnoldi avoids explicit matrix construction. If those three points are clear, the scalability story is clear.

Second, inspect the figures that visualize non-diagonal structure and layer coupling. Those are the core evidence that the method goes beyond diagonal or block-diagonal approximations. Pay particular attention to whether the value projection finding is stable across model families.

Third, read the joint corruption and post-corruption fine-tuning sections carefully. Those experiments are where cross-layer terms prove their practical value. A simple correlation with single-layer quantization damage would not be enough, because many weaker proxies could also achieve that.

A reasonable reading budget is 25–35 minutes. If time is tight, read the introduction, the method overview, the main experimental figures, and the complexity discussion. Two follow-up questions are worth keeping in mind: how reliable the empirical Fisher is as a Hessian proxy for pretrained LMs, and whether this low-rank Kronecker structure can be turned into a compression algorithm rather than remaining an analysis tool.68e:T981,HEAT makes the iteration count at each approximation site learnable. For every nonlinear function replaced by an iterative solver, the paper considers the sequence of intermediate approximations F0, F1, ..., Fn produced by successive solver steps. The iteration count is discrete and not directly differentiable, so the authors introduce a learnable distribution over possible step counts at each site. Instead of choosing a hard step count during training, the forward pass uses the expected approximation under that distribution. This makes the objective differentiable with respect to both the halting distribution and the model weights.

To bias the solution toward shallow approximations, the loss includes a KL penalty that pulls each site’s learned distribution toward a negative-binomial prior whose mode lies at low iteration counts. Task loss pushes in the opposite direction when more precision is actually needed. The result is a site-specific equilibrium: many locations collapse to fewer iterations, while sensitive locations retain more depth. The method also uses activation-range regularization so that intermediate values stay in numerically favorable regions for approximation, reducing error amplification.

A key design choice is joint adaptation. The paper argues that merely learning per-site iteration counts is not enough. If weights remain fixed, many sites cannot be pruned aggressively because the original model was never trained under those approximation errors. HEAT therefore fine-tunes the pretrained model under the same approximations it will face at encrypted inference time, allowing the weights to absorb part of the error introduced by shallower solvers. This is the main distinction from prior FHE work that either hand-tunes approximation fidelity or redesigns the network to be encryption-friendly.

The training procedure is staged. The paper describes a three-phase schedule that first stabilizes the iteration distributions, then jointly optimizes distributions and weights, and finally converts the soft distributions into deployable discrete iteration counts. This staged recipe matters because fully joint optimization from the start would mix approximation-policy drift with weight adaptation and can be unstable. Implementation-wise, all Fi come from a single solver rollout, and backward recomputes intermediate states from checkpointed inputs, keeping memory overhead manageable.68f:T630,The headline result is on encrypted GPT-2. HEAT reduces the total number of approximation iterations by 3.1×, lowers end-to-end decoding latency from about 54 s/token to about 38 s/token, and improves top-1 agreement with the plaintext parent model from 74% to 83%. That combination is important: the method is not simply trading away fidelity for speed, but recovering part of the lost accuracy through co-adaptation of weights and approximation budgets.

The most informative ablations compare three settings: fixed uniform iteration counts, learned per-site iteration counts without weight adaptation, and full HEAT with joint weight training. The gap between the second and third settings is central to the paper’s claim. Learning site-specific budgets helps, but joint training helps more because the model parameters internalize some of the approximation error. The paper also studies the effect of the KL regularization strength and the prior shape, which control the trade-off between preserving task quality and minimizing multiplicative depth.

Another useful empirical result is the learned heterogeneity across approximation sites. The model does not reduce all sites uniformly; instead, it allocates depth unevenly across layers and operations. That observation supports the main thesis that worst-case uniform approximation is systematically over-conservative. The site-level distributions are more revealing than the latency number alone, because they show that the gain comes from exploiting non-uniform error tolerance rather than from a generic compression trick.690:T4ad,Start with the introduction’s explanation of multiplicative depth and bootstrapping, because the rest of the method only makes sense once that bottleneck is concrete. After that, focus on three things: the exact loss decomposition, the staged training schedule, and the ablation comparing fixed budgets, learned budgets only, and learned budgets plus weight co-adaptation.

TIC-Bench organizes evaluation into three dimensions and eight task types. Logical Association includes Linear, Cyclic, and Convergent structures, covering single-chain tracking, revisiting earlier scenes, and merging multiple reasoning branches. Temporal Association includes Sequential, Retrospective, and Parallel settings, testing forward event tracking, backward evidence retrieval, and coordination across concurrent storylines. Spatial Association includes Map and Photo reasoning, where models must reconstruct relative positions from fragmented visual patches and interleaved textual descriptions. This design is useful for two reasons. It does not merely increase the number of images; it explicitly controls reasoning structure, which helps separate perceptual difficulty from evidence-organization difficulty. And it reduces the chance of answering from parametric knowledge alone, forcing stronger dependence on local contextual bindings. The paper also includes error analysis, highlighting abstraction errors and reasoning errors as dominant failure modes. That distinction is informative: the issue is not purely in visual recognition or purely in language reasoning, but in the intermediate cross-modal state representation that must preserve entity identity and support multi-step composition.694:T51c,TIC-Bench contains 2,280 questions spanning three domains and eight task types. The evaluation covers 10 state-of-the-art MLLMs and 15 inference settings, including standard and thinking variants for several open models. Three findings stand out. First, the human-model gap is large: the strongest model, GPT-5.5, reaches 59.9% overall accuracy, while the human baseline is 91.7%. That suggests the benchmark is not dominated by annotation noise; models genuinely lack this capability. Second, difficulty is highly structured. In logical tasks, Convergent reasoning is harder than Linear and Cyclic, indicating that branch merging is a persistent weakness. In temporal tasks, Parallel reasoning is the hardest, pointing to difficulty in maintaining multiple concurrent evidence streams. Third, the error analysis shows that abstraction and reasoning errors dominate over pure perception failures. This matters because it means a model may recognize local visual content correctly and still fail by losing entity mappings, confusing character states, or failing to combine distributed clues into a final answer. First is data curation. The authors collect 22,000 problems from 16 regional and international competition families plus online platforms, package them into executable evaluation environments, and explicitly exclude and deduplicate evaluation problems. They then use DeepSeek-V4-Flash to generate large synthetic reasoning-trace corpora: about 1.2M traces for the Nano model and 477,642 for the larger model. The key point is not just scale, but the organization of problems, reasoning, code, and feedback into long-context supervised examples.

Second is supervised fine-tuning. They start from Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B and perform long-context SFT to obtain competition-specialized models. Nano is a 30B-parameter MoE with 3B active parameters; Ultra is 550B with 55B active. The supervision appears to target not only final code generation but also intermediate problem-solving traces.

Third is reinforcement learning. RL is applied to Nano-CC, with rewards derived from executable evaluation, namely whether the generated program passes tests and how much score it obtains. This reward is attractive because it is automatic and closely aligned with the task objective. The downside is that it may favor search-friendly behaviors rather than robust one-shot generalization. The paper places RL after SFT, which is sensible: the action space in competitive programming is too large for pure RL to be stable without a strong initial policy.

Fourth is GenCorrect, the test-time closed-loop strategy. It is more than self-consistency. The system generates diverse candidate solutions, evaluates them, uses the feedback to refine later attempts, and operates under a limited submission budget. This is essentially verifier-guided search plus iterative program repair. It is especially well matched to IOI-style settings, where multiple submissions and partial credit are part of the environment.69c:T704,The main results are straightforward. On IOI 2025, Nemotron-3-Nano-CC improves from 130 Score@1 at baseline to 280 after SFT and 291 after RL. So SFT provides the dominant gain, while RL adds a smaller but real improvement. With five rounds of GenCorrect, the score rises to 468, above the gold threshold of 438.3. The size of that jump makes it clear that test-time search is a major contributor, arguably larger than RL in this setup.

Nemotron-3-Ultra-CC does not use code-specific RL. It reaches 304 with SFT alone, and 502.0 after five GenCorrect rounds. This suggests two things: larger base models still benefit from domain-specific SFT on hard coding tasks, and a strong base model plus strong inference-time search may be a more efficient path than a smaller model with additional RL.

The authors then build a competition-specific system for IOI 2026 and evaluate it live, before public release of the problems, under matched time, internet, and submission constraints. It reflects a full specialized system, including task-specific adaptation and inference strategy, not just the intrinsic capability of the underlying model.

It is a strong post-training and inference-system paper whose value for pretraining lies in what it reveals about executable supervision and reward quality.69e:T44d,DKL builds on task arithmetic. Given a base model θ_B and its instruction-tuned counterpart θ_I, the instruction-following vector is Δ_inst = θ_I - θ_B. New knowledge is learned by extended pretraining the base model on the target documents with the next-token objective, producing a knowledge vector Δ_know. The final model is obtained by adding the instruction vector and the knowledge vector to the base parameters, giving a model intended to retain instruction behavior while absorbing the new corpus. This avoids direct EPT on the instruct model, where instruction-following can be forgotten, and avoids generating massive synthetic QA for the entire corpus. A key implementation detail is embedding alignment: because the knowledge vector is trained from the base model but applied in a space involving the instruct model, token embeddings and chat-format tokens can introduce mismatch. DKL therefore uses the instruct model’s token embeddings during extended pretraining on the base model. Optionally, a small amount of synthetic QA supervision is added to improve recall at query time.69f:T4f0,The method is deliberately simple. It follows a read-compute-feedback-reread procedure. In the first pass, the model reads the original task and long context, then produces one or more reasoning traces. These traces are not assumed to be fully correct; they are treated as an observable textual proxy for latent task state. In the second pass, the collected traces are serialized as text T and prepended before the long-context block C. The model then rereads the context and answers. This is trace as state. The critical control is trace append: the second pass uses exactly the same trace text, but places it after the long context. That makes the comparison unusually clean. Both conditions have the same information content, similar token budget, and the same two-pass structure; the only difference is whether the trace can influence contextual encoding during rereading. The theoretical section provides the conceptual backbone. Using causal state update processors with finite working memory, the paper shows a worst-case exponential separation between condition-first and condition-last orders. The result is not a tight theorem about practical Transformers, but it serves as a strong design principle for causal sequence models operating on long contexts.6a0:T431,The empirical study spans 3 frontier models and 3 long-context benchmarks, yielding 27 reported model-task-metric combinations. The models are DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview, GLM-5.2, and Qwen 3.7 Max. The benchmarks are GraphWalks 256K, MRCRv2 8-needle, and NUB-1M, covering different long-context reasoning regimes. The headline result is strikingly consistent: trace as state outperforms trace append in 26 of 27 combinations. That consistency is the main empirical message. The paper also runs targeted ablations on GraphWalks 256K with DeepSeek V4 Pro Preview to test alternative explanations. These controls weaken the view that gains come merely from generic trace scaffolding or from leaking first-pass answers into the second pass. Instead, the evidence supports the placement hypothesis: putting the trace before the context is what allows it to function as state during rereading. The full paper appears to emphasize robustness across tasks more than one single large absolute gain, and the effect is strongest on tasks where maintaining evolving task state is central.6a1:T7e8,The setup is deliberately controlled. All models are trained on English Wikipedia, about 3.7B tokens, with article-level topic labels used to define three domains: a forget domain consisting of Biology articles, about 3.7% of tokens; an adjacent domain including Medicine and Health, Chemistry, and Earth and Environment; and a retain domain containing the rest. The architecture is fixed across runs: a 254M-parameter GPT-Neo-style transformer with 16 layers, hidden size 1024, 32 attention heads, and MLP width 4096. In each layer, the authors designate a tiny biology subnetwork: one attention head and 64 MLP hidden units. Everything else is treated as the non-biology subnetwork.

To control entanglement, they repurpose Selective Gradient Masking during pretraining. For biology examples, gradients to the non-biology parameters are zeroed after backprop, forcing biology knowledge to flow mainly into the biology subnetwork. For a sampled subset of non-biology examples, the biology subnetwork is zeroed in the forward pass, training the model to handle retain and adjacent data without relying on that specialized pathway. The remaining examples are trained normally. By varying the fraction of training steps that use SGTM, they produce six models with graded levels of disentanglement. This is the central design choice: the dataset and the downstream unlearning algorithms stay fixed, while the internal routing of knowledge during pretraining changes.

They then apply three standard unlearning methods to every model: Weighted Gradient Ascent, Weight Divergence Regularization, and RMU. The logic of the paper has two stages. First, show that the six models indeed span a meaningful range of disentanglement, using three separate metrics rather than relying on naming or training settings alone. Second, compare retain cost at matched forgetting levels. This makes the experiment much cleaner than prior studies that varied data mixtures or unlearning procedures and then attributed the outcome to entanglement.6a2:T5e8,The main result is consistent and easy to interpret: more disentangled models achieve better retain-forget trade-offs. At a fixed level of forgetting, the most disentangled model incurs about 4x lower retain cost than the most entangled one under WGA and RMU, and about 1.3x lower under WDR. That is large enough to suggest that entanglement is not a minor nuisance variable but a substantial driver of collateral damage in unlearning.

The experimental scale is moderate but well controlled: roughly 3.7B training tokens, 1024-token blocks, a forget domain that is 3.7% of the corpus, and a fixed 20% subsample of each test split used for unlearning sweeps and reporting. All models have the same 254M parameter count, which removes model-size variation as a confound.

Two details are especially worth noting. First, the adjacent domain is explicitly separated from the retain domain, which makes the setup more realistic than a simple biology-versus-rest split. It allows the paper to probe whether forgetting one domain also harms nearby knowledge. Second, the gain from disentanglement depends on the unlearning method: WGA and RMU benefit much more than WDR. That suggests an interaction between representation structure and the mechanics of the editing algorithm, rather than a single universal effect size. For a closer read, the exact definitions of the disentanglement metrics and the retain-cost / forget-level measures are important, because they determine how far the conclusions can be generalized.6a3:T435,This is a good skim for methodology rather than for direct algorithm adoption. Start with the introduction, where the paper clearly separates localization from entanglement and explains why earlier work did not isolate the latter. Then read the experimental setup carefully, especially the forward-pass and backward-pass interventions used by SGTM. That is the core experimental manipulation. After that, inspect the section that validates the disentanglement ordering across the six models; without that, the later unlearning comparison is much less convincing. Finally, read the retain-forget curves for WGA, WDR, and RMU and compare how sensitive each method is to the underlying representation structure.

If you only want the main takeaway, 20 to 30 minutes is enough. If you want to connect it back to pretraining, two follow-up questions are worth thinking about: whether controlled specialization hurts general modeling efficiency, and whether softer routing or optimization constraints could induce similar disentanglement in larger, more natural pretraining settings.6a4:T521,The method defines a Bayesian model over hypotheses h.
- Representation: each hypothesis is a pair (natural-language description, Python implementation). Language provides a compressible, flexible concept description; code provides an executable semantics.
- Prior p(h): favors shorter NL descriptions (an Occam/MDL-like bias implemented in the language channel).
- Likelihood p(e_t|h): scores how well the program’s execution matches the observed evidence at time t.
- Inference: exact posterior p(h|e_{1:t}) is intractable, so they use LLM-augmented Sequential Monte Carlo (LLM-SMC-S). Maintain K particles; for each new observation, use an LLM prompt as a bottom-up proposal q(h_{t+1}|e_{1:t+1}, particles), then importance-weight by prior×likelihood and resample; optionally “revise” particles to better fit new evidence.
- Inquiry: because the particle set encodes posterior uncertainty, the agent can choose questions/experiments that best discriminate among particles (information-gain style), closing the induction–inquiry loop.
Key distinction from common LLM reasoning setups: the LLM is not the final reasoner but a proposal generator; correctness pressure comes from executable constraints and Bayesian reweighting, and uncertainty is represented explicitly via multiple competing hypotheses.6a5:T8e7,APEx maintains two levels of experience. Instance-level memory stores summarized execution traces for concrete queries, preserving operational details that can later be retrieved. Category-level skills aggregate many experiences within a category-modality bucket and distill them into reusable procedural guidance. At inference time, a query q is routed to a bucket, relevant memories R_M(q) and the corresponding skill R_S(q) are retrieved, and both are packed into a structured context E(q). The Planner uses E(q) to generate a research plan. The Executor follows that plan through multi-turn tool interaction and produces a trajectory τ and a final answer. After execution, the trajectory is summarized into a new memory entry, and once enough fresh experience accumulates, the Distiller updates the category-level skill.

The key idea is not just hierarchical memory, but the Executor-Distiller-Planner loop. Planner converts retrieved experience into a task-specific plan, Executor interacts with tools, and Distiller abstracts new trajectories into procedural skills. These modules are trained with a three-stage alternating GRPO schedule rather than a single joint objective. The motivation is cross-module credit assignment: if everything is optimized end-to-end at once, it is difficult for final task reward to shape the quality of distilled skills in a stable way. Alternating optimization gives each module a cleaner relative-reward signal while the others are partially fixed. In that sense, skill distillation is treated as reward-guided policy learning, not prompt-based summarization.

Another notable component is skill-guided TTRL. During deployment, the Planner performs test-time reinforcement learning on unlabeled queries, while retrieved skills and memories act as procedural priors that regularize online adaptation. The model is therefore not exploring from scratch at test time; it adapts locally around previously distilled high-quality procedures. The resulting improved trajectories are then written back into memory and can later trigger skill updates. This is the main conceptual difference from standard memory-augmented retrieval: retrieval helps the current sample, but APEx is designed so that the current sample also improves future behavior.6a6:T64b,The headline result reported in the paper is an average score of 64.4% across deep research benchmarks. This is 14.7 points above GPT-5.4 and 3.0 points above the strongest memory-augmented baseline. For judging the method, the second comparison matters more, because it isolates the gain from experience organization and training rather than from a stronger base model.

The paper also highlights a context-efficiency result: a skill-only variant remains competitive while injecting fewer memory tokens. That supports the claim that category-level procedural skills are a more compact carrier of useful experience than flat trajectory retrieval. This matters for long-context agents, where the bottleneck is often not retrieval quality but context budget and retrieval noise.

From the full text, the experimental story appears to rely on three main ablation axes. First, replacing hierarchical experience with flat memory retrieval hurts performance, suggesting that instance memories and category skills play different roles. Second, removing reward-guided distillation or the alternating GRPO schedule degrades both skill quality and downstream task performance, supporting the claim that useful skills must be shaped by task reward. Third, removing skill-guided TTRL weakens online adaptation, indicating that test-time updates without procedural priors become high-variance exploration. The abstract does not provide all ablation numbers, so the main tables and appendix are the right place to verify effect sizes, benchmark composition, tool setup, and the exact definition of the no-ground-truth reward.6a7:T454,This is a skim paper rather than a line-by-line read. Start with the introduction and focus on how the authors separate episodic, reflective, and procedural memory, and why they insist that distillation must be coupled to downstream RL. Then jump to the method overview figure and trace the data flow: query routing, two-level retrieval, the Planner-Executor-Distiller loop, and TTRL. After that, read the alternating GRPO section carefully enough to understand which module is optimized in each stage, where the reward comes from, and why this is expected to be more stable than joint training. Finish with the main results and ablations, checking three questions: does hierarchical experience beat flat retrieval, does the skill-only variant really save context, and is the TTRL gain robust.

If time is limited, about 30 minutes is enough to understand the design. If you want to go deeper, inspect the appendix for retrieval details, bucket construction, reward design, and memory-update triggers. Those implementation choices are likely to determine whether the method transfers to other agent settings.6a8:T50c,The contribution is structured as definition → impossibility → quantitative characterization.
- Definition (epistemic Sybil resistance): marginal evidential contribution is measured by conditional mutual information I(Θ; Z | R). If it is zero, Z is merely an apparent new voice, not new evidence.
- Report-only identification barrier: different latent ancestry structures can induce the same observable report profile (including similarity/diversity patterns) yet require different Bayes-optimal posterior updates. Therefore, no aggregator that only sees report content can be generally correct.
- No-minting bound: descendants of fixed evidence cannot collectively contain unbounded information about Θ; there is a source-level ceiling.
- Gaussian shared-root model: reports are generated from a shared root signal plus extraction noise. The analysis shows (i) shared ancestry does not imply complete redundancy—repeated extraction can add information up to a ceiling; (ii) correlated extraction errors (e.g., agents sharing the same base model) accelerate saturation and reduce effective information gain.
- System implication: achieving epistemic Sybil resistance requires provenance interfaces or architectural constraints/estimation of dependence, not just text-based heuristics.6a9:T7de,The method has four layers. First, coordination is modeled as a bilevel game. The orchestrator is the leader, workers are followers, and the orchestrator emits a decomposition tau over subtasks. Workers generate local solutions, while the system seeks to maximize a global utility U. Because real systems are not independent across workers, the paper introduces weakly coupled decomposition using an interaction graph, pairwise coupling terms psi_ij, coupling strength kappa, and maximum neighborhood degree d_max. Under bounded coupling, the follower game becomes an approximate potential game, and the equilibrium slack is controlled by decomposition quality. Better decomposition means smaller mismatch between local incentives and global utility. Second, reflection is modeled as stochastic movement over a discrete semantic memory state space. The paper derives finite-time upper bounds for free-form reflection under a one-sided drift condition, proves worst-case tightness, and shows that without an additional persistent-harm condition, unconditional reflection cannot guarantee arbitrarily low error. Third, the paper studies the role of verification. It constructs two environments with identical text-generation laws but opposite semantics for the same reflections. Any gate that only sees the transcript, even if randomized and history-dependent, must behave identically in both environments and therefore cannot improve both. A grounded verifier, by observing external execution or environment feedback, can distinguish them and recover geometric convergence. Fourth, the paper proposes SRMA, Stochastic Reflective Memory Ascent. A candidate memory is committed only if a fixed grounded evaluation protocol certifies a strict decrease in verifier risk. Under calibration and non-degenerate corrective mass, the method achieves exact geometric or polynomial convergence rates. A confidence gate handles stochastic probes, and re-anchoring restores segment-wise convergence under piecewise stationarity.6aa:T467,The baseline objective interpolates standard next-token cross-entropy with a KL term between temperature-scaled teacher and student next-token distributions. The paper studies both forward KL and reverse KL, varying teacher size and the interpolation coefficient. The central analysis uses teacher predictive entropy as a diagnostic. Low-entropy teacher predictions tend to appear on procedural or highly constrained tokens, where the teacher distribution is sharp and informative. High-entropy predictions are common on unstructured web text and factual continuations with many plausible next tokens. In high-entropy regions, KD reduces the relative force of the one-hot ground-truth token compared with NTP, so it can slow the learning of facts that the student has not yet acquired. Switch Distillation follows directly from this analysis: use KD on low-entropy tokens and fall back to NTP on high-entropy tokens. The routing signal comes from the same teacher logits already needed for KD, so the method adds little overhead and differs from global fixes such as tuning alpha, changing KL direction, or scaling the teacher.6ab:T466,The controlled experiments use the OLMo-2 ecosystem, with 1B students and larger 7B/13B teachers, including instruction-tuned teachers. In pre-training, forward-KL distillation improves reasoning and factual recall over vanilla NTP. In mid-training, increasing distillation strength generally improves reasoning but hurts factual recall relative to NTP. This pattern is robust across teacher sizes, KL directions, and interpolation coefficients; no conventional KD objective Pareto-dominates NTP in mid-training. The entropy analysis supports the mechanism: teacher entropy varies strongly by data type, lower entropy correlates with higher-quality supervision, and the facts not yet learned at the start of mid-training tend to receive weaker teacher supervision. Switch Distillation improves the tradeoff. With an OLMo-2 7B Instruct teacher, it raises average reasoning by 71% and knowledge/commonsense by 19% over NTP, while reducing factual recall by only about 1 percentage point. After post-training, the gains persist: reasoning remains 32% higher, knowledge tasks improve by 20%, and the factual recall gap disappears.6ac:T867,The setup is simple and clean. Given a pretrained model of size N and a total annotation budget B, an allocation ratio r sends rB examples to SFT and (1-r)B to RL. Performance is written as P(N, r, B; tau). A standard formulation would optimize r* = argmax_r P, but the paper argues that this is the wrong target because post-training curves are often flat near the top. A tiny gain in measured score may not justify a full retraining run, and the exact argmax can be unstable under noise. The paper therefore defines the epsilon-near-optimal region: the set of ratios whose performance is at least (1-epsilon) times the best observed performance.

This shift enables three analyses. First, region characterization: the authors sweep allocation ratios across tasks, model families, and RL methods, then measure how wide the near-optimal region is under tolerances such as 2% to 10%. Second, scale transfer: instead of asking whether the exact optimum ratio matches across scales, they ask whether the near-optimal region found on a small proxy model covers high-performing ratios on a larger model. This is a much more stable transfer criterion. Third, asymmetric annotation cost: the default setup measures budget in number of labeled examples, but the paper extends the framework to cases where SFT and RL labels have different unit costs. Under that view, the effective optimum shifts, and the acceptable region can widen further when SFT data is relatively more expensive.

Relative to prior work, the novelty is in the problem formulation and the transfer criterion. Earlier work mostly reported broad trends, such as SFT being more important in low-data regimes and preference optimization becoming more useful at larger scales, but did not provide a principled near-optimal allocation framework or establish transfer from small to large models. Work on data mixture optimization and scaling-law extrapolation usually focuses on single-stage training, especially pretraining mixtures, not sequential SFT-then-RL coupling. The paper’s contribution is to turn a brittle tuning problem into a region-finding problem with practical transfer value.6ad:T6f4,The most important empirical findings are structural rather than benchmark-centric. First, the performance-versus-allocation curve typically has a broad plateau near its maximum. Even with small tolerances, such as a few percent from peak performance, the near-optimal region is already wide. Second, this region generally widens with model scale. Larger models are therefore more forgiving to imperfect SFT/RL splits. Third, transfer works better at the region level than at the exact-optimum level: a near-optimal region identified on a small proxy model tends to reliably contain high-performing allocations for a larger target model, even when the exact best ratio shifts. Fourth, the pattern is observed across tasks, model families, and both off-policy and on-policy RL settings, which argues against the effect being tied to one specific algorithm.

The paper also includes a useful cost sanity check. Using measured runtimes and L40S cloud pricing, per-example training compute cost is reported to range from about 2e-5 USD for the cheapest 1B SFT setting to about 3e-4 USD for 8B DPO. Compared with human annotation costs around 0.5 to 1.0 USD per example, compute is lower by roughly three to five orders of magnitude. Even compared with cheap synthetic annotation around 1e-3 USD per example, compute is still usually below annotation. This supports the paper’s decision to treat annotation as the dominant first-order budget axis.

The paper is less about headline absolute scores and more about curve geometry, region width, and transfer coverage. When reading the experiments, the key is not the single best number but how flat the top is, how the width changes with scale, and how much overlap exists between proxy-model and target-model high-performance regions.6ae:T563,Start with the introduction and preliminaries. The central conceptual move is the replacement of exact optimality with near-optimality. If that framing makes sense, the rest of the paper becomes straightforward. Anyone working on large-scale training pipelines can reuse the same lens for other multi-stage allocation problems, including continual pretraining versus SFT, SFT versus preference data, or allocation across multiple RL signal sources.6af:T778,The paper has two technical components: a measurement framework and a decoding intervention.

For measurement, the authors build a step-wise and position-wise analysis framework for masked diffusion language models. At each denoising step, the model predicts clean-token distributions for all positions, but only a subset of still-masked positions is committed. Using this structure, the paper tracks refusal-related token mass across denoising steps and response positions under harmful prompts. It distinguishes several events: whether refusal evidence appears at all, whether refusal tokens are committed, whether that commitment persists or gets overwritten, and how early commitments affect the final safety outcome.

This leads to the paper’s main conceptual finding: shallow-step alignment. The claim is that early denoising steps themselves form a safety-sensitive axis in dLLMs. Tokens committed early can strongly influence the final safety outcome even when they are not all at the leading response positions. Compared with shallow alignment in autoregressive models, diffusion models introduce an additional temporal dimension tied to denoising rather than surface order.

Based on that analysis, the paper proposes Refusal-Aware Early Commitment (RAEC), a training-free decoding method. RAEC changes only the commitment decision during decoding. If a refusal signal appears early and remains sufficiently strong and persistent, the decoder commits it early before later denoising dynamics can wash it out. Importantly, RAEC does not inject an external refusal template; it acts on refusal probability mass already produced by the model. This design is well matched to the diagnosed failure mode. If unsafe trajectories often contain weak or transient refusal evidence, then intervening at commitment time is a more targeted fix than retraining the model or attaching an external safety classifier.6b0:T6fc,The evaluation uses harmful-instruction benchmarks including JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT, with Llama-Guard-3-8B as the safety judge and Attack Success Rate (ASR) as the main metric. The tested models include masked diffusion LMs such as LLaDA and Dream.

The empirical findings come in three layers. First, the measurement results show that refusal signals are concentrated in early denoising steps and leading response positions, but these are not the same thing. Early-step commitments have a strong effect on final safety, supporting the shallow-step alignment hypothesis. The paper also includes intervention-style analyses: forcing early refusal commitment makes an unaligned base dLLM safer, while forcing early compliance commitment can push an aligned model toward unsafe outputs. That suggests early commitment is not just correlated with safety; it is a causal control point.

Second, the paper analyzes unsafe trajectories and finds that many of them do contain refusal evidence. The issue is that the refusal mass is weak, transient, or overwritten before commitment. Safe trajectories, in contrast, show stronger and more persistent refusal mass and much higher refusal-commitment rates. This is an important mechanistic refinement: the failure is often not “no refusal capability,” but “refusal evidence does not survive to commitment.”

Third, RAEC reduces ASR on both LLaDA and Dream while largely preserving utility. The provided text does not include the full result tables, so it would be unsafe to quote exact deltas here. When reading the original paper, the key numbers to verify are the ASR reductions on each benchmark, the utility trade-off on benign prompts, and the sensitivity to the thresholds controlling early commitment and refusal persistence.6b1:T57f,This is a good skim paper for readers interested in mechanism rather than only safety application. Start with the Introduction and Preliminaries to understand the commitment process in masked diffusion LMs: the model predicts all positions at every step, but commits only some masked positions. Without that, the later analysis is easy to misread.

Then focus on the measurement framework and the visualizations. Finally, check the benchmark tables for gains on LLaDA and Dream over JailbreakBench and StrongREJECT, and inspect the utility cost. A first pass should take around 30 minutes. If reading more deeply, pair the intervention experiments with the ablations.6b2:T47e,FFD combines content-aware scanning, a top-δ selection rule, and a fused selector-compute kernel. Instead of storing separate metadata such as centroids, partial-dimensional keys, or geometric bounds, it scans a compressed representation of the K cache itself. The K cache is decomposed into low-bit quantized thumbnails, used for fast query-key similarity estimation, plus a residual path for fidelity. The selection rule, top-δ, filters blocks according to their estimated contribution to the attention score sum. This differs from top-k, which imposes a fixed budget regardless of the attention entropy, and from top-p, which requires global probability accumulation. The paper argues that blocks whose contribution is below a numerically motivated threshold have negligible effect on the final attention output, and that the criterion can be approximately parallelized because LLM attention is often highly concentrated. At the systems level, FFD fuses scanning, selection, and attention computation into one kernel so that the compute phase reuses the selector’s intermediate estimates and avoids redundant HBM traffic and reduction bubbles.6b3:T6b6,The main idea is to decompose a standard MoE expert into composable internal sub-transformations and execute path compositions instead of whole experts. The paper builds on the common SwiGLU-style FFN expert used in models such as Mixtral and Qwen-MoE. In a vanilla expert, the input goes through parallel gate and up projections on the expansion side, then through element-wise gating, and finally through a down projection back to the hidden dimension. Standard MoE routing treats this entire computation as one atomic unit. PCoMoE instead turns it into a path-level execution space.

That creates a combinatorial problem: once internal components can be recombined, the number of possible paths can explode, which would hurt both quality and runtime. To control this, the paper introduces compatibility-aware gating and layer-wise pruning. Compatibility-aware gating suppresses low-value off-diagonal combinations, keeping only structurally plausible or useful path compositions. Layer-wise pruning further reduces the path space according to layer sensitivity, preserving more flexibility where the model is fragile and pruning more aggressively where redundancy is higher. Importantly, vanilla expert paths remain available, so the method augments rather than replaces the original execution graph.

The runtime design is a central part of the contribution. The authors propose a hardware-friendly execution engine that groups active paths by source and shares expansion-side operations, aiming to convert path-level flexibility into actual speedups instead of scheduling chaos. This system co-design is essential. Without it, the extra path freedom would likely be canceled out by dispatch and batching overhead.6b4:T4e5,From the provided full-text content, the main reported outcomes are end-to-end speedup and task accuracy. PCoMoE achieves up to 1.31x serving speedup, which is a meaningful gain if measured under realistic MoE serving conditions rather than isolated kernel benchmarks. The paper also claims up to 10% accuracy improvement over vanilla MoE baselines on downstream tasks. That number should be read carefully in the original tables, since it is likely task-specific or relative rather than a uniform absolute gain.

The most important ablations to inspect are likely the effect of compatibility-aware pruning, the sensitivity of different layers to path pruning, and the contribution of the runtime grouping strategy to actual throughput. Without those, it would be hard to tell whether the gains come from the path formulation itself or from a stronger execution backend. Another key point is the quality-efficiency frontier: whether PCoMoE is faster at matched quality, or more accurate at matched latency. Those are different claims with different implications.
