At scale, Pixel Linguist II is trained on 280M examples and is evaluated on English, cross-lingual, and multilingual Visual STS, ViDoRe visual document retrieval, and as a vision encoder inside multimodal LLMs. The model also remains robust when up to 80% of visual tokens are compressed, which matters for document retrieval and serving cost. The provided text does not include the full numeric tables, so the most reliable signal is the structure of the ablations and their failure cases.6eb:T816,The method has two stages. First is AHAF, Adversarial Hallucination Attribute Flipping. Instead of using adversarial perturbations for standard classification attacks, the paper uses PGD to flip the model’s object-existence judgment on the same image, for example from present to absent or vice versa. This produces paired images that are semantically almost identical, with differences concentrated around the visual cues that move the model across a hallucination boundary. That is the key distinction from ordinary contrastive fine-tuning with random negatives: random negatives change too many factors at once, such as scene, object identity, and background, so the model can still solve the task through coarse spatial shortcuts.

Second is ACFT, Adversarial Contrastive Fine-Tuning. The model is fine-tuned with a contrastive objective built on AHAF-generated pairs, pulling correct image-text pairs together and pushing apart representations associated with hallucination-inducing perturbations. The important design choice is not merely the use of contrastive loss, but the controlled negative construction. Positive and negative samples share nearly all image content; the only systematic difference is the perturbation that flips the hallucination attribute. That makes the learning signal much more focused on the visual decision boundary.

AHAF also serves as a probe. If tiny pixel-level perturbations can flip the answer, then the visual representation is already sitting close to a fragile decision boundary even on clean inputs. That observation is more general than the specific method: many hallucination mitigation techniques may improve outputs without actually moving the underlying visual representation into a more stable region.

Compared with prior methods, VCD, OPERA, and VTI are more inference-time or post-hoc control methods; RLHF and DPO variants mainly reshape output preference; ordinary OCFT lacks targeted negatives. ACFT differs by directly training against the diagnosed visual misalignment mechanism, with no extra inference cost.6ec:T7ee,The most informative evidence comes from three groups of experiments.

First, diagnostic evidence. On LLaVA v1.5, hallucinated samples show much worse image-text embedding alignment than correct samples: average cosine similarity is 0.158 for correct cases versus -0.122 for hallucinated ones. Grad-CAM analysis shows an inverted attention pattern. When the target object is present, hallucinated cases have more dispersed attention; when the object is absent, they show overly concentrated attention on irrelevant regions. Using normalized Shannon entropy over 500 hallucinated and 500 non-hallucinated samples, entropy is 5.1% higher for hallucinated cases when the object is present, and 6.2% lower when the object is absent. This supports a visual-perception failure rather than pure language-side fabrication.

Second, causal intervention. The paper perturbs the visual side directly. On POPE, adding Gaussian noise, downsampling the image, or replacing the visual encoder with a weaker one reduces average accuracy from 0.842 to the 0.739-0.822 range. Replacing it with a stronger SigLIP-SO400M encoder raises accuracy to 0.864. This is an important step beyond correlation: changing visual feature quality systematically changes hallucination behavior.

Third, mitigation results. ACFT uses only 0.9% of COCO for fine-tuning and outperforms VCD, OPERA, VTI, and post-training approaches such as LLaVA-RLHF and DPO variants on POPE and MME, while preserving general visual understanding. The full tables are not included in the provided excerpt, but the paper repeatedly emphasizes three properties: high data efficiency, zero inference overhead, and a clear gain over ordinary contrastive fine-tuning because the negatives are controlled rather than random.

For a careful read, the most useful experimental sections are the OCFT versus ACFT comparison, the target-versus-non-target similarity-gap analysis, and the encoder-strength ablations. Those explain why the method works, not just that it improves benchmark scores.6ed:T509,Read it as a diagnosis-to-training paper. Start with the two findings and the causal validation in the introduction. The key question is whether the authors really close the loop from observation to intervention. Then go to the AHAF construction in the methods: how the PGD objective is defined, how the perturbation is constrained so it flips the hallucination attribute rather than destroying semantics, and how the paired samples enter the contrastive loss. That is where the paper either becomes a targeted hallucination method or collapses into generic adversarial robustness training.

In the experiments, prioritize four parts: the image-text similarity and Grad-CAM entropy analysis, the visual-side intervention studies, ACFT versus OCFT and prior mitigation methods, and the retention of general visual comprehension. If time is limited, Figures 1 to 3 and the main result tables are enough to capture the main argument in about 25 to 35 minutes.

Two deeper questions are worth keeping in mind. First, does AHAF mainly improve local robustness around adversarial boundaries, or does it genuinely improve broader visual alignment? Second, will the same mechanism hold for natively pretrained multimodal models, or is it especially suited to connector-style systems such as LLaVA?6ee:T524,The method is Adaptive Multi-Reward Projection, or AMRP. Instead of using a fixed weighted sum of reward dimensions throughout training, AMRP updates the projection weights online based on training dynamics. It uses three signals.

The first is relative shortfall, which measures whether a reward dimension is lagging behind the others. If a dimension remains under-optimized, its weight is increased. The second is reward volatility, which tracks instability in a dimension. High volatility suggests that the policy has not stabilized there, so AMRP keeps attention on it. The third is recent progress, which measures whether a dimension is improving, stagnating, or regressing. Saturated and stable dimensions get down-weighted; stagnant or regressing dimensions get up-weighted.

This design addresses the two identified failure modes in a practical way. It does not eliminate the information loss of scalarization entirely, but it reduces persistent aliasing by making the projection time-varying rather than static. More importantly, it counters shortcut lock-in by reallocating learning pressure toward neglected dimensions. Compared with manual reward tuning or simple normalization, the key difference is that AMRP is driven by observed reward dynamics during training rather than by fixed prior assumptions.6ef:T4a0,The evaluation covers three multi-reward settings: rule-based mathematical reasoning, citation-grounded generation with automatic evaluators, and open-ended alignment using learned reward-model scores. The main empirical claim is that AMRP consistently improves downstream performance across all three, with especially strong gains in math reasoning and citation-grounded generation, and smaller but still consistent gains in the more correlated open-ended alignment setting.

The paper also provides mechanism-level evidence. It shows that under static aggregation, training is often dominated early by dense rewards such as format or length, while harder dimensions such as correctness remain under-optimized. AMRP changes the reward-profile dynamics by shifting weight toward lagging or unstable dimensions, which leads to more balanced profiles over time. Another useful result is compatibility: the method composes with PPO, GRPO, and GDPO, suggesting that it is best viewed as a reward-aggregation module rather than a replacement for the RL optimizer itself. The emphasis is less on one dramatic benchmark number and more on consistent gains plus healthier reward trajectories.6f0:T793,The method, TUSA, inserts a training-free cognitive arbiter between the base model policy πθ and the weak specialist πϕ. Instead of combining the two distributions at every step, the system first lets the base model propose a candidate token and then decides whether the specialist is allowed to intervene. The decision is made by a gate defined through a Joint Necessity Score.

That score combines two signals. The first is supervisor confidence, operationalized mainly through token-level entropy of the specialist distribution. Low entropy means the specialist has a sharper belief over the next token and is more likely to provide meaningful guidance. The second is semantic saliency. The paper argues that many decoding positions carry little semantic load, so spending intervention budget on function words or low-information tokens is wasteful even if the specialist is confident there.

The arbiter activates only when both conditions hold: the specialist is confident enough, and the current token is semantically important enough. This is stronger than a plain entropy threshold. Confidence alone would still trigger many low-value interventions; saliency alone would allow the specialist to overwrite the base model even when it is unsure. Their conjunction turns alignment into trust-based arbitration rather than continuous supervision.

Conceptually, the contribution is less about a new learned reward model and more about a new control logic at decoding time. Compared with dense guidance methods such as MARA-style token-level steering, TUSA changes three things: intervention becomes event-triggered rather than always-on; authorization depends on uncertainty-aware gating rather than fixed fusion; and the objective shifts from maximizing supervision coverage to minimizing harmful low-confidence interference. In that sense, the method is closer to abstention and selective prediction than to stronger supervision.6f1:T630,The experiments address two questions: whether weak specialists are indeed persistently uncertain, and whether sparse intervention outperforms dense intervention. Evaluations are conducted on Mistral- and Llama-family backbones over both general preference benchmarks and safety benchmarks.

First, the paper validates the phenomenon directly. Figure 2 shows entropy profiles of the specialist across domains. Entropy is frequently close to the theoretical maximum for a large fraction of tokens, and this high uncertainty often persists along the generation trajectory. This supports the claim that the confidence–intervention mismatch is structural rather than anecdotal.

Second, on end metrics, TUSA reduces intervention overhead by roughly 50% relative to the dense baseline. At the same time, it improves Preference Rate by up to 12.0% on general benchmarks and by up to 15.6% on safety benchmarks. The key point is that gains come from fewer but better interventions, not from stronger or more frequent overwriting.

Third, the analysis suggests that sparse gating better preserves valid reasoning paths from the base model. Dense methods are more likely to derail correct trajectories when the specialist is uncertain. Ablations indicate that removing either uncertainty or semantic saliency weakens performance, implying the two signals are complementary. The paper is especially useful for its utility–safety trade-off analysis: the method does not simply increase refusal behavior, but improves alignment while preserving more of the base model’s original competence.6f2:T42b,Read it with one question in mind: when should a decoding-time controller abstain? Start with the introduction and Figures 1–2. They contain the main empirical claim and explain why the paper is not merely proposing another gating heuristic. Then focus on the method section where the dense aligned policy is reformulated into a conditional intervention policy. The most important part is how the Joint Necessity Score is built and why both uncertainty and semantic saliency are required.

In the experiments, prioritize three pieces. First, the entropy distribution plots and trajectory-level uncertainty analysis. Second, the trade-off between intervention rate and preference/safety outcomes. Third, the ablations comparing full TUSA against entropy-only, saliency-only, and threshold variants. A quick read takes about 30 minutes. A deeper read should examine whether entropy is a sufficient proxy for local supervisory competence, and whether the same arbitration logic could be extended to verifier-guided decoding, reward models, or multi-supervisor systems.6f3:T671,OSW-FT keeps the standard expert trajectory as the optimization target, but rescales its loss online. For each query q, the current model runs K inference-only rollouts to estimate a pass rate p-hat(q). The usual SFT loss on the expert output o* is then multiplied by (1 - p-hat(q)). Queries the model already solves reliably get downweighted; unresolved frontier queries get larger updates.

The design choice is important. The method does not optimize on sampled trajectories, does not apply token-level reward shaping, and does not alter the training distribution. The rollout is used only to estimate a scalar weight. This sharply separates it from PPO/GRPO-style methods, where the sampled trajectories both define the learning signal and receive the update.

The theoretical framing is built for binary-verifiable reasoning. The authors start from expected correctness, apply the score-function trick, and introduce a query-dependent control variate. This yields a variance-reduced estimator whose optimal baseline depends on the model’s success probability on that query. That connection motivates why scaling the expert log-likelihood gradient by a function of success rate is sensible. They further argue that with finite K, the Monte Carlo estimate remains unbiased for the exact OSW-FT surrogate update, so rollout noise affects variance but not the target update itself.

Conceptually, this is best read as online difficulty-aware SFT rather than offline RL or reward-weighted regression. The online component estimates whether an example is still informative; the offline expert trajectory still specifies what the model should learn.6f4:T5a9,The experiments use Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 4B parameters on binary-verifiable reasoning benchmarks including AIME, AMC, MATH-500, and GPQA-Diamond. The empirical claim is deliberately modest: OSW-FT consistently improves over standard SFT at small-to-medium scales, but it is not presented as a universal replacement for GRPO.

The results support four main points. First, adaptive online weighting beats uniform SFT across multiple model sizes, which suggests that competence-aware reweighting is useful even when the supervision target stays fixed. Second, under limited rollout budgets, OSW-FT often offers a better compute-performance trade-off because it only needs a few inference-only samples per query and avoids the full RL optimization loop. Third, the comparison with GRPO is mixed in the expected way: OSW-FT is favorable in several low-budget settings, while GRPO remains stronger in some configurations. Fourth, the ablations matter: continuous success-rate weighting outperforms hard-thresholding and random weighting, indicating that the gain comes from a smooth online estimate of current competence rather than generic sample reweighting.

The provided full text excerpt does not include all table values, so exact benchmark deltas are not fully recoverable here. Still, the paper is clear about the pattern it wants to establish: consistent gains over SFT across 0.6B–4B models, especially when rollout budget is constrained.6f5:T486,The paper connects MH acceptance ratios to Bradley–Terry (BT) choice models. Under BT, the odds of preferring x over y equal exp(u(x)-u(y)), which matches the unnormalized density ratio needed by MH for a Gibbs target. The obstacle is that the algorithm cannot query the comparison probability itself—only draw Bernoulli preference samples. The authors prove an impossibility result: any fixed-budget plug-in estimator of the acceptance ratio (estimate win probabilities then substitute into MH) cannot implement the oracle acceptance rule and can arbitrarily distort the stationary distribution. Pref-MH avoids estimating probabilities and instead designs a randomized accept/reject mechanism whose marginal acceptance probability exactly matches the Hastings ratio implied by the preference odds (plus proposal correction). With this construction, detailed balance holds in expectation, yielding an exact stationary distribution while using only a fixed number of binary comparisons per transition. The method is stated for general state spaces and arbitrary proposal kernels, positioning it as a general-purpose MCMC wrapper around preference oracles.6f6:T4b6,The proposed mechanism is trait-direction drift:
- Define a teacher-side preference gap for each sample (p,r) as the log-likelihood difference between a biased system prompt and a set of neutral prompts, with a length-normalized variant to compare variable-length completions.
- Use an empirically motivated low-rank/logit-linear factorization of the prompt-by-sample log-probability matrix (via SVD-like geometry): prompt embeddings ψ(s) and sample embeddings φ(p,r) explain why certain “innocent” samples still carry trait signal.
- Argue (and test) that student SFT updates contain a component aligned with a recognizable trait direction; across steps this component accumulates beyond noise, producing measurable drift and eventually behavioral transfer (preference shifts or higher misalignment rates).
- Introduce probe-space corridor regularization: monitor the student’s coordinate along a probed trait/steering subspace and penalize deviations outside a corridor, limiting motion along the trait direction while keeping general task learning largely intact.
The paper also studies why cross-model subliminal transfer is weaker than same-model transfer, using diagnostics and interventions.6f7:T897,方法叫 FactAgent，核心由两部分组成：fact-centric agent state，以及基于 Bayesian fact utility estimation 的 dense process supervision。

先看 agent 形式。与标准 ReAct 只维护原始对话和工具返回文本不同，FactAgent 在状态里显式维护一个 fact store。每次 search 动作得到 observation 后，agent 不只是继续推理，还可以执行 assert 动作，把 observation 里的信息抽取成结构化事实，写入 fact store。这样，状态从“越来越长的文本历史”变成“问题 Q、当前 observation、累计事实集合 Ft”。作者把这些事实视为离散语义单元，而不是普通字符串，这一步是后续 credit assignment 的基础。

再看奖励构造。论文的关键不是直接给 assert 打启发式分，而是从 group rollouts 里估计事实的后验效用。具体做法是先把语义等价的事实聚成 cluster，避免同一证据因表述不同被分散统计；然后基于一组 rollout 的最终 outcome，用 Bayesian estimation 推断每个 fact cluster 与成功结果的统计关联。直观上，如果某类事实经常出现在成功轨迹里、较少出现在失败轨迹里，它的 posterior utility 就更高。随后，这个 fact-level utility 被映射回 step-level dense rewards，用来训练 policy。

这比直接做 token-level process reward 更适合搜索任务，因为搜索任务的有效中间单位不是 token，也不一定是整句 reasoning，而是“找到并确认了哪条证据”。作者因此把 credit assignment 的对象从 action surface form 转成 evidence semantics。和纯 outcome-based GRPO 相比，FactAgent 仍然利用 group rollouts，但不再让整条轨迹共享同一个粗粒度 advantage，而是通过事实聚类和后验估计，把奖励分配到真正有贡献的中间步骤上。

从设计取舍看，这个方法避免了额外训练 reward model，也不依赖人工标注每一步是否正确，代价则是需要可靠的事实抽取与聚类。如果抽取质量差，后验 utility 估计会被噪声污染。全文也承认这一点，因此 fact store 既是方法优势，也是误差传播的主要入口。6f8:T89d,FactAgent has two main components: a fact-centric state representation and a Bayesian utility estimation scheme for dense process supervision.

On the agent side, the paper departs from standard ReAct-style agents that keep only raw text history. The state explicitly includes a fact store. After a search action returns an observation, the agent can take an assert action that extracts structured facts from the observation and writes them into the store. The state is therefore represented as the question, the current observation, and the accumulated fact set. These facts are treated as discrete semantic evidence units rather than plain text snippets. This is important because the method assigns credit at the level of evidence semantics, not at the level of surface-form actions.

On the reward side, the paper estimates fact utility from grouped rollouts. Semantically equivalent facts are first clustered so that the same evidence is not split across multiple textual variants. Then, using final outcomes from a group of trajectories, the method performs Bayesian estimation of the posterior utility of each fact cluster. Intuitively, if a fact cluster appears disproportionately often in successful trajectories, its posterior utility increases. These fact-level utilities are then converted into dense step-level rewards for policy optimization.

This differs from standard outcome-based GRPO, where all steps in a trajectory inherit the same coarse trajectory-level signal. Here, group rollouts are still used, but the reward is redistributed through an explicit evidence layer. That makes the method better matched to search tasks, where the meaningful intermediate unit is often not a token or a reasoning sentence, but a retrieved and validated piece of evidence.

The design also avoids training an external reward model and does not require human annotation of intermediate steps. The trade-off is that the whole pipeline depends on the quality of fact extraction and fact clustering. If those are noisy, the posterior utility estimates can be corrupted. The paper is aware of this: the fact store is both the main strength of the method and the main source of possible error propagation.6f9:T5ef,The experiments use Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct backbones and evaluate on seven QA benchmarks. The headline result is that with the 7B backbone, FactAgent reaches an average EM of 51.2, outperforming the strongest baseline by +3.2 EM. The paper emphasizes that the gains are consistent across benchmarks rather than driven by a single dataset.

The more informative findings come from the analysis. The dense process supervision mainly improves evidence precision and retrieval quality. That matches the method design: the reward does not simply encourage more search, but encourages finding useful evidence and committing it into the explicit state.

The ablations likely cover the main components: removing the fact store, removing the assert action, disabling fact clustering, or replacing Bayesian posterior utility with simpler statistics. From the full-text description, the explicit fact representation and the utility estimation module are the most important contributors. Another practical point is that the method derives dense rewards directly from grouped rollout outcomes, without relying on an external reward model, which makes the training setup lighter and easier to scale.

The current evidence mainly supports search-heavy QA agents. Whether the same approach transfers to broader web agents, coding agents, or longer-horizon multi-tool settings depends on whether “facts” remain the right intermediate abstraction and whether fact extraction stays reliable in those environments.6fa:T427,Start with the introduction and preliminaries to see that the paper changes more than the reward function. It jointly changes the state representation, the action space, and the reward decomposition. Then focus on three technical pieces: how the fact store is defined, how the assert action extracts and writes facts, and how Bayesian utility estimation is computed from grouped rollouts. The key questions while reading are: what exactly counts as a fact, how semantic equivalence is handled, and how posterior fact utility is mapped back to step-level rewards.

In the experiments, prioritize the main results table, the analyses on evidence precision and retrieval quality, and the ablations on fact store and utility estimation. A skim in about 40 minutes is enough to capture the main idea. A deeper read should ask whether explicit intermediate state could replace part of free-form chain-of-thought in reasoning RL, and whether fact-level credit assignment could generalize to code execution states, web interaction states, or multimodal tool trajectories.6fb:T53e,The method has two main components. The evaluation pipeline samples from roughly 100k monthly production queries while balancing diversity and representativeness. Uniform sampling preserves the production distribution but keeps many near-duplicate templates. Diversity-first sampling increases coverage but distorts the service and task mix. The paper introduces a template-aware sampler: mask variable spans, cluster near-identical normalized prompts with LSH, select diverse examples within each template using greedy max-min over variable spans, and allocate budget proportional to the square root of template count. Scoring is task-specific. Classification and information extraction, about 63.2% of traffic, use reference-based evaluation with gold answers generated by Kimi-K2.5 and checked by annotators. Open-ended summarization and generation use side-by-side judging augmented with checklist-style rubrics. The training recipe starts from Qwen3-32B with a Cyrillic-dense tokenizer and runs in non-reasoning mode for latency and cost reasons. It performs a combined SFT stage, then trains separate GRPO experts for instruction following, function calling, and internal task-distribution alignment. The experts are merged with two-stage SLERP in weight space to avoid cross-domain reward interference from a single joint RL objective.6fc:T4a5,The deployed adapted model absorbed 50% of platform traffic six months after rollout, corresponding to 116 million requests per month from more than 200 internal applications. On benchmark construction, the template-aware sampler reaches a mean pairwise TF-IDF cosine distance of 0.953 while keeping Jensen-Shannon distances lower than pure diversity sampling, indicating better coverage without strongly drifting from production mix. For judging, a uniform side-by-side LLM judge has limited agreement with experts, with Cohen’s kappa around 0.62 and task-dependent errors. After task routing, the LLM task classifier matches human consensus 90.6% to 99.6% of the time. The final task-specific judging pipeline improves agreement: reference-based subtasks rise from kappa 0.63 to 0.88, and open-ended content-generation subtasks rise from 0.57 to 0.72. For content generation, explicit per-criterion grading plus an overall verdict reaches kappa 0.79. The authors also release an open-weight checkpoint trained without internal data and report that it is close to the deployed model on public benchmarks, suggesting that the recipe contributes substantially beyond private traffic data.6fd:T43e,1) Controlled conflict setup: a fact-retrieval prompt template that mimics multimodal RAG—textual supplied context (containing a plausible but counterfactual answer) + entity (either name text or an image) + query. Only the entity modality changes.
2) Dataset: a curated benchmark of 37K conflicting fact pairs across celebrities, buildings, and artworks.
3) Validity filtering: they keep only instances where the model can (a) identify the entity and (b) recall the parametric fact when no conflict is present, so the measured effect is conflict resolution rather than recognition failure.
4) Mechanistic claim: for textual entities, attention detects the conflict and suppresses early-layer MLPs associated with factual recall (building on the “MLPs store facts” line of work). For visual entities, entity resolution is slower, so the suppression does not happen in time, leading to more parametric answers.
5) Prompt interventions: CoT prompting does not close the modality gap; adding more image-grounded contextual information reduces the parametric bias for visual entities.6fe:T49c,They operate on Cross-layer Transcoders (CLTs), which learn a shared sparse dictionary spanning all layers (a cross-depth latent space), enabling analysis beyond single-layer SAEs.
They compare three latent-selection methods:
- ValSel: select latents with language-distinct activation magnitudes (mean activation differences), using an l-monolinguality score.
- FreqSel: select latents that activate more frequently for a target language, with a specificity threshold T and corpus/token coverage constraints (N%, M%).
- AnnSel: trace attribution graphs with Circuit Tracer, prune to high-importance paths, then filter latents by LLM-generated annotations that explicitly mention the target language (favoring interpretability).
Given per-language latent sets, they test four intervention families at inference:
- Target amplification (set target latents to mean nonzero activations from target-language data).
- Distractor zero ablation (zero latents for the context language or all non-target languages).
- Distractor direction ablation (remove residual projections along distractor latent directions; one-layer vs multi-layer).
- Combined interventions (e.g., Zero+Amp, 1L+Amp).6ff:T6bc,The main technical contribution is an analysis-ready perturbation framework plus a mechanistic probing pipeline. Existing adversarial summarization datasets are usually too coarse for causal tracing because they modify text at the sentence or document level. The authors instead build paired clean/corrupt summaries with explicit token-level modification maps. They define eight localized perturbation types spanning two quality axes, Readability and Adequacy, while controlling perturbation intensity through a parameter k and preserving exact token positions of edits.

Using this setup, they analyze two judge models: Themis, built on Llama-3-8B, and Prometheus, built on Mistral-7B. The experiments combine causal tracing, logit-lens vocabulary projection, and attention-head knockout. The central finding is a two-stage internal evaluation process. Lower layers, especially attention modules, are mainly involved in defect identification and signal routing. Upper-layer MLPs integrate those signals into a final rating, with the score becoming sharply encoded in the residual stream at a late layer. The paper also shows criterion-specific attention behavior: readability errors spread across nearby syntactic context, while adequacy-related perturbations stay more localized around the modified tokens.

Another useful result is the comparison with the base model. Fine-tuning does not appear to create the evaluation pipeline from scratch. The base Llama-3-8B already exhibits a routing-like substrate and late-layer score crystallization. Judge fine-tuning mainly modifies that substrate by suppressing low-layer MLP contribution at the last position and moving the crystallization point earlier by about two layers.700:T4b2,The most important results are mechanistic. Both judges show a consistent stage split: below roughly layer 15, attention dominates error detection and routing; around layers 25 to 26, the final rating becomes sharply represented. Themis writes the score in a more concentrated top-layer step, while Prometheus distributes the write across mid-to-late layers and applies an opposite-direction correction at the final layer. The comparison to base Llama-3-8B is also notable: the base model already contains much of the routing structure, and judge fine-tuning mainly reshapes information flow rather than inventing a new circuit.

The perturbation analysis further shows that different error types induce different attention patterns. Readability defects recruit broader local context, whereas adequacy defects remain more tightly centered on the perturbed tokens. This suggests that criterion-specific supervision could be a sensible design direction for future evaluator training.

If reading selectively, the key is not every individual attack category but the connection between token-level perturbation maps, score shifts, and layer-wise decomposition of attention, MLP, and residual contributions.701:T899,论文的技术路线分三步。

第一步是现象隔离。作者比较 released VLM 与对应 reference LLM 的文本能力差距，并引入 text-only further-training 对照，以及共享 base LLM 的 VL-versus-text matched trajectory，说明损失不是一般继续训练都会发生，而是和视觉模态适配强相关。损失最明显的不是开放式知识问答，而是那些对表面 token 格式、答案边界、最终输出规则很敏感的任务。

第二步是机制诊断。作者把问题归因到 attention-sink corruption。现代 LLM 往往会把大量注意力质量集中到少数早期位置，这些位置的 hidden state 又被少数高幅值固定特征维度主导，形成 sink。论文的假设是，这种 sink 有助于稳定每个位置对关键表面 token 的注意力分配，从而支撑格式敏感任务。VL fine-tuning 会扰动 query/key 投影 Wq、Wk；由于 logit shift 会随输入幅值放大，这种扰动在 sink 位置被特别放大，导致 per-head sink collapse。作者进一步分析不同 QK normalization 设计的差异：如果是 per-head QK-RMSNorm，可以直接去掉对原始输入幅值的显式依赖；如果只是 layerwise normalization，则每个 head 的尺度仍受整层能量分配影响，弱 head 会被进一步压缩，因此到 VL 训练开始前，某些 backbone 的 per-head sink 已经偏弱。

第三步是预测指标与干预验证。作者提出 Sink Strength，一个只在 base LLM 上通过少量 forward pass 计算的标量，用来量化 head-level sink concentration。这个指标不需要做任何 VL 训练，就能预测后续多模态适配后的文本能力损失。然后他们把 base-side sink weakness 与 post-VL gap perturbation 结合起来，区分“骨干先天脆弱”和“VL 更新额外破坏”两部分。最后做两个负对照：一是在预训练后给模型补装 QK-RMSNorm 再去做 VL 训练，发现不能复现原生架构自带的保护效果；二是对已经训练好的 VLM 做多种 weight merging，也无法把丢失的文本能力救回来。这说明问题更像训练过程中的 head-level 结构破坏，而不是事后线性修补能解决的。702:T843,The paper proceeds in three stages.

First, it isolates the phenomenon. The authors compare released VLMs against their reference LLM backbones on a text-only evaluation suite, and add text-only further-training controls plus a matched VL-versus-text training trajectory from the same base model. This is meant to show that the degradation is not just a generic consequence of continued training, but is tied to multimodal adaptation.

Second, it proposes a mechanism: attention-sink corruption. Many modern LLMs place a large fraction of attention mass on a few early positions. Those positions are dominated by a small set of high-magnitude feature dimensions and act as sinks. The paper argues that these sinks help stabilize attention allocation in ways that matter for tasks graded on exact output form. During VL fine-tuning, perturbations to the query and key projections, Wq and Wk, induce logit shifts that scale with input magnitude. Because sink positions have unusually large magnitude, the perturbation is amplified there, causing per-head sink collapse. The architecture analysis then distinguishes per-head QK-RMSNorm from layerwise normalization: per-head normalization removes explicit raw-magnitude dependence, while layerwise normalization can still compress weak heads because each head’s scale is tied to the layer’s total energy.

Third, the paper introduces a predictive metric and tests interventions. Sink Strength is a single scalar computed on the base LLM, before VL training, to quantify head-level sink concentration. It predicts how much text capability will be lost after VL adaptation. The authors then separate base-side vulnerability from update-induced corruption by combining pre-VL sink weakness with post-VL sink-gap perturbation. Finally, they run two negative controls: injecting QK-RMSNorm after pretraining and then doing VL training, and applying several post-VL weight-merging methods. Neither recovers the protection seen in native architectures, which suggests the issue is tied to training-time head-level dynamics rather than something easily repaired afterward.703:T64f,The study covers six released VLM–LLM pairs from families including Qwen, InternVL, and LLaVA-OneVision, with headline examples such as Qwen3-VL, InternVL3.5, Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, and LLaVA-OV, plus additional controls. The language backbone is extracted from each VLM and evaluated as a standalone causal LM on a nine-task text suite against a reference LLM.

Several results stand out. First, the text-capability gap reaches double-digit points on multiple format-sensitive tasks, while matched text-only further training causes much smaller degradation. That supports a modality-specific effect. Second, Sink Strength is a strong predictor of post-VL damage: the headline rank correlation is Spearman rho = 0.97, and correlations remain high across six pairs and four format-sensitive tasks, with rho >= 0.88. Third, the preserved-sink versus collapsed-sink split is sharp on instruction following: every preserved-sink backbone stays within 5.4 points of its reference LLM, while every collapsed-sink backbone loses at least 7.9 points. Fourth, native per-head QK-RMSNorm is associated with better sink preservation, but post-pretraining injection of the same module does not reproduce the benefit. Fifth, post-VL weight merging, including linear, spectral, and sparsified variants, fails to recover the lost text capability under the tested settings.

The strongest part of the empirical design is the control structure. The paper does not rely on a single correlation plot; it includes text-only controls, matched training trajectories, architecture comparisons, and negative controls for post-hoc repair.704:T4d0,Read it in the order of phenomenon, mechanism, prediction, and failed repair. Start with the setup and the definition of format-sensitive tasks, then move to the Sink Strength section. The important point is that Sink Strength is computed entirely on the base LLM, before any VL training, so it is a pre-adaptation diagnostic rather than a post-hoc explanation.

Then spend time on the mechanism section. The most informative part of the paper is the chain from sink positions to Wq/Wk perturbation amplification to degraded format-sensitive behavior. Also pay attention to the distinction between per-head and layerwise QK normalization. That architectural detail is central to the argument.

After that, inspect the ranking results and the preserved-sink vs collapsed-sink grouping, then read the two negative controls carefully. They are what make the paper more convincing than a simple predictor paper: adding QK-RMSNorm after pretraining does not recreate the benefit, and merging weights after VL training does not restore the lost capability.

A selective read takes about 40 minutes. If you want to understand Theorem 1, the margin calibration, and the normalization-granularity argument in detail, budget 70 to 90 minutes.705:T780,AnySearch formulates budget-aware search as a resource-constrained sequential decision problem. The state contains the interaction history h_t and remaining budget b_t. The action space has three actions: reason internally, call the search tool, or answer and terminate. Budget is charged only on external search calls, since search latency and retrieved-document tokens dominate cost relative to internal reasoning tokens.

The method uses a two-phase curriculum. Phase I is a scaffolded learning stage. The model receives explicit budget-state injection and structured reasoning prompts that encourage it to think about whether a search is necessary, how much budget remains, and how to allocate it. Budgets decay linearly during training so the policy sees a range of budget regimes instead of overfitting to a single point.

Phase II removes the scaffold entirely. Training inputs now match inference conditions: the model is given only the total budget and must autonomously manage allocation. To make this work across budgets, the paper introduces adaptive budget sampling. Rather than sampling budgets uniformly, it focuses more on budget levels where the current policy is weak, while retaining uniform smoothing for coverage. This is important because the target is not peak performance at one budget, but a stable performance curve over many budgets.

The reward is a composite objective combining answer accuracy and budget efficiency. Efficiency is measured with both absolute and relative signals. A key detail is the adaptive weighting of the efficiency term based on query difficulty, which prevents the policy from becoming overly conservative on hard questions. Without this, a strong efficiency reward would push the model toward under-searching; too weak a reward would collapse back to wasteful search. The paper’s solution is effectively a difficulty-aware trade-off controller inside RL training.706:T660,The evaluation spans 7 benchmarks and 3 backbone models. The main result is consistent improvement over baselines across all tested budget levels, together with generalization to budget values not seen during training. That unseen-budget result is more important than a single average score, because it suggests the model learned a transferable budget-allocation behavior rather than memorizing a few discrete budget settings.

The baselines include fixed-budget RL search agents, reward-shaping methods that try to reduce redundant tool use without an explicit budget interface, and BATS-style approaches that rely on an external budget tracker. AnySearch improves not only answer quality but also tool productivity, meaning each search call yields more useful information on average. It also achieves the lowest total token consumption, which indicates the gain is not coming from replacing search with excessive internal reasoning tokens.

The ablations address three central questions. First, whether the scaffold is truly internalized: after removing explicit budget tracking and structured prompts, performance remains strong, which supports the internalization claim. Second, whether the two-phase curriculum is necessary: removing either the scaffolded phase or the scaffold-free adaptation phase hurts cross-budget robustness. Third, whether each reward component matters: removing relative efficiency, absolute efficiency, or adaptive weighting degrades the accuracy–efficiency trade-off. The paper emphasizes consistency across the full budget range and generalization to unseen budgets more than isolated peak numbers.707:T515,A three-stage simulation pipeline:
1) Data-driven persona building: start from anonymized, aggregated behavioral signals (activity patterns, engagement, inferred demographics) and use an LLM to synthesize a structured persona profile (summaries, patterns, narrative descriptors) used as conditioning context.
2) Structured elicitation: present control/treatment variants (visual stimuli) plus a target metric (CTR/subscription) via carefully designed structured questions; each persona-conditioned agent outputs numeric scores per variant and persona-grounded rationales. Prompt format is treated as a key hyperparameter.
3) Statistical aggregation: aggregate per-persona score differences into a simulated treatment-effect distribution \(\mathcal{N}(\hat{\delta}_s, \hat{\sigma}_s)\), analogous to the normal approximation of the real experiment’s relative effect \(\mathcal{N}(\hat{\delta}_{rel}, \hat{\sigma}^2_{rel})\). Quality is mainly measured by sign agreement (improve/harm/no effect). The paper further studies persona-pool subsampling to reduce inference cost.
The main methodological distinction from prior systems is grounding personas in real behavioral signals (vs screenshot-derived synthetic personas) and systematically analyzing prompt format + persona depth/diversity + sampling.708:T467,AgentFactory formulates an agentic system \(s\) as a pair drawn from a joint space \(\mathcal{S} = \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{W}\):
- Model space \(\mathcal{M}\): includes selecting a foundation model from an available set, plus optional instruction fine-tuning choices—dataset \(\mathcal{D}\), hyperparameters \(\mathcal{H}\), and tuning method \(\phi\) (LoRA/QLoRA/full FT). For closed models, fine-tuning is disabled (empty \(d,h\)).
- Workflow space \(\mathcal{W}\): can be graphs, neural workflow representations, or executable code.
- Multi-objective evaluation: a vector of metrics \(\mathbf{g}(s_i)\) computed by evaluation functions \(\mathbf{G} = \{G_1,\dots,G_p\}\) (accuracy, cost, latency, etc.).
- Optimization: because the space is non-differentiable and partially observable, the framework uses an “LLM optimizer” to propose iterative modifications based on the history (trajectory) of candidate systems and their metric vectors.
The key delta vs prior automated workflow optimizers is explicitly incorporating model fine-tuning into the automated search loop and emphasizing multi-objective constraints.709:T7e4,The method is an alternating optimization framework called WHALE. The joint objective is to maximize verifier reward over trajectories induced by both model parameters θ and harness h. Directly updating both at once creates a credit-assignment problem: harness search is a slow proposal-evaluate-accept loop, while online finetuning alternates rollout collection and gradient updates at a much faster cadence. WHALE avoids this mismatch by decomposing the problem into two conditional subproblems:
1) update weights with the harness fixed;
2) search for a better harness with the updated model fixed.

For the weight phase, the paper uses online RSFT. Under the current harness, the model samples multiple trajectories per prompt, keeps only verifier-accepted rollouts, and trains with supervised learning on those accepted traces. This choice is more stable than direct policy-gradient style updates and fits existing SFT pipelines well.

For the harness phase, the paper uses Meta-Harness to search over executable harness programs while keeping the model fixed. The search space includes system instructions, tool schemas, context management, parser/execution logic, and termination policy, which is much broader than prompt-only optimization.

The paper also introduces adaptive WHALE. A fixed schedule must decide how long each phase should run, but that is hard to tune: if a phase is too short, it lacks evidence; if too long, it over-optimizes against a frozen counterpart. Adaptive WHALE enforces a minimum phase length, then switches when the current phase’s training signal stops improving. This is a sensible design because the bottleneck can shift during training.

Compared with prior joint-adaptation work, the main differences are clear. Earlier methods typically co-optimize weights and textual prompts. WHALE expands the optimization target to full executable harnesses and uses conditional alternation rather than concurrent co-adaptation, prioritizing stable attribution over raw update frequency.70a:T7b3,The evaluation covers three domains: SearchQA, mathematical reasoning with code execution, and chess puzzles. Baselines include weight-only optimization, harness-only optimization, and Fast-Slow Training (FST). Importantly, their FST implementation uses the same update methods and schedule as WHALE, but restricts the search space to system/user prompts. This isolates the effect of searching over a full harness.

Main results: WHALE improves over single-component baselines by 7.67 to 24.38 percentage points, and over FST by 4.15 to 13.00 points. That suggests the gain is not just from extra tuning, but from the alternating scheme plus the richer harness search space.

A particularly useful finding is the existence of different bottleneck regimes:
- In SearchQA, harness-only search can match the peak accuracy of weight-only training with far fewer rollouts. This indicates a harness-limited regime, where retrieval and context/control logic dominate.
- In Math, harness-only search barely helps until a small weight update is applied first. After that, the same harness search becomes effective. This is a weight-limited regime, where the model’s reasoning or code-use ability must cross a threshold before harness improvements matter.

This observation explains why stagewise optimization is weak: it assumes the bottleneck stays on one side for a long stretch, while the experiments show that the bottleneck can move.

The paper also compares alternating updates against stagewise optimization directly. Under matched budgets, small alternating updates outperform stagewise by 5.32 points on SearchQA and 9.16 points on Math, and surpass the final stagewise result after using only 29% and 49% as many rollouts, respectively. That is a strong sample-efficiency result.

Finally, adaptive WHALE beats the tuned fixed schedule on both evaluated domains, supporting the claim that phase duration should respond to the training signal rather than remain static.70b:Tac2,LoGo 的核心设计是每层同时有 local 和 global 两个分支，但两者不是两套完全独立的大模块。所有 token 都先走 local attention，只看一个受限窗口；global 分支只对被选中的 query 激活，被选中的 token 再把 local/global 输出做融合，未选中的 token 直接绕过 global 分支。这样做的关键点有四个。

第一，动态分配单位是 token，而不是层或头。论文把 attention span 当作 attention budget 的代理变量：一个 token 是否需要全局上下文，可以由当前隐藏状态预测。具体做法是用一个轻量 gate 为每个 token 产生标量偏好分数，表示它对 global span 的需求。

第二，路由不是固定阈值，而是自适应阈值控制全局激活比例。作者设定 target global ratio，在每个 batch 或序列内根据 gate 分数确定阈值，把 top-ratio 的 token 送入 global 分支。这样可以把计算预算直接绑定到“有多少 token 走全局”，而不是让 gate 自由漂移导致预算失控。相比用连续权重软混合，这种二值路由更容易把理论 FLOPs 节省转成真实 kernel 加速。

第三，训练时用了 progressive mask，也就是文中说的 P-mask。问题在于如果一开始就做硬路由，gate 还没学到有意义的偏好，容易让训练不稳定，或者过早把重要 token 切掉。LoGo 在训练早期延迟引入稀疏路由，先让 local/global 结构和 gate 有一个较平滑的学习阶段，再逐步过渡到目标稀疏度。这一点很像 conditional computation 里常见的 warmup/annealing 思路，但这里作用在 attention routing 上。

第四，只稀疏 global queries，不稀疏 KV。也就是说，所有 token 的 key/value 仍然保留在全局可见集合里，只是并非每个 query 都去访问它们。这样被选中的 token 仍然拥有精确的 full-context attention，而不是近似检索或压缩记忆；代价则主要按被选中 query 数量下降。这个设计比同时稀疏 query 和 KV 更稳，因为不会破坏信息可达性，也避免了额外的 memory selection 误差。

从与现有方法的区别看，静态 inter-layer hybrid 是某些层全局、某些层局部；intra-layer hybrid 是某些头全局、某些头局部；它们都把预算结构写死了。LoGo 则让同一层内不同 token 走不同 span。与 CoLT5、SMA 这类动态模块激活方法相比，LoGo 直接把“是否需要长程上下文”作为路由目标，而不是切换不同 attention 模块或受限 span 模块。工程上，作者还实现了 query-sparse Triton kernel，把只对部分 query 做 global attention 的结构真正映射到运行时加速，而不是停留在 FLOPs 账面节省。70c:Ta3b,LoGo builds each attention layer from coupled local and global branches. Every token always receives local attention over a restricted window. A lightweight gate predicts, for each token, whether global span is worth paying for. Selected tokens additionally go through the global branch and fuse local/global outputs; unselected tokens bypass the global branch entirely.

There are four important design choices.

First, the routing unit is the token. The paper explicitly uses attention span as a proxy for attention budget: if a token likely depends on long-range retrieval, it should be allowed to access the full sequence; if it is locally predictable, local context is enough. This differs from static layer-wise or head-wise span assignment.

Second, routing is controlled by an adaptive threshold tied to a target global ratio. Instead of using a fixed threshold or unconstrained soft gating, LoGo selects roughly the top fraction of tokens for global attention. This keeps compute predictable and directly links routing decisions to budget. It also makes it easier to convert FLOP savings into real speedups, because the global branch becomes query-sparse in a hard, structured way.

Third, training uses progressive masking (P-mask). Hard sparse routing from the start would make optimization brittle because the gate is initially untrained and may suppress important tokens too early. LoGo therefore delays the full sparse regime and gradually introduces routing sparsity after the gate has learned more meaningful preferences. This is a training-stability device, and it is one of the more important parts of the method.

Fourth, LoGo sparsifies only global queries, not keys or values. All KV states remain globally available, so any selected token still performs exact full-context attention rather than an approximation over compressed memory. This is a conservative but sensible design: it reduces compute without damaging information accessibility.

Relative to prior work, static inter-layer hybrids assign some layers to global attention and others to local attention; intra-layer hybrids assign some heads to global and others to local. Both impose a fixed per-token budget. LoGo instead lets different tokens in the same layer take different span routes. Compared with dynamic module activation methods such as CoLT5 or SMA, LoGo directly routes based on span demand rather than swapping among attention modules with the same restricted context. On the systems side, the paper also implements query-sparse Triton kernels so the reduced global-attention workload translates into actual runtime gains.70d:T695,The experiments are organized around three claims.

First, scaling behavior. The authors train models from 200M up to 3.3B parameters and report that LoGo consistently matches or slightly improves over a standard Transformer on language modeling. This matters because many dynamic-routing ideas look promising only at small scale; once moved into real pretraining regimes, instability or routing overhead often erases the benefit. Here the evidence suggests token-level span allocation does not break backbone scalability.

Second, matched-budget comparisons at around 1.5B scale. Under matched parameter count and attention FLOPs, LoGo is compared against a standard Transformer and static inter-layer and intra-layer local-global hybrids. The main result is a better performance-compute trade-off: strongest language-modeling results among the compared variants, competitive short-context recall, and clearer gains on long-range retrieval after context extension. The emphasis is not just raw quality, but quality at the same budget.

Third, implementation and ablations. Kernel benchmarks show that the query-sparse Triton implementation delivers practical speedups that are close to the theoretical FLOP reduction at long sequence lengths. Ablations cover progressive masking, adaptive thresholding, the target global ratio, and compatibility with static hybrids. Two takeaways stand out: performance is reasonably robust across global ratios, and LoGo can be combined with static hybrids to reduce both memory and compute. The analysis section also reports interpretable routing patterns, with tokens that require long-range access being selected more often for the global branch.70e:T45a,For a skim-level read, start with the introduction and Figure 1. The key idea is not generic sparse attention, but token-level span allocation with span treated as the budget proxy.

Then read the method sections on the gate, adaptive threshold, and progressive masking. The most useful questions are why the model needs a target global ratio, and why hard routing cannot be turned on from the beginning. Those choices explain most of the training and systems behavior.

In the experiments, prioritize three items: the scaling plots, the matched-budget 1.5B comparison table, and the kernel benchmark. Together they answer whether the method preserves Transformer-like scaling, whether it beats static hybrids under fair budgets, and whether the FLOP savings become real speedups. If time is limited, the most informative ablations are the ones on P-mask, global ratio, and the combination with static hybrids.

Each item is paired with an intentionally wrong user answer. For multiple-choice tasks, the wrong answer is sampled from incorrect options; for PathVQA, it is the inverse of the ground truth; for ClockQA, it is produced by perturbing the correct time. The evaluation covers single-turn and multi-turn pressure, five pressure conditions, and five LMRMs: GPT-5.4-Mini, Claude-Sonnet-4.6, Gemini-3-Flash-Preview, Mistral-Small-4, and Grok-4.2-Reasoning. A Type 0–5 failure taxonomy separates reasoning-level sycophancy from answer-level sycophancy. A sentence-level drift taxonomy then locates where capitulation starts: Visual Evidence Reading, Reasoning and Derivation, Uncertainty Expression and Reconsideration, User Belief Acknowledgment, or Answer Commitment. This design is stronger than final-answer scoring because it distinguishes perception drift, derivation drift, and last-step reversal.710:T519,For each intended theorem T, the authors construct a complete shadow set 𝒮={S1,...,Sn}. Each shadow theorem Si is chosen so that T implies Si, giving a forward checker. The set is complete only if the conjunction S1∧...∧Sn implies T, giving a backward checker. Both directions are encoded and mechanically verified in Lean, so completeness is not an informal annotation claim but a machine-checked property. During evaluation, the generated candidate theorem \hat{T} is appended with these checkers. It receives credit only if it type-checks and passes the implication tests induced by the shadow set. A notable design choice is the annotation workflow: experts do not write everything from scratch. LLMs first draft candidate shadows, experts revise them, and Lean verifies completeness. This keeps expert labor focused on correction and validation rather than blank-page authoring. The method is especially well suited to multi-conclusion theorems, bundled conditions, existence/uniqueness statements, and other structures where partial formalization can still compile. Compared with BEq+-style reference-based equivalence checks, SA-Pass is less tied to one canonical expression. Compared with compile rate, it explicitly tests whether the generated statement is neither too weak nor too strong.711:T51b,Three results matter most. An earlier 126-problem version was already used in the ICML 2026 AI4Math Challenge Track 4, which gives the benchmark some external validation beyond an internal case study.712:T51c,SCEval keeps the question, answer space, gold label, and modality channels fixed, and perturbs only the internal structure of one or more modalities. Text corruption means deletion or shuffling rather than removing the text channel. Visual corruption means noise, blur, or occlusion rather than replacing the image/video. Audio corruption means muting, distortion, or segment removal rather than dropping the audio stream. The benchmark uses 14 curated operators: four for text, seven for vision, and three for audio. It evaluates single-, dual-, and tri-modal corruption settings. For stochastic operators, the protocol averages over up to three random variants and also records the worst-variant gap, which is a useful way to expose seed-level fragility without making the main metric depend on one unlucky sample. The dataset is built from 300 candidates sampled from Social-IQ, OmniBench, and VALOR, then filtered by a third-party team down to 273 human-verified tri-modal examples. The filtering criteria are important: the clean item must be valid, the answer must be tri-modally supportable, and the corrupted inputs must remain interpretable to humans. Because the design is sample-paired, clean-versus-corrupted comparisons are made on the same underlying example rather than across shifted subsets.713:T433,The main results are behavioral diagnostics. First, structural corruption consistently reduces clean all-modality accuracy, showing that many apparent omni-modal gains are fragile to internal evidence damage. Second, text-vision joint corruption emerges as the most stable shared fault line, suggesting that this interaction is especially brittle across models. Third, degradation is non-additive and model-dependent: the effect of dual- or tri-modal corruption is not a simple sum of single-modality drops, which implies that different models rely on different evidence pathways. The most striking empirical pattern is that under fixed heavy visual noise, 14 of 15 models perform worse with mildly corrupted text (t30) than with heavily corrupted text (t70). The paper is careful not to over-interpret this, but the result strongly suggests that partially damaged text can be more misleading than obviously broken text. In terms of scale, the benchmark contains 273 human-verified base examples, each expanded into clean, single-, dual-, and tri-modal corruption conditions.714:T51f,The central method is LPS-TC, a lightweight proactive speech turn controller. They therefore split multi-round dialogues into individual turns with real preceding context and evaluate both chunk-level timing precision and turn-level interaction quality.715:T424,This is not a core pretraining paper, but it is relevant to optimization signal quality, reward hacking, and the pretrain-to-posttrain interface. First, it localizes proxy misalignment to the candidate-selection stage of discrete search, rather than the more familiar RLHF or preference-optimization setting. That perspective is useful anywhere a proxy objective drives search, data synthesis, or iterative refinement. Second, it shows that keeping the proposer fixed and changing only the selector can materially change the final outcome. That is a useful reminder for training and search systems: what matters is not the candidate pool alone, but the trajectory induced by the retention rule. Third, it offers a practical recipe for situations where no true reward is available: combine trajectory-aware proxies with reference regularization to reduce short-sighted optimization. The contribution is more mechanistic than foundational, but it is worth reading if you care about alignment optimization, synthetic-data search, or proxy-objective failure modes.716:T8b8,TACS leaves candidate generation unchanged and intervenes only in candidate selection. At step t, a standard gradient-based proposer generates a batch of suffix candidates from the current suffix. The baseline strategy evaluates each candidate with the current attack loss and keeps the lowest-loss one. TACS replaces this with a richer scoring rule built from three kinds of signals.

The first is the standard current-step quality term, L_now, typically the target-token cross-entropy over the training behavior set. This remains in the score because immediate optimization quality still matters.

The second is trajectory-aware information. From the provided text, two components are central. One is an auxiliary early-token loss, denoted as something like L_first, computed only on the beginning of the target response. The motivation is intuitive: jailbreak failure often reappears at the start of the answer, where refusal templates or safety scaffolds come back first. A candidate that already supports the early part of the harmful response may therefore be more promising than one with a slightly lower average loss. The other is a one-step improvement proxy, Δ1(a), intended to estimate whether a candidate leaves room for useful future progress rather than merely fitting the current step. Even without the full formula, the design intent is clear: score candidates by downstream search utility, not just current proxy fit.

The third ingredient is reference regularization. Inspired by ideas from ORPO-style regularized optimization, TACS stabilizes selection by comparing against a reference signal or reference distribution. The role here is not alignment in the usual sense, but preventing the selector from making overly aggressive moves based on noisy or misleading local proxy improvements.

An important practical point is that TACS does not require extra intermediate model queries and does not assume access to a true reward. It only reuses signals already available in standard suffix optimization. Relative to prior jailbreak work, the novelty is in the selector rather than the proposer. Relative to ordinary reranking, the target is not better single-step ranking but better multi-step search trajectories.717:T506,The main empirical claim is that, under the same search budget, changing only the candidate selector improves average attack success rate on HarmBench by nearly 10%. The paper presents this as evidence that selection-stage reward hacking is real and practically important.

The most important diagnostic result is the loss-ASR mismatch. During optimization, training loss decreases smoothly, but ASR remains low for a long stretch and improves only in delayed bursts. That pattern suggests current-step loss is a poor retention criterion. With TACS, the optimization trajectory becomes more stable and the ASR gains are more consistent, rather than depending on occasional lucky suffix updates.

The provided text does not include the full result tables, but the experimental framing is clear: same candidate batch, same observable signals, different selection rule. If the full paper follows that setup throughout, the most informative results are likely the overall ASR improvement, robustness across models or behavior sets, and ablations on the scoring components. In particular, the relative contribution of the early-token loss and the one-step improvement proxy would tell you whether the method is mostly a prefix-sensitive selector or a more general trajectory-value estimator.718:T4ee,This is best read with one question in mind: is the selector really the bottleneck? Then read the methodology section carefully, especially the candidate scoring function. It helps to separate the roles of the terms: L_now for immediate fit, early-token loss for prefix-level jailbreak viability, and Δ1 plus reference regularization for reducing myopic retention. The key is not the formula alone, but why each term should improve the mismatch between current proxy quality and future jailbreak success.

A useful skim should take about 20 to 30 minutes. If you work on RLHF, preference optimization, search-based data synthesis, or red-teaming, the paper is interesting because it makes reward hacking concrete at the selector level.719:T4fa,The study combines linear separability, geometric comparison, and causal steering.
- Data: matched answerable/unanswerable pairs in two formally checkable domains (math800, code800). fact800 (epistemic unanswerability) and FalseQA (false premise) are used only as boundary/transfer checks.
- Impossibility direction d_imp: at a chosen layer L, they build a 1D direction using a low-capacity probe variant (CosNSRT/GSRS-style). They fit PCA on answerable states (k=100), project all states onto the orthogonal residual space R to remove dominant answerable variance, then compute a mean-difference direction between A and U in that residual. Scoring uses cosine similarity and orientation-invariant AUC.
- Safety refusal direction d_ref,safety: reproduced from Arditi et al. (2024) as μ_harmful − μ_harmless, with behavioral verification.
- Geometry: measure cosine(d_imp, d_ref,safety) to test whether structural invalidity reuses the safety-refusal pathway.
- Causality: steer generation by injecting along ±d_imp and measure dose-responsive changes in invalidity-aware behavior, with random-direction controls.
- Origin analysis: base vs instruct model pairs to see whether the near-orthogonality is created by instruction tuning or already present in the base model.71a:T6fd,The paper uses Distributed Alignment Search (DAS) within the causal abstraction framework, instead of standard probing or sparse feature decomposition. The motivation is clear. Probes can read out information that is not actually used by the model, while SAE/CLT-style methods may surface interpretable features but still leave faithfulness and stability concerns. DAS searches for low-dimensional, causally relevant subspaces by intervening on internal states between paired examples and identifying the rotations and substitutions that best explain behavioral changes.

The experimental design is unusually important here. The authors build templated minimal pairs for three syntactic constructions across fifteen languages. Coverage is intentionally uneven where typology demands it: Chinese is excluded from number agreement because it lacks grammatical number, and German/Dutch require special handling in filler–gap templates because embedded verbs are clause-final. This matters because the paper is trying to compare mechanisms, not just outcomes, so template alignment and minimal-pair control are central to validity.

The workflow is: verify that the model behaviorally handles the construction, localize a causally implicated subspace within a source language, then transplant that intervention into the corresponding target-language position and measure whether behavior changes in the expected direction. The paper also includes controls such as random-label tests and mismatched interventions to show that the effect is not a generic perturbation artifact. A further step links transfer strength to typological similarity, leading to the claim that multilingual syntactic mechanisms are organized around typological hubs rather than arbitrary language-specific partitions.71b:T59b,The study spans 4 multilingual LMs, 15 languages, and 3 syntactic phenomena. The models differ in family, size, and training setup, which helps the authors argue that the findings are not tied to a single architecture or checkpoint. Before any interpretability analysis, they run behavioral validation to ensure the models actually exhibit the target syntactic competence on the constructed stimuli.

The main empirical findings come in three layers. First, cross-lingual mechanism transfer is consistently observed across all three constructions, not just in a few closely related language pairs. Second, transfer is graded rather than binary: stronger transfer tends to occur between typologically closer languages. Third, some languages behave like hubs, with interventions localized in those languages transferring more broadly to others. That suggests multilingual models may organize syntactic abstractions around a small number of reusable structural centers.

The controls are important. Random-label and other non-specific intervention settings substantially weaken the effect, which supports the claim that the discovered subspaces are causally tied to the target syntactic behavior rather than reflecting generic representation damage. This is not a benchmark-improvement paper, so the key numbers are intervention effect sizes, transfer success rates, and their relation to typological structure, not downstream task gains.71c:T74a,The analysis starts from the simplest binary geometry. For hidden states labeled factual vs hallucinated, define class means μ0 and μ1, and let δ = μ1 − μ0 be the mean-shift direction. The authors first test necessity: remove the component along δ and see whether classification survives. It does not; performance collapses to chance. They then test sufficiency: project onto δ alone and classify in 1D. That already recovers a large fraction of the signal, but still trails regularized logistic regression.

This motivates the second layer of analysis. In the binary case, Fisher LDA uses ΣW^-1δ rather than raw δ, so if within-class covariance is far from spherical, covariance-aware linear methods can outperform the pure mean-shift direction without invoking nonlinear structure. Since the hidden dimension is around 4,000, covariance estimation is nontrivial. The paper therefore compares raw mean-shift projection, shrinkage LDA, L2-regularized logistic regression, and a set of controlled alternatives designed to isolate mean-targeting, variance-targeting, and nonlinear effects. The result is that shrinkage LDA closes about 73% of the gap between the 1D mean-shift classifier and the full-dimensional classifier, supporting the view that most of the remaining gain is about covariance estimation under noise, not richer geometry.

LayerMix is then introduced as a practical consequence of the analysis rather than a major algorithmic invention. Since the signal is not confined to a single oracle layer but spread across a contiguous band of layers, LayerMix uses lightweight cross-validated aggregation across layers to identify and combine that informative band. The framing is intentionally modest: it is a strong, cheap baseline derived from the geometry, not a claim that multi-layer aggregation is itself the main scientific contribution.71d:T5fb,The experiments cover three 7B-scale models and three datasets under a paired-example protocol. The headline result is that removing the mean-shift direction δ drops AUROC to 0.499, essentially chance, which makes δ necessary for detection. Using only the 1D projection onto δ yields 0.834 AUROC, recovering about 78% of the above-chance performance. A practical L2-regularized logistic regression reaches 0.952 AUROC, showing that there is still useful structure beyond raw δ, but that structure remains largely linear and covariance-related.

The paper also reports Cohen’s d of roughly 1.2–1.6 along δ, even though that direction explains less than 3% of total variance. This is an important geometric point: discriminative signal can live in a very low-variance direction. In controlled comparisons against 12 alternative probe architectures, L2-LR matches or outperforms them, which supports the claim that many complex probes are mostly dealing with estimation noise rather than exploiting meaningful nonlinear structure. LayerMix reaches 0.954 AUROC without oracle-layer access and adds only about 35 seconds of overhead, suggesting that the main benefit comes from exploiting a distributed informative layer band rather than from more expressive modeling.

A good aspect of the paper is that it states its boundary conditions clearly. The conclusions are explicitly tied to the paired-example setting and should not be read as universal claims about all online or free-generation hallucination detection scenarios.71e:T423,The method reformulates the output projection plus top-k selection as maximum inner product search. Rows of the output embedding matrix are treated as token vectors, and the final hidden state is used as the query. Instead of evaluating all logits, the system retrieves likely high-score tokens using an approximate nearest-neighbor index. The authors evaluate FAISS-backed options and choose HNSW because it offers the best latency–recall trade-off in this high-dimensional embedding space. The index is built post-training from the static output embeddings and can be distributed with the checkpoint. At inference time, the HNSW ef parameter controls the speed–accuracy trade-off. To reduce harmful misses, the implementation explicitly scores selected special tokens, common punctuation, and structural words. Retrieved logits can be scattered into a sparse full-vocabulary tensor, which keeps the method compatible with existing decoding pipelines. Unlike Adaptive Softmax-style designs, this does not require architectural changes during pretraining.71f:T4bc,The method represents the CFG as a pushdown automaton. A PDA configuration consists of a finite control state and an unbounded stack. To handle tokenizer–grammar mismatch, the online state is extended to (q, gamma, rho), where rho stores the open prefix of a grammar terminal currently being matched. Offline, the method builds bounded stack summaries under a stack-height limit H and computes reachability-to-acceptance labels using Pre*-style saturation from pushdown-system analysis. It then turns the PDA into a weighted pushdown system. A terminal-consuming transition is assigned the minimum number of LLM tokens needed to generate that terminal; for regex terminals, the method first picks a shortest string in the regex language and computes its minimum tokenization length. Epsilon transitions have zero cost. These computations produce token-level upper-bound distances to acceptance. Online, SWYB combines model top-k candidates with automaton-proposed backup tokens, validates candidates through budgeted successor exploration, and uses the distance estimates for horizon-aware pruning and beam reranking. Any completed output returned by the decoder is guaranteed to be accepted by the target PDA.720:T75e,The benchmark construction pipeline is graph-based and deliberately audit-friendly. The corpus is first partitioned by a quality classifier into D_high and D_low. Instead of mining the retained high-quality pool, the authors search D_low for low-exposure facts that are more likely to reveal parametric memory limits. Documents in D_low become nodes in a graph. Support edges connect documents about the same specific fact, while conflict edges connect documents that give incompatible accounts for the same subject-attribute pair.

A naive all-pairs comparison would be quadratic, so the paper uses a two-stage narrowing strategy. First, an LLM assigns each document a knowledge-point label, and candidate comparisons are restricted within those clusters. Second, entity-based retrieval further reduces the candidate set. Only then are LLM judgments used to verify support and conflict relations. This is an important design choice: the LLM is used offline to structure the corpus and identify disagreements, not to provide evidence at evaluation time.

Verified conflict edges seed subgraph sampling and QA synthesis. Each question is paired with an answer set containing at least two verified accounts, and every answer must remain traceable to source documents, externally checked against authoritative public sources, and reviewed by human annotators. The evaluation is closed-book: no retrieval, no source passages, no tools.

The metric design is also central. The paper separates fact recall from account completeness. A model may recover one account and therefore show some memory of the fact, yet still fail the completeness criterion by omitting the alternative verified account. The authors then use the number of supporting documents on each side of a disagreement as an exposure proxy, which allows them to analyze how corpus prevalence relates to these two failure modes.721:T58e,ElephantBench contains 1,094 closed-book questions mined from naturally occurring disagreements in a low-exposure web corpus. Each item is source-traceable, externally verified, and human-reviewed. The evaluation covers 32 models. The headline result is that even the strongest model recovers both accounts on only 52.4% of questions. On nearly all of the remaining cases, the model does not fail by total ignorance; instead, it recalls one verified account while omitting the other. That makes incompleteness, not pure forgetting, the dominant error mode.

The most informative analysis is the exposure asymmetry study. By counting how many documents support each side of a disagreement, the paper approximates relative corpus exposure. The more prevalent account is more predictive of whether the model recalls the fact at all. The less prevalent account is more predictive of whether the model recalls the full set of verified accounts. This is a clean empirical link between corpus imbalance and partial memory retention.
