It observes harness-visible telemetry rather than hidden states, logits, or internal traces. The monitored system is a three-stage pipeline: a read-only feasibility gate, a planner, and a GUI executor. CURA converts the trajectory into a sequential risk process built from four families of task-agnostic signals: execution effort, reasoning semantics, execution physiology, and visual dynamics. Intuitively, these capture how much work the agent is doing, what kind of reasoning it is expressing, whether its action rhythm looks unhealthy, and whether the screen is changing in ways consistent with progress. The online detector is based on CUSUM, which accumulates evidence over time instead of making a one-shot judgment. Thresholds are calibrated with Learn-then-Test using successful trajectories only, yielding finite-sample false-alarm guarantees without requiring failure labels. This design choice is important: the goal is not to maximize retrospective AUROC, but to detect failure early under a controlled false-alarm budget. The paper also studies where signal enters the pipeline: some risk is measurable before the first action, more appears at the planning stage, but fast quiet failures and belief-level errors remain difficult for purely external monitoring. The authors further test common alternatives such as token-level log-probability confidence and single-screenshot LLM judging, and find them weak on this benchmark.724:T54e,Experiments are run on 361 OSWorld-Verified tasks. The monitored pipeline achieves a mean task score of 82.9 and a full-solve rate of 80.3% (290/361), above the human reference of 72.4 reported in the paper. The central empirical finding is the oversight gap: among 71 failures, 64 (90%) still end with a success claim; 61 of those 64 acknowledge no blocker; and the explicit failure affordance is never used in roughly 9,100 executor calls. As a retrospective baseline, token count is already strong at 0.802 AUROC, while CURA’s composite reaches 0.828, not a large offline separation. The online story is more favorable. Under matched false-alarm budgets, CURA detects more failures: at α=0.10, recall is 0.41 versus 0.34 for token-count triggers; at α=0.20, 0.56 versus 0.38. The paper also reports that at α=0.10, CURA detects 42.3% of failures a median of 31 steps before termination with a realized false-alarm rate of 0.066. Early-stage predictability is also quantified: gate-probe telemetry reaches 0.69 AUROC and plan-stage evidence 0.74.725:T713,方法上，作者把问题形式化成 call-decision test。每个样本先有 ASR transcript，再由 text LLM 给出 transcript-side label；同时系统还可以选择调用本地音频 encoder（CLAP、AST、WavLM）或 generative audio model（Qwen2-Audio、Qwen2.5-Omni、MOSS-Audio）。关键不是单独比较这些模型，而是训练一个 routing / selection policy，在固定开发集上决定何时保留 transcript 标签、何时看 encoder、何时发起 generative call。

论文设计了几种策略。transcript-first route 用 transcript 风险分数来决定是否升级到 generative model；风险分数由 transcript label 的开发集错误率估计、Whisper 不确定性、text-LLM label likelihood 不确定性、以及是否输出非法标签等特征组成。encoder-first route 则先让 CLAP 对所有波形打分，再把低 margin 样本送去 generative model。更强的 full selector 把问题写成 row-action 对上的 correctness prediction：用 L2 正则 logistic model 预测某个动作在某个样本上是否会答对，特征包括动作置信度、transcript 不确定性和长度、encoder/generative 标记、动作成本、动作身份等。CLAP 和 WavLM 的开发集预测采用 out-of-fold，避免 selector 直接吃到泄漏的监督信号。

最关键的对照是 matched no-call selector。它和 full selector 使用同样的训练协议、同样的开发集调参流程，只是把 generative actions 整体移除。这样 full-vs-no-call 的差异就能更干净地解释成“生成式音频调用本身的边际价值”，而不是 selector 更强、特征更多、或调参更充分。作者还把成本单独报告，不把 latency / privacy / hosted exposure 混进 accuracy 里。这个设计很工整，适合做接口层面的审计。726:T66a,主实验在 Dynamic-SUPERB VocalSound 六分类任务上进行，chance 为 0.167。开发集 480 条，holdout 240 条，并做了文件 stem、推测 speaker/session 等层面的无重叠检查。这个任务先验证 transcript 不够用：transcript-only 只有 0.296 accuracy。直接看音频模型时，Qwen2.5-Omni 达到 0.883，Qwen2-Audio 0.838，MOSS-Audio 0.808，zero-shot CLAP 0.762，AudioSet AST 0.404。到这里如果停下，很容易得出“必须用 generative audio model”的结论。

For each example, the system has an ASR transcript, a transcript-side label from a text LLM, optional local audio encoders such as CLAP, AST, and WavLM, and optional generative audio models such as Qwen2-Audio, Qwen2.5-Omni, and MOSS-Audio. The goal is not to compare these components in isolation, but to learn a policy that decides when to keep the transcript label, when to rely on encoder evidence, and when to make a generative audio call.

Several routing strategies are evaluated. A transcript-first route uses a transcript risk score built from development-estimated transcript error risk, normalized Whisper uncertainty, text-LLM label-likelihood uncertainty, and an invalid-label flag. An encoder-first route uses CLAP margins and sends low-confidence cases to a generative model. The strongest setup is a full selector: an L2-regularized logistic correctness model over row-action pairs, with features including action confidence, transcript uncertainty and length, encoder flags, generative-call flags, action cost, and action identity. CLAP and WavLM development predictions are generated out-of-fold to avoid leakage.

The decisive control is the matched no-call selector. It uses the same training protocol, the same development tuning procedure, and the same selection machinery, but removes all generative actions. That makes the full-versus-no-call comparison a clean estimate of the marginal value of generative audio calls, rather than a comparison confounded by different selectors or different tuning effort. Costs are reported separately from accuracy, which keeps latency, privacy exposure, and hosted-interface concerns from being folded into the main accuracy metric.728:T6f7,The main benchmark is Dynamic-SUPERB VocalSound, a six-way human-vocalization classification task with chance accuracy 0.167. The development split has 480 rows and the holdout has 240, with checks for overlap in file stems and inferred speaker/session groupings. The first result confirms that transcripts are insufficient: transcript-only accuracy is 0.296. Audio models are much stronger: Qwen2.5-Omni reaches 0.883, Qwen2-Audio 0.838, MOSS-Audio 0.808, zero-shot CLAP 0.762, and AudioSet AST 0.404. If evaluation stopped there, one could easily conclude that generative audio models are necessary.

The more informative comparison comes after adding supervised encoder controls. CLAP class-bias tuning reaches 0.792. A CLAP score probe reaches 0.796 accuracy and 0.784 macro-F1. A CLAP embedding probe reaches 0.850 and 0.849. AST embeddings reach 0.817 and 0.813. A WavLM-base+ probe reaches 0.854 and 0.853. A CLAP-WavLM correctness oracle reaches 0.938, and a joint CLAP-WavLM ridge probe reaches 0.896 and 0.892. These results show that discriminative audio representations already recover most of the benefit on this closed-set task.

The headline result from the abstract is the key one: on VocalSound, the supervised selector with the full action set reaches 0.900 accuracy, while the matched no-call selector still reaches 0.892. The gap is only 0.008, with a 95% bootstrap interval of [-0.025, 0.042]. In other words, once transcript and encoder evidence are available to the same development-selected policy, generative audio calls add little on this task. Inspecting per-head attention maps, the authors observe that full-attention heads tend to specialize into semantic roles, with some focusing more on foreground objects and others on background regions. Chunk-window attention shows much weaker specialization and more uniform grid-like patterns. This phenomenon is named Semantic Head Specialization (SHS).

To quantify it, the paper introduces SHS-Index, an AUROC-based metric that measures how well a head separates foreground from background tokens. The metric is then evaluated on 16 open-source visual encoders and VLMs, where it cleanly separates full-attention and chunk-window families. The authors also show that changing only the LLM backbone size in Qwen2.5-VL barely changes SHS-Index, suggesting that the signal is driven by ViT attention design rather than language model scale.

The paper then analyzes three structural factors that affect SHS: window interaction, token serialization, and local softmax allocation. Based on these findings, it proposes Ariadne Attention, which combines sliding windows, per-head sink bias, and row-column alternating serialization. The design logic is diagnostic-driven: identify what full attention preserves internally, then build a cheaper hybrid that retains more of that property.72b:T5da,VLAct is best understood as a recipe, not a new backbone family. The first component is preserving the VLM prior. The model uses shallow-layer protection to reduce destructive drift in early representations, and caption-data mixing to keep generic semantic anchors alive during robot continued pre-training. This is a deliberate choice: robot trajectories provide action supervision but poor coverage of open-world semantics, so relying on them alone would adapt faster but forget more. The second component is multi-head continuous action co-supervision. During continued pre-training, the same backbone is trained against multiple continuous action heads rather than a single head. The point is not to deploy all heads later, but to prevent the backbone from collapsing onto one head’s output geometry and to encourage head-agnostic action representations. The third component is a partially unified cross-embodiment action layout. Instead of fully separate robot-specific action spaces or an overly rigid global unification, the method aligns semantically comparable action dimensions where possible and uses a wrap-aware loss for periodic joints so angular variables are trained with the correct topology. This middle ground matters because embodiments are related but not identical. A notable design choice throughout the paper is that these mechanisms are used to shape the backbone during continued pre-training; downstream users can still attach whatever action head fits their own setup.72c:T4db,The evaluation spans simulation benchmarks, real-world robot settings, and unseen-embodiment transfer. Main numbers reported in the paper include 82.6% on LIBERO-Plus, 54.8% on VLA-Arena, and 92.5% on RoboTwin 2.0. On RoboDojo, VLAct reaches a score of 10.66 with a 7.60% success rate, ranking sixth by success and outperforming all explicitly designated WAM models according to the paper. A particularly strong data-efficiency result is that using only 20% of RoboCasa-GR1 data still surpasses the full-data GR00T-N1.6 baseline. The training setup is also intentionally modest: open-source data only and a 16-GPU run. The most important experimental control is that, across comparisons, only the VLM backbone weights differ; the action head, its fresh initialization, downstream data, optimizer, and fine-tuning budget are held fixed. That makes the attribution to continued-pretrained representations much cleaner. The ablations support the proposed failure-mode analysis: removing shallow-layer protection or caption mixing hurts prior preservation; removing multi-head co-supervision reduces transfer robustness; removing the partially unified action layout and wrap-aware loss weakens cross-embodiment sharing and periodic-joint modeling.72d:T8c1,方法设计很克制，核心是“保留标准 student update，只在严格筛选的条件下做 student-to-teacher adaptation”。训练仍然从 student on-policy rollout 开始：student 只看题目 x 采样解答 y，teacher 在同一条 partial rollout 上、但额外看到参考解 y*，输出逐 token 分布。标准 OPSD 部分不变，student 继续用 teacher 的 token-level target 做蒸馏更新。VISTA 新增的是 teacher 更新，而且只在两层筛选后发生。

第一层是 rollout-level gating。只有当 student rollout 通过 outcome verifier 时，这条 rollout 才被认为包含了值得 teacher 学习的 problem-only reasoning 轨迹。这里的判断不是“student 比 teacher 强”，而是“这条 rollout 至少在结果上成立，因此其中某些 student token 偏好可能比 reference-conditioned teacher 更贴近部署时可行的推理分布”。这样做避免把 teacher 拉向明显错误的 student 行为。

第二层是 token-level selection。即便 rollout 最终正确，也不意味着整条序列的每个位置都该拿来更新 teacher。论文用 teacher-student disagreement 的 KL 信号做位置选择，只在 top-k 个分歧最大的 token 位置上，把 teacher 向 student 适度拉近。这里的直觉很重要：真正需要修正的是 teacher 最不贴近 problem-only reasoning 的位置，而不是所有位置。若全序列都更新，teacher 很快会塌缩到 student，失去 privileged knowledge，后续也就无法继续提供互补监督。

从损失形式看，VISTA 复用了标准 OPSD 的同类蒸馏损失，没有再造一个复杂目标。它的创新不在 loss 公式本身，而在“哪些 rollout 能作为 teacher 反馈”“哪些 token 位置值得反馈”这两个选择机制。论文还把这一设计与已有方法区分得比较清楚：RLSD 是在 student 侧用 verifier reward 约束更新方向；TRACE 是限制 distillation 的 token span；DemoPSD 是在 teacher-student disagreement 时重加权 student target。它们都在减少 student 受坏 teacher 影响，但 teacher 本身仍是静态的。VISTA 则让 teacher 在受控条件下被 student 的成功行为校准，因此改变的是监督源本身。72e:T4a5,The main significance is conceptual and methodological. Conceptually, the paper reframes privileged distillation as a target-alignment problem rather than a simple stronger-model-supervises-weaker-model setup. That matters beyond reasoning post-training. Any setting with a conditioning gap between teacher and student—reference-conditioned teachers, tool-augmented teachers, retrieval-conditioned teachers, multimodal teachers supervising text-only students—faces the same issue. Methodologically, VISTA introduces a controlled feedback loop from student to teacher without discarding the standard OPSD student update. This is a meaningful contribution because it changes the supervision source itself, not just the student's robustness to bad supervision. Empirically, the gains are consistent across three Qwen3 scales, and the method stays lightweight: no extra sampling and no separate RL objective. For researchers working on pretrain/post-train interfaces, the useful lesson is that supervision quality depends not only on teacher capability, but also on whether the teacher distribution is calibrated to the student's observable information and feasible reasoning trajectories.72f:T9b5,VISTA keeps the standard OPSD pipeline intact and adds a tightly controlled student-to-teacher adaptation step. Training still begins with an on-policy student rollout: the student policy sees only the problem x and samples a solution y, while the teacher sees both x and the reference solution y*. Both models are evaluated on the same partial student rollout. The student update remains unchanged: it is still distilled toward the teacher's token-level distribution, exactly as in standard OPSD.

The new part is the teacher update, and it is gated twice.

First, VISTA applies rollout-level selection using an outcome verifier. Only student rollouts that pass verification are allowed to provide feedback to the teacher. The logic is not that the student is globally better than the teacher, but that a verified rollout contains evidence that some of the student's token-level preferences are compatible with successful problem-only reasoning. This prevents the teacher from being pulled toward clearly bad student behavior.

Second, VISTA applies token-level selection within each eligible rollout. Even a correct rollout should not be used wholesale. The paper computes teacher-student disagreement and selects the top-k positions with the largest KL discrepancy. Teacher adaptation is applied only at those sparse positions. This is the central design choice. The goal is to correct the teacher exactly where its distribution is most misaligned with successful problem-only reasoning, while preserving the rest of the teacher's privileged knowledge. If the teacher were updated densely across all positions, the teacher-student gap would collapse too quickly and the teacher would lose its complementary value as a privileged supervisor.

An important practical point is that VISTA reuses the same rollouts and the same family of distillation losses as standard OPSD. The novelty is not a new reward function or a complicated optimization objective. It lies in deciding which rollouts are trustworthy for teacher feedback and which token positions are worth adapting. This also distinguishes VISTA from prior methods. RLSD constrains student updates with verifier rewards; TRACE restricts distillation to selected spans; DemoPSD reweights the target toward the student when teacher and student disagree. All of them reduce student exposure to mismatched teacher targets, but the teacher remains static. VISTA instead calibrates the teacher itself using verified student behavior.730:T83a,The main experiments cover three Qwen3 model scales—1.7B, 4B, and 8B—on three competition-math benchmarks under a matched OPSD protocol. The headline result is straightforward: VISTA achieves the best Avg@12 average across the three benchmarks at all three scales. Relative to reported OPSD, the average improves by 0.6, 0.7, and 2.1 points at 1.7B, 4B, and 8B respectively. The largest gain appears at 8B, which suggests that teacher adaptation may become more valuable as model capability increases. Across the nine scale-benchmark combinations, VISTA is best in eight.

The ablations are more informative than the topline numbers. Removing verifier-gated rollout selection hurts performance, indicating that teacher adaptation cannot be safely driven by arbitrary student trajectories. Removing selective top-k position adaptation and updating the teacher more broadly also degrades results, which supports the paper's core claim: the benefit does not come from making the teacher more student-like everywhere, but from sparse correction at the most mismatched positions.

The analysis section appears to target the three failure modes identified in the introduction. First, the adapted teacher provides better support for validated student reasoning, meaning it assigns higher probability to successful problem-only continuations. Second, explicit reference attribution is reduced, which suggests less leakage from the teacher's privileged conditioning. Third, teacher capability is preserved, showing that sparse adaptation does not simply collapse the teacher into the student. These analyses matter because they connect the empirical gains back to the proposed mechanism rather than leaving the method as a black-box improvement.

The abstract does not expose every implementation detail, but the full paper is likely worth checking for the exact verifier setup, the top-k schedule, the distribution of teacher-student KL across positions, and how often teacher adaptation is applied. Those details will determine whether the method transfers cleanly to other reasoning or distillation settings.731:T6b4,Start with the introduction and read the definition of the teacher-superiority assumption carefully. The paper is only compelling if you buy the problem formulation. Pay attention to the two concrete mismatch modes: reference-conditioned token leakage and suppression of valid alternative reasoning paths.

Then move to the method section and focus on the two selection mechanisms: verifier-gated rollout filtering and KL-guided top-k token masking. The key is not mathematical complexity. The key is understanding why the student update is left untouched while the teacher is adapted only under sparse, trusted conditions.

After that, inspect the main results table to verify that the gains hold under a matched protocol rather than through extra compute or sampling. The most important ablations are the verifier gate and the top-k sparsity study. Those tell you whether the method is genuinely exploiting successful student trajectories or merely benefiting from an auxiliary regularization effect.

If you want to go deeper, look for figures or tables on reference attribution, teacher-student disagreement, and teacher capability retention. Those analyses are where the paper either validates or fails its own mechanism story.

A quick but useful read can be done in about 30-40 minutes: introduction, method, main table, and the two critical ablations. A deeper read should examine verifier design, rollout sampling details, teacher update frequency, and hyperparameter sensitivity. The most interesting follow-up question is whether this idea extends to broader teacher-student mismatches, such as retrieval-augmented teachers, tool-conditioned teachers, or multimodal teachers supervising unimodal students.732:T46a,The method, INSPIRE, has two coupled components. The first is Reference-Guided Student Internalization (RGSI). Instead of directly treating an external reference solution as the preferred response, the model is asked to understand the reference reasoning pattern and regenerate an answer in its own style. This is meant to preserve the policy model’s distribution while injecting the missing example-based reasoning signal. The second is stage-wise rubric-based preference training. Rather than collapsing quality into answer correctness, the paper defines a three-dimensional rubric: Method, Reasoning, and Correctness. Method checks whether the response actively uses an example-based analytical strategy; Reasoning evaluates coherence and completeness; Correctness evaluates the final answer. DeepSeek V3.2 is used as the judge to score each dimension independently. Training is then staged: first encourage adoption of the strategy, then refine correctness on top of that. The key distinction from one-shot DPO-style training is that the paper explicitly treats capability acquisition as sequential rather than simultaneous.733:T441,The experimental story is centered on consistency across model families and scales, plus ablations that isolate the contribution of RGSI and stage-wise training. According to the full text provided, the method improves performance consistently, with larger gains on problems where constructing examples, counterexamples, or boundary cases is especially relevant. The most important ablations compare: (1) direct external references as preferred samples vs RGSI-internalized responses, to test the distribution-shift hypothesis; (2) single-stage preference training vs the proposed staged training, to test the progressive-acquisition claim; (3) correctness-only preference signals vs the full rubric, to test whether method supervision matters; and (4) dimension-wise score trajectories, to see whether Method improves before Correctness. The excerpt does not include the full result tables, parameter counts, or exact benchmark numbers, so it would be unsafe to invent specific gains. The paper’s emphasis is on stable improvements and design validation rather than one headline metric.734:T465,ContextPilot expands the context-management action space and changes the RL procedure. On the tool side, it adds planning, long-term memory, and soft context offloading beyond search, deletion, and summarization. Planning gives the agent a global structure before later actions. Long-term memory stores scattered evidence in a reusable form. Soft offloading acts as adaptive compression or temporary externalization rather than hard deletion. On the training side, the paper introduces context-aware partial rollout. It identifies influential context-management actions using changes in context and policy entropy, then branches rollouts around these critical actions instead of exploring every action uniformly. For credit assignment, it estimates the advantage of an intermediate context-management action using rewards from subsequent branches. This gives a finer signal than assigning the final trajectory reward to every step. The training also uses trajectory snapshots and token-level loss masking so that edited contexts are represented without repeatedly optimizing tokens that already appeared in earlier snapshots.735:T4ff,The analysis uses the online-to-nonconvex conversion framework. The optimizer’s update rule is treated as an online learner, and the learner’s regret is converted into a Goldstein-style stationarity guarantee for nonsmooth nonconvex objectives. For a momentum matrix M = U Sigma V^T, the ideal Muon direction is the polar factor U V^T, which preserves singular subspaces and maps all positive singular values to one. This hard singular-value map is discontinuous. Finite Newton–Schulz replaces it with a polynomial map obtained by q iterations of an odd matrix polynomial, implemented with matrix multiplications rather than an SVD. The paper shows that this finite-depth map is the gradient of a smoothed spectral potential evaluated at the momentum matrix. This turns Muon into a gradient-based prediction algorithm. The discounted regret decomposes into a penalty term and a stability term. The penalty decreases as the smoothed potential approaches the nuclear norm; the stability term is controlled by the Lipschitz constant of the finite Newton–Schulz map. Choosing q = O(log(1/epsilon)) balances these terms. The key conceptual move is to use the finite-depth deviation from the exact polar factor as smoothing, rather than treating it only as approximation error.736:T448,The core metric is Token Economy Score, TES(Mr, Mb, T) = [Acc(Mr,T) - Acc(Mb,T)] / [GenTok(Mr,T) / GenTok(Mb,T)]. Mr is the reasoning-enabled model, Mb is the non-reasoning baseline, and GenTok is reasoning tokens plus final answer tokens. Input tokens are deliberately excluded because they are mostly determined by the benchmark prompt and evaluation harness rather than by the model’s reasoning behavior. TES is therefore a marginal metric, unlike absolute accuracy-per-token metrics such as Per-Token Intelligence. TES greater than 1 means the accuracy gain in percentage points exceeds the generated-token multiplier; values between 0 and 1 indicate positive but weak marginal efficiency; values at or below 0 indicate that reasoning is wasteful or damaging. The paper also defines deployment-facing quantities, including Reasoning Cost Share and Deployment Cost Multiplier, to connect token behavior with cloud and on-premises cost profiles. A key caveat is explicit: TES is a practical convention, not a universal utility function, and should be read with baseline and absolute accuracy.737:T4e7,The method, VIG-Sampler, is built on two empirical observations. First, candidate tokens that place stronger attention on image tokens tend to be both better grounded in the visual input and more useful for predicting the remaining masked tokens. Based on this, the sampler uses token-level image attention as the ordering score, prioritizing visually informative tokens over high-confidence but semantically weak ones. Second, when multiple tokens are decoded in parallel, their individual information gains do not add up cleanly because some of them are redundant. The paper argues that this redundancy is reflected in similar token-to-image attention distributions. VIG-Sampler therefore adds a similarity-based penalty during subset selection: if a candidate attends to the image in a way that is too similar to already selected tokens, its priority is reduced. This gives a simple two-part design: image-attention-based ranking for grounding, plus attention-similarity penalty for complementary information. Compared with certainty-based samplers, it avoids locking in punctuation, copulas, or other frequent low-content tokens too early. Compared with text-only info-gain samplers, it explicitly injects visual evidence into the decoding trajectory.738:Ta22,方法核心是“自参考的局部分支探索 + signed distillation”。在某个 on-policy 时间步 t_j，模型先按当前 ODE 预测得到一个确定性的下一状态；然后从同一个父状态出发，额外分出 K 个带噪声的 SDE 候选分支。每个分支只在当前步做随机探索，之后再用确定性 ODE 一路 rollout 到干净图像。这样做的目的很明确：把当前局部方向的好坏，转化为最终图像奖励的差异。

为了把终局奖励变成局部监督，作者同时从同一父状态做一条 deterministic ODE rollout 作为 baseline。每个分支最终得到的 reward 与 baseline reward 做比较，形成 normalized branch advantage。这样 advantage 不是绝对分数，而是“从当前状态出发，这个局部扰动比默认走法更好还是更差”。这一步很关键，因为它把不同 prompt、不同 reward 量纲、不同时间步上的分数差异压成了可比较的局部相对信号。

训练目标不是只拉近最好分支，而是 all-branch pull-push distillation。高 advantage 分支把当前 velocity field 拉向更优局部方向；低 advantage 分支则把模型从差方向上推开。相比只学 best-of-K，这种 signed objective 利用了更多探索样本，样本效率更高，也更像一个局部排序学习问题。但 signed update 容易不稳，尤其是“推开差分支”可能与“靠近好分支”方向冲突。为此作者加了 direction-aware attenuation：如果某个 repulsive update 会明显抵消 best branch 的主方向，就衰减其权重，避免训练在局部几何上自相矛盾。

另一个技术点是 SDE-variance normalization。因为不同时间步、不同噪声强度下，SDE 分支的位移尺度不同，若直接回归分支目标，loss 尺度会失衡。作者用 SDE 方差做归一化，使每步监督更接近统一量纲，并给出与 reward-tilted KL 最小化相关的解释：模型在每个局部状态附近，把概率质量往高奖励分支倾斜。

多目标部分也值得注意。已有一些 OPD 方法会为不同目标训练不同 teacher，再在 field level 做路由或融合。Self-OPD 不这么做。它先把多个 reward 归一化后在 scalar reward 层融合，只用融合后的分数对局部分支排序；真正回归的对象仍然是某条具体分支对应的 velocity target，而不是多个 teacher field 的线性组合。这样避免了不同目标梯度直接打架，也更符合“同一张图同时满足多个约束”的目标，而不是不同 teacher 各自擅长不同样本。739:T953,The method is built around self-referenced local branching plus signed distillation. At an on-policy step t_j, the current model first predicts the deterministic next state along the ODE trajectory. From the same parent state, it then spawns K stochastic SDE branches. Each branch explores only locally at the current step, after which it is rolled out deterministically to a clean image. The purpose is to evaluate whether a local directional perturbation leads to a better final sample.

A deterministic ODE rollout from the same parent state serves as a self-reference baseline. Final rewards from the K branches are compared against this baseline reward to produce normalized branch advantages. This is important because the signal becomes relative and local: not whether a sample is globally good, but whether a local move from the current state is better or worse than the default trajectory.

Training uses an all-branch pull-push distillation objective. Positive-advantage branches pull the velocity field toward better local directions, while negative-advantage branches push it away from poor ones. Compared with only regressing toward the best branch, this uses more of the sampled neighborhood and turns local exploration into a richer ranking signal. The downside is potential instability: repulsive updates can conflict with attractive ones. To address that, the paper introduces direction-aware attenuation, which downweights repulsion when it would substantially cancel the direction of the best branch.

Another key component is SDE-variance normalization. Since branch displacement scales vary across timesteps and noise levels, direct regression would produce poorly calibrated losses. Normalizing by SDE variance makes the per-step target more comparable across the trajectory and is connected in the paper to a reward-tilted KL view: locally shifting probability mass toward higher-reward branches.

For multi-objective alignment, Self-OPD avoids field-level fusion of multiple teachers. Instead, it normalizes and combines scalar rewards first, uses the composite reward only to rank branches, and still regresses toward a concrete trajectory-derived velocity target. This is cleaner for black-box rewards and better aligned with the actual goal: one image satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously, rather than separate experts excelling on different samples.73a:T55d,The experimental story, based on the provided full-text sections, is centered on single-reward and mixed-reward alignment, with comparisons against two families of baselines: direct RL methods and teacher-based OPD methods. The paper reports that Self-OPD outperforms both, with the advantage being especially visible in mixed-reward settings where one model is expected to satisfy text rendering, compositional correctness, and aesthetics at the same time.

The most informative comparisons are likely the following: (1) single-reward versus mixed-reward performance, to test whether the method really resolves objective conflict; (2) training stability against teacher-free RL, to validate the dense-supervision claim; (3) performance against teacher-based OPD, to test whether removing the teacher sacrifices or improves alignment quality; and (4) ablations on branch count K, pull-only versus pull-push, direction-aware attenuation, and reward fusion strategy.

The excerpt does not include the full result tables, model sizes, compute budget, or exact benchmark numbers, so it would be unsafe to invent precise gains. The numbers worth checking in the full paper are the reward improvements over RL baselines, whether all component rewards improve simultaneously under mixed objectives, and whether removing push or attenuation causes clear degradation or instability.73b:T44c,GRAS combines two changes. First, it improves the guided proposal. Prior GILC-style methods correct clean-token logits with a straight-through reward gradient, but the gradient is often estimated from a single noisy sample. For differentiable rewards, GRAS uses a Gumbel-Rao / Rao-Blackwellized reveal estimator to analytically average part of the reveal randomness and reduce variance. For non-differentiable rewards, it uses a leave-one-out baseline to reduce particle-level reward noise. These proposal changes add no denoiser calls. Second, it changes the search stage. Standard SMC/TDS-like resampling often uses a fixed temperature, although the spread of values differs across denoising steps. GRAS introduces AMC, an adaptive-temperature resampling rule that standardizes per-step values into group-relative advantages and lets a single scale parameter control selection pressure. Compared with simply stacking gradient guidance and search, the useful contribution is the accounting framework: variance reduction, adaptive selection, diversity cost, and denoiser budget are analyzed together.73c:T7e8,The proposed solution is RecursiveGPT, built around two ideas. The first is factorized embeddings, which reduce the share of parameters spent on the input and output vocabulary maps. This matters because when hidden size is reduced, Transformer block parameters shrink roughly quadratically, while embedding-related parameters shrink much more slowly. As a result, small standard LMs can spend a disproportionate fraction of capacity on token lookup rather than sequence computation.

The second idea is recursive weight sharing across depth. Instead of stacking many independently parameterized Transformer blocks, the model repeatedly applies a shared block for multiple recurrent steps. This increases the amount of computation performed on each token without a proportional increase in parameter count. The paper is explicit that this is not mainly a compute-efficiency argument in the serving sense; it is a way to scale computation under fixed data while keeping model size under control.

Architecturally, this is closer to ALBERT-style cross-layer sharing plus recurrent refinement than to a new sequence model family. The interesting questions are therefore in the implementation details: how many recursive steps to use, how to stabilize training with shared blocks and residual connections, whether step information is encoded explicitly, and how to choose the factorization dimension for embeddings. The paper studies these choices systematically in a BabyLM-like setup rather than presenting a single tuned model.

A notable aspect of the work is what it does not rely on. It does not primarily solve overfitting through aggressive recipe engineering such as unusually large weight decay, elaborate stopping heuristics, or late ensembling. Nor does it switch to a different objective such as masked LM or diffusion-style masked modeling. The claim is narrower and cleaner: even with a conventional causal LM objective, architecture alone can improve the compute–parameter trade-off in the limited-data regime.73d:T863,The experiments span roughly 10M to 100M words, model sizes from about 13M to 1.2B parameters, two corpora, and several evaluations including BabyLM-relevant benchmarks such as BLiMP and COMPS, with supplementary reporting on BLiMP Supplement, EWoK, and Entity Tracking. The most important result is not a single score but the shape of the scaling behavior.

First, there is a clear optimal model size, and that optimum depends strongly on both the data budget and the evaluation target. The best size at 10M words is not the same as at 100M words, and different downstream or linguistic evaluations prefer different scales. That is a strong empirical reminder that “bigger is better” does not transfer cleanly into the low-data regime.

Second, the paper shows that standard Transformers use parameters inefficiently when scaled down. As models get smaller, the fraction of parameters tied up in embeddings and the LM head rises sharply, while performance does not improve monotonically with total parameter count. Past a certain point, training loss may continue to decrease while validation and downstream metrics deteriorate. RecursiveGPT improves on matched standard Transformer baselines by allocating more of the budget to token transformation rather than to independent parameters.

Third, RecursiveGPT outperforms standard Transformer baselines at both 10M and 100M word budgets and remains competitive with strong BabyLM 2025 systems. The abstract does not list all numbers, but the body emphasizes consistent gains across the main evaluations. The ablations are important: both factorized embeddings and recursive depth help, but the larger benefit comes from adding computation through shared-depth recurrence rather than merely shrinking vocabulary maps.

Fourth, the training-dynamics analysis is useful. The paper documents the overfitting pattern directly: larger models fit the training corpus better but generalize worse, while recursive models make better use of extra compute under the same data budget. For researchers interested in limited-data scaling, these curves are more informative than the leaderboard comparisons.73e:T445,The authors formulate variable-length generation in a padded sequence space with an absorbing empty token, so autoregressive decoding can be viewed as a time-dependent transport from the empty sequence to complete samples. They then define a family of target distributions derived from the base LLM, including powered distributions for sharpening, product distributions for combining constraints, and tilted distributions using additional potentials. Two sampling algorithms are proposed. The Sequential Monte Carlo variant maintains a population of particles along an annealing path and uses importance weights plus resampling to avoid the degeneracy of one-shot importance sampling. The Replica Exchange variant runs chains at different temperatures or sharpness levels and swaps states across replicas, allowing high-temperature chains to explore while low-temperature chains focus on high-probability regions. Compared with Best-of-N, these methods use intermediate distributions and adaptive weighting rather than drawing many independent base-model samples and filtering them afterwards.73f:T76c,The main idea is affix-oriented cache reuse. Instead of restricting reuse to shared prefixes, the paper generalizes it to any shared contiguous span, or affix, which may appear at the beginning, middle, or end of the context. This is a natural systems opportunity created by bidirectional attention: unlike AR models, DLLMs are not inherently prefix-centric.

The key challenge is deciding which affix-token KV states become meaningfully stale as the masked generation tokens evolve. ACache introduces Anchor Tokens for this purpose. It measures the cross-attention importance from masked generation tokens to affix tokens, identifies a small request-specific subset of influential affix tokens, and recomputes KV states only for those anchors. The remaining affix-token cache is reused. In effect, the method turns a coarse full-span refresh decision into a sparse token-level refresh decision.

Implementation-wise, ACache is built on top of Fast-dLLM. It replaces periodic full-cache recomputation with selective anchor-token recomputation, so it is an incremental but targeted improvement over existing approximate caching frameworks rather than a completely new inference stack. The authors also implement a shared-prefix prototype in Nano-vLLM to test whether the gains survive under a more realistic serving environment with paged memory management and continuous batching.

Relative to prior work, the distinction is clear. dLLM-Cache uses asymmetric prompt/response refresh and feature-similarity-based partial recomputation for response tokens. dKV-Cache focuses more on decoded-token reuse with delayed block recomputation. Fast-dLLM improves the overall inference framework but still relies on periodic refresh. ACache is novel in treating shared context itself as the optimization target and shrinking the recomputation unit from an entire shared span to a request-specific token subset.740:T504,The main results operate at three levels. First, quality recovery: compared with direct affix-cache reuse, which causes noticeable degradation, ACache recovers most of the lost accuracy across multiple benchmarks while recomputing only around 20% of affix tokens. That number matters because it suggests the stale-cache problem is sparse enough to be exploitable. Second, system gains: in the Nano-vLLM shared-prefix prototype, ACache reduces recomputation latency by up to 55.7% and improves end-to-end throughput by up to 1.68x. This indicates that the benefit is not just a FLOP-level argument but can survive a realistic serving stack. Third, scope: the method applies to shared spans beyond prefixes, which is practically relevant because reusable text in production often appears as retrieved snippets, tool outputs, templates, or summarized dialogue history rather than only as a left prefix.

For a researcher, the most informative part is likely the ablation structure rather than any single headline number: how stable the anchor-selection rule is, how quality changes as the recomputation ratio varies, whether affix position matters, and how stale-cache error accumulates across denoising steps. If the paper includes those plots, they are the ones worth studying closely.741:T598,TwinKV defines importance through pairwise redundancy in key space. For each token, it counts how many non-adjacent tokens have a key vector with cosine similarity above a fixed threshold. A high twin count means the token is redundant; a low count means it is likely unique and harder to recover if evicted. Two design choices matter. First, the method operates on keys rather than values or hidden states, because eviction affects what can later be retrieved through attention, and keys are the retrieval addresses. Second, it excludes adjacent tokens to avoid trivial local similarity from contiguous text.

The more interesting systems idea is to use TwinKV as a repair pass rather than a standalone eviction policy. Given any existing method’s retained and evicted sets under a fixed budget, TwinKV looks for two types of mismatch: an evicted token with no surviving near-duplicate, and a retained token whose information is already duplicated among retained tokens. It then swaps them while keeping the budget unchanged. This is a low-intrusion design: it does not need the wrapped method’s internal scores, only its final keep set. The paper also distinguishes this from anchor-based approaches that score keys by distance from a single global reference point. Those methods measure outlierness relative to a centroid; TwinKV measures substitutability through local pairwise relations. That is a different inductive bias.742:T623,The experiments answer two questions. First, does attention track causal utility? Using chunk-level leave-one-out on real long-context QA, the authors measure how much removing a chunk hurts the log-probability of the correct answer and compare that with the chunk’s attention mass in the original forward pass. The correlation is effectively zero, which directly weakens the premise behind attention-based eviction.

Second, does TwinKV improve existing policies as a post-hoc repair? On Qwen3-4B, the method is composed with four recent eviction baselines: StreamingLLM, PyramidKV, SnapKV, and ExpectedAttention. Evaluation covers LongBench, LooGLE, RULER, and a short-context MMLU-Pro control set, at compression ratios 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7. The gains are conditional rather than universal: TwinKV improves a majority of evaluated cells for StreamingLLM (up to 64% of cells) and PyramidKV (57%), is closer to neutral for SnapKV (41%), and helps only a minority for ExpectedAttention (16%). The paper argues that ExpectedAttention is already near ceiling on several settings, leaving more room for harmful perturbation than for correction. Another consistent pattern is that TwinKV helps more under tighter budgets; at the loosest compression ratio, average gains are smallest. That fits the paper’s causal story: when every retained slot matters, preserving unique information becomes more valuable.

The empirical emphasis is on breadth of positive configurations and compatibility with multiple baselines, not on a single large absolute score jump on one benchmark.743:T49a,Start with the introduction and Figure 1. The most important takeaway is the causal probe against the attention-as-importance assumption; that diagnostic is more memorable than the repair rule itself.

Then read the leave-one-out setup in Section 2 carefully. The paper’s argument depends on how marginal utility is defined, at what chunk granularity, and how the correlation is computed.

Section 3 is the method core. Focus on why the authors choose a swap-based repair pass instead of rescoring all tokens globally, and why pairwise redundancy differs from centroid-distance scoring. If the goal is only to understand the method, this section is enough.

In the experiments, prioritize: the per-baseline win-rate pattern, the dependence on compression ratio, and the MMLU-Pro short-context control. Those results clarify that TwinKV is mainly a long-context memory repair mechanism rather than a general capability booster. A careful skim should take about 20–30 minutes. For deeper reading, inspect threshold sensitivity, the non-adjacency constraint, and any layer/head sensitivity analysis, since those details determine portability to other models and serving stacks.744:T8e2,The paper first performs a systematic diagnosis, then proposes a mitigation method. The study covers two representative MLLMs: Wan2.2 for multimodal generation and Qwen3-VL for multimodal reasoning. It evaluates multiple low-precision formats, including MXFP8, MXFP4, and HiF4, across a wide set of components: vision encoders, text encoders, attention blocks, feed-forward layers, multimodal projection layers, and MoE modules. The analysis shows that FP8 is nearly lossless, while FP4 degradation is highly heterogeneous. In Wan2.2, the visual generation backbone is the main bottleneck and the UMT5 text encoder is relatively robust. In Qwen3-VL, the vision encoder is especially sensitive, though the language backbone also degrades under FP4. Crucially, ablations separating weight-only from activation quantization indicate that activation quantization is the dominant source of performance loss.

Based on this diagnosis, the paper proposes Residual Fallback Quantization (RFQ). Unlike threshold-based outlier fallback methods, which detect large values and route them through a higher-precision path, RFQ uses a fully low-bit and differentiable decomposition. It first quantizes the activation into a primary FP4 representation, then explicitly computes the quantization residual and sends that residual through a secondary low-bit quantization path for reconstruction. Conceptually, the approximation is q(x) + q_res(x - q(x)), rather than a hard split between normal values and outliers.

This design has several practical advantages. It is differentiable and suitable for end-to-end training. It avoids threshold tuning, which is difficult when outlier behavior varies by module and evolves during training. It does not require full-precision fallback, making it more compatible with true FP4 execution. And because it models the current quantization error directly, it is better aligned with dynamic training-time activation statistics than PTQ-style calibration methods.

Methodologically, RFQ sits between static PTQ smoothing and mixed-precision QAT fallback. It accepts that FP4 cannot faithfully represent the full activation range in many MLLM modules, and therefore models the error instead of forcing the original distribution through a single quantizer.745:T644,From the provided full text, several empirical conclusions are already clear.

1. Precision formats separate cleanly in quality: MXFP8 is close to lossless, while MXFP4 and HiF4 incur substantial degradation. This suggests that 8-bit training/deployment is already fairly mature for current MLLMs, whereas 4-bit remains the hard regime.
2. Activation quantization hurts much more than weight quantization. The paper runs extensive ablations to isolate their contributions, and the main takeaway is that compressing weights alone is often manageable, but pushing activations to FP4 causes the major collapse.
3. Sensitivity is strongly module-dependent. In Wan2.2, the WanDiT visual generation backbone is the main failure point, while the text encoder is relatively stable. In Qwen3-VL, the vision encoder is the most sensitive, though language modules are not immune. This argues against a single uniform quantization strategy across the whole MLLM stack.
4. RFQ recovers a meaningful portion of the FP4 loss without using high-precision fallback. The abstract excerpt does not provide exact numbers, but the framing makes clear that RFQ primarily addresses activation-outlier-induced instability rather than offering a small average gain everywhere.

If the full paper includes detailed tables, the most informative numbers to inspect are the relative gaps among FP8, FP4, and HiF4 on both generation and reasoning tasks, and the decomposition into weight-only, activation-only, and joint quantization. For pretraining researchers, those diagnostics are more useful than a single final benchmark score.746:T574,Read this paper with diagnosis first and method second. Start from the experimental setup and module-level ablations before diving into RFQ details.

First, read the introduction and the main experimental tables to confirm that the study spans both generative and reasoning MLLMs rather than a single architecture. That context matters when interpreting which conclusions are likely to transfer.

Second, focus on the activation-versus-weight ablations and the ranking of module sensitivities. This is the highest-information part of the paper because it answers why FP4 fails, not just whether it fails.

Third, move to the RFQ formulation and implementation details. Pay attention to how the residual is quantized, what extra storage or bandwidth it introduces, and what the training and inference overheads are. If your interest is low-precision pretraining, these system costs matter as much as the recovered accuracy.

As a skim paper, 30 to 45 minutes is enough to capture the main message. First is dataset construction. Instead of scraping noisy online conversations or using lightly controlled crowdworkers, the authors hire professional script writers to produce complete human-to-human dialogues. The tasks are goal-directed but open-ended, such as tutoring, planning, or everyday assistance. They intentionally avoid heavy knowledge retrieval, coding, or tasks with a single correct endpoint. That design choice matters: if the task is too knowledge-bound, the benchmark becomes another factual QA test; if it is too rigidly task-scripted, it stops measuring natural conversation.

Second is annotation and metric analysis. UPHELD provides dense turn-level labels rather than only conversation-level scores. The labels target dimensions such as stylistic consistency, content consistency, and coherence. This lets the benchmark expose local failures inside a long interaction instead of averaging them away. The paper then compares several evaluation families: classical lexical/semantic metrics, single LLM-as-a-judge systems, and a learned mixture-of-judges built using UPHELD supervision. The main takeaway is that standard metrics and single judges correlate poorly with human judgments on realistic dialogue, especially for long-range conversational properties, while a simple learned ensemble tracks humans better. The interesting contribution is less the ensemble itself and more the empirical demonstration that synthetic-data-based judge validation does not transfer cleanly to real human-scale conversations.748:T46f,The most important results are about dataset scale, distribution, and metric validity. The error analysis also emphasizes failures caused by synthetic dialogue bias and judge leakage.749:T5d4,MemToC is built as a controlled post-tool-call benchmark derived from ToolHop.
- Data pipeline: start from ToolHop sub-questions with locally executable tool calls and verified intermediate answers; keep only self-contained facts with short verifiable answers.
- Pre-construct benchmark artifacts before evaluating any model: question q, verified gold g, executable call, and curated distractors to synthesize plausible incorrect tool returns. Two annotators independently review for self-containedness, answer leakage, answer validity, and distractor plausibility.
- For each model and each prompt wording variant, first elicit a closed-book answer m (forced to answer, no abstention) and score it against g to determine whether the model’s memory is correct.
- Then present the same question with an injected tool return r under four conditions: correct return, incorrect return (built from verified answers and human-validated distractors), error payload, and no return. Because r is injected, tool correctness is known a priori.
- This yields a source-correctness matrix where the “correct behavior” is well-defined (use correct tools, resist incorrect tools), with tool-error/no-tool as controls.
- Evaluation details include extraction-first answer matching and three instruction-wording variants with fixed question text.
- Mitigations: compare prompting vs SFT vs DPO, using cross-fitting over ToolHop chains so that each reported fine-tuned prediction is on held-out questions.74a:T525,The benchmark is organized around two aligned axes. On the agent side, these are aligned with Planning, Action, and Feedback. The key point is that the benchmark evaluates the intersection rather than simply relabeling math skills: planning is framed as capability selection, ordering, and next-step decision making; action as isolated execution of a single atomic capability; feedback as monitoring and revising an existing trajectory.
