The released pipeline is reported to reproduce on a single workstation with a 24GB GPU.772:T557,The work extends the Gemini-based Co-Scientist system into an execution-grounded multi-agent framework spanning hypothesis generation, experiment planning, tool use, result interpretation, and manuscript drafting. The key idea is not a new foundation model, but adaptive orchestration across domains with different verification costs and safety constraints. In materials science, the system interfaces with a semi-automated CVD setup, proposes candidate recipes under lab constraints, and relies on experts to select and execute promising options. In another materials setting, Gemini 3 Deep Think is used for fast inference and direct hardware control to drive single-attempt growth of 2D semiconductors. In biology, the system works with experts who iteratively refine the task framing, while the model predicts emergent swarming phenotypes of engineered E. coli from sparse imaging data and the predictions are checked against wet-lab measurements. In computer science, the system operates autonomously from a high-level research directive to discover an inference-time scaling architecture and evaluate it on medical benchmarks. The unifying design choice is selective autonomy: the system does not insist on full automation, but allocates decision authority between AI and humans based on execution risk, observability, and the availability of reliable feedback.773:T52e,The evidence is presented mainly as real-world case studies rather than a single standardized benchmark. In materials science, Co-Scientist proposes a non-hazardous precursor route for Ti3C2Tx MXene growth; after expert optimization and physical execution, the resulting structures show characteristics similar to Ti3C2Tx MXene, although the paper explicitly notes that further experiments are needed to confirm the atomic structure. In a second materials setup, the system uses Gemini 3 Deep Think for rapid reasoning and direct hardware control, achieving successful single-attempt growth of monolayer MoS2, MoSe2, and WS2 while adapting to lab constraints within minutes. In biology, the system predicts swarming phenotypes across IPTG concentration gradients and is quantitatively validated against unpublished wet-lab morphology measurements, with the claimed benefit of reducing combinatorial screening. In computer science, the system autonomously discovers an inference-time scaling architecture that outperforms six frontier models on HealthBench Hard and Professional and reduces potential clinical harm in blinded physician evaluation, though the excerpt does not provide the full numbers. Overall, the experimental contribution is breadth of deployment and grounding, not tightly controlled algorithmic comparison.774:T7f3,ASIL is presented as an agent-native interaction layer rather than a single backend. The core design choice is to expose software through the deepest feasible access path available for each application. On the observation side, the agent receives a structured JSON object containing task metadata, application state, interactive elements, environment context, navigation structure, and a concise textual summary. On the action side, the agent emits a schema-constrained JSON action with explicit type, target, and parameters. The key shift is from “where to click” to “what to modify / invoke / export.”

The implementation is organized around three realization paths:
1. file-based access, where structured file formats are read and modified directly;
2. scripting-based access, where native scripting runtimes or automation APIs are used;
3. service-based access, where backend APIs or service endpoints expose semantic operations.

The paper emphasizes four design principles: completeness, semanticity, stability, and composability. Completeness addresses the partial observability of screenshots. Semanticity aligns actions with meaningful software operations. Stability avoids UI-dependent identifiers and layout drift. Composability allows complex tasks to be solved through a sequence of higher-level operations rather than long GUI event chains.

A notable systems contribution is the onboarding framework: reviewed interface profiles are compiled into validated adapter contracts. This makes ASIL more than a one-off wrapper. It resembles tool schemas or MCP-style interfaces, but with a stronger emphasis on state observability and action closure.

Importantly, ASIL is also treated as a trainable environment. The authors run small-scale SFT followed by resource- and time-limited on-policy RL. Because states and actions are structured and directly checkable, reward design and rollout efficiency become much cleaner than in screenshot-and-click settings. That is the part most relevant to agent training dynamics.775:T689,The evaluation has three layers. First, the environment and benchmark: ASIL is instantiated across 15 applications, with 300 single-application tasks and 80 multi-application tasks. The authors also render GUI snapshots from the underlying software state at every step, so ASIL and screenshot-driven agents can be compared under the same task definitions and validators. This is an important design choice because it controls for task specification while changing only the interaction interface.

Second, the interface comparison: the abstract reports that ASIL reaches above 80 with closed models on the benchmark. The paper also includes repaired GUI / 50max results, matched native-interface baselines such as LibreOffice UNO and draw.io MCP, and independent validity checks to bound the comparison. The main empirical message is not just higher end performance, but shorter and more stable trajectories. GUI agents pay a large step budget and are fragile to grounding, focus, timing, and layout errors. ASIL compresses many multi-step GUI procedures into one or a few semantic actions.

Third, the training results: the authors run small-scale SFT plus resource-limited, time-limited on-policy RL on Qwen3.5-2B and Qwen3.5-9B, and report double-digit gains. They further confirm the trend on a curated 80-task hard suite. There is also an ablation over realization patterns, comparing file, scripting, and service access routes. Even without every number in the abstract, the important result is clear: once the interface is structured and semantic, smaller models become trainable for software operation in a way that is much harder under screenshot-based interaction.776:T4f1,For a quick but useful read, focus on three parts. First, the introduction and the interface-mismatch section: this is where the paper makes its real argument, namely that many GUI-agent failures are caused by the wrong observation/action interface rather than insufficient reasoning alone. Second, read the ASIL interface definition and realization methodology carefully, especially the observation/action schema, the three access paths, and the four design principles. That tells you whether the proposal is generalizable or just engineering around a few apps. Third, inspect the benchmark construction and the comparison protocol: shared validators, GUI rendering from state, native-interface baselines, and the hard-suite training results are the places where the paper either earns or loses credibility.

A practical reading order is: problem framing → interface design → benchmark construction → training experiments. In about 30–45 minutes, that should be enough to capture the main idea. The two deeper questions worth thinking about are: how much of the gain comes from better tool interfaces versus better state representations, and whether ASIL-like environments could become a source of continual pretraining or RL curricula for software agents.777:T792,GRAIN has three main components. First, it uses an explicit pipeline. Rather than letting the model mix extraction, graph construction, and computation inside unconstrained chain-of-thought, the task is decomposed into semantic parsing of the graph and task arguments, followed by tool execution with the appropriate graph algorithm. The motivation is straightforward: shortest path, matching, coloring, and related computations are deterministic; the real weakness of LLMs is the language-to-structure mapping.

Second, the method enforces structural invariance during training. The authors construct multiple isomorphic views of the same underlying graph: node identifiers may be random, semantic, aliased, or noisy, and the task description may range from standardized templates to more realistic narratives. The model is trained to recover the same intermediate graph despite these surface changes. This is more than ordinary augmentation, because the reward directly checks whether the predicted intermediate graph matches the ground-truth topology. That gives denser and more targeted feedback than final-answer supervision alone.

Third, GRAIN uses single-agent RL as a form of robustness distillation. The goal is not to build a multi-agent system, but to absorb into one model the robustness that would otherwise require repeated decomposition and verification across multiple agents. The RL objective jointly rewards correct structure recovery and correct tool invocation. The intended effect is to learn identifier-invariant and formulation-invariant parsing rules instead of memorizing templates.

The accompanying benchmark, GRIT, is also a substantial part of the contribution. It covers six graph problems across 31 real-world prototypes, with controlled multi-view variants for naming and narrative style. That makes it possible to separate failures of structure extraction from failures of downstream algorithmic solving.778:T6da,The experiments are built around robustness diagnosis rather than a single leaderboard number. The first result is that the robustness gap is real: under identifier shift and task-form shift, performance varies significantly even when the underlying graph is unchanged. Closed models tend to retain stronger average accuracy but still show unstable variance across naming schemes. Open models degrade much more sharply under non-canonical identifiers and realistic narratives. This is an important finding because it shows that strong performance on sanitized graph benchmarks does not imply reliable real-world graph reasoning.

Against baselines, GRAIN is reported to outperform standard CoT, SFT, and more expensive multi-agent approaches in out-of-distribution robustness while keeping latency and token cost lower. The most informative results are likely the breakdowns by naming scheme, narrative type, graph size, and task complexity. If the gains are consistent across those slices, that supports the claim that the reward is improving the language-to-structure stage rather than exploiting a narrow template.

A key ablation concerns the structural reward itself. The paper argues that rewarding intermediate graph correctness is better than rewarding only the final answer, and better than static supervision alone. The reason is intuitive: final-answer rewards are sparse and can be accidentally correct even when parsing is wrong, while structural rewards directly supervise semantic parsing quality. Although the abstract does not list all numbers, the central empirical message is that GRAIN yields more stable performance under surface perturbations and converts part of the robustness of complex multi-agent pipelines into a single model.779:T49e,A good skim has three stops. First, read the introduction and the GRIT setup carefully to understand what is actually being evaluated: not generic text-serialized graph reasoning, but robustness of language-to-graph extraction under naming and formulation shifts. Without that framing, the paper is easy to misread as just another graph benchmark. Second, read the method section with attention to the semantic parsing → tool execution pipeline and the definition of the structure invariance reward. In particular, check how the predicted graph is matched against the ground-truth topology, whether graph isomorphism is handled explicitly, and how node renaming is treated. Third, inspect the OOD splits and the ablations comparing CoT, SFT, RL, and multi-agent baselines.

If the goal is only to capture the main idea, 20–30 minutes should be enough. The deeper follow-up questions are more interesting: whether this kind of verifiable intermediate-structure RL can transfer to code dependency graphs, knowledge graph extraction, or tool-planning graphs, and whether invariance rewards could be connected to pretraining-time augmentation, canonicalization, or schema induction.77a:T459,1. **Spectral Probing Analysis**: At checkpoints along real training trajectories, the momentum buffer is decomposed into singular directions, and the loss-optimal step size along each direction is estimated on held-out data. The spectral profile is found to be highly anisotropic and stable: a 'volatile head' at the 'Edge-of-Stability' supports only small step sizes, while a 'tolerant bulk' permits much larger steps.
2. **Unified Perspective**: SGD allocates step size proportional to singular values (opposite to landscape suggestions); Adam's coordinate-wise rescaling mitigates but doesn't solve the mismatch; Muon's whitening to a uniform scale reallocates step mass from the head to the bulk.
3. **SAMuon Algorithm**: To exploit the bulk's capacity for larger steps, Spectral-Aware Muon (SAMuon) is proposed. It imposes a static, head-anchored prior on the whitened update. The full SAMuon fits a log-rank-linear shape via randomized SVD; the simplified SAMuon-lite uses power iteration to pin the head and uniformly amplifies the bulk. Both add no persistent state and negligible computational overhead.77b:T4dd,The authors define an exact conditional-marginal oracle model to isolate parallelization error from model approximation error. A deterministic adaptive policy chooses the next reveal set from the observed partial assignment. The selected variables are then sampled independently using their true conditional marginals rather than from their true joint conditional. Approximation error is measured by forward KL, which has a chain-rule decomposition aligned with the reveal process and corresponds to excess expected log loss. Serial depth is the minimum target-averaged number of rounds needed to meet a KL budget. The central proof aligns each round's KL contribution with the conditional total correlation of the variables revealed in that round. The identity applies to random and history-dependent reveal sets. The paper then turns the identity into upper and lower bounds for structured families: logarithmic exact sampling for Bernoulli walks via hierarchical bisection, logarithmic-in-length zero-error schedules for finite-order Markov chains with a factor depending on Markov order, linear expected depth for uniform random permutations at fixed error, and several binary-alphabet constructions with polylogarithmic to polynomial depth.77c:T53b,The theoretical results give the main evidence. For the Bernoulli walk, hierarchical bisection achieves exact sampling in logarithmically many rounds, while contiguous left-to-right schedules require linearly many rounds to maintain fixed accuracy. For uniform random permutations, every fixed-error policy needs a linear number of expected rounds; under a hard round cap, the optimal error reduces exactly to an integer-composition problem, yielding fixed-round asymptotics, a finite-blocklength pairs-first phase, and a joint scaling frontier. Over a binary alphabet, uniform balanced binary strings have depth on the order of squared log sequence length at any fixed positive error, while independent one-hot blocks give matching square-root-depth lower bounds against arbitrary deterministic value-adaptive policies. Rectangular block constructions realize polynomial exponents up to one half. The empirical section is diagnostic: it evaluates generic schedules and deployed decoding rules on 542 sequences from WikiText and model-generated text across four domains using a single 0.5B model and one sampling temperature. A paired self-sampling study on 231 held-out prompts compares teacher-forced pseudo-costs with output quality under an external autoregressive evaluator, and also tests a model-independent spaced-profile schedule.77d:T5f7,The core mechanism is Expert Folding. Instead of dropping an excluded source expert or rerouting it to a similar target expert without correction, ExFold projects the source contribution onto a retained target expert. The method is motivated by two empirical findings: many experts produce directionally aligned outputs on the same inputs, but their output magnitudes differ substantially. Directional alignment makes substitution plausible; magnitude mismatch makes naive rerouting inaccurate. Based on this, each layer is calibrated with two matrices from a single frozen forward pass on unlabeled text. The scalar-projector matrix stores directed source-to-target scaling factors. The projection-loss matrix measures reconstruction loss for folding one expert into another. At inference time, retained experts are selected according to the phase budget: K_pre dominant experts per token for prefill, and D dominant experts per batch for decode. Every excluded expert is then assigned to the minimum-loss retained target, and its contribution is folded into that target by absorbing the scalar projector into the router weight. This gives one shared folding operator across both phases. Compared with token-wise sparsification, the method does not only reduce executed experts; compared with expert-set consolidation, it does not bake compression into a fixed submodel; compared with similarity-based rerouting, it explicitly corrects scale mismatch. The implementation is integrated into vLLM with a lightweight CUDA kernel.77e:T4a9,The evaluation covers multiple MoE architectures and real vLLM serving workloads, focusing on TTFT, TPOT, and quality retention. The headline numbers are up to 1.41× TTFT speedup and 2.45× TPOT speedup while preserving about 99% of the original average quality. The larger decode gain is consistent with the method’s focus on reducing the active expert set under memory-bound conditions. The more informative part is the comparison structure. Against pruning or skipping baselines, ExFold degrades quality more slowly at the same budget, which supports the claim that explicit reconstruction matters. Against static merging methods, it remains adaptive to token-level or batch-level budgets instead of committing to one permanently compressed model. Against similarity-based rerouting, the directed scalar projector improves approximation when experts are aligned in direction but not in scale. The ablations indicate that both components—the loss-based target assignment and the scalar correction—are necessary. Another useful result is that the same calibrated matrices work for both prefill and decode, which reduces deployment complexity and supports the phase-unified formulation.77f:T493,Hydra is a common-schema instrumentation and analysis framework. The authors instrument both HuggingFace Transformers and llama.cpp so that two very different inference stacks emit the same per-prompt timing record. The canonical schema covers at least tokenization, prefill, per-token generation, de-tokenization, inter-token latency, and end-to-end latency. These phase boundaries are then fused with high-resolution telemetry from tegrastats and NVML, enabling attribution of CPU activity, GPU utilization, DRAM traffic, power, energy, and thermal behavior to the prefill and decode windows. Two design choices matter. First, the measurement interface is decoupled from execution configuration, so models, precisions, prompt lengths, and SoC generations can be swapped without changing the analysis pipeline. Second, the framework spans both the Python framework path and the GGML/C++ path, which makes the comparison more realistic for deployment. The instantiated study covers three Jetson generations—AGX Xavier, AGX Orin, and AGX Thor—two backends, 13 instruction-tuned models from seven families, and five execution formats: bf16, F16, Q8_0, Q6_K, and Q4_K_M.780:T46b,The paper is more about stable findings than about one best number. First, performance depends jointly on backend, architecture, precision, and sequence length; model size alone is not predictive enough. Hydra’s phase-level timing shows that backend overhead, quantized decode throughput, and input/output-length scaling affect different parts of the inference pipeline. Second, quantization often reduces DRAM traffic and model footprint, but it does not automatically reduce latency or energy on edge SoCs, because CPU orchestration, GPU effective utilization, shared-memory bandwidth, DVFS, and thermal limits also matter. Third, backend choice changes CPU-side runtime behavior enough to alter decode throughput and efficiency. Fourth, gains across SoC generations are not uniformly realized; newer hardware can improve throughput or energy efficiency in some settings, but backend overheads or thermal constraints can offset part of the benefit in others. A central empirical point is that phase-aligned telemetry is necessary: aggregate latency or run-averaged power hides meaningful differences between prefill and decode.781:T78d,The method has four stages.

1) Direction estimation. For each layer, the model collects hidden states from reflective and non-reflective examples and computes a standard mean-difference vector as an initial reflection direction. This follows the usual activation-engineering assumption that a behavior can be approximated by a linear direction in residual space.

2) Direction purification. This is the key technical step. The authors argue that the raw contrast direction mixes reflection with activation structure shared by reasoning states more broadly. They therefore apply PCA-based denoising to reduce sample noise and low-value variation, then orthogonalize the candidate reflection direction against a rank-one proxy for shared reasoning structure. A central empirical claim is that the raw direction has substantial overlap with this shared proxy, while the orthogonalized direction reduces that overlap to roughly an isotropic-random baseline.

3) Layer calibration. The method does not assume every layer is a good intervention site. On a small calibration set, it sweeps candidate layers and intervention strengths, then keeps the layers that consistently reduce reflection-like behavior without destabilizing generation quality.

4) State-dependent projection attenuation. Instead of adding or subtracting a fixed vector at every token, the method removes only the component of the current hidden state that lies along the learned reflection direction, with bounded magnitude. This makes the intervention conditional on how much reflection-associated signal is present in the current token state. Compared with constant shifts, this is a more selective suppression mechanism and is less likely to damage ordinary reasoning.

The design choice is deliberate: no retraining, no controller network, no modified decoding. The trade-off is that it needs a small reflective/non-reflective contrast set and a calibration pass.782:T6e1,The evaluation covers three open-weight Qwen-family checkpoints on two benchmarks, MATH-500 and GPQA-Diamond, with matched answer parsing and token accounting. The main comparison is against two closely related representation-level baselines, CREST and ReflCtrl.

Across six model-benchmark settings, Reflection Steering reduces reasoning tokens by 16.9% on average while largely preserving task performance. The cleanest result is on Qwen3-30B-A3B for MATH-500: a 21.8% token reduction with only a -0.1 point change in accuracy. The paper also reports paired equivalence testing and finds support for equivalence to the raw model within a ±1 point margin, which is stronger evidence than simply reporting a small average drop.

The paper’s own framing makes clear that the strongest accuracy-preserving evidence is on mathematical reasoning. On GPQA-Diamond, the token savings remain meaningful, but the trade-off is less clean. That makes sense: in math, reflection often appears as repeated verification after the solution path is already established, whereas in scientific reasoning, revision and reconsideration may be more tightly coupled to useful inference.

The ablations that matter are: (i) raw mean-difference direction versus purified direction, showing that orthogonalization against shared reasoning structure materially improves the accuracy-efficiency trade-off; (ii) fixed vector shifts versus projection attenuation, where the latter better preserves accuracy; and (iii) layer calibration, showing that intervention quality depends strongly on depth. This is not a paper about raising benchmark accuracy. It is about recovering tokens without paying much accuracy tax, and the right way to judge it is by the cleanliness of that trade-off.783:T6e6,The core method is residual-guided non-parametric optimization. The system starts from a fixed base verifier and iteratively improves it around observed mistakes. At each round, the current verifier is replayed on a construction pool, and disagreements with labels are collected as residuals. Recurring residual patterns are then abstracted into rule cards. Each card records a missing verifier bias together with support examples, counterexamples, applicability conditions, and abstention conditions. This is a key design choice: instead of directly updating model parameters, the method converts recurring failure modes into explicit knowledge units.

A rule card can follow one of two promotion paths. If the missing bias can be expressed as deterministic comparison logic—such as numerical tolerance handling, unit normalization, scientific notation conversion, or specific symbolic equivalence rules—it goes through code audit and replay validation, and if accepted becomes a code module. A code module is a deterministic verifier unit that returns Correct, Incorrect, or Abstain. If the bias cannot be fully codified and still requires model judgment, it is incorporated into the fallback verifier prompt rather than compiled into code. At inference time, the system first runs the module library; cases that can be decided explicitly are handled there, and only unresolved cases are sent to a fixed model-based fallback verifier.

What distinguishes this from prior work is not simply adding tools, but turning verifier improvement into a closed loop: residual discovery, rule-card drafting, replay validation, and promotion into either executable modules or prompt guidance. It sits between hand-maintained rule libraries and opaque judge-model behavior.784:T545,The paper evaluates on four reference-based verification benchmarks. The headline result is 93.05% macro accuracy, outperforming the reported rule-based, model-based, scientific, and tool-augmented baselines included in the study. The more informative result is the component ablation: compared with a prompt-only setting, adding code modules yields an additional +1.76 macro-accuracy gain. That suggests the benefit is not merely better prompting; explicit comparison logic is covering verifier blind spots that prompting alone does not fix. In addition, direct module decisions reduce fallback model calls by 32.13%, so the system improves both accuracy and inference efficiency.

The experiments are most convincing when read as evidence for two claims. First, recurring residuals do contain reusable verifier biases that can be extracted. Second, splitting those biases into deterministic modules versus prompt-level guidance works better than relying on a single prompt-only or model-only verifier. A careful reader should still pay attention to the relationship between the construction pool and the evaluation benchmarks: if they are too similar, rule extraction becomes easier. The replay-validation protocol, support/counterexample design, and cross-benchmark consistency are therefore important for judging how robust the method really is.785:T462,For a quick read, start with the motivating examples in the introduction, especially the discussion of when 1+3.14 should or should not be treated as equivalent to 1+π. Then read the method section with four objects in mind: residuals, rule cards, code modules, and the fallback prompt. Once the transitions among these four are clear, the whole system becomes easy to follow.

Each task is packaged as a self-contained unit with aligned components including a task description, fixed inputs, an execution environment, a deliverable contract, and a task-specific grader. The curation follows four principles: representativeness, complexity, diversity, and verifiability. In practice, that means tasks must resemble real professional workflows, require dependency-aware multi-step execution, avoid trivial template variation, and support automated, repeatable scoring through files, numerical checks, plots, or explicit acceptance criteria.

First, a diagnostic framework. In each trajectory, the agent retrieves candidate pages, inspects page images, writes source-linked findings into working memory, and finally outputs both a final answer and terminal memory. A frozen reader then sees only the question plus terminal memory and produces a memory-only answer. An official judge scores both the final answer and the memory-only answer against the gold answer, yielding binary indicators for answer correctness and memory answerability. This produces a four-cell analysis, with special attention to P_mmc, the fraction of answer-correct cases whose terminal memory is still not answerable. The key design choice is that memory quality is defined functionally—whether it preserves enough information for answering—rather than stylistically.

Second, the training algorithm AWM-GRPO. All compared agent variants share the same Qwen3-VL-4B policy, retrieval harness, tools, memory schema, prompts, and optimizer; only post-training and reward differ. For each sampled trajectory, the policy emits a final answer and terminal memory; the frozen reader answers from memory alone; the judge scores both outputs. GRPO then ranks trajectories using not only final-answer correctness but also memory-only answerability, preferring trajectories that both solve the task and leave behind answerable memory. This differs from answer-only GRPO, which optimizes the end result but is indifferent to the quality of the stored state. It also differs from direct memory supervision: instead of imitating a gold summary, the method supervises memory indirectly through its ability to support answering, which is closer to the actual role memory plays in an agent loop.791:T57a,The experimental setup is carefully controlled. The input to this stage is a per-frame spatial grid of visual features, preserving a 27x27 token layout instead of flattening everything into a 1D sequence upfront. The method has three main ingredients. First, the fast-weight parameterization is convolutional rather than MLP-based. Unlike TTT-MLP or SSM-style operators such as Mamba that process flattened sequences, the hidden state here is represented by two grouped convolution kernels, W1 and W2, which together define a time-varying convolutional mapping over the 2D feature grid. Grouping partitions channels into subsets, allowing specialization while keeping the update efficient. Second, the module uses causal inner-loop updates. For each frame, lightweight heads produce keys, values, queries, per-group learning-rate gates, and momentum coefficients. These signals drive gradient-style updates to the fast weights, and the updated convolutional mapping contextualizes the current stream using only preceding history. The causality claim is specifically about update ordering: each frame can only depend on accumulated past state, not future frames. Third, the model uses a hybrid frame selector. Instead of training an auxiliary scoring network, it derives change-aware importance directly from the inner-loop training signals, combining gradient-direction shifts and alignment-loss deltas with uniform sampling. This is meant to preserve both scene transitions and within-scene changes under a fixed frame budget. The full pipeline processes videos in chunks with state carried across chunk boundaries, normalizes importance after the full pass, selects a fixed number of frames, and then applies the original MLP projector to map selected visual features into the LLM embedding space.794:T5d6,The strongest part of the empirical section is the controlled comparison setup. The paper compares temporal Transformer, Gated DeltaNet, Mamba2, TTT-MLP, and TTT-Conv under the same baseline as much as possible, rather than mixing different backbones and training corpora. The headline numbers from the abstract are that TTT-Conv improves over TTT-MLP by up to 2.12 points on MLVU and over bidirectional Mamba2 by up to 3.04 points, while also outperforming attention-based and fixed-state recurrent resamplers across three benchmarks. The system handles videos up to 512 frames and compresses them to 128 frames for the LLM, with training reported on A100 40GB GPUs. Beyond the main scores, several analyses matter more than the topline. Convolutional fast weights consistently beat MLP-style TTT, suggesting that preserving 2D local interactions at the projector stage is useful. Causal update ordering is better than bidirectional alternatives, supporting the claim that temporal modeling should happen before compression and in the correct direction. The hybrid selector beats naive uniform sampling without requiring an extra learned scorer, which indicates that the inner-loop signals carry meaningful change information. Finally, the retention diagnostics show that fast weights are not reliable long-horizon memory. If a task requires exact evidence from far back in the video, explicit frame retention is still necessary. That boundary is one of the most useful takeaways in the paper.795:T44f,The paper formulates text generation as a finite-horizon MDP. The state is the prompt plus generated tokens, the action is the next token, the transition deterministically appends the token, and the reward is assigned by a verifier over the completed sequence. This makes RLVR different from many classical RL settings: there is little environment dynamics, but the horizon can be extremely long and rewards are often sequence-level. The analysis focuses on KL-constrained policy optimization as probability redistribution relative to a base reference model. To manipulate the initial distribution, the authors use SFT+ to increase the probability of a target string and SFT- to disrupt or suppress that behavior. They then run toy RLVR tasks, including target-string generation and math solving, under sparse, dense, and random reward signals. They also vary the prompt distribution, comparing narrow reasoning prompts against a broader Tulu-3-style pretraining distribution, and compare different model scales. Entropy and probability mass assigned to target behaviors are tracked throughout training.796:T90f,TailSFT 的核心很简单：在 SFT 时做 sequence-level filtering，把那些相对于初始策略已经“fit 得够好”的训练序列过滤掉，只对 under-modeled tail 继续更新。作者的出发点是，标准 cross-entropy 会继续奖励所有 demonstration 的概率提升，包括模型已经很容易采样出来的响应；而概率质量守恒意味着，这种继续加压可能把质量从别的潜在有用响应上挤走，导致 coverage 下降。也就是说，CE 和 coverage 不是同一个目标，甚至可能冲突。

论文先在理论上 formalize 了 coverage。设任务有二值可验证奖励，RL 初始阶段真正有用的是：对一个 prompt，模型在 k 次采样内至少出现一个 reward-bearing response 的概率，这正是 pass@k 的含义。large-k pass@k 越高，RL rollout 越容易拿到正信号。TailSFT 因而不再试图均匀提升所有监督样本的 likelihood，而是优先学习那些初始模型还不容易覆盖到的序列。

关键设计点有两个。第一，过滤是 sequence-level，而不是 token-level reweighting。因为 coverage 关心的是“完整响应是否可被采到”，不是局部 token 拟合。第二，过滤标准是相对于 initial policy，而不是相对于当前训练中的 policy。作者强调这一点并给出理论说明：若按当前策略动态过滤，训练过程会不断改变“谁算已经学会”，容易引入不稳定或错误的偏置；相对于初始策略做过滤，则更接近“保留初始模型已有覆盖、把增量学习预算投向尾部”的目标，并且能在文中的设定下给出优于标准 CE 和一些朴素过滤方案的 coverage 保证。

从算法形态看，TailSFT 是一个 drop-in SFT objective modification，不需要改模型结构，也不依赖 RL 阶段信息。实现上更像在 SFT 数据上做基于 base policy 的 hard example selection，但它不是为了提升训练时 loss 或 pass@1，而是为了提升后续 RL 可利用的探索起点。论文还提出了一个 coverage-ratio diagnostic，用 base model 和标准 SFT run 的统计量来判断 TailSFT 是否有望改善 coverage。这个诊断给了方法一个实用入口：不是所有数据集、所有任务都一定适合过滤，先看 coverage ratio 可以减少盲试。797:T85d,TailSFT is a sequence-level filtering method for supervised fine-tuning. During SFT, it removes sequences that are already sufficiently well fit by the initial policy, and concentrates updates on the under-modeled tail of the response distribution. The motivation is that standard cross-entropy keeps rewarding likelihood increases for every demonstration, including responses the model can already sample easily. Because probability mass is limited, pushing those easy responses further can reduce mass assigned to other potentially useful responses, hurting coverage.

The paper formalizes coverage in the setting of binary verifiable rewards. For a prompt x, what matters for RL initialization is the probability that at least one of k samples receives reward 1. This is exactly what pass@k measures. Large-k pass@k is therefore a proxy for how much positive learning signal RL can expect from the initialization under a realistic rollout budget.

Two design choices are central. First, filtering is done at the sequence level rather than the token level, because coverage is about sampling complete reward-bearing responses, not about local token fit. Second, filtering is defined relative to the initial policy rather than the current policy during training. This is not a cosmetic detail. The authors argue, and partially prove, that filtering relative to the initial policy better preserves useful pre-existing coverage and avoids the instability or myopia of more naive dynamic filtering schemes. Under their setup, this criterion yields better coverage guarantees than standard CE and simpler alternatives.

Operationally, TailSFT is a drop-in modification to SFT rather than a new architecture or an RL-dependent method. It resembles hard-example selection based on the base model, but the target is not better training loss or pass@1; it is better downstream RL initialization. The paper also introduces a lightweight coverage-ratio diagnostic, computed from the base model and a standard SFT run, which provides a sufficient condition for TailSFT to improve coverage. That diagnostic makes the method more actionable in practice.798:T5c1,The experiments are organized in three layers. First, the paper uses a controlled graph-navigation task to isolate the tension between CE and coverage. In that setting, filtering already-fit examples improves large-k pass@k even when cross-entropy becomes worse and pass@1 does not improve. This is an important result because it shows TailSFT is not just an empirical trick on benchmark tasks; it is optimizing a genuinely different objective.

Second, the method is tested on OLMo-3 7B for math and coding. According to the reported headline numbers, TailSFT improves pass@16 by up to 16.8 absolute points on coding and 3.1 points on math. More importantly, the gain transfers through RL: after GRPO, final pass@1 improves by up to 3.9 points. That is the strongest evidence in the paper, because it shows the method improves not only multi-sample accessibility but also the eventual post-RL model.

Third, the paper includes design ablations and diagnostics. It compares different filtering criteria and motivates why filtering relative to the initial policy is preferable to more naive alternatives. It also introduces the coverage-ratio diagnostic and shows that it can predict when TailSFT should help. A recurring theme in the results is the trade-off: TailSFT may sacrifice CE and small-k metrics in exchange for better large-k coverage and better post-RL performance. The paper treats this trade-off as a feature of stage-aware optimization rather than a weakness.799:T4ee,This one deserves a close read. Start with the introduction and the coverage formalization section. The paper only makes sense if you internalize the distinction between optimizing SFT loss and optimizing RL initialization quality. Then read the controlled graph-navigation section carefully; it gives the cleanest evidence that lower CE does not necessarily imply better downstream RL readiness. After that, focus on the TailSFT algorithm and the argument for filtering relative to the initial policy. The main empirical tables on OLMo-3 7B are the next priority, especially the pass@16 numbers and the final GRPO pass@1 gains. Finish with the coverage-ratio diagnostic, which is the part most likely to transfer directly into real training pipelines.

If time is limited, the minimum useful subset is: the coverage formalization, Algorithm 1, the graph-navigation figures, the main math/coding result tables, and the diagnostic figure. Good follow-up questions while reading are: whether the same idea extends to other stage boundaries such as pretrain-to-mid-train or mid-train-to-SFT; how filtering thresholds trade off against data diversity; and how the notion of coverage should change for multi-answer tasks, non-binary rewards, or process-based rewards.79a:T7b6,文章的组织方式比一般 survey 更像问题剖析。它先把 OPSD 放回方法谱系里：SFT 提供 dense 但 off-policy 的信号；RL/RLVR 变成 on-policy，但奖励稀疏；on-policy distillation 用外部 teacher 恢复 token-level dense signal；OPSD/SDPO 则把 teacher 换成“带 privileged information 的自己”。这条脉络讲得很清楚，也解释了 OPSD 为什么同时继承了 imitation learning、RL 和 privileged learning 的优点与缺点。

全文的主线是“一个症状，三个杠杆”。从给出的内容看，这个症状主要指 OPSD 中最突出的失败模式：dense self-distillation 信号会把模型过快拉向 teacher 条件分布，导致多样性下降、探索受限、甚至学到依赖特权信息的行为。围绕这个症状，文章把控制手段归纳为三类杠杆：
1）where to apply the signal：信号施加在什么 token、什么阶段、什么轨迹片段上；
2）what to show the teacher：teacher 拿到哪类 privileged information，参考解、hint、plan、环境反馈各自引入什么偏差；
3）when to let the guidance change：训练过程中 teacher guidance 是固定、退火、门控还是分阶段切换。

文章还专门强调 KL 方向的差异。它回顾了 forward KL 与 reverse KL 在 on-policy distillation 中的不同作用：forward KL 倾向覆盖 teacher 的多模态分布，reverse KL 更容易收缩到单一模式。MiniLLM 一类工作推动了 reverse KL 在 LLM 上的使用，但在 OPSD 场景里，这种 mode-seeking 倾向会进一步放大熵塌缩问题。这个讨论对理解为什么有些 OPSD 训练“看起来收敛很快，但泛化和探索变差”很关键。

从方法论上，这篇综述最有用的地方不是罗列论文，而是把很多后续变体放进统一因果框架：它们大多是在调节 privileged teacher 与 on-policy student 之间的信息落差，以及由此产生的偏置-方差-探索三角关系。79b:T86b,The paper is organized as a diagnosis rather than a catalog. It first places OPSD in a lineage: SFT gives dense but off-policy supervision; RL and RLVR move to on-policy learning but with sparse end-of-trajectory rewards; on-policy distillation restores dense token-level supervision using an external teacher; OPSD and SDPO replace that teacher with the same model under privileged conditioning. This framing is one of the paper’s strengths because it makes clear which advantages and liabilities OPSD inherits from imitation learning, RL, and learning with privileged information.

The main analytical frame is the title’s “one symptom, three levers.” The dominant symptom is that dense self-distillation can over-concentrate the student toward the privileged teacher distribution, reducing diversity and encouraging reliance on information unavailable at inference time. The three levers are then organized as:
1) where to apply the signal — which tokens, trajectory segments, or training phases should receive distillation pressure;
2) what to show the teacher — what kind of privileged information is exposed, such as reference solutions, plans, hints, or environment feedback, and what bias each introduces;
3) when to let the guidance change — whether teacher guidance should be fixed, annealed, gated, or staged over training.

A particularly useful part of the review is its treatment of KL direction. It revisits the difference between forward KL and reverse KL in on-policy distillation: forward KL encourages mode covering, while reverse KL is more mode seeking. In LLM distillation, reverse KL became popular partly through MiniLLM-style formulations, but in OPSD that same tendency can amplify entropy collapse. This helps explain why some self-distillation runs look sample-efficient and stable early on, yet end up with poorer exploration and weaker generalization.

The paper’s real contribution is conceptual unification. Many later variants are shown to be different ways of managing the information gap between privileged teacher and on-policy student, and the resulting trade-off among bias, variance, and exploration.79c:T64f,As a critical review, it does not present a new unified benchmark suite. Its empirical value lies in synthesizing what the literature has already established and where disagreement remains. The paper notes that early OPSD results in mathematical reasoning were promising: accuracy could approach RL-style training while using far fewer generated tokens. That promise explains the rapid growth of the area.

At the same time, the review argues that several failure modes are now well documented:
1) entropy and diversity collapse, where dense teacher supervision narrows the student’s output distribution;
2) capability regression, where previously acquired abilities degrade under repeated self-distillation, especially when the target style becomes too tied to reference solutions;
3) dependence on privileged information, where the student is implicitly trained against token-level distributions shaped by information unavailable at test time;
4) limited strategy discovery, where OPSD is better at sharpening reasoning patterns already present in the base model than at discovering genuinely new ones, in contrast to some RLVR settings.

The paper is careful about what is settled and what is still implementation-dependent. Outcomes vary with KL choice, the type of privileged information, whether guidance is annealed, and whether distillation is applied selectively to uncertain or erroneous tokens. If the practical question is whether OPSD can replace RL, the review’s answer is cautious: it offers dense supervision and token efficiency, but its bias is not something that disappears with minor tuning.79d:T793,The analysis targets the Thinker backbone of Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct: 48 layers, hidden size 2048, with audio encoder features injected at audio-token positions before the text Transformer continues processing. The authors do not train probes or modify the model. They apply a logit lens to intermediate residual states, projecting hidden states through the final untied output head and measuring the rank of target tokens in vocabulary space. They use token rank rather than raw probability because logit scale drifts substantially across depth.

A key design choice is to predefine the workspace band as layers 17-38, roughly 35%-80% of depth, following prior text-model workspace studies instead of tuning the band on audio data. Readout is taken at audio-token positions, and for each answer option they report the best rank achieved by its first token across those positions and layers.

The central control isolates audio evidence from text prior. The written question and options are kept byte-identical, while only the waveform is swapped among the true clip, a mismatched clip from the same category, or silence. Because audio features are injected at positions that precede the textual question/options in the causal stream, readouts at those positions cannot simply copy the later option text. This makes a strong case that readable option-related concepts in the middle layers are driven by the waveform.

The paper then studies five aspects: hidden multi-hop concept formation, multilinguality of the workspace, differences between direct audio input and text caption input, depth-wise emergence of audio-driven signals, and layer-deletion evidence about where listening, integration, and output delivery happen. The resulting picture is a three-band organization: early sensory access, middle verbalizable workspace, and late output alignment. Errors often appear early as text-mode priors and are rarely corrected later.79e:T8f2,The experiments are mainly controlled interpretability studies rather than benchmark-style evaluation. The model under study is Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct with a 48-layer Thinker backbone.

Five empirical findings stand out.

1. Hidden reasoning can be read without chain-of-thought. In the most striking example, for an audio clip whose verbatim transcription is essentially garbled, the middle-layer readout progresses through “water + gate,” then “scandal,” then “president,” and finally resolves to “Nixon.” This suggests that latent multi-hop semantic structure is already present before the model emits any answer.

2. The workspace is multilingual. On entirely English inputs, 38.5% of top-1 readouts are Chinese. The implication is that the intermediate workspace is not tied to the surface language of the prompt, but behaves more like a shared semantic space with multiple lexicalizations.

3. Audio preserves information that text captions lose. The authors compare direct audio input against feeding the model its own emotion-stripped caption of the same clip. The audio pathway recovers sound source, speaker role, and affective information that the text pathway does not. This supports the claim that the readable middle-layer content is not reducible to transcript text.

4. Audio-driven signals emerge at a specific depth range. The gap over text prior is near zero at input, becomes significant from roughly 12% depth onward, and is most cleanly separated from prior in the predefined workspace band (layers 17-38). The paper also argues that these middle-layer states are causally used before the final motor layers.

5. The answer is distributed, and hallucinations are born early. Layer deletion localizes “listening” to early entry layers and “delivery” to the final output layer, while no single interior layer is indispensable. A text-mode hallucination often takes over early and is usually not revised later.

The authors are careful about limitations: they use a logit lens rather than the more faithful Jacobian lens; they study one model family; the dataset slice is small and intentionally sound-dominated; and readout is sparse across audio positions. So the results should be read as mechanism evidence, not as a capability benchmark.79f:T4cb,For a quick but useful read, focus on three parts.

First, read the introduction and method carefully to understand the control logic. The most important point is how the paper separates waveform-driven internal content from prompt prior: byte-identical text, waveform-only swaps, and readout at audio-token positions that causally precede the options.

Second, inspect the qualitative case studies tied to the five findings, especially the Watergate/Nixon example, the multilingual readouts, and the audio-versus-caption comparisons. These examples carry most of the paper’s interpretability argument.

Third, read the depth analysis and layer-deletion sections. That is where the paper becomes relevant to pretraining researchers: it suggests that audio information enters a shared language-like workspace relatively early, and that hallucinations may crystallize before late layers have any chance to repair them.

A 30-45 minute skim is enough to extract the main ideas. If reading more deeply, the two questions worth pushing on are: how faithful the logit-lens readout is in the audio setting, and whether this middle-layer verbal workspace is specific to Qwen3-Omni or a broader property of multimodal language models.7a0:T46d,The pipeline has three stages. First, captions are generated on 200 COCO val2014 images, and object mentions are labeled as grounded or hallucinated using a COCO-based CHAIR scorer. For each object token, the method records image-token attention for all 1,024 attention heads in LLaVA-1.5-7B and ranks heads by the drop in image attention around hallucinated object words relative to grounded ones. Second, the strongest candidates are screened by single-head ablation, measuring the change in hallucination-token log probability. This yields a fixed set of 32 heads spanning 19 transformer layers. Third, two interventions are applied only to this set: a head-sliced LoRA adapter on the corresponding Q/K/V head dimensions, enforced with gradient masking, and an inference-time grounding controller that penalizes generation when the selected heads attend weakly to image tokens. The LoRA stage uses a DPO-style objective where COCO ground-truth captions are chosen responses and the model’s hallucinated captions are rejected responses. The reported LoRA configuration is rank 8, alpha 16, dropout 0.05, trained for three epochs.7a1:T517,MHS is built around a model-agnostic standardized hardware driver. The driver translates device-specific interfaces into simple primitives such as read, for retrieving temperature, images, curves, or other state, and write, for setting temperature, positions, laser parameters, or other controllable values. Devices are made discoverable in a standard format so that agents and instruments can find and communicate with each other across networks without custom translators. A second important design is the use of natural-language tags. Many hardware-relevant facts are not visible from code alone, such as the weight of a robot arm, operating limits, what the device can measure, and what can be safely adjusted. MHS lets users enter this information directly, or have an agent interview them about the setup. The driver then produces a reference file describing the device’s capabilities and enforced safety limits. Control is exposed through MCP, command-line interfaces, and code-file APIs. Online model reasoning is used for high-level supervision, monitoring, fault handling, and parameter updates, while long-running or fast operations can be compiled into deterministic scripts. This separation is important because physical control often needs low latency, reproducibility, and auditability.7a2:T4e0,The blog reports a research preview and partner deployments rather than a controlled benchmark with ablations. The reported integration claim is that MHS can reduce setup work from weeks or months to hours or minutes. Carnegie Mellon used MHS for serial dilution dose-response experiments and reports roughly a 3x speedup, with an agent orchestrating a liquid handler, plate reader, robotic arm, and monitoring cameras across three computers with incompatible interfaces. QuEra used MHS to give an agent control over parts of the laser system in neutral-atom quantum machines; the agent-developed controller recovered laser lock 99.3% of the time without human intervention. Other deployments include Genentech automating a BCA protein assay across a liquid handler, robotic arm, and plate reader; University of Washington work on remote monitoring, agent-supervised qPCR, and collision-free plate handoffs; HHMI Janelia unifying a microscopy rig that previously depended on seven vendor programs; and Tetsuwan integrating MHS with ResearchOS for a qPCR workflow. The evidence is promising but incomplete: there is no public standardized task suite, failure taxonomy, model comparison, or detailed safety incident analysis in the provided material.7a3:T40c,The technical core has two parts. First, the paper uses Scheffé response-surface models, which are designed for variables constrained to the probability simplex. A first-order Scheffé model represents additive domain effects. A second-order model adds x_i x_j terms, capturing pairwise deviations from additivity: a domain pair can be better or worse together than expected from their individual contributions. Because the number of interactions grows quickly with the number of domains, the paper uses sparse second-order Scheffé models, keeping the response surface interpretable and less prone to overfitting when proxy data are limited. Second, the paper treats proxy mixture choices as an optimal design problem. Instead of sampling candidate mixtures randomly, it constructs model-robust I-optimal designs. I-optimality minimizes average prediction variance over the experimental region, and the model-robust variant balances performance across candidate response models, such as additive-only and interaction-inclusive models.7a4:T50f,Geodesia-KV is a training-free family of cache policies. It partitions the cache into 64-token blocks and assigns each block to a monotone precision ladder: exact 16-bit storage, 8/4/2-bit scalar quantization, or a 1-bit centroid-like representation. Block importance is tracked through a causal EMA of observed attention mass, so allocation decisions depend only on the prefix. For GQA models, allocation is performed once per physical KV head by aggregating masses across the associated query heads.

The allocator is framed as a monotone rate-distortion problem. After a block leaves the recent window, it may be demoted but not promoted, since the dense copy is no longer kept. This design makes in-place compression possible and prevents hidden memory costs from a fallback representation. The bit depth is selected from attention mass and a reconstruction-error proxy: blocks with high attention mass or larger distortion risk receive more bits. The method also adds exact residuals for a small set of high-impact tokens, selected from prompt attention mass and value reconstruction error. The Compressed-Quest variant combines query-sparse page reading with compressed resident pages: exact key boxes are used for page ranking, while resident K/V tensors follow the graded representation.7a5:T42f,The experiments cover 3B and 8B checkpoints, with long-context evaluations on WikiText-2 and PG-19. A central experimental point is the causal Q=1 setup and separate accounting of resident and read rates. The authors show that chunked teacher forcing can alter the reported rate of a method such as KIVI; in their implementation, KIVI changes from about 5.03 bits/value with a 64-token chunk to about 5.69 bits/value with a 1024-token chunk.

On WikiText-2 with a 16k context, the 5-bit operating point of Geodesia-KV achieves lower perplexity at a lower bitrate than KIVI-4 on Qwen. The Compressed-Quest version improves perplexity while reducing resident cost, with a reported comparison of 9.83 versus 16.25 bits/value. The PG-19 study uses a preregistered window list and cluster bootstrap intervals to separate robust effects from small-window artifacts. The paper also reports native vLLM integration and practical resident-capacity gains on GQA and MLA models, along with several negative results for spectral, quantum-inspired, VQ, and static-protection variants.7a6:T85b,方法上有三个关键设计。其一是 extractive compression：模型不是重写代码和工具输出，而是从输入段落中选择要保留的 span，并配合一组固定的结构标记表示删除区域。这样做的目的很明确，不是追求语言自然，而是尽量保证 identifier、path、number、error string 这类 downstream edit 依赖的精确字符串不被改坏。文中对这一点做了审计，训练语料上 96.0% 的 identifier/path/number 来自输入拷贝，held-out SWE-bench Lite 上是 96.2%；如果排除作者刻意允许改写的一类对象，这个比例到 98.3%。

其二是 intent conditioning。每次压缩不是只看 segment 本身，而是同时输入当前任务 query，让模型优先保留 query 中点名的实体、文件、函数、报错线索。作者强调“什么重要”不是静态属性，而是相对当前 agent 目标定义的，这也是它和通用压缩器的主要区别。

其三是 pipeline 设计。系统先做 segmentation、kind classification 和 level labeling，再按 segment 单独压缩。压缩模型只看到 task + 单个 segment + kind/level tag，不直接接收数值 token budget；预算通过 system prompt 中的 level-to-ratio 表间接传达。作者原本设计了四级重要性标签 L0-L3，并希望不同 level 对应不同压缩率，但实验发现蒸馏后的 student 实际只学出了两个有效压缩带宽，四级设计没有按预期落地。这个负结果作者没有回避，反而是全文里比较有价值的部分。

数据方面，作者从 67,074 条 OpenHands 轨迹出发，经过五阶段流水线，构建出 45K segment distillation pool 和 40,606 条 teacher-validated compression examples，带有 intent-conditioned target、level label 和 must-keep annotation。训练上比较了三个匹配 backbone，最后选 4B；还尝试过对 drop supervision 加权，但结果适得其反，最终部署版本没有采用。更有意思的是，最终上线 checkpoint 不是训练 loss 最优，而是通过 OOD sweep 选出来的，说明这个任务里 loss 和真实可用性并不严格一致。7a7:T89d,The method has three main pieces. First, it uses extractive compression. Instead of rewriting code and tool outputs, the model selects spans from the input and uses a fixed set of structural markers to denote removed regions. The reason is straightforward: downstream edits depend on exact strings, so identifiers, paths, numbers, and error messages should be copied, not paraphrased. The paper audits this claim explicitly: 96.0% of emitted identifier/path/number-like tokens are copied from the input on the training corpus, and 96.2% on held-out SWE-bench Lite outputs; excluding the one category intentionally rewritten by design, the rate reaches 98.3%.

Second, the compressor is intent-conditioned. Each compression call receives both the current task/query and a single segment, so the model can prioritize entities, files, functions, and error clues named in the live task. The paper argues that importance is not intrinsic to a segment; it is defined relative to what the agent is trying to do now.

Third, the system is built as a pipeline. A gateway performs segmentation, kind classification, and level labeling, and the model compresses one segment at a time. The compressor sees the task plus one segment with kind/level tags, but no explicit numeric token budget. Budget control is only indirectly encoded through a static level-to-ratio table in the system prompt. The authors originally designed four importance levels, L0-L3, but report that the distilled student effectively learned only two usable compression bands. That negative result is one of the more informative parts of the paper.

On data, they start from 67,074 raw OpenHands trajectories and build a five-stage pipeline that yields a 45K-segment distillation pool and 40,606 teacher-validated compression examples with intent-conditioned targets, level labels, and must-keep annotations. On training, they compare three matched backbones and choose 4B. They also tried drop-supervision weighting, found that it backfired, and shipped without it. Notably, the deployed checkpoint was selected by an out-of-distribution sweep rather than by training loss, which suggests that lower loss did not reliably predict real utility.7a8:T53a,The evaluation has two layers. The intrinsic evaluation focuses on OOD holdout performance, including compression quality, must-keep retention, and identifier retention, with confidence intervals. One notable result is that at comparable budgets, the student does not underperform its own teacher on must-keep identifier retention, which suggests that distillation preserved the key exact-copy behavior.

The end-to-end evaluation plugs Paritok-4B into a coding-agent workflow under both raw-source and in-distribution line-numbered settings. The headline result is a 25.7% compression rate, meaning roughly one quarter of the original context is retained, while maintaining comparable single-shot solve quality. The paper describes this as roughly twice as aggressive as strong GPT-based compressors. Interestingly, the expected trade-off did not appear in the predicted form: instead of harder compression at equal quality, they observed slightly softer compression with higher quality, and no paired degradation was statistically resolvable over 300 instances.

That said, the scope is narrow. The conclusions are tied to coding-agent trajectories, the specific segmentation pipeline, and teacher-generated targets. The collapse from four intended levels to two effective bands also shows that fine-grained budget control remains weak.7a9:T6d8,The method organizes each logical KV page into a three-tier lifecycle: Recent, Anchor, and Stale. Recent and Anchor pages are stored in FP8, while Stale pages are stored in a 3-bit TQ3 format. Recent covers fresh tokens needed for local coherence and ongoing reasoning. Anchor is reserved for globally important regions such as system prompts, attention sinks, retrieved evidence, or structural headers. Stale holds older non-anchor content that should not be dropped. The key contribution is not merely mixed precision, but integrating mixed precision into the paged-attention runtime itself. Every live-request page remains addressable; pages are not evicted. Format-specific kernels compute partial attention statistics on different physical formats, and the outputs are merged through a stable global softmax merge, instead of reconstructing a unified dense cache first. The paper also keeps key/value asymmetry explicit: key distortion changes routing, while value distortion changes retrieved content, so the codec and kernel interfaces preserve separate treatment for K and V even if a deployment uses the same nominal tier for both. The controller uses page age, structural metadata, attention statistics, layer/head sensitivity, K/V role, and current memory pressure to decide transitions. Attention-based promotion is built on globally normalized page mass, not raw local scores, so pages from different physical partitions remain comparable. On the engineering side, the paper adds an ownership protocol, fallback paths, dense-shadow and physical-byte instrumentation, and a CUDA-graph-compatible heterogeneous decode path. That makes the contribution primarily a runtime integration story rather than a new compression formula in isolation.7aa:T5fa,The main evaluation is on Qwen3.6-27B using a single 96GB NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU. The paper first explains the compression opportunity from the model structure: Qwen3.6-27B has 64 language layers arranged as 16 groups of three Gated DeltaNet layers followed by one full-attention layer, so only 16 layers contribute attention KV. Each such layer has 4 KV heads with head dimension 256. Under this setup, the theoretical BF16 attention-cache cost is exactly 2.00 GiB per 32K-token sequence and 8.00 GiB per 128K-token sequence. Minima-KV reports 18.3 KiB of attention KV per live token in deployment accounting, which is a 3.50x reduction relative to BF16 and a 1.75x reduction relative to FP8. On quality, the paper reports profile-separated evidence. The clearly stated results include parity with the dense control on 16K RULER NIAH, less than 1% regression on 4K RULER NIAH, and LongBench v2 evaluation up to 64K context. One important caveat is highlighted by the authors: Qwen3.6 also has a separate per-sequence Gated DeltaNet recurrent state, which is not counted as compressed attention KV. That means the concurrency gain from KV compression is bounded by other fixed per-sequence allocations. This is an important systems point, because raw KV compression ratio does not translate directly into throughput gain. From the available full text, the evaluation is more deployment- and quality-oriented than analytically broad; there is limited evidence of cross-family validation or deeper generalization studies.7ab:T416,For a quick read, focus on three parts. First, read the Introduction and Background to understand that the paper is not just about quantization; it is about retention-preserving lifecycle management for KV pages. Second, read the hierarchy section carefully, especially the tier definitions, the globally normalized page-mass formulation, and the mixed-format softmax merge. Those are the most informative technical pieces. If time is limited, prioritize: (1) the Qwen3.6-27B KV cost breakdown, (2) the Recent/Anchor/Stale controller logic, and (3) the RULER NIAH and LongBench v2 quality results. A useful skim should take about 20–30 minutes. Two deeper questions are worth following up: whether the page-level normalized attention mass is stable enough as a control signal, and whether this kind of runtime hierarchy could eventually influence training-time long-range dependency modeling.7ac:T87f,方法分三步：generation、routing、refinement。先从同一个生成模型独立采样 n 条完整轨迹，再用 reward model 对整条轨迹打分。与直接按绝对分数阈值决策不同，SRD 采用 rank-normalized score，把候选按 reward 排序后映射到 [0,1] 区间，再用两个阈值 θ_low 和 θ_high 做三路路由：高分样本 Keep，中间样本 Refine，低分样本 Discard。这样做的动机是减少不同题目、不同 reward 尺度下绝对分数不稳定的问题。

真正的创新在 refinement。对进入 Refine 的边界样本，算法不会整条重采，而是沿轨迹按固定步长 m 检查 prefix-level reward 变化，寻找最早出现“相对前缀退化”的位置 j，把 j 之后的 suffix 截掉并重新生成。重生成时提高采样温度，目的是增加局部探索，避免原轨迹在同一错误模式附近反复采样。新 suffix 接回原 prefix 后，再重新打分并与其他活跃候选一起排序，只保留最终进入 Keep 的样本。

论文还给了理论分析。核心结论是，在温和假设下，SRD 相比 rejection sampling 有严格更高的期望最优轨迹质量，并带来约 1.28–1.36 倍的 sample efficiency 提升，且收益会随候选池增大而上升。文中把收益写成与 (1 + ρ·p_M/p_H) 相关的形式，其中 p_M、p_H 对应中等质量可修复样本与高质量样本的概率质量，ρ 则刻画 refinement 成功率。这个表达很重要，因为它说明 SRD 不是无条件占优：只有当“边界样本里确实存在可救前缀”且 reward 能识别退化位置时，局部重写才有意义。

和已有方法相比，Best-of-N 只会在末端选择，完全不回收中间结构；speculative rejection 会更早停掉低质前缀，但一旦拒绝就不可逆；Controlled Decoding 依赖 prefix-aware value function 在 token 级引导，而 SRD 不需要额外训练 value function，也不需要更大 teacher，只需生成模型加 reward model。代价是它仍然依赖完整轨迹采样和额外 reward 评估，且边界定位目前较粗，主要靠固定间隔扫描，不是细粒度 token-level attribution。7ad:T95d,SRD has three stages: generation, routing, and refinement. It first samples n complete trajectories from the same generator, then scores them with a reward model. Instead of using an absolute reward threshold, it converts rewards into rank-normalized scores in [0,1], and applies two thresholds, theta_low and theta_high, to route candidates into Keep, Refine, or Discard. The motivation is practical: absolute reward scales are often unstable across tasks and prompts, while rank is more robust.

The main novelty is the refinement stage. For borderline candidates routed to Refine, SRD does not resample the whole trajectory. It scans the trajectory at fixed intervals m, evaluates prefix-level reward behavior, and finds the earliest point j where quality appears to degrade relative to the preceding prefix. It then truncates the suffix after j and regenerates only that suffix, using a higher sampling temperature to encourage local exploration and avoid repeating the same failure mode. The repaired trajectory is rescored and reranked jointly with the remaining candidates, and is kept only if it survives the final routing.

The paper also provides a theoretical analysis. Under mild assumptions, SRD achieves strictly higher expected best-trajectory quality than rejection sampling and improves sample efficiency by about 1.28–1.36x, with gains increasing as the candidate pool grows. The gain is characterized by a term of the form (1 + rho * p_M / p_H), where p_M and p_H capture the mass of repairable medium-quality samples and already-high-quality samples, and rho reflects refinement success. This matters because it clarifies when SRD should help: only when there is a meaningful population of salvageable trajectories and the reward signal can identify degradation reliably.

Relative to prior work, best-of-N only selects at the end and never recovers partial structure; speculative rejection can stop early but is irreversible once a prefix is rejected; Controlled Decoding uses a learned prefix-aware value function for token-level steering, whereas SRD needs only a generator and a reward model, with no larger teacher and no separately trained value function. The trade-off is that SRD still requires full-trajectory sampling up front and extra reward evaluations, and its boundary detection is fairly coarse, based on interval scanning rather than token-level attribution.7ae:T6b0,The experiments cover MATH500, GPQA, HotpotQA, and AlpacaEval, spanning mathematical reasoning, science QA, multi-hop QA, and instruction following. The main empirical claim is about the accuracy-compute frontier rather than a single accuracy number: at matched or near-matched quality, SRD uses fewer generated tokens; under low compute budgets, it tends to outperform speculative rejection; under larger budgets, it approaches best-of-N quality at lower cost.

The clearest number stated in the paper is the theoretical 1.28–1.36x sample-efficiency gain. The full text indicates that the gain becomes more visible with larger candidate pools, because more borderline trajectories become available for repair. The ablations focus on two issues. First, reward calibration: when rewards are stable and ranking is reliable, conservative global rerouting works better because it identifies worthwhile candidates more consistently; when rewards are noisy, local self-comparison is more robust because it reduces misrouting from cross-sample score instability. Second, refinement boundary choice: truncating too early destroys useful context, while truncating too late leaves too little room for repair, so the interval size m and routing thresholds matter.

A useful experimental detail is that the authors test multiple generator–reward model pairings rather than tying the method to one specific model stack. That suggests SRD is a search-layer improvement rather than an artifact of a single base model. Still, many results are presented as tradeoff curves and relative gains, so readers who care about exact token costs and absolute per-benchmark deltas should inspect the main tables and appendix carefully.7af:T5a4,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the main method figure. The key idea is simple: SRD does not just sample more trajectories and pick one; it repairs near-miss trajectories by preserving good prefixes. Then read the routing rule and the regeneration-boundary definition. The use of rank-normalized reward, rather than absolute reward, is an important design choice because it determines how stable the method is across tasks.

After that, skim the theory section for the main proposition rather than every proof detail. Focus on the assumptions behind the sample-efficiency gain: the prevalence of repairable borderline samples, the success rate of suffix regeneration, and the reliability of reward ranking. Those assumptions define the regime where SRD should work. In the experiments, prioritize four kinds of figures: accuracy versus token budget, direct comparisons with best-of-N and speculative rejection, reward-calibration ablations, and sensitivity analyses for boundary choice, temperature, and routing thresholds. A useful skim should take about 30–45 minutes. If reading more deeply, two follow-up questions are worth pursuing: whether boundary detection can be upgraded from interval reward scans to token-level verifier signals or hidden-state anomaly signals, and whether SRD can be composed tightly with speculative decoding, process reward models, or MCTS-style search rather than only compared against them.7b0:T713,PuzzleKV partitions each per-head KV cache into fixed-length logical pages and independently factorizes completed pages using low-rank decomposition. Instead of forcing the entire prompt history to share one basis, each page gets its own local basis, which better preserves region-specific directions.

The implementation has several important pieces. First, the cache is hybrid: a small sink region and a recent window are kept dense, while older completed pages are stored in factorized form. This protects the most attention-sensitive tokens from compression artifacts. Second, the attention kernel is designed to operate directly on both dense and factorized pages, so the model does not reconstruct the historical KV cache back into full space before attention. That matters for bandwidth and runtime. Third, page conversion is incremental during autoregressive decoding: once a page is filled, it becomes eligible for decomposition and storage as factors. This makes the method compatible with online generation rather than only offline post-prefill compression. Fourth, the method is training-free and calibration-free. Unlike approaches that derive a fixed compression space from model weights or calibration activations, PuzzleKV builds the representation directly from the current request's page-local KV activations.

The paper's logic is straightforward: establish that page-level low-rank structure is common across models, layers, heads, and page sizes; show that page-local bases preserve information better than a global SVD baseline; then implement the idea in a mixed dense/factorized attention pipeline that can run during decoding. The trade-off is also clear: it gives up some of the maximal sharing of a global basis in exchange for finer-grained fidelity and more stable task performance.7b1:T49a,Experiments are run on Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, evaluated on RULER and LongBench. The headline result is that at roughly 60% of full KV storage, PuzzleKV retains more than 96% of Full-KV performance across all tested settings. When combined with per-factor INT4 quantization, storage drops to 18.7% of the original KV footprint while still retaining more than 93% of Full-KV performance. Compared with Global SVD, PuzzleKV shows substantial gains on RULER and competitive results on LongBench.

The more informative evidence is the structural analysis. The paper shows that for page size P = 32, the effective ranks needed for accurate reconstruction vary by layer and KV head but remain well below full rank throughout the evaluated models. It also studies reconstruction quality across different page sizes and ranks, supporting the claim that page-local low-rank structure is a robust property rather than an artifact of one configuration. From a systems perspective, the results suggest that page-wise decomposition does not destroy practical decoding quality, though the paper appears more focused on quality retention than on full end-to-end serving throughput.7b2:T429,This is a skim paper. Start with the introduction and the main workflow figure to understand why the page is used as both the memory-management unit and the compression unit. Then read the analysis establishing page-level low-rank structure; that is the empirical premise the whole method depends on.
