The OLMo experiments sharpen this into something close to a mechanistic statement. Along the same documented trajectory, adapter retention decays as continuation distance grows. The paper reports retention of 0.88–0.99 after a 46B-token continuation, but near no-adapter-floor performance after a 2.9T-token continuation. Subsequent annealing and model-soup merging add little extra damage. This turns portability from a vague family-level intuition into a distance-budget question.867:T9cb,The experimental scale is modest but well structured: 98 trainings and 193 evaluation cells, all run on a single RTX 4090, with per-query predictions, bootstrap confidence intervals, and energy logs released. The emphasis is clearly on reproducible decision measurement rather than brute-force benchmarking.

Several results stand out. First, specialists do not always become obsolete quickly. On intent classification, freezing retains 99%–101% of the attainable gain across nine upgrade hops. Over four generations, the retrained-specialist reference score moves by only 0.2 points, while zero-shot performance rises by 21 points. This suggests that some specialist value is tied mainly to task data, label taxonomies, or output conventions rather than to frontier base capability.

Second, other tasks are much more base-dependent. On text-to-SQL, the frozen specialist can forfeit up to 59% of attainable gain on a single hop, and its advantage over a newer base decays to zero within three generations. This motivates the paper’s data-bound vs base-bound distinction: some specialist moats are stable, others are rapidly eroded by improvements in the base model’s reasoning ability.

Third, naive porting can fail catastrophically. The paper gives a strong counterexample: between two architecturally identical checkpoints from independent pretraining runs, directly pasting the adapter drops intent classification from 92.8% to 42.9%, which is even worse than the 60.7% obtainable with no adapter at all. But when the target is a continued-pretraining descendant of the same weights, the same operation preserves near-reference accuracy. This directly challenges the common rule of thumb that same-family, same-shape transfer is safe.

Fourth, the OLMo validation reproduces the same pattern and localizes the boundary more precisely. Along the same training trajectory, port retention falls from 0.88–0.99 to the no-adapter floor as continuation distance increases; annealing and model-soup merge are not the main sources of damage. This is highly relevant for continual pretraining and checkpoint release strategy.

The paper also estimates a specialization half-life of roughly two to three generations at the 7–8B scale, and observes at least one actual crossing at 1.5–1.8B where cheap adoption of the new base overtakes the old specialist. The exact values are task-dependent, but this is much more concrete than the usual qualitative discussion around whether upgrades are worth it.868:T49b,Read this one with a concrete deployment or training question in mind. Start with the introduction and Figure 1, where the paper lays out the three intuitions it challenges: specialists do not always age quickly, porting is not always safe, and task differences are not well captured by a generative/discriminative split. Then read the benchmark setup and metric definitions carefully, especially retention, recovery cost, and specialization half-life. Without those definitions, the later conclusions can look like anecdotal observations.

In the experiments, prioritize the strategy comparisons across tasks and the evidence from both Qwen and OLMo supporting the claim that continuity, not architectural shape, governs portability. If you work on continual pretraining, checkpoint selection, adapter ecosystems, or practical model deployment, this is worth a full read. If you only need the main conclusions, 40–60 minutes on the main paper should be enough. The section around the independent-pretraining-run vs continued-pretraining-descendant comparison is the most important one to study closely, because it directly probes the limits of parameter-space transferability.869:T5a3,The method is an agentic LLM-as-judge setup. The data consists of pairs of revisions for the same declaration from Mathlib PRs: an earlier version that was sent back for revision, and the later version that was accepted. Importantly, each version is scored independently. The judge does not know the score of the other revision and is not explicitly told it is doing pairwise comparison, which reduces comparison leakage. The rubric decomposes proof quality into five dimensions: library leverage, automation fit, structural clarity, statement quality, and Mathlib conventions. Each dimension is scored from 1 to 10, then combined by a harness into a final score. The key design choice is tool grounding. The judge can query the exact Mathlib state at the relevant commit through bash, search for existing lemmas, inspect signatures, and check available APIs. That lets it reason like a human reviewer: is this proof reinventing something already in the library, should the statement be more general, is there a cleaner one-line invocation already available. This is materially different from a text-only judge because proof quality often depends on library context, not just the local proof text. For dataset construction, the authors used Claude Sonnet 5 to inspect historical PRs and identify cases with substantial revision differences that were not just linting or newly added declarations, then split them into development and test sets.86a:T5dc,The benchmark contains 218 declaration pairs in the test split and 123 pairs in the dev split used for rubric tuning. Six judges were evaluated, including three open-weight and three closed models, with three replicates per judge. Each evaluation allows up to 20 tool calls per sample to cap inference cost. The main metric is preference alignment: whether the judge assigns a higher score to the revision that Mathlib ultimately accepted. All models perform well above the 50% random baseline. Claude Sonnet 5 is best at 80.8%, while even DeepSeek-V4-Flash reaches 63.5%, with all sign tests reported at p < 1e-5. Among open models, muse-glimmer-30b gets 70.2% and inkling-small 69.3%, showing that the task is not exclusive to frontier closed models. The most useful experimental finding is the variance analysis. Re-running the same judge on the same declarations flips roughly one-fifth to nearly half of the verdicts. Some ablations look non-significant in one replicate, p = 0.34, and significant in another, p = 0.006. That means single-run judge benchmarks can easily overstate differences. The PR 11640 case study is also informative: the initial proof reconstructed a result already present in Mathlib, while the merged revision replaced it with a one-line call to H.restrictPreimage s. The judge found the existing declaration via tool use and consistently penalized the initial version on library leverage. This kind of semantic review cannot be replicated by linting or regex heuristics.86b:T9bd,Libra 的核心设计是 decoupled vision-language system：一套 vision system，一套 language system，中间用 cross-modal bridges 连接。关键不只是双塔，而是在每层内部把 self-modal modeling 和 cross-modal interaction 分成两种计算模式。

第一是 switch attention。作者区分两种场景：模态内部建模时，用标准 attention；跨模态交互时，不直接让一种模态去对齐另一种模态的原始特征空间，而是先通过 cross-modal bridge 把 Q/K/V 映射到新的交互空间，再做注意力。这么做的动机很明确：如果直接共享同一注意力空间，视觉和语言会互相拉扯，尤其在数据不平衡时更容易让弱势模态被强势模态同化。bridge 相当于给跨模态交互加了一个受控接口，保留各自表示的自治性。

第二是 switch FFN。它对应不同任务场景下的后续变换分流，用来进一步区分理解与生成、以及自模态与跨模态信息融合后的处理方式。虽然从摘要和引言看，具体实现细节需要结合方法章节确认，但设计意图很清楚：attention 负责信息路由，FFN 负责场景化变换，二者共同完成“共享框架下的计算解耦”。

在实例化上，作者给了两个版本。Libra-1 面向 understanding-only image-to-text。这里有两个值得注意的点：一是 supervision 采用 unified discrete autoregression，把视觉和语言都放进离散 AR 框架里，优先换取训练稳定性；二是 vision input 采用 hybrid tokenization，把连续视觉信号和离散 ID 结合起来，试图兼顾细粒度感知与离散序列训练的稳定性。这个选择说明作者并不完全相信纯离散视觉 token 足够表达感知细节。

Libra-2 扩展到 unified understanding + generation。按引言描述，它在 tokenization、representation、supervision 上又加了额外策略，目标是同时支持 image-to-text 和 text-to-image。这里最关键的不是“能不能统一”，而是统一后是否还能维持两边能力不互相伤害。Libra 的回答是通过结构分流降低干扰，而不是完全依赖数据配比去硬平衡。

如果和典型 unified MLLM 比，Libra 的区别在于它不把跨模态交互视为默认状态，而把它视为一种需要显式开关和专门映射空间的计算模式；如果和 cascade 比，它又没有把视觉生成完全外包给独立大后端，而是保留了端到端联合学习的可能。86c:Ta8b,Libra is a decoupled vision-language system with one vision branch and one language branch connected by cross-modal bridges. The key idea is not merely having two towers, but introducing two computation modes inside the model: self-modal modeling and cross-modal interaction.

The first component is switch attention. For self-modal modeling, Libra uses standard attention. For cross-modal interaction, it does not directly align one modality into the raw feature space of the other. Instead, queries, keys, and values are mapped through a cross-modal bridge into a dedicated interaction space before attention is computed. The motivation is clear: direct sharing of the same attention space can cause one modality, usually language, to dominate the other under imbalanced data. The bridge acts as a controlled interface that preserves modality-specific representations while still allowing information exchange.

The second component is switch FFN. It further separates computation after attention depending on the scenario, helping distinguish self-modal processing from cross-modal fusion, and likely also understanding from generation. The exact implementation details need the method section, but the design intent is straightforward: attention handles routing, FFN handles scenario-specific transformation, and together they realize decoupled computation within a unified framework.

The paper instantiates the framework in two versions. Libra-1 targets understanding-only image-to-text modeling. Two details matter here. First, supervision uses unified discrete autoregression over both vision and language, prioritizing training stability. Second, vision inputs use hybrid tokenization, combining continuous visual signals with discrete IDs to balance fine-grained perception and stable sequence modeling. This suggests the authors do not fully trust purely discrete visual tokens to carry enough perceptual detail.

Libra-2 extends the framework to joint multimodal understanding and generation. According to the introduction, it adds further strategies in tokenization, representation, and supervision to support both image-to-text and text-to-image. The central claim is not simply that these tasks can be unified, but that they can be unified without one side damaging the other, thanks to structural decoupling rather than only careful data balancing.

Compared with typical unified MLLMs, Libra treats cross-modal interaction as an explicit computation mode with dedicated mappings, not as the default state of every layer. Compared with cascade systems, it does not outsource visual generation to a separate large backend, so it preserves the possibility of end-to-end joint learning.86d:T597,From the available full-text fragment, the experiments are organized in two settings: Libra-1 for multimodal understanding and Libra-2 for joint understanding and generation. The paper claims that the architecture is effective in both settings and that the evaluation also covers tokenization, representation, and supervision choices.

However, the provided content does not include the later experimental tables, so it is not possible to responsibly report exact model sizes, training tokens, dataset scales, or precise gains over baselines. What can be stated with confidence is that the paper evaluates not only understanding-only settings but also unified generation settings, which is more complete than many works that stop at captioning or VQA. The separate Libra-1 and Libra-2 instantiations also indicate an important methodological point: a unified architecture does not imply a single training recipe; understanding-only and understanding-plus-generation require different supervision and tokenization choices.

If the full experiments include ablations, the most important ones to inspect are: removing switch attention or switch FFN, comparing hybrid tokenization against purely discrete or purely continuous visual inputs, and measuring whether unified training introduces a clear trade-off between understanding and generation quality. Without those ablations, the architectural claim would be much harder to assess.86e:T619,This is a skim-to-careful-read paper if you care about native multimodal pretraining rather than downstream VQA scores alone.

Start with the introduction and the architecture overview. The main point is not just building an MLLM that can generate images, but addressing training bias under modality imbalance in unified systems. Then read the switch attention and switch FFN sections carefully. In particular, check what the cross-modal bridge actually is: an independent parameter space, a low-rank mapping, or a gated projection. That determines whether the gain comes from inductive bias or simply from added capacity.

Next, compare Libra-1 and Libra-2. The important part is not the naming but how supervision, tokenization, and losses differ between understanding-only and joint understanding-generation settings. If reading selectively, prioritize the architecture figure, the tokenization design, the main result tables, and any ablations directly tied to modality imbalance. Expected reading time is about 35 to 50 minutes.

Three deeper questions are worth keeping in mind. First, whether hybrid tokenization is merely an engineering patch or evidence that current discrete visual tokenizers are still insufficient for unified AR modeling. Second, whether the switch modules help because they impose a better inductive bias or because they isolate parameters and reduce negative transfer. Third, whether this decoupled design still holds at much larger data scale, or mainly serves as a practical compromise under current multimodal data limitations.86f:T476,Re$^3$Cap treats multimodal retrieval as a semantic constraint mechanism.
1) Image-to-dataset retrieval: given an image v, retrieve Top-K similar image-text pairs R_v from a paired corpus D using an image retrieval model.
2) CRS (Caption Refinement Suggester): extract semantic elements that consistently appear across the retrieved captions; these act as “must-preserve / should-include” anchors.
3) CQA (Caption Quality Assessor): use the generated caption as a query to retrieve another set R_c; discrepancies between R_v and R_c are interpreted as hallucinations (caption introduces content that shifts retrieval away from the image-based neighborhood) or omissions (missing details that prevent alignment).
4) RL training uses CRS+CQA outputs to guide caption refinement, encouraging generation of new candidates rather than merely scoring existing ones.
Key differences vs common RL captioning: it avoids relying on a single VLM/CLIP scalar judge, does not require extra keyword annotations, and aims to reduce reward hacking by grounding feedback in retrieval-set consistency—assuming the retrieval model and corpus are reliable.870:T485,The framework, Multi-Turn Certified Robustness (MTCR), models conversation as a State-Adversarial MDP. Dialogue history is mapped to a continuous state; at each turn an adversary chooses a user message from an epsilon-bounded perturbation set; the LLM responds according to its policy; and the state is updated. Safety is defined by a predicate over the state space. The central quantity is k-turn certified robustness: the worst-case probability of staying safe for k turns under any adaptive adversary. A naive certificate gives a lower bound of p^k, where p is the worst-case single-turn certified safety probability. MTCR tightens this through embedding-space mode decomposition, separately certifying intra-mode safety and inter-mode transitions. It also introduces (alpha, beta)-safety persistence, a structural condition under which the degradation can improve from p^k to beta^k when beta is larger than the worst-case single-turn bound, with a linear characterization 1 - k(1 - beta) for interpretable horizon estimates. The paper also discusses tightness for non-overlapping decompositions and impossibility results without structural assumptions.871:T49c,The dataset contains 40 Korean conference sessions, 19 medical and 21 finance, with multilingual segments preserved when present. Each condition produces 2,598 to 2,765 QA items, a roughly 6% range. The main grid covers 9 models from five families, EXAONE, Gemma, Llama, Phi, and Qwen, ranging from 2.4B to 70B parameters. The main experiment has 72 LoRA runs, plus 12 full fine-tuning sanity runs and an 8-cell Whisper-medium STT-swap grid. The LoRA recipe uses rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05, 4-bit QLoRA, learning rate 2e-4, 3% warmup, 3 epochs, and effective batch size 16. Evaluation includes KMMLU, KMMLU-Pro, MMLU, four LLM judges, six blind human experts, STT substitution, and an LLM difficulty audit. QA quality improves by +0.18 according to LLM judges and +0.22 according to humans on a 1–5 scale, but the cross-model mean MCQA gain is not significant. Gains concentrate in model-family and domain-aligned settings. Replacing the internal STT system with Whisper-medium changes aggregate KMMLU by at most 1.32 percentage points on average. The difficulty audit finds that two strong LLM judges still cannot answer 7.8% of the public-sample QA items with confidence.872:T7ca,The setup is built around Qwen3-8B as a hybrid model. The same base model can be decoded in think mode, where it generates reasoning before deciding, or in no-think mode, where it emits a direct action token. This allows a relatively controlled comparison between a reasoning policy and a direct classifier without changing the model family. The task is binary intervention timing: given a prefix of a multi-party conversation, decide whether an assistant should speak now or remain silent. The dataset contains about 16,000 synthetic conversations expanded into roughly 173,000 token-level decision points, with only about 13% positive intervention labels, so the class imbalance is severe. The paper compares several training routes. One is direct decision-token SFT, which tends to produce a stronger classifier but suppresses reasoning. Another is a masked objective that preserves the model’s native reasoning, but only on cases the model already solves correctly; this means it receives little useful signal on failure cases and therefore struggles to improve beyond the base reasoning policy. A third route is think-mode RL, optimizing either accuracy or a behavioral faithfulness reward. The authors point out a key limitation of group-relative RL objectives: when all sampled rollouts agree, there is no learning signal, even if they all agree on the wrong answer. That leaves many confidently wrong prompts untouched. For auditing, the paper combines activation probes with behavioral interventions. Probes test when the decision becomes decodable in the hidden states, while interventions remove or replace parts of the generated reasoning to see whether the final action changes, which is a more causal test of whether reasoning matters. The paper also argues that several common metrics are misleading in this setting, including probability-based contribution scores, probe accuracy that ignores class imbalance, probing only at the end of reasoning, and uncontrolled flip tests.873:T613,The main empirical result is that the strongest action policy is the direct classifier that does not explicitly generate reasoning, while the reasoning policy is more auditable but less accurate, with the largest cost coming from missed interventions. That is the central capability–auditability tradeoff. In training experiments, decision-token SFT further strengthens the direct policy but pushes reasoning toward irrelevance. The masked objective cannot substantially beat the base reasoning policy because it only preserves reasoning on examples the model already gets right. Think-mode RL also fails to clearly surpass the base reasoning policy, not because RL is useless in general, but because the group-relative objective gives no gradient on prompts where all sampled rollouts agree, including confidently wrong ones. The audit results are also informative. For the reasoning policy, the eventual decision becomes decodable during the chain of thought, whereas for the direct classifier the decision is already decodable at the prompt stage. That supports the interpretation that the direct policy commits early, while the reasoning policy at least partially forms the decision during reasoning. The authors also stress that single-run comparisons can confuse seed variance with reward-objective effects, so multiple seeds or replicates are necessary when comparing RL variants. The excerpt provided here does not include the full numeric tables, but the paper is clearly organized around mechanism evidence rather than a single headline score.874:T588,The architecture has three parts: a frozen backbone LLM, a safety-specific LoRA adapter, and a learned gate that outputs a continuous routing score g in [0,1] from hidden-state representations. The adapter is not simply turned on or off. Its strength is scaled continuously inside the model, with the effective transformation written as h' = (W + gΔW)h. This makes the method closer to interpolation between the base model and a safety-adapted model, rather than hard switching or post-hoc filtering.

A key design choice is that the gate is trained jointly with the safety adapter. It is not an external moderation classifier. The gate directly modulates internal computation during generation. The paper adds two training ingredients to make routing discriminative. First, subtype-aware gate weighting gives different emphasis to different harmful and benign prompt categories, aiming to reduce false positives on safety-adjacent benign inputs. Second, a hard pairwise margin objective explicitly separates harmful and benign prompts in gating space. This is important because plain generation loss may not force a clean routing boundary. Compared with standard safety LoRA, the novelty is not the adapter itself but the input-conditioned continuous activation. Compared with guard-model pipelines, the novelty is that routing happens inside the model’s latent computation rather than as an external pre-filter.875:T755,The evaluation covers safety with HarmBench and XSTest, and utility with GSM8K, MMLU, and TruthfulQA, using Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Gemma-2-2B-it as the main backbones. The paper’s case is not built on one isolated metric. It is built on a better trade-off point.

On Llama-3-8B-Instruct, CLEAR reportedly drives HarmBench attack success rate close to zero. Against existing aligned variants in the Llama-3 and Alpaca families, CLEAR reaches 0.50% ASR, while the compared aligned variants remain around 15.50% to 24.00%. At the same time, it retains 73.46% on GSM8K, about 7 points higher than globally applied SFT and standard LoRA. That is the most important result in the paper because it suggests the utility gain is not coming from weaker safety, but from selective intervention.

On Gemma-2-2B-it, the same pattern appears and is arguably more informative for smaller models: GSM8K improves from roughly 38% under SFT/LoRA to 42%, and TruthfulQA MC2 rises from about 47% to 53%. This supports the idea that smaller models suffer more from global safety tuning and therefore benefit more from conditional routing.

XSTest is used to probe routing quality rather than end-task generation alone. The hidden-state gate, with fewer than 1M parameters, is claimed to achieve a favorable harmful-versus-benign routing trade-off. That matters because it distinguishes CLEAR from simply adding another classifier in front of the model.

The most important ablations to inspect are the comparisons against always-on LoRA, removal of the pairwise margin objective, and removal of subtype-aware weighting. The central question is whether utility preservation truly comes from conditional routing rather than from a weaker safety adapter. If the paper shows CLEAR maintaining similar or better ASR while preserving noticeably higher GSM8K or TruthfulQA, then the argument is strong.876:T412,Read it as a routing paper, not as another safety fine-tuning paper. Two details are worth deeper inspection if available in the full text: which hidden states feed the gate, and whether the routing score is prompt-level, layer-specific, or token-dynamic during generation.877:T55b,The method is a deterministic short-window probe. Starting from the last two tokens, the model predicts the next token by argmax; the window is rolled forward and the process is iterated, producing a discrete dynamical system. From 96 random two-token starts, the authors measure the fixed-point fraction φ, the proportion of trajectories that terminate in a fixed point. They also classify trajectory geometry into funnel, none, fragmented, and borderline, which gives a coarse structural summary of the attractor landscape. Prefixes are added as wrappers to every forward pass without changing the estimator, so the observed effect is attributed to the conditional distribution rather than to the readout definition. The paper compares raw, BOS, and ordinary text prefixes across six models and sweeps window size. The interesting part is that the paper is organized around failed factorizations. Prefix length is not a monotone driver. Two proposed content-side factors fail after widening the sample. Model-side hypotheses such as a universal direction, bidirectionality as a model property, and instruct-resistance also fail. Even the nearest mechanistic account, attention-sink strength, matches the sign of the fixed-point shift in only 2 of 5 models. What remains is pairwise and model-conditioned: the same prefix can push four models toward 0 and two toward 1.878:T61a,Training is modeled as a deterministic discrete-time dynamical system over a complete state S_t=(w_t,m_t,v_t,\tau_t), where w are parameters, m the first moment (momentum/Adam first-moment buffer), v the second moment, and \tau auxiliary deterministic state (clock/schedule).
- Forward sensitivity (transport): define q_t=\partial S_t/\partial \alpha for a source-strength parameter \alpha. The recurrence includes (a) injected source perturbations d_t (teacher-induced gradient changes) and (b) feedback through \partial G/\partial S because past perturbations alter w_t and therefore future gradients.
- Backward sensitivity (valuation): define a terminal observer O (in LLMs, a target-minus-reference candidate-string log-likelihood on a frozen prompt bank). Compute the costate p_T=(\partial O/\partial S_T)^\top and propagate it backward to obtain a per-step “future value” \lambda_t capturing how valuable a state perturbation at time t is for the final behavior.
- Exact transport–valuation identity: total behavioral change is expressed as a path integral pairing forward-propagated perturbations with backward-propagated values, making route dependence explicit.
- State surgery for causal identification: by transplanting components of the trainer state at a cut, they show the first moment m is the main carrier that continues to write source ancestry into weights after source removal. Transplanting m alone can change future trajectories while keeping current parameters/outputs unchanged; recovering terminal behavior requires (w,m) together.879:T492,CARD has three steps. First, for each axis such as belief, intent, or knowledge, the authors train L2-regularized logistic probes on per-layer, per-head activations at the final input token. Each example contains a matched statement and its negation, and the learned unit vector points from the negated statement toward the matched one. Second, they select the top K=56 layer-head pairs by held-out probe accuracy, roughly 7% of all heads, and use forward hooks to add a scaled version of the probe direction only at the final-token position and only in those head slices. The steering scale is alpha=+10 or alpha=-10 in units of the activation standard deviation along the probe direction. Third, they measure a different prediction axis after steering, for example steering belief while evaluating action. The main statistics are the true-belief versus false-belief accuracy gap shift and a mean-accuracy shift. The accompanying Relay Chain benchmark is a cooperative grid-world setup with belief, knowledge, intent, and action questions, plus success and counter partitions that separate constant-prior behavior, world-state tracking, and belief-conditional behavior.87a:T584,The work has two parts. First, a diagnostic analysis. On four ordinal benchmarks and four MLLM backbones, the authors probe frozen hidden states across layers and prompt protocols to test whether ordered labels are linearly recoverable. They then go beyond probe scores and analyze how the unembedding matrix filters the ordinal direction, and how much of that direction is retained by the digit-token row subspace W_S. This turns the gap between probe-readability and generation into a concrete output-subspace issue. Second, they propose Ordinal Lens Alignment (OLA), a frozen-backbone inference-time correction method. OLA does not modify the vision encoder, LM backbone, or original unembedding. It trains lightweight lenses on K mid-to-deep decoder layers, with the lenses anchored to the digit-token row space, produces layer-wise ordinal distributions, fuses them with learned softmax weights into an instance-specific P_OLA, and then applies a discrepancy-driven correction to logits only at the answer position and only over the target digit-token set. The design choices are deliberate: multi-layer lenses because ordinal structure emerges across depth and varies by instance; W_S anchoring because the goal is to reconnect latent evidence to the native output interface rather than to maximize free probe accuracy; and target-restricted correction to avoid disturbing the full vocabulary distribution.87b:T491,The strongest evidence is in the diagnostic section. Under the most informative setup, task-designed prompt plus last-token hidden state, all backbone-dataset combinations achieve probe SRCC of at least 0.756, with peaks including 0.938 on Adience with Qwen3-VL, 0.919 on Aesthetic with Gemma-4, and 0.843 on HCI with Qwen3-VL. In contrast, the digit-token row space retains less than 1.15% of the ordinal-direction energy across all 16 model-dataset pairs, which strongly supports the output-bottleneck claim. At the behavioral level, there is a 16 to 77 absolute-point accuracy gap between hidden-state linear probes and native digit-token outputs. That is large enough to argue that the main issue is not the absence of latent ordinal evidence. In method comparisons, OLA outperforms prompt-only, hidden steering, capacity-matched baselines, and offline-lens variants, and beats the LoRA-tuned OrderChain baseline in most settings while keeping the backbone frozen. For a closer read, the most useful checks are whether ACC, MAE, and SRCC improve consistently, and how much each component matters: number of layers K, W_S anchoring, and target-restricted correction.87c:T4ec,The paper proposes and documents the Salt method as a disciplined workflow rather than a new learning algorithm.
- Fixed deliverable bundle per iteration: (i) implementation, (ii) formal specification, (iii) kernel-checked proof that the implementation meets the spec, (iv) tests including adversarial controls to ensure the proof has “bite,” and (v) certificates—simplified restatements of the spec designed for human comprehension.
- The key contract is implication: the kernel proves the formal statement entails the certificate statement, so the certificate can only be weaker than what was proved. This makes statement-level human review tractable without trusting the full formal development.
- Emphasis on specification risk: correctness is meaningless if the spec is wrong; therefore the workflow centers on active interrogation, where the human queries the system and receives kernel-checked evidence (unfolding binders, justifying hypotheses, producing variants under changed assumptions).
- End-to-end verified stack culminating in a RISC-V tapeout, with strict provenance (commit-verified theorem trails) and append-only error logs.
The design choice is to optimize for controllable autonomy at AI speed, not for minimal formalization effort.87d:T48f,Daedalus-150M is a convolution–attention hybrid decoder. Out of 18 blocks, only 6 are full attention; the other 12 are short convolution blocks with kernel length L=3 depthwise conv and a fixed recurrent state of width L-1=2 timesteps, making their per-token decode cost independent of context length. Attention layers are interleaved across depth (a fixed C/A pattern) to preserve long-range retrieval at multiple representation levels. To further reduce cache traffic, attention uses grouped-query attention (12 Q heads, 4 KV heads). The model ties input/output embeddings to cut parameters and memory traffic, and uses a narrower FFN (2048, ~2.67×d_model) to reduce bandwidth-heavy matrices. The paper explicitly documents rejected options (MoE due to export/runtime constraints and lack of sub-1B precedent; position-free attention due to export format; distillation due to teacher-logit storage cost). A first-order CPU decode cost model is provided: per token, read quantized weights once plus KV-cache reads proportional to context length for each attention layer; this yields an analytic cache coefficient κ used to predict hybrid vs dense decoding costs.87e:T820,方法延续 FlashPrefill 的两阶段思路。先做 block-level 的粗粒度打分，再只对被选中的 block 做精细 attention。原始 FlashPrefill 用 probe queries 和 block mean-pooled key 来估计每个 key block 的重要性，并用基于峰值分数的动态阈值替代 Top-k/Top-p 排序，从而避免全局排序开销。它还保留 sink blocks、局部滑窗和最近块，以兼顾因果约束和常见注意力模式。

V2 的第一个关键改动是 mean correction term。原方法在极端稀疏时直接截断未选 block 的 softmax 分母和分子，忽略掉被剪枝块的质量，误差会迅速放大。V2 为每个 key block 预先计算 pooled K/V 统计量，用零阶近似去补偿被丢弃块对 softmax mass 和 value aggregation 的贡献。直观上，它不再把未选 block 当成完全不存在，而是用块均值代表其剩余贡献。这样做的好处是代价低，不需要恢复 token-level 计算，但能显著缓和高 sparsity 下的偏差。

第二个关键改动是 kernel 重写，目标是对齐 Hopper 时代的高性能 dense attention 实现。文中提到三点：PackGQA memory access、warp specialization、pingpong pipelining。前者针对 grouped-query attention 的访存组织，减少无效带宽和访存碎片；warp specialization 把不同 warp 分配给不同职责，提高流水并行；pingpong pipeline 则利用 Hopper 上的异步搬运和计算重叠机制，把数据准备和计算交替推进。作者明确说 V2 是按 FlashAttention-3/4 的实现思路重构，而不是停留在 FA2 时代的 kernel 结构上。

第三个关键改动是系统兼容性。V2 原生支持 paged KV cache 和 continuous batching，并集成到 SGLang 这类现代推理框架中。这个点很重要，因为很多 academic sparse attention 方法默认 contiguous KV layout，离真实 serving 很远；一旦接入 paged cache，索引、页表、batch 动态拼接都会改变 kernel 设计。V2 把这一层一起处理了，所以论文不只是算子 benchmark，而是端到端 TTFT 改善。87f:T8b0,FlashPrefill V2 keeps the two-stage structure of FlashPrefill. It first performs block-level coarse scoring, then computes fine-grained attention only on selected blocks. The original method uses probe queries and mean-pooled keys to estimate block salience, and replaces Top-k/Top-p sorting with a max-based dynamic threshold. It also preserves sink blocks, a local sliding window, and recent blocks to respect causal structure and common attention patterns.

The first major addition in V2 is a mean correction term. In the original truncation-based approximation, unselected blocks are simply dropped from both the softmax denominator and numerator. Under extreme sparsity, that discarded probability mass becomes too large to ignore. V2 compensates for pruned blocks using precomputed pooled K/V statistics for each block, effectively adding back a zero-order surrogate contribution. Intuitively, the method no longer treats pruned blocks as nonexistent; it represents their residual effect through block means. This keeps the correction cheap while significantly reducing approximation error at high sparsity.

The second major change is a Hopper-oriented kernel redesign. The paper highlights PackGQA memory access, warp specialization, and pingpong pipelining. PackGQA improves memory organization for grouped-query attention and reduces bandwidth waste. Warp specialization assigns different roles to different warps to improve overlap and utilization. Pingpong pipelining exploits Hopper-style asynchronous data movement and compute overlap. The authors explicitly position V2 as aligned with FlashAttention-3/4 implementation principles rather than older FA2-style kernels.

The third change is systems compatibility. V2 natively supports paged KV cache and continuous batching, and is integrated into SGLang-like serving frameworks. This is important because many academic sparse-attention methods assume contiguous KV layouts and do not survive contact with real serving systems. Once paged cache, page tables, and dynamic batching enter the picture, the kernel design changes materially. V2 addresses that layer directly, so the contribution is not just an operator benchmark but an end-to-end TTFT improvement.880:T620,The empirical story has three parts: speed, quality, and deployability. On NVIDIA H20 at 128K context in BF16, FlashPrefill V2 reports up to 27.19x speedup over FlashAttention-2 during prefill. Its FP8 variant reaches 47.26x. More importantly, even against a much stronger dense baseline aligned with FlashAttention-3/4, it still achieves 17.54x speedup in BF16 and 30.49x in FP8. That means the gain is not an artifact of comparing against an outdated dense kernel. The paper also notes that acceleration remains visible even at 4K sequence length, suggesting that sparse selection and launch overheads are kept low enough to matter outside only ultra-long contexts.

At the system level, after integration into SGLang, the method reduces end-to-end time-to-first-token by up to 4.8x at 128K with only marginal accuracy loss. This result is more convincing than raw kernel throughput because it includes the effects of paged KV cache, continuous batching, and framework-level scheduling.

On accuracy, the headline claim is that mean correction keeps degradation manageable even under extreme sparsity. The method section explains why: naive truncation drops the softmax mass of pruned blocks, while the correction restores an approximation of that contribution using block-level statistics. The excerpt provided here does not include the full downstream quality tables or exact error curves, but the intended contribution is clear: not zero-loss sparsification, but a much better quality-speed tradeoff in the high-sparsity regime where deployment actually benefits.881:T4d8,Read this paper with a systems lens. Start from the introduction and keep the three prototype gaps in mind: approximation quality, kernel efficiency, and serving compatibility. You do not need to follow every algebraic detail, but you should recognize that this is a cheap zero-order block-level correction rather than a heavier higher-order scheme. A solid skim should take 30–45 minutes; a reproduction-oriented read will take much longer.882:T655,FleetSieve treats profiling as downstream decision identification. For each workload-class/configuration cell, it maintains intervals for sustainable capacity and tail latency rather than a single estimate. It then solves two fleet allocations under the same resource constraints and lexicographic objective: a conservative allocation using lower capacity and upper tail bounds, and an optimistic allocation using upper capacity and lower tail bounds. The objective first enforces minimum fulfillment floors for critical classes when feasible, then maximizes the minimum satisfaction ratio, then total served goodput, and finally reduces fragmentation.

The key idea is the acquisition rule. FleetSieve does not measure the cell with the largest uncertainty, nor does it try to cover the grid uniformly. It measures the configuration expected to reduce disagreement between the conservative and optimistic downstream allocations. In other words, a cell with high uncertainty is not important if no plausible outcome would change the fleet decision. Conversely, a cell becomes important if resolving it could flip SLO feasibility or alter resource allocation for a critical workload.

The paper also introduces a conditional decision certificate with three states: Certified-Feasible, Undecided, and Certified-Infeasible. The wording is careful. The certificate is not distribution-free or unconditional; it is valid only under the empirical uncertainty model used to bound the unknown performance table. That restraint is a good sign: the method is presented as an engineering decision tool, not as a universal guarantee.883:T491,The evaluation is intentionally narrow and concrete: one 31B open-weight decoder model, one H100 node, FP8, a vLLM-based serving stack, speculative decoding disabled, and candidate TP degrees {2, 4, 8}. Each profiling cell is measured for 300 seconds. The main metric is how many profiling GPU-seconds are needed to recover the oracle aggregate fleet decision.

The headline result is modest but real: on the fixed H100 measurement grid, FleetSieve reaches the oracle aggregate decision with 22,200 GPU-seconds, a 6.9% reduction relative to uniform profiling. The paper is refreshingly explicit that gains are selective rather than universal: the reduction is larger for Chat and absent for Code. That matters because it clarifies when the method helps. If unresolved cells can still change the global allocation, decision-aware profiling is useful. If the allocation is effectively determined early, the extra machinery may not buy much. The experiments also show why joint modeling of capacity and tail latency is necessary: throughput-only profiling can certify configurations that look efficient but violate the actual SLO, which then corrupts fleet-level planning.884:T584,CacheRoute builds a periodically refreshed routing table that plans prefix affinity and expected load together, prioritizing cache stability over per-request reactive remapping.
- Inputs/abstraction: per-key arrival rates λ_b for business keys; R routable destinations (a destination is a model-server group; in the 70B setup, TP=2).
- Admission (warm set): admit the highest-rate keys into an affinity-managed warm set under a warm-prefix slot budget; non-admitted traffic falls back to cache-blind power-of-two choices.
- Load cap via replication: calibrate q_cap from a single destination’s latency/load knee. For each key, allocate enough destinations so the expected per-destination load contributed by that key is ≤ q_cap. Replication is primarily for load control (capping per-destination contribution), not for improving hit rate per se.
- Placement: assign admitted keys (and their replica counts) to destinations using LPT (longest-processing-time-first) list scheduling to reduce expected load imbalance.
- Control interval: keep the table fixed for a period to preserve cache warmth; avoid reactive spilling that would send the next request to a cold destination once a cap binds.
The novelty is not LPT or top-k admission individually, but the combined routing design and the empirical characterization of when planned affinity beats both cache-blind balancing and reactive cache-aware routing.885:T6ce,The work has two layers. The first is the Thinkingbox sandbox. A task is instantiated as a finite-horizon POMDP whose latent state includes backend state, simulated-user private state, evaluator-relevant event logs, and episode status. At each turn, the agent observes dialogue history and tool outputs, then either sends a user-facing message or issues a tool call with arguments. Tool calls execute inside isolated backend sessions. The system records side effects and runs hidden executable checks at the end. A key design choice is outcome-based evaluation: multiple trajectories may be valid as long as the final backend state, required side effects, and dialogue constraints are correct.

The second layer is Thinkingbox-bench, a 507-task benchmark spanning retail/e-commerce, travel/hospitality, auto insurance, neobank internal IT support, and consulting IT/HR support. Tasks are designed around recurring enterprise patterns: lookup-then-update flows, user clarification, confirmation before irreversible actions, policy-conditioned changes, and multi-tool coordination. Most tasks are graded through executable checks over terminal backend state. An additional subset of 30 tasks uses binary rubrics on the final response, covering required disclosures, confidentiality, and consistency between what the agent says and what it actually executed.

The reliability framing is central. pass@k measures whether at least one of k attempts succeeds, which captures discovery capability. pass^k measures whether all k attempts succeed, which captures repeatable reliability. That distinction is important because many agents can occasionally find a correct trajectory while remaining unstable under sampling noise or interaction variation.886:T56f,The main empirical result is a large discovery–reliability gap. The benchmark contains 507 tasks, and the authors evaluate 12 proprietary and open-weight models with 20 repeated trials per task. The strongest model reaches 65.36% pass@1, which is still far from dependable single-run performance. Its pass@20 rises to 91.12%, showing that many tasks are solvable at least once. But its pass^20 is only 25.25%, meaning only a quarter of tasks succeed in all 20 attempts. That gap is the central takeaway of the paper.

Because evaluation is tied to terminal backend state rather than a single final answer, the benchmark can expose failure modes that simpler tool-use benchmarks miss: updating the wrong entity, producing a convincing response while leaving the backend unchanged, missing a required side effect, introducing an extra side effect, executing high-impact actions before collecting confirmation, or generating a final message inconsistent with the actual execution outcome. The paper also includes evaluator ablations and failure analyses to show that fluent tool use is not the same as reliable work completion.

The provided excerpt does not include the full per-domain or per-model breakdown, but the headline numbers already show strong benchmark discrimination: this is neither plain function-calling nor pure dialogue evaluation; it is outcome-centric stateful execution.887:T461,The method treats response correctness as a binary classification problem. For each query-response pair from a fixed black-box LLM, the feature set includes: (1) one or more existing uncertainty scores, and (2) neighborhood-derived features computed from a labeled reference set. The reference set is embedded, k-nearest neighbors are retrieved for each query, and statistics such as neighbor correctness and cosine similarity are added as features. A lightweight classifier is then trained to predict the probability that the current response is correct.

A key design choice is that the paper does not insist on a single learner. Instead, it compares simple classifiers and concludes that the best learner is task-dependent. This is important: the paper is not claiming a universal parametric confidence model, but a supervised calibration layer over existing UQ signals. Relative to standard zero-shot UQ, the shift is clear: uncertainty scores are treated as imperfect features, not as final confidence estimates. The neighborhood features inject local empirical risk information that zero-shot methods cannot access.888:T736,The method, NAPE, starts from a log-mel spectrogram, splits it into non-overlapping patches, and projects each patch into a latent embedding. This yields a 2D grid of patch embeddings. Since the backbone is a causal Transformer over a 1D sequence, the grid must be serialized with a scanning order. The model then predicts the embedding of the next patch from the prefix, using a lightweight predictor head. Training uses negative cosine similarity to a stop-gradient target embedding, rather than L2 regression or classification over discrete acoustic tokens.

The most interesting technical point is that scanning order is treated as a first-class design choice. In images, rasterization is often a convenience. In audio spectrograms, time and frequency axes play very different roles, so the serialization order changes both the available causal context and the inductive bias. The paper studies four scanning strategies and shows that this choice materially affects transfer performance and training behavior. The trade-off is intuitive: if the order destroys temporal continuity, the model no longer follows natural acoustic evolution; if it only marches along time, it may underuse local time-frequency structure. Making this axis explicit is one of the paper’s main contributions.

Architecturally, the setup is deliberately minimal: a single causal encoder plus a predictor head, with no teacher branch, no EMA target network, no reconstruction decoder, and no extra variance/covariance regularization. This is the key difference from much of prior audio SSL. The model is not trained to reconstruct masked content or to match a teacher representation. It is trained to model audio as a sequential latent process, which makes it much closer in spirit to language modeling and easier to align with unified multimodal pretraining recipes.889:T5a7,Pretraining is done on AudioSet, with downstream evaluation on ESC-50, Speech Commands V1/V2, and IEMOCAP. The paper reports three model sizes: Small (19M), Base (85M), and Large (303M), mainly to test whether the objective scales. According to the full text, NAPE reaches state-of-the-art or near-state-of-the-art performance on several tasks, and importantly it also performs well under linear probing, not just full fine-tuning. That matters because next-embedding prediction does not explicitly optimize for linear separability.

The ablations are more informative than the headline numbers. The paper studies scanning order, model scale, and objective/architecture choices. The main takeaways are that scanning order matters a lot, temporally aligned serialization is usually stronger and more stable, and performance improves consistently from Small to Large without obvious breakdown of the objective. The fact that this works without a decoder, tokenizer, or teacher is itself an empirical result. The qualitative analyses, including attention maps and embedding-space structure, suggest that the model captures meaningful acoustic boundaries and local spectro-temporal patterns. The excerpt provided here does not include the full numeric tables, so I will not invent exact margins, but the paper clearly does more than present a single best result: it builds a fairly complete empirical case for simple causal latent prediction in audio.88a:T473,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the main method figure. If time is limited, about 30 minutes is enough to capture the main idea: method figure, scanning-order ablation, main benchmark table, and one qualitative section. If the goal is to assess relevance for unified multimodal pretraining, spend extra time on the serialization design and the cosine latent-prediction loss, because those are the pieces most likely to transfer to broader next-latent frameworks.88b:T50d,The analysis starts from standard flow matching. A time-dependent vector field vθ transports a simple prior p1, usually noise, to the data distribution p0 through an ODE. Standard training fits the conditional velocity along interpolation paths. FlowDPO-style methods avoid exact likelihood computation by replacing log probabilities with timestep-wise flow regression errors, then applying a DPO-like pairwise objective to winner and loser samples. The paper shows why this can be unsafe: the preference update can alter the terminal endpoint of the flow in directions that are normal to the pretrained data manifold. Optimal flow matching recovers the terminal data distribution, but a preference update leaves the manifold whenever its induced terminal displacement has a nonzero normal component. ThermoDPO addresses this by adding a temperature-controlled winner-side anchor. As the temperature τ goes to zero, the objective recovers rejection sampling fine-tuning. For τ>0, it decomposes into a temperature-scaled FlowDPO term plus a nonnegative anchoring term. This makes the alignment–preservation trade-off explicit. The weighted variant, ThermoDPO-weighted, fixes practical weighting issues near t=0 and comes with a bound on a reconstruction-based surrogate for manifold drift.88c:T858,方法叫 R²-OPD，关键设计有三步。第一步，用 teacher-independent 的 process reward 估计 reasoning progress。做法不是只看最终答对与否，而是对连续推理状态采样后续 continuation，比较从不同中间状态继续生成时的 solve probability 变化，把某段推理对最终解题概率的边际贡献当作 progress signal。作者强调 raw process reward 噪声很大，原因一是 Monte Carlo continuation 采样方差，二是中间 reasoning span 的边界本身不稳定。

第二步，做 sign-consistent span merging。原始轨迹先被切成 reasoning spans，然后把 process reward 符号一致、相邻的 span 合并成更大的 segment。这样做有两个目的：一是减少对细粒度边界估计的依赖，二是让后续比较发生在更稳定的语义单元上。文中给了理论说明：如果内部边界估计有误差，合并后这些误差在段内会相互抵消；同时对 token-level divergence 做段内平均，也能在弱相关假设下降低局部方差。

第三步，用 ranking conflict 做 reward filtering，而不是 reward replacement。对每个合并后的 segment，作者聚合 token-level reverse-KL distillation loss，得到该段“偏离 teacher 的惩罚强度”；同时用 process reward 给出该段“推进解题的贡献”。如果两个排序冲突，例如 progress 更高的段反而被蒸馏损失惩罚得更重，就说明 teacher guidance 在这一局部可能不可靠。R²-OPD 不把 process reward 加到 loss 里，也不重写 OPD objective，而是把这些冲突段的 distillation reward mask 掉，只保留 progress 与 distillation 一致的部分继续监督。这个选择很关键：它把 process reward 用作校验器而不是训练主信号，降低了高噪声 reward 直接驱动优化的风险。

从实现上，论文基于 reverse-KL OPD，并采用 support-restricted 近似来计算 token-level KL，只在学生或师生联合的 top-H support 上做分布匹配，避免全词表计算。R²-OPD 叠加在这个标准 OPD 框架之上，因此兼容现有 on-policy 蒸馏流水线。88d:T866,The method, R²-OPD, has three main components. First, it estimates reasoning progress using teacher-independent process rewards. Instead of relying only on final correctness, it samples continuations from successive intermediate reasoning states and measures how the probability of solving the task changes. This gives a marginal contribution estimate for each reasoning span. The paper emphasizes that raw process rewards are noisy because continuation-based estimation has Monte Carlo variance and because fine-grained reasoning boundaries are themselves unstable.

Second, it performs sign-consistent span merging. The trajectory is segmented into reasoning spans, and adjacent spans with process rewards of the same sign are merged into larger segments. This reduces sensitivity to noisy internal boundaries and creates more stable units for calibration. The theoretical discussion argues that internal boundary estimation errors can cancel within merged segments, and that averaging token-level divergence over a segment reduces local variance under weak dependence assumptions.

Third, it detects local ranking conflicts between progress and distillation penalty, and uses those conflicts for filtering. For each merged segment, token-level reverse-KL distillation losses are aggregated into a segment-level penalty for deviating from the teacher. Process reward gives a segment-level estimate of reasoning advancement. If a higher-progress segment is penalized more heavily than a lower-progress one, the two signals disagree in ranking, indicating that teacher supervision may be unreliable there. Instead of adding process reward into the objective or replacing OPD, R²-OPD masks distillation rewards on the most inconsistent segments and keeps teacher guidance elsewhere.

This design choice is the core idea. Process reward is treated as a reliability probe rather than a primary training signal, which avoids directly optimizing against a high-variance reward. The implementation is built on reverse-KL OPD with support-restricted approximation over a top-H token set, so the method can be layered onto standard practical OPD pipelines.88e:T776,The experimental section is aimed at validating the signal-calibration hypothesis rather than demonstrating a large-scale model jump. The tasks are reasoning-heavy, and the comparisons include vanilla OPD, variants that directly incorporate outcome or process rewards, and alternative filtering or weighting strategies.

Three findings stand out. First, the mismatch is real: the paper provides qualitative examples and aggregate analysis showing that some intermediate spans increase downstream solve probability while receiving stronger distillation penalties because they diverge from the teacher distribution. This is especially visible on harder reasoning problems.

Second, the gains come from removing bad supervision rather than injecting another reward. Compared with directly mixing process rewards into optimization, the filtering-based approach is more stable and more consistently helpful. The explanation is straightforward: raw process rewards are noisy, so using them as direct optimization targets can distort learning, whereas using them only to suppress clearly inconsistent teacher signals is safer.

Third, the ablations support the two main design choices: sign-consistent merging and segment-level averaging. Without merging, conflict detection becomes more brittle because boundary noise leaks into the comparison. With token-level filtering instead of segment-level filtering, lexical fluctuations create more false conflicts. The paper also studies the masking ratio and shows that more masking is not always better; excessive filtering removes useful teacher transfer.

The most transferable idea is that auxiliary supervision does not always need to enter the loss directly. It can be used to gate, filter, or calibrate another training signal. That pattern may carry over to synthetic data filtering, RL signal gating, and teacher-ensemble arbitration.890:T616,The central move is to treat interpretability as a measurement-design problem. The unknown \(x\) can be an effect vector, a local gradient map, or an interaction matrix, depending on the chosen basis and intervention family. Each row of \(A\) corresponds to an intervention, \(\tilde y\) is the observed response, and \(w\) collects what the linearized measurement model misses. Importantly, the framework does not force all methods to estimate the same target; instead, it provides a shared language for how measurements are obtained and how their errors should be analyzed.

The paper then studies when such measurements are useful. It analyzes recoverability conditions, the role of intervention scale and mask density, and the point at which first-order local measurements must be replaced or augmented by interaction-aware ones. A key concept is calibration dimension: the smallest declared correction family needed so that a baseline map can predict finite-scale held-out interventions. If a low-dimensional correction suffices, a local map may still be operationally useful after calibration. If not, the residual indicates missing interactions, a poor basis, or an inadequate measurement family.

Another important concept is the observer: an estimate that is meant to guide interventions. The paper argues that an observer should be judged not by whether it reconstructs an appealing internal story, but by whether it predicts intervention effects at the scale where control will actually be applied. This links interpretability directly to control.891:T45b,The experiments are designed to validate the framework rather than to win a benchmark. The most informative quantitative result is in the finite-scale correction setting: at a larger intervention scale, a one-dimensional fitted gain improves mean held-out attribution-patching \(R^2\) from 0.818 to 0.960, close to sparse recovery at 0.969. This supports the paper’s claim that some local maps are not fundamentally wrong, but need an explicitly declared finite-scale correction.

A second key result comes from the two-HMM wind-tunnel control experiment. With controller and actuator fixed, closed-loop target error tracks observer error across ten observer variants with Spearman correlation 0.95. This shows that interpretability error is not merely descriptive; it propagates into control error. The specificity test adds an important caveat: improving the target state alone is not enough, because an observer can still induce larger movement in a nuisance state. If your interests are closer to mechanistic analysis of LLMs, two issues are worth deeper attention. One is basis choice: the framework starts after a basis is proposed, but whether the target is sparse or recoverable depends heavily on whether the basis is heads, neurons, residual directions, or learned features. The other is intervention scale: many attribution methods are valid only infinitesimally, while practical steering and editing use finite interventions. The paper’s held-out intervention tests are aimed exactly at that gap.893:T73a,CAMA has two main components: correlation-aware evidence decoupling and missing-evidence recovery.

The first component is query-conditioned latent-source arbitration. Instead of treating each retrieved memory as an independent vote, the method maps memories into latent evidential factors or slots. The intuition is that multiple memories may express the same underlying source of evidence, just through different agents, timestamps, or phrasings. CAMA uses neural dependency inference to estimate whether memories are redundant under the current query, and combines this with provenance-based symbolic priors derived from source chains, dependency links, or write traces. Hypothesis support is then aggregated at the latent-factor level rather than the raw-memory level, reducing repeated counting of the same evidence.

The second component is sequential evidence recovery. The paper argues that the initial retrieval set is itself biased: similarity-based retrieval tends to over-select correlated memories and miss independent evidence that could overturn a false majority. CAMA therefore does not restrict arbitration to the initial top-K slice. Instead, it learns a recovery policy that, under a budget, decides whether to expand retrieval or trace provenance/dependency links to acquire additional independent evidence. This is a sensible design because it treats the current evidence set as a biased sample rather than a complete basis for decision-making.

Methodologically, this is not a new LLM architecture. It is a combination of evidence aggregation, symbolic provenance, and sequential retrieval policy for multi-agent memory arbitration. The main novelty is making dependence modeling query-conditioned and latent-source based, rather than relying on static heuristics such as agent identity, timestamp, or semantic similarity alone.894:T4fe,The experiments are designed to show that CAMA suppresses false majorities caused by correlated memories and outperforms standard baselines on long-term multi-agent memory benchmarks. The baseline families appear to include majority voting, confidence or relevance weighting, and retrieval-augmented reasoning methods. The qualitative result is straightforward: when memories share sources or propagate through the system, conventional aggregation overestimates support for a hypothesis, while CAMA is better able to recover the correct arbitration by grouping correlated evidence and recovering missing independent evidence.

Exact numbers should be taken from the main tables, the recovery-budget ablations, and the experiments removing provenance priors.895:T471,ClosureBench is built around “logic primitives + executable semantics + controlled instance generation.”
- Task space: 26 categories derived from explicit graph-relational primitives such as reachability/transitive closure, degree, set operations, connectivity (e.g., SCC-related queries), and aggregation over reachable sets.
- Exact labels: each query is implemented as a short program whose execution yields the reference answer. The paper mentions implementations in Ein (tensor-contraction style graph ops) and an equivalent Python/NetworkX version.
- Constructive generator: instances are produced on demand with separate structural and surface seeds, allowing independent control of graph structure and linguistic realization.
- Difficulty control: three orthogonal axes—number of nodes, edge density, and query depth/compositional level—so evaluators can hold two fixed and sweep the third to localize failure modes.
- Interface: models only see natural-language questions and must output JSON; the underlying program is hidden, keeping the benchmark focused on reasoning rather than program induction from code exposure.896:T4ab,The experiments use code-generation tasks because hidden unit tests provide an exact oracle while remaining unavailable to the operators. The data comes from MBPP+ and HumanEval+. The loop runs on 75 MBPP+ training tasks. Evaluation uses 428 unseen tasks: 75 held-out MBPP+ tasks, 228 additional MBPP+ tasks, and 125 HumanEval+ tasks. A naive operator-generation loop is highly redundant: five runs produce 183 flagging operators but only 96 distinct flag sets. Scoring all 295 authored operators at the narrow interface yields no discovery. EvalCEGAR admits an operator in six of eight runs, and all six admitted operators help on the 428 unseen tasks. For composition, the authors enumerate about 2.3M subsets and show that the loop’s original composition objective can rank near the 5th percentile, whereas an untuned class-weighted objective reaches the 91st percentile or above.897:T4e6,SESSE is a five-stage pipeline. Stage 0 runs the judge holistically on a development set and collects examples where the judge disagrees with the reference label. Stage 1 prompts the same judge to derive conditional evaluation sub-questions from those errors, using a format such as: if a condition applies, which response better satisfies a given property, A, B, or NA. These criteria require neither human-written rubrics nor oracle responses. Stage 2 embeds the candidate questions and clusters them into k thematic groups. Stage 3 ranks questions within each cluster using greedy farthest-first traversal, producing a diversity-ordered bank that can be truncated at different depths. Stage 4 asks an LLM to summarize each cluster into an abstract protasis and merges near-duplicate clusters through binary equivalence checks. Stage 5 first selects relevant clusters for a new example, then answers selected concrete sub-questions with A/B/NA votes. NA votes are ignored; A/B majority gives the final preference; ties are abstentions and are excluded from the accuracy denominator. The key distinction from prior rubric or specialist-judge methods is that the criteria are induced from the judge’s own failure distribution without parameter updates.898:T590,The method has three main pieces. First, a library of 14 semantics-preserving transformations, including control-flow rewrites, dead-code injection, and identifier renaming. These are meant to cover both realistic refactorings and stress-test perturbations. Semantic preservation is operationalized through per-test equivalence on the project test suite rather than formal program equivalence, which is pragmatic and aligned with SWE-bench acceptance. Second, a randomized variant sampler applies selected transformations at sampled locations to create independent perturbed repositories. This is intentionally not an adversarial search procedure. The point is to show that even simple, unguided local rewrites already hurt agents, so the measured effect is a lower bound. FM-Bench is a deterministic football-management simulator where an LLM agent operates through 26 schema-generated tools. Across roughly 340 to 400 decision stops over 20 in-game years, the agent drafts players, trades, negotiates contracts, invests in facilities and youth development, sets lineups, and manages finances under board pressure. Each stop is a fresh conversation; the only persistent memory is a self-authored notebook, so long-term memory curation is part of the task. The environment is built to instantiate four demands of management: hidden information, cumulative consequences, a counter-adaptive environment, and multi-objective pressure. To keep this measurable, the authors use equal-endowment drafting, sealed-bid conflict resolution, and capped revival. Scoring is fully programmatic and cumulative.
