For a single-answer task with answer-space size k, a reference-free judge implicitly solves the problem with grading-context competence c. If it is wrong, its internal answer is assumed to be uniformly distributed over the other k-1 answers. The judge score is then whether the candidate answer matches the judge’s internal answer. Under this model, TPR is c and FPR is (1-c)/(k-1), giving AUC = 0.5 * (1 + c - (1-c)/(k-1)). This yields a necessary condition: c must exceed 1/k for the judge to discriminate above chance. The paper also shows that marginal AUC can be confounded by item difficulty; a scorer that only reads difficulty can appear useful. The proposed measurement therefore uses a within-question estimator, comparing correct and incorrect candidates for the same question, with question-clustered bootstrap uncertainty. The judge is run as a non-intervening probe: the real optimizer still accepts or rejects candidates using the verifier, while the judge only records scores.89f:T426,The headline findings are straightforward and useful. First, augmentation and automation rankings are only moderately correlated overall, with a model-level rank correlation of about 0.48. Second, the correlation varies sharply by task, from -0.04 on travel planning to 0.85 on tax preparation, showing that the overlap between being a strong solver and a strong assistant is task dependent. Third, assistance is not always beneficial. The paper reports that GPT-5-mini ranks first on average in both regimes, but in augmentation the unaided worker baseline, where GPT-3.5-Turbo works without any external help, achieves the second-best average rank. That means some assistance harms performance, likely because it is too complex, poorly calibrated, or mismatched to the worker. The task-level reversals are especially informative: for example, Claude-Opus-4.8 is among the strongest direct solvers on market trends analysis with mean rank 2.05, yet among the weakest assistants on the same task with 8.15, while GPT-4.1 shows the opposite profile on counseling.8a0:T44d,The paper evaluates on MMAU, MMAR, MMSU, and MMAU-Pro. It reports that the alignment-only model can match or exceed more heavily post-trained open-source audio-language models while using substantially less data. On the instruction-following split of MMAU-Pro, freezing the LLM helps preserve its original instruction-following behavior. The ablations are more informative than the aggregate scores: scaling alignment data mainly helps open-ended reasoning tasks; closed-set recognition saturates quickly when the encoder lacks the needed information. Encoder sweeps show that benchmark performance tracks the capability emphasized during encoder pretraining. LLM sweeps suggest the recipe transfers across model generations, with a caveat that the generator used for synthetic responses should be well matched to the target LLM. The paper also finds that dense synthetic captions per sample are not strictly necessary; diverse open-source captions can work when aggregated. The provided content does not include full per-task numbers or dataset sizes, so the result tables should be checked directly.8a1:T5df,The proposed method is geometric iterative retrieval. It has three main ingredients. First, the model predicts per-layer continuous codebook vectors rather than discrete indices or a single full latent. This preserves the semantic hierarchy of RVQ while exposing the geometry of the codebook space. Second, training uses a CLIP-style symmetric contrastive objective instead of MSE. For each layer and time position, the predicted vector is trained to be closer in cosine similarity to the true codebook vector than to negatives from the batch. This addresses two failure modes at once: classification treats all wrong entries as equally wrong, while regression encourages mean-seeking behavior. Third, the method replaces the standard additive RVQ conditioning assumption with a self-attention aggregator over previously predicted lower layers, allowing non-additive cross-layer interactions. The backbone is a 12-layer bidirectional DeBERTa-v3 with hidden size 1536. During training, causal masking along the codebook axis lets the model learn all higher-layer predictions in one forward pass using ground-truth lower-layer conditioning. During inference, prediction proceeds autoregressively over RVQ layers: each continuous prediction is snapped to the nearest codebook entry and then used to condition the next layer. Compared with diffusion-based resynthesis, the key difference is that the iterative axis is aligned with the codec hierarchy itself rather than an externally imposed noise schedule.8a2:T401,Experiments are run on DAC codec restoration for both speech and music. The method is compared against single-pass token prediction, MSE regression, cosine regression, and related learned baselines. The main empirical result is consistent: geometric iterative retrieval achieves the best LSD among learned baselines and is preferred in double-blind human listening tests. The ablations support three claims: 1) iterative continuous prediction is better than one-shot continuous regression, so the refinement structure matters; 2) contrastive retrieval works better than direct vector regression, suggesting that codebook geometry is better exploited through retrieval-style objectives; 3) self-attention aggregation improves over simple additive conditioning, indicating that the codec's additive residual structure is not the right inductive bias for the predictor. Inference takes D-1 deterministic steps, matching standard coarse-to-fine RVQ prediction and avoiding the longer sampling chains typical of diffusion methods.8a3:T912,方法部分的关键不在于引入一个复杂新目标，而在于把 capability imbalance 对应到三个彼此独立的失真源，然后一一修正。

第一部分是 token-share balancing。作者观察到，按 prompt 均匀采样并不能带来按优化强度均匀训练，因为 OPD/RL 类目标是 token 级求和，长序列天然占据更多梯度份额。于是他们不再用固定 batch 内样本数控制 domain 配比，而是直接设定 weighted token-share target，让不同 domain 按目标 token 份额分配优化预算。这里的重点是“按 token share 控制”，而不是简单 oversample 短任务，因为 oversample 只在静态长度分布下近似有效，训练过程中 reward 强度变化后仍会漂移。

第二部分是 gap-aware allocation。即便初始 token 预算拉平，不同 domain 的 student-teacher gap 会以不同速度收敛。若仍固定配比，已经接近收敛的 domain 会继续消耗预算，而落后 domain 得不到补偿。作者因此用剩余 gap 来动态调度预算，把更多更新分给还没追上 teacher 的 domain。这里他们特别强调，不能只做 naive reward normalization，因为那会把预算错误地推向“看起来 reward 大但其实已接近收敛”的部分，文中给了一个在 step 74 直接训练崩掉的反例。

第三部分是 student reward refresh。标准多步 rollout reuse 会在多个 gradient step 中重复使用同一批 rollout 上基于旧 student 计算的 reward/advantage。对于依赖 student log-prob 的 OPD 信号，这会迅速变 stale，尤其在不同 domain 收敛速度不同的时候，staleness 会进一步放大预算失真。作者的做法是缓存 teacher states，但在每个 gradient step 前重新计算 student log-prob，从而刷新 student-dependent reward 组件。这样保留了 teacher 侧缓存带来的效率，又避免了 stale advantage。

全文还有一个重要的负结果：作者专门测了 token-level teacher disagreement，结论是它不像很多人预想的那样是主导瓶颈。也就是说，多 teacher 之间监督不一致并不是主要矛盾，真正的问题是训练信号如何被分配、何时失真、何时过时。这一点让方法更像“优化与预算控制”问题，而不是“多专家冲突消解”问题。8a4:T78a,实验设计很扎实，重点在于把 integration gap 定量化。基座是 SmolLM3-3B-Base，先做三域 mixed-SFT，再训练三个 domain RL teacher，然后用 oracle routing 做 M-OPD。这样 deployment 时的 RouteOPD/RouteRL 可以作为上界或参考，避免把路由错误混进结论里。

核心结果有几组数字需要记住。标准 naive M-OPD 在六个 benchmark 上平均分 28.05，而把每个 domain 单独蒸馏后再按路由部署可到 31.55，说明单域蒸馏本身没那么难，难的是统一到一个 student。作者进一步用 recovery 指标衡量 student 从 mixed-SFT 到 RouteRL 可获得提升里实际拿回了多少，naive M-OPD 只恢复 35.6%，Open-MOPD 提升到 83.4%。这是全文最能说明问题被真正修复的数字。

分 domain 看，instruction following 的退化最严重：相对 RouteOPD 参考低 6.16 分，且退化幅度是 math 的 3.3 倍，并且最早进入 plateau。作者给出的机制证据也很直接：IF 虽然占 20.3% 的输入 prompt，但只贡献 0.99% 的 gradient tokens。这个数字几乎把“按 prompt 平衡不等于按优化平衡”讲透了。

消融实验是文章最值得看的部分。作者分别验证了三种失真源：
1) 序列长度差异会直接造成 token budget 倾斜；
2) 即便初始 token 配平，随着 student 对不同 teacher 收敛速度不同，预算会在几十步内再次漂移；
3) rollout reuse 带来的 stale student reward 会进一步恶化这种漂移。

在方法消融上，token-share balancing、gap-aware allocation、student reward refresh 是累积增益，而不是互相替代。文中还展示了 naive reward normalization 在 step 74 崩溃，说明“简单把 reward 拉平”不是稳妥修复。作者强调他们的方法额外开销很低，尤其 refresh 只重算 student log-prob、缓存 teacher states，因此在 8×A100-80GB 的学术环境里可复现。8a5:T411,This is valuable because it turns an industrially relevant but poorly explained practice into a measurable optimization problem. The contribution is less about a new distillation slogan and more about a clean mechanistic decomposition: sequence-length imbalance, convergence-rate imbalance, and reward staleness. That decomposition matters beyond this paper. It informs how to think about token budget allocation, mixture weighting, and training dynamics at the pretrain/post-train interface. The work also provides an open and reproducible recipe at an academic compute scale, which is rare for RL-heavy post-training pipelines. The gain is not cosmetic: under the paper’s recovery metric, the student goes from recovering only 35.6% of the available RouteRL improvement over mixed-SFT to 83.4%. That suggests the limitation is largely in the optimization protocol, not simply teacher quality or student capacity. Anyone working on unified post-training, continual capability integration, or multi-objective RL should read this carefully.8a6:T819,The method is strong because it maps each observed failure mode to a specific correction instead of introducing a monolithic objective.

First, token-share balancing addresses the fact that prompt-balanced sampling does not imply optimization-balanced training. In OPD-style objectives, longer responses contribute more token-level loss and therefore more gradient mass. The authors replace implicit prompt-level balancing with an explicit weighted token-share target across domains. The point is not just to oversample short tasks. Oversampling is only a rough proxy under a fixed length distribution, while token-share control directly targets the quantity that drives optimization.

Second, gap-aware allocation handles the fact that even if raw token budgets are equalized at the start, they drift quickly because the student closes the teacher gap at different speeds in different domains. A fixed allocation then wastes updates on already-converged domains while under-training lagging ones. The proposed mechanism dynamically steers budget toward domains with the largest remaining student–teacher gap. The paper also shows why naive reward normalization is not enough and can even destabilize training by funneling budget into the wrong places.

Third, student reward refresh fixes staleness introduced by multi-step rollout reuse. In standard OPD/PPO-like training, the same rollout is reused for several gradient steps, while token-level rewards or advantages depend partly on student log-probabilities. Those student-dependent terms become stale quickly, especially when domains move at different rates. The authors cache teacher states for efficiency but recompute student log-probabilities before each gradient step, refreshing the student-side reward component at low overhead.

An important negative result is that token-level teacher disagreement does not appear to be the dominant bottleneck under their metric. That matters. It shifts the framing from “multi-teacher conflict resolution” to “optimization budget allocation and signal freshness.”8a7:T7c0,The experimental setup is carefully controlled. Starting from SmolLM3-3B-Base, the authors build a three-domain mixed-SFT model, train three RL teachers, and then run oracle-routed M-OPD. This gives clean references such as RouteOPD and RouteRL, so the integration gap can be measured without confounding routing errors.

The headline numbers are clear. Naive M-OPD reaches an average score of 28.05 on six benchmarks, while distilling each domain separately and deploying with routing reaches 31.55. So single-domain distillation is not the main issue; unifying capabilities in one student is. Using their recovery metric—how much of the RouteRL-over-mixed-SFT improvement is actually recovered by the unified student—naive M-OPD recovers only 35.6%, whereas Open-MOPD reaches 83.4%.

The domain breakdown is especially revealing. Instruction following suffers the largest degradation: it falls 6.16 points below its RouteOPD reference, which is 3.3 times the degradation seen in math, and it plateaus earliest during training. The mechanism-level evidence is unusually concrete: instruction-following prompts account for 20.3% of inputs but only 0.99% of gradient tokens. That single statistic captures why prompt balancing is not enough.

The ablations are the core of the paper. They show that: (1) sequence-length differences directly skew token budget, (2) even initially balanced token shares drift apart within tens of steps because domains converge at different rates, and (3) stale student-dependent rewards from rollout reuse further worsen the imbalance. On the method side, token-share balancing, gap-aware allocation, and student reward refresh provide cumulative gains rather than redundant ones. The paper also includes a useful failure case where naive reward normalization collapses training at step 74. The implementation remains practical: the full pipeline is reproducible on 8×A100-80GB, and the refresh mechanism is cheap because teacher states are cached.8a8:T5d4,Read it in three passes.

First, get the evaluation frame right. Focus on the introduction and setup until RouteRL, RouteOPD, M-OPD, and the recovery metric are fully clear. Those references are essential; otherwise the later diagnosis can look like ordinary ablation work.

Second, spend time on the diagnosis section. This is where the paper earns its value. Pay attention to the evidence that catastrophic gradient conflict is not the main culprit, how prompt share diverges from gradient token share, why concise instruction-following tasks stall early, and how student–teacher gaps evolve differently across domains. The per-domain training curves and token-share statistics are more informative than the final leaderboard-style numbers.

Third, read the method section together with the corresponding ablations. Each module fixes a different distortion source: token-share balancing for length bias, gap-aware allocation for unequal convergence rates, and student reward refresh for stale rewards under rollout reuse. It helps to compare these choices against standard PPO/OPD practice, especially how advantages are computed and reused.

If time is limited, prioritize the problem-definition figures, the per-domain result tables, the instruction-following token-share analysis, the step-74 collapse example, and the cumulative ablation. A careful 60–90 minute read is enough to capture the main mechanism. The appendix is worth checking if you care about reproducing the pipeline.8a9:T44e,Two pillars: controlled ablations and a supervision decomposition.
- Controlled setup: keep the student always in non-thinking mode during both training and evaluation; vary only the teacher’s generation mode (thinking vs non-thinking) and the teacher’s access to references (correct, incorrect, none, or from other problems).
- Decomposition: for trajectories generated by the student at checkpoint c, compare next-token distributions:
  T = teacher with reference, N = teacher without reference, S_c = student.
  Using log-probability vectors, decompose total teacher supervision direction:
  D_tot = (T − S_c) = D_ref + D_rec,
  where D_ref = (T − N) captures reference-induced supervision and D_rec = (N − S_c) captures “recovery” supervision independent of the reference.
- Alignment analysis: measure how much D_ref aligns with D_tot and how student prediction changes align with these directions over training.
- Controls: swap in contexts/references from other problems to test whether apparent alignment is spurious and to avoid over-attributing effects to the correct reference.8aa:T5da,The method combines activation patching and attention analysis across 29 languages, five open-source model families, and six checkpoints. The experimental design is deliberately controlled. The authors build verb inventories from morphological resources such as UniMorph, then create zero-shot prompts with a common template like “Conjugation of the verb X in present tense: pronoun conjugation,” adapted to each language. This is less natural than free-form text, but it preserves token-position alignment between clean and corrupted prompts, which is important for causal patching. They distinguish two recovery metrics: a broader target-form recovery metric, which asks whether patching a head helps restore the context-appropriate target token, and a stricter minimal-pair inflection recovery metric, which isolates restoration of the inflectional contrast itself. For each language, they identify the attention heads causally implicated in agreement, then compare these head-level signatures across languages. The key claim is not just that overlap exists, but that overlap varies systematically with overt inflection. Languages with clear person/number marking show stronger circuit similarity. English behaves as a bridge case: its third-person singular cases align more with strongly inflecting languages, while its non-inflecting cases do not. The paper also examines attention patterns of overlapping heads and finds that they play similar routing roles, not merely similar locations.8ab:T4f8,The study covers 29 languages, five model families, and six checkpoints. The initial lexical inventory spans 34 languages, with the number of verb lemmas per language ranging from 56 to 23,782 and averaging about 1,750. The evaluation focuses on four person/number contrasts: 1sg↔2sg, 1sg↔3sg, 1pl↔3pl, and 3sg↔3pl; English has overt inflection in only two of these. The main findings are threefold. First, languages with overt subject-verb agreement show substantial overlap in the heads implicated in agreement, especially under the stricter minimal-pair inflection metric. Second, languages with weak or absent person-based inflection are much less similar to that shared signature, which argues against a simple “all multilingual processing is shared” story. Third, model family, size, and instruction tuning affect the absolute pattern but do not overturn the main trend. The provided text does not include the full numerical tables, so exact similarity values or head counts should be taken from the original figures rather than inferred here. The most important empirical artifacts to inspect are the language-by-language similarity matrices, the comparison between broad recovery and inflection-specific recovery, and the English bridge-case breakdown.8ac:T566,The analysis extends prior work on diffusion over mixture distributions by giving each cluster its own low-dimensional Gaussian structure. The first key step is to express the mixture score as a posterior-weighted average of cluster-wise scores. This turns denoising into a dynamical Bayesian classifier: at high noise, posterior mass is spread across clusters and the trajectory explores; once the signal-to-noise ratio crosses a threshold, the posterior concentrates and the trajectory commits to a single cluster with high probability. The threshold is shown to occur at SNR of order Theta(log(KD)/D). The second key step is to split the reverse process at this commitment time. Before commitment, the analysis handles inter-cluster ambiguity; after commitment, it studies denoising within one cluster and exploits its low intrinsic dimension. This yields KL error bounds whose dominant dimensional dependence is linear in the maximum intrinsic dimension across clusters, with only logarithmic dependence on D. Relative to prior single-manifold or purely qualitative mixture analyses, the novelty is the joint treatment of multimodal phase transition and intrinsic-dimension-sensitive KL bounds. The limitation is also clear: the framework relies on strong assumptions, especially Gaussian components, separation conditions, and regularity needed to control discretization error.8ad:T698,DART-SD has three main components. First, it builds an Interaction-State Transition Graph from teacher rollouts. Nodes are not single actions; they are cumulative interaction states, defined by the task-relevant information acquired so far. To make this possible, the method introduces information atom abstraction: tool outputs are canonicalized, semantically equivalent responses are mapped to the same atom, and non-informative outputs such as status-only or empty responses are collapsed away. This lets trajectories with different action orders but the same acquired information land on the same node, which naturally captures the diamond topology induced by order-independent sub-goals. Second, for a failed student rollout, the method performs success-reachable projection and identifies the Critical Topological Breakpoint. Instead of cutting by timestep, it asks whether each cumulative student state still lies in the region from which success is reachable in the empirical graph. The CTB is the point where the rollout leaves that success-supported region. Third, starting from a recovery anchor near the CTB, the method retrieves a success-supported continuation from the ISTG and applies localized supervision only to the recovery segment, while preserving the valid prefix. Training is progressive self-distillation: the student rolls out, exposes its current capability boundary, receives CTB-guided local correction, and gradually extends the length of valid interaction prefixes. Compared with vanilla SFT, supervision is localized. Compared with RL, the method does not rely on sparse reward propagation; it uses explicit graph structure extracted from teacher behavior.8ae:T47e,The study evaluates on five benchmarks and two model scales. The main empirical claim is consistent improvement over supervised and RL baselines, along with fewer redundant tool calls and longer valid interaction prefixes. The full numerical tables are not present in the provided text, so it would be unsafe to invent exact gains, parameter counts, or data sizes. From the paper content that is available, the important experimental takeaways are: first, DART-SD helps most in tasks with multiple order-independent sub-goals, where linear imitation tends to over-penalize alternative valid paths; second, many failed student trajectories already contain long correct prefixes, so local recovery is more efficient than rewriting the whole trajectory; third, using cumulative interaction states matters, and weaker action-level graph variants lose performance; fourth, progressive self-distillation outperforms one-shot correction, suggesting that the student’s recoverable frontier expands over training. For practical use, the original tables should be checked for benchmark-specific gains, tool-call reduction, and consistency across model sizes.8af:T40f,The analysis covers 1,338 public agent trajectories on PostTrainBench, spanning seven benchmarks, four base models from 1.7B to 4B parameters, and 20 agent configurations across five scaffolds. Each trajectory has a 10-hour budget on one NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU. The main finding is strategy lock-in. The high-level strategy is usually fixed at the beginning, before code and experiments provide feedback, and the rest of the run is spent on local adjustments. The pattern depends more on the agent scaffold than on the task: 80.7% of Claude Code trajectories converge on full-parameter SFT, while 89.6% of Codex CLI trajectories converge on PEFT. The experience scaffold improves execution, with reported gains of +12.6 points on GSM8K and +40.8 on HumanEval, but does not make strategies adaptive. Human review can redirect the initial strategy before training begins, yet agents still fall back to local adjustment after training starts. Spending 2–8x more inference tokens helps easier tasks but gives almost no gain on the hardest one.8b0:T52f,SkillGate introduces two disjoint credit channels within a single policy-gradient update. The task channel uses the usual group-normalized outcome advantage, but removes the entire skill-read tool call from its support. In other words, task success or failure no longer directly updates the tokens that name the chosen skill. The selector channel applies an action-local advantage only to the token span corresponding to the chosen skill name. That selector signal is positive only when the trajectory issued a single read and the selected skill matches the oracle-correct one; it is then centered within the prompt group to reduce between-group difficulty effects. Two implementation details matter. First, rollout-time span attribution records the exact token span of each skill-read action so the support partition is exact in practice. Second, length-invariant reweighting gives equal batch-level loss weight to the two channels and equal share to each read action, preventing selector learning from weakening on longer trajectories. This differs from finer reward shaping: the paper is not slicing the same reward more finely, but separating two decisions that are justified by different evidence. It also differs from pre-execution retrieval methods, because the target here is the policy’s own in-episode skill choice.8b1:T4ac,The paper first audits the failure mode, then validates the method. In the audit, it analyzes 12,800 on-policy trajectories from a standard outcome-only RL run and reports three key findings. First, share: the median token share of the selected-skill name is only 0.14% of a trajectory, and this shrinks further with horizon. Second, sign: about two in five of those tokens receive negative advantage; on the longest trajectories, a correct choice is punished more often than rewarded. Third, value: within matched prompt groups, making the correct read is still worth +11.2 points in task success, so the decision is important despite receiving weak and noisy credit. The method is then evaluated on five agent benchmarks. The headline number in the provided text is trial success improving from 47.0% to 53.2%. The gains appear concentrated in long-horizon settings with similar-looking candidate skills and noisy downstream execution, which matches the proposed diagnosis. The most important ablations are likely the ones isolating support partitioning, local selector advantage, and length-invariant weighting. The paper’s claim is that all three are needed for the effect to hold robustly.8b2:Taaa,技术方案由两部分组成：capability-specific data pipeline 和 capability-aligned curriculum scheduling。

先看数据管线。作者没有把所有样本混成一个大池子统一清洗，而是设计了三个可互操作的数据引擎。

第一是 T2I data engine，目标是建立广覆盖的 text-image grounding。全文提到它会做概念覆盖扩展、长尾重平衡、多粒度 caption 对齐，以及 dense caption 构造。这里的关键不是单纯提高 caption 质量，而是让 T2I 数据承担“概念底座”的角色，为后续结构化生成、文本渲染和编辑提供可迁移的视觉词汇与语义对齐。

第二是 image-editing data engine。作者把编辑监督视为多种操作类型的组合，因此不是只收集 source-target pairs，而是为不同编辑类型设计专门构造流程，同时从自然相关图像中挖掘真实关联，并用专家生成样本补足稀缺编辑类型。更重要的是，编辑指令在词汇和描述结构上与 T2I caption 对齐，这样编辑任务可以复用 T2I 已学到的概念表示，而不必在编辑数据里重复覆盖全部视觉概念。

第三是 knowledge-grounded data engine。它通过知识图谱引导的数据获取，把视觉模式与命名实体、结构化知识关联起来。这个设计针对的是一般图像生成模型常见的知识薄弱问题：模型能画出“像某物”的图，但未必能稳定绑定实体、属性和关系。

再看课程调度。作者提出五阶段 curriculum，沿能力依赖顺序逐步扩展训练混合。起点是大规模 T2I，用来建立基础视觉语义对齐和基本生成先验；随后加入结构复杂、知识相关、文本密集的样本，发展结构构图、知识绑定和文本渲染；在 T2I prior 稳定后，再引入 editing data，学习 reference preservation 和 controlled transformation；之后通过 continual training 与 SFT，把 mixture 转向更小、更平衡、更精细的数据子集，并让图像分辨率随内容复杂度提升。这里有四个共同演化轴：任务组成、视觉概念分布、数据质量、图像分辨率。

全文里另一个值得注意的点是 active refinement loop。课程不是一次性写死，而是通过 capability-aware evaluation 把失败模式映射回对应数据引擎，做 targeted retrieval、expert construction、resampling，再把修正后的数据重新注入后续训练。这使它更像一个闭环数据系统，而不是静态配方。

与常见做法相比，这篇工作的区别不在于某个过滤器或 captioner 更强，而在于它把“数据样本”提升为“能力单元”，把“任务数据集”改写成“可迁移监督源”。8b3:Tc0e,The framework has two main parts: a capability-specific data pipeline and a capability-aligned curriculum schedule.

On the data side, the authors build three specialized but interoperable engines instead of throwing all samples into one global pool.

The first is a T2I data engine for broad text-image grounding. It expands concept coverage, rebalances long-tail distributions, aligns captions at multiple granularities, and uses dense captions where needed. The important design choice is that T2I data is treated as the conceptual base layer. It is not only for standalone text-to-image quality; it is meant to provide reusable visual vocabulary and semantic alignment for later capabilities such as structured generation, text rendering, and editing.

The second is an image-editing data engine. Rather than collecting generic source-target pairs only, the paper describes specialized pipelines for different edit types, mining realistic associations from naturally related images, and using expert-generated examples for sparse edit categories. A key interoperability choice is that editing instructions are aligned with T2I captions in vocabulary and descriptive structure. This allows editing supervision to reuse concepts already learned from T2I data instead of duplicating full concept coverage inside editing datasets.

The third is a knowledge-grounded data engine. It links visual patterns to named entities and structured knowledge through knowledge-graph-guided acquisition. This targets a common weakness in image generators: they may produce plausible imagery without reliably binding entities, attributes, and relations.

On the curriculum side, the paper proposes a five-stage schedule that follows the dependency order of capability acquisition. Training starts with large-scale T2I data to establish broad visual-semantic alignment and a basic generative prior. It then adds structurally complex, knowledge-grounded, and text-rich examples to develop composition, knowledge grounding, and text rendering. Once the T2I prior is stable, editing data is introduced to learn reference preservation and controlled transformation. Later continual training and supervised fine-tuning shift the mixture toward smaller, more balanced, and more refined subsets, while image resolution increases with content complexity. The schedule evolves jointly along four axes: task composition, visual concept distribution, data quality, and image resolution.

A notable systems idea is the active refinement loop. The schedule is not fixed once and for all. Capability-aware evaluation maps observed failures back to the relevant data engine, which then performs targeted retrieval, expert construction, or resampling. The refined data is fed back into later training mixtures. This makes the proposal a closed-loop data system rather than a static recipe.

Compared with standard data-pipeline work, the novelty is not a better filter or captioner in isolation. The novelty is the shift from task datasets to transferable supervision sources organized around capability dependencies.8b4:T712,The provided full-text excerpt is mostly from the introduction, so it does not expose the full result tables or exact numbers. It would be unsafe to invent model sizes, corpus sizes, or precise gains. Still, the experimental logic is clear from the paper’s framing.

First, the paper should test the independent and complementary value of the three data engines. The key question is whether T2I, editing, and knowledge-grounded supervision each improve distinct capabilities, and whether joint capability-oriented training is better than simply mixing task-specific datasets built in isolation. The most informative outcomes would be gains in text rendering, knowledge binding, complex composition, and edit faithfulness.

Second, because the paper emphasizes dependency-aware curriculum, an important comparison is likely between the proposed staged schedule and baselines such as fixed mixtures, random mixtures, or task-isolated training. What matters here is not only final quality but also convergence speed, emergence order of capabilities, and stability after introducing editing, continual training, and SFT.

Third, the active refinement loop should be evaluated through failure-driven data augmentation or targeted resampling. If the paper includes case studies, the useful question is which failure modes can be repaired by routing them back to the right data engine, and which ones reveal that the capability decomposition is still incomplete.

The real value of the experiments is whether they validate the organizational principle. If the results only show that more curated data helps, the contribution is limited. If they show that organizing data by capability dependencies is more sample-efficient or more transferable than organizing by task silos, the paper becomes much more interesting.8b5:T54a,For a skim, start with how the paper defines capabilities and the dependency structure between them. If you work on multimodal pretraining data systems, the data-engine definitions, curriculum schedule, and failure-feedback loop deserve a closer read.8b6:T6d9,The technical core is a time-dependent Rasch/IRT-style model of vocabulary acquisition. Each word j has a difficulty δ_j. Each child i has an ability θ_i(t) composed of a baseline efficiency ξ_i, an acceleration term κ_i log(t/a0), and a waking-hours term H that links developmental time to cumulative exposure. Word production probability is determined by the gap between child ability and word difficulty. The central modeling move is to interpret growth on ratio-scale variables with real zeros, so log transforms have a direct meaning in terms of returns to experience rather than being a generic curve-fitting trick.

Three design choices matter. First, the model is built on interpretable units such as tokens heard per hour and vocabulary size in word types. Second, word difficulty is estimated freely rather than reduced to frequency, which lets the analysis isolate whether learning efficiency itself changes over development. Third, the authors compare four nested models: no acceleration, no individual efficiency variation, no individual acceleration variation, and the full accelerating accumulator. This is important because it separates true acceleration from apparent curvature induced by heterogeneity.

A major strength, visible only in the full paper, is that the model is fit to item-level longitudinal CDI data rather than aggregate vocabulary counts. That means word difficulty, age of acquisition, and child trajectories are jointly constrained. The paper also checks robustness with hierarchical pooling, 2PL IRT variants, alternative item selections on CDI forms, and linear-time growth alternatives. The high κ estimates survive these changes, which makes the result much harder to dismiss as a parameterization artifact.8b7:T77e,The empirical analysis uses five longitudinal Wordbank datasets covering American English, Norwegian, and Japanese, with monolingual typically developing children aged 8–36 months. Total N is 1,841, and each child has at least three longitudinal administrations. The study focuses on reported production rather than comprehension because it is available over a wider age range and is more reliable.

The full accelerating model wins on all five datasets. Relative to the next-best ablation, the item-level leave-one-out expected log predictive density improves by more than 760 in every dataset, which is a large gap for this kind of model comparison. The estimated acceleration parameter κ is far above the pure-accumulator value of 1 in every case, roughly 10.6 [10.5, 10.8] to 13.3 [13.2, 13.3]. These estimates remain essentially unchanged in larger data settings, hierarchical pooling, 2PL IRT variants, and alternative CDI item selections. Linear growth models do not fit better.

There is also substantial between-child variation in acceleration, with σ_b ranging from 3.2 to 6.6, yet the fitted population distribution places 99.5% of children above κ=1. The authors are careful about what can and cannot be inferred at the individual level: typical CDI series are too sparse to estimate a child-specific κ precisely, but adding a population acceleration term improves trajectory prediction for 91.9% of children when at least five prior CDIs are available.

One of the most useful interpretive results is the conversion from acceleration to exposure requirements. The model implies that the number of exposures needed to learn a word drops sharply over development. Later-acquired words are not simply easier; the learner is more efficient. In the LM comparison, even models trained on child-directed speech do not show this accelerating pattern and instead look closer to constant proportional returns.8b8:T487,Start with the model definition and Figure 1. A careful read takes about 60–90 minutes.8b9:T49e,MoNe attaches a fast-weight neural memory to each decoder layer of a frozen Transformer. The context is split into fixed-size segments, with T=512 in the paper. During the context-reading phase, segments are processed sequentially and each layer updates its own memory through localized gradient updates; backbone weights are never modified. The memory module is a per-head SwiGLU MLP rather than a single linear map, giving it more capacity to store associative structure under a small parameter budget. During generation, the original context tokens are not reread. Query tokens are projected with the frozen Wq, used to read the final fast-weight state, and converted into memory tokens. After RMSNorm and learned head-wise gating, these tokens are projected through the frozen Wk and Wv and concatenated with the query’s normal attention entries. This gives O(N) preprocessing, approximately O(1) query cost with respect to context length, and a KV footprint that does not grow with N. Compared with RAG, it is less tied to locally retrievable chunks. Compared with architectures such as Mamba, TTT, or Titans, it is designed as a plug-in for existing pretrained Transformers.8ba:T8c2,LinCa follows a Decompose-Predict-Reconstruct pipeline. The motivation comes from empirical analysis: hidden features in diffusion models show strong heterogeneity across models, timestep segments, and feature dimensions. Some components evolve smoothly and are suitable for higher-order extrapolation; others are unstable and exhibit abrupt changes, making direct prediction unreliable. The difficulty is that these components are interleaved in the original feature space, so simple manual partitioning does not work.

To address this, LinCa introduces a lightweight invertible network that maps cached features into a new representation space. In that space, features are decomposed into sub-components with different continuity and predictability properties. Stable components are predicted from historical caches using polynomial extrapolation, and the prediction order is matched to the component rather than shared globally. Unstable components are not extrapolated; they are simply reused from the nearest cache. The processed sub-components are then mapped back to the original feature space through the inverse transform. The role of invertibility is important: it prevents information loss during decomposition and allows the training objective to be defined directly on reconstructed features.

A second key design is timestep segmentation. Instead of training one global predictor for the entire denoising trajectory, the method splits timesteps into several segments and trains isomorphic but independently parameterized predictors for each segment. This matters because early, middle, and late denoising stages often have very different hidden-state dynamics, and a single predictor tends to fail in some regions.

Training overhead is intentionally small. LinCa does not need to load or finetune the original diffusion model. It only uses a small set of pre-generated intermediate features as supervision. The paper reports 100-200 feature samples, less than one hour of training on a single 12GB GPU, and parameter overhead below 0.2% of the base model. From a systems perspective, this keeps much of the deployment convenience of training-free caching while replacing brittle heuristics with a lightweight learned predictor.8bb:T782,The evaluation covers FLUX.1-dev, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-Edit, and HunyuanVideo, and also tests compatibility with distilled and quantized models. The main result is that LinCa preserves generation quality much better than prior caching methods at high acceleration ratios while keeping nearly the same runtime profile. Reported speedups include 5.51× on FLUX.1-dev, 6.95× on Qwen-Image, 7.08× on Qwen-Image-Edit, and 5.50× on HunyuanVideo, with the paper describing the quality loss as near-lossless.

The most important evidence is not the headline speedup table but the validation of the paper’s core premise: heterogeneous feature dynamics. The useful experiments are the ones showing (1) different predictability across timestep segments, (2) different continuity patterns across feature dimensions within the same layer, and (3) lower prediction error from decomposed, differentiated prediction compared with a uniform predictor. If those analyses are convincing, then the gains are not just from adding a larger auxiliary model but from matching the predictor to the actual dynamics.

For ablations, the key questions are: whether invertible decomposition is necessary, whether component-specific prediction orders outperform a shared order, whether segmented predictors beat a global predictor, and whether 100-200 training samples are already enough to saturate performance. If the paper reports FID, CLIP-based metrics, video quality scores, or editing consistency, the most informative comparison is quality at matched speedup against methods such as FORA, ToCa, and TaylorSeer, rather than absolute quality alone.

A clear limitation is that this remains an inference-time patch; it does not change the sampling algorithm itself. Its gains depend on temporal continuity in hidden features, so the room for improvement may shrink under extremely low-step samplers or models with highly irregular dynamics.8bc:T412,This is a skim paper. Start with the introduction and the feature-dynamics visualizations, especially the figure that shows heterogeneity across timesteps and dimensions. The whole paper stands or falls on whether that observation is empirically well supported. Then read the method overview and focus on three ideas: invertible decomposition, differentiated prediction, and segmented training. If those are clear, the main design is clear.

In the experiments, prioritize the main comparison table and the ablations. The main table tells you whether LinCa is actually more stable than prior caching methods; the ablations tell you where the gain comes from. A useful 20-minute read would cover the introduction, the dynamics figures, the method diagram, the main results, and the key ablations. If you care about diffusion LMs or unified multimodal generation systems, also check the compatibility experiments with distillation and quantization, since that determines whether LinCa is a composable systems module rather than a one-off trick.8bd:T83e,The method, AViTS, stands for Adaptive Spatiotemporal Token Selection. At resolution transition points, it assigns each latent token a joint importance score and uses that score to decide which tokens are upsampled earlier.

The first component is spatial importance. Instead of relying only on local latent structure or one-step statistics, AViTS explicitly uses latent-text attention. The intuition is straightforward: if a visual token consistently responds strongly to the text condition at low resolution, it is more likely to correspond to prompt-relevant objects, attributes, or edit targets, and should therefore receive high-resolution compute earlier. The paper suggests that this signal is aggregated rather than taken from a single layer or step, which makes it more stable.

The second component is temporal importance. The paper measures token-level step variance, namely how much a token representation changes across diffusion steps. Tokens with large variation are still evolving and likely need further refinement; tokens with small variation are closer to convergence and can be deferred. This complements attention-based importance because some regions may not be the strongest text-aligned areas but still require continued updates for editing fidelity or fine-detail recovery.

The third component is fusion and selective upsampling. AViTS combines the spatial and temporal signals into a unified spatiotemporal importance score, then performs importance-aware selective upsampling: high-importance tokens are promoted to high resolution earlier, while low-importance tokens are delayed. This differs from prior partial upsampling methods that mostly depend on local structure heuristics, edge cues, uncertainty proxies, or single-step latent statistics. AViTS jointly models conditional semantics and cross-step dynamics.

Importantly, the framework is presented as an add-on policy for dynamic-resolution DiTs rather than a backbone redesign. It is reported to work with FLUX, Qwen-Image-Edit, and FLUX.1-Kontext-dev, and to compose with distillation, quantization, and feature caching.8be:T618,The main experimental story is the efficiency-quality trade-off rather than a single headline metric. The paper reports up to 6.34x acceleration on FLUX, nearly 9x FLOPs reduction on Qwen-Image-Edit and FLUX.1-Kontext-dev, and up to 14.76x acceleration when AViTS is combined with distillation. The claim is that these gains come with limited degradation in generation and editing quality.

Two empirical parts matter most. First, the paper provides the analysis that motivates the method. On both FLUX.1-dev and Qwen-Image-Edit, attention-based spatial importance and step-variance-based temporal importance show strongly long-tailed distributions, indicating that only a small subset of tokens are truly critical. The visualizations further suggest that attention highlights instruction-relevant semantic regions, while high step variance concentrates on areas requiring fine-grained modeling or modification.

Second, the method appears to include ablations comparing spatial-only, temporal-only, and fused scoring. Even without all table values in the prompt, the paper’s narrative makes clear that the joint score is more reliable than either signal alone. Another useful result is composability: AViTS works not only for text-to-image generation but also for image editing, and it stacks with distillation, quantization, and feature caching. That consistency is more interesting than the raw speedup number, because it suggests the method is exploiting a fairly general structure in token importance rather than overfitting to one model or one sampler.8bf:T405,For a quick read, start with the introduction and the empirical motivation around token-importance heterogeneity. Figures 2 and 3 are the key entry point. Then read the method section with attention to three details: how the attention signal is aggregated, how step variance is computed across timesteps, and what extra memory or bookkeeping this introduces. Those implementation choices determine whether the method is practically attractive.

Finally, look at the main efficiency-quality comparisons, the ablations on scoring strategies, and the results combined with distillation, quantization, and caching. For a deeper read, the most interesting follow-up question is whether this spatiotemporal importance score can be generalized to multimodal token pruning or adaptive compute allocation during training.8c0:T806,The method has two main components. The first is DVBP. The authors estimate the input activation covariance of each layer in an online manner, avoiding the need to store all activations. They then eigendecompose the covariance matrix and use random matrix theory, specifically the Marchenko-Pastur law, to identify the noise-dominated part of the spectrum. Those spectral components are filtered out, producing a denoised covariance matrix. Variance scores are then computed from this denoised covariance and used to rank neurons. The key point is that the original VBP relies on diagonal variance terms, but those diagonals are themselves corrupted by global spectral noise; denoising at the spectrum level leads to more stable rankings, especially under aggressive pruning.

The second component is OB²C. Starting from the Optimal Brain Compression reconstruction objective, the authors incorporate the mean-shift bias compensation directly into the objective instead of treating it as a separate post-hoc fix. With this formulation, the layer-wise Hessian reduces exactly to the input activation covariance matrix. This matters because it turns a generic second-order reconstruction problem into one that can be solved from calibration activations alone. Given a pruning mask, the method then solves for the optimal update of both the remaining weights and the bias so that the output reconstruction error is minimized after low-variance neurons are removed. Compared with original VBP, the difference is not just a better bias correction; the remaining weights are also allowed to absorb information from the pruned features. Compared with standard OBC, the explicit bias term makes the formulation better suited to the case where low-variance features behave like near-constants.

Operationally, the full pipeline is: use denoised covariance for more reliable neuron ranking, then use the same covariance for second-order recovery. The design is fairly clean, and the reuse of one statistical object across both stages is the main technical appeal.8c1:T635,The experiments cover DeiT, Swin, and ConvNeXt backbones across Tiny, Small, and Base scales. The main comparison is against the original VBP under different structured pruning ratios. The headline result is that the gain widens as pruning becomes more aggressive. At 50% structural reduction, Tiny models retain roughly 80% Top-1 accuracy, while Small and Base models stay above 90%; relative to VBP, the improvement reaches up to 7.33% on Swin-S and 29.46% on ConvNeXt-T. These numbers suggest that the method mainly helps in the high-compression regime, which is consistent with the paper’s diagnosis that VBP fails because of noisy ranking and insufficient compensation.

The most informative ablations are of two kinds. First, whether spectral denoising alone improves neuron ranking. The paper shows that denoised variance by itself already outperforms raw variance at high pruning ratios, indicating that covariance noise is not a minor issue but directly affects pruning decisions. Second, whether OB²C improves over mean-shift-only compensation. The results show that bias correction alone is insufficient; jointly updating the remaining weights reduces reconstruction error and improves final accuracy. If the paper includes layer-wise or module-wise analyses, the gains are likely more visible in MLP/channel pruning settings, where the low-variance-as-near-constant assumption is most plausible.

A clear limitation is that all experiments are on vision models rather than LLMs. So the transferable value is mostly in the method, not in the empirical conclusions themselves.8c2:T5cf,They propose a two-stage selective evaluation policy with joint threshold calibration.
- Setup: an examinee model produces an answer; a judge outputs a binary verdict. A held-out calibration set provides ground-truth evaluation labels (human or reference-based matching). Define a Bernoulli failure indicator for whether the judge verdict matches ground truth.
- Mode 1 (parametric judging): the judge decides using only its internal knowledge and emits an uncertainty/confidence score. If uncertainty is below threshold τ1, accept the verdict.
- Mode 2 (retrieval-augmented judging): otherwise, trigger web search, re-judge with retrieved evidence, and accept if uncertainty is below τ2; else abstain.
- Risk control: thresholds (τ1, τ2) are calibrated on the labeled calibration set using Clopper–Pearson upper confidence bounds to ensure the error rate (framed as FDR / false discovery among accepted verdicts) is bounded by a user-specified α with high probability.
- Key technical point: they argue the Bernoulli structure required for the CP bound still holds under the two-threshold routing scheme, so the finite-sample guarantee extends without extra distributional assumptions.
- Compared to prior selective prediction: prior work is typically single-threshold accept/abstain; here retrieval is an intermediate action, and the two thresholds are jointly calibrated to increase coverage under the same risk constraint while concentrating retrieval cost on uncertain cases.8c3:T48e,The work has three components. First, PROBE-Sim is a tabletop simulator built with PyBullet and Blender-EEVEE, using a UR5 robot with a Robotiq gripper. Scenes contain 15 tightly packed objects sampled from 1,796 scanned assets across 481 categories, with object metadata such as names, colors, categories, and physical descriptions. The design emphasizes physical realism, scalable procedural generation, and verifiable ground truth. Second, PROBE-Bench contains 150 tasks spanning six question types: Count, Find, Compare, Size, Reduce, and Beneath. Agents can call perception tools such as scene parsing and object finding, and manipulation tools such as grasp-and-remove and pushing. The important design choice is that perception and manipulation are embedded in a single agent loop, so the model must decide when to inspect, when to manipulate, and when to answer. Third, Probe-Agent distills successful tool-use trajectories from a strong teacher, Gemini 3.1 Pro, into smaller open-weight students such as Qwen3-VL and NVILA via supervised fine-tuning. Distilling only successful trajectories is meant to teach stable strategies rather than noisy exploration.8c4:T5ae,The benchmark construction pipeline is the main technical contribution. Instead of directly scraping product demos or manually inventing tasks, the authors use a multi-stage process. They first identify AI-native startups with evidence of funding and real adoption, using that as a proxy that users genuinely delegate these workflows to AI. They then interview deep users to recover actual usage contexts, task goals, inputs, constraints, expected deliverables, and acceptance criteria. Domain experts convert those validated scenarios into benchmark instances that are reproducible, answerable, and evaluable. A final quality-control stage checks realism, answerability, evaluability, and discriminative difficulty. The result is a 97-task benchmark spanning six major domains.

The evaluation protocol is equally important. Each task is scored with multiple independent rubrics covering functionality, structure, formatting, and domain-specific quality, rather than a single holistic score. The reason is straightforward: real work products must satisfy several coupled requirements at once, and a single score can hide severe failure on one dimension. The authors also evaluate representative models under a unified agentic harness to reduce confounding from system-specific tooling. The novelty here is not an algorithmic method but the coupling of task sourcing, task abstraction, and deliverable-level evaluation into one coherent benchmark design.8c5:T4c7,The headline result is that even the strongest model completes only about 30% of tasks under the unified harness. That is a strong signal that current general-purpose agents are still far from reliably producing professionally usable deliverables. Performance varies substantially by domain, with Finance, STEM & Computer Science, and Education & Humanities emerging as especially difficult. This suggests that high-constraint, expertise-heavy, and strongly structured tasks remain major weaknesses.

The paper’s analysis points to a few recurring failure modes. One is complex instruction following: models often capture the broad objective but fail to satisfy many detailed constraints simultaneously. Another is domain-specific expertise: the issue is not generic fluency, but instability in professional content, terminology, conventions, and reasoning. A third is deliverable completion: systems can often produce something plausible-looking, yet still fall short of a directly usable final product. The emphasis is less on leaderboard separation and more on showing that once task sourcing becomes more realistic and scoring becomes more faithful, the apparent capability ceiling of current agents drops materially.8c6:T6cb,There are two main technical ideas. The first is lifecycle decomposition. The authors organize harness risk into six operational phases: Harness Configuration, Capability Extension, Runtime Operation, State Persistence, Action Control, and Incident Recovery. This is useful because it re-groups agent failures by harness responsibility. Configuration covers connectors, credentials, gateways, and policy templates; capability extension covers plugin selection, installation, updates, and permissions; runtime operation covers adversarial content in emails, webpages, documents, and tool outputs; state persistence covers whether transient malicious content gets written into durable memory or policy state; action control covers high-impact actions such as payments, deployments, deletions, OAuth grants, and outbound communication; incident recovery covers rollback, credential rotation, state repair, and evidence preservation. The second idea is the benchmark protocol itself. HarnessRisk contains 128 sandboxed cases spanning those six phases. Each case combines a benign user goal with an adversarial instruction embedded in an untrusted workflow artifact. The agent operates through a three-turn owner workflow with case-specific files, tools, persistent state, and mock services. Every run starts from a fresh environment and real network access is disabled. Evaluation is split into Utility, Attack Success Rate, Persistence, and Detection. That separation is important because it allows the benchmark to show that successful task completion and safe execution are not the same thing. The evaluated unit is not a bare model but a deployed model-harness configuration: three harnesses, six models, and fourteen total configurations.8c7:T43c,The most important empirical findings are qualitative but strong. First, high utility can coexist with high attack success. That is the central result: task completion alone is a poor proxy for safety. Second, Harness Configuration is the most vulnerable phase across all three harnesses. The reason is not that runtime attacks disappear, but that configuration-time manipulation can weaken security-sensitive parameters before the rest of the workflow even begins. Third, model safety rankings change substantially across harnesses, showing that permissions, state representation, tool exposure, and authorization context materially alter the risk profile of the same underlying model. The benchmark also measures Persistence and Detection, which extends evaluation beyond one-shot unsafe actions to durable compromise and explicit risk recognition. Even without all table values here, the experimental design makes clear that the paper is testing whether attacks remain in long-term state and whether the system notices them, not just whether a single malicious action is triggered.8c8:T478,The paper defines a self-consistency hypothesis, H_SC, over a finite set of text-described items. Each item is treated as an atomic alternative; the audit does not assume linear, additive, smooth, or feature-based utilities. The only economic structure is quasi-linearity in money: the utility of an offer equals the item’s utility minus its listed price. Two query types are compared. Item queries ask for the maximum willingness to pay for a single item. Offer-pair queries ask for the signed price change that would make the user indifferent between two priced offers. If a shared dollar utility exists, differences between item-query estimates should agree with the compensation elicited directly from offer-pair queries. The paper provides a joint bootstrap test measuring deviation from the best-fitting shared utility, plus two local diagnostics. P1 checks path consistency among offer-pair judgments. P2 checks whether offer-pair judgments match price-adjusted differences of item-query judgments. The diagnostics report statistical evidence, dollar-scale effect sizes, price-normalized magnitudes, and supported preference reversals.8c9:T619,The study compares three models in the GPT-5.4 to GPT-5.6 Sol line over three migration edges: 5.4→5.5, 5.5→Sol, and 5.4→Sol. The setup is intentionally controlled to mimic a real dependency upgrade: all request parameters are fixed and only the model identifier changes. Reasoning effort is set to medium for all models, no output-length cap is imposed, and each model-item pair is sampled independently K=50 times.

The evaluation uses 900 public benchmark items spanning graduate-level knowledge, olympiad mathematics, and instruction following. The paper first screens for items with headroom, excluding cases that are always correct or always incorrect across all models, since those items carry little information about migration-induced change.

At the item level, the method estimates pass probabilities for each model and classifies each item into four categories: reliably improved, reliably regressed, practically equivalent, or inconclusive. The classification uses both a practical-significance threshold and FDR control. A key strength is that the authors do not stop at nominal hypothesis testing. They build a label-permutation null and rerun the entire classification pipeline at matched sample size, so the calibration applies to the full decision procedure rather than to an isolated test statistic.

For instruction following, the same responses are scored under both strict and loose verifiers. This is an important design choice because it helps separate semantic capability changes from output-format or protocol-compliance changes.8ca:T4f0,The main empirical result is simple and strong: all nine migration-benchmark cells contain both reliable improvements and reliable regressions. No upgrade is uniformly better.

The headline numbers are informative. Even migration edges with positive aggregate score changes contain up to 8.3% reliably regressed items. Conversely, edges with negative aggregate changes still contain up to 10.7% reliably improved items. In other words, the net score hides substantial bidirectional churn.

The instruction-following results are especially revealing. On the latest migration, the same edge shows a 3.9-point regression under strict scoring but only a 0.04-point regression under loose scoring, widening the strict-loose gap by 3.9 points. That suggests a large fraction of the measured regression comes from exact compliance with verifier expectations rather than from a broad semantic failure.

Methodologically, the use of 50 repeated samples per item is one of the paper’s main strengths. It allows the authors to distinguish stable pass-probability shifts from sampling noise.
