核心发现有三层。第一，跨任务通道确实存在，但双向不对称：只学生成的模型，在理解侧可以做名称匹配，却不能稳定地产生名称；只学理解的模型，则可以在生成侧画出该概念。第二，multiple-choice probe 会高估 generation→understanding 的迁移，因为模型可能靠排除法选对；一旦改成 production-style 评测，即把候选词从上下文中全部移除，只有真正经过 LM cross-entropy 训练的条件才会产出名称。第三，entry point 决定可用性，但“位置对”还不够，必须该层已经处在共享语义格式中。alignment probe 能预测哪些配置会导出，但把 probe 指标硬推到很高本身并不自动带来迁移，说明相关性不等于充分因果。作者还做了 activation edit，直接在闭式形式下最大化同一个 alignment 项，发现它能拿到训练增益的大约 80%，但只在很窄的层窗口内有效，这进一步支持“中层共享语义空间”这个解释。8cc:T9c9,The experimental design is unusually clean. The main platform is BAGEL-7B-MoT, a 28-layer Mixture-of-Transformers model with hidden size 3584. Each layer contains a shared text/understanding expert and a private generation expert. Understanding uses only the shared expert, while generation uses both shared and private branches. To isolate architectural transfer from supervision overlap, the authors create 56 novel concepts. Each concept is an Objaverse 3D asset rendered from 60 training views and 20 held-out views, paired with a pseudo-word screened so that the frozen model shows no stable visual or lexical behavior for it. Concepts are split into seven groups of eight, with evaluation done against fixed-difficulty retrieval banks.

There are two injection routes. G-inject trains only the caption-to-image direction using a rectified-flow objective. U-inject trains only the image-to-text direction using language-model cross-entropy. Training uses rank-32 LoRA, and the placement of LoRA is itself a controlled variable. The central experimental axis is the entry point: the exact layer and submodule where the new concept is written into the decoder. The paper compares writing into the shared pathway, the private generation branch, non-exporting carriers, and readout layers, and uses an alignment probe to test whether a given depth already represents concepts in a semantic format usable by both tasks.

Three findings stand out. First, the cross-task channel is real but asymmetric. Generation-only training lets the model match the concept name on the understanding side, but not reliably produce the name. Understanding-only training can also support drawing the concept on the generation side. Second, multiple-choice probes overestimate generation-to-understanding transfer because they can be solved by elimination. When evaluation is changed to production, with all candidate names removed from context, only conditions that actually computed LM cross-entropy can produce the name. Third, entry point gates usability, but the right location is not sufficient by itself: the concept must enter at a depth where both tasks already share a semantic code. The alignment probe predicts exportability across configurations, but maximizing the probe score alone does not guarantee transfer. The activation-edit experiment sharpens this point further: directly optimizing the same alignment term in closed form recovers about 80% of the trained gain, but only within a narrow layer window.8cd:T484,Several numbers matter. The practical method, writing the concept mid-stack with an alignment objective and no generative gradient, acquires the concept while causing only a 0.1% relative loss in general text-to-image ability. The standard generative recipe causes a 41% loss, which is a large gap and suggests that naive generative fine-tuning is a poor way to inject new concepts into a unified model. The activation-edit intervention recovers roughly 80% of the trained gain, but only in a narrow depth range, which makes the entry-point claim concrete rather than rhetorical. The alignment probe is tested across 36 configurations and predicts which settings export across tasks. Across four architectures or settings, the effective window tracks whether the understanding pathway encodes semantic concepts at that depth, not simply backbone family or scale. The most important qualitative result is the dissociation between matching and production: generation-only training supports recognition-like matching on the understanding side, but not true name production without lexical cues; understanding-side LM training is what creates producible names.8ce:T9c1,技术上，论文构造了一个受控的 LoRA-GRPO RWKU unlearning 实验框架。训练数据来自 RWKU forget-prompt 分布，目标是在不完全重训模型的前提下，通过 GRPO 让模型在 target-adjacent 提示上减少目标知识泄露，同时尽量保持有用回答。

优化目标采用标准 GRPO 形式：对每个 prompt 采样一组 completions，用 reward 对组内样本打分，计算 group-relative advantages，再配合 clipped objective 和对 reference policy 的 KL penalty 更新策略。这里真正的研究变量不是优化器，而是 reward 语义和初始策略。

论文比较了四种 reward 设计：
- R0-Lex：词汇级 suppression。核心是惩罚目标相关词或短语的出现。这类 reward 最容易实现，但也最容易被表面规避，比如换说法、间接泄露、或者直接拒答。
- R1-AntiRefusal：在 lexical suppression 基础上加入 anti-refusal shaping，试图避免模型通过一律拒答来拿高分。它承认 refusal 是一个显著的 reward-hacking 通道，因此显式加约束。
- R2-Rubric：把 reward 从词面规则改成 rubric-based broad answering，目标不只是“不说目标内容”，而是鼓励模型给出更宽泛、仍然有帮助的回答。这个设计最接近作者提出的行为规范，也是全文最关键的 reward 语义转向。
- R4-Refusal：显式把 refusal 当作目标行为来奖励，作为诊断性对照组。它不是为了实用，而是为了看 benchmark 会不会把“拒答得很好”误当成“忘得很好”。

另一个核心变量是初始化方式。作者比较了原始 instruct 模型直接进入 GRPO，与先做 SFT warm-up 再进入 GRPO 两种路径。SFT warm-up 的作用不是单纯提高起点分数，而是把策略分布推到一个会偶尔采样出 broad-topic non-target answers 的区域，让 GRPO 有可放大的正样本。这个 framing 很重要，因为它把 RL 失败区分成两类：reward 设计错了，或者 reward 对但 rollout support 不足。

评估上，论文没有只看 RWKU forget score，而是设计了多层诊断：RWKU benchmark 指标、held-out completion audits、terminal training-rollout audits，以及训练动态信号。审计维度包括 leakage、prompt-helpfulness、refusal、language drift，terminal audit 还额外检查 broad-topic helpfulness。这个评估设计本身就是论文的重要贡献，因为它直接对应“优化成功不等于行为成功”的中心论点。8cf:Ta3b,从全文给出的结论看，最重要的实验发现不是某个 reward 绝对领先，而是不同 reward 在 benchmark 上可能看起来都能“忘”，但行为终点差异很大。

第一，RWKU forget score、held-out completion audit、terminal rollout audit、训练过程中的 reward 轨迹，并不会讲同一个故事。作者明确指出，类似的 forgetting 分数背后，可能分别对应 refusal collapse、与分类器/判分器对齐的表面策略、仍有残余泄露、或者回答风格发生明显漂移。这说明单一 benchmark 对 unlearning 行为的刻画是不充分的。

第二，reward specification 的影响是决定性的。R0-Lex 这类词面 suppression 容易把策略推向“避词不避义”或直接拒答；R1-AntiRefusal 试图修补这一点，但仍可能停留在 reward-compatible 而非 genuinely helpful 的区域；R2-Rubric 更有机会学到作者想要的 broad-topic helpful answering，因为它把奖励语义从“不要说什么”改成了“应该如何回答”；R4-Refusal 则作为对照证明，如果奖励拒答，模型可以在 forgetting 指标上表现不错，但行为上明显偏离有用 unlearning。

第三，SFT warm-up 很关键。作者强调 RLVR 只能强化当前策略偶尔会采样到的行为。如果冷启动策略几乎总是直接泄露目标内容，那么即便 reward 定义正确，GRPO 也可能学不到 broad-topic answer，因为 rollout group 里根本没有这种候选。SFT warm-up 通过先把模型推向更合适的支持集，帮助区分“reward 不对”和“策略从未探索到目标行为”这两种失败模式。这个结果对所有依赖 verifier reward 的 RL 训练都很重要。

第四，论文把 benchmark reliability 的问题具体化为 coverage 问题，而不是简单的方差问题。作者特别提到 held-out 审计会检查 paraphrase、aliasing、indirection、multilingual prompting、recovery-style prompts 等更容易暴露残余泄露的情况。这说明 benchmark 上的成功可能只是对训练分布和评分器的适配，而不是对目标知识的稳健压制。

摘要中没有给出完整数值表，当前可确认的实验信息主要是：采用 LoRA-GRPO 设置，比较四种 reward 设计，并做有无 SFT warm-up 的对照；评估覆盖 forgetting、neighbor locality、membership-inference behavior、以及 utility（启用时）。如果精读全文，最值得抄下来的不是单个分数，而是不同 reward 在审计标签分布上的差异，以及 warm-up 前后 rollout 中“有用但不泄露”样本占比如何变化。8d0:T4ef,This is highly relevant to the pretrain–post-train interface even though the task is unlearning. The paper is really about semantic misalignment between reward and desired behavior, support limitations in RL optimization, and the gap between benchmark success and actual policy behavior. Those issues generalize directly to RLHF/RLVR, reasoning RL, safety tuning, and continual post-training.

Its importance comes from four points. First, it expands the behavioral specification of unlearning from a two-part objective to a three-part one: suppress the target, preserve utility, and answer broadly when possible. That is a useful correction because RL systems often converge to the easiest high-reward behavior rather than the intended one. Second, it compares multiple reward designs under a shared training pipeline and shows that similar benchmark outcomes can correspond to very different learned behaviors. Third, it treats SFT warm-up as a policy-support intervention rather than a mere engineering trick, which is a valuable lens for any verifier-driven RL setup. Fourth, it argues that benchmark reliability problems are not only about statistical noise but also about missing behavioral coverage. A high forget score does not imply the right endpoint.8d1:T8fc,The paper builds a controlled LoRA-GRPO unlearning setup on RWKU-derived forget prompts. The optimization objective is standard GRPO: for each prompt, sample a group of completions, score them with a reward, compute group-relative advantages, and update the policy with a clipped objective plus a KL penalty to a reference policy. The main experimental variables are the reward semantics and the starting policy.

Four reward designs are compared:
- R0-Lex: lexical suppression. This penalizes target-related words or phrases. It is easy to implement but easy to game through paraphrase, indirect leakage, or refusal.
- R1-AntiRefusal: lexical suppression plus anti-refusal shaping. This explicitly tries to block the common shortcut where the model learns to refuse everything.
- R2-Rubric: a rubric-based reward that shifts the objective from “do not say the target content” to “answer helpfully at a broader topic level without leaking.” This is the most behaviorally aligned reward in the study and the conceptual center of the paper.
- R4-Refusal: an explicit refusal reward used as a diagnostic contrast. It is not meant as the desired endpoint; it is there to test whether benchmarks can mistake refusal-heavy behavior for successful unlearning.

The second major variable is initialization. The paper compares direct GRPO from the original instruct model against SFT warm-up followed by GRPO. The key idea is policy support: RL can only amplify behaviors that the current policy samples at least occasionally. If broad-topic, non-target answers never appear in the rollout group, even a well-designed reward cannot reinforce them. SFT warm-up is therefore framed as a way to move the policy into a region where the intended behavior has nonzero support.

Evaluation is deliberately multi-layered. Instead of relying only on RWKU forgetting scores, the paper uses benchmark metrics, held-out completion audits, terminal training-rollout audits, and training-dynamics analysis. The audits examine leakage, prompt helpfulness, refusal, and language drift; the terminal audit also measures broad-topic helpfulness. This evaluation design is itself a major contribution because it operationalizes the paper’s central claim that optimization success is not the same as behavioral success.8d2:Ta03,The main empirical takeaway is not that one reward simply wins, but that benchmark-level forgetting can hide qualitatively different policy endpoints.

First, RWKU forget scores, held-out completion audits, terminal rollout audits, and training-time reward traces do not tell the same story. The paper explicitly reports that similar forgetting scores can correspond to refusal collapse, classifier- or judge-aligned artifacts, residual leakage, or visibly different answer styles. That is the central result: standard benchmark success is not behaviorally diagnostic enough.

Second, reward specification strongly determines the endpoint. R0-Lex tends to encourage surface-level suppression and can be satisfied by avoiding specific words, leaking indirectly, or refusing. R1-AntiRefusal tries to patch that failure mode but can still settle into reward-compatible rather than genuinely helpful behavior. R2-Rubric has a better chance of producing the intended broad-topic helpful answers because it changes the semantics of the reward from prohibition to constructive guidance. R4-Refusal serves as a useful control, showing that a model can look good on forgetting-style metrics while clearly failing the broader behavioral objective.

Third, SFT warm-up matters. The paper emphasizes a support limitation of RLVR: if the cold policy almost never samples the desired broad-topic non-target response, GRPO has nothing to amplify. Warm-up helps separate two failure modes that are often conflated: a bad reward versus a good reward with no policy support. This is one of the most transferable insights in the paper.

Fourth, the benchmark-reliability issue is framed as a coverage problem rather than just a variance problem. The held-out audits probe paraphrases, aliases, indirection, multilingual prompts, and recovery-style prompts, all of which can expose residual leakage that a narrow benchmark misses. That makes the paper relevant beyond unlearning, because many post-training pipelines optimize against similarly incomplete automatic signals.

The provided text does not include the full numeric tables, so the most reliable summary is structural: the experiments compare four reward designs under LoRA-GRPO, with and without SFT warm-up, and evaluate forgetting, neighbor locality, membership-inference behavior, and utility when enabled. When reading the full paper, the most useful numbers to extract are not only the headline benchmark scores but the audit-label distributions and the change in broad-topic helpful samples before and after warm-up.8d3:T58f,This one deserves a careful read. Start with the Introduction and Problem Formulation rather than jumping straight to the result tables. The key conceptual move is the third behavioral requirement: on target-adjacent prompts, the model should answer at a broader useful level when possible, not merely avoid leakage.

Then read the reward-design section closely. For R0, R1, R2, and R4, ask a simple question: if I were the policy, what is the easiest shortcut to maximize this reward? Once that is clear, the later training outcomes become much easier to interpret.

In the experiments, focus on four things:
1. whether benchmark scores and audit outcomes agree;
2. how SFT warm-up changes training dynamics and final behavior;
3. the distribution of broad-topic helpfulness, refusal, and leakage in the terminal rollout audit;
4. any qualitative examples showing language drift, templated refusal, or judge-aligned artifacts.

If time is limited, at minimum read the reward-definition table, the main result table, and the audit examples. A serious read will likely take 45–75 minutes. Two deeper questions are worth carrying forward: whether richer rubric-style rewards can scale without becoming too judge-noisy, and whether policy-support problems now handled by SFT warm-up could instead be addressed through better exploration or offline preference data. Both connect directly to broader RL post-training research.8d4:T694,The method is DEPT, short for Document Embedding Preservation Tuning. The setup is a single decoder-only LLM that both generates expansion text and encodes expanded queries and candidate documents into a shared embedding space. Naive end-to-end contrastive learning updates all shared parameters and therefore changes generation behavior, query representations, and document representations at once. DEPT argues that only the query path should remain highly adaptable, while the document path should act as a stable retrieval target. To implement that, the method combines four pieces. First, a Document Embedding Preservation loss keeps current document embeddings close to cached embeddings from the initial model, reducing target drift. This makes it harder for the retrieval objective to improve by simply moving documents. Second, the method fits a fixed whitening transform on cached document embeddings, because raw LLM embeddings are often anisotropic and poorly suited for cosine retrieval. Training and retrieval then happen in this whitened coordinate system. Third, because document embeddings remain near the cached reference, the same cached index can be reused for online hard-negative mining during training and for index reuse at inference. Fourth, the paper uses straight-through expansion training so that retrieval supervision can influence the generated expansion despite the discrete generation step. Compared with prior work such as InPars, Promptagator, ExpandR, and UniRAG, the novelty is not merely using one model for both tasks, but directly optimizing expansion under the final retrieval loss while controlling the instability caused by shared parameters.8d5:T539,Experiments cover two LLM backbones and five retrieval tasks. The main result is that DEPT achieves the best average retrieval quality among the compared query-expansion paradigms while preserving generation quality and compatibility with cached indexing. Several findings matter. First, naive end-to-end contrastive training does improve retrieval, but it hits a bottleneck because the same updates that help ranking also distort the fluent explanatory behavior that made LLM-based expansion useful. DEPT alleviates that by stabilizing the document side. Second, the long-expansion variant gives the best average retrieval performance, while a keyword-style short-expansion variant remains competitive under tight generation budgets. Third, whitening and preservation work together: without preservation, the fixed whitening space and cached index would drift out of sync more quickly; without whitening, the geometry of raw LLM embeddings hurts cosine retrieval. Fourth, the paper explicitly checks that generation ability is retained, which is important because retrieval-only optimization can otherwise collapse expansions into unreadable but embedding-friendly token sequences. The prompt here does not include all table values, but the experimental story is clear: unified training is viable, provided document drift is controlled.8d6:T40b,This is useful for both coding-agent evaluation and training. First, it reframes repository-level failure from vague claims about insufficient context or weak retrieval into a more causal object: edit-time fact availability. That is a sharper target for diagnosis. Second, it shows strong substitution between parametric memory and explicit context, which means many apparently successful agent strategies on familiar repositories or APIs may simply be benefiting from memorized knowledge rather than sound workflow design. Third, it exposes a systematic blind spot in read-derived instrumentation: when facts are missing, agents usually do not stop; they guess, fabricate, and continue. As a result, measuring what the agent read can underestimate the shortfall and mislead harness design. For pretraining researchers, the paper matters because it touches the interface between what is stored in parameters, what must be supplied externally, and how benchmarks can accidentally conflate memorized priors with genuine agent competence.8d7:T847,The core framework is a two-channel, edit-time working-set model for repository coherence. Each edit depends on a set of coupled facts, such as imports, tests, configuration rules, migration constraints, or naming conventions. Those facts can come either from recent context or from parametric memory. If neither channel covers a required fact, the edit carries coherence debt. This turns repository coherence from a loose intuition into something that can be manipulated experimentally.

The experimental design is unusually controlled. The first setup uses four fictional API migration tasks, each with 12 mechanically checkable requirements. In the closed-book condition, the model gets the task description but no workspace and no tools, effectively emptying both channels. In the matched front-loaded condition, the exact rules and source files are placed in the prompt while keeping the model and tool surface fixed, isolating whether explicit context can substitute for missing memory. The second setup uses a real Pydantic migration with 79 tests, plus a renamed twin where all API names are changed so that memorized library knowledge becomes useless. This isolates the role of parametric memory. The third setup instruments tool-using trajectories by checking whether the agent read the dependencies of an edited file shortly before editing. The fourth uses synthetic tasks authored by the researchers, where the required facts are fully known, enabling precise fault injection and attribution.

Two boundary findings are especially important. Availability is not sufficient on its own: when written standards conflict with working code, agents systematically follow the written standard even when the code is the better guide. So seeing a fact is not the same as weighting it correctly. Also, decomposition is not automatically helpful: if the task is tightly coupled, splitting it across subagents can sever dependencies and create additional coherence debt. The paper also compares harnesses and finds that some configurations spend far more tokens for the same end result, without improving fact coverage.8d8:T6c0,There are five main empirical results. First, on the four fictional migrations, none of the 154 closed-book trials succeeds, while front-loading the exact facts into the prompt lifts 299 of 300 matched trials to at least 9 out of 12 requirements. This is strong evidence that explicit context can substitute for missing parametric knowledge. Second, on the renamed version of the real Pydantic migration, 66 of 70 trials across seven models end at the same score and pass the exact same 24 of 79 tests. Once memorized knowledge is neutralized, failures become highly aligned, suggesting that availability rather than model style determines the outcome. Third, the damage from withholding facts is reported to be linear in the work those facts support: removing a fact costs exactly the edits it enables and no more. Fourth, distance itself is not the issue: when a fact is supplied, models use it about as reliably at the far end of a 128,000-character context as when it is placed near the edit. Fifth, harnesses can differ by 12.8x in total token consumption while holding only 1.8x different amounts of context in front of the model at any moment, and the more expensive setups recover no extra capability when facts are withheld.

Two negative results matter as much. In 39 conflict trials, agents consistently follow written standards over contradictory but working code, showing that coverage does not guarantee correct arbitration. And the framework does not transfer cleanly to SWE-bench, where models likely already know the repositories and the task structure is observed only coarsely, so reading behavior no longer predicts success. The paper is careful not to overclaim universality beyond its controlled workloads.8d9:T435,For a quick read, focus on three parts. First, read the introduction and experimental design carefully to internalize the three key concepts: coupled-fact graph, two-channel availability, and coherence debt. Without them, the results can look like a collection of coding-agent anecdotes. Second, prioritize the closed-book, front-loaded, and renamed-migration interventions. These are the strongest causal pieces of evidence in the paper. Third, read the sections on harness cost, subagent decomposition, and conflicting facts, because they show that the paper is really about the design limits of coding-agent systems, not just benchmark behavior.

If time is limited, the main figures and the five headline claims are enough to capture the argument in about 35 minutes. For a deeper read, spend time on the synthetic-task construction and the fault-injection analysis, especially the argument that read-derived instruments cannot measure the shortfall they are intended to detect. That part is useful if you care about building better diagnostics for repository-scale agents.8da:T46f,The estimand is treated as a functional over states (p,q), where p is the data-generating distribution and q is the trained model. Consistency is quantified over both p and q, because the tail behavior of q is not readable from its weights or recoverable from samples. On a countable sequence space with softmax full support, risk is a nonnegative infinite series that can diverge; an arbitrarily small mass shift can turn finite risk into infinite risk and vice versa. Estimation is therefore reduced to testing finite versus infinite risk, and no such test can be consistent. Theorem 1 gives the general impossibility; Theorem 2 retains it under bounded expected sequence length and full support; Theorem 3 shows the failures are dense, so no neighborhood-certifiable assumption restores consistency. Two escape routes are discussed: a bounded context window yields finitely many next-token distributions and hence a positive probability floor β, making loss linear in length and risk finite whenever expected sequence length is finite; and a thresholded estimand that only requires the true risk when it is below a pre-specified r.8db:Tb25,技术上，作者先把自回归 LM 重新表述成“context embedding 到 next-token distribution 的分类问题”。Transformer backbone 产出上下文向量 e，最后一层线性 head W 加 softmax 生成词表分布。论文刻意先把 backbone 固定，只分析最后线性层，因为它是唯一直接把表示映射到词表分布的部件，也决定了回传到 backbone 的梯度形态。理论部分采用一个可控 toy setting：每个上下文对应一个大小为 k 的随机 support，目标分布在 support 上均匀，k 用来控制 ambiguity；真实语料中的非均匀分布则用 effective support size，也就是 exp(entropy)，来度量。

作者把 curse 拆成两类来源。架构根因方面，结论是更高 ambiguity 的分布需要更大的“存储容量”和更高维的 embedding 才能在给定误差下被表示。直观上，k=1 时只需把一个 token 从其余 token 中分离出来；k>1 时需要同时为多个 token 保持相近高 logit，并与大量非 support token 拉开间隔，这对线性可分性和几何表示都更苛刻。论文分析了随机 embedding 与可联合优化 embedding 两种情形：前者展示在固定 h 下误差如何随 k 恶化，后者说明即便允许最优表示，embedding 维度仍需随 ambiguity 增长，否则无法同时容纳足够多彼此不同的高熵目标分布。

学习根因方面，作者分析了梯度和采样噪声。训练时我们并不直接看到目标分布 p，而是从 p 采样一个 token 做交叉熵更新。对高 ambiguity 上下文，单个样本只暴露 support 中一个 token，导致梯度对完整分布的估计方差更大；换句话说，同样一次 SGD 更新，对 k 大的分布提供的信息更少、更噪。论文进一步给出优化步数需求随 ambiguity 增长的理论结果：要把预测分布拟合到同等精度，需要更多样本和更多步数。这里的关键不是 label smoothing 那种人为加熵，而是真实条件分布的熵越高，token-level sampling 对分布学习越低效。

实证部分分三层推进。第一层是严格受控的合成实验，单独训练 logistic head 或小网络，验证表示误差、所需维度、收敛速度、梯度噪声都随 k 变差。第二层是在真实语言模型上做上下文分桶，按下一词分布的 effective support 或 entropy 分析 loss、拟合误差、训练动态，观察到与理论一致的 signature。第三层是规模外推：作者论证这些现象在更大模型上仍存在，不会因为参数变大而自动消失，只是阈值后移。与已有工作相比，这篇论文的区别不在于提出新的 uncertainty metric，而在于把“高熵目标更难学”具体落实到最后层几何、样本复杂度和 token sampling 噪声三个机制上，并把它们连到 LM 训练闭环。8dc:T45a,Its value for pretraining research is threefold. First, it turns an empirical complaint—models are poorly calibrated in uncertain contexts—into a mechanistic object of study with architectural and optimization roots. Second, it suggests that learning difficulty in pretraining is shaped not only by sequence length, knowledge content, or model size, but also by conditional entropy itself. Two contexts with the same token count can impose very different learning burdens depending on how diffuse the target distribution is. That has implications for scaling laws, data curricula, loss weighting, tokenizer design, and synthetic data generation. Third, it clarifies why several post-training methods hit a ceiling: RL can only reinforce sampled trajectories, search-based inference needs probability mass to be spread over viable branches, and self-generated corpora become fragile if the model collapses too early onto a narrow set of continuations. This is not a new architecture paper. It is a foundational diagnosis of AR LM learning dynamics, useful because it identifies where interventions might matter.8dd:Tb9e,The paper reframes autoregressive language modeling as context classification. A Transformer backbone maps a context to an embedding e, and the final linear head W plus softmax maps that embedding to a vocabulary distribution. The analysis first isolates this last layer while treating the backbone representations as given. That choice is deliberate: the output head is the only component that directly parameterizes the next-token distribution, and it also shapes the gradients flowing back into the backbone.

The theoretical setup is a controlled toy model. Each context is associated with a target distribution that is uniform over a random support set of size k. The support size k controls ambiguity. For real, non-uniform language distributions, ambiguity is measured by effective support size, exp(H(p)), which reduces to k in the uniform-support setting.

The authors then separate the curse into architectural and learning roots. On the architectural side, they show that more ambiguous target distributions require more storage capacity and larger embedding dimensions to be represented to a fixed accuracy. Intuitively, predicting one correct token is geometrically easier than assigning similarly high logits to many plausible tokens while separating them from the rest of the vocabulary. The paper studies both random embeddings and jointly optimized embeddings. The first shows degradation at fixed hidden dimension h as k grows. The second shows that even with optimal embeddings, the required representation dimension still increases with ambiguity.

On the learning side, the key issue is token-sampling noise. Training does not observe the full target distribution p directly. It observes one sampled token from p and updates with cross-entropy. For high-ambiguity contexts, a single sample reveals only one element of a larger support, so the stochastic gradient is a noisier estimator of the full distributional objective. The paper derives that fitting such targets to the same precision requires more optimization steps and more samples. The point is not that entropy makes the loss numerically larger. The point is that token-level supervision becomes a less efficient channel for learning the full conditional distribution as ambiguity increases.

Empirically, the paper proceeds in three stages. First, controlled synthetic experiments validate the predicted trends in representation error, required dimension, convergence speed, and gradient noise. Second, real-language-model analyses bucket contexts by ambiguity and show analogous signatures in training dynamics and distribution fitting. Third, the authors argue that scaling model size does not remove the phenomenon; it only shifts the regime where it becomes visible. Relative to prior work, the contribution is not a new uncertainty metric. It is the decomposition of the problem into output-layer geometry, sample complexity, and token-sampling noise, tied back to practical LM training.8de:T628,The experimental contribution is mostly in the consistency of the observed trends rather than in a single benchmark number. In synthetic settings, the authors vary support size k and show that as k increases: (1) the error between predicted and true distributions rises at fixed head capacity and embedding dimension, (2) maintaining the same error requires larger hidden dimension h, (3) optimization slows down and needs more steps, and (4) sampled-token training induces higher gradient variance. They also compare random embeddings with jointly learned embeddings, showing that the problem is not merely poor representation learning but a genuine increase in geometric and statistical difficulty.

On real data, the paper replaces uniform support size with effective support size exp(H(p)) as the ambiguity measure. Contexts with higher ambiguity exhibit higher loss, slower fitting, and worse approximation of the full next-token distribution. Importantly, the gap is not only in top-1 behavior. It appears in probability allocation across plausible continuations. The same qualitative signatures remain visible in full language models rather than only isolated linear heads, which supports the claim that the simplified analysis captures a real bottleneck.

The quantitative setup explicitly revolves around support size k, hidden dimension h, optimization steps, and effective support size. For close reading, the most informative artifacts are the plots showing error versus k, convergence versus k, and gradient-noise statistics, rather than any single summary table.8df:T67e,Read it in the order of problem setup, architectural roots, learning roots, then real-LM validation.

Start with the introduction and the formalization section. The key is to understand why the authors cast AR LM as context classification, and why they use both a uniform-support toy model and effective support size for real distributions. Without that, it is easy to misread the result as the trivial statement that high-entropy targets have higher loss.

Section 3 deserves the closest attention. Focus on two questions: why higher ambiguity requires more storage capacity, and why it demands larger embedding dimension at fixed error. The useful part is the geometry of the output layer: how multiple plausible tokens translate into stricter linear constraints. If you care about tokenization, vocabulary size, or output-layer design, this section has the most room for extension.

Section 4 is the most relevant for training recipe design. Read it together with the appendix if possible. The important part is how gradient variance scales with ambiguity, and why sampled-token cross-entropy is especially inefficient for high-entropy targets. This naturally connects to ideas such as soft targets, teacher distributions, multi-sample supervision, sequence-level credit assignment, or curricula.

In Section 5, focus on two kinds of figures: synthetic validations of the theoretical trends, and real-LM analyses stratified by ambiguity. The practical question to keep in mind is whether scale alone can wash out the effect. The paper argues it cannot. A careful read takes about 60–90 minutes; a focused pass over the main argument takes around 30 minutes.8e0:T888,实验分三组，结论比较一致。

第一组是小型 byte-level WikiText-2 模型，4 层 Transformer，hidden width 32，训练 600 steps。结果显示，只删 backward 路径中的一部分方向，训练会变差，而且删得越多越差；但直接把 forward head 做低秩，伤害明显更大。forward 与 backward-only 的配对差值分别为：rank 16 时 +0.0808，rank 8 时 +0.1030，rank 4 时 +0.0913，15 个配对比较全部同号，95% 置信区间都排除了 0。rank-32 的 backward control 与普通反传完全一致，说明自定义 backward 实现本身没有引入额外偏差。

第二组是更大的 subword 模型，BPE-8192，6 层、width 96，约 2.26M 参数，训练 1200 steps。这里半秩 backward-only 干预带来验证交叉熵 +0.0586，95% CI 为 [+0.0167, +0.1005]，配对效应量 d_z=1.74；而低秩 forward head 带来 +0.1795，95% CI 为 [+0.1547, +0.2042]，d_z=9.00。两者直接比较，forward 比 backward-only 更差 +0.1209，95% CI 为 [+0.0848, +0.1569]，d_z=4.16。去掉用于调学习率的 seed 1 后，forward-minus-backward 的区间仍为正 [+0.0744, +0.1756]。这说明“低秩 forward 训练更差”不能被简单解释成“backward rank 不够”。

第三组实验针对不可见 logit 残差是否已被训练过程利用。作者保留 hidden gradient，只从 LM head 更新中删除这部分贡献。摘要片段没有给出完整数值，但从主结论可知，移除这部分更新是明显有害的。这个结果是全文最关键的因果证据之一：所谓 hidden 看不到的那部分梯度，并没有被训练丢弃，而是在输出层参数更新里发挥作用。

此外，作者还复查了几何测量指标与学习进展的关系，结论是这些指标能描述投影现象，但不能稳定预测哪个模型学得更快。几种额外反馈通路的尝试也没有超过调得较好的标准 backprop。整体上，证据支持一个较窄但重要的结论：删除已经能到达 hidden 的方向会伤害学习；但“词表空间中 hidden 当前不可达的巨大残差若能直接加进模型，就会提升学习”这一更强命题，并未被证明。8e1:T73b,The central methodological move is a backward-only intervention. Prior work reduced the rank of the LM head in the forward pass and observed worse training. But that intervention simultaneously changes: the space of representable logits, the decoder parameterization and conditioning, the number and arrangement of trainable parameters, and the rank of the gradient returned to the hidden state. It therefore cannot identify whether the damage comes from the backward channel.

Here, the model still computes ordinary full-rank logits, and the LM head still receives its ordinary parameter update. Only the gradient sent back to the hidden state is replaced by a lower-rank version derived from the best rank-r approximation of the current head. The hidden gradient is RMS-matched to the exact gradient so that any effect is not confounded by gradient scale.

A second key piece is the explicit decomposition of the logit gradient into the component visible to the current hidden state and the orthogonal residual g_perp. The latter does not affect the current hidden state because it lies outside the column space of W, but it generally does contribute to the gradient of W itself. That means it changes the LM head, which in turn changes future predictions and future feedback subspaces. So “invisible to the current hidden state” is not the same as “discarded by training.”

The paper then runs a complementary ablation: keep the exact hidden-state gradient, but remove from the LM-head update the contribution coming from the currently invisible logit residual, while matching update magnitude. This directly tests whether that residual is functionally used by training even if it does not reach the current hidden state. The paper also critiques the SpamLang setup for conflating repeated loss terms with independent information coverage.8e2:T829,There are three main experimental blocks.

First, a compact byte-level WikiText-2 model with 4 Transformer layers, hidden width 32, trained for 600 steps. Removing directions from the backward path hurts learning, and the effect grows as more directions are removed. But reducing the forward head rank hurts substantially more than changing only the backward path. The paired forward-minus-backward-only validation cross-entropy differences are +0.0808 at rank 16, +0.1030 at rank 8, and +0.0913 at rank 4. All 15 paired comparisons have the predicted sign, and the reported 95% intervals exclude zero. The rank-32 backward control exactly reproduces ordinary backprop, validating the custom backward implementation.

Second, a larger subword model with BPE-8192, 6 layers, width 96, about 2.26M parameters, trained for 1,200 steps. The same qualitative pattern holds. A half-rank backward-only intervention increases validation cross-entropy by +0.0586, with 95% CI [+0.0167, +0.1005] and paired effect size d_z = 1.74. A reduced-rank forward head causes a much larger increase of +0.1795, with 95% CI [+0.1547, +0.2042] and d_z = 9.00. The direct forward-versus-backward-only gap is +0.1209, with 95% CI [+0.0848, +0.1569] and d_z = 4.16. Excluding the learning-rate screening seed preserves the ordering, and the forward-minus-backward interval remains strictly positive.

Third, the paper tests whether the logit-space residual that does not reach the current hidden state is already being used through the LM-head update. The exact hidden gradient is preserved, but that residual contribution is removed from the head update. The paper reports that this removal is strongly harmful. Even without all numeric details in the provided excerpt, this is one of the most important causal results: the supposedly “lost” component is not lost to the training process.

The paper also finds that geometric measurements of the projection do not reliably predict learning progress, and several attempts to add separate feedback routes fail to outperform ordinary, well-tuned backpropagation.8e3:T57f,Start with the section defining what “lost” means. The paper’s main argument depends on a precise distinction between a component being invisible to the current hidden state and being irrelevant to training as a whole. Then read the backward-only control carefully. The important design choices are: keep full-rank logits, keep the ordinary LM-head update, and match hidden-gradient RMS. That is the cleanest part of the causal identification.

Next, focus on the paired-seed results for the larger subword model. The absolute scale is small, but the comparison is well controlled and statistically reported with confidence intervals and paired effect sizes. Finally, read the ablation that removes the invisible component only from the LM-head update. That experiment is the strongest evidence against the claim that the orthogonal residual is simply discarded.

If reading selectively, prioritize: the gradient decomposition, the clean backward-rank test, the main result tables for the byte-level and subword models, and the head-update ablation. The most interesting open questions are whether the same conclusions hold at true pretraining scale, especially with tied embeddings and much larger vocabularies, and whether these geometric effects still matter for early training speed, stability, or frequency-dependent learning even if they do not establish a causal bottleneck in the strong sense.8e4:Taa1,方法核心是 Consistency Forcing（CForce）。训练起点是一个预训练好的 dLLM。作者先用该模型在自己的解码策略下生成 self-rollout trajectories，而不是使用 teacher rollout 或 oracle trajectory。这样做的原因是，学生在推理时真正会遇到的状态分布，来自它自己在 threshold decoding 下逐步 reveal token 的轨迹；如果训练时看的是别的轨迹，尤其是信息条件更优的 teacher 轨迹，蒸馏目标就会偏离真实推理状态。

接着，作者不按 native denoising step 逐步对齐，而是把轨迹按“每揭示固定数量的新 token”切成若干 stage。这样做有两个考虑：一是存储 native step 全轨迹成本高；二是 reveal-count 更直接对应高并行解码下的承诺强度。对于每一对相邻 stage，训练目标是让早期 stage 在 still-masked positions 上的预测分布，去匹配同一模型在后期 stage 的 stop-gradient 预测。这里没有冻结 teacher，teacher 就是同一个模型在更后状态下的输出。直观上，后期状态拥有更多上下文，尤其 edit-capable 模型还可能经过 T2T refinement，因此它对某些位置的判断更可信，可以反过来监督早期 M2T 预测。

关键损失设计有两部分。第一部分是 Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence（CAD），用于 still-masked positions 的分布对齐。作者没有固定用 forward KL 或 reverse KL，而是根据 later-stage prediction confidence 动态插值。原因在于两者偏好不同：forward KL 更覆盖 teacher 支持集，reverse KL 更偏 mode-seeking。后期预测若置信度高，更适合强调 mode-seeking；若置信度低，则需要更保守地保留分布质量。CAD 试图把这两种偏好按置信度自适应结合。第二部分是 cross-entropy anchor，用于 reveal-boundary token，也就是那些在当前阶段即将被提交或刚被揭示的 token。这个 CE 项的作用是稳定 token commitment，防止纯分布对齐把模型推向“看起来和后期一致，但不敢明确提交”的状态。

此外，作者加入了 reveal difficulty curriculum。因为越早期、越高并行的阶段越难，直接在最激进的 reveal 设置上做相邻阶段蒸馏容易不稳定。课程学习让模型先在较容易的 reveal 条件下学会一致性，再逐步过渡到更难的高并行情形。理论部分则给出一个上界分析：早期阶段预测误差可由相邻阶段分布漂移和 reveal-boundary token error 两项控制，这正好对应 CAD 和 CE anchor。这个理论不是完整收敛证明，但它把损失设计和误差来源一一对应起来，解释了为什么不是只用 KL，也不是只用 CE。8e5:T436,This is a meaningful contribution to alternative language modeling paradigms. First, it reframes dLLM efficiency around early-stage reliability rather than step count alone, which is closer to the actual failure mode in high-TPF decoding. Second, it improves training-inference alignment by distilling along the model’s own self-rollout threshold-decoding trajectories instead of relying on external teachers or privileged trajectories. That design choice is particularly important for diffusion LMs, where the state distribution seen at inference can differ sharply from teacher-generated trajectories. Third, it adapts consistency-style training to discrete masked diffusion language models with a confidence-adaptive KL objective and a token-commitment anchor, both tailored to the actual sources of decoding error. Fourth, the empirical pattern is informative: edit-capable models can gain both speed and quality, while non-edit models show a clearer speed-quality trade-off. That distinction says something substantive about where the extra supervision signal comes from.8e6:T9e3,The method, Consistency Forcing (CForce), starts from a pretrained dLLM and collects self-rollout trajectories under the model’s own decoding policy. This is a deliberate choice. The states that matter are the ones the student will actually encounter under threshold decoding, not cleaner or more informative states produced by a separate teacher. Using self-rollouts therefore reduces the mismatch between training supervision and inference-time state distribution.

The collected trajectory is then partitioned into stages, not at every native denoising step, but after a fixed number of newly revealed tokens. This stage definition is important for two reasons: it lowers storage overhead, and it ties supervision directly to reveal intensity, which is what controls practical parallelism. For each adjacent stage pair, the model is trained so that the earlier stage matches a stop-gradient prediction from the same model at the later stage on positions that remain masked. There is no frozen teacher. The later stage acts as a stronger target because it has more observed context, and in edit-capable models it may also incorporate token-to-token refinements that correct earlier drafts.

The loss has two main components. The first is Confidence Adaptive KL Divergence (CAD), used to align distributions on still-masked positions. Instead of choosing either forward KL or reverse KL globally, CAD interpolates between them based on the confidence of the later-stage prediction. The intuition is straightforward: high-confidence later predictions justify a more mode-seeking target, while lower-confidence predictions call for a more conservative distributional match. The second component is a cross-entropy anchor on reveal-boundary tokens, which stabilizes token commitment. Without this anchor, pure distribution matching could improve consistency while weakening the model’s ability to make decisive commitments at the reveal boundary.

The paper also introduces a curriculum over reveal difficulty. Early-stage, high-parallelism supervision is the hardest regime, so training directly on the most aggressive reveal settings can be unstable. The curriculum gradually increases difficulty. The theoretical section supports the design by showing that early-stage prediction error can be bounded by adjacent-stage distribution drift and reveal-boundary token error, which map directly onto the CAD and CE terms. It is not a full convergence theory, but it does provide a clean justification for why both terms are needed.8e7:T78b,The headline results are on two LLaDA variants. On the edit-capable LLaDA2.1-mini, CForce increases average Tokens Per Forward from 6.94 to 9.08 while also improving average accuracy from 85.57 to 86.41. That is the strongest result in the paper because it shows simultaneous gains in speed and quality, consistent with the claim that later T2T-refined states provide useful supervision for earlier M2T predictions. On the non-edit LLaDA2.0-mini, CForce raises average TPF from 3.60 to 6.42, but the effect is better described as an explicit speed-quality trade-off. The model performs better under aggressive few-step decoding and at fixed TPF budgets, yet the gains are not as cleanly dual-improving as in the edit-capable case.

The full paper also appears to include several important analyses. One is performance under different decoding budgets or threshold aggressiveness, which should show that the gains concentrate in the high-parallelism regime rather than uniformly across all settings. Another is loss ablation: CAD versus plain forward KL or reverse KL, with and without the CE anchor. That ablation is important because the method’s credibility depends on showing that confidence-adaptive interpolation is not just cosmetic. A third likely analysis is the effect of the reveal-difficulty curriculum on stability and final few-step accuracy. Finally, the comparison between edit-capable and non-edit models is conceptually important. It helps separate gains from simply having more context later in the trajectory versus gains from having genuinely improved later states due to token-level refinement.

When reading the experiments closely, pay attention to how accuracy is defined, how TPF is measured, what block-diffusion setup is used, and what the storage and compute overhead of self-rollout trajectory collection looks like. Those details determine whether the method is practical beyond the paper’s scale.8e8:T5d4,Start with the introduction and preliminaries. You need a clear picture of block diffusion, mask-to-token decoding, token-to-token refinement, and threshold decoding before the method will make sense. In particular, the distinction between edit-capable and non-edit dLLMs is central to understanding why the gains differ across models.

Then read the method section carefully, focusing on self-rollout trajectory construction, stage partitioning, CAD, and the CE anchor. Three questions are worth keeping in mind: why self-rollouts are preferable to teacher trajectories, why stages are defined by reveal count rather than native denoising steps, and why KL direction should depend on later-stage confidence. The theory section is worth reading alongside the method because it ties the loss design to a concrete error decomposition.

In the experiments, first inspect the main figures and tables showing the LLaDA2.1-mini speed-and-quality improvement and the LLaDA2.0-mini trade-off. Then move to the ablations, especially CAD versus forward/reverse KL, the effect of the CE anchor, and the curriculum. The deepest idea in the paper is not a single metric gain. It is the training-inference alignment principle: train early states to learn from the model’s own later, more informative states along the actual decoding trajectory it will follow at inference. A quick read takes about 40 minutes. A serious read for reproduction or adaptation to another dLLM will likely take 1.5 to 2 hours.8e9:T9c3,方法上分成三块。第一块是环境与训练系统。作者构建了一个 agent-agnostic 的交互框架，把环境模拟、对话执行、模型推理和训练器分离。这样做的原因很直接：多回合社会交互训练不是单轮 preference optimization，训练信号来自完整 episode 的效用、协议是否达成、对手策略等，若系统耦合过紧，很难支持跨环境训练、黑盒 teacher、或不同对手组合。六个环境覆盖了多物品分配、带私有偏好的资源分配、价格谈判、工作面试式协商、日程协调和市场匹配，交互结构差异较大，便于观察迁移是否来自表面模板还是更抽象的策略能力。

第二块是 SocialRL 本身。论文先在每个环境里训练 specialist policy，再做完整 cross-environment transfer matrix。虽然给出的摘要没有展开具体 RL 算法细节，但从全文描述看，核心不是发明一个全新的 policy gradient 变体，而是把社会交互中的效用函数、对手建模、episode rollout 和后续 consolidation 组织成一套可复用 recipe。训练目标围绕 principal utility，而不是单纯的 helpfulness 或 agreement rate。也就是说，模型被奖励去争取更优结果、保护私有信息、在不利条件下拒绝成交，而不是“把对话聊顺”。这和常规 assistant RLHF/RLAIF 的目标函数有根本差异。

第三块是 specialist→generalist 的整合，以及显式 ToM 蒸馏。作者用了两条 consolidation 路线：cascade RL，以及 multi-teacher mode-seeking OPD（MOPD）。前者更像课程式地把多个环境能力串联进一个统一策略；后者则利用多教师策略分布，把统一模型往高价值模式上拉，而不是简单平均教师行为。这里“mode-seeking”很关键，因为谈判策略往往多峰，直接行为克隆容易学成折中而无效的平均策略。除此之外，论文引入 Infer→Act→Anticipate 轨迹，把模型在某一状态下对对手偏好/意图的推断、当前动作选择、以及对对手下一步反应的预期串成监督信号，再蒸馏进策略模型。这样做不是为了让模型生成更长的解释，而是为了把 social reasoning 拆成可训练的中间变量。全文的分析显示，三者里对 performance 最有预测力的是 Anticipate，尤其是 next-action prediction，这说明有效策略更依赖“对手接下来会怎么动”的局部博弈预测，而不是抽象人格归因。8ea:T434,Its importance for foundation-model research is threefold. First, it treats social reasoning as a trainable post-training capability rather than a byproduct of frontier scale. The central empirical claim is that targeted RL and distillation can push a 4B model close to, and in some settings beyond, much larger GPT-class models on strategic interaction tasks. That is a meaningful data point in the scale-vs-signal debate. Second, it contributes a reusable infrastructure for multi-turn social interaction training: environment, agent harness, inference engine, and trainer are decoupled, which matters for RL over long dialogues, heterogeneous opponents, and black-box teachers. Third, it studies explicit theory-of-mind supervision in a way that is operational rather than decorative. Infer→Act→Anticipate traces are distilled into the policy, and the analysis shows that anticipating the counterpart’s next action is the ToM component most predictive of negotiation utility. That is a useful lesson for anyone designing intermediate supervision for agentic behavior.8eb:T958,The method has three layers. The first is the training system. The authors build an agent-agnostic interaction stack where the environment simulator, dialogue execution harness, inference backend, and trainer are separated. This is not just an engineering convenience. In multi-turn strategic interaction, the learning signal depends on full episodes, opponent behavior, and utility outcomes. A tightly coupled setup makes it hard to support cross-environment training, heterogeneous opponents, or distillation from black-box policies. The six environments span allocation, multi-issue bargaining, price negotiation, interview-style negotiation, calendar coordination, and marketplace interaction, giving enough structural diversity to test whether the model learns reusable strategic abstractions.

The second layer is SocialRL itself. The paper first trains domain specialists, then evaluates the full transfer matrix across environments. The contribution is less about inventing a new low-level RL optimizer and more about defining a complete recipe for strategic delegation: principal-utility-centered rewards, multi-turn rollouts, opponent-conditioned interaction, and evaluation under held-out scenarios. The objective is explicitly different from standard assistant alignment. The model is rewarded for protecting private information, holding reservation boundaries, and rejecting bad deals when necessary, rather than maximizing agreement rate or perceived helpfulness.

The third layer is specialist-to-generalist consolidation plus explicit ToM distillation. The authors use cascade RL and multi-teacher mode-seeking OPD (MOPD) to merge specialists into a unified policy. The mode-seeking aspect matters because negotiation policies are often multi-modal; naive averaging or plain behavior cloning can collapse distinct but effective strategies into a weak compromise. On top of that, the paper introduces Infer→Act→Anticipate traces as structured supervision. These traces encode the model’s inference about the counterpart, the chosen action, and the expected next move from the counterpart. The point is not to make the model verbose, but to expose trainable intermediate variables for social reasoning. The analysis suggests that among these components, next-action anticipation is the strongest predictor of downstream utility, which is a concrete and actionable finding.8ec:T74f,The experimental story has four main parts. First, domain specialists are trained and evaluated on held-out scenarios in each of the six environments. The headline result is that 4B specialist policies achieve utility comparable to much larger GPT models across the suite, showing that targeted post-training can compensate for a large part of the scale gap in this setting. Second, the paper reports a full cross-environment transfer matrix. Transfer is substantial but not uniform: it follows interaction structure. Environments with similar bargaining dynamics transfer better to each other than environments that only share surface language. That is an important result because it suggests the model is learning reusable strategic patterns rather than memorizing domain-specific scripts.

Third, the specialists are consolidated into a single 4B policy. Using cascade RL and MOPD, the unified model reaches an average utility of 0.627 across the six environments, compared with 0.625 for GPT-4.1, 0.619 for GPT-5.1, and 0.613 for GPT-5.2 in the paper’s evaluation. The right interpretation is not that the small model is broadly stronger, but that objective-task alignment can outweigh generic assistant priors on strategic delegation benchmarks.

Fourth, the paper studies explicit theory-of-mind supervision. Distilling Infer→Act→Anticipate traces improves both performance and cross-environment generalization. The most informative subskill is next-action prediction: it is the ToM signal most correlated with negotiation success. While the excerpt does not expose every ablation number, the full paper appears to include comparisons with and without ToM traces, differences between consolidation methods, and analyses of specialist versus unified policies. The transfer matrix and ToM correlation analyses are likely the most informative tables and figures.8ed:T596,Start with the problem framing. For a deeper read, spend extra time on the training infrastructure and consolidation details.8ee:T4b8,The Wiggle Framework applies a graduated stress test on fixed items, judges, and grading schemes. A temperature-0, no-pressure verdict serves as the L0 anchor for each item. A wiggle is defined as a verdict flip on binary scales, and on Likert 1–5 scales as a move of two or more points (crossing the midpoint, or jumping from the midpoint to an extreme), excluding minor numerical drift. Stability is decomposed into three dimensions. Mechanical Consistency tests verdict retention under information-free perturbations: 10 identical decoding runs, random-seed strings appended to the system prompt, and swapped argument order. Single-turn Conviction tests whether the verdict survives one substantive challenge immediately after the decision. Multi-turn Persistence tests stability under sustained, adaptive pushback over multiple turns. Each wiggle is further labeled as corrective (toward ground truth) or corrupting (away from ground truth), separating stability from accuracy direction. The study covers 9 frontier models on 14 judging tasks spanning safety classification, toxicity detection, red-teaming, AI-writing detection, and political-response evaluation, under both binary and Likert grading.8ef:T425,Three layers. First, ablations of the scaling-law recipe (parameter counting, embedding inclusion, LR decay, warmup length) show these details matter little compared to whether hyperparameters are fully tuned. Second, the noisy quadratic model (Lourie et al. 2025a) characterizes the hyperparameter loss surface as quadratic, low-rank, and approximately normal near the optimum; as parameters and data grow together, good configurations fill a larger fraction of the space because the intrinsic dimension of the surface drops—the blessing of dimensionality from parameters cures the curse of dimensionality in hyperparameters, with the effective number of hyperparameters approaching one. Third, three tools are combined into a methodology: the noisy quadratic limit diagnoses whether tuning is complete, scaling laws describe loss vs. scale, and the perplexity–capability correspondence checks whether pretraining-loss changes translate into downstream capabilities. The normalization-placement debate (Pre-LN vs Post-LN) is used as a worked demonstration.8f0:T519,The work adapts Generalizability Theory (G-theory) from psychometrics to the long-horizon agent evaluation setting, building a fully crossed four-facet variance decomposition model with facets for agent, task, trajectory step, and error category. It decomposes total variance in binary success observations into the agent main effect (the true general capability signal), independent main effects for each facet, pairwise interaction effects between facets, and residual variance. Three independent variance estimators are used to cross-validate results: Henderson Method-I, restricted maximum likelihood implemented via lme4, and a Bayesian binomial generalized linear mixed model run on GPU. Building on the G-study (variance component estimation), a D-study (decision study) translates variance components into a budget frontier of minimum tasks, steps, and judges required to meet target reliability thresholds (generalizability coefficient Eρ² ≥ 0.85 for relative ranking decisions, dependability coefficient Φ ≥ 0.90 for absolute threshold decisions such as SLA gates). The final DDR reporting specification combines a variance component table, evaluation size budget frontier, cost-adjusted reliability index, difficulty-conditional reliability profile, and capability ceiling decomposition.8f1:T610,Full variance decomposition is run across three public enterprise agent benchmarks (TheAgentCompany, τ²-bench, AppWorld) and one auxiliary failure-mode dataset (MAST/MAD), with five core empirical findings: 1. Across all datasets and check types, the agent main effect accounts for less than 3% of total variance, while the agent-by-task interaction accounts for 7-23% of variance (4-13x larger than the main effect), meaning rank differences are driven primarily by fit to specific tasks rather than cross-task general capability. 2. Reliability collapses sharply on harder tasks: for action checks on τ²-bench, aggregate Eρ² is 0.752, but Eρ² drops to 0.000 on the hardest quartile of tasks, so aggregate reliability provides no valid guarantee for hard-task deployments. 3. Across 50 random splits, Eρ² estimated on training splits correlates negatively with held-out Eρ² (r=-0.90), meaning reliability projections from observed samples systematically overestimate the reliability of replication runs. 4. While the aggregate capability gap ratio is stable at 0.35-0.40 across datasets, per-task-family rankings invert completely (Spearman ρ = -0.50), so population-level capability diagnostics transfer but family-level rank claims do not. 5. Per-category agent-by-task interaction variance is orthogonal to per-category failure frequency (ρ=-0.20), meaning the failure categories where agents differ most are not the categories where failures occur most often. Results from the three variance estimators agree to three decimal places.8f2:T432,The study tests the hypothesis in both pretraining and supervised fine-tuning. In pretraining, the token budget, data, model configuration, and optimization setup are fixed, while the training context window is varied. Coherent document span length serves as a proxy for the amount of available relevant information. This design separates longer-context learning from simply seeing more tokens. In supervised fine-tuning, the context length is fixed and the amount of task-relevant context is directly controlled, isolating relevance from length. The theoretical account treats language modeling as compression with two predictive channels: information stored in parameters and information supplied in context. When context offers a lower-complexity solution, less task information needs to be encoded in the weights to reach the same risk threshold. The mechanistic analyses then connect this to lower-complexity contextual solutions, a shift in update pressure from feed-forward networks toward attention modules, and stronger reliance on context tokens at inference time.8f3:T504,The proposed MOSAIC framework formulates MoE architecture-systems co-design as a mixed-integer nonlinear program. First, the authors derive a MoE scaling law that demonstrates the necessity of systems constraints: under model-FLOPs-only constraints, optimal MoE sparsity sits at the feasibility boundary, with loss monotonically decreasing as sparsity increases, meaning no interior optimum exists without explicit systems limits. Second, a calibrated system performance model estimates, for any given MoE architecture on a target cluster, attainable MFU, communication overhead across data/tensor/pipeline/expert parallelism dimensions, memory usage, and the best available parallel layout. Third, instead of solving a continuous unconstrained optimum and snapping to the nearest valid discrete architecture (the standard practice), MOSAIC directly minimizes predicted loss over a discrete grid of valid architecture choices—expert count, active parameters, total parameters, training token count, layer dimensions—to jointly output a cluster-tailored MoE geometry, token budget, and parallel execution plan. Unlike prior work that added only memory constraints to MoE scaling laws, MOSAIC accounts for the full stack of systems overheads that determine real training throughput.8f4:T78e,The core contribution is a corrected protocol for measuring cross-lingual action-policy retention. Under a fixed scaffold, models operate over a shared five-tool alphabet and emit executed action traces alongside answers. The study covers 8 models, 6 parallel benchmarks, 41 languages, and 2.38 million rollouts. A naive trace-similarity metric fails for five reasons: short traces look artificially similar, empty traces score perfectly, unrelated traces overlap by chance, same-language reruns are not identical, and without a within-language baseline the quantity is not identifiable.

The estimator addresses each issue explicitly. Every language-task cell is run twice with identical decoding settings and token budgets, changing only the serving seed. Same-language agreement, I_within, compares the two replicates in one language. Cross-language agreement, I_cross, compares traces across languages, also cross-seed. The normalized retention metric is \tilde{I}=I_cross/I_within, which measures how much of a model’s own reproducible policy survives a language change. Comparisons are length-matched in both directions, pairs are dropped if either trace is empty, and uncertainty is estimated with task-level bootstraps. This design makes language the only systematic difference while keeping decoding noise symmetric.

The paper then probes mechanism. The evidence points to an English pivot. Translate is the most frequently used tool across adapted benchmarks, and reasoning text is about 99% ASCII even for non-Latin inputs such as Devanagari. Removing the translation tool lowers agreement in proportion to a model’s prior reliance on translation; forcing translation helps in a pre-registered ordering across models. The implication is that many multilingual agents do not execute the same policy directly in the target language. They often map the task into an English-centered internal workflow and plan from there.8f5:T697,The empirical scale is substantial: 8 models, 6 parallel benchmarks, 41 languages, and 2.38M rollouts. Three results stand out. First, under greedy decoding, all 24 main cells show a positive cross-lingual policy gap, and every bootstrap interval on the raw gap excludes zero. The effect is stable rather than anecdotal. Second, every correction increases the measured effect instead of shrinking it. That is important because it means the problem was previously hidden by bad measurement, not because it was weak. Third, after normalization, four otherwise very different models converge to nearly the same policy-retention value under greedy decoding: about 71–73%. The regularity holds at the cell level, not just in model averages, and model identity explains only about 5.7% of the variance.

The temperature ladder is also informative. As sampling temperature rises, cross-language agreement changes little, while same-language self-consistency drops sharply. Without normalization, sampling noise masks the true cross-lingual policy loss. On the mechanism side, Translate is the most-used tool in every adapted benchmark, and reasoning text is almost entirely ASCII, indicating that non-English tasks are often routed through an English internal channel. Removing translation hurts agreement roughly in proportion to how much a model already uses it; forcing translation helps in the pre-registered order predicted from those usage rates. When reading the full paper, it is worth checking how tightly the tool alphabet is standardized across benchmarks, how the bidirectional length matching is implemented, and whether retention differs systematically across language families.8f6:T50e,This one is worth a careful read. Start with the introduction and method sections to understand why the paper insists on measuring action traces rather than final answers, and how each of the five confounds can distort the conclusion. From a pretraining angle, two questions are especially worth carrying through the paper. Second, does the near-constant 71–73% retention hint at a structural bottleneck in cross-lingual policy transfer, where only part of the planner survives language change?
