This is the strongest experimental insight in the work.9eb:T4c0,First, a unified theoretical perspective is established: the second derivative of cross-entropy loss equals the squared gradient (Fisher information metric, the only canonical local geometry of KL divergence), and all high-performing Transformer optimizers effectively condition gradients by the square root of this metric, equivalent to dividing by the estimated standard deviation of gradient estimates. Ember is built on two core design choices: 1) Remove Adam's first-moment EMA entirely and use instantaneous gradients — ablation shows this change improves performance while saving V×D memory; 2) Leverage the observation that row-wise gradient energy of token interfaces is an unbiased estimator of token occurrence probability p_i, and row-wise Fisher scales with p_i², so full V×D second-moment buffers are unnecessary. Only V row-wise and D column-wise second-moment EMAs are maintained to approximate curvature. Key differences from prior work: Adafactor uses similar second-moment factorization but has more hyperparameters and is not purpose-built for token interface geometry; Muon only applies to linear layers and relies on singular value decomposition, making it unsuitable for embedding tables.9ec:Ta9b,方法上，PAW 由三个部件组成：伪程序生成器、LoRA 编译器、冻结解释器。整体流程不是让一个模型直接根据规格输出答案，而是先把规格整理成更稳定的中间表示，再生成任务专属参数，最后由小模型执行。

第一步是 pseudo compiler。它使用一个未训练的 4B Qwen3，通过固定模板把用户规格改写成 pseudo-program。这个 pseudo-program 由两部分组成：一段更清晰、去歧义的任务重述，以及少量输入输出示例。这样做的原因很直接：原始用户描述常常含糊、冗余、带 typo，直接拿来生成权重不稳定；先做一次离散化重写，相当于把自然语言规格投影到更规整的任务空间。

第二步是 LoRA compiler。这是论文真正训练的核心模型，也是一个 4B Qwen3 级别编译器。它读取原始规格和 pseudo-program，然后输出一组可注入解释器的 LoRA 参数。论文把这一步看成“从任务描述到神经二进制”的编译。相比前作用 prefix-tuning KV cache 作为程序表示，这一版改用 text-to-LoRA。作者明确比较后认为 LoRA 更强，因为它不是只在输入侧加条件，而是直接改变解释器内部线性层的行为，控制粒度更细，容量也更高。

第三步是 interpreter。解释器是冻结的小模型，主实验用 Qwen3-0.6B。运行时输入包括用户样本 x、pseudo-program 的离散部分，以及编译得到的 LoRA。也就是说，程序是“离散 token + 连续参数”的混合体。作者强调这个混合设计不是实现细节，而是关键抽象：离散部分负责鲁棒地表达任务语义，连续部分负责补足文本无法精确指定的行为边界。

训练数据方面，论文发布了 FuzzyBench，规模 1000 万样本，分 29 个主题版本，覆盖 800 多类模糊文本任务，包括分类、格式转换、解析、模糊匹配、自然语言命令、agent 工具使用等。数据是逐步扩展构建的，目标不是单一 benchmark，而是覆盖“可由自然语言规格定义、但难以用规则精确实现”的函数空间。这个数据设计很关键，因为编译器学的不是某个任务，而是从规格泛化到新任务的映射。

从建模角度看，PAW 和直接 instruction tuning 的区别在于：它不把所有任务都压进一个统一前向过程，而是显式生成任务特定权重；和元学习或 ICL 的区别在于：任务适配结果被固化成可保存、可版本化的程序文件；和普通 LoRA 微调的区别在于：LoRA 不是通过梯度优化得到，而是由编译器一次前向生成。这使它更像 hypernetwork 驱动的条件参数化系统。9ed:T4eb,Its value for pretraining research is mostly architectural and paradigm-level. PAW reframes weights as a program representation, not just a repository of general capability. Instead of paying inference-time reasoning cost on every input, it shifts substantial work to compile time: a larger compiler maps a task spec into a small task-specific adapter, and a lightweight interpreter executes it repeatedly. That is a meaningful alternative to the standard autoregressive pattern of “one general model, one prompt, one forward pass per request.” The reported result that a 0.6B interpreter plus compiled adapters can match or exceed direct prompting of a 32B model suggests that some capability currently expressed as online contextual reasoning can be externalized into offline task specialization. For pretraining, this opens several directions: PEFT modules as executable intermediate representations, datasets for spec-to-weight compilation rather than only next-token prediction, and a cleaner separation between universal pretrained competence and compiled task-local behavior. It also connects naturally to hypernetworks, conditional weight generation, and the question of when in-context learning can be converted into persistent parameter updates.9ee:Tb25,PAW consists of three components: a pseudo-compiler, a LoRA compiler, and a frozen interpreter. The system is not just prompting a model with a better template; it explicitly compiles a task into a hybrid neural program.

Stage 1 is the pseudo-compiler. An off-the-shelf 4B Qwen3 model, kept untrained, rewrites the user specification into a pseudo-program. This pseudo-program contains a cleaned task restatement plus a handful of input-output examples. The motivation is practical: raw user specs are ambiguous, verbose, typo-prone, and often unstable as direct conditioning signals. The rewrite step creates a more canonical discrete representation of the task before any weight generation happens.

Stage 2 is the LoRA compiler, the main trained component. It is also built on a 4B Qwen3-scale model. Given the original spec and the pseudo-program, it emits a LoRA adapter to be injected into the interpreter. This is the actual “program binary.” The paper positions this as a shift from text-only task conditioning to generated parameterization. Compared with the authors’ earlier prefix-tuning-based precursor, the current version uses text-to-LoRA and reports better performance. That choice matters: prefix tuning mainly conditions through the input side, while LoRA changes internal linear transformations of the interpreter and therefore offers finer control and more representational capacity.

Stage 3 is the interpreter, a frozen small LM, with Qwen3-0.6B as the main instantiation. At execution time, the interpreter receives the input x, the discrete pseudo-program tokens, and the compiled LoRA. So the program is explicitly hybrid: a discrete component for semantic anchoring and a continuous component for behavioral precision. The paper argues that this split is not incidental. The discrete part protects against ambiguity in the original spec, while the continuous part captures nuances that text alone cannot pin down reliably.

Training relies on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset released with the paper. It is built incrementally across 29 thematic versions and covers more than 800 categories of fuzzy text tasks, including classification, format conversion, parsing, fuzzy matching, natural-language commands, and agentic tool use. This dataset is central because the compiler is not learning one task family; it is learning a mapping from task descriptions to executable task-specific parameterizations.

Conceptually, PAW differs from standard instruction tuning because it does not force all tasks through a single shared forward policy. It differs from ordinary LoRA finetuning because the adapter is not obtained by gradient descent per task, but generated in one shot by a compiler. And it differs from pure in-context learning because the adaptation result is persistent, versionable, and distributable as a file.9ef:T80d,The headline result is the main accuracy-cost tradeoff. The paper reports that a Qwen3-0.6B interpreter running PAW programs reaches 73.78% exact match, outperforming direct prompting of Qwen3-32B at 68.70%, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory. That is the key empirical claim: for this family of fuzzy functions, offline task compilation can be more effective than repeatedly invoking a much larger general model.

Deployment numbers are also concrete. In quantized form, the shared interpreter base is about 430MB in GGUF format, and each compiled program is about 23MB as a LoRA adapter. The system runs at around 30 tokens per second on a MacBook M3. The paper also describes a smaller GPT-2-based path that runs fully client-side in the browser via WebAssembly. These details matter because the work is making a systems claim about software packaging and local execution, not only a modeling claim.

The case studies cover output triage, custom classification, fuzzy search reranking, agent preprocessing, and creative generation. The agent preprocessing setup reaches 93% on ToolCall-15. The point is not a single benchmark win, but evidence that PAW is not limited to narrow label classification; it can also support tasks with tool-selection and preprocessing structure.

The paper further shows modality generality: by replacing only the compiler with a vision-language model and keeping the same interpreter, PAW can handle image-conditioned fuzzy tasks. That suggests the executable representation is not tied to text-only specifications; cross-modal understanding can be absorbed by the compiler while execution remains unified.

On ablations, the abstract already states that LoRA outperforms prefix-tuning as the program form. The most important experimental signal is not the absolute score itself, but the fact that a frozen 0.6B interpreter plus generated task weights can cross the performance level of direct prompting on a 32B model. That strongly supports the paper’s central thesis about compile-time specialization.9f0:T6b5,Start with the introduction and the formal definition of Programs as Weights. The key thing to internalize is that the “program” here is neither a prompt nor a finetuned checkpoint in the usual sense. It is a hybrid executable object: pseudo-program tokens plus PEFT parameters. If that abstraction is missed, the rest can look like ordinary adapter generation.

Then read the compile pipeline carefully. Focus on why the pseudo-compiler is left untrained, why the LoRA compiler is trained separately, and why the interpreter is frozen. Those design boundaries reveal the authors’ decomposition of the problem into semantic normalization, parameter synthesis, and execution.

In the experiments, prioritize the main comparison tables against direct prompting, model scale, and alternative program representations. The 0.6B interpreter versus 32B direct prompting result is the central validation point. After that, read the case studies to judge whether the method covers a genuine class of software functions rather than a narrow benchmark slice.

For deeper study, four questions are worth tracking. First, whether FuzzyBench adequately represents the real distribution of fuzzy functions or contains templated biases. Second, whether generated LoRAs have interpretable structure, for example clustering by task family in a low-rank subspace. Third, how much responsibility is carried by the pseudo-program versus the continuous adapter. Fourth, where compile-time specialization stops being enough and online reasoning is still necessary, such as long-horizon reasoning, open-ended generation, or strong compositional generalization. Reading with those questions in mind will make the paper much more useful.9f1:T46b,The authors construct an end-to-end mechanism around BPE fragmentation. Space insertion is used as a clean probe because it preserves all original characters while forcing BPE segmentation changes. The perturbation is optimized greedily to reduce a safety logit gap, rather than sampled randomly. The gap is measured at the first generated position: refusal tokens include I, Sorry, As, No, Unfortunately, and cannot, while compliance tokens include Sure, Okay, Here, and Step. A positive gap indicates a refusal tendency. The authors are careful to treat this as a first-token refusal trigger, not as a full behavioral safety metric. They then separate trigger flips from actual harmful generations. Activation patching is used to localize the disrupted signal, which appears mainly in the last roughly 30% of layers. A data audit of three public alignment datasets finds no intentionally fragmented inputs. Targeted mutation further isolates safety-critical words as the main locus of disruption. The defense study evaluates DPO and SFT-style augmentation and shows that neither gives a clean selective fix across model families.9f2:T4cc,The main experiments cover five model families: Qwen-3-4B, Qwen-2.5-7B, Gemma-3-4B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Mistral-7B, with additional cross-scale evidence from Qwen-2.5-72B. On refused HarmBench prompts, an optimization targeting safety-token fragmentation flips the first-token refusal trigger in 80–100% of cases. Among those trigger flips, 48% produce genuinely harmful outputs, with per-model rates from 29% to 65%. The gap-behavior ROC-AUC ranges from 0.66 to 0.98, with a pooled value of 0.84, indicating that the logit gap is informative but not sufficient. A Unicode no-split control is 2.2 times weaker, supporting the claim that the effect is tied to BPE segmentation rather than visual noise alone. Activation patching localizes the disrupted refusal signal to the last about 30% of layers. The alignment-data survey finds zero intentionally fragmented inputs in three datasets. In the defense experiments, no configuration in a 68-cell DPO grid closes ASR in a seed-stable way; a four-seed Mistral retraining run with 438 pairs still shows a 20–37% seed spread. SFT augmentation reduces ASR for 3 of 5 families, but it also increases refusal on benign prompts, which the authors expose with a Conv-Benign diagnostic.9f3:T71f,Several design choices matter. The source data is not arbitrary English web text but the actual high-quality split of Nemotron-CC, chosen because prior baseline work found it to be one of the strongest open English pretraining sources. This is important: by starting from a strong source corpus, the paper avoids conflating source-data noise with translation quality. The authors uniformly sample about 155 million documents, around 100B English tokens, and translate the same source set into each target language, which naturally creates a multi-way parallel corpus. On the translation side, they do not rely on a single model family. Instead they optimize over quality, throughput, and language coverage: Tower+ 9B and 72B for stronger-coverage higher-resource settings, and OPUS-MT/HPLT-MT for broader lower-resource coverage. Before production, they run a small human fluency study over seven languages and six candidate systems using blind ratings on matched source documents. Tower+ ranks highest, while general-purpose instruction LLMs lag clearly behind, so those are removed from the production pool. That decision matters because one of the paper’s later findings is that translation-system quality does affect downstream pretraining, even when standard benchmarks fail to expose it. The corpus preserves source-document alignment and, for some languages, multiple row-aligned translations from different systems. This makes the resource useful not only for per-language pretraining but also for controlled cross-system and cross-language experiments. The training setup is also fairly disciplined: reference LLMs are trained under matched budgets on translated data and native baselines, then compared on token efficiency, MT-system choice, benchmark blind spots, and phenomenon-specific Norwegian evaluations.9f4:T756,Four result groups stand out. First is scale and coverage. MultiSynt/MT spans 36 languages and about 4.8T target-language tokens; for many lower- and medium-resource European languages it exceeds the largest comparable open native resource by more than an order of magnitude. Second is pretraining efficiency. On standard multilingual base-model benchmarks, models trained on MultiSynt/MT reach the final score of the HPLT 2.0 native-data baseline using about 72% fewer training tokens, and at a matched 100B-token budget they outperform it by roughly 15% relative. That is a strong indication that translated data can be highly information-dense. Third is evaluation blindness. A fluency-sensitive LLM-as-judge setup cleanly recovers the ranking of translation systems, while standard multiple-choice benchmarks largely fail to separate them. An embedding-space nearest-neighbor analysis further shows that benchmark items tend to sit closer to MultiSynt/MT documents than to HPLT documents, suggesting that benchmark distribution alignment may inflate the apparent strength of translated-data pretraining. Fourth is capability boundary analysis. On Norwegian tasks involving idioms and culturally grounded knowledge, native-data models remain better throughout training. On Norwegian commonsense reasoning, however, translated-data models close the gap and eventually overtake the native baseline. This is one of the most useful findings in the paper because it decomposes the usual criticism of translationese into something operational: translated data is not uniformly worse, but it is weaker on local cultural grounding and idiomatic expression. The overlap experiment between Tower+ 72B and 9B also matters: the downstream gap is small enough that 9B becomes the default production choice, which is relevant for cost-quality trade-offs in large-scale corpus construction.9f5:T5ab,A good reading order is data construction, then training results, then evaluation critique. Start with Section 3. The important parts are not the mechanics of translation at scale but the choices: why Nemotron-CC HQ was used as the source, why the final production pool combines Tower+ with OPUS/HPLT-MT, and why preserving parallel alignment matters for later controlled analysis. Then read Section 4 carefully, since this is where the pretraining value is established. Pay attention to how token efficiency is measured, whether budgets are matched fairly, and how much downstream difference remains between translation systems. After that, read Section 5 with care, because it changes how the earlier gains should be interpreted. Section 5.1 compares LLM-as-judge with standard benchmarks, Section 5.2 gives the embedding-space diagnostic, and Section 5.3 breaks down Norwegian performance into cultural knowledge, idioms, and commonsense. Together they show that benchmark gains should not be read as proof that translated corpora fully replace native corpora. If time is limited, prioritize Figure 1, Figure 3, Figure 6, and the main tables in Sections 4 and 5. Two deeper questions are worth carrying forward: whether the best recipe is a translated-native mixture rather than either source alone, and how multilingual evaluation should separate fluency, cultural grounding, and reasoning instead of collapsing them into a single benchmark score.9f6:T959,方法核心是把数据配比优化写成带协变量的连续处理因果推断问题。每次 proxy 训练 run 记为三元组 (X, T, Y)：X 是训练前可观测的数据状态，包含质量、难度、复杂度、风格等统计特征；T 是各域 mixture；Y 是训练后的下游性能。作者强调 X 不能包含任何训练后模型信息或评测结果，否则会破坏因果设定。

处理变量 T 不是直接用 simplex 上的原始比例，而是先做 log-mixture 变换 z=log(t+ε)。这样做有两个原因：一是经验 scaling law 常表现为边际收益递减，log 空间更适合局部线性近似；二是 compositional data 在 simplex 上直接回归不稳定，Aitchison 风格的几何处理更自然。随后作者不去拟合完整响应面 μ(x,z)，而是在历史 mixture 支持域附近采用 partially linear approximation：Y≈g(X)+θ(X)^T z+noise。这里 g(X) 表示由数据状态决定的基线性能，θ(X) 是状态条件化的边际数据回报向量。θ_k(X)>0 表示在当前数据状态下提高第 k 个域占比通常有利，θ_k(X)<0 则意味着可能存在负迁移或技能冲突。

为了从观测到的历史 run 中识别 θ(X)，作者使用 Double Machine Learning 和 causal forest。具体思路是先分别拟合 outcome model 和 treatment model，对 Y 与 T 关于 X 的可预测部分做 orthogonalization / residualization，再在残差空间里估计局部线性效应。这样做的目的是把“数据池本身更好，所以性能更高”与“某个域比例更高，所以性能更高”分开，减少混杂偏差。得到 CATE 估计后，作者不是直接跳到新的最优配比，而是做 trust-region 约束下的保守更新，避免由于局部估计噪声把 mixture 一步推到训练支持域之外。这一点很关键，因为历史 proxy run 只有有限覆盖，过度外推很容易失真。

与 RegMix 一类方法相比，差别不在于用了更复杂的回归器，而在于目标函数变了。RegMix 更像学习一个静态全局 surrogate；CausalMix 学的是“在给定数据状态下，沿哪个方向改 mixture 更可能带来真实收益”。这使它天然更适合数据池变化、模型规模迁移和解释分析。论文还把 CATE 用于分析域间相互作用，而不是只输出一个配比建议，这让方法从纯黑盒调参器变成了可诊断工具。9f7:T9f8,CausalMix formulates each proxy training run as a triplet (X, T, Y), where X is the pre-training data state, T is the domain mixture, and Y is the downstream performance after training. A key modeling choice is that X contains only pre-training statistics of the data pool, such as quality, difficulty, complexity, entropy, or style, and explicitly excludes any post-training model signal or evaluation outcome.

The treatment is not modeled directly on the simplex. Instead, the paper uses a log-mixture representation z = log(t + epsilon). This choice is motivated by two considerations: empirical diminishing returns are often closer to linear in log space, and compositional data are better handled with geometry-aware transforms than with raw simplex coordinates. Rather than fitting the full response surface mu(x, z), the paper adopts a partially linear local approximation, Y ≈ g(X) + theta(X)^T z + noise. Here g(X) captures the baseline performance implied by the data state, while theta(X) is the state-conditioned marginal return vector. Positive theta_k(X) means increasing domain k is locally beneficial under state X; negative values indicate local negative transfer or domain conflict.

To identify theta(X) from observational proxy runs, the paper uses Double Machine Learning and causal forests. The idea is to first model the predictable parts of both outcome and treatment from X, then residualize them and estimate the local linear effect in the orthogonalized space. This is the crucial step: it tries to disentangle “this pool performs better because the pool itself is better” from “this pool performs better because the mixture changed.” Once the conditional effect is estimated, the method performs a conservative trust-region update rather than jumping directly to an unconstrained optimum. That design is sensible because historical proxy runs only cover a limited region of the mixture space, and aggressive extrapolation would be unreliable.

Compared with methods such as RegMix, the main difference is not just a stronger regressor. The target itself changes. RegMix-style methods learn a static global surrogate from mixture to performance. CausalMix instead estimates a local, state-conditioned causal direction for how to move the mixture under the current pool. That makes it more suitable for distribution shift, transfer across model scales, and interpretation. The paper also uses the estimated CATEs to analyze domain interactions, which is more informative than returning a single recommended mixture.9f8:T5de,The core experimental setup uses 512 proxy runs of Qwen2.5-0.5B to fit the causal model, then tests whether the learned update rule transfers to unseen data pools and larger model architectures. From the provided text, these are the only hard numbers that can be confirmed directly: 512 runs and a 0.5B proxy model. The central empirical claim is that, unlike static-distribution mixture optimizers, CausalMix does not require retraining the proxy search from scratch when the data pool changes.

The reported findings, as described in the paper text, fall into three buckets. First, transfer: the learned causal update generalizes to unseen pools and larger models. Second, interpretability: the estimated conditional treatment effects reveal a conflict between factual-knowledge-heavy data and complex logical reasoning, and show that math and coding data become beneficial only above certain quality thresholds. Third, optimization behavior: trust-region updates appear more stable than aggressive reweighting, which is consistent with the local nature of the estimator.

What still needs to be checked in the full results section are the decisive quantitative details: which baselines were compared, the absolute and relative gains, how large the transfer models are, which data-state features matter most, and how much each component contributes in ablations. In particular, the necessity of DML, causal forests, log-mixture parameterization, and trust-region updates should be verified carefully.9f9:T659,This one is worth a close read. Start with the methodology and keep the three variables straight: X is the data state, T is the mixture, and Y is post-training performance. Once that framing is clear, the rest of the paper becomes much easier to parse. The next thing to focus on is why the paper estimates local marginal returns theta(X) instead of fitting a global response surface. That is the conceptual center of the work. If you have worked on data mixture or curriculum learning, the key insight is not the causal vocabulary by itself, but the explicit separation between pool-state effects and mixture effects.

In the experiments, prioritize four parts: the main transfer results on seen versus unseen pools and across model scales; the ablations removing data-state features, DML, trust-region constraints, or replacing the method with plain regression; the CATE visualizations supporting the skill-conflict and quality-threshold claims; and any case studies showing how the recommended mixture shifts under different pool states. Those sections will tell you whether the method is merely plausible or actually robust.

If time is limited, read Figure 1, the method overview, the main result tables, and the interpretability figures first. The most interesting follow-up questions are whether the chosen data-state features remain stable enough for real deployment, whether the same framework can scale from SFT to pretraining, whether the local linear assumption survives with more domains and sparser support, and whether this causal optimizer can be combined with online data selection or mid-training annealing.9fa:T8cf,The core technical scheme consists of four parts, with the key difference from prior methods being full adaptation to GRPO’s critic-free structure and the current RLHF setup without explicit off-policy corrections: 1. Behavior-policy-aware GRPO surrogate objective reconstruction: Unlike traditional GRPO derivations that assume equivalence between the behavior policy and the current learner policy, it explicitly disentangles the stale behavior policy φ (used to generate rollouts) from the learner parameter θ, and defines the surrogate gradient mapping ℋ(θ,φ) to avoid conflating the surrogate gradient with the total derivative of the distribution-dependent population objective, providing a rigorous foundation for lag bias analysis. 2. Per-step staleness bias quantification: Under three assumptions (local boundedness, distributional smoothness, behavior-policy smoothness), it strictly proves that the per-step surrogate gradient bias induced by stale rollouts scales as O(Sη), where S is the maximum rollout lag step count and η is the learning rate — meaning the single-step training safe region is controlled by the product Sη. 3. Conditional collapse-time scaling law: It distinguishes two types of constraints: the batch-level clipping radius from GRPO’s importance sampling ratio, and the learner drift threshold over the training horizon. Training stability is divided into two regimes: when Sη is small enough that per-step staleness bias stays within the tolerance of batch clipping, the collapse time follows a Tη horizon law (T is the total training step count), and the maximum stable learning rate is nearly independent of S; when Sη exceeds the batch clipping tolerance, stability is directly bounded by Sη. 4. Two-constraint stability rule: Combining the two regimes, it provides an actionable hyperparameter configuration formula η ≪ min{R_batch/(S·G_upd), R_crit/(T·G_upd)}, where R_batch is the batch-level clipping radius, R_crit is the critical drift threshold, and G_upd is the per-step gradient magnitude. This explains the industrial observation that the maximum stable learning rate sometimes appears independent of lag magnitude, which only occurs in scenarios dominated by the horizon constraint.9fb:T5a9,Prioritize the following sections for intensive reading: 1. Introduction: Focus on the throughput motivation of asynchronous GRPO, the core limitations of existing analyses, and the observational background of the two-phase "stable-then-collapse" training dynamic. 2. Behavior-policy-aware GRPO surrogate reconstruction: Focus on the definition logic of ℋ(θ,φ), and clarify the core reason why traditional GRPO derivations cannot handle staleness. 3. Per-step staleness bias proof: Pay attention to the applicability boundaries of the three assumptions — for example, when policy updates are overly aggressive, the local boundedness assumption fails and the conclusions no longer hold. 4. Conditional collapse-time scaling law derivation: Focus on the switching condition between the two regimes, i.e., the tradeoff logic between the batch-level clipping constraint and the horizon drift constraint. 5. If the full experimental section is available later: Prioritize training stability curves under different lag step counts S and learning rate η settings to verify the two-phase dynamic and the validity of the two-constraint rule. Worth further exploration: extending the framework to GRPO scenarios with universally added KL regularization, adapting it to multimodal RLHF setups, and combining it with explicit off-policy correction methods such as V-trace to increase the maximum allowable lag step count S for higher training throughput.9fc:T6bd,The method has three layers. The first is empirical diagnosis. The authors show systematically that in ELF, more repetition often coincides with lower Gen-PPL. When repeated spans are stripped out, model rankings can reverse; the smallest model looks best largely because it repeats the most. The second layer is mechanism analysis. They rewrite self-conditioning as a feedback recurrence: the denoiser predicts a clean estimate, and that estimate becomes part of the next-step input. Linearizing this loop around sampling trajectories and inspecting the Jacobian reveals a dominant slowest-contracting mode that is nearly one-dimensional and strongly aligned with repetitive trajectories. They also run direct causal probes: increasing feedback strength alone raises repetition while lowering Gen-PPL, which supports the claim that the loop creates the pathology that the metric then rewards. The third layer is the fix, ACE (Attractor-Contrast-Escape). ACE subtracts a single fixed direction d from the self-conditioning feedback at every step. That direction is estimated without labels, auxiliary models, or retraining: collect feedback states from high-repetition trajectories and low-repetition trajectories, then take the difference of their means. The paper also derives a closed-form usable steering window so the intervention is strong enough to escape the basin but not so strong that it destroys semantics. A key design choice is where to intervene. ACE acts on the latent feedback state, not at token decoding, because the repetition is already formed upstream in continuous space before argmax readout. That makes it fundamentally different from repetition penalties, n-gram blocking, or decode-time heuristics.9fd:T5ab,Three result groups matter most. First is metric pathology. ELF-B reports a Gen-PPL of 19.5, but after removing repetition the score rises to 27.7, enough to change the apparent ranking against larger models. Sample-level analyses also show that more repetitive generations receive better GPT-2-based perplexity scores, confirming that the scorer favors the degenerate outputs. Second is mechanism validation. Increasing self-conditioning feedback strength increases repetition and further lowers Gen-PPL, which supports the proposed causal chain. The Jacobian analysis shows that the problem is dominated by a single slow-contracting direction, and sharper sampling settings deepen the basin. Third is ACE performance. A direction estimated once on the smallest model transfers well across inference settings and model scales; its cosine similarity to per-configuration re-estimated directions is reported between 0.82 and 0.96. Under the paper’s defect-controlled evaluation, ACE reaches human-clean text at 1.5x to 5x lower compute cost while maintaining competitive quality on accepted samples. The same direction-estimation recipe also recovers useful controls on Plaid and LangFlow, suggesting the issue is not ELF-specific but tied to self-conditioned continuous DLMs more broadly. The appendix tables on repeated 4-grams are also important: the degeneration is not mild local repetition but long loops that can persist for hundreds of words.9fe:T549,Read it along three threads. First, go through Section 3 and the associated tables to understand how severe the Gen-PPL failure is. Focus on how model rankings change before and after repetition stripping, and on the sample-level correlation between repetition and scorer perplexity. Second, spend real time on Section 4. This is the center of the paper: the dynamical reformulation of self-conditioning, the linearization, the Jacobian spectrum, and the feedback-strength ablations. Without that section, ACE can look like just another steering trick, which would miss the point. Third, read Section 5 carefully because the evaluation protocol is part of the contribution. The paper does not merely report lower repetition; it proposes a more defensible comparison based on a human repetition threshold, quality on the accepted set, and compute-to-clean. Figure 1, Table 4, Table 16, and Table 17 are the first items to inspect. If time is limited in the appendix, prioritize the derivation of the usable steering window and the transfer results across models and samplers. Two follow-up questions are worth keeping in mind while reading: whether the one-dimensional attractor is induced mainly by the training objective or amplified by the inference recipe, and whether training-time variants of self-conditioning could remove the issue at the source.9ff:T4c8,Anthropic frames Fable 5 and Mythos 5 as two deployments of the same base model. Fable 5 is the general-use version with strong safeguards. Mythos 5 has fewer safeguards and is limited to trusted Project Glasswing partners for defensive cybersecurity. The Fable 5 safeguard stack uses defense in depth. Some mechanisms are trained into the model so that it refuses dangerous requests. Others are external classifiers that monitor an interaction and block potentially harmful cybersecurity requests or outputs. The classifiers are intentionally set with a large safety margin: a request must look clearly safe to avoid being blocked. This reduces room for jailbreaks, but also blocks some benign coding, debugging, and defensive-security requests. After Amazon researchers reported a prompt-based bypass that made Fable 5 identify vulnerabilities and, in one case, produce exploit demonstration code, Anthropic trained a new classifier targeted at that behavior. If Fable 5 blocks a request, the user is notified and the request is routed to Opus 4.8. Under a mean-field assumption, the high-dimensional policy state is summarized by the expected reward p(theta)=E[R], whose evolution is governed by a one-dimensional drift g(p) with a stable fixed point. A second-order backward-error expansion of the discrete update then yields a stochastically forced damped oscillator. The effective mass, damping, and stiffness are given in closed form from optimizer hyperparameters plus one measured curvature scale. Momentum supplies inertia. Off-policy lag from delayed refresh adds inertia while reducing damping. Group size enters as a noise temperature rather than as a determinant of the mean trajectory. The familiar single-exponential reward saturation law appears as the overdamped limit of this oscillator. Keeping the inertial term explains an early slow-start inflection that a single exponential cannot represent.a06:T53c,LOTUS inserts K learnable padded latent blocks, each with c latent tokens, between the question and the answer. The whole sequence is processed R times by the same Transformer backbone, reusing weights across iterations. This recurrent-depth design converts a length-N explicit CoT into R rounds of parallel dense computation, with R much smaller than N.

The central training signal is parallel cross-entropy supervision on the post-loop latents. Each latent position is read through the base model’s own LM head and trained to predict the corresponding gold CoT token. This gives the latent trace a direct token-level target. The design differs from autoregressive latent methods such as Coconut, CODI, and SIM-CoT because it does not generate latent thoughts one by one. It also differs from methods such as PCCoT and KaVa, which reduce sequential bottlenecks but rely on more indirect grounding signals such as teacher hidden states or compressed KV-cache targets.

The paper also introduces LOTUS-aux, where the same supervision is routed through an auxiliary decoder conditioned on all latents and trained with teacher forcing. The auxiliary decoder is used only during training. It can match the direct route at the 3B scale, but it degrades on smaller backbones, which makes the direct LM-head route the more robust design choice.a07:T443,The main model is Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct. On GSM8K, LOTUS comes within 1 point of explicit CoT. On the out-of-domain math average, it surpasses explicit CoT while reducing thought-phase latency by 2.5x in the math-expression setting. On a more verbose natural-language CoT stress test, it matches explicit CoT accuracy and reduces thought-phase latency by 6.9x.

The ablations support two key claims. First, direct parallel supervision is important; without CoT-token grounding, the latent trace is less reliable as a reasoning carrier. Second, the looped architecture needs enough block width and loop depth. The benefit is not obtained simply by inserting latent tokens into a standard forward pass.

The interpretability analysis is also notable. Reading post-loop latents through the base LM head recovers most gold intermediate tokens, and sometimes assigns probability mass to alternative valid reasoning steps that were not used as training targets. This is evidence that the latent states are aligned with language-level reasoning rather than only optimized for final-answer accuracy.a08:T514,The analysis first disentangles two correlated but distinct signals: position-level predictive entropy measures the model's total uncertainty at a sequence position, while sampled token probability measures the likelihood of the specific token that was generated at that position. High-entropy positions can produce both high- and low-probability tokens; low-probability tokens can appear either at high-entropy positions (where the model is uncertain, providing useful learning signal) or low-entropy positions (where the model is highly confident but sampled an outlier, producing noisy, unstable gradients). The Relative Surprisal Index is defined to combine both signals, measuring the relative unexpectedness of the sampled token against the model's full predictive distribution at the position. Under mild assumptions, RSI has a direct analytical connection to the magnitude of token-level policy gradients, making it a direct proxy for token importance. The RSI-S selection scheme filters two categories of unproductive tokens before gradient updates: low-surprisal tokens at low-entropy positions (already mastered, near-zero gradient) and high-surprisal tokens at low-entropy positions (outlier samples, unstable gradients), retaining only tokens that provide stable, useful learning signal.a09:T430,All runs use rsLoRA with rank 32, alpha 64, no dropout, and adapters on all attention and feed-forward projection matrices. This separates the optimization question from the details of pipeline scheduling. The technical contribution has three main parts. The paper also provides convergence analysis for Linear Minimization Oracle algorithms under delayed updates, including the Error Feedback variant.a14:T8ff,方法上，作者做了一个相当干净的分解。先把验证集 loss 写成 contextualized token instance 的平均：每个 token 在某个 scaling 轴 a 上都有一条损失轨迹 ℓ_i(a)，这里 a 可以是训练步数 T、数据规模 D、模型规模 M。然后不直接看 L(a)，而是看其导数 L'(a)，因为导数更直接对应“哪里发生了学习”。

核心观察有两个。

第一，单个 token 的 loss 轨迹不是平滑幂律，而更像带平台期的 sigmoid：在被学会之前长期维持较高 loss，到了某个局部区间快速下降，之后进入新的平台。sigmoid 的中心可以定义为该 token 的 learning time，导数则形成一个局部 pulse，表示学习事件发生的强度和范围。

第二，把不同 token 按 learning time 对齐后，这些 pulse 的形状相当相似。也就是说，token 之间的主要差异不在“怎么学”，而在“何时学”。于是全局 loss 导数可以近似写成：一个共享的局部学习 pulse，与 learning-time spectrum 的卷积或叠加。若 learning-time spectrum 本身是长尾甚至近似幂律，那么聚合后的全局 loss 就自然呈现幂律缩放。

这比已有解释更进一步的地方在于，它把“数据难度长尾”从抽象叙事变成了可测量对象：不是直接测 token 难度，而是测 token 在不同轴上发生学习转变的时间分布。作者还系统比较了三种假设：
1. 幂律主要来自整体优化动力学；
2. 单 token loss 自身按幂律下降；
3. 不同 token 在不同时间被学会。
全文证据支持第三种解释占主导。

更有意思的是，作者没有停在解释层面，而是把 learning-time signal 用回训练。具体做法是：估计样本中 token 的学习事件集中在哪个训练区间，然后针对目标区间上调这些样本权重、下调贡献较小的样本权重，以此改变后续优化轨迹。这相当于一种基于 token-level learning dynamics 的 data curriculum / mixture reshaping。

和传统 curriculum 的区别在于，传统方法多按静态难度、质量或来源分桶；这里按“何时会被学到”分桶。这个视角更贴近 scaling 过程，也更可能解释为什么同样的高质量数据在不同训练阶段边际收益不同。a15:T534,This is a meaningful contribution to pretraining science because it turns scaling laws from a purely macroscopic empirical regularity into a token-level dynamical picture.

First, it offers a concrete microscopic explanation for aggregate loss scaling. That matters because many practical decisions in pretraining, such as compute-optimal allocation, curriculum design, and continued pretraining schedules, are currently guided by global curves with limited mechanistic interpretation.

Second, it introduces a new control signal for data scheduling. Instead of weighting data by static quality heuristics, perplexity, or source labels, the paper proposes using token-level learning-time concentration: samples are valuable at a given stage if many of their tokens are about to be learned in that stage.

Third, it sharpens the usual “heavy-tailed difficulty” narrative. The heavy tail appears primarily in the spectrum of learning times, not in the shape of individual token-loss trajectories. That distinction is important because it changes what one should try to optimize: the timing distribution of learning events, rather than only average token difficulty.

If the findings hold up broadly, this paper is more than another scaling-fit exercise. It provides a reusable lens for analyzing and steering pretraining dynamics.a16:T81e,The technical setup is elegant. Let the validation loss along some scaling axis a be the average over contextualized token instances: each token i has a loss trajectory l_i(a), where a can be training steps T, data scale D, or model scale M. Instead of analyzing only L(a), the paper studies its derivative L'(a), because the derivative reveals where learning is actually happening.

The first empirical observation is that individual token losses are not well described as smooth power-law decay. For many tokens, the trajectory looks like a sigmoid: a high-loss plateau, then a localized drop, then a lower-loss plateau. The center of that sigmoid defines a learning time. Its derivative forms a localized learning pulse.

The second observation is that once token trajectories are aligned by learning time, the pulse shapes are highly similar across tokens. In other words, tokens differ much more in when they are learned than in how the local transition unfolds. This leads to the main decomposition: the global loss derivative can be reconstructed from a shared pulse shape plus the distribution of learning times. If the learning-time spectrum is long-tailed, the aggregate loss naturally exhibits power-law-like scaling.

This is stronger than the usual qualitative argument about heavy-tailed language structure because it identifies a measurable latent variable: the timing of token learning events along each scaling axis.

The paper also goes beyond explanation. It uses the measured learning-time signal to reshape the training distribution. Samples whose token-level learning events concentrate in a target interval are upweighted, while samples with little contribution to that interval are downweighted. This changes the subsequent optimization trajectory and serves as a dynamics-aware curriculum or mixture adjustment.

That differs from standard curriculum learning, which usually relies on static difficulty or quality scores. Here the organizing principle is temporal usefulness: not just whether a sample is good, but when it is likely to produce learning.a17:T65b,The experimental scope is one of the paper’s strengths. The authors run more than 110 pretraining experiments on real-world corpora and modern LLM architectures, totaling 1,178 A100 GPU-days. Model sizes range from 290M to 6B parameters, and training budgets range from 1B to 300B tokens. The analysis is carried out along three axes: training steps T, data scale D, and model scale M.

The main empirical findings are:

1. Token-level trajectories are transition-like. A large fraction of contextualized token losses are well fit by sigmoids, indicating localized learning events rather than smooth monotonic decay.

2. The derivative view reveals localized pulses. After alignment by learning time, token-level derivatives share a similar pulse shape, suggesting that the main source of variation is timing rather than pulse morphology.

3. The learning-time spectrum is long-tailed. Many tokens are learned early, progressively fewer are learned later, and this spectrum largely determines the shape of the aggregate scaling curve.

4. Shared pulse plus measured spectrum can reconstruct the empirical loss derivative along all three axes, T, D, and M. This is the core validation of the decomposition.

5. Learning-time-guided data reweighting changes the optimization trajectory and yields an 11% acceleration in validation-loss reduction relative to the original distribution.

For pretraining researchers, the most important point is not a single benchmark number. It is that the explanatory model and the intervention line up: the same token-level signal that explains scaling also provides a handle for improving it.a18:T59c,This one deserves a careful read.

Start with the introduction and Figure 1. That figure contains the whole conceptual structure: sigmoid-like token learning, pulse derivatives, and the learning-time spectrum behind the global curve.

Then read the decomposition section closely. Pay attention to why the authors move to the derivative domain, how they define learning time, how they fit sigmoids, and how they distinguish among the three competing hypotheses.

Next, inspect the three-axis results for T, D, and M. Do not only look at fit quality. Check whether the pulse shape is truly stable across axes and whether the learning-time spectrum remains heavy-tailed in each setting.

After that, read the data-reshaping experiment carefully. The practical questions are: how expensive it is to estimate learning times, whether the method requires prior pilot runs, and what exactly the reported 11% acceleration is normalized against.

Finally, spend time on limitations. Important ones include: whether all tokens are well modeled by a single sigmoid transition, how repeated or multi-stage learning events are handled, how sensitive the findings are to tokenizer choice and data deduplication, and whether results up to 6B parameters extrapolate to frontier-scale models.

If time is short, read Figure 1, the decomposition method, the main T/D/M results, and the reweighting experiment. A full careful read is about 60–90 minutes.a19:T558,The core reframing models repeated samples for a single prompt as cluster sampling rather than i.i.d. draws, building on Kish’s design effect and de Finetti’s exchangeability theorem. It disentangles three quantities confounded by nominal sample count: (1) The modal ceiling π_mode for answer selection: without a perfect verifier, plurality vote converges to the model’s most frequent answer for a given problem. If that modal answer is incorrect, additional samples only increase confidence in the wrong answer (anti-scaling), so selection accuracy is capped at the fraction of problems where the model’s modal answer is correct. (2) The correlation ceiling 1/ρ: within-problem response correlation ρ means n correlated samples have an effective sample size of n/(1+(n-1)ρ), which saturates at a hard upper bound of 1/ρ regardless of sampling budget, governing the accuracy of model performance estimates from sampling. (3) Between-problem difficulty heterogeneity ρ_b shapes the coverage curve; previously reported power-law coverage curves under i.i.d. assumptions are recovered as the special case where within-problem correlation ρ_w = 0. The framework strictly separates estimation (sampling to measure model accuracy) from selection (sampling to return a single answer), and provides a rule for optimal compute allocation across sampling budget.a1a:T523,The method has a training component and an inference component. On the training side, Multi-block Teacher Forcing concatenates a clean prefix with a bounded group of consecutive noisy blocks, instead of corrupting only the current block. Noisy blocks inside the group can attend to one another through a Group-Aware Dual-Stream Mask, while preserving block-causal generation constraints. The dual-stream design separates the prediction view from the conditioning content view, so the model can use neighboring noisy blocks without leaking the target token. MultiTF also uses a more aggressive and randomized noise scheduler inside each group, creating heterogeneous slot-wise noise patterns similar to inference: front slots may be nearly solved while later slots remain heavily masked. Blocks are partitioned into groups with varying sizes so the model sees different running-set sizes and relative slot positions. On the inference side, the Block Buffer keeps a fixed number of physical block slots. Future blocks enter by activating idle slots, and completed front blocks are committed to the KV cache before their slots are reused. This keeps input shape static, supports CUDA Graph replay, preserves prefix caching, and turns higher TPF into wall-clock throughput rather than only a nominal parallelism metric.a1b:T470,Key empirical findings reported in the paper include:
- Literature-level discrepancy: for LLaDA-8B-Instruct on GSM8K, reported accuracy can differ by up to ~9 percentage points across studies even when the decoding method and generation configuration are claimed to be the same, indicating evaluation details dominate.
- Prompt-template sensitivity: tiny template changes can cause large score swings; parallel decoding methods exhibit larger variance and ranking reversals.
- Speed–quality trade-off persists: under the authors’ more rigorous settings, existing parallel decoding/step-reduction methods consistently underperform the single-token decoding baseline in quality, undermining “no degradation” claims.
- Other knobs matter: increasing generation length is not reliably beneficial and can hurt under some templates; few-shot prompting can overestimate parallel decoding gains; hardware differences can yield inconsistent comparisons.

Core observation: Correct solutions are stable fixed points of the discrete flow denoising process — re-noising a correct solution and solving it returns the original answer, while incorrect solutions drift significantly. This stability signal acts as a high-AUROC self-verifier without requiring external labels or checking tools. 2. Test-time scaling paradigm: Generate multiple candidate solutions and filter correct ones via a re-noise, re-solve, consistency-check stability pipeline to directly improve solve rates. 3. Inference-time self-conditioned refinement: Feed the complete previous prediction as conditioning at each denoising step, so a single sampling run iteratively converges to a stable fixed point, adding cross-refinement-step memory to flow models without requiring multiple independent sampling runs. 4. (2) Experience-aware policy optimization: the GRPO objective is adjusted per token based on local experience injection intensity, modulating clipping ranges and KL constraints to account for the mixed sampling distribution and prevent training instability. MLFM uses a Brownian bridge as the stochastic interpolant between an embedded partially masked sequence and the embedded clean sequence. This choice is important for two reasons. First, the latent state evolves jointly across positions, so the model is not forced into the position-wise independence approximation used by standard masked diffusion models. That makes few-step generation better aligned with the true dependency structure of language. Second, at the boundary of the Brownian bridge, the interpolant reduces to the embedded partially masked sequence, which matches the input structure of pretrained MDMs. This enables warm-start adaptation from a large masked diffusion model instead of training a flow LM from scratch. Training follows the stochastic-interpolant / flow-matching view: the network learns a conditional velocity field that transports the continuous latent state toward clean token embeddings while conditioning on observed, unmasked tokens. Inference adds two mechanisms. The first is a new form of classifier-free guidance. Rather than only contrasting conditional and unconditional predictions, the method noises clean tokens inside the reference velocity so that the contribution of clean context can be isolated more cleanly. The second is online token promotion: once the posterior mode at a position exceeds a confidence threshold of 1-ε, that token is immediately committed and its clean embedding is inserted into the state. This means resolved tokens become usable context for later denoising steps instead of remaining noisy until the end. That is the main behavioral difference from standard FLMs, which keep decoding all positions throughout generation, and from standard MDMs, which iteratively unmask in discrete space but still rely on factorized reverse transitions.a21:T4ce,The experiments adapt a pretrained 1028M-parameter MDM from Nie et al. performance.a25:T5b1,DMuon is a drop-in distributed Muon module orthogonal to the host training framework and parallelism strategy. Its design has four layers. (1) Owner-centric communication optimization: one owner rank is selected per full matrix. Non-owners aggregate their shards to the owner via a single all-gather, the full Newton-Schulz iteration runs on the owner, and updated shards are then scattered back. Communication volume is minimized while exact optimizer semantics are preserved, addressing the root issue that per-shard computation cannot perform orthogonalization. (2) Shape-adaptive execution stack: combines batched Gram Newton-Schulz execution (computing MM^T / M^TM first then iterating, reducing arithmetic), symmetry-aware specialized kernels (halving work on symmetric Gram matrices), and DSL-driven autotuning to deliver high utilization across heterogeneous matrix shapes. (3) Computation-aware load balancing: owner assignment is formulated as a measured-cost optimization problem. A runtime profile captures the nonlinear costs introduced by batching, kernel selection, and autotuning, then performs global assignment to balance work across owners. (4) Drop-in interface: exposes only a standard optimizer API to existing pipelines, natively supports ZeRO, FSDP2, and tensor parallel sharding without modifying the main training loop. DMuon performs no algorithmic approximation; update rules and convergence behavior are identical to naive Muon.a26:T49d,Close read. Worth further investigation: portability of this framework to other matrix-aware optimizers (Shampoo, SOAP variants), and owner assignment strategies for the large expert-matrix populations in MoE setups.a27:Ta28,方法上最关键的是 two-tower 设计。作者从同一个预训练 Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint 复制出两份网络。context tower 保持原始 AR 结构并冻结，负责对 prompt 和已提交 token 做因果建模，持续维护每层的 KV cache 以及 Mamba state。denoiser tower 则是可训练的 diffusion 模块，针对当前待生成 block 的 [MASK] 初始化序列做 T 步迭代去噪。

生成过程是 block-wise autoregressive。序列被按块生成：过去块一旦“提交”，就进入 context tower 的干净历史；当前块在 denoiser 中反复细化，直到 token 变干净后再提交。这样既保留了跨块的 AR 因果结构，又允许块内并行生成。

架构创新主要有四点。第一，layer-aligned cross-attention。denoiser 的第 i 层直接访问 context tower 第 i 层的表示，而不是只读最后一层 hidden state。作者的理由很直接：两塔从同一 checkpoint 初始化，同层表示处在相近抽象层级，逐层对齐比“末层广播”更自然，也让 denoiser 在不同深度都能拿到条件信息。第二，块内 bidirectional attention。当前 noisy block 内部取消因果 mask，使 token 彼此双向可见；但对过去 clean blocks 仍保持因果约束。这让 denoiser 更像条件填空器，而不是被迫按 AR 方式在块内单向传播。第三，time conditioning。作者把图像 diffusion transformer 常用的 adaLN-single 引入语言去噪器，用 timestep 生成 scale/shift/gate，对每层做调制。额外参数只有约 1.5M，在 30B 骨干上几乎可以忽略，但能显著改善采样质量。第四，Mamba 层的条件接入。attention 层通过 cross-attention 读 context KV；Mamba-2 层则用对应 context tower 的 Mamba state 作为初始状态。也就是说，两塔的耦合不只发生在 attention 子层，而是覆盖了混合骨干里的两类主要计算单元。

论文还讨论了几个设计取舍。作者测试了 parameter-free 的 bidirectional Mamba：同一组预训练 Mamba 权重分别做左右两个方向扫描，再平均输出。这个设计几乎不增参数，但会把 SSM FLOPs 近似翻倍。实验显示收益很小，所以最终保留 causal Mamba，只在 attention 上做双向块内建模。MoE routing 基本沿用骨干已有机制，噪声感知主要通过 adaLN 调制进入专家路由前的表示，而不是重写路由器。推理时只有 context tower 维护跨块 cache，因此序列长度相关内存与 AR 基线同阶；额外成本主要是固定的第二塔权重和当前块去噪计算。a28:Tac7,The central idea is a two-tower architecture built from two copies of the same pretrained Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B checkpoint. The context tower is frozen and remains a causal AR model over the prompt and previously committed tokens. It maintains per-layer KV caches and final Mamba states. The denoiser tower is trainable and performs masked diffusion over the current block, starting from a block of [MASK] tokens and refining it over T denoising steps.

Generation is block-wise autoregressive. Past blocks are committed and become clean causal context. The current block is refined in parallel inside the denoiser. Once the block is sufficiently clean, it is committed, the context tower consumes it causally, and generation moves to the next block. This preserves AR structure across blocks while enabling parallel generation within a block.

There are four notable design choices. First, layer-aligned conditioning: denoiser layer i attends to context-tower layer i, rather than conditioning only on the final hidden state. Since both towers start from the same pretrained checkpoint, same-depth layers are expected to live at similar representational levels, making aligned cross-attention a sensible pairing. Second, bidirectional attention inside the noisy block: tokens under refinement can attend to one another without a causal mask, while still attending causally to past clean blocks. This turns the denoiser into a conditional infilling module rather than a left-to-right decoder. Third, timestep conditioning via adaLN-single: the denoiser is modulated by the diffusion timestep using scale/shift/gate parameters generated from t. The added parameter cost is tiny, about 1.5M on top of the 30B backbone, but it improves sampling quality. Fourth, Mamba-state conditioning: attention layers consume context KV caches, while Mamba-2 layers are initialized from the corresponding context-tower Mamba states. So the coupling spans both attention and state-space components of the hybrid backbone.

The paper also studies design trade-offs. A parameter-free bidirectional Mamba variant is tested by running the same pretrained Mamba weights left-to-right and right-to-left and averaging outputs. It nearly doubles SSM FLOPs and yields only marginal gains, so the final model keeps Mamba causal and uses bidirectionality only in attention. MoE routing is inherited from the backbone, with noise awareness entering through timestep-conditioned activations rather than a redesigned router. At inference time, only the context tower keeps sequence-length-dependent cache state across blocks, so cache scaling remains comparable to the AR baseline; the extra cost is mainly the fixed second tower and the iterative denoising compute for the current block.a29:T7ff,The experimental story has three main parts. First, this is a large-scale validation rather than a toy setup. The backbone is Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, a 52-layer hybrid model with 23 Mamba-2 layers, 6 self-attention layers, and 23 MoE layers. TwoTower is trained on top of this 30B-class model with about 2.1T additional tokens, compared with roughly 25T tokens used to pretrain the original backbone. So the work is not retraining a diffusion LM from scratch; it is converting a strong AR asset into a diffusion-capable generator with a moderate extra budget.

Second, the key result is the quality-throughput trade-off. The model retains most of the AR baseline’s quality while delivering substantially higher decoding throughput. The mechanism is important: at the default operating point, the model commits multiple tokens per refinement step early in decoding, rather than advancing by exactly one token as in AR decoding. The wall-clock gain therefore comes from block-wise parallel progress, not from lower per-step complexity alone.

Third, the ablations support the final recipe. Timestep conditioning improves sampling quality. Layer-wise aligned conditioning is better motivated than using only the last hidden state, and the paper presents it as a meaningful architectural choice rather than a cosmetic one. Bidirectional Mamba brings only small gains relative to its extra FLOPs, which justifies the final decision to keep Mamba causal. Another useful engineering takeaway is that a frozen context tower is already strong enough to provide the conditional signal; most of the extra training is spent on learning how to denoise given AR representations, not on relearning language knowledge.

The paper reframes late-layer under-utilization as a property of residual signal routing rather than a generic optimization failure. That matters because it changes what kinds of interventions are plausible: if the issue is missing gradient diversity, rescaling gradients is not enough. This has implications for how to think about depth scaling, deep supervision, early-exit designs such as LayerSkip, and parameter allocation across depth. The second contribution is more practical: it suggests that uniform-width stacking may be a poor match to how training signal is distributed, and that tapering width with depth can improve deployment efficiency at fixed training FLOPs. The pruning result is also relevant because it uses accumulated training gradients as an online structural importance signal, avoiding expensive post-hoc analysis. This is not a recipe-changing result on the scale of a new optimizer or tokenizer, but it is a serious attempt to connect training dynamics, architecture shape, and pruning through one structural hypothesis.a2c:T6f2,The technical story has three parts. First, the paper defines GFA in Pre-LN residual Transformers. Writing the network as x_{l+1} = x_l + F_l(x_l), the input gradient at layer l can be expanded as a sum over identity and downstream functional paths. The key quantity is not the full combinatorial path count, but a tractable proxy: how many distinct downstream signal channels are aggregated into a layer’s gradient. This fan-in decreases with depth. With deep supervision, the imbalance becomes even stronger because shallow layers receive additional gradient hierarchies from auxiliary heads. Second, the paper tests the hypothesis with both correlational and interventional evidence. It first shows that average per-layer gradient norm correlates with eventual functional importance, but then argues norm is only a proxy. In the ablative intervention, the authors artificially amplify late-layer gradient magnitudes; this does not restore late-layer importance. In the constructive intervention, they increase structural path counts through layer repetition; this does restore importance. That contrast is the central argument of the paper. Third, they derive two methods from the GFA account. CascadeFormer uses a depth-tapered width schedule: earlier layers are wider, later layers narrower, under a fixed training-FLOP budget. The idea is to allocate capacity where gradient composition is richer. CascadeFlow Pruning accumulates training gradients over time and uses them as a proxy for structural importance to rank and remove layers. Unlike post-hoc pruning methods based on activation similarity, one-shot sensitivity tests, or simple depth heuristics, CFP uses information gathered throughout training and does not require an extra analysis phase after pretraining.a2d:T579,The experiments include models trained from scratch up to 1.2B parameters. The paper first presents observational evidence: in pretrained LLaMA, deeper layers show higher representational similarity, and in LayerSkip-style architectures the marginal utility of later layers drops sharply. The main method results are on the authors’ own training runs. For CascadeFormer, under matched training budget, the model reaches perplexity comparable to a uniform-width baseline while reducing inference latency by 8.6% and increasing throughput by 9.4%. That is the clearest practical result: better deployment shape without paying extra training cost. For CascadeFlow Pruning, accumulated training gradients outperform standard pruning heuristics on perplexity and rank stability, while remaining competitive on downstream accuracy. The abstract does not expose all numbers, but the full text emphasizes that the ranking induced by accumulated gradients is more stable across checkpoints and evaluation settings than simpler heuristics. The optimal controller applies two corrective forces to the live iterate: pulling it toward the estimated optimum, and pulling it toward consistency with the accumulated trajectory average, to prevent the live weights from drifting too far from the average. Since the exact optimal controller requires unavailable quantities during training (true optimum location, loss Hessian), practical heuristics are applied: the EMA of iterates is used as a proxy for the optimum, reducing the control term to a simple pull of live weights toward their EMA. The resulting PACE algorithm requires only one extra copy of model weights, identical to standard EMA overhead, with no additional complex state. Formal analysis establishes two key results: (1) for general convex losses with unbiased gradients, PACE achieves the standard SGD convergence rate up to a constant factor dependent on EMA strength, meaning it is never substantially worse than SGD; (2) in the quadratic setting used for derivation, PACE strictly reduces the limiting mean squared error of the averaged estimator relative to uncontrolled SGD with EMA, with arbitrarily large improvements possible on specific quadratic instances.a34:T5ee,Start with the problem framing to understand the core misalignment between standard optimization targets and the deployed averaged model, the most important conceptual contribution of the work. 第二部分是 cliff token 的统计判定。作者不是简单要求 pot_{t-1}-pot_t 超过固定阈值，而是要求它至少超过 0.1，并且通过一侧 two-proportion z-test 的 95% 置信检验。等价地，阈值写成 0.1 + 1.645 * SE_t，其中 SE_t 由相邻两个位置的 rollout 成功率估计方差决定。这样在 pot 接近 0.5、方差较大的区域，判定门槛会更高；在 pot 接近 0 或 1 的区域，门槛较低。作者明确想避免把 rollout 噪声误判成 cliff，这比固定 0.2 或 30% drop 的规则更稳。

第三部分是 cliff taxonomy。作者根据该 token 是否是 greedy choice，以及该位置分布熵的高低，把 cliff 分成 deterministic、uncertain、sampled-off 三类。可以把它理解为三种不同失败机制：deterministic cliff 表示模型高置信地走错；uncertain cliff 表示模型自己也不确定，错误 token 出现在高熵竞争位置；sampled-off cliff 则更像采样偏离，模型的 greedy 也许不会错，但采样选到了坏分支。这个分类不是装饰性的，因为后面的干预和训练结果表明三类 cliff 的可修复性不同。

在干预上，作者做了两种关键验证。其一是删除第一个 cliff token 后重新采样，观察 pass@64 是否恢复；其二是保留 cliff token 但只重采样后续，观察是否仍然无法完全恢复。这个设计直接检验“cliff 是触发点而不是伴随现象”。其后又提出 Cliff-DPO：把 cliff 位置的好坏 token 构造成偏好对，分别在不同 cliff 子集上训练，比较哪类 token 监督真正有用。与一般 process supervision 不同，这里监督信号被压缩到单 token 位置，目标更尖锐。a3f:T83d,The method has three main components. First, it defines token-wise potential. For a prompt, a partial reasoning prefix, and a ground-truth answer, the model rolls out N continuations from every token position and measures the fraction that end with the correct answer. This gives pot_t at each token t. The paper uses N=64 and computes this densely over the full trace, not just at a sparse subset of positions. The cost is high, but the localization is precise.

Second, it introduces a statistical criterion for cliff detection. A token is not labeled a cliff simply because pot_{t-1} - pot_t exceeds a fixed threshold. Instead, the drop must be at least 0.1 and pass a one-sided two-proportion z-test at 95% confidence. This yields an adaptive threshold of the form 0.1 + 1.645 * SE_t, where SE_t depends on the estimated variance of the rollout success rates at adjacent positions. The point is to avoid false positives in high-variance regions, especially around intermediate potential values.

Third, the paper proposes a taxonomy of cliff tokens: deterministic, uncertain, and sampled-off. The categorization uses whether the token is the greedy choice and the entropy of the local token distribution. Intuitively, deterministic cliffs correspond to confident but wrong decisions; uncertain cliffs arise at ambiguous, high-entropy positions; sampled-off cliffs reflect failures introduced by sampling away from a better-ranked continuation. This taxonomy is not cosmetic. It becomes central in the intervention and training results.

The causal validation is well designed. The authors delete the first cliff token and resample from that point, then compare this with keeping the cliff token fixed and only resampling the suffix. If recovery happens only when the cliff token is removed, that supports the claim that the token is a trigger rather than a post hoc marker. They then build Cliff-DPO by constructing preference pairs around cliff positions and training on different cliff subsets separately. Compared with generic process supervision, this is a much sharper token-level supervision signal.a40:T6fa,The study covers seven models and three math reasoning benchmarks: Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-4B, Qwen3-0.6B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.2-1B, and Gemma-3-4B, evaluated on GSM1K, MATH500, and AIME 2025. Token-wise potential is estimated with 64 rollouts per position.

The most important result is the causal intervention. Deleting the first cliff token and resampling restores pass@64 to 1.0, while keeping that token and only resampling the continuation fails to fully recover. That is the strongest evidence in the paper: cliff tokens behave like actual failure triggers, not merely locations where failure becomes visible.

A second result is the cross-model taxonomy analysis. Deterministic cliffs appear relatively scale-invariant, whereas uncertain and sampled-off cliffs better reflect model-specific gaps or scale asymmetries. In practical terms, some errors persist even as models scale because they are confident misgeneralizations, while others are more about uncertainty or decoding-induced branch selection.

A third result comes from Cliff-DPO. Training on uncertain and sampled-off cliff subsets improves reasoning performance, while training on deterministic cliffs does not. The full excerpt does not include every hyperparameter or table entry, but the qualitative conclusion is already informative: token-level supervision helps when the failure is near a ranking boundary or caused by sampling, and helps much less when the model is confidently wrong.

The paper also reports that the adaptive threshold varies roughly from 0.18 to 0.24 depending on the local potential regime, with stricter thresholds in higher-variance middle regions. This is a small but important implementation detail because it explains why the method is more robust than fixed-drop heuristics.a41:T500,Read it in the following order: definition, causal validation, taxonomy, then Cliff-DPO.

For deeper reading, it is worth thinking about two extensions: how sensitive token-wise potential is to the rollout decoding policy, and whether the same framework transfers beyond math reasoning to code or multimodal reasoning traces.a42:T8c7,The article starts from older learning-curve literature, including Amari, Hestness, and Rosenfeld, to make the point that power-law behavior predates modern LLMs. In that framing, scaling laws are empirical descriptions of how error changes with capacity, data, and compute. It then revisits Kaplan et al.: test loss scales as a power law with parameter count N, dataset size D, and compute C, and the joint form implies that overfitting is largely controlled by a ratio like N^(alpha/beta)/D. The important caveat is that Kaplan’s compute-optimal recommendation depends on the experimental range and fitting procedure, which pushed the optimum toward larger models trained on relatively fewer tokens.

The Chinchilla section is the core. It breaks down three fitting strategies. Method 1 fixes model size and varies the token budget to identify the best token count per model. Method 2 uses IsoFLOP profiles, comparing different N–D allocations under fixed total compute. Method 3 fits a parametric joint loss function directly. The article explains why these are not interchangeable: token sweeps reveal undertraining more directly, IsoFLOP studies align better with real compute allocation, and parametric fits are efficient but sensitive to functional assumptions and sampling coverage.

A particularly useful part is the discussion of fitting pitfalls. If experiments are concentrated in a narrow region, especially one that is effectively data-infinite or strongly model-limited, the fitted exponents can be systematically biased. If partially trained runs are treated as if they reflected compute-optimal behavior, the resulting recommendation will favor oversized, undertrained models. The toy simulation makes this concrete: even when the ground-truth law is known, limited coverage and noise can produce stable but wrong exponents. That is the real reconciliation between Kaplan and Chinchilla: not a simple contradiction, but different estimation procedures operating under different regimes.

The final section on why power laws appear is interpretive rather than formal. It argues that away from tiny-scale and saturation regimes, many error terms behave approximately scale-free, which makes log-log linearity empirically robust.a43:T625,This is a synthesis article rather than a new empirical paper, so the emphasis is on reinterpreting existing results and fitting procedures. It revisits Kaplan 2020: Transformer language models with roughly 768M to 1.5B non-embedding parameters, datasets from 22M to 23B tokens, trained with 3k-step warmup and cosine decay. One key Kaplan conclusion was N_opt ∝ C^0.73, implying that a 10x compute increase should scale model size by about 5.5x but tokens by only about 1.8x. The article highlights that this is exactly the recommendation later corrected by Chinchilla because it leaves models substantially undertrained.

For Chinchilla, the main takeaway is that compute-optimal scaling is much closer to growing parameters and training tokens in the same rough order, meaning smaller models trained on more data under a fixed compute budget. The excerpt provided here does not enumerate every number from the original Chinchilla study, but the experimental lesson is clear: once token sweeps or IsoFLOP comparisons are done carefully, many Kaplan-style large-model points are revealed to be undertrained, which shifts the optimum toward more tokens and fewer parameters.
