The deeper questions to keep in mind are whether reflective remasking scales to larger language models, whether HR can be combined with external memory or verifiers, and whether this capability should eventually be moved earlier into pretraining rather than added only in post-training.a96:T8c4,The paper starts by separating recursive training into three paradigms: replace, accumulate, and selection. Replace uses only newly generated synthetic data and is already known to collapse quickly. Accumulate keeps the original real data and appends later generations, which can prevent variance blow-up in theory, but in low-resource settings the real seed set is often too small to dominate later synthetic rounds. The main focus is selection: generate a candidate synthetic pool, score it with a verifier, and keep only the “good” subset for the next round.

The key move is to model the verifier’s reference distribution explicitly as a biased local observation rather than an approximation to the global truth. Under this view, the selection operator is not a denoiser. It is a directional projection toward the local manifold. Samples are retained in proportion to how well they match the silo’s own support, so repeated selection trims away globally important but locally underrepresented regions. The paper argues that this is not a transient artifact. In recursive training, the bias compounds and drives diversity contraction at an asymptotic power-law rate, with worsening Wasserstein distance to the true global distribution.

To mitigate this, the authors propose a collaborative verifier framework under a no-raw-data-sharing constraint. Instead of pooled verification, they build proxy reference distributions across silos using Wasserstein geometry. Two constructions are emphasized: geodesic interpolations between local empirical distributions, and Wasserstein barycenters across multiple silos. These proxies are then used as collective references for scoring synthetic samples. The design choice is important. Simple feature averaging, parameter averaging, or majority voting would not preserve distributional geometry well enough, especially for tail coverage and mode structure. Wasserstein proxies are intended to recover a more faithful global reference at the distribution level while respecting silo boundaries. The paper also notes that access to the true global distribution would theoretically fix the problem, but that option is unavailable in the target regime, which is why collaborative proxies matter.a97:T6d2,The experiments are designed to validate mechanism rather than to chase a single downstream score. Section 6 is the main place to read. The setup simulates low-resource recursive training with multiple silos and compares no selection, local selection, global-reference selection, and collaborative selection based on geodesic or barycenter proxies.

The main findings are consistent with the theory. Local selection can improve short-term alignment with the silo’s own data, but it accelerates global diversity loss: variance contracts, tail modes disappear, and Wasserstein distance to the true distribution grows. This degradation compounds across generations rather than appearing as a one-off effect, matching the paper’s power-law collapse analysis. When selection is performed against a global reference, collapse is much weaker, which isolates the real issue: not selection per se, but insufficient reference coverage. Under the realistic no-sharing constraint, both Wasserstein geodesic and barycenter proxies outperform single-silo selection, with larger gains when silo heterogeneity is stronger.

The right way to read the results is to inspect the main tables and generation-wise curves in Section 6: Wasserstein distance, variance evolution, diversity coverage, and ablations over silo count, resource level, and heterogeneity. The most informative signal is the trajectory shape over recursive rounds. Local verification often looks acceptable early on, then collapses faster later; collaborative proxies mainly help by preserving tails and improving long-horizon stability.a98:T797,Read it in four passes: setup, mechanism, mitigation, validation.

Start with the Introduction and Preliminaries. The important point is not the generic model-collapse background, but the paper’s reframing: selection is only as good as the reference distribution behind the verifier. Keep the replace / accumulate / selection distinction clear, because the later claims depend on it.

Then read Section 3 carefully. This is the conceptual center of the paper. Focus on how the authors formalize local-prior-driven biased filtering, and why that bias becomes diversity contraction under recursion. Subsection 3.2 is especially important because it links the selection bias to asymptotic power-law collapse. Pay attention to which assumptions are doing the work: low-resource verification, fragmented support, and the monotonicity of the selection rule.

Next, read Section 4 on the Wasserstein collaborative framework. The key question is not the algebra itself, but why geodesic interpolation and barycenters are the right objects here, instead of simpler pooled statistics or ensemble voting. The interesting technical issue is what exactly the proxy restores: mean location, support coverage, tail mass, or all three.

Finally, read Section 6 with an eye on dynamics rather than endpoint scores. Prioritize the generation-wise plots for variance, Wasserstein distance, and diversity coverage. If time is limited, first compare local selection, collaborative selection, and global-reference selection; then look at the difference between geodesic and barycenter proxies.

Two follow-up questions are worth carrying forward. One is whether the same verifier-bias logic applies to judge models, reward models, and synthetic-data filters used in modern post-training loops. The other is whether distribution-level collaboration can be extended beyond raw data distributions to tokenization space, embedding space, or text-generation manifolds.a99:T846,Gefen has two main components.

The first is shared second-moment estimation. The paper starts from a theoretical analysis on a two-layer MLP and studies when two parameters with a large mixed Hessian entry should also have similar squared-gradient magnitudes. The key result is that, under feasible Hessian bounds, increasing the magnitude of the mixed Hessian contracts the admissible ratio of squared gradients toward 1. This gives a clean design principle: parameters that are strongly coupled in curvature are natural candidates for sharing Adam’s second-moment estimate. Since explicit Hessian computation is intractable in large models, Gefen uses the structure of the first-step squared gradients as a proxy. For each parameter tensor, it flattens the tensor, enumerates proper divisors p of the tensor length n, reshapes g0^2 into consecutive blocks of size p, and computes an intra-block heterogeneity score E(p). Small E(p) means the squared gradients within each block are similar, so replacing element-wise v with one shared scalar per block should incur limited distortion. Larger p gives more aggressive sharing and lower memory, so the method selects p by balancing compression against heterogeneity. An important empirical observation is that E(p) is not necessarily monotonic in p; some larger divisors align better with real structural patterns such as attention heads or channel groups. That is why automatic search can outperform hand-written grouping rules.

The second component is first-moment compression. Instead of using a generic low-bit quantizer, Gefen reuses the same block partition and quantizes the first moment m with a learned codebook. The assignment is solved exactly with dynamic programming. Two design choices matter here. First, the codebook is learned rather than manually specified. Second, reusing the same partition avoids introducing another independent block-size hyperparameter. In effect, Gefen is a joint optimizer-state compression scheme: structured sharing for v and codebook-based quantization for m, both built around an automatically inferred block structure.a9a:T6d7,The main empirical claims are threefold. First, memory: Gefen reduces optimizer-state memory by about 8× relative to AdamW, corresponding to roughly 6.5 GiB saved per 1B parameters. That is the headline systems result. Second, quality retention: across both LLM and non-LLM models, the method maintains performance comparable to AdamW, with some settings showing slight gains. The introduction explicitly states that Gefen achieves the lowest memory footprint among compared methods while keeping quality and throughput comparable or better. Third, the automatic grouping mechanism appears to capture real structure rather than arbitrary compression. Beyond the toy theory, the appendix shows similar behavior in real tensors, including attention and convolutional layers, where the discovered partitions produce more homogeneous squared gradients within blocks.

The most relevant baselines are AdamW, Adam-mini, and quantized optimizer variants. Adam-mini reduces memory through manually specified sharing patterns, but requires architecture information such as the number of attention heads and depends on tensor naming. Gefen removes that dependency. Quantized optimizers often rely on hand-crafted codebooks and an extra block-size hyperparameter; Gefen replaces those with a learned codebook and exact dynamic programming. Another practical point is overhead: the grouping pattern is inferred once from the first-step gradient rather than recomputed throughout training, so the method avoids a large recurring cost. When reading the experimental section, the most informative comparisons are final loss or perplexity gaps versus AdamW, throughput changes, and ablations for shared-v only, quantized-m only, and automatic versus manual grouping.a9b:T5f0,Read it in three passes: theory, algorithm, then experiments.

Start with the theoretical section and focus on the central statement: large mixed-Hessian entries force the ratio of squared gradients toward 1. You do not need every proof detail on the first pass, but it is worth understanding the assumptions, the scope of the result, and why the authors argue that the same phenomenon appears beyond the toy MLP setting. This is the part that justifies block-wise sharing as more than an engineering shortcut.

Then move to the algorithm section. Three details deserve careful attention: why the first-step gradient g0 is sufficient to infer a useful sharing structure; how the heterogeneity metric E(p) is defined and used to trade off distortion against memory; and why first-moment quantization is tied to the same partition, with dynamic programming used for exact assignment. If you care about implementation and recipe design, this is the section to study closely.

For experiments, prioritize the main result tables, memory accounting, throughput comparisons, and ablations. The key question is not whether Gefen wins by a tiny metric margin, but whether it preserves AdamW-level optimization under an 8× state reduction, and whether it does so broadly across model families. The appendix visualizations of squared-gradient structure in attention and convolution tensors are also useful; they help assess whether the automatic partitioning is discovering meaningful structure or merely fitting first-step noise.a9c:T4c9,NULLs partitions MLP neurons into shared backbone neurons and a pool of sparsely activated sinks. Each source identity is deterministically mapped to a sparse mask over the sink pool. During training, examples from that source activate the shared backbone plus the source’s masked sinks. The implementation is close to standard pretraining: the main extra operation is an elementwise mask over MLP activations. Unlike per-source modules, NULLs does not allocate a separate parameter block per source; sparse masks over a common sink pool provide combinatorial control, so the number of controllable sources can be much larger than the number of sink groups. The mechanism relies on training dynamics. A fact unique to one source produces gradients on both the backbone and that source’s sinks, but the backbone receives interfering updates from all other sources, while the relevant sinks see far less interference. The unique fact is therefore fitted by the sinks earlier. Once fitted there, the gradient pressure on the backbone decreases, reducing leakage into shared weights. Facts repeated across many sources keep reinforcing the backbone. At deployment, unlearning a source means disabling its corresponding sinks.a9d:T4ba,The paper presents two main case studies. In the Wikipedia setting, it trains an approximately 1B-parameter model on a corpus where about 6 million articles are treated as separate sources. The key test is single-article unlearning without broader topic erasure. Disabling the target article’s sinks sharply reduces recall of facts unique to that article, while preserving semantically related knowledge from other articles. Post-hoc unlearning baselines tend to remove related knowledge at a similar rate as the target knowledge. In the Harry Potter setting, the source is coarser and more topical. NULLs supports instantaneous removal by disabling the relevant sinks, and the removal is more robust to an adversarial relearning attack; the paper notes that standard gradient unlearning can be reversed in fewer than 10 gradient steps. On general natural-language benchmarks, NULLs matches a standard Transformer closely, suggesting that the sink mechanism does not impose a visible cost on broad capability. The most important experimental details to inspect are sink capacity, mask sparsity, source granularity, mask overlap, and the relationship between factual recall suppression and perplexity changes.a9e:T56d,The probe suite contains 686 prompts across six regimes. The strengthened run uses 5 seeds and 20 prompts per regime, giving 100 traces per regime, with prompt-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. For prose, code, math, and factual regimes, token-level tie-aware Kendall tau_b is moderate, roughly 0.43 to 0.60. The ordering becomes more left-to-right as the analysis bin gets coarser; for example, in R1, tau_b rises from 0.59 at bin size 4 to 0.91 at bin size 64. There is no discontinuity at 16 tokens, so 16 is not supported as a privileged architectural block. The observed order remains below a pure block-sequential control, which is around 0.94 to 0.96, indicating real sub-block disorder. Accept batches are large, around 13 to 26 content tokens per call, so many token pairs are tied. The JSON regime is different: token tau_b is -0.044 with a 95% CI of [-0.086, -0.00], which is closer to order-independent behavior. Commit confidence is predictive on GSM8K, with AUROC 0.749 and a 95% CI of [0.602, 0.879], but not on factual recall, where AUROC is 0.471 with a 95% CI of [0.383, 0.544]. Generations typically finish in a small number of accept-calls, far below the 48-step budget, and at entropy well below the 0.1 bound. On scorable regimes, accuracy is comparable to the matched AR sibling Gemma-4 26B-A4B, although the comparison is not powered as an equivalence test.a9f:T4f1,1. Under free dynamics, the critical grokking norm ||W||_c is highly concentrated, varying only 1-2% across a 2x range of training fractions and 10x range of learning rates. 2. Clamp experiments confirm causal control: networks generalize at every fixed norm in the 0.85-1.15||W||_c range, with no required hard threshold. Grokking time follows an exponential law T_grok ∝ e^{αρ} with R²>0.99 across this range; weight norm controls a ~19x span of grokking time, while learning rate acts as a secondary modulator with only ~2x effect. 3. Across 5 prime moduli, all tasks collapse to a shared exponent α≈7.5 when normalized by relative norm ρ (R²=0.996). The law enters sub-exponential saturation for ρ>1.25, with a minimum norm floor at the smallest task size. 4. The law replicates on unnormalized attention models with α≈15 (R²=0.999). LayerNorm decouples total weight norm from function scale, leaving only the functionally relevant unembedding norm concentrated and aligned with the law. 5. Sparse parity (a non-Fourier task) replicates the core finding that norm controls timing rather than acting as a hard threshold. 6. Fourier feature concentration rises in lockstep with norm relaxation, temporally aligning with circuit formation timelines.aa0:T679,For each behavior, the authors build a matched contrastive dataset with positive examples that elicit the behavior and negative examples that suppress it. At a chosen layer of a decoder-only Transformer, they take the last-token residual-stream activation and compute paired contrast vectors between positive and negative examples. These vectors are centered and decomposed with SVD. Instead of representing a behavior by a single steering direction, the method represents it as a top-k low-rank subspace.

A key step is removing decision-aligned variance. The leading singular components can reflect the model’s final positive-vs-negative decision rather than behavior-specific structure. The paper defines a scalar decision margin using the log-probability difference of label strings, identifies components aligned with this margin, and separates them from the behavior subspace analysis. This is meant to avoid conflating decision readout with the internal representation of the behavior.

The diagnostic then studies two quantities. The first is geometric overlap between behavior subspaces, measured through projection-style or principal-angle-style comparisons. The second is decision coupling, which measures how strongly a behavior subspace is connected to the model’s decision direction. Projection-based interventions are applied to a source behavior subspace, and the induced changes are measured on target behaviors. Overlap explains whether an intervention can reach another behavior; decision coupling explains whether that shared representation actually affects the output. Their combination accounts for asymmetric intervention effects.aa1:T4d7,The evaluation compares five memory substrates: none, markdown, vector, graph, and git. It covers GPQA-Diamond and MATH-500, two transfer regimes, two backbones, and sample sizes up to n=500. The memory hypothesis is rejected for novel problems: no substrate reliably improves accuracy. An early git trend of about +15 percentage points at n=40 failed a pre-registered replication. A similarity sweep explains the null result. Memory helps sharply only when the retrieved case is a near-duplicate of the test problem, around cosine similarity above 0.8, with gains of roughly +12 to +13.5 points. With a roughly 4.5x stronger backbone, the near-duplicate gain increases to about +22.5 to +28.5 points, while the method-transfer region remains null. Accuracy is moved more reliably by test-time sampling and model strength; self-consistency gives about +3.4 points at n=500. The paper’s GPQA headline result, 47.0% versus 33.0%, is attributed to MCQ-aware expansion and a larger compute budget, not to memory. On the substrate side, git preserves accuracy parity with other stores and adds about 15 ms per write. A merge demonstration shows that contradictory lessons surface as git merge conflicts instead of being silently concatenated.aa2:T9b3,方法叫 WebGraphMix。核心设计很朴素：先在 Common Crawl 的 host-level hyperlink graph 上给每个 host 算结构中心性分数，再把属于这些 host 的文档映射回预训练语料，最后按 central / peripheral 的比例构造训练 mixture。

图的定义是 host 级而不是 page 级。每个节点是一个 host，例如 wikipedia.org；有向边表示 host 间超链接。作者用的是 Common Crawl 的 host graph，规模 13.9M nodes、439.6M directed edges。之所以选 host-level，而不是 page-level，一是规模可控，二是 host 级位置更稳定，也更适合和大规模语料中的文档来源对齐。

中心性主要试了两类：Betweenness centrality 和 Katz centrality。Betweenness 强调一个节点是否位于大量最短路径上，适合刻画“桥接不同社区”的 host；Katz centrality 则考虑来自邻居及更远节点的影响衰减，偏向刻画全局连接中的重要性。作者也试了 PageRank，但没有看到提升，这一点和 DCLM 里 PageRank 信号效果一般的观察一致。这个负结果其实很有信息量：对预训练数据来说，‘被很多节点指向’未必等于‘提供更有用的学习信号’，而桥接性和结构位置可能更关键。

拿到中心性分数后，作者把语料按 host 分桶，构造几种 mixture：只采 central、只采 peripheral、以及 central/peripheral 的混合，尤其关注 50/50 这种简单配比。这里的关键不是做复杂的连续权重优化，而是先用可解释的结构分区，观察能力变化方向。

更有意思的是它和内容质量信号的结合方式。论文把 centrality 与 DCLM-fasttext 质量分类器做 multiplicative 和 divisive 组合打分。虽然全文细节公式需要结合方法节看，但直觉上是在问：如果一个文档既来自结构中心 host，又被内容分类器判为高质量，是否更值得采样；反过来，是否可以通过除法或重加权避免某一类信号完全主导。实验结果表明这种组合优于单独使用任一信号，说明 web graph topology 与文本内容质量确实捕捉到不同维度。

从方法取舍看，这篇工作刻意避免训练额外模型，也不做下游驱动的 mixture search。优点是轻、稳、可迁移；代价是 centrality 只是 host 级粗粒度信号，无法区分同一 host 内部页面质量差异，也可能把大型聚合站点的结构优势和真实文本价值混在一起。aa3:T85a,实验设置比较扎实，且控制得干净。作者把 WebGraphMix 接进标准化的 DCLM pipeline，训练了 400M 和 1B 两个规模的模型，分别用 8B 和 28B tokens。tokenizer、shuffle、优化器、训练流程都保持一致，尽量把变量压到“数据选择”本身。评测用的是 DCLM CORE v2 的 23 个任务，覆盖较广。

关键结果有几组。

1. 单独看 central vs peripheral 的能力偏置：
在 1B 模型上，采样结构更中心的 host 文档，相比 uniform sampling，在 Symbolic & Algorithmic Reasoning 上提升 +1.4%。而采样更边缘的 host，则在 Science & Factual Knowledge 和 Commonsense & Reasoning 上更好。这个结果很重要，因为它说明图位置不是单调的‘越中心越好’，而是不同区域承载不同能力相关信号。

2. mixture 优于单边采样：
用 betweenness centrality 做 50% central + 50% peripheral 的混合，在 23 个任务平均分上达到 41.4%，而 uniform sampling 是 39.8%。这是 +1.6 个点的平均提升。对预训练数据配方来说，这个幅度不小，尤其考虑到方法几乎不增加训练时成本。

3. 与内容质量信号结合进一步提升：
把 centrality 和 DCLM-fasttext 质量分类器结合后，平均分提升到 43.8%。也就是说，相比 uniform 的 39.8%，总提升达到 +4.0 个点；相比只用 graph mixture 的 41.4%，还有 +2.4 个点增益。这是全文最关键的结果之一，因为它直接支持“图结构信号与内容质量信号大体互补”。

4. 计算成本：
完整 Common Crawl host graph 的 centrality 计算总共不到 9 GPU 小时。这个数字很关键，它说明方法不是理论上可行、工程上很重，而是真的可以作为预训练前处理步骤。

如果看消融，最值得注意的不是某个 centrality 指标谁赢得更多，而是三件事：PageRank 无明显收益；betweenness 的解释性更强且效果稳定；central/peripheral 的混合优于只押一边。它们共同说明，图结构信号的价值在于提供能力互补的数据子集，而不是简单排序出一批‘最好网页’。aa4:T4ac,This is a meaningful pretraining paper. Its contribution is not a more elaborate scorer, but a new selection axis: web-graph position. That matters for three reasons.

First, it provides a signal that appears complementary to content quality. When graph centrality is combined with the DCLM-fasttext quality classifier, performance improves beyond either signal alone. That suggests topology is not just a noisy proxy for existing quality scores.

Second, it sharpens the discussion around data mixtures and capability allocation. Central hosts seem to favor reusable abstractions and bridge-like information, while peripheral hosts contribute long-tail and specialized knowledge. The result is not 'higher quality is better' in a generic sense, but 'different structural regions induce different capability trade-offs.'

Third, the method is lightweight enough to matter in practice. Computing centrality on a 13.9M-node, 439.6M-edge host graph takes under 9 GPU hours and can be reused across many training runs. That is a much lower barrier than training multiple proxy models.

Overall, this looks like a credible addition to the pretraining data toolbox rather than a narrow benchmark trick.aa5:T938,The method, WebGraphMix, is simple by design. It computes structural centrality scores on the Common Crawl host-level hyperlink graph, maps those host scores back to documents in the pretraining corpus, and constructs mixtures that emphasize central hosts, peripheral hosts, or combinations of the two.

The graph is defined at the host level rather than the page level. Each node is a host such as wikipedia.org, and each directed edge indicates that one host links to another. The graph contains 13.9 million nodes and 439.6 million edges. This choice is important: host-level graphs are much more tractable than page-level graphs, and host identity aligns naturally with large-scale corpus provenance.

The paper mainly studies betweenness centrality and Katz centrality. Betweenness captures whether a host lies on many shortest paths and therefore acts as a bridge across otherwise weakly connected regions. Katz centrality measures global influence with distance decay. The authors also tried PageRank but did not observe gains, which is itself informative. For pretraining, being heavily linked may not be the same as providing broadly useful learning signals; bridge structure may matter more than raw popularity.

Once centrality scores are computed, documents are partitioned by host score and sampled into different mixtures: central-only, peripheral-only, and mixed settings such as 50/50. The point is not to solve a continuous optimization problem, but to create interpretable structural slices and observe how they affect learned capabilities.

A particularly useful part of the paper is the combination with content-based quality signals. The authors combine centrality with the DCLM-fasttext quality classifier using multiplicative and divisive scoring. The exact formulas matter less than the design intent: reward documents that are strong under both signals, while preventing one signal from completely dominating the other. The gains from this combination indicate that graph topology and textual quality capture different aspects of pretraining value.

The trade-off is clear. The method is cheap, unsupervised, and portable, but host-level centrality is coarse. It cannot distinguish high-value and low-value pages within the same host, and it may conflate structural prominence with actual textual usefulness for large aggregator sites.aa6:T87d,The experimental setup is strong and well controlled. WebGraphMix is integrated into the standardized DCLM pipeline. Models are trained at 400M and 1B scales with 8B and 28B tokens respectively. Tokenization, shuffling, optimization, and training procedures are held fixed so that the main variable is data selection. Evaluation uses the 23-task DCLM CORE v2 benchmark.

Several results stand out.

1. Central and peripheral regions favor different capabilities.
At 1B scale, sampling from structurally central hosts improves Symbolic and Algorithmic Reasoning by +1.4% over uniform sampling. In contrast, sampling from peripheral hosts improves Science and Factual Knowledge as well as Commonsense and Reasoning. This is one of the paper's most important findings: graph position is not a monotonic quality ranking. Different parts of the web graph support different capability profiles.

2. Mixed sampling beats one-sided selection.
Using betweenness centrality, a 50% central plus 50% peripheral mixture reaches 41.4% average across the 23 tasks, compared with 39.8% for uniform sampling. A +1.6 point average gain is substantial for a data-selection intervention with almost no training-time overhead.

3. Graph structure and content quality are complementary.
Combining centrality with the DCLM-fasttext quality classifier raises the average to 43.8%. That is +4.0 points over uniform sampling and +2.4 points over the graph-only 50/50 mixture. This is the strongest evidence that topology provides information largely orthogonal to content-based quality scoring.

4. The preprocessing cost is low.
Computing centrality over the full host graph takes fewer than 9 GPU hours in total. This matters because it makes the method operationally plausible for real pretraining pipelines.

The most informative ablations are not about tiny differences between centrality metrics. They are: PageRank does not help, betweenness is stable and interpretable, and central-peripheral mixtures outperform either extreme alone. Together these results suggest that graph structure is useful because it exposes complementary data regions, not because it identifies a single best subset.aa7:T5cc,This one is worth a careful read. Start with the introduction and the method overview to lock in the main hypothesis: central hosts expose reusable abstractions, while peripheral hosts preserve long-tail knowledge. Then read the graph construction details, the definitions of betweenness and Katz centrality, and the mapping from host scores to document sampling. Pay attention to why the paper chooses host-level structure and why it avoids training a document scorer.

For the experiments, read in this order: the main comparison table with uniform, central-only, peripheral-only, 50/50 mixtures, and the combined graph-plus-fasttext results; then the capability breakdowns, especially Symbolic and Algorithmic, Science and Factual, and Commonsense; then the centrality-metric comparison including the negative PageRank result; and finally the compute-cost discussion.

A few deeper questions are worth carrying through the paper. Is host-level centrality too coarse, and would page-level or hybrid scoring work better? Does the best central-peripheral ratio change with model size, token budget, or training stage, suggesting a curriculum or annealing schedule? Can graph structure be integrated with deduplication, quality filtering, and domain mixtures into a more systematic recipe? And why exactly do central hosts help symbolic reasoning: because of more tutorial-style text, more reusable templates, or stronger cross-domain connectivity? Those are good follow-up directions.aa8:T990,论文围绕 WINO 做系统复评。WINO 的思路是：先用 confidence-based adaptive unmasking 逐步生成 token，再根据已生成 token 在当前上下文下的置信度，把低置信 token 重新 mask，给模型一次改写机会。作者没有提出新 remasking 规则，而是把问题拆成三个层次来检查。

第一层是公平比较。作者指出，早期 WINO 结果缺少一个关键 baseline：强 confidence-based unmasking 本身，例如 Fast-dLLM。若不和这种强基线比较，很容易把“更聪明地决定先解哪些 token”带来的收益误记到 remasking 头上。于是论文在相同模型、相同解码预算下，直接比较 Fast-dLLM 与 Fast-dLLM+WINO，考察 remasking 的边际贡献。

第二层是机制诊断。作者追问：为什么 remasking 常常没用？他们的解释不是 remasking 选错了位置，而是更深一层——模型在这些被挑出来重做的位置上，往往提不出比原 token 更好的候选。也就是说，confidence 能发现“不太确定”，却不等于模型具备“重新采样后会更好”的能力。对于 absorbing masked diffusion，这个问题尤其自然，因为训练过程只学习从部分 mask 状态恢复原 token，并没有显式训练“撤销已作决定并在更完整上下文下重选”的行为。

第三层是解码条件依赖性。作者把评估扩展到 stochastic generation，考察温度采样、不同 block size、以及 learned Bernoulli unmasking policy。这里的核心观察是：remasking 的效果高度依赖 unmasking policy。若底层 unmasking 已经是偏确定性的 confidence policy，remasking 的空间很小；若 unmasking policy 本身更随机、更容易引入局部错误，remasking 才更可能修正这些错误。相应地，WINO 在 learned Bernoulli policy 上的收益明显大于在 deterministic Fast-dLLM 上的收益。

这篇论文还有一个重要点是把质量和多样性一起看。作者指出，confidence-based unmasking 已被发现会导致 diversity collapse，而 remasking 在 stochastic setting 下虽然能提高 pass@1，减少部分随机错误，但会进一步压缩样本多样性。也就是说，它改善的是单样本命中率，不一定改善采样分布质量。这个取舍对 diffusion LM 很关键，因为并行生成的一个卖点就是在给定延迟下提供更灵活的采样，而不是把输出进一步推向近似贪心。aa9:T883,实验部分的主线很清楚：重新比较 WINO 与强基线，并把评估从标准 greedy 扩展到 stochastic decoding。

在标准采样设置下，也就是短 block length、greedy decoding 或接近确定性的解码条件，WINO 与 Fast-dLLM 基本持平。作者的结论不是“完全无效”，而是“边际收益可以忽略，尤其一旦把 remasking 带来的额外 latency 算进去”。这点很重要，因为 diffusion LM 的核心卖点之一就是吞吐和并行度；如果一个修正机制带来额外步数，却没有换来稳定质量提升，那它在系统层面就站不住。

机制实验进一步支持上述判断。作者检查了被 remask 的位置在下一轮是否真的会被替换成更优 token，发现很多情况下模型并不能提出更好的替代项。这说明瓶颈不在 confidence estimator，而在底层 reverse model 的条件建模能力。换句话说，remasking 只是在暴露模型不会 revision，而不是自动赋予 revision 能力。

在 stochastic generation 下，结果更复杂。使用非零温度时，WINO 可以修复一部分采样噪声导致的错误，因此 pass@1 有提升；但与此同时，多样性下降更明显，延续并加重了 confidence-based unmasking 已知的 diversity collapse。这个现象说明 remasking 更像一个“去随机化”装置：它能把明显偏离高概率模式的 token 拉回来，但代价是样本分布更窄。

当 WINO 与 learned Bernoulli unmasking policy 结合时，收益明显大于与 deterministic Fast-dLLM 结合时。作者据此认为，remasking 的有效性不能脱离 unmasking policy 单独讨论。若前者是后验修正，后者决定了前面到底制造了多少可修正错误。

从全文节选里看不到完整的模型参数量、数据规模和所有具体数字表格，因此不能在这里可靠填入精确百分比或延迟倍数。但论文给出的定性结论很稳：1）标准 greedy/短块设置下，WINO 对强基线几乎没有净增益；2）随机采样下，pass@1 可能提升，但多样性进一步塌缩；3）在 learned Bernoulli policy 上，remasking 的边际价值显著更大。aaa:T483,This matters a lot for alternative language modeling paradigms, especially masked diffusion and related any-order generation. The value of the paper is not a new algorithm but a correction to an emerging narrative: masked dLLMs do not become reliably self-correcting just by adding a training-free remasking heuristic. The key point is that remasking only helps if the underlying model can actually propose a better replacement token after the position is masked again. If the reverse model lacks that conditional revision ability, remasking mostly adds steps without adding quality. For pretraining research, the implication is direct: if we want diffusion LMs to support robust revision, that ability may need to be built into the training objective, the forward process, the decoding policy, or post-training, rather than assumed to emerge from a post-hoc heuristic.

The contribution is mainly careful re-evaluation and mechanism clarification. It is not a paradigm shift by itself, but it should change how future papers choose baselines, report latency-quality tradeoffs, and reason about whether revision should be learned or decoded heuristically.aab:Ta49,The paper performs a systematic re-evaluation of WINO. WINO works by combining confidence-based adaptive unmasking with a confidence-based remasking step: after some tokens have been generated, low-confidence decoded tokens are masked again so the model gets another chance to fill them in. The authors do not propose a new remasking rule. Instead, they decompose the question into three layers.

First, they enforce a fair comparison. They argue that earlier WINO evaluations missed the most important baseline: strong confidence-based unmasking on its own, such as Fast-dLLM. Without that baseline, gains from better unmasking order can be mistakenly attributed to remasking. So the paper compares Fast-dLLM directly against Fast-dLLM+WINO under matched model and decoding budgets, isolating the marginal value of remasking.

Second, they diagnose the mechanism. Why does remasking often fail to help? Their answer is not merely that the wrong positions are selected. The deeper issue is that, at many remasked positions, the model cannot produce a better alternative token than the one it already chose. Confidence can identify uncertainty, but uncertainty does not imply that the model has a superior replacement available. This is especially natural in absorbing masked diffusion, where training teaches the model to reconstruct original tokens from partially masked inputs, but does not explicitly train it to revoke previous decisions and re-decide under richer context.

Third, they study dependence on decoding conditions. The evaluation is extended to stochastic generation, varying temperature, block size, and unmasking policy, including learned Bernoulli unmasking. The central observation is that remasking effectiveness is highly policy-dependent. If the base unmasking policy is already deterministic and confidence-driven, there may be little room left for remasking to improve anything. If the unmasking policy is more stochastic and introduces more local errors, remasking has more opportunities to repair them. Consistent with that view, WINO helps much more on top of learned Bernoulli policies than on top of deterministic Fast-dLLM.

A further strength of the paper is that it evaluates quality and diversity together. Confidence-based unmasking has already been linked to diversity collapse, and the paper shows that remasking can intensify this effect. Under stochastic decoding, WINO may improve pass@1 by correcting some sampling-induced errors, but it also narrows the sample distribution further. So the gain is not a free quality improvement; it is often a trade of diversity for single-sample accuracy.aac:T9a7,The experimental story is clean: re-compare WINO against a strong baseline, then extend the evaluation from standard greedy decoding to stochastic generation.

Under standard sampling settings, meaning short block lengths and greedy or near-deterministic decoding, WINO performs roughly on par with Fast-dLLM. The paper does not claim remasking is universally useless; the claim is narrower and more important: its marginal gain is often negligible once the extra latency from remasking is included. That matters because one of the main motivations for diffusion LMs is throughput and parallelism. If a correction mechanism adds decoding steps without delivering stable quality gains, it weakens the systems case for using it.

The mechanism analysis supports this conclusion. The authors inspect whether remasked positions are actually replaced by better tokens in subsequent steps and find that this often does not happen. That points to a limitation of the underlying reverse model rather than the confidence estimator. In other words, remasking exposes the absence of revision ability; it does not create that ability.

Under stochastic generation, the picture becomes more nuanced. At non-zero temperature, WINO can repair some errors introduced by sampling noise, so pass@1 improves. But diversity drops further, extending and worsening the diversity collapse already known for confidence-based unmasking. This suggests that remasking often acts as a de-randomization mechanism: it pulls samples back toward high-probability modes, which helps single-sample accuracy but narrows the output distribution.

When WINO is paired with learned Bernoulli unmasking policies, the gains are meaningfully larger than when it is paired with deterministic Fast-dLLM. The paper therefore argues that remasking cannot be evaluated in isolation from the unmasking policy. The latter determines how many correctable mistakes are created upstream.

The excerpt provided here does not include the full parameter counts, data scales, or all numeric tables, so I cannot safely reproduce exact percentages or latency multipliers. But the qualitative findings are clear and stable: (1) under standard greedy/short-block settings, WINO adds little over a strong confidence-based baseline; (2) under stochastic decoding, pass@1 can improve while diversity collapses further; and (3) remasking is substantially more useful with learned Bernoulli unmasking than with deterministic Fast-dLLM.aad:T5f0,This one is worth a careful read. Its impact is on recipe selection, model ranking, and the pretrain-to-posttrain interface.

First, it explicitly separates benchmark failure into knowledge failure and format-following failure. That matters because many low scores from base models are not evidence of weak pretraining; they are often caused by unparseable outputs or failure to follow the benchmark interface.

Second, the paper proposes an extremely lightweight soft-prompt tuning protocol that pushes format compliance close to saturation while keeping the model frozen. This makes benchmark scores a better proxy for latent knowledge rather than instruction-following polish.

If this finding holds broadly, it is a strong practical tool for early-stage pretraining recipe selection, where fully post-training every candidate is too expensive.ab2:T7bd,The core idea is simple: freeze the entire LLM and prepend a tiny learnable soft prompt, allowing the model to discover an internal continuous prompt that best matches the benchmark format. The soft prompt is not treated as a capability upgrade, but as an evaluation calibrator that removes benchmark-induced penalties unrelated to knowledge.

Concretely, the method uses a soft prompt of length 10, with each vector living in the model’s embedding dimension. For a 7B model, this is about 0.0006% trainable parameters. The base model remains fully frozen; only the soft prompt is optimized. Tuning is very short, around 80 optimization steps using 640 data points. The method is architecture-agnostic in the practical sense that it only requires access to the embedding input and does not depend on a special decoder head or model-specific adaptation module.

Two design choices are central. First, the paper introduces disentangled metrics: knowledge accuracy and format-following accuracy are measured separately. This lets the evaluator tell whether a model failed because it lacked the answer or because it failed to present it in a parseable form. Second, brief soft-prompt tuning is used as a proxy for base-model selection. The point is not to maximize benchmark scores per se, but to estimate which pretraining recipe will produce the strongest model after downstream post-training.

Compared with prompt engineering, soft prompts search a continuous space and avoid brittle dependence on wording. Compared with full post-training, they barely change the model and therefore act more like a way to surface existing knowledge than to inject new knowledge. Compared with few-shot prompting, they do not rely on manually crafted exemplars and are less constrained by superficial prompt templates. The paper also notes that even post-trained models can still benefit from soft prompts, which suggests that benchmark scores often contain interface noise even after alignment.ab3:T748,The experimental setup is fairly broad: 7 models and 7 benchmarks, including model families such as Llama-3, Qwen-3, Olmo-3, and Mistral-3, with tasks spanning math reasoning, reading comprehension, and factual QA. Several findings stand out. First, with only about 80 tuning steps, 640 examples, and 10 soft-prompt vectors, format-following accuracy reaches the 90–100% range. That strongly suggests that many benchmark failures of base models are interface failures rather than knowledge failures. Second, after soft-prompt tuning, the gap between base models and their post-trained counterparts narrows substantially on these benchmarks. The authors’ analysis and experiments conclude entropy is dominant, mismatch is negligible (Fig.3).
2) Entropy bound insight:
- Under common greedy target-only verification (draft proposes argmax tokens; verification uses only target probabilities without caching draft probs), acceptance is upper-bounded by max_y p(y). As entropy increases, max probability drops, producing a near-linear acceptance decline.
- With probabilistic rejection sampling, acceptance becomes the distributional overlap sum_v min(p(v), q(v)), which is much less sensitive to entropy shifts because it depends on global overlap rather than peak mass.
3) Training objective alignment: CE/KL-trained MTP drafts are not optimized for rejection-sampling acceptance since they only indirectly affect overlap. The paper proposes an end-to-end TV (total variation) loss that directly optimizes the multi-step overlap relevant to rejection sampling, improving acceptance and keeping it entropy-invariant.
4) Deployment recipe: do a lightweight pre-RL MTP training phase with e2e TV loss, then use rejection sampling during RL rollouts; no online MTP training during RL, reducing memory/latency overhead.ab6:T419,Its importance is less about a new preference optimizer and more about a new control surface for post-training. If some concept is merely spuriously correlated with preference labels, or if optimizing it induces off-target behavior, then the training signal should be adjusted so that this concept no longer provides useful evidence for the update. The paper connects this to probabilistic-inference views of post-training: shaping learning means controlling which evidence is admissible when distinguishing preferred from dispreferred generations. The forward process starts from a data sequence and randomly drops tokens with a time-dependent rate. The reverse process starts from a reference distribution and grows the sequence through insertion jumps. Using CTMC time reversal, the ideal reverse rate can be written in terms of the forward rate and time marginals; since the marginals are unknown, the work parameterizes the reverse rate with Transformer models and derives an evidence lower bound on the data likelihood. Two reverse parameterizations are proposed. 训练上，作者不是从零训练，而是从一个预训练 AR teacher 蒸馏。难点在于：联合离散采样没有直接可微的 likelihood 目标，也不能简单做逐位置 CE。论文提出 progressive self-forcing distillation。可以把它理解为一种逐步增强条件依赖的蒸馏过程：模型学习在给定前缀和噪声的情况下，生成未来多个位置；训练时通过逐步引入模型自身已生成的 token 作为后续位置条件，缓解 exposure bias，并让模型学到 next-k 内部的联合结构，而不是只学每个位置的独立边缘。这里“self-forcing”相对 teacher forcing 的区别在于，后续位置并不总是喂真值，而是逐渐让模型对自己生成的中间结果负责。这样做的原因很直接：如果始终用真值上下文训练，多 token 联合生成时会在测试阶段出现条件分布错位；如果一开始就完全自回馈，训练又容易不稳定。progressive 设计是在稳定性和分布匹配之间取中间点。

架构上，作者强调 fully causal，并尽量复用 AR backbone 与标准 serving 基础设施。直观上，它不是做一个双向 masked model，也不是 diffusion U-Net，而是在 Transformer 因果骨干上增加适合 next-k 联合生成的头部/解码结构，使得位置编码、KV cache、causal mask、现有部署栈都还能沿用。这一点很重要，因为如果建模范式要求完全不同的 serving stack，工业落地成本会很高。论文还讨论了为什么固定长度输出是设计原则之一：它牺牲了 speculative decoding 那种“有时一次接受很多 token”的上界，但换来了 batch 内步调一致、张量规则、调度简单，这在高负载吞吐场景里反而更有利。

从方法定位看，K-Forcing 和 Medusa/Hydra 这类多头预测不同。后者通常仍服务于 AR 验证或辅助草稿，最终依赖 target model 的逐步接受机制；K-Forcing 直接把 next-k 联合采样作为主生成对象。它和 diffusion LM 的差别也不只是“步数更少”，而是建模对象不同：K-Forcing 试图直接采样联合条件分布，diffusion LM 常见实现更接近对多个位置的边缘或近似联合做迭代修正。abd:T48f,The paper targets a specific bottleneck that standard AR language modeling does not address well: high-load batch serving. The question is not merely how to shave off single-request latency, but whether one can change the statistical modeling layer so that each forward pass emits multiple future tokens in a regular, fixed-length manner, thereby reducing decoding steps and improving throughput without collapsing generation quality. The authors argue that the two main alternatives each have a structural mismatch with this setting. Speculative decoding is attractive for latency, but its variable acceptance length creates desynchronized batches, irregular tensors, and KV-cache realignment overhead. Diffusion LMs can reveal multiple tokens, but they usually rely on iterative denoising over per-position marginals or approximate factorizations, so they still require many refinement steps. K-Forcing is framed as the problem of learning a conditional push-forward map that transforms independent noise into a joint sample of the next k tokens, conditioned on the prefix, while preserving fixed-length outputs and compatibility with causal serving infrastructure.abe:T4af,Its importance lies less in replacing AR training outright and more in opening a new modeling direction for inference-efficient language generation. First, it moves the acceleration discussion from systems and kernels to statistical parameterization: instead of making each AR step cheaper, it reduces the number of steps. Second, the fixed-length design is directly relevant to industrial serving, where throughput under heavy batching is often more important than interactive latency. Third, it offers a middle ground between standard AR decoding and iterative non-AR paradigms such as diffusion LMs: the model still reuses a causal backbone and AR teacher supervision, but learns a joint next-k sampler rather than a one-token conditional distribution. The contribution is therefore conceptual and empirical. It does not yet look like a drop-in replacement for frontier AR models, since quality degradation remains visible and k is still small, but it demonstrates that a modeling change alone can deliver nearly 3x throughput gains in batch serving. That is a meaningful result for future work on multi-token generation, joint sampling, AR distillation, and serving-aware pretraining objectives.abf:T9d3,The central idea is to cast next-k generation as an implicit generative model. Given a prefix x_{1:t}, the model does not explicitly parameterize the full joint distribution p(x_{t+1:t+k} | x_{1:t}) in a tractable form. Instead, it samples a set of independent base noise variables u_{1:k} (uniform noise in the paper) and applies a conditional mapping F_theta(x_{1:t}, u_{1:k}) that directly outputs k discrete tokens. This push-forward view avoids explicit normalization over a combinatorial joint space and avoids the iterative reverse process used by diffusion models.

Training is done by distilling from a pretrained AR teacher rather than training from scratch. The main difficulty is that joint discrete sampling does not naturally admit a simple tokenwise cross-entropy objective. The paper introduces progressive self-forcing distillation. The intuition is to gradually train the model to condition not only on the prefix but also on its own partially generated outputs when producing later positions within the k-token block. This is meant to capture intra-block dependency and reduce train-test mismatch. Pure teacher forcing would expose the model only to gold intermediate context, which is misaligned with test-time joint generation. Pure self-conditioning from the start would be harder to optimize and less stable. The progressive schedule is therefore a compromise between optimization stability and distribution matching.

Architecturally, the model is fully causal and intentionally close to standard AR infrastructure. It is not a bidirectional masked LM and not a diffusion-style denoiser. The design reuses a causal Transformer backbone, along with standard positional handling, causal masking, and serving machinery, while adding the machinery needed to emit a joint k-token sample in one pass. This compatibility point matters: if the modeling gain required a completely different serving stack, the practical value would be much lower.

The paper is also careful about what makes K-Forcing different from prior multi-token methods. It is not simply a Medusa- or Hydra-style auxiliary head that proposes several tokens for later AR verification. Those methods still rely on an acceptance mechanism tied to AR decoding. K-Forcing instead treats joint next-k sampling as the primary generation object. It also differs from diffusion LMs in what it tries to model: a direct conditional joint sampler, rather than an iterative denoising process over token marginals or approximate joint states.ac0:T6a1,Experiments are conducted on LM1B and OpenWebText, with the main message being a clear quality-speed trade-off. For k between 2 and 4, K-Forcing reduces the number of decoding passes and yields substantial throughput gains across low-, medium-, and high-load serving regimes. The headline result is a throughput improvement of up to roughly 3x, at the cost of modest but visible degradation relative to the AR teacher. Smaller k values preserve quality better, which makes k a practical deployment knob rather than a fixed modeling choice.

A strong point of the evaluation is that it measures serving throughput directly, not just perplexity or offline generation quality. That aligns with the paper's claim: the contribution is not that K-Forcing beats AR on language modeling metrics, but that fixed-length joint decoding is better matched to throughput-oriented serving than variable-length speculative acceptance. The experiments also span different load regimes, which helps show that the gain is not confined to a narrow operating point.

The ablations appear to focus on the role of progressive self-forcing, the effect of different k values, and the quality gap to the teacher as generation proceeds. The main takeaway is that progressive self-forcing is important for both stability and quality retention; naive parallel token prediction does not learn a sufficiently good joint structure. Another useful observation is that reducing k often hurts throughput less than it helps quality, leaving a practical middle regime. In scale terms, the paper uses standard corpora such as LM1B and OpenWebText and is positioned as a proof of feasibility rather than a frontier-scale training study.ac1:T6d4,Start with the introduction and the section analyzing why existing acceleration methods struggle in batch serving. That section contains the paper's sharpest argument. The discussion of speculative decoding is valuable because it ties variable acceptance lengths to concrete systems consequences: ragged tensors, desynchronized positions, and KV-cache realignment. The discussion of diffusion LMs is equally important because it clarifies that the issue is not just speed, but the lack of direct next-k joint sampling.

English, Spanish, and back-translated English variants are trained to contain the same underlying corpus knowledge while differing in language or wording. This setup is meant to remove common confounders such as data coverage and training budget. They then analyze standard MCQA scoring, where the selected option is the one with the highest log P(a_i | q), optionally normalized by characters or tokens. The flaw is that this probability is computed over one arbitrary answer string. ParaEval changes the evaluation protocol by generating multiple paraphrases for every option, including both correct answers and distractors. Each option receives the score of its most favorable paraphrase, and the model then chooses among options. The same idea is also applied to generative evaluation by expanding the reference set. The key distinction from prompt-sensitivity work is that ParaEval targets the scored answer surface form, not only the wording of the prompt.ac3:T465,Its value is primarily as an evaluation asset and a diagnostic study. For foundation-model researchers, the benchmark matters because Office automation is a strong stress test for long-horizon tool use: it requires precise parameter settings, stateful multi-step execution, and cross-application workflows. Unlike many existing agent benchmarks, the tasks are not synthetic and the scoring is not based on subjective LLM judges. OfficeEval is derived from the Level 1 and Level 2 MS Office practical exams in the NCRE. The benchmark contains 200 tasks spanning Word, Excel, and PowerPoint, and preserves the original rubric structure and point allocations. These are not short QA items. Each task requires a sequence of interdependent operations on real documents, spreadsheets, or presentations, such as formatting, formulas, pivot tables, chart customization, mail merge, animation settings, and layout edits. The full benchmark is decomposed into 7,118 machine-gradable criteria, and performance is reported as Score Rate (SR), the percentage of rubric points earned.

The evaluation compares two paradigms. The first is single-turn code generation, where the model receives the task and relevant files and outputs code in one shot. The second is an autonomous coding-agent setup, where the model can iteratively plan, write code, execute it, inspect outcomes, and revise. This distinction is important because it separates raw model competence from the recovery and iteration benefits provided by an agent scaffold.

Another strong design choice is the bilingual setup. Since the original tasks are in Chinese, the authors also construct English-translated versions of all tasks, documents, and scoring criteria. This allows them to test whether language understanding is the main bottleneck or whether the harder issue is Office-specific semantic execution.

The paper's most informative methodological addition is its error taxonomy. Instead of reporting only aggregate scores, it distinguishes execution crashes from logic or operation errors. Execution failures include code crashes and environment-level failures. Logic errors correspond to cases where code runs but the resulting Office artifact does not satisfy the rubric. This turns the benchmark into a diagnostic instrument rather than just a leaderboard.ac5:T701,The headline results are straightforward. Text is tokenized with a standard language tokenizer. Images are mapped into discrete visual sequences through a unified tokenizer. The tokenizer starts from a frozen SigLIP2 encoder, using its semantic visual features as the basis for quantization. A stack of attention blocks projects these features into a compact latent space. Discretization is done with Finite Scalar Quantization, avoiding an explicit learned codebook and its associated collapse issues. A symmetric projection module maps quantized features back to the original feature space for reconstruction and alignment. The tokenizer is trained with complementary objectives: the paper explicitly describes a captioning loss for language alignment and a pixel reconstruction loss for visual fidelity, and it also emphasizes semantic discrimination and reconstruction-oriented supervision. A 7B autoregressive model is then trained on large-scale text, image, and interleaved multimodal sequences with next-token prediction. The final stage applies GRPO using strong multimodal models as reward models for text-to-image generation and editing. The policy being optimized is the visual-token predictor, not a separate diffusion generator.ac9:T42a,The method builds on a standard self-distillation loss. The solver samples a reasoning trace y for a question x. The student distribution is πθ(·|x,y<t), while the self-teacher distribution is πθ(·|x,c,y<t), where c is additional context. The model minimizes a per-token divergence between these two distributions, with stop-gradient on the teacher branch. Prior analysis shows that, for KL-style divergences, the gradient resembles a policy-gradient update, but the advantage is token-specific rather than constant across the whole rollout as in GRPO. The proposed context, StepAlignFB, is generated by a frozen critic that reads the solver’s actual trace and produces step-by-step critique aligned to that trace. This differs from using a reference solution. A reference solution may be high quality, but it often diverges from the solver’s path in wording, decomposition, or intermediate choices. Step-aligned feedback instead addresses the rollout the model actually produced, so the contextual teacher shifts its distribution near the relevant errors.aca:T578,The audit is clean and well targeted. The authors study three high-redundancy MoE LMs: OLMoE-1B-7B-0924, Qwen1.5-MoE-A2.7B, and DeepSeek-V2-Lite. These models span major MoE design choices: different load-balancing objectives, different top-k activation ratios, scratch training versus dense upcycling, and the presence or absence of shared experts. At five representative layers per model, they evaluate four standard observational metrics: utilization rate, activation norm, mean routing weight when active, and activation standard deviation. These are corpus-level expert summaries. They then compare them against token-level interventional effects using router-aware ablation. For an expert active at token t, they zero that expert’s output and measure the resulting next-token loss change, ΔL_i^(t), as the functional-importance target. They also report residual-stream displacement, the gap norm, as a representation-level effect size. To rule out lack of statistical power, they add a stronger control: instead of using population-averaged routing summaries, they use the token-conditioned routing weight g_i(x_t) itself. This gives routing-derived signals their best possible chance. The key design choice is that the comparison is made on the same token, layer, and active-expert event, so the paper is genuinely testing whether observational rankings predict interventional consequences.acb:T466,The main result is a strong null. Across 60 metric-layer combinations—four observational metrics, five layers, three models—none reaches Bonferroni-corrected significance. First, the taxonomy is extended beyond the 12 dimensions of ESSENTIAL-WEB with two new ordinal dimensions: timeliness and cultural specificity. Timeliness measures how temporally durable a document’s value is, from highly time-sensitive content to fully evergreen material. Cultural specificity measures how tightly content is tied to a particular cultural or geographic context. The paper validates that these are genuinely new signals: pairwise NMI with existing dimensions is low, with timeliness reaching at most 0.21 and cultural specificity at most 0.11. This is an important systems choice: the goal is not only label quality, but making semantic annotation cheap enough to run over production-scale corpora. Third, they introduce a two-pass search framework for compound filters. Because each taxonomy dimension is ordinal and can be thresholded in multiple ways, exhaustive search over conjunctions and disjunctions is combinatorially expensive. Pass 1 evaluates dimensions independently at small scale to identify the strongest single signals. Pass 2 constructs compound filters from the top-performing dimensions and evaluates them at the same scale. Only the most promising candidates are then taken to full scaling-law style experiments. First, it reframes gen-PPL conceptually. A frozen AR scorer assigns high probability to sequences that are locally predictable under its learned conditional structure. That is not equivalent to text quality. Quality includes long-range semantic consistency, discourse structure, information content, and human plausibility. A sequence can be easy for the scorer to continue token by token while still being globally poor. The commonly paired empirical unigram entropy guardrail does not fix this, because it only filters out crude low-entropy collapse. It does not prevent sequences that use a reasonably broad vocabulary but combine tokens in shallow, low-quality ways.

Second, the authors build explicit counterexamples. This is the core technical move. They construct a suite of zero-parameter, deliberately naive samplers that do not learn a text distribution at all, yet achieve extremely strong gen-PPL. The exact sampler designs matter less than the broader point: by directly exploiting what the scorer finds predictable, one can manufacture outputs that score well while remaining incoherent to a human reader. This demonstrates that the failure is in the metric definition, not in a particular model family.

Third, they propose a replacement evaluation protocol centered on distributional comparison rather than scorer-based token likelihood. Instead of asking whether a generated sequence is easy for an AR model to predict, they ask whether generated samples statistically resemble human-written samples. The paper recommends distributional metrics such as MMD and energy distance, drawing from two-sample testing and divergence estimation. The key shift is from single-sample scoring to comparing generated and reference distributions. That aligns much better with the actual goal of unconditional generation and is harder to game through local predictability hacks.ad1:T683,The most important experimental result is the existence proof: on LM1B and OpenWebText, the zero-parameter naive samplers achieve gen-PPL numbers competitive with or better than recently published diffusion and flow-based language models, while maintaining non-degenerate empirical entropy. So this is not a trivial collapse case where the sampler repeats a few tokens. It passes the standard entropy guardrail and still produces poor text. That directly invalidates the common interpretation of low gen-PPL as evidence of high-quality generation.

A second important result is the clear decoupling between human-perceived quality and gen-PPL. Through examples and quantitative comparisons, the paper shows that sequences ranked highly by gen-PPL can be semantically weak or incoherent. This is not presented as a rare pathology but as a broad failure mode induced by the metric.

A third result comes from re-benchmarking recent non-AR models under distributional metrics. Once evaluated by sample-distribution similarity rather than scorer predictability, the picture of progress changes. Models that looked strong under gen-PPL do not necessarily remain strong, and models that better match human text distributions can be separated from those that merely exploit the scorer. The most informative thing to inspect is not the absolute ranking itself, but how rankings change between the old and new protocols.

From an experimental design standpoint, two details are worth noting. The paper uses both LM1B and OpenWebText, covering different text regimes, and it does more than criticize: it provides reproducible adversarial baselines plus an alternative protocol.ad2:T49c,Start with the introduction and the formal discussion of what gen-PPL actually measures. The largest model uses 460 routed experts with top-12 routing, and activates 5.93B parameters per token path, roughly five percent of the stored parameters. Each stage is initialized from the previous trained model. The paper emphasizes preserving the learned interfaces during growth, rather than treating expansion as a mostly random reinitialization. Two supporting design choices matter for the memory budget. The model uses BrahmicTokenizer-131K, a 131,072-token byte-level BPE tokenizer, and replaces a conventional learned embedding table with a Kronecker input embedding. A standard lookup table at this vocabulary and width would require about 537M trainable parameters. The Kronecker projection uses about 33.55M trainable parameters and constructs embeddings from frozen byte and position bases through a trained projection. It also avoids materializing a reconstruction table that would otherwise occupy about 2.15GB per GPU, or about 17GB across the node.ad4:T85f,方法核心是 OPDLM 和其中的 On-Policy Distillation。学生模型来自一个 ARLM checkpoint，但把 causal attention 改成 bidirectional attention，使其可以对被 mask 的任意位置做条件建模。教师模型则保留原始冻结 ARLM。关键难点在于，AR teacher 和 DLM student 的状态空间不同：teacher 习惯在完整左前缀上做 next-token prediction，student 则在部分已知、部分 mask 的序列状态上做去噪。作者的处理方式不是把 teacher 直接搬到随机 mask 状态上，而是让 student 先按自己的 diffusion 解码策略 rollout 出一条反向去噪轨迹，从中采样一个部分去噪状态 x_t，再对其中仍被 mask 的位置做蒸馏。

蒸馏目标的构造很讲究。对每个 masked 位置 i，student 输出该位置的 token 分布；teacher 则读取终态序列 x_0 中该位置之前的 causal prefix，给出 AR 条件分布，作为该位置的监督信号。也就是说，teacher 提供的是“如果按 AR 方式生成到这里，应该偏向哪些 token”，student 学的是“在当前部分去噪状态下，对这些尚未恢复的位置给出与 teacher 一致的分布”。这样做同时解决两件事：一是知识保留，因为监督直接来自原 AR 模型的 logits，而不是只靠 diffusion NELBO 重新学；二是 train-test mismatch，因为训练样本来自 student 自己的 on-policy rollout，而不是离线随机 mask。

论文还加入 rollout-length curriculum。直觉上，训练初期学生模型还不稳定，如果一开始就在很长的去噪轨迹上做 on-policy 学习，状态分布会太差，蒸馏信号也更噪。于是作者逐步增加 rollout 长度，让学生先在较短、较容易的轨迹上对齐，再扩展到更接近真实推理的状态。这个设计和序列决策里的 curriculum / DAGGER 风格很接近，但这里的监督源是冻结 AR teacher。另一个值得注意的点是，作者把 OPDLM 明确定位成 general-purpose DLM 和 task-specific DLM 两种用法：既可以把通用 AR 基座转成通用 DLM，也可以在特定任务上做更便宜的转换。ad5:T802,The central idea is OPDLM, trained with On-Policy Distillation. The student starts from an ARLM checkpoint whose causal attention is replaced with bidirectional attention, enabling denoising over arbitrary masked positions. The teacher is the original frozen ARLM. The main challenge is that the teacher and student do not share the same state space: the teacher predicts the next token from a causal prefix, while the student denoises partially observed sequences.

The paper resolves this by letting the student generate its own reverse denoising trajectories. At each training step, the student rolls out a trajectory under its own diffusion decoding policy, and one partially denoised state x_t is sampled from that trajectory. Distillation is then applied only to the still-masked positions in x_t. For each masked position i, the student predicts a token distribution conditioned on the partially denoised sequence, while the teacher provides target logits conditioned on the causal prefix of the terminal sequence x_0 up to position i. In effect, the teacher says what an AR model would prefer at that position, and the student learns to match that preference on the states it will actually encounter during inference.

This design addresses both mismatches at once. Knowledge retention improves because supervision comes directly from the original AR teacher rather than from relearning everything through a diffusion NELBO. Train–test mismatch is reduced because training states are on-policy student states, not uniformly random masks. The paper also introduces a rollout-length curriculum: early in training, the student is supervised on shorter and easier trajectories, and the rollout horizon is gradually increased as the model stabilizes. That choice is important for optimization, since long on-policy trajectories from an immature student would otherwise create noisy and low-quality supervision. The framework is presented both as a general-purpose AR-to-DLM conversion method and as a cheaper task-specific DLM adaptation method.ad6:T597,The most informative results are about efficiency and the necessity of on-policy training. On efficiency, the headline number is striking: OPDLM-8B uses only 0.066B training tokens and 4.2 × 10^18 FLOPs, while establishing a new known Pareto frontier on AIME-24. Relative to prior DLM or AR-to-DLM conversion systems such as LLaDA-8B, Dream-7B, SDAR-8B, and Fast-dLLM-v2-7B, the required training tokens are reduced by roughly 15× to 7,000×. That is not a marginal saving; it turns conversion into something much closer to heavy post-training than continued pretraining.

On task performance, the paper evaluates across general-purpose and reasoning-heavy settings, including math and coding, and also studies task-specific conversion. The emphasis is not on claiming the single best absolute score everywhere, but on maintaining strong performance under dramatically lower training cost. The key ablation compares on-policy and off-policy distillation, and on-policy consistently wins, directly supporting the train–inference mismatch argument. Additional appendices study smaller-scale settings, the effect of teacher size, multi-seed evaluation on GPQA-Diamond and AIME variants, and comparisons against standard supervised fine-tuning. The inference section also shows that the converted DLM can exploit multi-token decoding, so the method is not merely changing the training loss while keeping AR-like inference behavior.ad7:T527,Read it in the order of problem setup, method, efficiency evidence, and ablations. First, benchmark construction: the authors assemble 43 benchmarks with more than 30,000 questions spanning math, coding, puzzles, causality, theory of mind, strategic reasoning, and multi-turn tool-use settings. The key constraint is that models are prevented from emitting reasoning tokens before the answer, so the setup aims to measure latent reasoning rather than explicit CoT. Second, capability scaling via task-completion horizons: following and extending prior horizon work, they estimate the human time required for tasks that a model completes with 50% success rate. To make this credible, they explicitly model uncertainty in human solve times using a mix of real human timings, collected baselines, and calibrated model-based estimates, then propagate uncertainty through hierarchical bootstrap over benchmarks, problems, model stochasticity, and time estimates. Third, they define a reasoning-token horizon using o3-mini as an anchor reasoning model: task difficulty is measured by the minimum number of reasoning tokens the anchor needs to solve the task within k attempts. 这个框架和传统做法的区别有三点。其一，传统 recipe 往往只看模型参数量、token 数或经验 warmup 规则，而这里显式把“checkpoint 当前状态”作为一等公民。其二，传统超参迁移通常依赖同架构、同数据、相近训练阶段的经验复用；这里试图用 loss-based coordinate 把不同生命周期的 checkpoint 放到统一坐标系。其三，很多 CPT 调参默认先固定 batch 再找 LR，或者反过来分步搜索；这篇工作把二者都写成 compute 的函数，目标是一次性 zero-shot 给出配置。

从全文表述看，这个方法隐含几个前提。一个前提是 target-domain loss 与有效 compute 之间存在足够平滑、可拟合的关系，否则 C_pre 的反演会不稳。另一个前提是 proxy 模型上发现的最优超参函数在更大模型和不同架构上保持形状稳定，只需做尺度迁移。论文声称 Dense 和 MoE 都验证了这一点，但阅读时需要特别留意：这种稳定性到底是“趋势一致”，还是参数化形式和系数都能可靠迁移。这里决定了方法是 recipe 级工具，还是只是一种较好的初始化器。ae2:T8e2,The method has two stages.

Stage 1 is empirical law discovery. The authors train small proxy models under continued pre-training across a range of compute budgets and hyperparameter settings, then identify how the optimal learning rate and batch size evolve as training proceeds. The main empirical pattern reported in the paper is that the optimal batch size increases monotonically with compute budget, while the optimal learning rate decreases accordingly. Rather than fitting hyperparameters directly against steps, the framework uses standard loss-compute scaling relationships to derive mappings from compute to optimal hyperparameters. This is an important design choice because compute is a more transferable coordinate than raw step count when model size and setup vary.

Stage 2 is quantifying the initial optimization state. This is the key conceptual move. A checkpoint inherited from prior pre-training is treated as a point on a continuous target-domain training trajectory. The paper maps the checkpoint’s validation loss on the target domain to an equivalent amount of pre-training compute, denoted C_pre. Planned continued pre-training compute is C_cpt, and the total effective compute becomes C_total = C_pre + C_cpt. The optimal learning rate and batch size are then predicted zero-shot by plugging C_total into the scaling laws discovered in Stage 1.

Compared with standard practice, the framework differs in three ways. First, it explicitly models checkpoint state instead of relying on model size, token count, or inherited recipes alone. Second, it uses a loss-based coordinate system to place checkpoints from different lifecycle stages onto a common axis. Third, it aims to predict both LR and batch size jointly, instead of doing sequential search or fixing one while tuning the other.

The method does rely on nontrivial assumptions. The target-domain loss-to-compute curve must be smooth enough to invert reliably. The proxy-discovered hyperparameter laws must also transfer in shape across larger scales and different architectures. The paper claims this holds for both dense and MoE models, but the strength of that claim depends on whether only the trend transfers or the actual parameterized law remains accurate enough for zero-shot use.ae3:T78f,The experimental story has three layers.

First, the paper needs to show that the scaling regularities actually exist. The key question when reading the figures is whether this is merely local monotonicity or a clean functional law over a broad compute range.

Second, the paper needs to validate equivalent pre-training compute. The central claim is that checkpoints from arbitrary prior states can be mapped to C_pre using target-domain validation loss, and that this quantity is sufficient to predict good hyperparameters for future CPT. The most informative comparisons are against heuristic recipes and explicit grid search, ideally across multiple starting checkpoints. 第一步是构造连续 CoT 目标。作者假设训练数据里有显式文本 CoT d1:L 和最终答案 x1:N。先用一个 encoder 把文本 CoT 压缩成长度为 K、维度为 D 的连续表示 e1:K。这里的 e-space 更像“压缩后的思维表示”，适合承载语义，但未必适合直接做 prompt-conditioned AR 生成。

First, the model defines a continuous target for chain-of-thought. Given supervised examples with prompt q, explicit textual CoT d1:L, and answer x1:N, an encoder compresses the textual rationale into a continuous sequence e1:K of length K and dimension D. This e-space is optimized for semantic compression, but it is not necessarily easy to model autoregressively conditioned on the prompt.

Second, the paper introduces an LLM-facing thought space u1:K that is easier to sample and score causally. Instead of modeling e directly, NF-CoT maps e to u through an invertible transformation Fθ. In the u-space, the thought sequence follows a causal Gaussian density: each latent thought token is generated left-to-right with mean and variance conditioned on the prompt and previous thought tokens. Because the transformation is invertible, the exact density of the original continuous thought can be computed via the change-of-variables formula. This is the key design choice. The flow is not used merely as a generic density estimator; it bridges a semantically meaningful compressed space and an autoregressively tractable space.

Third, the model jointly generates latent thoughts and textual answers using a shared causal LLM backbone. On top of the backbone, one head models the continuous thought density and another head models the answer tokens. Training maximizes the joint likelihood of latent thoughts and answers. Since the thought likelihood is tractable, the same interface also supports policy-gradient optimization directly in the continuous reasoning space.

Relative to prior work, the distinctions are sharp. Compared with Coconut-style methods, NF-CoT is stochastic and likelihood-based rather than deterministic hidden-state rollout. Compared with diffusion-based latent reasoning, it supports one-pass left-to-right sampling instead of iterative denoising. Compared with two-stage VAE-plus-generator pipelines, it more tightly couples latent-thought generation with the causal LM backbone and answer generation.ae7:T65d,The evaluation is conducted on code reasoning and program synthesis benchmarks: MBPP, MBPP+, HumanEval, HumanEval+, and LiveCodeBench v6. The exact numbers matter less than the closed loop the paper demonstrates: explicit CoT supervision is compressed into continuous thoughts; those thoughts are modeled with exact likelihood; inference remains causal and one-pass; and the same latent space can be refined with policy gradients.
