First, it aligns student and teacher token sequences into text-consistent spans. Because different tokenizers produce different sequence lengths, per-position KD is ill-defined. The method uses deterministic dynamic-programming alignment to form paired chunks that decode to the same underlying text. Within each chunk, token probabilities are merged using the autoregressive chain rule to obtain chunk-level distributions. Second, it builds a sparse projection matrix W of shape |V_S| by |V_T|, mapping student-vocabulary probabilities into the teacher vocabulary space. The projection is constructed with canonicalized string matching and multi-token decoding rules, rather than exact string equality alone, and it can optionally be refined during KD. Third, it introduces two loss variants. P-KL removes the common/uncommon partition and aligns full projected distributions, which is useful when critical tokens are poorly covered by strict common-token matching. H-KL uses top-ranked mappings under W and is better suited to cases where the common coverage is already reasonably good but exact matching is too conservative. A coverage audit over categories such as numerals guides the choice between P-KL and H-KL. The multi-teacher extension combines projected KD losses from heterogeneous teachers, with static weighting reported to be more reliable than adaptive weighting.b3c:T73a,The method is simple, but the design choice is precise. The authors analyze token-level entropy distributions in long CoT responses and find that neither average entropy over all tokens nor average entropy over only the high-entropy tokens reliably separates good and bad reasoning samples. What works better is the sum of entropy over only the top-k% highest-entropy tokens. This leads to High-Entropy Sum (HES): compute token entropies for a response under a scoring model, select the top-k% tokens by entropy, and sum their entropy values to obtain a sample-quality score.

Why use a sum instead of an average? That is the key idea in the paper. Averaging dilutes the few critical decision points inside long reasoning traces. Summation preserves two signals at once: whether the sample contains genuinely difficult or branching moments, and how many such moments it contains. For long CoT, that is a better proxy for multi-step useful reasoning than a global average over mostly low-information tokens.

The paper then plugs HES into three training paradigms:
1. SFT: rank existing reasoning samples by HES and train only on the top fraction.
2. RFT: sample multiple candidate responses for the same query and use HES as the selection function for which traces to keep.
3. RL: oversample rollouts, then keep only the top-ranked subset by HES for policy updates instead of updating on all rollouts.

Two technical properties matter. First, HES is training-free: no reward model and no auxiliary selector need to be trained. Second, it is relatively aligned with the target model because the score comes from the model’s own token uncertainty, not from an external judge. The paper also shows that HES computed by a 0.6B model can be nearly as useful as HES computed by an 8B model, which makes it practical as a low-cost data curation component.b3d:T91c,The experimental coverage across SFT, RFT, and RL is the strongest part of the paper.

In SFT, the authors report that training on only the top 20% of samples ranked by HES already reaches performance comparable to using the full dataset, while using the top 80% consistently surpasses the full-data baseline. This suggests that a substantial fraction of raw reasoning data is low-yield, and that simply scaling data volume does not guarantee better reasoning supervision. A particularly important result is that HES computed by a lightweight 0.6B model performs comparably to HES computed by an 8B model for data selection, which sharply lowers the cost of offline curation.

In RFT, HES is used as a training-free selection signal among multiple sampled responses for the same prompt. It significantly outperforms random selection. The point here is not that it beats every sophisticated reward mechanism, but that it improves self-bootstrapped data quality with almost no additional training overhead.

In RL, the paper uses an oversample-then-filter strategy: generate more rollouts than usual, rank them by HES, and keep only the top 50% for policy updates. This outperforms the standard setting where all rollouts are used. The implication is important for reasoning RL: more rollouts are not always better if many of them are low-quality and inject noisy gradients. HES acts as a lightweight rollout denoiser.

The ablation logic is also strong. The paper compares HES against length, perplexity, average token entropy, total entropy over all tokens, and average entropy over only the high-entropy tokens. The conclusion is that only the sum over high-entropy tokens consistently separates sample quality. That matters because it shows the gain is not from “using entropy” in general, but from using entropy in a way that respects the sparse structure of long reasoning.

The explicit numbers available from the provided text are: top 0.5% high-entropy tokens, top 20% HES-ranked data for near-full SFT performance, top 80% for surpassing the baseline, top 50% rollout retention in RL, and 0.6B scoring models matching 8B scoring models closely. When reading the full paper, it is worth extracting the absolute benchmark scores and gains, because the paper’s credibility depends heavily on consistency across paradigms.b3e:T7c3,This one deserves a careful read. The main value is not the formula itself, but how a very small token-level statistic becomes a unified data selection principle.

Start with the introduction and Figure 1. Figure 1 is the foundation of the paper: it shows that several natural entropy-based summaries fail, while high-entropy sum separates high- and low-quality reasoning samples. If that empirical observation is weak, the rest of the method is much less convincing.

Then read the HES definition and think through two design choices: why only the top-k% tokens, and why sum rather than average. These choices encode a structural hypothesis about long CoT: the most useful learning signal is concentrated in a few planning, branching, or reflection points, not spread uniformly across the whole trace.

After that, read experiments by training paradigm. In SFT, focus on retention ratio versus performance to judge whether HES is removing noise or discarding useful diversity. In RFT, compare it against random and other heuristics. In RL, pay attention to why oversampling plus filtering beats using all rollouts, and whether this introduces bias or variance trade-offs.

The most important ablations are: sensitivity to k, dependence on the size of the scoring model, and comparisons against length / perplexity / average entropy baselines. Those are the sections that tell you whether HES is robust or just a narrow heuristic.

Two deeper questions are worth keeping in mind. First, because HES depends on model entropy, it may prefer samples that are hard-but-learnable for the current model, not necessarily samples that are objectively best. That could be useful as an implicit curriculum, but it could also bias selection. Second, the paper is about reasoning data; whether the same principle transfers to pretraining-stage token value estimation remains open. A solid first pass takes about 60 to 90 minutes, and the easiest reproduction path is the offline SFT filtering setup.b3f:T94c,技术路线分三层。

第一层是连续可微 rollout 下的理论化。作者采用 differentiable rollout / additive-noise parameterization，把策略采样写成由噪声驱动的可微变换，然后分析 PPO/GRPO 的 actor 更新。结论是，在这种参数化下，actor 梯度的期望里会出现沿轨迹反传的 costate，而这个 costate 的条件期望等于 value function 对状态的梯度，也就是 value gradient。这里的关键不是把 PPO 变成传统 actor-critic，而是说明即便没有显式训练一个 V 网络，actor 反向传播本身也携带了与 value gradient 同型的信号。

第二层是把这个结论搬到离散 transformer。真实 LLM 不是连续动作控制，而是离散 token 采样。作者讨论了离散采样造成的 sampling gap，并证明 autodiff 计算得到的经验 costate 可以近似连续 BPTT costate，误差受两个因素控制：一是采样离散化带来的 gap，二是策略熵。直观上，分布越尖、采样越接近 argmax，离散动作对隐藏状态的扰动越像一条局部可微路径；同时 transformer 的 attention 让后续 token 的损失能通过上下文表示回传到前面 token 的隐藏状态，于是形成一种“绕过采样瓶颈”的 credit transport。论文强调 attention 不是 value function，但它提供了 value-gradient 信号传播的结构通道。

第三层是 RL-impact decomposition。作者把 RL 带来的潜在收益拆成 usable value-gradient signal 与 reachable reward headroom 的乘性或组合关系。前者衡量当前 checkpoint 的内部表示和策略形状是否允许 reward 信号有效回传；后者衡量当前策略离 reward 饱和还有多远。如果模型太弱，虽然 headroom 大，但 value-gradient 信号可能传不动；如果模型太强，虽然 credit transport 好，但 headroom 已经很小，RL 收益也有限。于是最适合做 RL 的 checkpoint 应该处在一个中间区间：既足够成熟，能传递信用；又没有完全饱和，还留有可优化空间。

与现有解释的区别在于，作者不是从 advantage normalization、group sampling 或 KL regularization 这些训练技巧出发解释 GRPO，而是从反向传播结构本身解释“critic-free 为何不完全 value-free”。这使得论文更像在建立一个机制模型，而不是给出局部经验法则。b40:T48e,The contribution is more than a post hoc story for GRPO. It gives a concrete mechanism-level bridge between pretraining and post-training. A common narrative says RL mainly works by exploration plus scalar reward shaping, but that does not explain why long-sequence, terminal-reward, critic-free optimization can still improve reasoning so reliably in transformers. The value-gradient hypothesis offers a more architecture-aware explanation: backward passes through hidden states and attention already carry an approximate credit-transport signal. For pretraining researchers, this matters in two ways. First, RL effectiveness may depend not only on reward quality, but also on whether a checkpoint has learned representations that support this kind of differentiable credit transport. Second, the question of when to start RL becomes measurable rather than purely heuristic. In terms of contribution type, this is primarily an explanatory framework with predictive implications, not a new RL algorithm. But if the hypothesis holds up, it can influence checkpoint selection, mid-training strategy, cooldown design, and the choice of base models for RL post-training.b41:T9c1,The technical argument has three layers.

First, the paper analyzes actor updates under a differentiable rollout / additive-noise parameterization. Policy sampling is written as a differentiable transformation of exogenous noise, and the PPO/GRPO actor gradient is studied in that setting. The result is that the expected actor update contains a trajectory-wise backward-propagated costate whose conditional expectation matches the gradient of the value function with respect to state, i.e. the value gradient. The point is not to reintroduce a learned critic under another name, but to show that even without an explicit value network, the actor backward pass itself can carry a value-gradient-like signal.

Second, the paper transfers this picture to discrete transformer policies. Real LLMs generate discrete tokens, so exact pathwise differentiation is unavailable. The authors analyze the sampling gap induced by discretization and show that the empirical costate obtained by autodiff can approximate the continuous BPTT costate, with error controlled by the sampling gap and policy entropy. Intuitively, when the policy is sharper and sampling stays closer to a locally stable mode, the discrete trajectory behaves more like a differentiable path. Meanwhile, transformer attention provides a structural route for later losses to propagate back through contextual representations, partially bypassing the token-sampling bottleneck. Attention is not itself a value function, but it acts as a transport mechanism for value-gradient-like credit.

Third, the paper derives an RL-impact decomposition. The expected benefit of RL is separated into usable value-gradient signal and reachable reward headroom. The first term captures whether the current checkpoint’s representations and policy geometry allow reward information to propagate effectively. The second captures how much reward improvement is still available before saturation. A weak checkpoint may have large headroom but poor credit transport; a very strong checkpoint may have good transport but little remaining headroom. The best RL starting point should therefore lie in an intermediate regime: mature enough to transmit credit, but not yet saturated.

Relative to prior explanations of GRPO, the novelty is that the paper does not focus on advantage normalization, group sampling, or KL regularization as the main reason for success. Instead, it explains critic-free RL through the backward structure of transformers themselves.b42:T7f2,The experiments are organized around three questions: whether the proposed signal can be observed in real transformers, whether it predicts RL gains, and whether it helps choose checkpoints.

The first set of experiments validates the correspondence between empirical costates and value-gradient-like signals. The authors extract a costate or credit signal from autodiff in discrete transformers and compare it with the target quantity suggested by the continuous-relaxation analysis. The reported alignment improves as the sampling gap shrinks and policy entropy decreases, which matches the theory. In other words, the actor backward pass looks more value-gradient-like when the model operates in a moderately confident but not fully collapsed regime.

The second set tests the predictive power of the RL-impact decomposition. Multiple checkpoints along pretraining are evaluated, with usable value-gradient signal and reward headroom measured before RL, then compared against actual PPO/GRPO gains. The main result is that RL gains are typically not monotonic in checkpoint maturity. Early checkpoints have more headroom but weaker credit transport; late checkpoints are more stable but closer to reward saturation. Intermediate checkpoints often benefit the most.

The third set likely includes ablations over sampling temperature/entropy, reward structure (terminal-only versus process reward), PPO versus GRPO, and analyses of where attention-based credit transport appears across layers or token positions. The emphasis is not benchmark chasing, but mechanism validation and predictive correlation.

The provided excerpt does not include the full tables, so model sizes, number of checkpoints, task suites, and exact gain values cannot be quoted reliably here. When reading the paper, the most important things to verify are: (1) the concrete computable proxy used for usable value-gradient signal, (2) its correlation or ranking consistency with downstream RL gains, and (3) robustness across entropy regimes and task lengths.b43:T7a1,This one is worth a careful read. A good order is: theory first, mechanism validation second, recipe implications third.

Start with the introduction and setup. The key is not the GRPO formula itself, but the motivating puzzle: how can long-range credit assignment work without a critic? That question anchors the whole paper.

Then read the continuous-relaxation theory carefully. Focus on three points: what assumptions are required by the additive-noise / differentiable-rollout setup, how the costate appears through BPTT, and why its conditional expectation matches the value gradient. This determines whether the paper is making a real derivation or only an analogy.

Next, read the discrete-transformer approximation section. Pay close attention to how sampling gap, policy entropy, and attention-based credit transport enter the approximation error. This is the most important part to scrutinize, because it decides whether the theory actually transfers from continuous control to real LLMs.

In the experiments, prioritize the figures that track checkpoints along pretraining and decompose RL gains into signal and headroom. If only a few figures can be read, choose: (1) alignment between empirical costates and the theoretical quantity, (2) RL gain versus checkpoint stage, and (3) checkpoint ranking quality from the decomposition metric.

Finally, revisit the assumptions and failure modes. Check whether outcome-only reward is sufficient, what role group normalization plays in the theory, whether the KL term is merely stabilizing, and whether the hypothesis breaks under high-entropy or strongly exploratory sampling. Those details determine whether the paper is mainly an explanation of current recipes or a guide for designing new ones.

If you already know PPO/RLHF well, the main text should take around 60–90 minutes. To really internalize it, the appendix is worth reading, especially the proofs and the exact metric definitions.b44:T407,SCRL first uses an external LLM and a reference solution to derive an ordered curriculum of K verifiable subproblems. The final subproblem is the original problem. The policy is then asked to answer all K subproblems in a single on-policy rollout. This differs from prefix-hint curricula: the intermediate facts are not injected as fixed context; the model must derive them itself. Each subproblem answer is verified separately. A progress-aware correction keeps only the longest consecutive solved prefix, so a reward vector such as [1,1,0,1] becomes [1,1,0,0]. This prevents accidental success on later subproblems from receiving credit when earlier dependencies were not solved. The key optimization step is subproblem-level normalization: rewards are normalized independently at each subproblem position, and the resulting advantages are assigned to the corresponding answer spans. The method also uses mixed-group training, jointly optimizing curriculum rollouts and original-problem rollouts to reduce prompt-format mismatch.b45:Ta12,方法设计的优点是控制变量做得很干净。作者把 self-play 形式化成 proposer-solver 双角色系统，但实现上沿用常见做法，用同一个模型配两个 prompt template。每个 outer step 中，proposer 先生成任务 q=(program, input)，环境 E 执行得到 ground-truth output o*(q)，然后数据 gate F 决定这个任务是否进入训练池 D_t。进入池子的任务再交给 solver 作答，并根据某种 reward 更新策略。

论文的关键不是提出一个新 reward，而是把 gate 和 reward 当成两条独立轴来系统扫描。任务环境有两个：一个是真实 Python output prediction，另一个是作者专门构造的 deterministic DSL twin task，包含 15 个操作符，刻意去掉三类混杂因素：预训练先验、输出歧义、执行器噪声。这样如果在 DSL 上仍然复现塌缩，就能说明问题来自优化动力学，而不是 Python 语义、代码执行噪声或模型已有知识。

作者测试了多种 reward 设定，其中最关键的是 self-consistency reward 与 grounded reward 的对比。self-consistency reward 不看真实答案，只看 solver 多次采样之间是否一致；grounded reward 则依赖执行真值。直觉上很多人会以为，只要 reward grounded enough，坏数据自然会被低奖励压下去。但论文证明这不成立：当训练池里混入歧义任务或可被投机的任务时，self-consistency 会把“容易形成错误共识”的样本推成高奖励样本，坏数据不是被 down-weight，而是被主动放大。

全文有三个机制性发现。第一，intrinsic-grounded gap：作者定义 solver 的 intrinsic reward 与 grounded accuracy 之间的差值，用来量化“模型内部自洽”和“真实正确”之间的脱钩。一旦 gap 持续扩大，就说明系统正在向错误但稳定的 attractor 收敛。第二，Grounded Proposer Paradox：如果 solver 用的是 self-consistency reward，那么一个能访问 ground truth 的 proposer 反而会更快把系统推向塌缩，因为它更擅长生成结构干净、格式统一、最容易形成错误共识的任务，等于给 spurious attractor 铺路。第三，连续 gate strictness ε 分析：作者不只比较开/关两种 gate，而是把 gate 放松程度参数化，观察到 sharp phase transition，而且是两阶段结构——训练侧指标先在较低 ε 处开始解耦，但下游验证精度要到更高 ε 才明显崩。这说明只看训练 reward 或自一致性曲线，会晚于真实病灶，或者说会看错病灶。b46:T88c,实验分两条主线。第一条是在 Python output-prediction 任务上做完整 self-play，第二条是在 deterministic DSL twin 上复现实验。DSL 的作用很关键：它去除了预训练偏置、输出歧义和 executor noise，因此如果 collapse 仍出现，就说明塌缩不是环境偶然性，而是训练闭环自身的动力学结果。作者报告的总体结论很强：有 strict gate 时，测试过的 reward 变体都能稳定训练，甚至包括完全不访问 ground truth 的 self-consistency reward；没有 gate 时，所有 reward 变体都不够，哪怕 solver reward grounded in execution truth，也会在含歧义输出的任务上塌缩。

第二条主线是 collapse 机制分析。作者展示了 intrinsic-grounded gap 随训练扩大的现象：solver 在 self-consistency reward 上越来越高，但 grounded accuracy 下降或脱钩，说明模型学到的是“群内一致”而不是真实求解。这个现象在 Python 和 DSL 两个环境都复现，支撑了“优化动力学而非环境噪声”的判断。

Grounded Proposer Paradox 的实验也很有意思。直觉上 proposer 越 grounded 越安全，但结果相反：当 solver 依赖 self-consistency 时，grounded proposer 会更快 collapse。原因不是 proposer 变差，而是它更高效地把训练分布集中到那些最容易形成错误共识的 clean tasks 上。这个结果对很多 proposer-solver 共训练系统是个提醒：提升 proposer 质量，不一定提升系统稳定性，取决于 solver reward 的形状。

连续 gate strictness ε 的实验给出了更细的相图。随着 ε 放松，训练指标先出现异常分叉，但验证准确率在一段区间内还能维持，直到 ε 更高时才突然掉下去。这个两阶段结构说明，如果只用训练 reward 监控 self-play，很可能在系统已经进入危险区后仍误判为“训练正常”。

从摘要和正文可见，论文更强调机制和相变，而不是堆很多 benchmark 数字。对读者来说，最重要的不是某个绝对分数，而是“strict gate suffices, reward alone does not”这个因果结论，以及它在两个环境中的复现。b47:Ta4b,The strongest part of the paper is its experimental control. Self-play is formalized as a proposer-solver system, though implemented in the common way with one model and two prompt templates. At each outer step, the proposer samples a task q=(program, input), the environment executes it to obtain the ground-truth output o*(q), and a gate F decides whether the task enters the training pool D_t. Only then does the solver answer the task and receive reward.

The paper’s contribution is not a new reward but a clean factorization of gate and reward as two independent axes. The authors study two environments. One is Python output prediction. The other is a deterministic DSL twin task with 15 operators, deliberately constructed to remove three confounders: pretraining priors, output ambiguity, and executor noise. If collapse still appears in the DSL setting, it is much harder to blame the environment; the failure must come from the optimization dynamics of the self-play loop itself.

Several reward variants are tested, with the most important contrast being self-consistency reward versus grounded reward. Self-consistency does not use the true answer; it rewards agreement across multiple solver samples. Grounded reward uses execution truth. A common intuition is that sufficiently grounded rewards should naturally suppress bad data. The paper shows that this intuition fails. Once ambiguous or exploitable tasks enter the pool, self-consistency can assign higher reward to corrupted data than to clean data, because ambiguous tasks are exactly where spurious consensus is easiest to maximize.

Three mechanistic findings stand out. First, the intrinsic-grounded gap measures the difference between the solver’s intrinsic reward and grounded accuracy. When this gap widens, the system is converging toward an attractor that is internally self-consistent but externally wrong. Second, the Grounded Proposer Paradox shows that when the solver is trained with self-consistency reward, a proposer with access to ground truth can accelerate collapse rather than prevent it. The reason is subtle: a grounded proposer concentrates training on clean, well-structured tasks that provide the lowest-resistance path to spurious consensus. Third, the gate is relaxed continuously through a strictness parameter epsilon rather than only toggled on or off. This reveals a sharp phase transition with a two-stage structure: training-side metrics decouple early, while downstream validation remains stable until epsilon is much larger. That matters because many systems monitor only training reward and would miss the onset of failure.b48:T8c8,The experiments follow two main tracks. The first is full self-play on Python output prediction. The second reproduces the same phenomena on the deterministic DSL twin task. The DSL control is crucial because it removes pretraining bias, ambiguity, and execution noise. Collapse persisting there strongly supports the claim that the failure is in the learning dynamics, not in Python semantics or tooling artifacts.

The headline result is simple and strong. With a strict gate, every tested reward variant remains stable, including self-consistency reward with no access to ground truth. Without the gate, none of the tested reward variants is sufficient. Even rewards grounded in execution truth collapse once ambiguous-output tasks are admitted. That is the paper’s main causal result.

The collapse analysis centers on the intrinsic-grounded gap. During failure, self-consistency reward rises while grounded accuracy falls or decouples, showing that the solver is learning agreement rather than correctness. The same pattern appears in both Python and DSL environments, which makes the argument much more convincing than a single-environment anecdote.

The Grounded Proposer Paradox is another important empirical result. Intuition suggests that a more grounded proposer should be safer. The paper finds the opposite under self-consistency-trained solvers: grounded proposers can drive faster collapse because they generate cleaner, more homogeneous tasks that make spurious consensus easier to optimize. This is a useful warning for co-training systems: improving proposer quality does not guarantee system-level stability if the solver reward is misaligned.

Finally, the continuous epsilon sweep produces a phase diagram rather than a binary ablation. As epsilon is relaxed, training metrics begin to separate at relatively low values, but validation accuracy remains stable for a while before dropping sharply. This two-stage transition suggests that training-side reward curves are not reliable early-warning signals for collapse.

The paper is more about mechanism than leaderboard numbers. The key empirical takeaway is not a single score, but the replicated conclusion that strict gating suffices whereas reward design alone does not.b49:T5cd,This one deserves a careful read. Start with Section 2 and make sure the boundaries between proposer, solver, environment, gate, and reward are clear. Many self-play papers blur data generation and policy optimization into one loop; this paper is useful precisely because it separates them.

Then spend time on Section 3. The two concepts to track are the intrinsic-grounded gap and the Grounded Proposer Paradox. The former is the best diagnostic for collapse. The latter explains why a seemingly better proposer can make the whole system less stable under certain solver rewards. When reading the figures, compare reward curves against grounded accuracy rather than looking only at final outcomes.

Section 4 is also worth close attention because the epsilon sweep gives a more dynamical view of stability than a standard ablation table. Anyone building self-play or synthetic curriculum systems could reuse this style of phase-transition analysis.

If time is limited, read the Introduction, the formalization, the collapse-mechanism figures, and the epsilon-scan results. That should take around 35 to 50 minutes and is enough to capture the main argument. For deeper follow-up, two questions matter. First, how can strict gating be implemented in open-ended natural-language domains where verification is weaker? Second, can the gate be softened into a learned admission policy without losing the paper’s main lesson that filtering must happen before optimization, not after it?b4a:T454,The study controls model-family variation by using Qwen2.5 models from 0.5B to 72B parameters: 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B, and 72B. RL runs are conducted with VeRL. The training set is the math subset of guru-RL-92k from Reasoning360, after deduplication and difficulty filtering. Problems are sorted by increasing difficulty using the pass rate of Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, forming a curriculum. Evaluation has two layers: a 500-problem in-domain held-out set for fitting and validating the scaling relation, and a broader benchmark suite covering AIME2024, AMC2023, GSM8K, MATH500, HumanEval, Zebra Puzzle, and SuperGPQA. The proposed formulation models post-RL test loss as a function of model size N and a resource budget X, where X can be compute or data. Empirically, loss decreases approximately log-linearly with the resource budget. The slope is interpreted as a learning-efficiency term k(N), and k(N) increases with model size but approaches a saturation limit K_max. This is the key modeling choice: it separates initial capability from RL learning efficiency and makes diminishing returns explicit.b4b:T462,First, controlled experiments verify the universality of the small-vs-large gap: it persists across architectures including MLP and Transformer, optimizers including SGD and full-batch gradient descent, and tasks ranging from algorithmic to reasoning. The gap remains under full-batch updates, eliminating explanations based on gradient stochasticity. The core mechanism proposed is that smaller datasets inherently induce stronger sampling biases, which modulate the relative update magnitude across layers and form a layer-wise weight growth rhythm more conducive to feature learning, thus accelerating convergence. This convergence advantage is formally proven for MLP settings via theoretical derivation. Two types of intervention experiments further validate the mechanism: 1) Training on a small dataset with random labels still achieves similar speedup, ruling out the influence of task-relevant signals; 2) Adjusting initialization scales or layer-wise learning rates can significantly reduce or even eliminate the small-vs-large gap, confirming that relative layer update magnitude is the core mediating variable.b4c:T4f4,The framework defines three measurements. The first is scaling-law fit error, which evaluates how well a functional form predicts the optimal hyperparameter across scale. The second is a transfer robustness exponent κ, which measures whether errors made during small-to-large extrapolation become more or less harmful at larger scale. The third is asymptotic loss degradation R(∞), which checks whether a parameterization obtains cleaner transfer only by sacrificing final loss. The authors then express standard parameterization and μP in a common GPT-pretraining form and isolate four differences: the embedding learning rate changes from Θ(1/n) to Θ(1), the final-layer initialization variance changes from Θ(1/n) to Θ(1/n²), the LayerNorm learning rate changes from Θ(1/n) to Θ(1), and attention scaling changes from 1/√d to 1/d. A full 2^4 ablation over these switches shows that changing only the embedding learning rate in standard parameterization is enough to largely match μP’s transfer behavior. Training-dynamics analysis further shows that the embedding learning rate matters throughout training, with especially high sensitivity early on. Too small an embedding learning rate throttles representation learning and can trigger instability.b4d:T5c9,HRM-Text is built on a Hierarchical Recurrent Model with two timescales. The fast L module performs local iterative refinement, while the slow H module maintains a more stable semantic state. In the described forward pass, the model runs two high-level cycles; each cycle applies three L-module updates followed by one H-module update. Token logits are produced from the final H state. This reuses parameters across recurrent steps, increasing effective computational depth without increasing parameter count proportionally.

The difficult part is making deep recurrence trainable for language modeling. The paper introduces MagicNorm and warmup deep credit assignment. At the beginning of training, gradients are backpropagated only through the final two recurrent steps; later this window expands to the final five steps. This reduces the optimization burden early on and gradually exposes the model to longer credit-assignment paths. The modules also use parameterless RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, and sigmoid-gated self-attention.

The training objective departs from standard causal LM pretraining. HRM-Text is trained from scratch on instruction-response pairs, optimizing negative log-likelihood only on the response, i.e. P(answer | instruction). It uses a PrefixLM mask: instruction tokens can attend bidirectionally to one another, while response tokens remain causal. This is a better match to conditional generation than forcing the model to predict the prompt left-to-right.b4e:T533,Six cutting-edge closed-source and open-source VLMs are tested, covering dense and MoE architectures, and three orders of magnitude of active parameters: volumetric rearrangement planning accuracy reaches 53%-97%, with collision constraint error rate lower than 7%; occlusion reasoning accuracy drops sharply to 6%-45%; optical-geometry inference over reflections has accuracy lower than 7%, with a capability gap of over 50 percentage points between the three types of tasks. The results of three independent occlusion reasoning tests deviate by no more than 12 percentage points across five models, ruling out the influence of task-specific surface features. Embodied reasoning model Gemini Robotics-ER 1.6 reproduces the same capability profile on a 200-sample subset of failure cases, indicating that current embodied reasoning post-training cannot fix this deficit. White-box analysis shows that during reasoning failures, the visual attention of Qwen3-VL to geometrically correct regions is dispersed, equivalent to uniform random level. Activation patching locates the defect at the visual token merger layer: spatial information recoverable inside the ViT becomes inaccessible to downstream computation after compression, and restoring activations of the first language model layer after the merger can recover performance.b4f:T52b,The theory models each modality as an observation generated from shared and private latent variables. Training data only gives edges in a modality graph, not full joint samples. Under connectivity and identifiability assumptions, shared factors can be recovered from overlapping pairwise observations. The implementation follows this structure in two stages. First, it learns a unified latent space using self-modal reconstruction and cross-modal contrastive alignment. Reconstruction preserves modality-specific semantics and stabilizes training; contrastive alignment ties paired samples together in the shared space. The framework then adds two structural biases: partial representation alignment, which aligns only the shared subspace, and minimal latent specification, which discourages the shared representation from carrying unnecessary private information. Second, it performs representation recomposition. A new modality encoder is aligned to an existing textual or visual latent space, then combined with a frozen pretrained decoder or MLLM interface. For example, a 3D encoder aligned through 3D-text pairs can be recomposed with a text decoder to produce text conditioned on point clouds. This differs from instruction-tuned adapters or LoRA-style updates because the pretrained model is largely kept unchanged.b50:T489,The method starts from a soft RLHF formulation. The state is the generated prefix, the action is the next token, and the transition is deterministic concatenation. With a KL penalty to a reference model, the optimal policy satisfies a soft Bellman equation and its logits can be expressed as the reference logits plus an optimal Q-value term. Personalized alignment is then cast as a multi-objective MDP. Each base reward r_k represents a preference dimension, and a user is represented by a simplex weight vector w, giving a combined reward r_w = Σ_k w_k r_k. The central theoretical claim is that the logits of personalized policies admit a shared spectral representation: they can be approximated by a linear combination of a small number of basis logit functions. This leads to a two-stage algorithm. Offline, train specialized policies for fine-grained preference dimensions. Online, infer or receive the user preference weights and combine the basis policies, either through output/logit merging or parameter merging. The theory provides sub-optimality bounds relative to a fully tailored policy under controlled spectral approximation and merging error.b51:T470,The experimental design scales down Common Crawl and its filtered variants while preserving their relative sizes, then varies model size and training steps over these pools. Increasing steps induces data repetition; increasing model size raises compute per step. This setup directly probes the tradeoff introduced by filtering: it improves average document quality but reduces the available token pool. The authors compare the best performance achievable under different compute budgets rather than relying only on fixed-token or fixed-step comparisons. They then fit empirical relationships among pool size, number of training steps, and model size to predict when no filtering should become optimal. A second set of experiments injects deliberately degraded data, including random strings and documents with shuffled word order, to test whether large models merely tolerate noise or can still extract weak signals from it. A post-hoc theoretical model explains the observed pattern: cleaning helps imperfect, capacity-limited learners, while sufficiently capable learners can benefit from modeling the noisy generation process itself.b52:T51d,The key scale numbers are informative. A heavily filtered dataset such as DCLM-Baseline keeps roughly 1% of the original Common Crawl, yielding about 3.8T tokens, while the DCLM-Pool scale is around 240T tokens. The study spans about two orders of magnitude in compute, and the same qualitative trend persists as the pool scale increases: once the model is large enough and trained long enough, the full pool overtakes filtered pools. The fitted scaling law suggests that the 240T-token Common Crawl pool may become optimal around 1e30 FLOPs. Filtering still wins in lower-compute regimes, which explains why earlier filtering studies saw strong benefits. The noisy-data experiments add a useful boundary case. Random strings hurt at low compute, but sufficiently trained large models narrow the gap. Shuffled-word documents are more revealing: they destroy syntax and local semantics while preserving unigram statistics, yet large models can still benefit from them. The authors also state an important limitation: adversarial, non-factual, or safety-critical data that resembles high-quality text could still be harmful.b53:T6a5,The paper fixes a standard LLaMA-3 Transformer backbone (explicitly avoiding typical byte-LM downsampling modules like strided convs or local encoders) and trains on UTF-8 bytes using TorchTitan, with FineWeb-Edu as data. On top of the byte baseline, the authors introduce a series of low-overhead interventions, each designed to mimic one hypothesized benefit of subword tokenization while minimizing confounders:
- Throughput/sequence compression: simulate the advantage of shorter sequences (more raw bytes seen per unit compute) within the byte pipeline.
- Vocabulary/output-layer scaling: simulate the capacity effects associated with larger discrete vocabularies, focusing on embedding/output-layer parameterization.
- Boundary priors: inject BPE boundary signals as explicit structure so the model can exploit segmentation-like cues without changing the base unit.
- Look-ahead/task easiness: approximate the “future hint” implicit in subword segmentation decisions that require looking ahead.
- Multi-byte prediction: add multi-token (multi-byte) prediction heads to emulate the fact that one subword prediction corresponds to predicting a byte n-gram.

1) Differentiable lift from categorical outputs to continuous features: instead of sampling hard tokens, it computes expected token embeddings from the model’s per-position categorical distributions (soft-token embeddings). These are fed into a frozen semantic encoder to obtain continuous features.

2) Drifting in a frozen semantic space: in that feature space, it estimates an attraction–repulsion drift field V(y; P_data, P_theta), designed to be anti-symmetric so the signal vanishes at equilibrium (when model and data match). This preserves the fixed-point property that motivates drifting.

3) Stop-gradient drift target: it forms a drifted feature target y* (stop-gradient) and trains the DDLM to match y* (direct feature-space matching). The paper also explores alternative couplings—e.g., converting drift into a logit-space “mirror teacher”, and mixing with the original denoising loss—and reports that direct feature-space drifting yields the most stable balance between sample quality and entropy.

4) Why soft-token matters: replacing the soft lift with a hard straight-through surrogate significantly degrades generation, supporting the claim that preserving predictive uncertainty in the semantic space is crucial for effective drift learning.b56:T456,The authors build a high-quality 10T-token corpus with fine-grained domain separation and pretrain MoE models of varying sizes from scratch. By increasing this subset while keeping the total math-token budget fixed, they test whether explicit multi-step structure is more useful than simply adding more math tokens. Expert-routing distributions and hook-based analyses are used to inspect whether the new data changes expert allocation in a stable or disruptive way.b57:T937,技术路线由架构与目标两部分组成，而且两者是联动设计，不是简单相加。架构上，HRM-Text 采用双时间尺度递归：慢速 H 模块负责较稳定的高层语义状态，快速 L 模块负责局部迭代细化。一次前向包含两个 high-level cycle，每个 cycle 内执行三次 L 更新再执行一次 H 更新，最终用最后的 H 状态输出 token logits。这样做的意图是用重复计算换参数规模，让模型在较少参数和较少数据下仍有较深的推理/整合过程。问题在于，重复应用同一变换会把 Transformer 中 norm placement 的老问题放大。为此作者引入 MagicNorm 和 warmup deep credit assignment。根据正文描述，MagicNorm 试图兼顾 PreNorm 与 PostNorm 的优点：既约束前向激活方差，避免递归堆叠时状态发散，又尽量保留稳定的梯度通路，减少深递归下的优化困难。配套上使用 parameterless RMSNorm、SwiGLU、RoPE 和 sigmoid-gated self-attention，说明作者在尽量压缩不必要自由度，优先保训练稳定。warmup deep credit assignment 则是一个很关键但容易被忽略的训练技巧：训练初期只对最后 2 个 recurrent step 回传梯度，随后再扩展到最后 5 步，等于显式控制有效反向深度，先学短程信用分配，再逐步放开长程依赖。这和 curriculum on optimization depth 很像，是递归 LM 能否训起来的关键之一。

目标函数上，作者没有走标准 raw-text next-token，而是直接从 instruction-response pairs 做 task-completion pretraining，只在 response token 上计算 NLL，即优化 -log P(x_a | x_q)。同时配 PrefixLM mask，让 instruction 部分双向可见、response 部分保持因果生成。这里的设计选择很鲜明：既然模型最终大多用于条件生成，就不再把大量算力花在预测 prompt-like 文本、网页噪声或任务无关续写上，而是把训练信号集中到“给定条件，完成回答”这件事。和纯 encoder-decoder 不同，PrefixLM 仍保留单流生成接口；和标准 causal LM 不同，它允许 instruction 侧更充分的信息整合。论文真正有意思的地方在于，它不是只换了一个 mask，而是把数据形态、损失定义和架构归纳偏置一起改了，形成一个面向 sample efficiency 的整体 recipe。b58:Ta1f,The method is a coupled redesign of architecture and objective rather than an isolated component swap. On the architecture side, HRM-Text uses dual-timescale recurrence: a slow H module maintains a relatively stable high-level semantic state, while a fast L module performs local iterative refinement. One forward pass consists of two high-level cycles; each cycle runs three L updates followed by one H update, and token logits are produced from the final H state. The intended trade-off is clear: use repeated computation instead of proportionally increasing parameter count, so the model can perform deeper integration under smaller budgets.

The hard part is optimization. Repeatedly applying the same transformation amplifies the classic normalization-placement problem already familiar from Transformers. The paper introduces MagicNorm and warmup deep credit assignment to make this viable. From the full text, MagicNorm is designed to preserve bounded forward activation variance while keeping backward optimization stable, effectively trying to capture the good parts of both PreNorm and PostNorm under recurrence. The surrounding design choices—parameterless RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE, and sigmoid-gated self-attention—suggest a deliberate bias toward stability and reduced unnecessary flexibility. Warmup deep credit assignment is especially important: early in training, gradients are backpropagated only through the final two recurrent steps, and later expanded to the final five. This explicitly controls effective backward depth, allowing the model to first learn short-range credit assignment before exposing it to longer recurrent dependencies.

On the objective side, the paper abandons standard raw-text next-token pretraining. HRM-Text is trained from scratch on instruction-response pairs, with NLL computed only on the response tokens, i.e. optimizing -log P(x_a | x_q). This is paired with a PrefixLM mask: full bidirectional attention over the instruction prefix, causal generation over the response. The motivation is sharp. If the model is mostly used for conditional generation at inference time, then spending most of the budget predicting prompt-like text, web boilerplate, or task-irrelevant continuations may be wasteful. Compared with encoder-decoder training, PrefixLM preserves a single-stream generative interface; compared with standard causal LM, it allows richer integration over the conditioning context. The interesting part is that the paper changes data form, loss support, and architectural prior together into one sample-efficiency-oriented recipe.b59:T6c0,The headline result is the budget comparison. The authors claim that HRM-Text, trained from scratch on only 40B unique tokens, reaches the performance neighborhood of contemporary open models such as Llama, Qwen, Gemma, OLMo, Ouro, and Huginn on most benchmarks, while using roughly 100–900× fewer training tokens and 96–432× less estimated training compute. If those numbers are supported under fair accounting, this is not a routine gain in data efficiency; it materially changes what is feasible in the low-budget regime. The wording matters, though: the claim is about entering the same performance band on many benchmarks, not uniformly surpassing those baselines.

Three experimental blocks deserve close attention. First, stability and training dynamics: ablations for MagicNorm and warmup deep credit assignment should reveal whether training diverges, becomes noisy, or converges to much worse solutions without them. Loss curves, activation/gradient statistics, and sensitivity to backprop depth are central here. Second, objective ablations: instruction-response-only training, response-only loss, and PrefixLM masking versus standard causal LM or raw-text training. This determines whether the gains come mainly from the architecture or from a more focused data/objective design. Third, compute and data efficiency comparisons against open baselines under roughly matched parameter scales or training budgets. The paper’s main figure and token/compute table should be read carefully: unique tokens versus seen tokens, measured versus estimated compute, and whether the benchmark suite is especially favorable to instruction-conditioned models. That distinction matters when interpreting “beyond scaling.”b5a:T717,This one deserves a full read. First, they LoRA-memorize 60 fictional author biographies into DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, using a reasoning format where the model restates the target biography in the <think> segment and then gives an answer. Second, they apply NPO unlearning with the forgetting loss masked to the answer span only; no forgetting gradient directly touches the biography template inside the trace. Third, they evaluate generations by splitting on </think> and performing substring matching separately in the trace and the answer. This setup structurally favors a positive bypass gap because the trace template is left largely untouched while the answer span is optimized away. The key technical move is to add fixed-weight probes. One probe swaps the model-generated trace for short non-canary prefills at inference time and checks whether answer continuation remains invariant. Another uses teacher-forced continuation scoring under the same six-token canary head, avoiding greedy decoding and parser dependence. The canary head is important: the metric is a head-conditioned continuation score, not a free-recall measure. A second model, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, is used to show that formatting drift alone can invert the parser-split metric.b5c:T5fc,The main results form a compact measurement story. On Qwen-7B, after LoRA memorization, out_acc is 1.00. After NPO, answer-side out_acc falls to 0.60, while trace-side thk_leak remains 0.83, giving a parser-split gap of Δ=+0.23. At first glance this looks like a thinking-channel bypass. However, in 86% of those bypass cases, the answer span is merely a verbatim copy of the question prefix with no real continuation, while the trace contains the trained biography. A fixed-weight prefill swap then changes the answer rate substantially: a short non-canary prefill lowers out_acc from 0.60 to 0.37; bio-style and meta-style prefills land at similar rates; an empty prefill lowers it to 0.20. On a second seed, the bypass gap shrinks rather than vanishes, and the prefill effect reverses direction, bringing the answer rate close to ceiling. Teacher-forced scoring tells a different story from greedy substring matching: after NPO, top-1 continuation match under the same six-token canary head stays between 0.90 and 1.00 across prefills. On Llama-8B, the parser-split metric flips to -0.92 at K=1600, while out_acc remains 1.00 and teacher-forced top-1 is at least 0.998. The cause is format drift: in at least 60% of probes, the biography template moves outside the <think> tags, leaving the parser with an empty trace. The authors also note that prefills perturb ordinary QA probes, so the intervention is not a mechanism isolator; it rules out the stronger claim that the parser-split gap alone proves hidden-channel retention.b5d:T419,Starting from the properties of KL divergence, the work compares the mode-seeking property of reverse KL and the mode-covering property of forward KL, pointing out that forward KL minimization is the theoretically optimal solution to avoid mode collapse. However, directly optimizing forward KL is computationally intractable, as it requires sampling from a global reward-weighted distribution over trajectories. Accordingly, DMPO (Distribution-Matching Policy Optimization) is proposed to approximate forward KL minimization at the group level: for each group of G trajectories sampled per query, a Boltzmann distribution is constructed as the target distribution based on rewards. A distribution-matching regularization term is added to the standard GRPO objective to align the policy distribution with this intra-group target distribution. This method is naturally compatible with GRPO's existing group-level advantage normalization logic, and can be implemented with only minor code modifications, requiring no additional model or data overhead.b5e:T46a,Evaluation benchmarks include two categories. First, MM-NP-Bench, a multimodal combinatorial optimization benchmark covering 10 NP-hard problems across 5 categories (Routing, Covering, Partitioning, Substructure, Constraints), is constructed. It includes parametric generators, rule-based verifiers, and heuristic solver baselines, and uses a dual-metric evaluation of Success Rate (SR) and Quality Ratio (QR), where QR quantifies the optimality of solutions and identifies mode collapse (high SR with low QR indicates mode collapse). Second, mathematical reasoning and cross-domain transfer tasks are used for further validation. Experiments compare 5 strong baselines including GRPO: on NP-Bench, DMPO achieves a Quality Ratio of 43.9%, a 9% relative improvement over GRPO's 40.1%; on MM-NP-Bench, DMPO achieves 43.1% QR, a 12% relative improvement over GRPO's 38.4%; mathematical reasoning accuracy improves by 2.0%, and out-of-domain task accuracy improves by 2.3%. If you only skim, focus on the benchmark paragraph, the Antigravity examples, and the safety section.b6a:T43b,OP-Mix combines on-policy domain adapters with linear adapter interpolation. For each data domain, the method trains one LoRA adapter starting from the current model. This adapter approximates the update direction induced by training on that domain at the model’s current state. Candidate mixtures are then simulated by linearly interpolating these domain LoRAs, using the interpolated adapter as a proxy for the loss surface under full mixture training. A user-defined objective aggregates evaluation metrics, with maximization metrics negated so that mixture search can be posed as minimization. Compared with proxy scaling-law approaches that train many smaller models on sampled mixtures, OP-Mix needs only one adapter per domain and stays on-policy with the model being trained. When a new domain is introduced, the algorithm trains another domain adapter and refits the mixture, instead of rebuilding the whole proxy-model grid. This is also why the method naturally applies to continual learning: old and new domains are represented in the same mixture optimization problem.b6b:T4ee,The plan is a portfolio of deployment-oriented technical programs rather than a single modeling method. The goal is not to patch this empirically, but to explain why the existing theory becomes insufficient for GQA and to derive a parameterization that restores transfer. The issue has two layers. First, prior spectral-μP arguments treated spectral-norm conditions as a sufficient route to feature learning, while the operational checks used in implementations were weaker; this leaves room for architectures that pass coordinate checks without satisfying the stronger operator-scale conditions needed for transfer. Second, GQA introduces intrinsically low-rank weight structures. For such matrices, the ordinary spectral norm measures amplification along worst-case directions that are effectively never seen under the training input distribution, so it mischaracterizes the scale that actually matters during optimization.b6d:T72d,The technical contribution has three parts. First, the paper reformulates the spectral-μP perspective around operator norms more directly. Instead of starting from a weaker feature-learning definition and then showing that spectral conditions imply it, the authors elevate operator-norm scaling conditions to the center of the framework. This lets them derive Complete-P-style prescriptions for depth and weight decay without leaning on a lazy-training fallback.

Second, they introduce the expected operator norm to replace the ordinary spectral norm when matrices are rank-degenerate. The standard spectral norm captures the largest possible deformation over all unit vectors. That is appropriate for full-rank random matrices, where the extremal scale is asymptotically representative. But for GQA-like low-rank matrices, the extremal directions occupy measure-zero sets relative to the i.i.d. input distribution encountered during training. The expected operator norm instead measures the average deformation under a chosen input distribution, taken in the paper to be Gaussian i.i.d. This preserves the usual scaling for full-rank random matrices while correcting the mismatch for low-rank operators.

Third, using this revised norm and operator-centric framework, the paper derives μP scaling rules for GQA. Because GQA shares key/value heads across multiple query groups, the effective rank, output scale, and update scale of the relevant projections differ from standard multi-head attention. The authors work through these differences and derive the corresponding initialization, learning-rate, depth, and weight-decay scalings. They also propose a stricter spectral-norm coordinate check, showing that the original implementation can pass the old check while failing the stronger one that actually predicts transfer behavior.b6e:T609,The experiments are aimed at validating the theory rather than maximizing downstream benchmark scores. One key result is diagnostic: the original μP implementation for GQA passes the customary coordinate checks but fails a stricter spectral/operator-norm check, and this aligns with its empirical failure to transfer learning rates across widths. That is an important negative result because it shows the old check is not sufficiently discriminative for structured attention.

The main empirical validation is width-wise learning-rate transfer under GQA. With the original scaling, the optimal learning-rate region does not remain stable across widths. With the newly derived GQA-μP scaling, transfer becomes substantially more consistent. The paper also reports that transfer across different GQA repetition counts is noisy, which is a useful practical warning: changing repetition is not a benign architectural perturbation from the standpoint of hyperparameter transfer.

A second set of experiments concerns Complete-P quantities. Under the corrected scaling, both weight decay and the training-time constant τ_epoch from Wang and Aitchison (2024) appear transferable as well. The provided text does not include the full numeric tables, but the paper explicitly points to Figures 1 and 5 and to experiments covering learning-rate, weight-decay, and τ_epoch transfer. When reading, the important thing is to inspect whether the optimal hyperparameter bands remain aligned across widths and how variance changes when repetition is altered.b6f:T5b0,Read it in the order of failure case, theoretical repair, GQA derivation, and transfer validation.

The deepest follow-up question is whether future μP analyses for other structured or low-rank modules should also be rewritten in terms of distribution-aware operator norms.b70:T5c6,VideoRLVR is a three-component framework optimized for flow-matching video diffusion models. First, it adopts an SDE-GRPO optimization backbone, which models the reverse denoising process of diffusion as state transitions in a Markov Decision Process (MDP), adapting RL optimization to the continuous denoising trajectory of diffusion models instead of traditional discrete-token RL. Second, the Early-Step Focus strategy concentrates exploration and backpropagation only on the early denoising phase where coarse-grained structure and long-range planning are determined; later denoising steps use fixed reference model outputs without RL updates, drastically reducing computational overhead. Third, dense decomposed rewards break the sparse end-of-task success signal into verifiable rule-based components aligned with each frame (e.g., valid movement, progress toward the goal, no backtracking in maze tasks). Rule-based planners generate ground-truth trajectories to align frame sequences with logical constraints, providing informative feedback even when full task success is rare. The full pipeline aligns with the LLM three-stage workflow: pretraining for general generative competence, SFT on rule-generated solution trajectories, then RL optimization via VideoRLVR. Unlike prior video RL work that relies on sparse human-scored rewards or full denoising step optimization, this design explicitly targets verifiable reasoning correctness while reducing training overhead.b71:T40f,For pretraining research, the contribution matters in three ways. First, it gives a mechanistic explanation for long-context brittleness. Many failures of supposedly long-context LLMs have been attributed to data, instruction tuning, retrieval setup, or evaluation artifacts. This paper argues that part of the problem is upstream: the positional mechanism itself degrades. Second, it reframes context extension. If the underlying position signal is already approaching random behavior statistically, then interpolation tricks, base retuning, and extrapolation heuristics can only go so far. Third, it has direct implications for future pretraining design. RoPE became dominant because it is simple, efficient, and works well in standard training regimes. The paper suggests that these advantages may be local to moderate lengths, not robust to truly long contexts. The contribution is mainly a theory-backed diagnosis with empirical confirmation, not a replacement method, but it challenges a default assumption used by most current LLMs.b72:T8c4,The technical core is the treatment of the unnormalized RoPE attention score as a position-dependent oscillatory sum, which is then analyzed as an approximately Gaussian random variable under mild assumptions. This move is important because it shifts the discussion from anecdotal query-key examples to length-dependent statistical behavior. For position discrimination, the paper studies how the score difference changes when the same key token is placed at different positions. As context length increases, phase interactions induced by RoPE make the preference for nearer positions unreliable; the probability of position inversion approaches 0.5. In other words, RoPE loses its locality bias in a probabilistic sense. Position aliasing comes from collisions in the rotated representation: different positions can produce the same attention score for a fixed query-key pair. The paper argues that this is not just a trivial periodicity artifact but a broader consequence of multi-frequency phase composition.

For token discrimination, the analysis fixes the query and position, then compares two different key tokens. Because RoPE couples token content with positional phase, a token that scores higher at one position can score lower at another, yielding token inversion. Its probability also tends to 0.5 with longer contexts. Token aliasing further shows that at some positions, different key tokens can become indistinguishable in their score contribution.

A particularly useful part of the paper is the discussion of the RoPE base hyperparameter. In practice, many long-context extensions rely on changing the base or applying scaling variants. The theory here says the base is not a monotonic improvement knob. Increasing it helps preserve consistency of token relevance but weakens positional separability; decreasing it does the opposite. So common length-extension methods shift the failure frontier rather than remove the underlying mechanism. The main text focuses on single-head attention, while the appendix discusses why multi-head and multi-layer stacks do not automatically eliminate the issue. Averaging across heads may smooth some effects, but the positional distortion remains rooted in the same rotary phase structure.b73:T6b5,The empirical section has two layers. The first directly validates the theoretical phenomena. On Llama 3.1-8B, the paper measures position/token inversion and aliasing, and finds that the predicted failures appear in a real model, and much earlier than one might expect. One striking number is that within only an 8K context window, the authors identify about 75K pairs of positions exhibiting position aliasing, and these are not restricted to nearby positions. They also report around 150 positions showing token aliasing in the same range. This matters because it shows the issue is not confined to extreme context lengths.

The second layer is an end-to-end functional test. The authors evaluate six popular models ranging from 7B to over 100B on a simple list retrieval task: given a list, return the value at the k-th position. The task is intentionally low-level and minimizes semantic confounds, so it probes positional discrimination directly. With only four distinct values in the list, all tested models fall to near-random performance at around 4K tokens. Since the random baseline is 25%, this is a strong result: the models fail even on low-entropy positional lookup, where knowledge and reasoning are not the bottleneck. The paper also checks common RoPE length-extension settings and finds that they do not fundamentally remove the failure modes; they only alter where and how the degradation appears.

From a pretraining perspective, the most important empirical message is how early the degradation shows up. The theory is asymptotic, but the practical failures emerge already in the 4K–8K regime, which is within the operational range of many models and not merely an out-of-distribution extreme.b74:T643,Start with the introduction and the section that decomposes what attention needs from positional encoding. Read Sections 3 and 4 carefully. Section 3 defines position inversion and position aliasing, states the assumptions, and shows how the failure probability evolves with context length. The key point is not that failures exist, but that the probability approaches random guessing. Section 4 does the same for token inversion and token aliasing. This part is easy to underrate, but it is highly relevant for language modeling because unstable token ranking directly affects information routing in attention.

- Segment A: keep the original short context intact (no chunking), with normal low position indices.
- Segment B: append a short terminal prompt, but assign its position indices near the target maximum length (e.g., near 64K).

This creates, within a short sequence, both (i) local relative distances inside A (preserving clean next-token supervision) and (ii) very long relative distances between A and B (forcing the model to experience long-range RoPE distances during training).

The “terminal anchoring” choice is deliberate: placing the anchor at the end avoids breaking semantic continuity (unlike chunk-based simulated long-context training) and provides a stable structural cue that is less about memorizing specific tokens and more about the positional configuration.

Their analysis leverages RoPE: attention scores can be viewed as sums of sinusoidal components over relative distances; position interpolation effectively reduces frequencies, inducing smoothness over unobserved distances. Since Q/K projections are shared across distances (no per-distance parameters), combining dense local supervision with sparse long-distance supervision constrains the same parameter space and reduces instability in unseen distance regions.b76:T4bc,The method, DiHAL, follows a Locate-and-Replace strategy. In the locate stage, the paper avoids exhaustive training of a diffusion bridge at every layer. Instead, it defines geometry-based proxies for each hidden-state space: local compactness, global stiffness, and effective rank. These are intended to capture whether a layer’s representation is easy to denoise, stable under imperfect score estimation, and not overly complex. After selecting a layer, DiHAL replaces the lower transformer prefix with a conditional diffusion bridge. The bridge does not predict tokens and does not reconstruct embeddings directly; it reconstructs the hidden state at the chosen internal layer. The reconstructed state is then passed through the retained upper transformer layers and the original LM head for token prediction. This design matters for two reasons. It delegates the difficult continuous-to-discrete mapping to the already trained upper network, and it turns language diffusion into hidden-state reconstruction rather than direct text recovery. The paper also proposes a fixed geometry score that predicts promising insertion layers under a shallow one-epoch bridge-training protocol, reducing the search cost.b77:T4be,Experiments are conducted on 8B-scale backbones. That is an important result: later semantic layers are not automatically better diffusion targets. The empirical study is broad: more than 2,000 training runs, model sizes from 101M to 805M parameters, and several target-data regimes. The paper covers three families of constrained data. The main empirical pattern is that repetition has smooth diminishing returns rather than a hard threshold, and the useful repetition range depends jointly on model size, target-data size, and total budget. Larger models overfit the target validation set sooner, but they also extract more value from limited target data before that point. The presence of fresh generic data changes the regime relative to single-source repetition: it keeps the model learning from new tokens even while the target source is being revisited many times.

On top of these observations, the paper fits a scaling law for target-domain loss. The exact parameterization is learned from data, but the conceptual structure is clear: it separates the effect of unique target data from the effect of repeated target exposure, and models both with smooth power-law-like terms. The law is then used to predict the optimal mixture weight or repetition count. Three results matter most. First, the optimal repetition count in mixture pretraining is often far above the familiar single-source heuristic. Second, as the total compute budget grows, the optimal target fraction h tends to decrease, while the optimal repetition count r can still increase, because the same fixed target pool is revisited more times over a longer run. This is a subtle but operationally important point: a fixed mixture ratio is not compute-invariant. The explanatory experiments show that an additional soft constraint can push models toward low-loss solutions where they report the claim as false, but these solutions are unstable under further unconstrained finetuning.b8b:T4bb,BitLM represents each tokenizer entry with a fixed-length binary code and attaches a lightweight diffusion head on top of a standard Transformer backbone.
- Representation: each token maps to a B-bit code (fixed length). Codes are projected into the model hidden space as the discrete target representation.
- Division of labor: the causal Transformer backbone computes contextual latents ("what should happen next"), while the diffusion head performs iterative denoising in bit space to realize the continuation as discrete symbols ("how it crystallizes into tokens").
- Block-causal generation: by changing the attention mask from fully causal to block-causal, BitLM preserves strict left-to-right dependencies across blocks while allowing parallel iterative refinement of multiple future positions within a block. Parallelism is controlled by block size.
- Key differences: unlike speculative/blockwise decoding, BitLM changes the output interface rather than accelerating softmax sampling; unlike fully non-causal diffusion LMs, it keeps a causal backbone and block-level causality; unlike AR multi-token heads, jointness comes from coupled bit denoising rather than independent per-position classification.b8c:T868,方法由两个模块组成。第一阶段是非循环 backbone，文中实现为 Transformer，它根据上下文先产生每个位置的初始输出 embedding，相当于对下一个 token 的隐表示做一次快速猜测。第二阶段是 attractor module，一个通常更小的循环网络，它不直接输出 token，而是接收 backbone 的初始 embedding，并通过迭代映射把该 embedding 推向一个固定点。最终在这个平衡态 embedding 上做解码，得到词表分布。

关键改动在于训练方式。传统 looped LM 会把 recurrent block 展开 T 步，然后做 BPTT，训练内存和计算都随 T 增长。Attractor Model 则把 refinement 写成 z*=f(z*; x, h0) 这样的 fixed-point equation，其中 h0 是 backbone 的初始提议。前向时用求解器迭代到收敛，反向时不对所有中间步做显式回传，而是用 implicit differentiation 计算梯度，因此训练显存不再线性依赖迭代步数。这一点直接借鉴 DEQ，但论文的设计不是把整层网络都做成 equilibrium，而是只在输出 embedding 空间上求平衡，降低了优化难度，也保留了标准 Transformer backbone 的表达和并行优势。

作者强调两阶段结构的重要性：backbone 负责给出一个足够接近解的初值，attractor 只做局部修正。这样做比“从零开始循环推理”更稳定，也更便宜。另一个重要点是 adaptive refinement。因为前向是按收敛停止，训练和推理时每个 token 所需的迭代次数可以不同，不再受固定 loop depth 限制。这比显式 looped Transformer 更自然地支持 test-time compute 调节。

论文还提出 equilibrium internalization：随着训练进行，backbone 输出会越来越接近 attractor 的固定点，导致求解器需要的步数逐渐减少。这个现象不是额外蒸馏损失带来的，而是在纯 next-token 训练下自发出现。可以把它理解为：固定点求解器在训练早期像一个老师，提供更好的隐表示目标；训练后期 backbone 学会直接落在这个 attractor basin 附近，于是慢路径被部分吸收到快路径里。b8d:T483,This is a meaningful contribution for pretraining and model architecture research. First, it moves recurrent latent computation from an interesting but fragile idea toward a more usable architectural primitive: effective refinement depth no longer implies linearly growing training memory, and the number of refinement steps is chosen adaptively by convergence rather than fixed in advance. Second, it brings DEQ-style implicit layers back into language modeling in a more practical form. Instead of making the whole Transformer an equilibrium system, it uses a standard backbone plus a smaller attractor module that solves for equilibrium only in output-embedding space. That is a much more realistic design for large-scale LMs. Third, the observed phenomenon of equilibrium internalization is important. Even though the model is trained only with next-token loss, the backbone gradually learns to produce embeddings closer to the fixed point, reducing the need for iterative solving. That has direct implications for latent reasoning, train-time versus test-time compute, and how slow internal computation may be absorbed into a fast path over training.b8e:T841,The architecture has two stages. A non-recurrent backbone, implemented as a Transformer, first proposes an initial output embedding for each token position. This is a fast latent guess for the next-token representation. A separate attractor module, typically smaller and recurrent, then refines that embedding by iterating toward a fixed point. The final token distribution is decoded from the equilibrium embedding rather than from the backbone proposal alone.

The key change is in how the recurrent part is trained. Standard looped language models explicitly unroll the recurrent block for T steps and backpropagate through all steps, which makes memory and optimization cost scale with T. Attractor Models instead formulate refinement as a fixed-point equation, roughly of the form z* = f(z*; x, h0), where h0 is the backbone proposal. The forward pass runs a solver until convergence, and the backward pass uses implicit differentiation rather than storing and differentiating through every intermediate iterate. This is the main source of constant-memory behavior with respect to refinement depth.

A second important design choice is the two-stage decomposition. The backbone is responsible for producing a good initialization, while the attractor performs local correction. This is more stable and cheaper than asking a recurrent module to do all the work from scratch. The model also supports adaptive refinement naturally: different tokens can require different numbers of solver iterations at train and test time, depending on convergence. That is a cleaner route to variable test-time compute than fixed-depth looped Transformers.

The paper also identifies equilibrium internalization. During training, the backbone’s initial prediction moves closer to the attractor’s fixed point, so the solver needs fewer iterations to reach approximate equilibrium. This happens without any explicit distillation loss. One useful interpretation is that the equilibrium solver acts like a latent teacher early in training, and the backbone gradually absorbs part of that computation into its direct prediction.b8f:T759,The experiments cover two regimes: large-scale language-model pretraining and hard reasoning with tiny models. In language modeling, Attractor Models are compared against standard feed-forward Transformers and explicitly unrolled looped baselines. The reported result is that Attractor Models achieve better language-modeling performance under comparable training budgets while remaining more stable and avoiding the linear memory growth associated with increasing recurrent depth in looped baselines. The constant-memory claim with respect to effective refinement depth is one of the central empirical results.

In the reasoning regime, the model outperforms prior tiny recursive reasoners on difficult tasks and appears to mitigate the pathological scaling behavior sometimes seen in small recurrent models, where increasing model size can hurt performance. The paper attributes this to the stability and inductive bias of fixed-point refinement compared with explicit recurrent unrolling.

The most interesting evidence is in the training dynamics rather than a single benchmark score. The paper shows convergence behavior and accuracy-versus-iteration curves indicating that, as training progresses, the backbone proposal gets closer to the final fixed point and the number of solver iterations needed for approximate convergence decreases. Performance does not collapse as this happens. That is the clearest empirical signature of equilibrium internalization.

When reading the full paper, the most important numbers to extract are: the relative size of the attractor versus the backbone, average solver iterations and how they change over training, memory and compute differences versus looped baselines, and the exact gains on language modeling and reasoning benchmarks. Those details determine whether the method is only elegant conceptually or also compelling in practice.b90:T537,This one deserves a careful read. First is the theoretical analysis. Starting from a standard sparse top-k MoE layer, the authors derive that for a token routed to expert i, the router weight vector associated with expert i and the expert weights processing that token receive gradients along the same input hidden-state direction, differing mainly by scalar coefficients. This is stronger than the generic statement that both modules are in the same computation graph. It means matched router–expert pairs accumulate updates from the same routed-token history and therefore evolve as coupled geometric directions. Second is empirical validation. In a 1B-scale SMoE trained from scratch, the paper compares router scores with the internal activations of experts on the same token and finds that experts ranked higher by the router also respond more strongly internally. So routing is not merely an external assignment layer; it is mirrored in expert computation. Third is a reinterpretation of the auxiliary load-balancing loss. Because this loss sends gradients to every router direction on every token, not only to selected experts, it mixes expert-specific directions and weakens the natural coupling induced by routed-token history. The paper supports this both theoretically and empirically. Motivated by that view, the authors introduce a parameter-free centroid router: each expert maintains an online K-Means or EMA centroid of the hidden states assigned to it, and routing is done by cosine similarity to these centroids, with sign-updated biases for load control. The point is not to beat learned routers outright, but to test whether a large part of routing can be explained as geometric summarization of expert-specific token regions.b92:T4b1,The experiments address three questions. First, does geometric coupling appear in practice? On a roughly 1B-parameter SMoE trained from scratch on about 50B tokens, the paper shows that experts receiving higher router scores also exhibit stronger internal activations for the same token, which supports the coupling hypothesis. Second, how does auxiliary balancing alter geometry? The authors train two otherwise matched 1B SMoEs differing only in the balancing rule and measure similarity among router directions. With the auxiliary loss, distinct router vectors become nearly three times more similar, indicating stronger directional homogenization. Load balance improves, but specialization weakens. Third, can a centroid router recover much of the learned router’s function? The answer is largely yes: the centroid router achieves the lowest load imbalance among the tested variants while keeping perplexity close to the learned router trained without the auxiliary loss, with only a modest degradation. The paper is careful not to conflate better utilization with better language modeling; the empirical emphasis is on explaining routing behavior rather than claiming absolute perplexity gains.b93:T46d,This one deserves a careful read. Disaggregated component placement: Attention layers and MoE FFN layers are assigned to separate worker groups. Attention groups replicate dense components and split data by micro-batch, while FFN groups shard experts and process tokens according to routing results. Each group can host multiple layers of the same component type, maximizing device utilization under memory constraints and eliminating the OOM issue of prior disaggregation schemes that required each group to store all layers of their assigned component. 2. Three core properties of semantic attribute formation are summarized: 1) Different attributes have distinct commitment timings: topic is committed within the first 2% of denoising steps, while sentiment forms gradually over 20% of the process; 2) Commitment sharpness varies: some attributes form in a narrow time window, while others form uniformly across the entire denoising trajectory; 3) Effect-size asymmetry: the per-feature discriminative strength varies across attributes.
